Mr. President,

Excellencies,

Ladies and gentlemen,

The faultlines in our world are widening.

Cracks have become canyons.

Over the last decade, wars erupted with devastating consequences and dragged on with despicable cruelty.

Civilians were targeted.

Human rights trampled.

Hunger weaponized.

Humanitarians killed.

International law cast aside.

Geopolitical divides have deepened.

Inequalities have intensified.

Trust has frayed.

The climate crisis went from distant warning to daily reality.

And artificial intelligence moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it.

These are not separate crises.

They are chapters of the same story.

The story of power.

Who has it.

Who is denied it.

How it is used.

And how it is changing.

Excellencies,

Power is being reshaped in three fundamental ways.

First, among States.

New centres of economic, political and technological influence have emerged.

Second, we are witnessing an extraordinary transfer of power away from governments to a handful of private corporations and individuals.

Their reach now extends across politics, economies, information flows, technological development, and the civic space on which societies depend.

And, third, humans are increasingly handing over power to machines – with Artificial Intelligence agents going rogue, and lethal autonomous weapons going from science fiction to military reality.

Yet our institutions and systems of global governance continue to reflect the power realities and interests of a largely bygone age.

That is the defining challenge before us.

At the very moment when humanity faces an unprecedented convergence of threats, our mechanisms for collective action are under growing strain.

Excellencies,

We are clearly moving towards a multipolar world.

And that movement is irreversible.

But there are different ways that multipolarity can take shape.

One possibility is a world of fragmentation and transactionalism.

A world of rising tensions and deepening mistrust.

Of fractured markets and weakened institutions.

Of shrinking cooperation and zero-sum calculations.

In many respects, that is the trajectory we are on today.

But there is another path.

A path towards networked multipolarity.

A world built on interdependence – and sustained by a dense web of economic, political, social and technological connections.

A world in which multiple centres of influence coexist within a common framework of international law and shared rules.

Such a world can help us avoid hegemonic tendencies and what I have called the Great Fracture:

The division of the world into two rival blocs with separate economic, technological and security systems.

A networked world recognizes that no power can solve today’s challenges alone.

Of course, competition will remain a permanent feature of international relations.

But competition does not have to mean confrontation.

Healthy competition can drive innovation, strengthen resilience, and expand opportunity.

But only when it operates within frameworks that preserve stability and enable cooperation where cooperation is indispensable.

Building a networked future begins with a recognition, especially by superpowers:

That their power isn’t so super.

That their power has limits.

The events of recent years have made that unmistakably clear.

Military power alone cannot secure peace.

Economic power alone cannot command stability.

And technological power alone cannot guarantee security.

A networked multipolar world can create the conditions for more balanced and representative global problem-solving.

But it requires a multilateral system centred in the UN that is balanced and representative.

Strong, effective institutions that reflect the realities and the progressively changing relative weight of countries and economies in today’s world – not the power arrangements of 80 years ago.

Fortunately, we are not starting from scratch.

We already have a binding foundation:

The Charter of the United Nations.

And the principles that give it life.

The primacy of international law.

Upholding human dignity.

And the pursuit of justice in all its dimensions.

These are the backbone for the effective, legitimate and responsible exercise of power in the 21st century.

Excellencies,

It comes down to this:

Will we act to ensure that power is governed by law or by force?

By cooperation or coercion?

By responsibility to young people and future generations or indifference to their fate?

Because the defining challenges of our age are not separate from the question of power.

They are expressions of it.

And they will determine whether we drift deeper into division and instability – or move toward cooperation, justice and collective security.

Looking ahead, our future will be shaped by how we address four great tests of power:

The power over war and peace.

The power that concentrates wealth and drives inequality.

The power fuelling climate chaos and the war on nature.

And the power unleashed by artificial intelligence.

Excellencies,

The first great power test in the 21st century is peace and security.

Peace is far more than the absence of conflict.

It is the presence of restraint of power by law.

It is the recognition, as enshrined in the UN Charter, that force cannot be the final arbiter of whose lives, rights and future matter.

Today that principle is under profound strain.

Across the Middle East, conflicts are cascading.

So-called ceasefires have amounted to little more than “lesser fires” – with civilians continuing to pay the price.

Enough is enough.

I appeal to the leaders in this Chamber to maximize this High-Level week for deescalation and dialogue.

Together, let's send a clear message from this Hall:

The fighting must stop.

Humanitarian aid must flow.

And navigational rights and freedoms must be fully restored in accordance with international law.

Amid the turmoil engulfing the region, we must not lose sight of the devastating situation in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

It is nearly three years since the abhorrent terror attacks by Hamas on 7 October.

What followed was an onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza, with a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as Secretary-General.

The International Court of Justice has issued legally binding provisional measures in the case entitled: “Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip.”

In an advisory opinion last year, the Court was clear that the United Nations needs to be allowed to perform our mandates in Gaza – and for our staff and humanitarian personnel to be protected.

All parties must comply with international law and the Court’s orders.

Meanwhile violence, displacement and settlement expansion by Israel in the Occupied West Bank are bulldozing the path to peace and raising the spectre of ethnic cleansing.

We cannot allow the two-State solution to disappear before our eyes.

In Ukraine, Russia’s full-scale invasion has subjected a sovereign country to a brutal war in blatant violation of the Charter.

Civilians continue to be killed far from the frontlines.

Mainly in Ukraine, but also more recently in parts of Russia – homes, energy and water systems, and transport have come under repeated attack, threatening food and energy supply chains globally.

In Sudan, a war for raw power fed by outside actors has become a war on civilians:

Millions displaced.

Hunger spreading.

Drones striking hospitals and homes.

Sexual violence and ethnically driven attacks escalating.

And a country being torn apart as the world looks away.

And in Myanmar, another crisis is at risk of slipping from global attention with: escalating violence; mass displacement; and expanding transnational crime.

Excellencies,

These and so many other conflicts show what happens when power gets out of control, force outpaces diplomacy, military budgets soar, and accountability goes out the window.

The test before us is whether power will be exercised with the law – or beyond it.

We must pass that test:

We must defend the Charter without double standards.

Protect civilians without exception.

Ensure humanitarian access without obstruction.

Shield humanitarian personnel without fail.

Advance nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament without delay.

And demand accountability without fear or favour.

We must also reform the Security Council so that it reflects today’s world with the legitimacy and effectiveness that today’s challenges demand.

The Security Council was designed in the aftermath of World War II.

But the world has fundamentally changed since then.

A change that is far from reflected in the Security Council.

The most stunning example is Africa.

When the UN was founded, most of Africa was still under colonial rule.

Today, Africa still has no permanent representation on the Council.

A 21st century Security Council without permanent African seats is unjust and indefensible.

This must change.

Excellencies,

The second test of power is inequality.

Inequality is often framed as an economic problem.

It is a power problem.

Power over opportunity, resources, voice.

Never has humanity possessed so much wealth, knowledge, and technological capability.

Yet for billions, progress remains out of reach.

They see prosperity around them, but not for themselves.

They are told globalization expands horizons, but they experience exclusion.

They are promised that technology will unlock new possibilities, yet many fear it will take away their livelihoods.

Meanwhile, billions of people still live without the essentials embedded in the Sustainable Development Goals.

Food.

Clean water.

Education.

Decent work.

Health care.

Dignity.

Excellencies,

No country should be denied a sustainable future because it is on the wrong side of a deeply unequal financial system.

Yet so many throughout the developing world are being crushed by unsustainable debt.

Battered by disasters they did little to cause.

And locked out of affordable finance.

That is why we have pushed relentlessly:

For reform of the international financial architecture – which is not a technical debate, but a question of representation, fairness and power.

For debt relief that is timely, effective and just.

For Multilateral Development Banks that are bigger, bolder and better equipped to provide affordable long-term finance at scale and massively leverage private finance.

For Special Drawing Rights to benefit countries that need them most.

Excellencies,

No discussion of inequality can ignore its most universal form:

The inequality between women and men.

Everywhere, women and girls continue to face discrimination, violence, exclusion and abuse.

Around the world:

Their rights are being rolled back.

Their voices silenced.

Their bodies turned into battlegrounds.

And their freedoms treated as bargaining chips.

This is an outrage –and a profound waste for humanity.

Peace is more durable when women are at the table.

Economies are more dynamic when women have equal opportunity.

Societies are more resilient when girls can learn, lead and live free from fear.

And institutions are more effective when power is shared equally.

Over the last decade, we achieved an enormous milestone.

I am proud to report to you today that the United Nations achieved gender parity for the first time in history across all senior leadership...all headquarters... and all professional staff.

It happened because we removed barriers, challenged assumptions, and refused to accept that power must look as it always has.

At every step, we never compromised on quality and competence.

Equality is not a dream. It is a decision.

If the United Nations can change:

So can Governments.

So can Parliaments.

So can businesses.

So can peace processes.

And so can this General Assembly.

Excellencies,

The third great power test is the climate crisis.

In many ways, it is the most profound intergenerational power imbalance of all:

One generation consuming the future of the next.

One group profiting, while those least responsible suffer first and worst.

Three years ago in the mountains of Nepal, I sounded the alarm on accelerating glacier melt – warning that the rooftops of the world are caving in.

Some dismissed it all as overstating dangers.

But – as tragic events have shown – impacts are arriving sooner, hitting harder, and spreading further than many anticipated.

Now we face a near certain breach of the 1.5 degree limit, with a supersized El Niño speeding straight for humanity.

The dangers are real.

But so is the hope.

The last decade has fuelled one of the most promising shifts in power of our time.

The rise of clean energy.

The sun belongs to no one.

The wind cannot be embargoed.

Innovation can come from everywhere.

This is a profound rebalancing of power relations.

Renewables are now the cheapest source of new electricity in most of the world.

And the most viable path to energy security, independence and sustainable growth.

Excellencies,

A future beyond fossil fuels is in sight.

The question is how.

Will it be a just and orderly transition built on international cooperation – or chaotic and costly leaving people and countries behind?

Today I call on every government to adopt a national plan to transition away from fossil fuels aligned with 1.5 degrees, with clear timelines and protection for affected workers and communities.

We know fossil fuel interests won’t step aside on their own.

For decades, Big Oil has treated the atmosphere as an open sewer – and cashed in on the consequences.

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, five major Western oil companies have pocketed nearly half a trillion dollars in profits.

Compare that with just 34 billion dollars in international public adaptation finance for developing countries in the latest year reported.

Meanwhile, everyday people are paying more for energy, food and insurance.

We have seen this kind of abuse of power before.

When the harms of Big Tobacco became undeniable – governments acted.

The climate crisis demands the same determination.

Those who polluted the most – and profited the most – must do far more to repair the damage they caused.

Polluters must pay.

And to the leaders, cities, civil society and citizens working to hold them accountable:

You are on the right side of history.

Keep going.

And governments must keep going on all fronts:

To end deforestation.

Invest in grids and storage.

Cut methane emissions.

But these actions are not enough:

We need climate justice with a focus on adaptation and finance.

Developed countries must respect their commitments.

They must triple adaptation finance.

And make the Loss and Damage Fund work at scale.

We must also ensure that the mining of critical minerals does not dig deeper into the inequities of the past.

Producing countries and affected communities must retain a far greater share of the value created from their resources.

No more plundering.

No more exploitation.

Excellencies,

The fourth power test is technology, and above all artificial intelligence.

For centuries, power came from territory.

Then industry.

Then finance.

Today, power increasingly comes from data, computing capacity and algorithms.

This new power is highly concentrated.

It is advancing at extraordinary speed.

And racing ahead of our ability to understand its full consequences.

In 2017, AI was barely on the world’s radar.

Yet in my first address to the opening of the General Assembly, I warned – and I quote: “Artificial intelligence is a game changer that can boost development and transform lives in spectacular fashion. But it may also have a dramatic impact on labour markets and, indeed, on global security and the very fabric of societies.”

Unquote.

Here we are, almost a decade later.

AI is indeed a game changer – with enormous promise to advance medicine, accelerate scientific discovery, expand opportunity, and improve lives.

Make no mistake.

The danger is not technology.

The danger is technology without accountability:

Capability without oversight.

Decision-making without transparency.

And that danger cannot be minimized.

The very developers building these systems are now pulling the alarm.

Excellencies,

The first duty of government is to protect its people.

Governments must assume their responsibilities.

And governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity.

To establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation.

Not despite geopolitical rivalry – but precisely because of it.

At a pivotal moment during the Cold War, strategic rivals came to recognize the need to manage shared existential risks.

They built mechanisms to reduce misunderstandings, manage escalation, and prevent catastrophe.

Artificial intelligence demands the same clarity of purpose and sense of urgency.

Those countries leading this technological revolution must share information on emerging safety risks.

Cooperate on testing and evaluation.

And work towards common safeguards that protect us all.

But because this affects us all, global coordination is indispensable.

And there is only one place where every country has a voice in shaping our common future:

The United Nations.

Through the Global Digital Compact, you agreed for the first time on universal principles for AI governance.

Through the Global Dialogue on AI Governance, we created a platform for governments, scientists, industry leaders and civil society to work together.

Through the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, we have brought together global expertise to ensure that policy is guided by evidence.

Just yesterday, the AI Scientific Panel released a thematic brief on AI safety and risks from loss of human control.

Building on these efforts, we must take the next steps.

First, to advance the conditions for the responsible pacing of AI and the additional safeguards needed to address risks.

Second, to work towards a multilateral AI Risk Management Framework, supported by credible and independent oversight.

And in all our efforts, we must ensure no country is left behind.

Artificial intelligence must be shaped by humanity, with humanity, and for all humanity.

And as we confront the challenges ahead, let us not retreat from two fundamental principles.

Let us say with one voice:

Children must never become the test subjects for unregulated systems.

And let us resolve that life-and-death decisions must never be surrendered to machines.

Killer robots must have no place in our future.

Excellencies,

Peace and security.

Inequality.

Climate.

Artificial intelligence.

These are the four great power tests of the future.

And they are linked.

War deepens inequality, destroys development and accelerates hunger.

Inequality determines who has the means to face climate and other shocks and who is left exposed.

The climate crisis fuels instability and displacement.

Artificial Intelligence could help solve all these challenges, or make them worse.

Excellencies,

Across all four tests, the decisive issue is power.

Power over force, money, energy, technology, rules and the future.

That is why the UN Charter – and the work of the United Nations – matter more than ever.

The United Nations exists because power requires rules – and humanity needs a place where power answers to principle.

And the Charter leaves no room for selective reading.

The Charter created an Organization rooted in three pillars.

Peace.

Development.

And human rights.

These are not competing agendas.

They are one reality:

There is no peace without development.

No development without peace.

And no peace or development without human rights.

To pretend that peace can be separated from dignity, opportunity and rights is an illusion.

But defending this truth does not mean defending the status quo.

The Pact for the Future and the UN80 initiative are about making the UN:

More responsive.

More effective.

More coherent.

More transparent.

More focused on results.

More disciplined with resources.

And more present where people need us.

The world does not need a weaker United Nations.

It needs a UN strong enough to face the world as it is – and determined enough to build the world as it should be.

Excellencies,

After ten years, I hold one conviction even more strongly than when I arrived:

The greatest power is not the power to dominate.

It is the power to build a future that works for everyone.

Our shared future will be forged by whether humanity can govern power wisely.

By upholding the law before impunity becomes normalized.

By ending wars before they consume generations.

By tackling inequality before societies fracture.

By accelerating climate action before tipping points are crossed.

And by governing artificial intelligence before it governs us.

This is the challenge before this General Assembly, the United Nations, and humanity itself.

Excellencies,

In the face of global catastrophe more than 80 years ago, the United Nations was created as an act of defiance.

The defiance of people who refuse to surrender the future to fear.

The defiance against the self-defeating notion that might makes right.

The defiance of countries that know our futures are bound together.

The defiance of hope.

I will carry that spirit of resolve and determination through each of the 100 days I have left in office.

But commitment to the values and principles of the United Nations does not begin with a mandate.

And it does not end with one.

They are greater than any office – and they endure beyond any title.

So, on January 1st, when I am no longer Secretary-General, be sure of this:

Wherever I will be, whatever I will be doing – I will keep championing the conviction that peace is possible.

That human dignity is universal.

That the power of law must prevail over the law of power.

And that our common future is worth fighting for.

I will continue to stand up for the values of the United Nations Charter.

And I will never... ever give up.

Thank you.

Mr. Secretary-General,

Former Presidents of the General Assembly,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Forty years ago, I stood in this very Hall as a newly minted member of the Cabinet of the 41st President of the General Assembly, Mr. Humayun Rasheed Choudhury.

At the time, President Choudhury said, and I quote: “In recent years there appears to have been a crisis of confidence in the United Nations itself... there is a general feeling that the United Nations today needs revitalizing in a number of aspects in order to bring it into line with the priorities of a changing world.”

This shows that questions about multilateralism and the effectiveness of the United Nations are not new. They have been part of this place since the first stone was laid.

Yet, through it all, the United Nations has persevered. Not because it is perfect, but because it is irreplaceable, and because the alternative is simply unfathomable.

The world of 1945 was in peril. The Second World War, the colossal devastation wrought by it, and the Holocaust, left humanity bankrupt, morally and fiscally.

Something had to change. And this place was that change.

It ushered in a long era of diplomacy, which continues: Member States coming together to work through their problems because they knew that the alternative, guns blazing and bombs dropping, simply was not an option.

Perhaps the clearest evidence of its achievement is here in this very Hall.

In 1945, 50 nations participated in the San Francisco Conference. Today, eight decades later, the Organization has 193 Member States. The UN has brought together humanity under one roof; this is unprecedented in human history.

The core promise of this institution, its raison d’être, was and remains to prevent the unimaginable: a third world war. The fact that we have avoided such calamity is among the greatest achievements this institution could ever deliver.

(BRIEF PAUSE) But survival alone cannot be our sole measure of success.

Outside these walls, people are not asking whether the United Nations still exists.

They are asking whether it works.

Yes, there have been wars and conflicts that we could not prevent, and issues we could not resolve. The Palestinian issue continues unresolved for decades. Wars and conflict and their aftermath are ravaging Sudan, Gaza, Ukraine, Myanmar, and the Middle East.

But even as those wars raged, the United Nations stayed and served.

I’ve seen this in my own country, where the United Nations country team in Cox’s Bazar is striving to do more with less to support Rohingya refugees in the camps.

Just recently, a representative from a war-torn nation said to me: “Your peacekeepers from Bangladesh were not just blue helmets.

They built roads and communities.

They fed children.

They helped rebuild societies and put us on the road to proper governance.”

In Iraq, the United Nations system helped nearly five million people return home. It rehabilitated hundreds of schools, electricity stations and water-treatment plants.

And right now, in Haiti, the entire United Nations family is delivering amid immense security and governance challenges.

These stories rarely make the headlines, but we should never lose sight of what is working.

(BRIEF PAUSE) At the same time, let us not turn a blind eye to where we have fallen short, particularly in a world where challenges seem to multiply by the day.

The war in Gaza has left over 70,000 people dead, including thousands of children.

Humanitarian support has been a fraction of what is needed.

The ongoing wars across the Middle East and Europe have consequences far beyond the frontlines.

And the heartbreaking disaster in Nepal and China, was not just an isolated event, but yet another horrible climax to our collectively insufficient response to climate change.

The circumstances and politics of these crises differ. But our commitments under the Charter do not.

The principles of multilateralism, international law, the protection of civilians and humanitarian access cannot be applied selectively, not if we want the world to trust us.

It is precisely at such times that we must honestly confront our setbacks, however profound, not with blame, cynicism or blind hope, but with action, sober reflection, clear-eyed realism and pragmatism.

That is how we chart these turbulent waters. And that is how we rebuild trust in this institution, the central focus of this 81st session.

(BRIEF PAUSE) So how do we build back trust?

Trust is not given. It is earned.

And we earn trust, I believe, in three ways.

First, by being unapologetically realistic about where we are falling behind; Second, by taking a foundational look at the reforms of the Organization to deliver better; and Third, by making our work more inclusive and engaging all relevant stakeholders for effective delivery.

Let me elaborate.

(BRIEF PAUSE) On my first point, we must be frank about where the challenges lie and what needs to be fixed, even when the necessary changes may prove painful.

Consider peace and security. Under the UN Charter, the Security Council bears primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security.

Yet when the Council is unable to act, Member States turn to the General Assembly.

We saw this as early as 1950 with the “Uniting for Peace” resolution, and we have seen it more recently through the Assembly’s Veto Initiative.

These two principal organs of our Organization are complementary, not competing.

The Charter provides for an appropriate balance between them. Both chambers must do their respective part.

To be fair, the Security Council, when it acts, proves its strength and effectiveness.

It helped liberate Kuwait, ended civil war in El Salvador, supported Namibia’s independence, led rebuilding of Cambodia, and stabilized conflict-affected countries through peacekeeping.

Yet when the Council is unable to act on important matters, the effectiveness of our Organization as a whole is called into question.

In 1945, humanity placed its trust in the Council in good faith, giving it the extraordinary responsibility of maintaining international peace.

The Council accepted that responsibility and entered into a compact.

It must now hold up its end of the bargain.

This is what the people of the world expect. And in their eyes, when the Security Council works, the United Nations works.

The promise of 1945 still binds us today. I call on the Security Council to step up, to lead as we need it to lead and to act when we need it to act.

Linked to this is the question of Security Council reform.

I will support the General Assembly-led Intergovernmental Negotiations in its work to make the Council more representative, transparent and reflective of the geopolitical realities of our time.

Ensuring fair representation for underrepresented regions must remain a priority.

Nowhere is this more important, right now, than in Africa.

After eight decades, the largest region by number of Member States and a key focus of UN Peacekeeping, is underrepresented on the Security Council.

Africa needs to be at the table, not on the menu.

Africa cannot be asked to wait indefinitely for its rightful place on the Council.

Ending Africa’s underrepresentation, now, is a question of fairness, justice and, ultimately, the credibility of this Organization.

(BRIEF PAUSE) Turning to development, and particularly the Sustainable Development Goals, we are right to focus on the challenges.

Last year OECD donors spent about $175 billion on development assistance... a 23% drop year-on year.

And yet military expenditures approached $3 trillion.... capping 11 straight years of growth.

All the while progress on the SDGs has stalled at just over a third of targets, and developing countries are now paying the price for supply chain disruptions they did not cause and cannot cure.

The contrasts could not be more stark. We must better prioritize how our resources are spent by augmenting development assistance, addressing debt burdens, reforming the international financial architecture, fulfilling our Sevilla and Paris commitments.

And implementing the programmes of action for LDCs, LLDCs, SIDs, as well as the AU’s Agenda 2063.

Because where we have done so, the results are clear:

Over the past decade, nearly one billion people have gained access to safely managed drinking water.

Electricity now reaches 92 per cent of the world’s population.

And internet access has risen from 40 per cent to 74 per cent.

Behind these figures are healthier children, more resilient communities, greater opportunities for women and girls, and renewed hope.

These gains show that accelerating the SDGs is possible when developing countries and development partners work in concert.

This indeed is a shared responsibility.

Developing countries must also intensify their own efforts through domestic resource mobilization and plug any leakage or corruption, including capital flight — A plague that, until recently, undermined development in my own country under a repressive, authoritarian regime.

(BRIEF PAUSE) Turning to human rights, we should acknowledge that these are central to the other two pillars: they can promote peace and security and advance sustainable development.

And we recognize one of the most urgent assaults on human dignity today: hate speech that incites violence.

It is a growing threat to regional and global peace, and it is on the rise.

Hateful narratives are spreading like wildfire across borders and into homes at unprecedented speed and scale. They target women and girls, minorities, migrants, refugees and persons with disabilities, often for political gain.

New and emerging technologies are used to amplify lies, manipulate public debate, spread hatred and give incitement to violence faster and farther than ever before.

We must choose dialogue and tolerance and foster a culture in which human rights are respected not only in law, but in our daily interactions.

And we must stop the cherry picking of those rights that fit our respective cultures or the politics of the day. Whether it is islamophobia, antisemitism, homophobia, or misogyny, it’s all the same... hatred, repackaged and relabelled.

Let us use the tools of our age not to deepen fear, but to widen understanding and advance human dignity, for everyone, everywhere.

(BRIEF PAUSE) My second point: making the United Nations fit for the future, which requires a more foundational approach to reform.

The UN80 Initiative is a constructive start.

But it is only a start.

Moving positions on a budget sheet may deliver savings.

Merging or renaming bodies may reduce duplication.

Streamlining structures may improve efficiency.

These steps are important and often necessary for good housekeeping, but they are not enough; we need to dig deeper to address the problems beneath the superstructure, because the United Nations’ reform challenges are chronic and fundamental.

On 24 November 1949, four years after the founding of the United Nations, this Assembly adopted resolution 310 (IV), entitled “Problem of the Proliferation and Overlapping of the Programmes of the United Nations and of the Specialized Agencies”.

It urged Member States “to refrain from initiating new projects other than those which are urgently required and which can be effectively carried out”.

Yet we have not paid sufficient attention to our own decision. We have since created thousands of mandates, of which 4,000 are still active, irrespective of whether they were required or could be effectively carried out.

We cannot continue treating a chronic ailment with temporary painkillers when what we need is a deeper diagnosis and a more profound plan for transformation, even if that plan proves painful.

And here I must be equally candid: this will happen only if Member States take charge.

Time and again, we say that United Nations reforms must be Member State-led. But too often, Member States fail to take the wheel.

Passive ownership is not enough.

If we do not claim proactive ownership of this place, we cannot expect it to heal.

So let us engage.

Let us take charge, fix our own house, respect sovereignty of Member States, and together deliver the transformation we need.

(BRIEF PAUSE) As we decide what must change, we must also recognize what already works.

Again and again, Member States tell us that the United Nations works well at the country level, emergency situations, and in keeping and building peace.

We should build on that success.

We should strengthen the United Nations’ country-level work and draw increasingly on local capacity, including qualified national institutions and individuals.

We should ensure that all activities at country level, from development support to peacekeeping, are properly integrated and produce the highest synergy.

We should ensure avoidance of turf battles among different parts of the UN, and exercise care to select resident coordinators that are fit to lead the teams.

We want to have full value for money.

The Organization’s financial viability is also a chronic concern. We must ensure that it receives sufficient resources on a sustained basis and that all countries pay their dues on time and without conditions.

We must also recognize that dues to the United Nations come from hardworking people around the world.

Every penny must therefore be properly accounted for.

Every penny must be invested to achieve impact on the ground for the people we serve.

(BRIEF PAUSE) The role of the Member States, supported by the Secretariat is essential to delivering our work, but not sufficient.

This brings me to my third point: building a more open and inclusive United Nations.

We know that the United Nations of today, and the world it serves, are profoundly different from those of 1945.

Nowhere is the pace of change more evident today than in artificial intelligence.

AI can be a powerful accelerator of human progress; therefore, we must not close the door to innovation.

At the same time, we must address AI’s potential harms, including job losses and widening of the digital divide. We cannot also rule out the possibility that AI, particularly artificial general intelligence, or AGI, could affect human survival.

That demands prudent and reliable guardrails, based on scientific evidence, to safeguard the global public interest, while allowing innovation to go forward.

Governments must remain at the heart of this endeavour.

But governments do not have a monopoly on expertise, capital, technology, innovation or influence. Much of that experience and capacity already lies with businesses, innovators, civil society and others.

We need to unlock the doors of the United Nations to those developing and using AI.

Not someday. Now. We are falling further behind each day.

AI differs from earlier proliferation challenges in one critical respect: it is already embedded in nearly every facet of our lives, in our water systems, electricity grids, health records, economies and militaries.

We cannot allow an arms race for control of AI to carry us over the precipice.

There is clear precedent for United Nations engagement with world-changing developments.

We did so on nuclear non-proliferation; through the Montreal Protocol to protect the ozone layer; and with the United Nations Declaration on Human Cloning in 2005.

We need experts, innovators, industry leaders, scientists, civil society, and academia all working together on the issues of our times.

(PAUSE) Excellencies,

Ladies and gentlemen,

We have an opportunity in this session to show that we have learned from what works; that we are prepared to confront what does not; and that we can build a United Nations capable not simply of surviving change, but of shaping it.

To seize that opportunity, we must be realistic enough to confront hard truths, bold enough to reform, and inclusive enough to bring the right people to the table.

That is how, in my view, we will renew trust in our Organization and make it fit for future.

The task is not easy, nor can it be done overnight. Then we must persist over the long-haul.

Eighty-one years ago, President Truman expressed the hope that the United Nations would endure for nine decades.

Here we are, at the beginning of the UN’s ninth decade. Let us dedicate ourselves to the task of rebuilding trust and confidence in the United Nations so that it lives up to that incredible potential for many decades to come.

I thank you.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary General,

Your Excellencies,

Every generation believes the challenges they face are unmatched.

Perhaps for us that is true.

We are at a unique moment in history; the scale of knowledge and the speed of change are unprecedented. Every day brings another crisis, another tragedy, another emergency, demanding our attention.

One study shows that average screen attention has fallen from 2.5 minutes in 2004 to just 47 seconds today.

العر␀␀␀␀ه About The King Initiatives By His Majesty Media Centre The Hashemites About Jordan About The King Initiatives By His Majesty Media Centre The Hashemites About Jordan العر␀␀␀␀ه Press Room Speeches from the Throne Speeches Interviews Letters Photo Gallery Of course, a screen is not the world, but that says something about our world today: that attention has become a scarce asset, and where we choose to direct it has never mattered more.

And in this chamber, attention is more than a cognitive resource. It is a geopolitical one.

It determines which conflicts receive sustained diplomacy and which fade from the agenda.

Whether a ceasefire holds after the cameras leave.

Whether humanitarian suffering remains intolerable, or becomes familiar.

And whether the world steps up, or scrolls and strolls away.

History rarely catches us entirely by surprise. More often, it catches us focused elsewhere.

Economic disparity, food insecurity, climate change disasters. None of these challenges emerged overnight.

The warning signs have been there. The question is whether our attention lasts long enough to act.

And what we neglect has a habit of shaping our future.

Your Excellencies,

We see the cost of that neglect every day.

In my region, from Lebanon to Yemen, to Sudan, protracted conflict is deepening humanitarian suffering.

And if anyone had any doubt that a crisis in our part of the world stays there, just look at the energy and grocery bills of ordinary families, from Mumbai to Madrid to Minnesota.

The Iran war has shown how quickly instability can disrupt trade, investment, and lives beyond the region.

Then there is Gaza.

For decades, I have stood before this Assembly and warned of the dangers of leaving the Palestinian-Israeli conflict unresolved.

But the international community chose to manage the conflict, not confront it.

And every new Israeli violation was treated as “temporary”, diverting attention from the reality being created on the ground. Until temporary became permanent, and permanent became policy.

Of course, this is not the world’s only injustice. But one of the world’s longest-running occupations forces a basic question: If international law can be ignored for decades, then what exactly is that law worth?

And how can we enforce it if we won’t even call out its violations?

In Gaza, the evidence is overwhelming: In the first 300 days of the socalled ceasefire, at least 300 Palestinian children were killed. Jordan’s field hospitals have also been targeted. President Trump has pushed hard for peace and a path to end this war. But this Israeli government keeps moving the goalposts, continuing its attacks and destruction of civilian infrastructure, refusing to withdraw, and squeezing Palestinians into barely a third of Gaza.

This can no longer be dismissed as temporary military measures, or a consequence of war. Accountability begins when we call things what they are: an attempt to erase Palestinian life and impose a new territorial reality in Gaza.

And while the world has been focused on Gaza, something extraordinarily dangerous is unfolding in the West Bank.

Some may think we have seen this before.

Settlements. Violence. Displacement. More of the same.

But it is not. Nor is it simply an escalation. This is a fundamental shift.

What was once a creeping process has exploded into something far more aggressive.

Settler violence is rampant. Palestinians are being beaten, shot and terrorised. Homes torched. Property destroyed. Families driven from their land.

And Israel is tightening its grip on more of the West Bank, seizing land, expanding settlements and pushing Palestinians out.

It is time to see what is happening for what it really is. Because when the language is sanitised, the actions become normalised.

Demolishing Palestinian homes to expand illegal settlements is not “law enforcement.” It is forcible transfer.

Appropriating occupied land is not “land registration.” It is de-facto annexation.

A choking network of checkpoints and barriers is not “security” infrastructure. It is a system of subjugation.

Systematic attacks on Palestinian communities are not “settler unrest.”

The Israeli government ‘criticises’ the violence before international audiences. They call those responsible a “handful of rioters.” They assure us that Israel is a country governed by law.

Yet, what’s happening on the ground says otherwise: Israeli soldiers stand by as settlers attack Palestinians, often protecting the attackers or joining them. They have blocked ambulances from reaching the injured. They have targeted international journalists who are trying to say the truth.

And when soldiers watch, enable, and sometime even participate in violence against civilians, this is no longer about “a handful of rioters.”

And the question is no longer whether a few extremists are breaking the law. The question is, is this the behaviour of a democratic state governed by law?

What is unfolding across the West Bank is not a series of isolated acts. It is elements of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land.

And there is a name for that: forced displacement.

And that is a war crime.

Your Excellencies,

If we are to resolve the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, the world must abandon some illusions:

The first is that Gaza and the West Bank are separate stories. They are not.

They are two fronts of the same Israeli strategy. In both, Palestinians are being killed. In both, the reality on the ground is being remade. Gaza through destruction. The West Bank through de-facto annexation.

The objective is the same: To make a viable Palestinian state impossible.

Another illusion is that this Israeli leadership’s rejection of Palestinian statehood is a position that might yet change. It is not. It is being cemented on the ground.

This government has been accelerating settlements and land seizures.

But it began long before. Since Oslo, the map has changed—piece by piece, settlement by settlement.

And the most dangerous illusion:

That the Arab world never sought peace.

The Arab Peace Initiative in 2002 offered Israel normalisation with 57 Arab and Muslim states, including Iran and Iraq at the time, in exchange for peace and Palestinian statehood.

For over twenty years, that offer has stood. The obstacle hasn’t been the absence of a partner for peace, but the absence of an Israeli government willing to accept it.

This Israeli government understands the power of attention. And lately, it has not liked the attention it’s been getting.

When confronted with evidence of wrongdoing, rather than change course, it opts for distraction, discrediting its critics.

It has also tried to cast this conflict as a war of religions; Islam on one side,

Judaism and Christianity on the other. It is not. This is about whether Palestinians—Muslims and Christians—are entitled to the same rights as everyone else.

Distractions will not fly anymore; people across the world are paying attention.

The question now is: will we act?

Because the world’s political inaction is not for lack of options. So, let’s call it what it is: a choice.

We have tools:

Sanctions, asset freezes, embargoes, diplomatic isolation. And we have a record of using them elsewhere.

Yet with Israel, resolutions end where they begin: on paper.

The result is a state without restraint.

This government’s sense of impunity has reached terrifying levels: It no longer feels compelled to ask, “Can we get away with this?” It already knows the answer.

And that is precisely why no one in this Assembly should assume its ambitions stop at Palestine.

This Israeli government’s expansionist appetite is now a regional threat.

And today, Syria is the warning the international community is choosing not to see.

Repeated incursions. Creeping territorial expansion. New facts imposed on the ground, including around vital water resources.

Step by calculated step, Israel is testing how far it can go. And every time the international community looks away, Israel learns that it can go even further across border lines and legal limits.

For Jordan, there is no ambiguity. Any threat to our northern border, or our water security, is a threat to our national security. Jordan will not look away; we will protect our security, our water, and the interests of our people.

And the question here is: If Israel continues its antagonistic approach in Southern Syria, will the international community stand by, and let that happen?

Your Excellencies,

Some things demand our immediate attention. Others demand sustained attention. Injustice demands both.

Jordan understands this all too well.

We know what it means to live in a region where one crisis arrives before the last has receded.

And we know that we cannot choose between responding to the emergency before us and building the future beyond it.

So, we are doing both.

We are strengthening connections from the Gulf to the Mediterranean as a hub for trade, industry, and technology—while responding to humanitarian crises.

We are confronting terrorism in the region and beyond—while developing our own defences and remaining a frontline against threats like narcotics.

We are protecting Christianity—its communities and heritage—in its native and historic land, while promoting the true image of Islam against the voices of hate.

And through it all, we will not abandon our commitment to a just peace.

We will continue to support Palestinian resilience.

We will continue supporting UNRWA.

And we will continue to uphold the Hashemite Custodianship and historic and legal status quo at Muslim and Christian holy sites in Jerusalem.

Most importantly, Jordan is striving to build a different model:

Principled, open and steady.

At a time when certainty is rare and politics can shift by the day.

A country the world can count on: true to our principles, true to our word, ready to talk to everyone, and ready to work with anyone seeking peace.

However, our bias towards diplomacy will never supersede our commitment to human values, and should not be taken for granted or mistaken for weakness.

My friends,

Whether in Gaza, Sudan, Ukraine, or anywhere people live with war, displacement, and fear.

Whether a crisis began weeks ago, or has endured for decades.

Our principles cannot change with the world's attention.

Military force cannot deliver meaningful solutions. It cannot feed the hungry, return the displaced, or build peace. Nor can it repair our planet, manage mass migration, or guide technological progress.

That requires institutions that command legitimacy. And it requires trust.

Trust between nations. Trust in agreements. Trust that rules will actually be enforced.

Destroy that trust, and every challenge becomes harder.

Preserve it, and cooperation becomes possible.

And in a world competing for our attention, we must be deliberate about where we direct it, and vigilant about what seeks to distract it.

The future is shaped not only by what we do, but by what we choose to ignore.”

The Jordanian delegation at the 81st Session of the UNGA included Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi, Director of the Office of His Majesty Alaa Batayneh, and Jordan’s Permanent Representative to the UN Walid Obeidat.

“We are compelled to change the current understanding where international law is applied differently to the strong and the weak” 22.09.2026 Addressing the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, President Erdoğan said: “We are compelled to change the current understanding where international law is applied differently to the strong and the weak. Let us not forget that an international system where wrongdoers get away with it and, worse still, where impunity has become the norm, is doomed to decay.”

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan addressed the 81 session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

President Erdoğan said: “I pray to Almighty that the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly will be a blessing for all of humanity, especially the oppressed. I would like to thank H.E. Ms. Baerbock who has completed her term as President of the General Assembly, and I wish H.E. Mr. Rahman success as he assumes the Presidency. I extend my congratulations and gratitude to my dear friend, H.E. Mr. Guterres, who has served as Secretary-General of the United Nations for nearly 10 years with impartiality and, above all, with courage.

First and foremost, I would like to express my sadness over a matter: The esteemed President of the State of Palestine, officially recognized by the overwhelming majority of the member states, H.E. Mr. Mahmoud Abbas, has been unable to take his place in this hall for two consecutive years. This injustice against our st Palestinian brothers and sisters wounds the consciences. I wish to reiterate that, even though Mr. Abbas cannot be present here in person, we will, just as we did last year, continue to serve as the voice of the free and sovereign State of Palestine and to proclaim the struggle of the Palestinian people to the world from this podium. Hereby, I once again call upon all countries that have not yet recognized the State of Palestine to reconsider their decision.

When the Charter of the United Nations was signed on 26 June 1945, Member States declared with great hope: ‘We the peoples of the United Nations determined to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, which twice in our lifetime has brought untold sorrow to mankind; to establish the necessary conditions under which fundamental human rights, the dignity and worth of the human, justice and respect for the obligations arising from this Charter can be maintained; to live in peace with one another with the spirit of good neighborhood; and to unite our strength to preserve international peace and security.’ More than 81 years have passed since the Charter was signed; yet humanity still yearns for the day when the powerful resolve of that time will truly come to life.

There is no need to look too far... A glance at the picture of just the past year is enough. Consider this: The past 12 months have gone down in history as one of the bloodiest periods of the last 30 years, marked by over 60 conflicts and wars. From Gaza to Ukraine and Russia, from Myanmar to Darfur, from Iran to Lebanon, 250,000 people have lost their lives. Many more have endured indescribable suffering. Hundreds of thousands have been forced to leave the lands where they were born and raised. In Gaza alone, over the past three years, 74,000 of our brothers and sisters—most of them children and women—have fallen victim to Israel’s state terrorism. The people of Gaza are still searching for their loved ones beneath the rubble; they are uncovering the bodies of their spouses, children, mothers and fathers. Innocent children who have lost their arms and legs in Israeli attacks are trying to attend school and hold on to life with prosthetics made of wood. In hospitals in Gaza, more than 70 percent of generators are currently out of service due to fuel shortages.

As a father and a grandfather who cherishes his children and grandchildren dearly, I must state the following from this podium with my heart torn apart: Gaza today is not merely the world’s largest graveyard for children... It is also the territory with the highest rate of child amputees in the world. Gaza is the most inhumane and most shameful concentration camp of our time. Even after the ceasefire reached through the efforts of President Trump and the contributions of countries, including our own, the number of Gazans killed has exceeded 1,500. Although the Palestinian Resistance Movement has agreed to move to the second phase of the peace plan, the Israeli Government is unwilling to halt the occupation.

Meanwhile, in the West Bank, we are witnessing the most severe period of settler terrorism. In Al-Quds,

Muslims and Christians are being prevented from accessing their holy sites. There is an attempt to destroy UNRWA, a joint initiative of us all. Today, I will openly express certain realities here, without placing any barrier between my heart and my words: Let no one take offense, nor feel slighted or resented. This is not Tayyip Erdoğan’s personal issue... This is a humanitarian issue; it is a matter of conscience for us all.

Before us stands a genocidal mentality that can never get enough of killing. Before us stands an extremely dire situation. No one who holds humanity, compassion and mercy in their heart, with a sense of justice and conscience, can turn a blind eye to this reality.

This scene, which ought to shake us all to the core, tells us this: The United Nations, established 81 years ago to maintain peace and security, has become unable to fulfil this mission, or rather it has been made unable to do so. The Organization continues to lose blood. Those who have placed their hopes in the United Nations in Palestine, Lebanon, Sudan and other crisis areas are deeply disappointed. But I would like to remind you that one day, everyone will have to seek refuge in humanity’s collective conscience.

Today, we may feel safe, prosperous and at peace. We may live in comfort, far away from conflict zones and crisis areas. But none of us knows what tomorrow will bring or what might happen to us. That is why I find this year’s General Assembly theme, which focuses on restoring confidence in the international system, exceptionally accurate.

We support the sincere efforts of the Secretary-General in this direction, including the UN80 Initiative. We expect this commitment for reform to be maintained during the tenure of the next Secretary-General. Of course, I would also like to state a fundamental truth quite clearly here... If we genuinely wish to boost confidence in the United Nations, the necessary steps are evident: Children in Gaza must be safe. When Palestinian children look up at the sky, they will see kites soaring freely, not fighter jets, UAVs or drones.

Children in Lebanon will not wake up in the middle of the night to the sound of bombs. The labor of Asian workers will not be exploited by ruthless capitalists. Our African brothers and sisters will feel just as safe and full of hope for their future as the citizens of prosperous countries. Only in this way, trust in the United Nations can be restored. Let’s recognize that a system in which the will of more than 190 countries is subject to the whims of five countries is neither fair nor capable of fully establishing trust. The Security Council must absolutely be reformed in accordance with the principle that ‘the world is bigger than five.’

While we must keep pace with rapidly advancing technology, we also bear the arduous yet noble responsibility of building a fairer order. At this point, I want to share with you here some basic principles:

First and foremost, we are compelled to change the current understanding where international law is applied differently to the strong and the weak. Let us not forget that an international system where wrongdoers get away with it and, worse still, where impunity has become the norm, is doomed to decay.

Second; at every stage where the international will is obstructed in resolving crises, we must use regional ownership to open a new path. As Türkiye, in every instance, such as the Black Sea Grain Corridor, where we have acted upon this principle, we have achieved result; we contributed both regional and global security. Third; we must absolutely reestablish an approach that places cooperation and open diplomacy at the center of relations among states. History has shown us, through bitter experiences, that there is no winner in a political approach built upon mistrust. Fourth; we must jointly build a new paradigm that offers solutions to the increasingly deepening income inequalities around the world. We believe that the path to this lies in joint development, solidarity and connectivity. Societies connected to one another through roads, trade, energy networks and joint production will eventually be united in peace and stability as well.

Finally, by reasserting a human-centered understanding of technology, we must prevent new barriers to be erected between those who possess technology and those who do not. It must be understood that technopolarization and digital hegemony serve neither the interests of the United Nations-centered system nor those of the states that constitute its core.

As Türkiye, we do not confine ourselves with merely articulating these principles. With every step we take, we seek a fairer and more humane international system. Through the Defense Alliance we have established with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, based on the understanding of regional ownership, we are both strengthening solidarity among us and aiming to generate solutions to the problems in our region from within the region itself. We are maintaining our efforts with the relevant actors to bring an end to the climate of conflict and war that has been ignited in the Gulf. I strongly underline that dangerous attempt such as spreading these conflicts to neighboring regions serves no one’s interests.

As for Gaza, we remain determined to uphold our commitments we made in Sharm el-Sheikh one year ago. We must begin the reconstruction of Gaza without delay. In this regard, I call upon you to exert greater pressure on Israel. Let everyone now understand and accept this: Attempts to strangle the State of Palestine will fail. Allah willing, we shall see those auspicious days where an independent State of Palestine, based on the 1967 borders, with territorial integrity and East Al-Quds as its capital, is established.

After 14 years of oppression, Syria embarked on a new path with the December 8 Revolution. Under the leadership of President Sharaa, we are witnessing that Syria is moving toward its goal of becoming a safe and peaceful country, despite all forms of internal and external provocation. We will continue to stand by the brotherly Syrian people on this journey. In Iraq, another neighboring country, we fully support the efforts to strengthen the state authority and consolidate stability. We are working with Iraq on strategic transportation and energy projects that will enhance the welfare of our region, particularly the Development Road Project.

As for the Russia-Ukraine war, it is our sincere hope that it comes to an end with Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity being upheld. We continue our contacts with the parties with a view to restoring safety of navigation in the Black Sea, ensuring food security, and preventing the war from spreading to a wider geography. I would like to particularly emphasize that recent attacks against commercial vessels in the Black Sea, regardless of who carries them out, are unacceptable. We believe that freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz must be maintained.

In the Aegean Sea and in the Eastern Mediterranean, we wish to see existing issues resolved on the basis of good-neighborly relations and in accordance with international law. Our proposal for an Eastern Mediterranean Conference will contribute to establishing a common ground. On this occasion, I once again repeat the call I have made at the United Nations General Assemblies: The sovereign equality and equal international status of the Turkish Cypriot people must be recognized, and the inhumane isolation to which they have been subjected must finally come to an end. I call upon the international community to recognize and establish political, diplomatic, and economic relations with the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus.

Türkiye, thanks to its growing defence industry, and its resilient economy, continues to be an island of stability amid conflicts in its vicinity. As an integral part of Europe, our country plays a significant role in ensuring the welfare and security of the continent. The NATO Ankara Summit, which we successfully hosted in July, was a concrete manifestation of our commitment to our common security. A Europe that the security architecture excludes Türkiye cannot, I’ll say this clearly, be stronger or safer. We are shaping our future with the European Union precisely through this strategic vision. We expect the same vision from the European Union as well.

The Balkans is a region that we have strong historical, cultural and human ties with. Within the Balkans Peace Platform, we are taking joint steps to deepen our cooperation. Our stance on the South Caucasus is also quite clear: We hope for the establishment of lasting peace between Azerbaijan and Armenia. We commend and support the commitment to a solution demonstrated by Mr. Aliyev and Mr. Pashinyan. We are also resolutely advancing the normalization process with Armenia.

RESOLVED” I would also like to express with pleasure that: The Organization of Turkic States has become an exemplary model of regional cooperation that is growing in strength year by year. The 13th Leaders’ Summit, to be held in Ankara on 30 October, will, Allah willing, open new doors and new horizons for the Organization.

The 4th Türkiye-Africa Partnership Summit, which we will organize in Libya in December, symbolizes our institutional partnership we have been building for over 20 years.

In South Asia, it is important that all disputes, including the Kashmir issue, be addressed through dialogue, within the framework of United Nations charter and the relevant resolutions. Provided that constructive action is taken, every issue can be resolved. The same applies to tensions on the African continent. We fully support efforts for a ceasefire and lasting peace in Sudan, as well as efforts to strengthen security, development and institutional capacity in Somalia. Maintaining stability and tranquility in Libya is our priority. It is imperative that the ongoing reconciliation process be led and owned by Libyans.

As Türkiye, we maintain our support for the success of this process as well. Meanwhile, through our Asia Anew Initiative, we continue to strengthen our relations with our partners in the Asia-Pacific region. We regard the elevation of our relations with ASEAN to the level of Dialogue Partnership as a concrete outcome of this approach. Likewise, we are developing our relations with the countries of Latin America and the Caribbean on the basis of mutual respect, partnership and a win-win understanding.

We all derive our livelihood and the source of our life from the nature. Yet our world stands on the threshold of serious environmental and climate-related threats. Air, water and soil, as well as many living species, are being affected by the climate change. While developing countries and the Pacific region are experiencing the climate crisis to their very core, they unfortunately face serious difficulties in accessing the funding they need. This November, we will host COP31 Summit in Antalya. At the Summit, we will ensure that climate justice is given particular prominence. Through the partnership we have developed with Australia, we aim to make COP31 an “Implementation COP,” where financial commitments are fulfilled, technology transfer is accelerated, and promises are translated into concrete steps. Taking this opportunity,

I invite you to the COP31 Leaders’ Summit.

The Zero Waste Movement launched by my wife, Mrs. Emine Erdoğan, in 2017 with the slogan “The World is Our Common Home” has since evolved into a global campaign to raise awareness. It is a fact that there are undoubtedly many ways to tackle the climate crisis. The Zero Waste Movement is the strongest bridge where all these paths meet. I believe that, with your support, this bridge will become even stronger.

I would also like to draw your attention to the following fact: Another threat as serious as climate change is the spread of a culture of waste fueled by the desire for consumption. Every year, 5.8 trillion plates of food end up in the bin worldwide, meaning that over 2 billion tons of food are wasted. We cannot speak of justice in a world where tons of food are thrown into the garbage on one side while hundreds of millions of people collect food from garbage on the other. As Türkiye, we are ready to make every possible contribution both to preventing waste and to ensuring global food security. With this understanding, we nominated Dr. Mehmet Mehdi Eker for the position of Director-General of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. I am confident that you will not withhold your support.

It is also worth noting that: As our world changes rapidly, humanity has simultaneously begun to face new social threats. Islamophobia, which is spreading like the plague in the West, is at the forefront of these issues. Most of all, Muslim women and girls are subjected to greater discrimination in recent years. We regard the headscarf bans introduced in schools by certain countries as an attack on women’s most fundamental rights. Rising xenophobia, cultural racism and anti-Semitism are also toxic trends that must be combated with determination. Global gender-neutralization policies as well have turned into a siege targeting innocent children, alongside the family institution. We can break this siege only by protecting the family consisting of women and men. Türkiye will continue to take initiatives in protecting families and children, despite attacks from lobby groups.

Another threat that undermines social peace is the spread of disinformation on social media. Standing up for the truth has become more important today than ever before. We are also facing the same risk with artificial intelligence, which is becoming increasingly difficult to control. It is long overdue to establish a common international legal framework for artificial intelligence. It is crucial to accelerate the work being carried out to draft and bring into force the United Nations International Convention on Artificial Intelligence.

The realities I have spoken of here today with an open heart will undoubtedly upset some people, disrupt their comfort, and unmask their lies. I also know very well that they will resort to all kinds of perception management operations in an attempt to silence our voice. In the words of a late poet: ‘They think that if we remain silent, the issue will disappear/But even if we remain silent, history will not./History may remain silent, but the truth will not./They believe that if they get rid of us, the problem will be solved./Yet even if they get rid of us, they would not be able to escape the pangs of their conscience./Even if they were to escape the pangs of their conscience,/They would not be able to escape the pangs of history,/Even if they were to escape the pangs of history,/They would not be able to escape the wrath of Allah.”

As Tayyip Erdoğan, as the President of a great nation guided by its conscience, its history and its compassion, Allah willing, for as long as Allah grants me life, I shall continue from this rostrum to defend the rights of the oppressed, the aggrieved and the voiceless; to be their voice; to speak on their behalf; and to fight for them. If necessary, we will endure hardship; if necessary, we will pay the price. But we will not remain silent in the face of injustice, and we will never consent to oppression.

When we look at the course of the world, we can see that there are two paths before us: Either we will deepen uncertainty through fear, conflict and isolation... Or we will build the future together through justice, solidarity and common will. It is, of course, easy to punch the darkness. The difficult thing is to light a candle that will dispel that darkness. Türkiye has chosen the second path and hopefully will follow it with patience. May Allah ease our way and be our guide and helper, I pray. I invite our friends listening to us in this hall and from every corner of the world to embrace this shared vision of the future. Until we meet again, I salute you all once more with respect.”
