Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Distinguished Heads of Delegations,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

At the outset of my speech, I would like to sincerely congratulate Dr. Khalilur Rahman on being elected as the President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly and wish him further success.

• • • As you are all aware, last year the international community marked the 80th anniversary of the United Nations.

For 80 years, this unique global organization has been standing at the forefront of safeguarding peace, security and development.

Although our Organization brings together all countries of the world and serves as the principal platform for international cooperation, wars and tensions still persist in various regions.

Armed conflicts and humanitarian crises in different parts of the world, including Ukraine, Iran, Sudan and Palestine, demonstrate the complexity of the current international environment and require all of us to work together to strengthen peace, security and sustainable development.

Kyrgyzstan is a country that believes in the power of dialogue and the peaceful settlement of conflicts.

Our country stands ready to serve as a mediator in addressing complex and contentious issues.

In recent years, Central Asia has clearly demonstrated to the world its ability to resolve complex interstate issues peacefully.

Today, Central Asia is becoming an example of constructive interstate cooperation, as well as economic, infrastructural and technological development.

In this regard, we are ready to share the experience we have accumulated along this path.

• • • Distinguished Heads of Delegations,

For the first time in its history, Kyrgyzstan has been elected as a member of the United Nations Security Council for the 2027–2028 term.

Taking this opportunity, I would like to express my profound gratitude to all countries that supported our candidacy.

The support of 142 Member States not only confirms Kyrgyzstan's readiness to contribute to international affairs but also demonstrates the growing role of Central Asia in international relations.

This achievement is clear evidence that even small states can make a meaningful contribution to addressing global challenges.

We fully understand that membership in the Security Council is not a privilege or award – it is a great responsibility.

One year ago, standing at this stage, I stated with confidence that “Kyrgyzstan is among those states whose experience enables them to put forward substantive issues for consideration by the Security Council.”

We do not forget the promises we have made and will make every effort to implement them fully.

Therefore, I would like to reiterate: “Kyrgyzstan firmly adheres to international law, justice and the protection of human rights, and supports the multilateral system based on mutual respect, balance of interests and responsibility toward future generations.”

We intend to work closely with every country and remain committed to productive cooperation.

• • • Distinguished Colleagues,

As you all may know, since the establishment of the United Nations in 1945, its Member States and leaders have attempted to undertake systemic reforms.

Reforms have ranged from expanding the membership of the Security Council to modernizing mechanisms of governance, peacekeeping and the protection of human rights.

These initiatives continue to be actively discussed at the international level.

However, despite numerous efforts and years of discussion, the institutional structure of our Organization continues to face various challenges.

Therefore, I believe that expanding the membership of the Security Council is one of the reforms that the international community expects. I consider it fair to grant two permanent seats to the African continent with population of more than one billion people, and one permanent seat to Latin America.

Today, the world has changed.

At the same time, a number of developed countries have also expressed their aspiration to become members of the Security Council.

I believe that the requests of these countries should also be consider ed.

• • • Another issue, in my view, is the weakness of effective mechanisms for ensuring the implementation of the decisions of the Organization.

The systematic failure to implement the Organization's decisions undermines the legitimacy of multilateralis m’s concept, creates the impression that international law is not binding, and encourages disregard for international obligations.

Therefore, we must expand and strengthen the authority of the United Nations.

In this regard, we propose to redevelop the United Nations mechanism for the implementation of decisions and accountability.

First and foremost, it is necessary to establish, within the framework of the General Assembly, the permanent public registry of the implementation of resolutions and obligations by Member States.

This Registry could include the following information and ensure the implementation of such measures as:

The first — systematically record and verify the level of implementation of adopted decisions.

The second — establish the obligation for Member States to regularly submit report in accordance with agreed standards.

The third — provide analytical reviews on sectors and regions.

The f ourth — ensure transparency and equal access to information for all States.

• • • The Registry could be administered by the United Nations Secretariat, with the support of independent experts.

If decisions of the Organization are systematically not implemented, I propose the gradual response mechanism.

The first stage — an official notification to the concerned State, followed by consultations with the relevant bodies of the Organization.

The second stage — the deployment of a monitoring mission to the country concerned to assess the objective obstacles preventing the implementation of the decisions and to prepare recommendations.

The third stage — consideration of the case — right here — at a plenary meeting of the General Assembly to determine the status of the concerned State in terms of its systematic implementation or non-implementation of United Nations decisions.

The fourth stage — the initiation of appropriate procedures under the Charter of the United Nations with regard to States that fail to comply with the requirements.

In particular, the matter could be referred to the United Nations Security Council for consideration of restrictive measures provided for under international law, including:

The first - temporary restrictions on participation in United Nations programs.

The second - recommendations to review existing formats of cooperation.

And other diplomatic measures, where appropriate.

• • • Distinguished Colleagues,

I believe that when cases of systematic non-implementation of United Nations’ decisions are considered, the permanent members of the Security Council should voluntarily refrain from using the veto.

If a mechanism designed to ensure the implementation of the Organization's decisions is systematically blocked by permanent members through the use of the veto, such practice would no longer be consistent with the spirit of the UN Charter and the principle of equal responsibility of Member States.

Therefore, we should once again consider the possibility of voluntarily restraining the use of the veto in matters related to the implementation of the Organization’s decisions.

This approach could promote universality, the equality of all states regardless of their size, the primacy of diplomacy and avoid the double standards.

In order to implement this initiative, I propose establishing the open working group within the General Assembly with the participation of the interested Member States.

The working group could conduct intergovernmental consultations and prepare a report on possible models for the proposed mechanism.

Following these consultations, the General Assembly and the Security Council should consider adopting the relevant resolutions and decisions.

The strategic objective of this initiative is to ensure that the decisions of the Organization are treated not merely as political recommendations, but as genuine international obligations.

Improvement of their implementation would strengthen the rule of international law and reinforce confidence in the United Nations.

Kyrgyzstan is ready to initiate interstate discussions on the development of such a mechanism.

Starting from January 1, 2027, as a member of the United Nations Security Council, we intend to formally submit all these proposals to the relevant Committee.

• • • Distinguished Colleagues,

I would like to address separately the issue of sanctions.

As we have all observed, today sanctions are, in some cases, used by individual countries as an instrument of interference in the internal affairs of sovereign states.

The negative consequences of unjustified unilateral sanctions also affect small countries such as ours, which are at the stage of formation and development, and this raises concern among other small states as well.

In certain cases, such practices lead to interference in the internal affairs of independent states and contradict to the fundamental principles of international law.

Some major states, in pursuit of their own interests, put pressure on smaller countries such as Kyrgyzstan, attempting to force them to bargain over certain matters and issuing ultimatums.

In this context, I would like to take this opportunity to note the decision made by the President of the United States His Excellency Mr. Donald Trump after taking office to halt funding of non-governmental organizations around the world.

As a result, interference by NGOs in the internal affairs and policies of developing States has practically ceased.

President Trump’s decisions have created conditions for strengthening the sovereignty of States and enabling them to independently choose their own path of development.

Therefore, taking this opportunity today, I would like to express my appreciation to Mr. Trump for ending the funding of NGOs.

• • • Distinguished Colleagues,

Decisions to impose sanctions should be taken in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations and exclusively within the mandate of the Security Council.

We believe that the mandate to impose sanctions against a state should belong exclusively to the United Nations.

In my view, this is the only possible way to improve the international sanctions system.

First and foremost, we should introduce a mandatory mechanism under which all sanctions measures are reviewed in advance by the Organization.

The prior review of sanctions initiatives would help ensure that their potential humanitarian, economic and social consequences are taken into account.

An important element of the proposed mechanism should be the enhanced transparency and accountability.

States initiating sanctions should clearly indicate the legal basis for such measures, explain their necessity and objectives, and define clear criteria and conditions for their eventual removal.

I believe it would be appropriate to establish, under the auspices of the United Nations, the unified international mechanism for monitoring sanctions and reviewing them on a regular basis.

Only then can the central role of the United Nations in maintaining international peace and security be strengthened and its mandate enhanced.

This would also help eliminate the risk of sanctions being used arbitrarily by one country against another for political or economic gain.

No state should act arbitrarily.

The United Nations must be strong.

Every country should tremble when the United Nations intends to impose sanctions. Only then the strict international order can be established in the world.

Otherwise, some decisions of the United Nations may no longer be taken seriously, while states simply act according to their own discretion.

Every decision of the United Nations should be implemented without delay.

If a state fails to implement such decision and other countries cease cooperation with it, the effectiveness of sanctions will increase.

Only then will decisions can be implemented promptly, and the United Nations will become a strong and respected organization.

Otherwise, existing sanctions will become a sort of children's toy.

• • • Dear Friends,

As we all know, climate change, that has become a global challenge, continues.

The average temperature of our planet and the number of climate -related emergencies are rising rapidly, while their negative impact on energy, agriculture, food security and the economy as a whole has reached a significant scale.

Kyrgyzstan is a mountainous country.

We are particularly vulnerable to the effects of melting glaciers.

This is not an abstract threat.

It is an environmental challenge of regional significance.

I believe it is extremely important and necessary to unite international efforts in addressing climate challenges and the problems facing mountainous regions.

In this regard, on October 21–23, 2027, Bishkek will host the Second Global Mountain Summit, “Bishkek+25.”

Taking this opportunity, I invite all of you to participate in the Summit.

The Summit will serve as the concluding event of the Five Years of Action for the Development of Mountain Regions for 2023–2027 term.

During my meeting with United Nations Secretary -General Mr. António Guterres in Bishkek on August 31, 2026, I proposed organizing this Summit jointly with the Organization.

These efforts demonstrate our country's leading role among mountain states and its commitment to unite international efforts to address their challenges.

Therefore, Kyrgyzstan stands fully ready to serve within the United Nations as the voice of small and developing countries in addressing the climate -related challenges affecting mountainous regions.

• • • Distinguished Heads of Delegations,

Continuing the topic of climate change, I would like to draw your attention to another environmental challenge.

As we all know, global problems and disasters often have their origins at the local level.

This issue concerns the unique high -altitude Lake Issyk-Kul, which is part of the UNESCO Biosphere Reserve and is included among wetlands of international importance under the Ramsar framework.

Today, this invaluable natural water reservoir is under severe climatic stress.

Over the past 170 years, the water level has fallen by almost 14 meters, while over the past five years the rate of decline has reached approximately seven centimeters per year.

101 rivers historically flowed into the lake, but today only around 30 flow throughout the entire year.

The main source of water for Lake Issyk -Kul is the glaciers of the Tien Shan mountains.

Over the past 70 years, more than 30 % of the region's mountain glaciers have melted.

Nearly 20 % of this reduction has occurred within just the past seven to ten years.

This process poses a direct threat to the biodiversity of the region and economic stability of hundreds of thousands of people.

As part of our efforts to preserve Lake Issyk -Kul, Kyrgyzstan is mobilizing all available domestic resources.

In particular, the State Concept for the Sustainable Development of the IssykKul Ecological and Economic System until 2030 is being implemented.

Strict environmental restrictions have been introduced, and pilot projects have been launched to monitor the depth of the lake using underwater robotic technologies.

Large-scale efforts to clean the lakebed and its waters are continuing on a regular basis.

The scale and speed of climate change exceed the capacities of any individual mountain country and require consolidated international action.

The loss of Lake Issyk-Kul would not be merely a local tragedy.

It would become an irreversible environmental loss for the entire region.

In order to understand the potential scale of this environmental challenge and the costs associated with preventing it, it is important to look at the fate of the Aral Sea and Lake Chad, both of which have suffered severely over recent decades.

(Pictures) Please take a look.

Not so long ago, the Aral Sea and Lake Chad, just like Issyk -Kul today, were full and reservoir with full of water.

Today, they have largely dried up.

For us, these examples must serve as a clear warning.

Taking this opportunity, I officially call upon the United Nations, international financial institutions and donor countries to support our initiative to establish, under the auspices of the Organization, the Special joint trust fund for the preservation of Lake Issyk-Kul.

In order t o demonstrate our commitment through concrete action, we are prepared to contribute 10 million US dollars from the state budget to this fund.

• • • In our culture, there is a concept known as “Amanat.”

It means the duty to carefully preserve what our ancestors have entrusted to us and to pass it on to future generations.

In this sense, it would be fair to state that Lake Issyk-Kul is our shared climate Amanat.

We are not asking for help.

We are proposing a joint global partnership to preserve this unique natural resource of the Earth.

Before it is too late, let us unite our efforts and resources within the framework of this trust fund.

• • • Distinguished Participants,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

The challenges before us are shared. Therefore, our response to them must also be collective.

We stand at the threshold of a new era of change.

Safe, just and sustainable future can be built only through collective action.

The destiny of our planet and future generations is the responsibility of each and every one of us.

This year, Kyrgyzstan celebrates the 35th anniversary of its independence.

Throughout this period, our country has faced many different challenges.

Since then we chose cooperation over confrontation, creation over destruction, and embarked upon the path of sustainable development.

There is one thing we must all remember: peace does not come about by itself.

Therefore, let us turn our words into action - concrete steps that improve people's lives and protect nature.

Let us build together a world in which dialogue is stronger than weapons, mutual respect is stronger than fear, and cooperation among nations delivers tangible results for all humanity.

Thank you for your attention.

In the name of God.
The most gracious, the most merciful, your Excellency, president of the General Assembly, Your Excellency.

Secretary general, ladies and gentlemen, may the peace, mercy and blessings of God be upon you.
I extend my congratulations to His Excellency, Mr. Khalilur Rahman, on his assumption of the presidency of this session and wish him every success.
I also thank Her Excellency Miss Annalena Baerbock for her efforts in presiding over the work of the previous session.
I would also like to commend the efforts and endeavours of His Excellency Mr. António Guterres the Secretary General, throughout his term of office.

I would also like to express our appreciation to the staff of the United Nations system for their efforts amid difficult and complex circumstances.
I stand before you today at a time when our region is going through one of its most dangerous phases.
You are all aware of the dimensions of the crisis in the Gulf and its repercussions on the entire world, the crisis we are currently facing should come as no surprise to anyone.
It is the cumulative result of years of postponing crisis management through temporary solutions and unrealistic policies.

Our perspective has always been that the way to resolve disputes is through dialogue and negotiations to reach just fair solutions grounded in international law, grounded in respect for the sovereignty of states and the rights of peoples.
This remains our position in the aftermath of the wars.
We've been witnessing the state of Qatar through its role as a trusted mediator and peace facilitator, has consistently warned that time does not resolve lingering conflicts in the absence of a just settlement.
Rather, it doubles their costs.

Ladies and gentlemen, at the heart of the dangerous situation we are witnessing lies the absence of a regional system of collective security, one that respects the sovereignty, security and territorial integrity of states one that promotes the peaceful settlement of disputes and the non-interference in the internal affairs of states.
We have previously called from this very podium for the establishment of such a system, and we reiterate that call after recent events have demonstrated the urgent need for it.
In the absence of such a system, it has become possible for a war to erupt owing to considerations unrelated to the interests of the countries of the region.
It has become possible for one party to drag its neighbors into a war that is not theirs, targeting their vital assets and installations.

Despite their strenuous efforts to avert escalation.
It has become possible for an international waterway through which nearly a quarter of the world's energy trade passes to be closed.
It has also become possible for the lifelines of the global economy to be turned into tools of pressure and bargaining with people on every continent bearing the cost, despite being far removed from the causes of the conflict.
This is a crisis that drives up the prices of food and medicine, and affects the livelihoods of peoples who have nothing to do with any of this.

Despite all those developments which could have been avoided, we remain deeply convinced and our conviction is based on realistic considerations.
Convinced that the crisis in the Gulf can be resolved through diplomatic means by reopening the Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation and returning to negotiations in order to avert war, paving the way toward a lasting solution that ensures security and stability for the entire region, including Iran, while opening prospects for cooperation across various fields and ensuring non-interference in the internal affairs of states.
The opportunity for a peaceful diplomatic solution, which we believe is both possible and realistic, must not be missed.
Your excellencies, while we're doing everything within our power to address the situation through diplomatic efforts, we have strengthened our steadfastness to defend our sovereignty, our territory and our people and the foundations of normalcy.

We have devised resilient, flexible economic plans and remained committed to our development projects.
Despite the severe adverse impact of the war and the heavy price it has exacted at every juncture and in every crisis.
We have chosen to combine resilience with flexibility and to place the interests of our nation, our people and those residing on our sole soil above all else.
Our values are not mere slogans we proclaim, but a reality we live by.

They are values that we put into practice.
At their core is the conviction that the dignity of the nation cannot be compromised, and that wisdom and firmness are two sides of the same coin.
This approach is firmly anchored in our nation.
This approach has been championed by the leaders of Qatar, from the founder, Sheikh Jassim bin Mohammed bin Thani, to His Highness Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, our Emir from 1995 to 2013.

May Allah have mercy on his soul.
He passed away this year and was mourned with profound affection and gratitude by his people and all peace loving nations and people across the region and around the world.
On this occasion, I would like to thank the United Nations General Assembly for convening a special session in honor of his memory and in recognition of his legacy, the experiences and challenges we have confronted have demonstrated that resilience is the outcome of prior planning, preparedness and investment in people and national capabilities.
Accordingly, over the years, we have worked on assessing risks, securing supply chains, strengthening the capabilities of our national institutions, developing strategic reserves and forging trusted international partnerships.

Recognizing the nexus of peace, security, development, human rights and the rule of law.
The State of Qatar maintains its investment in development, education, health, security and economic diversification in conformity with the Qatar National Vision 2030.
Your Excellencies.
There can be no talk of a just international order, as long as Palestine remains a blind spot within it.

What has transpired in Gaza is genocide in every sense of the word and the stain of shame on the conscience of humanity as a whole.
Future generations will be astonished by the enormous gap between the scale of the catastrophe and the level of the international response to stop it.
Yet the catastrophe persists.
An Israeli leaders have now begun to openly proclaim that the most appropriate solution is to displace the population, which they call migration.

When the extent of global public revulsion at the practices of the Israeli occupation becomes evident.
Instead of looking in the mirror, they resort to hurling accusations indiscriminately, indiscriminately, in all directions, at times invoking accusations of anti-Semitism and at others resorting to conspiracy theories and accusing other powers and states of being responsible for creating their negative image.
It's as though there were no means of communication, as though Israeli soldiers had not boasted, through both sound and visuals of their crimes, and as though images of the crimes against humanity committed in Gaza had not been circulated by an entire generation of young people across the world, East and west.
From the very first day, the state of Qatar has done its utmost as a mediator to stem the bloodshed, to alleviate the suffering of civilians, and to release the prisoners and detainees until a cease fire was achieved.

Today, we continue our efforts to consolidate it and to move towards lasting peace.
As Palestinian factions agreed to arrangements for the collection of weapons as stipulated in the agreement, Israel, for its part must fully honour its commitments in their entirety.

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Thirty-five years ago, Lithuania returned to its rightful place in the global community of sovereign states. By joining the United Nations, we reaffirmed our strong commitment to the global order based on international law, territorial integrity, state sovereignty, and human dignity.

It was a glorious moment for a nation well taught by historical experience that freedom and independence cannot be taken for granted. They must be constantly – and consistently – defended.

Today, I am standing here to speak for the same dream that inspired Lithuania in 1991. The vision of a more just, secure, and peaceful world.

Today, I am backing up the principles of the United Nations which, sadly, are being put under increasing pressure.

Recent years have brought us numerous high-intensity and far -reaching conflicts that dominate the global affairs on a scale not seen in decades.

We witness geopolitical instability in Europe, the Middle East, and elsewhere. It is made worse by growing nuclear ambitions in the Middle East and Asia, as well as the irresponsible transfer of military-related goods, dualuse items, and sensitive technologies.

In recent months, Iran has continued attacking neighbouring countries, often through its proxies, while actively impairing the freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. These actions constitute a serious threat to regional and international peace and security. We reaffirm our full solidarity with the Gulf Cooperation Council states and Jordan. We call on Iran to halt its nuclear and missile programs, as well as its collaboration with armed groups across the Middle East.

Lithuania commends all efforts to find a solution ensuring the freedom of navigation. We will contribute with our demining capabilities to the international maritime missions in the Strait of Hormuz.

As regards the situation in the Gaza Strip, my country supports international efforts to maintain and consolidate the ceasefire. The Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, including the deployment of the temporary International Stabilisation Force, provides the guidelines to follow.

Lithuania reiterates the importance of full demilitarisation and calls on Hamas and other non -state armed groups to disarm and permanently decommission their weapons. Humanitarian aid must also be allowed to reach those in need safely, and without obstruction.

To this day, the two -state solution remains the only way towards a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace. In this light, it is crucially important to abstain from any further actions incompatible with a credible political process.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

The one conflict that poses the greatest threat to the world order is Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, supported by its proxies.

In the twelve years since the illegal occupation of Crimea, Russia has escalated from clandestine operations and limited warfare in Eastern Ukraine to massive military operations, mass killings, and, ultimately, the largest drone attacks against civilian infrastructure the world has ever seen.

The current stage of the war, which began with the full -scale invasion in February 2022, has already lasted longer than the First World War.

In the last 55 months, Russia has suffered 1.5 million military casualties. In the last year, it has gained 0.3 percent of Ukraine’s territory at the cost of over 400 thousand soldiers killed and wounded.

Yet all these enormous efforts, all th at blood and tears, basically came to nothing. Ukraine is still standing proudly as an independent state. The Ukrainian language, culture, and national identity are alive and thriving.

In all but name, Russia has already lost the war. Yet its leadership does not allow itself to admit defeat, fearing international legal accountability and possible revenge from its own people. As the inevitable approach es, the stakes get higher, and the Kremlin regime increasingly finds itself cornered.

How much more Ukrainian civilian lives will be sacrificed on Russia’s war altar? How many people will be tortured, sexually assaulted, thrown into dark dungeons, never to see the sunlight again? How many children will be illegally separated from their parents and sent to Russia to suffer indoctrination?

We do not know the answers, yet we must all feel the deep pain brought by this brutal and pointless war. And we all should join our forces to draw Ukraine’s victory closer.

For it is only Ukraine’s final victory, safeguarding its sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, that could ensure the global peace, security, and the credibility of the United Nations charter.

What we cannot allow is a brute force prevailing over international law. We cannot tolerate any longer Moscow’s colonial aspirations, which undermine global food security and driving up food prices.

Russia’s imperial ambitions reach far into Europe, Africa, and Asia. No country should consider itself immune from this threat.

Naturally, Lithuania witnesses many dangers up close. In recent months,

Russia’s war of aggression has led to numerous violations of our air space by combat drones. Russia has also intensified hybrid attacks, disinformation, and sabotage efforts.

Where Russia advances, opening Pandora’s box of new techniques for destabilization, other hostile actors follow, learning new skills and ideas.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Attacks on information integrity pose an especially troubling challenge to every society. Disinformation, foreign information manipulation and interference, and the falsification of history erode trust, restrict civic space, and target journalists and human rights defenders. As a result, human rights, democracy, and security suffer.

This risk is further enhanced by the development of artificial intelligence. As we all know, AI has a huge potential for transformation, especially in the field of economy. Whole sectors, including those related to defence and security, might get radically changed or destroyed almost overnight. As any instrument, AI is also increasingly used by those seeking to cause harm and destruction.

Lithuania strongly believes that the future of AI must not be determined by authoritarian control, technological coercion, or the malicious use of data.

We are therefore investing in trusted AI capabilities, promoting responsible AI deployment, and advancing the Vilnius Convention – the world’s first legally binding international treaty on artificial intelligence.

By demonstrating how shared principles can be translated into concrete legal commitments, we hope to contribute significantly to the United Nations Global Dialogue on AI Governance.

Lithuania invites the international community to unite in addressing significant legal, ethical, and strategic challenges posed by artificial intelligence. With even major technology companies sending warning signals that control of AI might slip out of humanity’s hands, the time is ripe for collective action.

Together, we must ensure that AI serves human dignity, sustainable development, and international security, rather than becoming a new instrument of inequality, manipulation, or conflict. At any cost, human accountability, international law, and peace and security must be safeguarded.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

The credibility of the United Nations depends on its ability to respond firmly to aggression, unlawful conquest, forced deportations, and crimes against humanity, and also to coordinate the global response to the growth of AI.

If we are serious about preserving peace, we must defend justice and strongly support those fighting for their freedom.

I am grateful to the Secretary General, His Excellency António Guterres, for his long-lasting service and his focus on reforming the United Nations into a more effective, modern, and responsive organization.

This is the correct path to follow. There is no other way. No nation can confront today’s challenges alone. Aggression cannot win. It is only through multilateralism, solidarity, and the unity of all Member States that we can uphold peace, security, and the rules-based international order.

It is also important to learn from the many lessons of history. Today, too many seem unwilling to recognize and confront the past crimes committed by totalitarian regimes, including Soviet crimes.

This is a fundamental flaw. We must remember the past so as not to repeat it!

That is why Lithuania is promoting the concept of historical remembrance.

My personal wish is to see the Pan-European Memorial to all victims of the 20th century totalitarian regimes unveiled in Brussels as soon as possible.

There is one lesson Lithuania, having survived and overcome numerous occupations and waves of repression, can share with the international community. Freedom can be delayed, but it cannot be extinguished; justice can be challenged, but it cannot be defeated.

This, I believe, is a message that goes far beyond an experience of a single person, or a nation. It speaks to the whole humankind, united in our shared dignity.

At a time of growing global uncertainty and power politics, we need even more multilateralism grounded in international law, the UN Charter, and universal human rights. We need to resist the law of the strongest collectively, in order not to fall under the yoke separately.

The time to act is now. And I believe – I want to believe – that we have what it takes to make the world a more just, secure, and peaceful place to live!

Thank you.

Mr President, Mr Secretary-General, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

Former Secretary-General Kofi Annan once said: “Whatever our differences, [...] we stand or fall together. ” When we forget this, disorder is what happens.

Last year, from this very podium, I stated that foreign policy is based on three pillars: values, interests, and power.

This year, I come with something simpler. A choice. Co-operation or conflict.

In today’s world, co-operation is undermined by a lack of trust, disregard for rules, and the weakening of institutions.

Conflicts are spreading, bringing suffering, violence, and injustice.

According to some accounts, there are currently 65 active armed conflicts – more than at any time since the end of the Cold War.

Competition will always be there. Nations compete now harder than they did a generation ago. That doesn’t worry me. What does, is that more and more of them now compete against the rules on which the international order rests.

So, this speech defends the rules. And it calls for co-operation. Small nations need it to survive. Large nations need it to stay great.

Upholding the most basic rules, values and institutions is our best option to ensure that competition does not escalate into conflict. And that co-operation gains ground.

Now, I want to begin by analysing how the world is changing today. And as a pragmatic Finn, I will always try to deal with the world as it is, because it often helps in building a world that I wish we would have. In other words, a world we can build together.

I will then make a few suggestions about what we should do next.

*** We should all be steadfast defenders of multilateralism. As Strobe Talbott reportedly remarked, multilateralism is hell, and can be a real pain in the neck. But it is the best option for humanity as a whole.

We need multilateralism in order to address our shared agenda, ranging from armed conflicts and climate change to sustainable development and artificial intelligence.

Currently, however, we seem to be going the other way: towards a non-cooperative multipolar world order.

This order, as it turns out, is based on zero-sum deals, transactions, and unrestrained power. This is a short-sighted approach.

Tempting as it may be for some, such a multipolar order will ultimately lead to conflict. It will turn against us, whether you represent a great power, a middle power, or a small state, like Finland.

Between these two approaches, there is a third option: plurilateralism. It means building ad hoc coalitions when global co-operation is unattainable.

And this is my first observation today: the emergence of flexible forms of co-operation around different themes and interests. Be it in the economy, climate, defence, or technology.

Coalition-building can be a force for good. But with one condition: it should not challenge multilateralism, but build on it. It should support the UN system, not substitute it.

The Coalition of the Willing for Ukraine is particularly close to my heart. It is a group of countries working to end Russia’s war of aggression. The war is unlawful, unjustified and unprovoked. Its solution will have far-reaching consequences for Ukraine and beyond.

The Coalition works for a just and lasting peace in Ukraine in accordance with the UN Charter. It seeks to uphold the basic tenets of the international order.

My second observation is that everywhere I travel, I hear the word ‘realignment’.

Whether it is in Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Asia, or the Americas, nations are seeking new alliances and partnerships.

This is a logical consequence in times of uncertainty and transformation. You seek security where you can get it.

We are seeing an intensification of regional integration akin to what we saw in the immediate aftermath of World War II.

Regional organizations like the African Union, Gulf Cooperation Council, Mercosur, ASEAN or the EU build trust.

When integration is not feasible, other forms of co-operation can prove essential. We Finns are happy to point to the historic signing of the Helsinki Final Act in 1975. It brought together 35 nations in the midst of the Cold War and laid the foundations for what would later become the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe.

There was no trust. There were deep disagreements. And outright hostility. Yet there was room for a process that reduced tensions and built common ground.

I believe regions, such as the Middle East, where conflicts are raging today, may consider something similar.

Even in the face of conflict and grievance, a region may be able to agree on principles that foster cooperation and prevent further conflict.

My third observation is that a new economic world order is taking shape.

Instruments once used for economic integration – including trade, technology, energy, investment, and supply chains – have become instruments of geopolitical competition.

There was perhaps, at times, a naïve belief that interdependence would bring about stability and peace. Now, the focus on opportunities has been replaced by the focus on threats.

We have entered a world of coercion, where dependencies are vulnerabilities. Countries seek chokepoints that can be weaponized to pressure others.

But dependencies are complex. No nation, not even the biggest ones, can go it alone. All coercive actions come at a cost.

And even if a mightier state dominates in one domain, a smaller state can respond in another.

In the new geopolitical environment, the economic order of the post-World War II era is seeking new forms.

The new order must be based on a realistic understanding of the power balance in the world.

We in the West must acknowledge that the Global South and East are an expanding economic and political force.

Many nations around the world have made remarkable advances in competence and know-how. We should put this collective expertise to work for the global common good.

Countries are right to be wary of dangerous dependencies. But our focus on threats should not lead us to abandon co-operation.

We should strive for an economic world order built on institutions and agreements. Multilateralism is also needed in the global economy.

*** It is all well and good to diagnose the problem: too many nations now compete at the expense of basic rules, and that is why the world has slipped into disorder.

But it matters more to find a prescription which would bring us back to order, stability and cooperation.

Thus, I will offer you three remedies for a world in disorder. To begin with, we need to go back to the basics of international law.

On my recent visit to India, I came across a quote from Mahatma Gandhi: “The breach of one rule inevitably leads to the breach of other rules”. These words resonate all too strongly today.

We have moved back to a world defined by raw power and narrow self-interest.

Rules and values seem to be taking a back seat. Some are ready to throw in the towel, prepared to accept the defeat of the international rules-based order.

That is an exaggeration. International law has been questioned and challenged before. It has never been a perfect system.

But we must admit that we are at a critical juncture. Fundamental norms are being questioned in a way that erodes confidence in the entire multilateral system.

Therefore, the first remedy for a world in disorder is rule of law.

Today, international norms are often presented as an obstacle to the pursuit of national interests. This is both wrong and dangerous.

International law has never been merely an effort to achieve universal justice, but neither can it be reduced to a mere instrument of domination.

It is not only about values, nor only about interests, but about both.

Despite the rhetoric, no major power is likely to give up its ability to shape the rules.

Even when actors claim to abandon rules, they rather seek to replace existing rules with ones more to their liking.

Therefore, we will not face a world without rules. But we could be facing a world with less predictability, less restraint – a world based on rules that are more permissive for the powerful.

For the collective benefit of the nations in this Hall, we should continue to defend the rule of law and uphold its most fundamental principles. They include the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of nations; freedom of navigation at sea; and accountability for the most serious international crimes.

The second remedy is about humanitarian principles.

The world today has an unprecedented capacity to meet humanity’s most pressing needs.

Since the establishment of the United Nations, poverty has declined, access to basic education has expanded, literacy has increased, and child mortality has fallen.

Yet, we are witnessing tyranny, disregard for the vulnerable, and violence against civilians in many parts of the world. Poverty and distress are still widespread.

For example, Sudan is devastated by war. Millions have been displaced, and many face famine.

Gaza continues to be one of the world’s most acute humanitarian emergencies, marked by mass displacement, the destruction of infrastructure and a lack of essential services.

Haiti struggles with armed violence and extreme weather events, causing a displacement crisis, a hunger crisis, and a health crisis.

We must not grow indifferent to wars and human suffering, but instead channel our efforts into preventing conflicts, upholding human rights, and strengthening sustainable economies.

Our growing material prosperity should not come at the expense of our ethical responsibilities.

The third remedy is about language and the way we treat each other.

Unfortunately, there is no shortage of examples of those who use dismissive language to describe others and entire groups of people.

Too often, those with the most provocative rhetoric receive the greatest visibility.

Provocation is rewarded with attention. Excess is misinterpreted as courage. Exaggeration as the truth.

Language can foster co-operation, but it can also break trust and turn competition into conflict.

The recipe is simple, but necessary: avoid polarization, strengthen trust, and listen to others.

We need dignified foreign policy. And that starts here, at the United Nations.

*** Ladies and Gentlemen,

I would like to thank Secretary-General Guterres for his service and his dedication to reforming and rationalising the UN system. This work must continue.

Every Secretary-General is shaped both by their era and by their own actions.

I was reminded of this recently when reading the biographies of former Secretaries-General U-Thant and Kofi Annan, both highly influential leaders who navigated an era of great-power tensions.

Let me put forward a few suggestions for the new Secretary-General’s consideration, whoever she may be, and for the international community at large.

Since my first speech here two years ago, I have consistently called for a reformed Security Council.

The world has changed, so should the UN.

There should be, at least, two new permanent seats for Africa, two for Asia-Pacific and one for Latin America.

No single state should have veto power. And, if a member of the Security Council violates the UN Charter, its voting rights should be suspended.

The world needs a functioning UN Security Council. To move forward, we need to break the impasse and be open for creative solutions.

The need for reform also extends to the global economic architecture. It, too, must be updated to reflect today’s power balance.

We have to make sure international economic co-operation continues to be rules-based, legitimate, and representative. Multilateral solutions are needed in an increasingly multipolar world.

We must also bring the United Nations back to peace mediation. The Secretary-General, as MediatorIn-Chief, will have a key role.

The UN’s legitimacy as a mediator is unique. Together, the UN and its Member States can accomplish what neither can achieve alone.

The UN needs to be at the centre of rule-making and institution-building. Regional integration and thematic coalitions can and should support it.

Artificial intelligence is the most consequential technology in the history of mankind. It will impact science, the economy, politics, security, and the very essence of our humanity.

Humans can and should be in the driver’s seat. We have a choice: we can compete, co-operate or slow down. For me, co-operation is the best way forward.

This is why Norway and Finland have, together with leaders from nations around the world, launched a call for companies, governments, regional organisations and the UN to develop mechanisms to control frontier models of AI.

My country, Finland, wants the United Nations to succeed and will remain strongly engaged in its work.

Therefore, we are standing for election to the Security Council from 2029 to 2030.

We are motivated by our belief in the UN Charter and the values it stands for. We will prioritize peace, people, and partnerships.

We are willing to take on the responsibility of the Council membership at a time that calls for more peace. We want people and nations to thrive. We believe in dialogue and co-operation.

Finally, let me make a procedural proposal. The foundations of the United Nations were built in San Francisco over 80 years ago.

Today, we must restore balance to the world order. We must recommit to the fundamental principles of the international order. And we must embrace co-operation over conflict.

What the world needs now, is a new San Francisco moment. A moment where world leaders come together to chart the way forward. A process to achieve this should start with the new SecretaryGeneral.

Thank you.

Madam president, excellencies, first and foremost, allow me to extend my warmest congratulations to His Excellency Doctor Khalilur Rahman on his election as president of the General Assembly.

He can certainly count on Luxembourg's full support throughout his tenure.
Madam president, the theme that has been chosen for this general debate can hardly be more timely.
When I try to paint an honest picture of the world we live in, one thing strikes me in particular trust is under growing strain.
Trust between nations, trust between people, and, perhaps most importantly, trust in our ability to work together.

And yet, I believe that trust is precisely where we should begin Not because trust is easy, but because every lasting achievement of the international community has begun with a decision to trust.
This is my first address to this Assembly as Head of State of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, I assumed office less than a year ago.
It is therefore a particular honor to stand before you today and to reaffirm from this podium the importance Luxembourg attaches to the United Nations and to a rule based international order grounded in the rule of law.
But this moment also makes me reflect on what the United Nations means from the perspective of my own generation.

As a relatively young man who has had the privilege of traveling the world, I have been fortunate to meet people from very different cultures, backgrounds, and traditions.
These experiences have left me with a simple and lasting conviction.
We can learn a lot from each other, and I remain convinced that it is only by working together that we can overcome the many challenges our world is facing today.
This conviction is not naive.

I am fully aware of the difficulties confronting us, but precisely because the world is becoming more difficult, I believe we must resist the temptation to give up on cooperation.
There has never been a time when communication between people in different parts of the world was so easy.
Millions of young people have virtual friends and acquaintances across continents through social media, gaming, and countless other forms of connection.
We have never been so connected, and yet we seem increasingly unable to trust one another.

This should make us reflect.
Is it still possible to build a world order in which respect and the willingness to work towards common goals can prevail over the pursuit of self-interest and power?
I believe it is, but it will require determination, dialogue and a willingness to look beyond immediate interest.
And this is why the United Nations matters.

Madam Presidents.
Luxembourg has believed in this principle from the very beginning.
81 years ago, still deeply marked by the horrors of the Second World War Luxembourg was among the 51 founding members that came together in San Francisco to lay the foundations of a new international order.
At the time, we were the smallest country represented.

We have prospered in the peace that Europe enjoyed for decades after 1945, and we have never forgotten that the peace could not be taken for granted.
It was built generation after generation by those who chose cooperation over confrontation.
Today, that peace is being challenged once again.
Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine has brought war back to our continent.

It is a stark reminder that peace requires constant commitment, and that the principles on which our international order was built must be defended.
The United Nations itself was born from that choice.
Its charter called upon us to unite our strength to maintain international peace and security, and above all, to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.
81 years later, that promise is under considerable pressure, but it has not failed.

Multilateralism may be imperfect, but disenchantment should lead us to reform, not to dismissal.
The question is, therefore, not whether we still need multilateralism.
The question is whether we have the courage to make it better.
Madam president.

Madam president, this brings me to a question that is very dear to my heart.
What kind of world do we want to bequeath to future generations?
We often talk about young people as if they came from the future.
Truth be told, they are already shaping the present.

Therefore, it is incumbent upon us to ask ourselves if we're really preparing a future that is going to earn their trust.
My personal experience has done nothing but reinforce this conviction.
This year I had the privilege of succeeding His Majesty King Carl Gustaf of Sweden as honorary chair of the World Scout Foundation.
My long standing commitment to the Scout movement has taught me a great deal about the power of intergenerational dialogue, solidarity, and the values of the Scout movement.

It's also taught me something absolutely fundamental.
Placing our trust in young people means giving them responsibilities, allowing them to take action.
They are growing up in a world in which there are extraordinary possibilities.
But it's also a world where uncertainty runs deep.

Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are already transforming our way of life and the way in which we work.
The enthusiasm they give rise to also goes hand in hand with the very real concerns, the current debates about the most extreme risks of AI remind us that technological progress cannot be divorced from responsibility.
As we confront these transformations, we should endow our young people with the means to develop their critical thinking skills and their creativity.
And this is exactly what education is supposed to do transmit knowledge and competencies, but also to teach young people to call things into question, to open up to others and to shoulder your responsibilities.

Against this backdrop, I believe that we should have one guiding principle.
Human beings should be at the heart of all of our decision making.
We must protect the rights, security, and the well-being of all.
We should also listen to young people, ask them what we can build, working hand in hand through different cultures and generations.

I saw for myself everything that young people are capable of accomplishing.
When we give them our trust, we give them responsibilities and the necessary space to take action, as well as when we encourage them to work together This is why Luxembourg supports the UN's youth delegate programme, as well as the United Nations Youth Office.
It is also why our commitment to education, science and culture remains so important, in particular through our term on the Executive Board of Unesco for the period 2025 2029.
It is precisely these qualities which allow trust to flourish.

Madam president, Luxembourg's commitment to the United Nations is underpinned by all three pillars peace and security, human rights and development.
Solidarity must be translated into deeds.
We continue to allocate 1% of our national income to development cooperation.
We're also building long term partnerships with vulnerable countries.

We remain committed to the multilateral humanitarian system, as well as to all those who are providing assistance where it is most needed.
The same level of responsibility applies to peace and security.
Conflicts affect all human beings women, children, older persons, persons with disabilities, as well as people who are already vulnerable.
Protecting civilians and defending human rights cannot take a back seat to other considerations.

Luxembourg has Unstintingly worked to contribute to this effort through peacekeeping operations humanitarian interventions protecting children affected by armed conflict, the women peace and security agenda, as well as the mine clearance humanitarian activities in Ukraine.
The experience we gained as an elected member of the Security Council in 2013 and 2014 showed us that elected members can make a real difference, especially when the permanent members of the Security Council are divided.
It is for this reason that Luxembourg is asking for member states to place their trust in it, as it seeks a Security Council seat for the 2031 2032 period.
We do this humbly, but firm in our conviction, our conviction that a small country can offer up a different perspective, can bring different positions closer together and help find common ground.

When this is particularly difficult, it is the same conviction which guides our commitment to human rights at a time when respect for human rights is being subjected to growing pressures, we must resist the temptation to see it as something that's up for discussion.
Human rights are neither a privilege reserved for the few, nor the expression of one culture, of one political system.
They are the very bedrock of human dignity.
Our commitment is also concrete.

As a member of the Human Rights Council for the period 2022 2024, Luxembourg took the full measure of just how important it is to defend human rights through multilateralism.
We continue to support the office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, as well as efforts aimed at clarifying the fate of persons who were disappeared in Syria.
Madam president.
Restoring trust also means making our institutions worthy of that trust.

The Security Council must become more representative, more effective, and more accountable to the entire membership of the United Nations.
Africa in particular, and it was said many times today, should have a stronger voice.
And when the Security Council is paralysed.
The General Assembly must be able to play its rightful role.

The United Nations must reform so that it can deliver more effectively, particularly when resources are constrained.
But reform must never become an end in itself.
The purpose of institutions is to serve people Ultimately, the test of multilateralism is not how many resolutions we adopt or how many meetings we hold.
It's whether a child is safer because of our decisions.

Whether a young person can receive an education, whether a family can live in dignity, whether a small country can believe that international law will protect it when power alone cannot.
This is why trust matters, and this is why Luxembourg will continue to defend multilateralism.
Because we know what happens when it fails.
Madam president, climate change reminds us, perhaps more clearly than any other challenge, that we cannot solve global problems by acting alone.

It transcends borders and generations.
Small island developing states are already experiencing consequences that threaten their very existence.
Luxembourg may be landlocked, but we are deeply committed to this common effort, including by drawing on the expertise of our financial centre in green finance.
Our interests may differ, but our future is shared.

Madam president, the world is becoming more fragmented.
The international order is under strain.
We need to recognise this reality.
But we should not mistake a world of competing centres of power for a more just or stable international order.

For Luxembourg, the answer is clear Our experience has taught us that international law and multilateral institutions give countries, whatever their size, a voice and place at the table.
It is not about resisting a changing world, but to make multilateralism fit for that world.
I believe this is ultimately what the United Nations asks of us, not that we agree on everything, not that we abandon our national interests, but that we recognise that there are challenges for which no nation, however powerful, can find lasting solutions alone.
We can look at the imperfections of multilateralism and conclude that it no longer works, or we can reform it fairly, strengthen it, and make it worthy of the trust that future generations will place in us.

I know which choice I want to make, because this is the world I want to leave to my children.
A world where dialogue is stronger than confrontation, where respect between nations allows differences to become sources of strength rather than division.
Where international law protects weeks, protects the weak as well as the strong.
If we restore trust, if we listen to the next generation, and if we have the courage to act together, the United Nations can continue to be more than a reflection of the world as it is.

It can remain an instrument for building the world we want to leave behind a world worthy of the trust of those who will inherit it.
Young people do not expect us to solve every challenge, but they do expect us to try.
They expect us to act with responsibility.
And above all, they expect us not to lose faith in our ability to shape a better future.

And that is the promise we should make to the next generation.
Thank you.

Your Excellencies, Heads of State and Government,

Distinguished Delegates,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Allow me to congratulate His Excellency Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the Eighty -first Session of the United Nations General Assembly, in the hope that, with his vast experience and profound knowledge of our international organization, he will render valuable service to the United Nations, which faces complex challenges that must be overcome in order to resume its central role in addressing the major issues of contemporary international relations.

I also congratulate Ms. Annalena Baerbock, who preceded you in the discharge of these noble duties and spared no effort, during the term she carried out with undeniable competence, to preserve the role of the United Nations in addressing the issues that most concern the international community today.

I would also like to congratulate His Excellency the Secretary-General, António Guterres, who has been working tirelessly and devoting himself with persistent dedication to the great global causes, building bridges for dialogue in the search for peaceful solutions to the problems facing humanity today.

We highlight his exemplary contribution as a man of dialogue, an advocate of the United Nations Charter and of International Law, a tireless advocate of the need to protect the planet from the harmful effects of climate change, and a champion of the global debate on the global governance of artificial intelligence.

Mr. President,

Excellencies,

The United Nations General Assembly is always held in the month of September; this year's session, however, takes place 25 years after the terrorist act that destroyed the twin towers in New York and struck other targets on American territory, causing thousands of civilian deaths and injuries, some of whom continue to bear physical and emotional scars to this day.

I take this opportunity once again to condemn terrorism in all its forms, wherever it occurs. In addition to terrorism, which remains active in some countries, particularly in Africa, the situation of global peace and security has been worsening year after year, bringing us to the present moment, in which we note with deep concern that the world has taken a course that brings it alarmingly close to a global conflict.

Over the years, Angola has sought to make its contribution to the building and consolidation of peace in Africa and in the world, but the current situation in no way reflects the aspirations of peoples for harmony and understanding among nations.

Among these contributions to peace are several initiatives undertaken in Africa, of which I highlight the “ 21st Extraordinary Conference of the African Union on Strengthening Conflict Prevention and Resolution Mechanisms in Africa”, recently held in Luanda, which opened a serious and sound prospect for resolving the problems affecting peace and stability on the African continent.

Also deserving particular attention is the holding, in July of this year in Luanda, in partnership with the United Nations Alliance of Civilizations, of the Third Edition of the “Initiative Call for Peace, an End to Wars and Respect for International Law”.

In this same context, Angola will host next October the “Pan-African Forum for the Culture of Peace and Non Violence, Luanda Biennale”.

My country takes seriously our commitment to matters concerning peace, the conflicts resolution through dialogue, respect for the norms governing international relations and the defence of International Law, sparing no effort to bringing the conflicting parties closer together and build consensus in Africa.

We remain available to render our attention and contribution to resolving the conflicts that persist on the continent.

Our paradigm for peacebuilding initiatives is based on the search for realistic and sustainable solutions, within the principle of African solutions to conflicts in Africa.

We call for the eff ective implementation of Security Council Resolution 2719, which must ensure predictable, adequate and sustainable financing for African Union -led peace support operations authorized by the United Nations Security Council, because investing in Africa’s capacity to prevent and resolve conflicts is also an investment in international peace and security.

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

This session of the General Assembly is of particular significance to my country, as it is taking place in the year in which we celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of the Republic of Angola’s admission as a full member of the United Nations Organization, in December 1976.

At that time, it was a historic achievement for the Angolan people, who waited more than twelve months from the date of the proclamation of their National Independence for the country to be accepted as a full -fledged member of the international community.

That event, of great significance for the history of my country, took place in a global context in which Angola became a victim of confrontation between the world powers, in the struggle for control of spheres of influence within the spirit of the Cold War.

Our entire journey towards the attainment of peace in 2002 was closely linked to the disputes of that period, which hampered the fulfilment of the dreams of Angolans and their plans to build a prosperous nation committed to its development.

These facts belong to the past, but they have left us with a wealth of experience and lessons that we have drawn upon to build peace, understanding and reconciliation among all Angolans and to chart the course of our foreign policy.

Peace and national reconciliation is now a reality, as shown demonstrated through concrete gestures, including the holding of award ceremonies honouring the main political leaders of the national liberation struggle and representative members of all segments of civil society, within the framework of the 50 th anniversary of National Independence.

Still within this framework, a monument in memory of all victims of the political conflicts that occurred in Angola, from the proclamation of National Independence until the achievement of peace in April 2002, will be inaugurated next October in Luanda.

Mr. President,

Excellencies,

In our time, we are witnessing a downgrading and violation of the rules governing international relations, with the logic of force, intimidation and the imposition of values stemming from the unilateral vision of certain countries prevailing in the defence of their exclusive interests.

Instability being experienced in various regions of our planet is a direct consequence of this stance, as it can be seen in the conflicts currently unfolding in Europe, the Middle East, the Persian Gulf and Africa, while tension is mounting in the Asia-Pacific region.

From what we have observed, we do not discern encouraging signs regarding the likelihood of reaching any peace agreement in the near future in the wars between Russia and Ukraine, in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict in the Middle East and in the Persian Gulf.

We condemn the genocide against defenceless populations, the elderly, women, children, bedridden patients, health professionals, journalists and workers of international humanitarian organizations, who are often deprived of access to the most basic human rights and to essential goods for life, such as water, food and medicines.

The expulsion of the Palestinians from their homes and lands through the expansion of Jewish settlements in the West Bank must elicit the strongest international outrage and condemnation.

Attempts to dominate entire countries and regions of the globe by force of arms are leading the world towards catastrophe.

The food security, energy and humanitarian situation of countries and of the world in general has deteriorated considerably following the outbreak of the wars against Ukraine and, more recently, against Iran.

The toll of the wars is disastrous, judging by the consequences arising from the strangulation of freedom of maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, a situation that has created a serious risk of disruption to logistics supply chains in general, and to food and energy supply chains in particular, with devastating effects on the most vulnerable countries.

Today, we live in an environment of global anarchy in which the use of force prevails over the force of reason and of law, in blatant opposition to the norms governing international relations.

In view of this, there is every need for profound reflection within the United Nations, the only institution on the planet with legitimacy and which brings together all the nations of the world, in order to find the best solutions for achieving global peace.

Our appeal is for us to act with wisdom and courage to restore the central role of the United Nations in its responsibility and irreplaceable mission in maintaining world peace.

Ladies and Gentlemen We are concerned by the unjust manner, indicative of great human insensitivity, in which Cuba has been treated over decades, as a victim of an embargo that continues and worsens the living conditions of the Cuban people.

Cuba is not a terrorist State; it neither produces nor possesses nuclear weapons, chemical or bacteriological weapons that could constitute an imminent or real threat to the national security of other countries, including neighbouring countries.

On the contrary, Cuba contributed to the fall of South Africa’s racist and segregationist apartheid regime, a regime broadly and unanimously condemned by the international community and consequently became one of the signatories to the Quadripartite Agreements of New York of 22 December 1988.

As the embargo is chiefly responsible for the calamitous situation in which Cuba and the Cuban people find themselves, and since it is inhumane, unfair and violates all the principles and norms of International Law, we once again call for an end to the embargo against Cuba.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Today, we are witnessing the direct involvement of certain permanent members of the United Nations Security Council in the bloodiest and most destructive conflicts of our time in Europe and the Persian Gulf, which is a cause for concern and a bad example for the rest of the world.

Those countries rendered a great service when they freed humanity from the horrors of Nazism, fascism and the Holocaust, and should therefore preserve that capital and legacy as liberators.

At a time when good governance of countries is widely advocated, the governance of the world likewise calls for a new, more democratic and just world order, one that is not based solely on the power of the restricted club of victors of a war that took place eight decades ago.

Since then, the World has come to know a different reality: new countries have emerged, which at the time were colonies and which today are strong economies with significant advances in science and technology.

It is therefore becoming increasingly pressing and urgent to undertake a profound reform of the United Nations Security Council, in which Africa, Latin America and Asia should be adequately represented as permanent members with all the powers inherent therein.

In this context, the Republic of Angola reaffirms its full support for the common African position enshrined in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration.

The voice of Africans must be heard in all circumstances, at all times, in strategic decision -making processes on issues of peace, global security, financing for development, as well as climate issues and the global governance of artificial intelligence.

Mr. President,

Excellencies,

Peace and development are inseparable, which compels us to consider strategies that can help accelerate the implementation of the 2030 Agenda.

The important decisions adopted under the Pact for the Future and the Seville Commitment can help advance development programmes in Africa.

However, in order to achieve concrete results in this area, it is essential to ensure affordable financing, debt relief, technology transfer, capacity -building and greater participation in international financial institutions.

African countries spend far more resources on the exorbitant costs of debt servicing than they are able to invest in health, education and infrastructure development programmes.

This situation obviously limits productive investment, deepens inequalities and economic disparities, and threatens economic and social stability.

In view of this, it is imperative to correct these distortions, and I therefore reiterate the call for the immediate reform of the international financial architecture, in order to make it fairer, more equitable, democratic and geared towards the progress and well-being of humankind.

These challenges are inherently complex and are further exacerbated by climate change, which has a severe impact on Africa, with severe and prolonged droughts, floods, desertification, food insecurity and population displacement.

This situation clearly illustrates the need to establish predictable, affordable and additional climate financing, without further aggravating the debt of developing countries.

Today, peoples and nations have an opportunity to make a qualitative leap in their overall living conditions, through fair mechanisms to support development and the tools that artificial intelligence provides to improve education, health, agriculture, public services, scientific research and economic productivity.

In this regard, I consider that the Global Digital Compact opens new prospects for cooperation to bridge the digital divide, expand digital public infrastructure, promote training and innovation, strengthen cybersecurity and build more inclusive, secure and human -centred governance of artificial intelligence.

To that end, I believe there is a need to strengthen North South, South-South and triangular cooperation, in order to make the digital revolution an instrument of inclusion, sovereignty and development, rather than a source of dependence and inequality.

Excellencies,

We are drawing close to the end of the tenure of the current Secretary-General and the appointment of the next one, an act of great importance, given that the person chosen must possess the qualities of independence, integrity, competence and courage to build consensus, uphold the Charter, promote conflict prevention, lead the necessary reforms and seek solutions to address the Organization’s financial crisis.

The Republic of Angola reaffirms its commitment to the United Nations, convinced that only at the level of this institution will it be possible to safeguard the achievements of recent decades in respect for International Law.

Only within the framework of the United Nations can we make progress in seeking peaceful solutions to the conflicts ravaging the world, within a framework in which multilateralism serves as the mechanism for bringing together ideas, political will and initiatives conducive to global peace.

We, political leaders and rulers of today, will be judged in the future by our ability to replace confrontation with dialogue, predatory competition with cooperation, exclusion with solidarity and the force of arms with the force of law.

Only in this way will we build a more just, peaceful and inclusive international order, capable of ensuring progress and well-being of humankind, leaving no one behind.

No weapon is more powerful than diplomacy, since all others are used only to destroy lives, infrastructure, dreams and life plans, whereas diplomacy is the only weapon that exists to unite, repair, build and save lives, peoples, nations and humanity.

For this reason, the United Nations Organization must equip itself with the appropriate tools and means to fulfil the theme of this 81 st session of its General Assembly, namely, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation and Empowering It to Become an Organization That Delivers for All”.

Thank you very much for your attention.
