Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Distinguished delegates,

Ladies and gentlemen,

At the outset, I wish to extend my sincere congratulations to Mr. Khalilur Rahman on assuming the important role of the President of the eighty-first session of the United Nations General Assembly and to convey my best wishes for the successful session.

This session of the General Assembly is convening on the eve of the 65th anniversary of Mongolia’s full-fledged membership in the United Nations.

In 1961, Mongolia made history by raising its national flag with the golden Soyombo at the United Nations and becoming the 101st member of the United Nations, the guarantor of global peace and security and the beacon of hope and trust for the world's nations.

Mongolia welcomes the convening of the eighty-first session of the United Nations General Assembly under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All,” reaffirming its belief in the central role of the United Nations in fostering mutual trust, mutual respect, and cooperation among the nations and peoples of the world.

Mongols say, “If you do your best, fate will do the rest.”

The United Nations is an organization based on the trust and commitment of each Member State, and the UN is strengthened by their dedication and sustained efforts.

Therefore, it is incumbent upon us, Member States, to uphold the mission of the United Nations with a sincere heart. Rather than simply expecting support and assistance, we must remain deeply conscious of our own responsibilities and duties and dedicate our wholehearted efforts to strengthening the United Nations.

It is through trust and hope, dedication and commitment, and engagement and participation of every Member State, that we can strengthen the United Nations. A stronger United Nations, in turn, will deliver more efficiently towards global peace, security, and sustainable development, thereby creating conditions for all Member States to benefit.

As the conflicts and confrontations flash across the world, the walls of distrust rise higher, and the chasm of misunderstanding grows deeper, it is becoming crucial to shape and develop international relations not through a form of multi-polarity that risks driving the world toward division, but through a multi-pillared principle that respects the pluralism inherent in each nation's history, culture, civilization, core national interests, and chosen path of development.

Eight centuries ago, our ancestors established the great "Pax Mongolica," promoting, for the first time, the idea to the world that nations could mutually recognize one another's values and that peoples of diverse civilizations and faiths could coexist. This historic contribution of the Mongols to the advancement of humankind continues to be recognized by the international community.

Let us strengthen multilateral cooperation through the multi-pillar principle inspired by the ideas of "Pax Mongolica," so that we may restore our trust and hope through shared responsibility, reform the United Nations with a common purpose, and build a better, more peaceful world through the strength of our collective action.

Mr. President,

Despite the remarkable heights of development and progress humanity has reached, our planet is currently confronted with more than 90 armed conflicts, around 30 of which are international, demonstrating that global peace and security remain unstable and th at geopolitical and geostrategic competition continues to intensify.

This results in the disruption of global economic supply chains, a rise in thein the prices of energy, fuel, raw materials, and food, as well as economic strains on nations around the world.

All of this is weakening the international order established since the Second World War, changing the universally recognized norms of international law, and undermining the stability of multilateral relations and cooperation.

Mongolia shares the view expressed by United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres in his Annual Report on the Work of the Organization that in a world marked by turbulence, division and uncertainty, the United Nations is more necessary than ever.

Hence, Mongolia underscores the tangible progress made under Secretary-General’s UN80 initiative to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of the United Nations in response to the challenges of our time, and reaffirms its active support for this initiative.

The effectiveness of the United Nations, the decisiveness of its actions, and the ability of nations to unite their efforts will ultimately depend upon us, the Member States.

Mongolia is confident that the soon-to-be-appointed Secretary-General will steadfastly uphold the purposes and principles of the United Nations and international law, ensure that the voices and positions of all Member States are equally heard and reflected, and provide strong leadership in restoring trust and managing transformation within the United Nations.

Believing that reform of the Security Council should be at the core of broader United Nations reform, Mongolia maintains its principled position in support of expanding the number of both permanent and non-permanent members of the Security Council, ensuring equitable representation of developing countries in the Council, and promoting greater openness and transparency in its work.

Mongolia is one of the 58 countries that have never served as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council.

Therefore, Mongolia aspires to actively participate in the work of the Security Council and contribute to finding collective solutions to the problems and challenges facing the international community.

In manifestation of this aspiration, I officially announce from this rostrum today that Mongolia is presenting its candidature for a non-permanent seat of the UN Security Council for the term 2048-2049.

Mr. President,

On behalf of the people of Mongolia, I extend my heartfelt gratitude to the United Nations and its system organizations for their valuable contributions to our country’s development and progress and their longstanding constructive cooperation over the 65 years since Mongolia’s accession to the United Nations as a full-fledged member.

Mongolia has been contributing with honor to the efforts on strengthening international peace and security, advancing social and economic development, and protecting human rights - the core pillars of the United Nations.

For instance, more than three decades ago, in pursuit of its foreign policy to ensure national security through political and diplomatic means, Mongolia declared its territory nuclear-weapon-free.

Since then, Mongolia has consistently pursued policies and taken actions to verify this status legally. In this spirit, the United Nations General Assembly adopts, on a biennial basis, the resolution entitled "Mongolia's international security and nuclear-weapon-free status," initiated by Mongolia in 1998.

Furthermore, Mongolia has made tangible contributions to global efforts to maintain international peace and security through its active participation in United Nations Peacekeeping Operations and other international missions, having deployed more than 23,000 military and police personnel to hotspots around the world since 2002.Even today, our troops are serving in the "Gang Suppression Force" multinational police and military mission deployed to Haiti.

Mongolia has been actively advancing the implementation of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325, “Women, Peace and Security,” and has become one of the few countries to have reached 15 percent women’s representation among its military personnel serving in United Nations Peacekeeping Operations.

Since 2006, when Mongolia deployed its first female peacekeeper to the UN mission in Western Sahara, Mongolian women have made valuable contributions to global peace over the past two decades through their courage, resilience, and ingenuity.

In this connection, Mongolia plans to host the second international conference on "Women's Participation in UN Peacekeeping Operations" in Ulaanbaatar in 2027.

I am pleased to highlight Mongolia’s active leadership within the United Nations in advancing the interests of landlocked developing countries, drawing greater international attention to their special needs and unique circumstances, and cooperating with th ese countries to ensure that their voices are heard on the global stage.

Mongolia has launched several important initiatives in this regard, including serving as one of the founding members of the Group of Landlocked Developing Countries at the United Nations and the establishment of the International Think Tank for Landlocked Developing Countries in Ulaanbaatar.

To translate the Awaza Programme of Action into tangible outcomes, it is essential for landlocked developing countries to align the Programme with their national development agendas and make full use of available resources and opportunities to accelerate regional integration and cooperation.

We also call upon the international community, banks, financial institutions, and development partners to provide credible assistance to landlocked developing countries through their support and collaboration.

Mr. President,

As the deadline for the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development approaches, the 2026 SDG report shows that only 36 percent of the Sustainable Development Goals are on track or making moderate progress, while 15 percent are regressing.

It is deeply regrettable that, according to the latest report of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, released at this critical time, global military expenditure has reached an all-time high of 2.9 trillion USD.

It is time for all of us to ponder and reflect with common sense on what progress could have been achieved in the development of human society if this huge budget and funds had been spent on tackling pressing issues such as combating global warming and cli mate change, and improving education, health, food security, and advancement of women and children.

According to the Sustainable Development Report 2026, Mongolia has achieved 68.8 percent of the SDGs, reflecting the tangible results of our efforts and the progress we have made in recent years.

As a country experiencing the adverse impacts of climate change first-hand, Mongolia has remained steadfast in contributing to global collective efforts to protect and preserve our natural environment.

In this regard, Mongolia is successfully implementing a series of national policies and initiatives, including the “Billion Trees,” “Food Revolution,” “White Gold,” “Blue Gold,” and “Healthy Mongolian,” aimed at restoring degraded land, expanding forest resources, protecting soil, water and pastureland, ensuring food supply and security, and supporting sustainable rural development.

Mongolia’s “Billion Trees” National Movement goes far beyond tree planting and afforestation; it is a comprehensive, nationwide initiative aimed at combating desertification and land degradation, scaling up land restoration, expanding forest resources, protecting soil fertility, water resources and biodiversity, mitigating the adverse impacts of climate change, improving food supply, and creating employment opportunities.

Furthermore, the United Nations General Assembly resolution initiated by Mongolia proclaiming 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists provides an opportunity to raise global awareness of the importance of rangeland ecosystems, support the livelihoods of pastoralists, strengthen sustainable food systems, conserve biodiversity, and preserve the cultural heritage of nomadic peoples.

In this regard, Mongolia, with its millennia-old tradition of nomadic pastoralism, took the initiative to convene the Global Pastoralist Gathering and Conference in Ulaanbaatar.

The Gathering brought together around 400 herders from 57 countries, whose opinions and fruitful discussion of challenges and solutions culminated in the adoption of the Ulaanbaatar Declaration.

Moreover, in August, Mongolia successfully hosted the seventeenth session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification in Ulaanbaatar, under the theme “Restoring Land, Restoring Hope.”

Restoring Mother Nature to its pristine state and creating conditions for future generations to live in a healthy environment with confidence and contentment must be a noble duty of humanity.

Mother Nature and healthy soil are the guarantee of humanity's existence, and the foundation of food and water resources, livelihood, and sustainable development.

Healthy soil means healthy food, and healthy food means healthy people.

Therefore, desertification, land degradation, and drought should not be viewed merely as environmental issues but should be addressed holistically in connection with food supply and security, water resources, livelihoods, sustainable development, and global peace and security.

In this spirit, as the Presidency of UNCCD COP17, Mongolia has advanced the Steppe Action Agenda, built upon three interconnected flagship initiatives: the Rangelands Flagship Initiative, the Water-Land Nexus Initiative, and the Nature-based Solutions for Sustainable Infrastructure Initiative.

Particularly, we regard the Rangelands Flagship Initiative as a landmark global movement that opens a new chapter in the history of rangeland conservation.

This initiative is special in raising global awareness that the protection, sustainable management, and restoration of rangelands are of strategic importance for building resilience to climate change, ensuring food security, and maintaining balanced ecosystems.

The nomadic way of life that we Mongols have inherited and carried forward over thousands of years embodies a comprehensive set of values and wisdom for living in harmony with nature and preserving it in its pristine state.

Today, we Mongols aim to share with the world our cultural heritage and the traditional knowledge and experiences gained from living in harmony with nature, thereby contributing to enhanced adaptation and resilience to climate change.

Mr. President,

Mongolia consistently adheres to the principle of resolving any conflicts through diplomacy and multilateral dialogue, while maintaining longstanding friendly relations with the countries of the region.

Building on this distinctive advantage, Mongolia held the 11th International Conference of the Ulaanbaatar Dialogue on Northeast Asian Security this year.

The Ulaanbaatar Dialogue has evolved into a unique platform for strengthening trust and confidence-building across Northeast Asia, facilitating multilateral discussions among government delegates and scholars, not only on traditional security challenges such as political and disarmament matters, but also on a broad range of issues including energy, infrastructure connectivity, green development, and humanitarian cooperation.

Furthermore, as an active member of the United Nations, Mongolia has contributed to international cooperation to advance gender equality, strengthen women’s political participation and leadership, and increase their representation at decision-making levels.

In recent years, Mongolia has established a tradition of hosting international events dedicated to women in our country, including the International Conference on Strengthening the Role of Women in Peacekeeping in 2022, the Female Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in 2023, and the World Women’s Forum in 2024, in collaboration with the United Nations, and the World Women Entrepreneurs’ Forum in 2025.

Hence, I am confident that the World Women Parliamentarians’ Forum, to be held in Ulaanbaatar on October 12-13 this year, will substantially contribute to strengthening women’s political leadership and inter-parliamentary cooperation, thereby advancing gender equality and accelerating progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals.

I cordially invite you to participate in this important event at a high level and with broad representation.

Mongolia will continue to serve as a solid bridge for partnership, cooperation, and solidarity in advancing women’s social and political leadership and participation at all levels.

Mr. President,

Mongolia has consistently championed and supported numerous initiatives within the international community aimed at preserving and promoting cultural heritage, traditional knowledge, and the shared values of humanity.

For instance, in 2025, at Mongolia’s initiative, a United Nations General Assembly resolution proclaiming World Horse Day was adopted, which recognizes the invaluable contribution of horses to the history, civilization, and socio-economic development of peoples around the world.

Moreover, last July, the Cemetery Complexes of the Xiongnu Nobility, Mongolia’s first statehood, were inscribed in the UNESCO World Heritage List, reflecting international recognition of their historical and cultural significance.

It is my pleasure to underline that Mongolia is serving for the first time as a member of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee for the term 2026-2029.

Moreover, this year marks the 820th anniversary of the Great Mongol Empire founded by Great Chinggis Khaan, Man of the Millennium, King of Kings.

The United Nations General Assembly resolution adopted on the occasion of the eight hundred years of Mongolian statehood highly values and emphasizes the contribution of Mongols to the history of humankind by “recognizing the richness of nomadic civilization and its important contribution to promoting dialogue and interaction among all forms of civilization, and that nomadic civilization influenced, inter alia, societies across Asia and Europe and, in turn, absorbed influences from both East and West in a true interchange of human values, the important role in the development of extensive trade networks and the creation of large administrative, cultural, religious and commercial centers.”

This demonstrates that these historical contributions embodied progressive ideas that could serve as a foundation for today’s collective efforts to safeguard peace and stability.

For example, the renowned Mongolist Władysław Kotwicz, in his work “Mongols are the promoters of the idea of global peace from the early 14th century,” noted that Öljeitü, IlKhan of the Mongol Empire, in his letter sent to King Philip IV of France in 1305, eloquently underscored the value of harmonious relations among nations and peoples in the thoughtful words, “What could be better than true concord?”

History is the foundation upon which we reflect on the past, shape the present, and build the future, and it is the memory of our statehood.

Scholars advise that studying the establishment of “Pax Mongolica” by Great Chinggis Khaan and his successors, as well as the history of its foreign policy and diplomacy, offers good practices and enduring lessons.

Hence, we, the Mongol people, who are guarding the sacred hearth of the Great Mongol Empire, wish to call upon from this mighty rostrum of the United Nations that if the nations of the world can bring together their efforts, it is possible to establish a Pax Globalica, a Global Peace, embodying the vision of the Pax Mongolica, which, eight centuries ago, laid the foundation for nations to coexist in peace and for humanity to flourish.

The role and contribution of the United Nations in further strengthening mutual understanding, mutual trust, and mutual respect among world nations, and in fostering a peaceful world free from war and conflict, where all can prosper together, are becoming increasingly critical than ever.

Therefore, let us work together to empower the United Nations, the guarantor of world peace and security and a source of hope and trust for the nations of the world, into a strong and respected Organization capable of bringing Pax Globalica!

May the eternal blue sky bless humankind forever with peace across the world.

Thank you for your attention!

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, and distinguished delegates,

The United Nations, which has a history of upholding human dignity and pioneering the way for future generations, now stands at a grave crossroads.

The glacial flooding in Nepal that claimed many lives and destroyed the foundations of people’s livelihoods evidences that the climate crisis is a reality of today, not tomorrow.

Persistent armed conflicts around the world, including those in Ukraine and the Middle East, continue to threaten the survival of humanity.

Emerging technologies such as drones are rapidly transforming warfare and posing serious challenges to human rights and the international law-based order.

Tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz are undermining the fundamental principles of ‘free and safe navigation’ and heightening the vulnerability of energy supply chains.

“The United Nations was not created in order to bring us to heaven, but in order to save us from hell.”

These words of the second Secretary-General of the UN, Dag Hammarskjöld, compel us to ask ourselves:

Is the United Nations today capable of saving humanity from war, poverty, and disaster?

Is the United Nations living up to its promise of restoring peace and achieving sustainable development?

Ironically, the geopolitical crisis brought on by the turbulence in international order has reminded us of the cherished value of multilateral cooperation and international norms.

In an era of fragmentation marked by fierce competition for immediate survival, values such as cooperation, mutual prosperity, and solidarity can sound like hollow outcries.

However, like the founders who, having witnessed the ravages of war, conceived the United Nations, the deeper the crisis, the more we need to return to the basic principles of the UN.

Last year, I proudly announced from this podium that the Republic of Korea, which will be a beacon of light for global citizens, has returned to the international community.

Today, I stand here to make clear the Republic of Korea’s bold resolve to lead the effort to restore the spirit of the United Nations and reconnect the world, as a nation that has risen through the solidarity of the international community.

The worldwide popularity of K-culture serves as an example demonstrating that universal empathy is possible, showcasing the potential of global connection.

The stories and content that grew out of Korea’s unique experience have become a ‘language of solidarity’ that crosses borders.

Just as culture has connected people across borders, so too can nations reunite in the face of common problems.

The Republic of Korea will build on the power of empathy and solidarity that culture has brought to light. We will harness that power to address the common challenges facing all of humanity.

To that end, allow me to set out the three visions of the ‘K-Initiative’ toward fulfilling this commitment.

First, the ‘Global AI Universal Basic Society.’

The Artificial Intelligence revolution is both a massive opportunity and a crisis for humanity. While it can be a core driver of new prosperity and sustainable development, it will only deepen inequality and imbalance unless we are properly prepared for it.

Young people around the world, in particular, are facing growing anxiety about their employment and their future as the pace of change becomes increasingly difficult to keep up with.

This boils down to a clear direction for the new era we seek to build. It is the ‘AI Universal Basic Society’ where everyone can benefit from technological progress.

The Republic of Korea is pursuing an AI transformation that will ensure stronger protection of fundamental rights across fields such as social security, labor, housing, and culture, beginning with our ‘AI Universal Basic Health’ program.

I believe this resonates with the core spirit of the UN Sustainable Development Goals, which prioritizes the guiding principle of “leaving no one behind.”

It also harnesses the AI revolution as a new driver to accelerate the realization of ‘economic, social and cultural rights.’

The Republic of Korea will build the ‘Global AI Hub’ platform to share this vision with the international community, in collaboration with international organizations, multilateral development banks, the business sector, and academia.

The Republic of Korea envisions a ‘Global AI Universal Basic Society’ where no country or individual is left out from access to the basic benefits of AI development. We will take the lead in shaping AI into a tool for solving the shared challenges we face, such as the climate crisis, public health, food insecurity, and refugee issues.

Second, the ‘green transformation.’

The climate crisis is often referred to as a ‘global group project shared by all 8 billion people on Earth.’

A single country cannot tackle this challenge alone. At the same time, abandoning growth cannot bring everyone on board.

The Republic of Korea announced its ‘2035 Nationally Determined Contributions’ as part of its active participation in the Paris Agreement and UNcentered climate action.

The ‘Korea Green Transformation’ strategy aims to convert our industrial structure, creating a virtuous cycle in which carbon neutrality leads to new growth engines and decent jobs.

We are ready to share our experience and best practices with the international community. Co-hosting the ‘4th UN Ocean Conference’ with Chile in 2028 reflects our commitment to leading discussions on the sustainable development of our oceans.

Third, the coalition for global energy supply chains.

Recently, there have been repeated blockades of sea routes in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. This has underscored the stark reality that the weaponization of key energy and logistics supply routes can send severe shockwaves to the lives of ordinary people around the world.

Freedom of navigation and safe passage through international straits is a right grounded in international law and serves as a bedrock of the global economy.

Attacks on merchant vessels and threats to the lives and safety of crew members cannot be justified under any circumstances.

While making greater use of existing frameworks such as the International Energy Agency, the Republic of Korea will build a more robust framework of cooperation for energy supply chains to prevent the supply chain crisis from escalating into a broader threat to the global economy and people’s livelihoods.

By nature, these problems cannot be resolved by any one of us alone. At the same time, we cannot afford to sit idly by and wait for all nations to arrive at a single solution.

The most urgent and realistic path is for countries with the capacity and willingness to supply global public goods to join hands and broaden the scope of cooperation.

I would like to call this a ‘Partnership of Constructive Contributors.’

I am not seeking to propose a new organization, nor an exclusive grouping. The idea is to respect the functions of the existing international order and the UN, work together in a flexible and open manner in areas where each country has particular strength, and expand our ties of cooperation into new areas.

By continuing to build on the achievements of collaborating ‘separately yet together,’ we can move beyond geopolitical rivalry, deadlock, and fragmentation, and rebuild trust in multilateralism.

The United Nations must evolve with the times.

Agreements reached at the negotiating table must translate into real change on the ground, so that people around the world can feel their impact in their daily lives.

We must reduce duplication across organizations and programs, accelerate decision making, and direct limited resources where they are needed most.

In this spirit, the Republic of Korea supports the ‘UN 80 Initiative,’ which will improve efficiency, prioritize field operations, and deliver greater results.

We also support the reform of the UN Security Council, so that it operates in a more effective, democratic, and accountable manner.

The Republic of Korea will live up to its responsibility and position to deliver results that can be vividly felt by people around the world across the UN's three pillars of peace, development and human rights.

Through the ‘Busan Global Partnership Forum,’ we will continue to support inclusive growth, share Korea’s development experiences such as the Saemaul Undong, and continue to make sustainable and innovative investments.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, and distinguished delegates,

When it comes to peace on the Korean Peninsula, the Republic of Korea knows firsthand the change that the United Nations has brought about.

Thirty-five years ago, the two Koreas were admitted to the UN as members on this very stage. It was a crucial turning point that laid the foundation for peaceful coexistence, freeing us from the relentless rivalry and confrontation that followed our division.

One year ago, I stated from this stage that the Republic of Korea would begin a new journey toward ‘peaceful coexistence and shared growth on the Korean Peninsula.’

Today, as we set out on this new journey, I would like to present to the international community the three blueprints for the road to peaceful coexistence on the Korean Peninsula.

First is inclusive peaceful coexistence built on mutual respect. Based on the respect for each other’s systems and acknowledgement of our differences, we will explore ways for shared growth through cooperation.

We will continue to respect the North on the international stage and seek cooperation wherever possible. We hope that opportunities will emerge for us to work together in the international community, in areas such as public health, disaster response, and the climate crisis.

Second is stable peaceful coexistence that renders conflict unnecessary. We will work to institute mechanisms for preventing crisis and managing conflicts.

Reestablishing basic channels of communication and building trust will be the first step toward a stable peaceful coexistence.

Third is responsible peaceful coexistence contributing to world peace.

We will go beyond building a Korean Peninsula free from war and nuclear weapons to promoting stability and cooperation in Northeast Asia, while actively contributing to global efforts to build a world free from war and conflict.

The most critical task is to bring an end to this decades-old war on the Korean Peninsula and establish a lasting peace regime.

For decades, the two Koreas, along with key countries such as the U.S. and China, have recognized the need for a peace regime on the Korean Peninsula and discussed ways to achieve it.

Fortunately, President Trump’s resolve has recently created a hard-won opportunity for change.

I hope the long-suspended dialogue between North Korea and the U.S. can resume without delay. We will lay the groundwork for this to develop into a dialogue among the parties aimed at ending the war on the Korean Peninsula and transitioning to a peace regime.

I am confident that the dialogue for establishing a peace regime on the Korean Peninsula can provide a valuable framework not only for normalizing relations among the parties concerned, but also for fostering shared growth through multilateral cooperation and promoting stability and cooperation in Northeast Asia.

In this process, we will begin with a stop to further advances in North Korea’s nuclear and missile capabilities, followed by their reductions in the medium term, moving toward a Korean Peninsula free from nuclear weapons over the long term.

I hope that the United Nations, which created a pivotal moment for peaceful coexistence on the Korean Peninsula thirty-five years ago, and the Security Council, which has safeguarded the peace and stability of the international community, will once again play a responsible and constructive role.

As a direct party to peace on the Korean Peninsula, and as a pacemaker, my government will exert every effort to open and sustain the path toward dialogue.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, and distinguished delegates,

The true performance of UN does not lie solely in the figures and charts of reports, or in the declarations made in conference rooms.

The raison d'etre of UN will be proven only when children's laughter replaces gunfire, when young people can enjoy the opportunity to learn, work, and take on new challenges, and when anyone, anywhere, can choose to live the life they want.

In 2015, the international community adopted the Sustainable Development Goals as our shared commitments for a bright future.

As we approach the 2030 deadline, now is the time to chart a new path forward for the next generation.

It is imperative for young people, our future generation, to define problems together, formulate solutions, and become co-designers who can lead the action.

We need to bring more youth voices into international decision-making by widening opportunities for participation and communication, as well as making bold investments in the potential of the next generation.

The Republic of Korea can testify more vividly than anyone else, to the noble power of solidarity embodied by the United Nations.

Our own experience of achieving industrialization and democratization in the wake of war stands as proof of how the world can bring about miraculous changes with one mind and one heart of the international community.

We are ready to repay that solidarity with greater responsibility and contribution.

We will reconnect a divided world, build a future that leaves no one behind, and chart a course for the next generation to dream of a better tomorrow.

The Republic of Korea stands ready to lead the way toward a peaceful coexistence on the Korean Peninsula, and toward “a United Nations that delivers for all.”

Thank you for your attention.

Mr. President,

Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished delegates,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Mr. President, let me congratulate you on the assumption of the high office of President of the 81st session of the General Assembly of the United Nations.

Expressing appreciation to your predecessor for her stewardship of the 80th session of the General Assembly, I wish her every success in her future endeavors.

Secretary–General, as you approach the conclusion of your tenure, the Republic of Suriname commends the dedicated service to humanity, showcased while in office. We also remember with warmth your visit to Suriname, expressing the importance of the United N ations’ engagement with our country and the Caribbean region. We wish you well, in the path before you.

Mr. President,

Standing before this Assembly, I am reminded that, while some efforts have been made from this rostrum over the past year, these have not yet matched the scale of the challenges confronting our world.

We will have to increase and strengthen efforts and commitment to the process of trans formation and strengthening of the UN in order to restore the trust that our organization will really be capable of delivering peace, inclusion and development in the world.

Suriname is firmly committed to the upholding of International Law, as we depend on a rules -based international order, without which, l ike many other vulnerable nations, we simply cannot exist as sovereign countries.

The consistent application of i nternational law and the strengthening of its institutions is also essential to maintain international peace and security, protect human rights and ensure sustainable development for all.

Mr. President,

As mentioned before, t he international community is experiencing profound uncertainty, including energy and food security crises, leading to intensified displacement of many people globally.

Armed conflicts continue to claim innocent lives, while geopolitical tensions escalate. Children are living through unimaginable horrors. The United Nations has not been able to prevent this or end the continuation.

Other developments, for example in the Strait of Hormuz, demonstrate how quickly wars can affect energy markets, suddenly and steeply increasing the cost of energy, adversely impacting economic and social developments in our countries.

Common people suffer when food and energy prices rise, so the quality of life of our people is directly threatened, even by wars in regions far from their home.

Suriname, therefore, calls for a renewed commitment to the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, namely the peaceful resolution of disputes.

Mr. President,

Dialogue is paramount for safeguarding a solid and proven UN system. The people of Cuba, a Caribbean country, are adversely affected by the current situation in their country.

Suriname calls on the parties involved to remain committed to dialogue and negotiation, to end the economic, commercial and financial embargo. We plea for continuing of negotiations in order to prevent further escalation and to reach a resolution, that will benefit the people of Cuba.

We also call for sustained international support for Haiti to restore security, constitutional order and democratic governance. Suriname supports solutions that place the Haitian people at the center.

The UN80 process rightly emphasizes mandate rationalization, institutional coherence and efficiency.

Reform must protect and improve the United Nations' capacity to deliver and also make the system easier to navigate. It should not reduce support where it is most needed.

Equally important, is the overdue reform of the Security Council, hence Suriname reiterates its call for making it more representative, more accountable and more capable of acting.

Africa, the Republic of Suriname supports your demand, for just permanent representation. Likewise, we underscore the relevance of a dedicated representation for Small Island States and Low-Lying Coastal Developing States.

Mr. President,

Regional and international partnership s remain indispensable to achieve our economic and social objectives as Suriname continues to actively engage in various regional bodies and mechanisms including CARICOM, CELAC, ACTO and Brasilia Consensus.

As Suriname prepares to be the Chair of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) in 2027, we are also committed to further strengthen our partnership globally in different areas of shared interest.

Our regional priorities are practical: food and energy security, climate resilience, improved connectivity, and movement of skilled people, transportation of goods and services. These are essential to economic integration and to our ability to withstand external shocks.

Mr. President,

The pursuit of restorative justice gained new momentum with the adoption of the resolution on Slavery and Transatlantic Trafficking of Enslaved Africans, in this Hall in March of this year.

This development is relevant for Suriname. And equally important for the countries of the Caribbean region.

The discussion is no longer about whether slavery and colonialism have caused lasting consequences. We know we are living them.

We increasingly must focus on how to overcome these effects and on the question of what form reparation should take to achieve that. How will countries that have benefited from slavery and colonialism compensate the affected.

It is therefore that the CARICOM ten -point plan for restorative justice is now of eminent importance.

Mr. President,

Suriname occupies a unique position. We are carbon negative and remain the world’s most forested country with over 90 per cent forest coverage.

High Forested and Low Deforestation countries, like Suriname, should not first have to lose forests, before climate finance institutions recognize the value of protecting them.

Conservation costs cannot be borne only by the countries protecting ecosystems whose benefits are shared globally.

I will continue my plea for just and effective climate finance, because our forests are under even more pressure than when I addressed this meeting last year.

I stated that the forest face s competition of rich natural resources like gold, diamonds and other precious minerals.

We are now confronted, however, with a new threat of people who also want to clear parts of our rainforest for large-scale agriculture.

At this very moment my government is introducing legal and institutional measures to better protect our forests and the immediate living environment of the Indigenous Peoples and Tribal Communities. Their knowledge and participation are important at all stages of development.

Last year at this rostrum I noted that Suriname is diversity.

At a time when diversity is too often manipulated as a source of division, Suriname has chosen the path to recognize the distinct histories of its people while strengthening their unity and their shared responsibility for the future.

Our experience affirms that diversity, when grounded in equality, mutual respect and meaningful participation, is not an adversity; it is a source of national resilience and prosperity.

Last month, the Republic of Suriname observed its first National Heritage Month under the theme, "Hoe wij hier ook samen kwamen, hoe wij samen verder gaan”, meaning “However we came here, united we move forward”.

This initiative was conceived not merely to celebrate our culture, but as a deliberate national undertaking centered on growing inclusion, mutual respect and unity. This process is also relevant for the global community.

Mr. President,

The development of Suriname’s offshore natural resources including oil and gas, will present significant opportunities to accelerate national development and improve the well being of our people.

Yet, we are equally conscious that oil and gas cannot and should not become the only foundation of our economy.

Our approach is therefore clear. We must transform temporary resource wealth into lasting national prosperity using resource revenues strategically to strengthen our economy and make it more resilient, through diversification.

Additionally, we will need to improve our energy security.

Although we are preparing for gas to shore, renewable energy will be part of our national energy mix.

Mr. President,

Besides the expected economic and energy transition, we must also prepare for the transformation driven by artificial intelligence.

Only if we can implement AI responsibly, Suriname will be able to benefit from the opportunities of this technology and mitigate its risks.

Mr. President,

With only four years left to achieve the S ustainable Development Goals, we may question whether we were too ambitious or if we should have done much more.

Political will, international peace and a ccelerated implementation are required, supported by financing, technology and partnerships that produce measurable results.

Equally important is to have a mechanism in place for global commitments after 2030.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates,

Finally, as the United Nations approaches change in its highest leadership, current realities and approved mandates require the next Secretary -General to portray strong commitment to multilateralism, dialogue, and the rule of law.

Many capable candidates, including women leaders who have taken up the challenge, have been put forth and for the first time in history we have a female candidate from the Caribbean. CARICOM endorses this candidate.

We are at that time in history where trust in the United Nations must urgently be restored.

We make efforts to protect our forests, use our natural wealth responsibly, strengthen the Caribbean Community and promote dialogue.

We will do what we can and call on more influential members of the United Nations, to help maintain peace.

Only a United Nations, capable of safeguarding international peace and security will deliver for all.

I thank you.

Gran Tangi.

May God bless you all.

1. I congratulate His Excellency Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the eighty-first session of the General Assembly.

2. President Rahman assumes this responsibility at a moment that demands principled and steady leadership, and he has Sierra Leone’s full support.

3. I pay tribute to His Excellency Secretary-General António Guterres, who is in the closing months of his mandate.

4. He has served this Organisation with steadfastness, moral clarity and the courage to speak difficult truths.

5. I also commend Her Excellency Amina Mohammed, the Deputy Secretary-General, for her exemplary service and distinguished representation of Africa on the global stage.

MR PRESIDENT,

6. Nearly twenty-five years ago, Sierra Leone completed disarmament and formally declared its civil war over.

7. The formal declaration matters, but peace became real in more practical ways: in the families that returned home, in the communities that learned to live together again, in the citizens who chose the ballot and in institutions that slowly earned back confidence.

8. The United Nations stood with us through disarmament, elections and the long work of peacebuilding.

9. We know what international cooperation can make possible because we have lived it.

10. That experience taught us that trust cannot be commanded by declaration.

11. Trust grows when promises are honoured, when the law protects everyone, when institutions serve their people, and when citizens can see a future for themselves.

12. Sierra Leone brings that lesson to this Assembly at a time when trust between nations, in institutions and in multilateral cooperation is under profound strain.

MR PRESIDENT,

13. In this year’s theme, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation:

A United Nations That Delivers FOR ALL,” the words “FOR ALL” carry its defining moral weight.

14. The words “FOR ALL” ask not only whether the United Nations can act, but also whom its actions reach, whose voices shape them, and whose dignity they protect.

15. An institution may act quickly and still fail those it was meant to serve.

16. Delivery worthy of the UN Charter must reach those furthest from power and recognise the equal worth of every nation and every human life.

17. That is the standard by which the world will judge us.

MR PRESIDENT,

18. That standard begins with TRUST. Trust is the currency of multilateralism.

19. Trust is gained when the law protects the vulnerable as firmly as it restrains the powerful.

20. International law must not change with geography or bend according to the identity of the accused.

21. In the Middle East, the UN Charter and international law must guide us. Civilians must be protected, humanitarian access ensured, aggression and occupation ended, and freedom of navigation safeguarded.

22. The inalienable right of the Palestinian people to selfdetermination must be realised through a viable State of Palestine living alongside the State of Israel in peace and security.

23. That same commitment to peace requires progress on nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation through diplomacy.

24. In Sudan, civilians continue to endure atrocities and displacement, underscoring the cost of delayed action.

25. Sierra Leone calls for their protection, unhindered humanitarian access, accountability, and a Sudanese-led political process that safeguards the country’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity.

26. In the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, agreements have not yet silenced the guns or allowed millions to return home.

27. Across West Africa and the Sahel, terrorism feeds on poverty, exclusion, unemployment and weak institutions.

28. These conflicts differ in origin and circumstance, but they carry a common warning.

29. Military action may contain a threat, but it cannot, by itself, build lasting peace.

30. When hunger, exclusion and despair deepen, insecurity takes root.

31. The connection between peace and development must therefore move from our resolutions into our budgets.

32. In 2025, global military expenditure reached almost 2.9 trillion United States dollars, the eleventh consecutive annual increase.

33. Nations have legitimate security needs, but the speed with which the world finds resources for war, compared with prevention and development, reveals a grave disorder in our priorities.

MR PRESIDENT,

34. The credibility of international law also depends on who has a voice in applying it.

35. That credibility weakens when the institutions entrusted with the law preserve an unequal distribution of power.

36. The Security Council still reflects the world of 1945. Africa, home to more than 1.6 billion people and the subject of much of the Council's work, still has no Permanent Seat.

37. Africa seeks its rightful place because the Council cannot be fully legitimate or effective while an entire continent remains permanently absent from its highest level of decision-making.

38. No durable global solution on peace, climate, food, energy or technology can be built without African leadership.

39. The Common African Position, espoused in the Ezulwini Consensus and Sirte Declaration, calls for no fewer than two Permanent Seats, with all the rights and privileges of permanent membership, including the veto if it is retained, and five NonPermanent Seats.

40. As Coordinator of the African Union Committee of Ten, Sierra Leone will continue to advance that position.

41. Years of Intergovernmental Negotiations without realising the reform have tested the credibility of the process.

42. Before this session concludes, Member States should have a consolidated model, which we committed to in the Pact for the Future.

43. Sierra Leone speaks with the authority of service. During our term on the Security Council in 2024 and 2025, we worked as a voice of reason and a bridge across division.

44. We convened the Security Council’s first high-level debate on redressing the historical injustice against Africa, placed conflict-related food insecurity at the centre of its agenda and, with Guyana, co-drafted the unanimously adopted Resolution 2807 on Youth, Peace and Security, strengthening young people’s role in conflict prevention and peacebuilding.

MR PRESIDENT,

45. Representation becomes meaningful when it changes decisions and improves lives.

46. The imbalance within the Security Council is also present in International Financial Institutions, whose structures still bear the imprint of an earlier age.

47. Developing countries need fairer voting power, stronger representation and increased capital within these institutions, together with affordable finance, concessional resources and fairer debt treatment.

48. They must also participate equally in shaping the rules of international taxation. Sierra Leone therefore supports a UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation.

49. Through ECOSOC, Sierra Leone will champion a development system that responds more effectively to Africa’s priorities.

MR PRESIDENT,

50. Restoring trust and delivering for all must also embrace the unfinished cause of reparatory justice.

51. In March, this Assembly adopted a resolution led by Ghana and supported by the African Union and the Caribbean Community, recognising the trafficking and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity.

52. For Sierra Leone, this history is neither abstract nor distant.

53. From Bunce Island, in our own river estuary, thousands of Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic into enslavement.

54. Freetown, our capital, would later become a home for formerly enslaved and liberated Africans. This history is woven into our nation's identity.

55. However, the consequences did not end with abolition. Their legacy continues to be reflected in enduring disparities in wealth, power and opportunity across our world.

56. Reparatory justice is therefore not a plea for charity. It calls for acknowledgement, formal apology, the return of cultural heritage, fair redress and guarantees of non-repetition.

57. Sierra Leone stands with Africa, the Caribbean and the wider African diaspora in advancing this cause, not to remain captive to the past, but to build a more just and equitable future.

MR PRESIDENT,

58. The same principle of fairness applies to Africa's critical minerals.

59. Critical minerals are indispensable to the global energy transition, yet too much value is still added elsewhere.

60. Processing at source, fair value chains, technology transfer and local industry would turn natural wealth into skilled work, stronger economies and hope for our young people.

61. The green transition must not reproduce the extractive terms of the past.

62. For the youth, this is immediate. A young person without work, opportunity or a stake in the future becomes vulnerable to the recruiter, the smuggler and the dangerous journey across the Mediterranean.

63. Jobs, skills and dignity are therefore part of any serious policy for peace and development.

MR PRESIDENT,

64. Sierra Leone does not ask of the world what it does not demand of itself. We carry these same principles into our work at home.

65. Through Feed Salone, we are increasing domestic food production and strengthening food security.

66. Through Free Quality School Education, we are widening the path from the circumstances of a child's birth to the possibilities of that child's future.

67. In 2024, we enacted the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act and subsequently championed the proclamation of 27 November as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage.

68. A girl in Sierra Leone is no more or less precious than a girl anywhere else. Protecting her childhood, education and freedom is part of what development means.

MR PRESIDENT,

69. A girl’s future, like the future of every young person, will be shaped by forces already remaking our world: climate change, artificial intelligence and the energy transition.

70. The meaning of ‘FOR ALL’ becomes more urgent as we decide how these transformations will be governed.

71. Artificial Intelligence can improve education, healthcare, agriculture and public administration.

72. It can also widen inequality if infrastructure, knowledge and rule-making remain concentrated in a few countries.

73. Developing nations must help shape the standards that will govern technologies affecting their people.

74. Climate Change presents the same moral question in harsher form: who benefits, who decides, and who pays?

75. In Shenge, on Sierra Leone's southern coast, families watch the sea take land, fishing grounds and the graves of their ancestors.

76. For them, climate change is the disappearance of home in the present.

77. Those who contributed least to the climate crisis are bearing some of its greatest costs.

78. Accessible and predictable climate finance, support for adaptation, and effective arrangements for loss and damage are obligations of justice.

79. They are also investments in global stability.

80. Fairness in transformation depends on the institutions that govern it.

81. Sierra Leone therefore supports the UN80 Initiative and wider reforms that make this Organisation more effective, accountable and responsive.

82. Efficiency matters and reform must preserve the capacity to act.

MR PRESIDENT,

83. The choice of the next Secretary-General offers another test of institutional effectiveness and equality.

84. In eighty years, every Secretary-General has been a man.

85. The women put forward for this office have placed their competence beyond dispute.

86. What remains is the will of this Organisation to live by the equality it asks of others and entrust a woman with its highest office.

MR PRESIDENT,

87. Our insistence on a capable United Nations comes from experience.

88. For Sierra Leone, this Organisation is part of our living history. It stood with us when our country was broken and helped us make peace durable.

89. In this Hall, a Small State has the same vote as a great power.

Imperfect as it is, that equality remains one of humanity’s boldest promises.

90. Sierra Leone will continue to contribute personnel to United Nations peace operations, uphold international law, support mediation and peacebuilding, defend the rights of women and girls, and serve as a bridge wherever Member States seek one.

91. We will also continue to support the institutions of international justice.

92. In this regard, Sierra Leone has nominated Professor Charles Chernor Jalloh, a distinguished international jurist, endorsed by the African Union and ECOWAS, for election as a Judge of the International Court of Justice.

93. We respectfully seek Member States' support on 3 November.

MR PRESIDENT,

94. The United Nations was created in a world of unequal power, yet it rests on a radical idea: nations differ in size and strength, but their peoples do not differ in human worth.

95. A United Nations that delivers ‘FOR ALL’ makes that equality felt beyond this Hall.

96. Nearly twenty-five years ago, Sierra Leoneans placed their trust in peace because they believed tomorrow could be different.

97. People around the world are asking something similar of us now.

98. They need reason to believe that cooperation still works, that law still matters, and that promises made here will be honoured in their lives.

99. Let this session give them that reason.

100. The words 'FOR ALL' should not remain at the end of this year’s theme. They must become the measure of our work.

I THANK YOU.

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

It is an honour and a pleasure to address the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly on behalf of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

We are a symbol of a nation that has survived severe trials but has not lost its path towards a better future.

In the period f rom 1992 to 1995, my country was subjected to aggression, joint criminal enterprises, genocide against Bosniaks, crimes against humanity and other war crimes.

Following the end of the aggression in 1995, destructive forces have sought, through blockades, obstruction and other means, to halt the progress of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are slowing down our path towards a modern European state, but they cannot stop it.

Today, Bosnia and Herzegovina stands at the doorstep of the European Union (EU) and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO).

These are our strategic foreign policy objectives, unanimously defined by the state authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Unfortunately, there are still those seeking to realise greaterstate projects at the expense of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

During the aggression, they attacked our country by military means; today, they do so by political, diplomatic and other means.

It is very important that the UN courts have established the nature of the war waged against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Final judgments, including those concerning joint criminal enterprises, have established that this was an international armed conflict. Judgments of the highest UN courts have established that genocide was committed against Bosniaks. They also stand as judgments on the greater -state policies that, through a joint criminal enterprise, sought to divide and destroy Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent, sovereign, indivisible and internationally recognised state.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

We live in a world of injustice, insecurity and intolerance.

The strengthening of authoritarian populism, the aggression against Ukraine, the suffering in Gaza, the war in the Gulf region, the catastrophic situation in Sudan and other flashpoints have brought humanity into a profound crisis, marked by great uncertainty and fear. We must not remain silent in the face of injustice.

The world did not respond adequately to the aggression against Ukraine and the genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, just as it did not during the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The aggression of the Russian Federation against Ukraine is a flagrant example of a violation of the UN Charter and international law, while Gaza is humanity’s greatest defeat in the twenty-first century.

The greatest global crises are directly interconnected and have the same root: the erosion of international law.

Disrespect for international law cannot lead the world towards prosperity and a better future.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Without identifying the causes of the crisis facing contemporary humanity, we cannot solve its problems.

The politics of force cannot bring progress to humanity. Instead of force, we need respect and the strengthening of the existing international norms, rules and institutions that we have built over more than 80 years.

The multilateral system today faces a serious challenge – a crisis of institutional trust.

Trust is weakening because some actors in the international community undermine the values enshrined in the UN Charter.

The future of humanity does not lie in policies of violence and human rights violations.

Conflicts and wars are not the purpose of our civilisation. Let us build a culture of dialogue, cooperation and peace.

In this context, I believe it is of utmost importance to: ▪ reaffirm the importance of the UN Charter; ▪ revitalise the role of the UN as the global centre for coordination and cooperation; ▪ support the reform process and strengthen the credibility of the UN; ▪ consistently implement the Sustainable Development Goals; ▪ build mutual trust, inclusiveness and a democratic vision of leadership; ▪ and strengthen preventive diplomacy at a time of numerous tensions and conflicts.

Let respect for international law, peace, solidarity, sustainable development and justice be the path that we follow together.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

We in Bosnia and Herzegovina call upon all UN Member States to focus on: ▪ reaffirming relations between states on the basis of international law; ▪ ensuring respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms; ▪ promoting peace and social progress; ▪ combating hate speech and all forms of discrimination; ▪ strengthening policies for the prevention of genocide, crimes against humanity and other war crimes; ▪ advancing the rights of women and children; ▪ and strengthening gender equality, better healthcare and education.

The world must return to the fundamental principles upon which the UN is founded.

Respect for human dignity.

The sovereign equality of states.

The peaceful settlement of disputes.

Respect for international law.

These are not unrealistic propositions; they are the only possible foundations of a stable world.

Bosnia and Herzegovina is a reliable and responsible member of the UN.

Among other things, I would like to remind that Bosnia and Herzegovina is: ▪ aware of climate change and committed to contributing to global efforts; ▪ committed to the transition towards renewable energy sources and the reduction of harmful gas emissions; ▪ and determined to combat all forms of terrorism.

We in Bosnia and Herzegovina know that peace cannot be taken for granted.

Peace must be safeguarded every day. It requires responsibility of political leaders, respect for the law and a readiness for dialogue.

There must not be one standard for large states and another for small states.

If we want to preserve trust in the international order, the rules we establish together must be applied equally.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Bosnia and Herzegovina is the only country in Europe where genocide was committed after the Second World War.

In May 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted the Resolution designating 11 July as the International Day of Reflection and Commemoration of the 1995 Genocide in Srebrenica. This Resolution represents a profoundly moral and civilisational act by the UN General Assembly. The adopted Resolution is equally important for the UN and for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

It is particularly dangerous that the leadership of the Republic of Serbia glorifies the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić.

The monster Ratko Mladić is not a hero, but a convicted war criminal.

The institutional glorification of this war criminal is an anti -civilizational and unacceptable act.

It amounts to identifying Serbia’s state leadership with one of the worst butchers in European history.

It is an indication that Serbia has not abandoned the ideology and policies that lead to aggression and genocide.

It is a direct assault on the values of the UN, whose court delivered a final judgement against this war criminal.

Let me remind you that Serbia is the only state in the world that has been found by a UN court to have violated the UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.

I call on the UN and EU and other international actors to clearly condemn this conduct and take concrete measures against those who institutionally glorify convicted war criminals.

Unfortunately, the ideology and policies that led to the genocide against Bosniaks continue to threaten Bosnia and Herzegovina.

From the podium of the UN General Assembly, I wish to publicly warn the international public that the current leadership of the Bosnian entity Republika Srpska continues to threaten the peace and security of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the region.

We must stop this destructive policy together.

The victims of the genocide and the employees of the Memorial Centre Srebrenica are facing unacceptable pressures from the police of the Republika Srpska.

We must not allow that the police and other institutions of Republika Srpska which committed the genocide against Bosniaks, today threaten the survivors and those that are preserving the memory on the victims of the genocide.

Those seeking to destroy the Dayton Peace Agreement are attempting to create the conditions for the secession of the Bosnian entity Republika Srpska.

In the period ahead, they will intensify their activities, primarily with the aim of: ▪ weakening and abolishing the mandate of the High Representative of the international community, which is also envisaged by the Dayton Peace Agreement; ▪ weakening the institution of the Constitutional Court of BiH; ▪ and seizing the state property of Bosnia and Herzegovina, contrary to national and international law.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Bosnia and Herzegovina is an unconquerable state.

There is not a single map of Southeast Europe from the past 1,000 years on which Bosnia or Bosnia and Herzegovina does not appear.

Bosnia and Herzegovina is home to people who love freedom more than their own lives.

Finally, as the Chairman of the Presidency of BiH, I wish to emphasise that I am proud of the brave people of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

These are people who have suffered injustice, yet they continue to fight for justice.

These are people who have been victims of lies, yet they continue to fight for the truth.

These are people who support the struggle for justice, freedom and human dignity throughout the world.

These are the honourable and proud people of my homeland, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Thank you for your attention.
