Mister President Excellencies,

Distinguished Delegates,

Mabrika, good afternoon.

I bring greetings to this Assembly from the People and Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica. I congratulate you, Mr. President, on your election and on the theme chosen for this eighty -first session of the General Assembly: “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers For All.”

This theme speaks directly to the defining challenges of our time.

We are living through an age of profound transformation. Technology is changing how we work, communicate and understand the world. Climate change is reshaping economies, communities and entire ecosystems.

09/21/2026 Final Statement Conflicts are destroying lives and displacing families. Economic uncertainty is deepening inequality, while progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals has stalled.

These challenges are not unfolding in isolation. They are interconnected, global in scale and beyond the capacity of any one nation to address alone.

They demand stronger cooperation and renewed confidence in multilateralism.

Yet, Excellencies, at the very moment when collective action is most urgently needed, this Organization stands at a crossroads.

The question before us, therefore, is whether we possess the courage, solidarity and political will to shape that change and guide our world towards peace, justice and shared prosperity.

09/21/2026 Final Statement The UN already Delivers for All.

I strongly believe that most right -thinking individuals would agree that the UN System has substantially delivered for all countries over the several decades of its existence.

For more than eighty years, this organization has embodied humanity’s highest collective aspiration, that countries, large and small, rich and poor, can work together to prevent conflict, protect human dignity and improve the lives of their people.

The United Nations provides shelter and protection to people enduring conflict, displacement and natural disaster. It supports education, healthcare, peacekeeping, elections and development in communities that might otherwise be forgotten.

These achievements matter and must never be dismissed or diminished.

What the United Nations does not currently do enough, is deliver at the transformative level.

09/21/2026 Final Statement Too often, humanity, and the institutions we have created to serve us, have had to concentrate on managing one crisis after another, without giving enough attention to the conditions that allow them to persist.

Excellencies, there is no question that managing crises is necessary. It brings relief, restores hope and saves lives. But we cannot stop there. Our responsibility must also be to address the root causes of these problems and build systems that are fairer, stronger and better able to serve our people.

The true test of this Organization, therefore, is not only how well we respond after people have suffered. It is also whether we can work together to prevent that suffering in the first place.

This is not to dismiss what has already been achieved. It is a call for us to build on that progress, strengthen our cooperation, and deliver the meaningful change that our people expect from us.

09/21/2026 Final Statement A fundamental question that one must ask is “ Can the international system still deliver?”

For Dominica, this is not an abstract question. When a hurricane destroys our infrastructure, when international energy prices rise, when access to capital becomes more expensive, when global markets change or when climate finance remains beyond our reach, the consequences are felt immediately - in our homes, in our businesses, in our schools and hospitals, and in the very lives of our people.

Yet, Mr. President, I do not come before this Assembly to speak only of vulnerability. I wish to speak of transformation and resilience.

Dominica has made a choice. We have chosen not only to rebuild after disaster, but to build differently, build better, buil d stronger. We have chosen not only to adapt to climate change, but to demonstrate what a climate-resilient economy and country can look like. And we have chosen to move from dependence to greater self-reliance.

09/21/2026 Final Statement Mr. President,

In 2017, Category Five Hurricane Maria demonstrated with devastating force the vulnerability of small island states like Dominica. The economic and human consequences were enormous.

Hurricane Maria however, also taught us an important lesson: Resilience should n ever begin after the disaster. Resilience must begin before disaster.

The international community must therefore move from a model that primarily finances reconstruction after catastrophe, to one that invests systematically in resilience before disaster strikes.

For Dominica, this means resilient roads and bridges, resilient buildings, reliable communications, modern water systems, strengthened health infrastructure and disaster-ready communities.

09/21/2026 Final Statement But resilience is not only physical. A resilient country must have resilient institutions. It must have resilient public finances. It must have resilient energy systems and must have resilient food systems.

Above all, a resilient nation must have people who possess the skills and confidence to withstand shocks and move forward.

That is the Dominica that we are building.

Excellencies,

Dominica has begun the transition from imported fossil fuels to renewable energy. Our geothermal power plant is now in commercial operation, and increasing the renewable share of our electricity generation to approximately 84 percent. We are well on our way to achieving 100% renewable energy by 2030.

09/21/2026 Final Statement This is more than an energy project. It is economic transformation. It demonstrates that small states can lead in the transition to clean energy.

Every barrel of oil that we no longer need to import, strengthens our resilience to international price shocks. Every unit of clean electricity we produce strengthens our energy security.

Affordable, reliable renewable energy can become a foundation for new industries, new investment, new employment and greater competitiveness.

The lesson is important beyond Dominica. We need international finance that recognises the transformative nature of renewable energy investment in vulnerable countries.

We need financing mechanisms that allow countries such as Dominica to move faster. And we need partnerships that allow the energy transition to become an engine of economic development and growth.

09/21/2026 Final Statement Our ambition is not merely to generate clean electricity. Our ambition is to use clean energy to transform our economy.

Finance Must Change Mister President,

The international community has become very good at recognising vulnerability. We have become less successful at financing the transformation that vulnerability requires.

Too often, the cycle is predictable: A disaster occurs. Infrastructure is destroyed and economic activity collapses. We then mobilise resources to rebuild what was lost, often through borrowing that substantially increases debt to rebuild what we could have made more resilient from the outset. This is not an efficient financial model.

The best time to build resilience is before disaster. The best time to finance transformation is before crisis. And the value of resilience should be 09/21/2026 Final Statement measured not only by what we build, but by what we prevent from being destroyed.

Mister President,

Dominica does not come to the United Nations asking to be treated as a victim of vulnerability. We come asking to be recognised as a partner in transformation. We must finance potential - not merely manage vulnerability.

And this is not only about Dominica. It is about whether the global financial system is capable of recognising a different development model.

A model in which resilience is an investment. Nature is an asset.

Connectivity is productive infrastructure. Clean energy is economic opportunity. And prevention is financially smarter than reconstruction.

That is the proposition we place before this Assembly. It is time that the international financial architecture evolves. Dominica joins its voice with those countries that continue to advocate for the use of multidimensional 09/21/2026 Final Statement vulnerability as a practical and fair basis in determining access to development finance.

We call for greater and easier access to concessional financing and grants for adaptation.

We call for stronger disaster clauses in sovereign debt instruments.

We call for financing mechanisms that can be activated rapidly when disasters strike.

And we call for a fundamental shift in the way the international community views investment in resilience.

Every dollar spent preventing the destruction of a road, a hospital, a school or a water system is an investment in future development. Dominica is prepared to serve as a demonstration country for this approach.

09/21/2026 Final Statement We are prepared to work with international partners to show what happens when finance is designed around transformation rather than vulnerability.

Mister President,

Dominica has long spoken of becoming the world's first climate-resilient nation. Today, I wish to take that ambition further. We invite the international community to partner with us in making Dominica a living laboratory for climate resilience and sustainable development.

Bring us the technology; Bring us the research; Bring us the investment; Bring us the innovation.

And together, let us demonstrate what a resilient small island economy can look like. Resilient housing; Smart and renewable energy systems; Climate-smart agriculture; Modern water management; Digital public services; Resilient infrastructure; Nature -based adaptation; And new industries powered by clean energy.

09/21/2026 Final Statement This should not be a relationship based simply on donor and recipient. It should be a relationship based on partnership, innovation and shared learning. Dominica has lessons to learn from the world. But we also have lessons to offer the world.

Transformation Must Create Opportunity Mister President,

Transformation is ultimately about people. A resilient economy must create opportunity for young people. Young people want to inherit a country that is not merely protected from disasters, but one in which they can build businesses, work in new industries, participate in the global economy, and build meaningful lives at home.

That is why our investments in energy, connectivity, digital transformation, tourism, agriculture and resilience must ultimately converge around one objective: creating opportunity.

The Wider Challenge to Multilateralism 09/21/2026 Final Statement Excellencies,

The challenges before us extend beyond climate and finance. We meet at a time when war continues to devastate communities and ruin lives. When humanitarian crises are multiplying. When international law is under pressure. When trust between nations is strained.

We cannot speak about development without speaking about peace.

Without peace, development is tenuous.

We believe in the principles of the United Nations Charter. We believe in respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states. We believe in the peaceful settlement of international disputes. We believe in dialogue.

And we believe that internati onal law must apply equally to all nations, and must be applied consistently.

09/21/2026 Final Statement Small states must never become collateral damage in the competition among larger powers. The security of a small nation is no less important than the security of a large one.

The credibility of multilateralism depends on fairness. But it also depends on delivery.

The true test of multilateralism is not whether we can agree in this room.

It is whether our agreements can transform lives outside this room.

Restoring Trust That is why I welcome the central challenge of this 81st General Assembly, “restoring trust”.

Excellencies,

The world does not need another generation of promises that remain unfulfilled. It needs delivery. It needs institutions that respond faster. It 09/21/2026 Final Statement needs financing that reaches vulnerable countries more efficiently. It needs partnerships that produce measurable results. And it needs a multilateral system that people can believe in again.

For Dominica, restoring trust means closing the gap between international commitments and the lived experience of our people.

It means ensuring that when the world says it supports climate resilience, resources actually reach the communities that need them.

It means ensuring that when we call for sustainable development, financing mechanisms do not make sustainability harder to achieve.

And it means recognising that the challenges confronting small island states are not marginal issues. They are an early warning of the challenges that the wider world will increasingly face.

09/21/2026 Final Statement The United Nations must remain a place where every country - large or small - can believe that its voice matters. But the United Nations must also remain a place where ambition can become action.

Mister President,

We must also confront the serious challenges facing the Sustainable Development Goals.

The SDGs represented a promise that, by 2030, we would make meaningful progress in ending poverty and hunger, improving health and education, advancing equality, protecting our planet and building more peaceful and inclusive societies.

Today, that promise is at risk. Conflict, climate change, debt distress, inflation and persistent inequality have pushed the Goals further out of reach for many developing countries.

09/21/2026 Final Statement But this is not the time to abandon the 2030 Agenda. It is the time to renew our commitment and concentrate on delivering results that people can see and feel in their daily lives.

For Dominica, we have incorporated the SDG’s as priorities in our National Resilience Development Strategy 2030, our Climate Resilience and Recovery Plan and our wider development agenda.

We see sustainable development in the homes we have built for vulnerable families; in our investment in geothermal energy as cleaner, more affordable and reliable energy.

We see it in our efforts to strengthen education, expand technical and vocational training and better prepare our young people for the world of work. We see it in our support for farmers, entrepreneurs, agro-processors and tourism operators who are creatin g jobs and building stronger local industries.

09/21/2026 Final Statement We also see it in our work to protect our forests, marine resources and natural environment. For Dominica, these resources are part of our identity, but they are also essential to our food security, our tourism product and the livelihoods of our people.

Excellencies,

The challenges before us cannot be overcome by any one country acting alone. They require a strong and effective United Nations, renewed international cooperation and a firm commitment to multilateralism.

We need a United Nations that does more than respond to crises after lives have been lost and communities destroyed. We need an Organization that works with determination to prevent conflict, advance sustainable development, confront injustice and protect those who are most vulnerable.

We need a system in which every country, regardless of its size, wealth or influence, has a voice and a meaningful place at the table. We need 09/21/2026 Final Statement multilateralism that is not selective in its concern or uneven in its response, but fair, effective and responsive to the needs of all people.

Our development must include young people, women and girls,

Indigenous Peoples, persons with disabilities, the elderly and communities that have too often been left behind.

If the United Nations is to deliver for all, it must first see, hear and include all.

Multilateralism is our best hope for addressing challenges that cross borders, threaten our shared future and demand collective action.

We therefore remain committed to peace, climate action, sustainable development and the dignity of every human being. We remain ready to work with all nations, in a spirit of mutual respect and shared responsibility, to build a fairer, safer and more resilient world.

09/21/2026 Final Statement Mister President Let this Eighty -first Session be remembered as the moment when we collectively renewed our faith in cooperation, and matched our words with action.

Let this Eighty-first Session be remembered as the moment when vulnerability was met with solidarity, promises were honoured and trust was rebuilt through meaningful delivery.

Above all, let this Eighty-first Session be remembered as the moment when this family of nations found the courage to act together and recommitted ourselves to ensuring that no country, no community and no person was left behind.

Ayahora, thank you.

I thank you for the courtesy of your attention.

President of the General Assembly.
United Nations Secretary general, heads of State and Government.

Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen.
Switzerland is a country of mountains, valleys and different languages.
Part of our history, therefore, meant learning to live with what divides us.
We didn't make the mountains disappear.

First we learnt to climb them, then to cross them.
To do so, we built roads, bridges and tunnels.
And we realized that a natural boundary is not necessarily a dividing line.
It can also be a pathway that connects us.

This very simple experience seems to me to have something to teach us about the world in which we live.
Because we are going through a time of upheaval.
The international order established in the aftermath of the Second World War is under severe constraints Conflicts are multiplying and becoming deadlocked.
The most fundamental principles of the United Nations Charter.

The prohibition of the use of force and respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity are being openly violated.
Added to this are transformations that are reshaping our societies.
Climate change and the increase in the number of disasters, humanitarian crises, inequalities and also technological upheavals, notably artificial intelligence which are often advancing faster than our collective ability to assess their implications.
At the same time, multilateral institutions are having to respond to an increasing number of crises while facing pressure, pressure on resources and an erosion of trust.

The theme of this 81st session of the General Assembly Restoring Trust, managing transformation, a United Nations that delivers for all, therefore aptly sums up the task before us to restore trust to support transformation, and to demonstrate through concrete results that cooperation remains possible.
This erosion of trust extends far beyond the realms of peace and security.
We are also seeing it in the global economy.
Protectionism is on the rise.

Supply chains built up over decades of interdependence are being reorganized or fragmented as a result of geopolitical tensions The multilateral trading system has been weakened, and the WTO can no longer fully carry out some of its essential functions Yet what is at stake here is not merely a technical issue of trade policy.
The question is whether relations between states will continue to be governed by common rules, or if they will increasingly depend on the weight and power of each individual state.
For Switzerland, this is a fundamental issue.
That is because my country is an open economy with few natural resources.

A large part of its prosperity, therefore depends on trade, but also on the stability and predictability of the rules that make such trade possible.
Economic resilience requires us to diversify relationships, forge new partnerships, and keep trade between different regions of the world as open as possible.
This is particularly important for economies with fewer resources or limited market access.
Access to markets knowledge and technology can create opportunities that would not otherwise exist.

These abstract concepts encompass quite concrete realities a business that can take on an apprentice, a family that can secure a more stable income, a producer who can trade beyond their local market.
Young people for whom the range of possibilities suddenly widens.
That is also what we mean when we talk about a global economy.
Trust is built when the rules offer everyone a genuine opportunity to participate.

It is also built when states continue to engage in dialogue.
Switzerland is neutral.
This neutrality goes hand in hand with a steadfast commitment to the UN charter, international law and the UN's three pillars peace and security, human rights and sustainable development.
Our experience has also taught us that dialogue is not a sign of weakness.

Engaging in dialogue does not mean glossing over disagreements or abandoning one's principles.
Engaging in dialogue means maintaining contact.
When positions begin to diverge.
A bridge does not require the two banks of a river to become alike.

It simply allows us to cross from one to the other.
In times of tension, this possibility often becomes essential.
Dialogue is a tool for de-escalation when crises erupt.
Above all, it can serve as a means of prevention before crises arise.

It is in this spirit that Switzerland will continue to offer its good offices and provide spaces where those who are no longer on speaking terms can.
When.
When circumstances permit.
Resume dialogue.

Geneva is one such space.
It is home to the UN, the WTO and numerous other international organizations, as well as scientific ones, humanitarian actors, representatives of civil society and permanent missions of almost every country in the world.
Every day, people from different backgrounds representing interests that are sometimes at odds with one another come together here.
They do not need to agree in order to talk to one another.

That is exactly what gives such a place its value.
Switzerland will therefore continue as the host state to ensure that Geneva remains open, accessible and inclusive for large states and small for the North and the South.
But inclusion is not merely about having a seat at the table.
It also means being able to make a real contribution to decisions that will affect one's own future.

This is the case with international cooperation.
Every society must be able to shape its future in accordance with its history, needs and priorities.
Cooperation is not about imposing one's own values or a single model.
It is valuable when it creates partnerships, facilitates the sharing of expertise, and strengthens everyone's capacity to act independently.

It is less about doing things for others than doing things with them.
This principle takes on particular significance in the face of current technological revolutions.
AI is the most obvious illustration of this.
It offers considerable new possibilities in science, the economy, medicine, education, and the management of resources But it also highlights the risk of a new divide between those who have the skills and infrastructure needed to participate in this transformation, and those who are likely to feel only its effects.

We must ensure that technological progress broadens opportunities without widening the gaps.
This means that as many countries and societies as possible must be able to benefit from advances in AI, develop their skills and contribute to the debate on the rules that will govern its development and use.
This is exactly the aim of the Geneva AI summit, which will take place on the 21st and 22nd of June 2027 under the motto Bridging Innovation and Trust.
These two concepts must go hand in hand.

Innovation in which society is no longer have confidence risks being rejected Conversely, rules that would prevent all innovation would deprive us of enormous potential.
Our responsibility, therefore, is to strike a balance to enable progress and promote its benefits, while creating the conditions for the reliable and responsible development and use of these technologies.
Artificial intelligence thus reminds us of a simple truth.
Certain changes are so far reaching and so fast moving, that no single state can manage all of their consequences by itself.

We need institutions capable of dealing with issues that transcend national borders.
We need multilateralism.
But multilateralism will only retain its credibility if it is also able to evolve.
Switzerland therefore supports efforts to reform the UN system as part of the UN 80 initiative This reform must make the UN more coherent, more effective and more results oriented, while respecting the powers and responsibilities of member states.

The UN must focus its efforts where its action brings real added value.
When problems transcend borders.
When national or regional capacities are insufficient, or when a universal institution is needed to provide a common framework.
The key question is therefore a simple one how can we ensure that the resources, expertise and energy invested in the multilateral system yield better results for those it is meant to serve?

Because our institutions do not exist for their own sake, they exist for the people, for those who live in fear of conflict, for those who have lost their home following a disaster, for those seeking work or building a future for themselves, for the children whose lives depend on access to education and the new opportunities we are creating today.
It is on this scale that the value of multilateralism is ultimately measured.
Ladies and gentlemen, Your Excellencies, we cannot make the diverging interests of our countries disappear.
We cannot erase disagreements, rivalries, or borders, nor can we remove all of the mountains that stand between us.

But we can determine how we wish to tackle them.
We can preserve open dialogue rather than erect more barriers.
We can keep the channels of communication open.
Rather than resign ourselves to silence, we can ensure that technological progress creates more opportunities rather than new divisions.

And we can reform our institutions rather than accept their gradual demise.
Switzerland will continue to play its part, using the means at its disposal by upholding international law, promoting dialogue, providing its good offices, supporting effective multilateral institutions, and by remaining a country where the world can continue to come together and engage.
We do not claim to have all the answers, but our experience in the Alps has taught us one simple thing.
While a mountain might separate us, it can just as easily be crossed.

Crossing it brings people together.
Coming together encourages dialogue, and dialogue fosters trust.
Perhaps this is where our shared responsibility begins.
To keep open the pathways that allow us, in spite of our differences, to continue moving forward, hand in hand.

Thank you very much for your attention.

Mr. President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

On behalf of the Party, State and People of Viet Nam, I warmly congratulate H.E. Dr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly. I am confident that under his leadership, this session will be a great success. I also highly appreciate the contributions of H.E. Ms. Annalena Baerbock,

President of the 80th Session of the General Assembly.

I wish to pay special tribute to Secretary -General António Guterres for his dedicated service to the United Nations and the international community. Throughout nearly a decade of formidable challenges, he has steadfastly upheld the values of the Charter, while working alongside Member States to strengthen the role and effectiveness of the United Nations.

Mr. President, Excellencies,

The world is undergoing profound shifts in the international order, with many risks and uncertainties. The tendency towards the use or threat of force and the arms race, particularly the modernization of nuclear weapons and the development of new technology weapon s, are heightening the risks of confrontation, miscalculation and conflict, even of large-scale wars.

At the same time, the global economy is becoming increasingly fragmented, amid mounting barriers to trade, investment and technology. Supply -chain disruptions and economic instability are narrowing development opportunities for many countries.

Climate change, natural disasters, pandemics and emerging technological risks continue to pose direct threats to people’s lives and livelihoods, as well as to the development and stability of many nations.

Shifts in the balance of power and development inequalities are placing growing strains on international relations. Instability is further exacerbated when competition goes unchecked, commitments are left unfulfilled and international law is applied select ively.

An erosion of trust is further impeding efforts at cooperation.

What should concern us is not only how the international order is changing, but where that change will take our world. Change is inevitable, for it is part of the objective course of history. Conflict and confrontation, however, are not inevitable. From our own history,

Viet Nam understands profoundly the cost of war, the value of independence, and the power of reconciliation and cooperation.

It is therefore my belief that the theme of this Session, “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all,” aptly reflects the urgent demands of our time.

Mr. President,

From the losses of the Second World War, humanity created the United Nations with the aspiration to prevent war, safeguard peace, promote cooperation, and place relations among nations on a foundation of common principles. Over the past eight decades, despite its limitations, the United Nations has helped sustain dialogue, advance decolonization, uphold the right of peoples to self-determination, and support development.

These achievements must be preserved and carried forward. Our institutions must be reformed to keep pace with the times, while the fundamental principles of the United Nations Charter must be respected and reinforced. What we seek is a more equitable, democratic and inclusive international order, where every country has a voice and every nation has the opportunity to develop.

The mission of our generation is to help shape and manage change so that competition does not turn into confrontation, differences do not lead to conflict, and advances in science and technology do not create new divides.

In that spirit, I wish to put forward four major priorities:

First, we must restore trust among nations on the basis of respect for the UN Charter and international law.

The UN Charter and international law form the foundation of the international order. They must be respected fully, consistently and without selectivity. All States must respect one another’s independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity and right to choose th eir own path of development; refrain from interference in internal affairs; and refrain from the threat or use of force inconsistent with the UN Charter.

Restoring trust does not require countries to erase their differences, but rather to manage those differences responsibly. Crises must be prevented. Competition must be kept under control. Dialogue must be sustained. Commitments must be honored and fully implemented. Major powers should lead by example in respecting international law, exercising restraint and responsibly addressing common challenges.

The United Nations must remain at the center of these efforts.

In every conflict, civilians must be protected, international humanitarian law must be respected, and humanitarian access must be ensured. Viet Nam supports the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination and the two-State solution, with an indep endent State of Palestine living peacefully alongside the State of Israel, in accordance with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions.

In the Asia-Pacific, nearly six decades of ASEAN’s development have demonstrated that countries can transform suspicion into trust, confrontation into dialogue, division into cooperation, and individual strength into collective strength.

In that spirit, Viet Nam remains steadfast in its commitment to resolving disputes, including those in the East Sea, by peaceful means and in accordance with international law, particularly the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. Viet Nam is resolute in safeguarding its sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction. The seas and oceans must remain spa ces of peace, cooperation, connectivity and sustainable development.

In the same spirit of peace and respect for peoples’ right to development, Viet Nam has always stood in solidarity with the State and People of Cuba. We call upon the United States to end the unilateral embargo and sanctions and the energy blockade against Cuba, and to remove Cuba from the list of State Sponsors of Terrorism. We also call upon the international community to support Cuba in overcoming the sanction-driven crisis.

Second, we must advance development that is equitable, humane, inclusive and sustainable.

International commitments must be translated into action and bring people lives of peace, security, dignity and happiness. It is for this reason that the Pact for the Future and the 2030 Agenda, our promises to present and future generations, must be implemented earnestly and in full.

Commitments on financing for development, including the Sevilla Commitment, must be translated into concrete measures: expanding access to long -term financing at affordable cost, supporting countries burdened by debt, and amplifying the voice of developing countries in international financial and monetary institutions. The multilateral trading system must be strengthened in an open, equitable and transparent manner, ensuring development opportunities for all countries.

Climate action must be accorded its rightful place in development cooperation, particularly through adaptation finance, technology transfer and a just energy transition.

Development must be people-centered and leave no one behind. Growth must go hand in hand with social progress and equity, environmental protection and the safeguarding of people’s livelihoods, particularly in vulnerable countries and communities. Global progress must uphold the spirit of humanity in relations among nations, safeguard their legitimate interests, and respect differences in history, culture and development conditions.

Third, we must proactively shape technology governance so that progress serves humanity and our common development.

Science, technology, digital transformation and artificial intelligence are opening up unprecedented opportunities, while also presenting new challenges. The future of technology does not automatically guarantee equity. Technological progress must help narrow divides and expand development opportunities, rather than create new forms of dependency or new sources of conflict.

We need to develop inclusive, safe, transparent and accountable principles and governance frameworks to ensure that technology serves people, while respecting national sovereignty, digital sovereignty and the right to development. Developing countries must be able to participate substantively in rule -making, receive support for infrastructure and digital capacity, and enjoy equitable access to the benefits of scientific and technological progress.

Viet Nam’s hosting of the Opening for Signature of the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime in Ha Noi in 2025 reflects our desire to make substantive contributions to global digital cooperation. Viet Nam stands ready to work with partners to streng then cooperation and build capacity in preventing and combating cybercrime, so that people may live safely and benefit from technological progress.

Viet Nam also stands ready to support international initiatives on green and digital transformation and the development of effective governance frameworks, so that science and technology can truly become drivers of shared development.

Fourth, we must strengthen multilateralism and the central, indispensable role of the United Nations.

The strength of the United Nations does not lie in its ability to replace the responsibilities of States, but in its legitimacy and capacity to build consensus, establish norms, develop rules, and mobilize global efforts to address common challenges.

For the United Nations to adapt to the transformations of our time, Viet Nam supports efforts to reform the Organization, particularly the General Assembly, the Security Council and the Secretariat, with a view to enhancing effectiveness, prioritizing structural reform and streamlining the apparatus, while fully harnessing the Organization’s advantages in advancing global agendas and safeguarding the interests of developing countries.

Mr. President,

The perspectives I have just shared are drawn from the experience of Viet Nam itself.

Viet Nam’s nearly half -century journey alongside the United Nations mirrors the transformation of our own country. From being primarily a recipient of invaluable assistance during the years of reconstruction and Doi Moi, Viet Nam today is increasingly making proactive contributions to our common endeavors, while deepening and broadening our substantive relations with the United Nations. Vietnamese military personnel and police officers have served, and continue to serve, in United Nations peacekeeping operations, carrying our nation’s aspiration for peace to places where peace remains fragile.

Our tradition of independence and self -reliance provides the foundation for Viet Nam to strengthen its strategic autonomy and proactively pursue international integration.

Looking towards our goal of becoming a developing country with modern industry and upper-middle income by 2030, and a developed, high-income country by 2045, Viet Nam is establishing a new development model based on productivity, quality and added value; with science, technology, innovation and digital transformation as key drivers; and w ith economic growth closely linked to cultural development, social progress and equity, and environmental protection.

Autonomy also means proactively adapting and cooperating with the world on an equal footing. Viet Nam therefore pursues the consistent foreign policy of independence, autonomy, self -reliance, peace, friendship, cooperation and development, and of multilateralization and diversification of external relations. Viet Nam will remain steadfast in upholding the UN Charter and international law, promoting dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes, and deepening its participation in United Nations peacekeeping operations. Viet Nam is working together with fellow Member States to build a united, self-reliant and resilient ASEAN, and is actively preparing to host APEC in 2027, contributing to peace, cooperation and development in the region and the world.

As a member of the United Nations Human Rights Council, Viet Nam champions dialogue and cooperation in promoting and protecting human rights and in ensuring that all people can share in the fruits of development. Viet Nam stands ready to share its experien ce in poverty reduction, agricultural development and climate change adaptation, and to work with partners to broaden cooperation for common interests.

Mr. President, Excellencies,

The world will continue to change. The direction of such change will depend on the choices we make and the responsibilities we shoulder today.

Viet Nam chooses peace, cooperation and development. We will work steadfastly with all nations to strengthen the United Nations, uphold international law, and translate our shared commitments into tangible benefits for our people.

Viet Nam believes that, with a strong United Nations, together we can build a more peaceful, equitable, inclusive and better world for all. On th is journey, Viet Nam will remain an active member, a trusted partner and a responsible nation, ready to contribute to the common endeavors of the international community.

Thank you.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished Delegates,

Good evening.

Mr. President,

I warmly congratulate you on your election to lead the eighty-first session of this General Assembly. You assume this high office at a defining moment for our Organisation and for humanity. Seychelles assures you of its full support and wishes you every success in guiding our work.

Mr. Secretary-General,

As this is the final General Assembly you will address in your current capacity,

Seychelles extends its profound gratitude for your decade of dedicated stewardship.

You have consistently championed a United Nations that is more effective, responsive, and grounded in the needs of the people we serve.

Mr. President,

The theme of this session strikes at the core of our contemporary global crisis: trust has eroded, yet structural transformation is urgently upon us.

In a world increasingly fractured by geopolitical rivalry, the answer cannot be a retreat into isolationism. It must be a revitalized commitment to multilateralism. The United Nations must prove that dialogue can bridge division, that international law must prevail over force, and that collective action achieves what unilateralism never can.

Seychelles approaches the world guided by an enduring, foundational principle: we are a friend to all, and an enemy to none.

Our commitment to non-alignment is not passive indifference; it is an active choice for peace. It is the conviction that principled diplomacy, mutual respect, and international law are the true foundations of global stability.

Small states like ours do not seek strategic competition—we seek shared solutions.

This requires a multilateral system that is principled yet practical, ambitious yet accountable, and representative yet effective. In short, a United Nations that delivers for all.

If multilateralism is to deliver, it must first secure the peace upon which all human progress depends. Without peace, sustainable development is an illusion. Conflict destroys lives, uproots communities, and diverts vital resources away from healthcare, education, and climate resilience.

We must reject the normalization of perpetual conflict and the selective application of international law. International law must apply equally to all—without exception, bias, or double standards.

This principle is vital to maritime security. The oceans are the lifeblood of global trade.

When maritime routes are threatened by piracy, geopolitical friction, or armed aggression, the shocks ripple far beyond regional waters, devastating vulnerable island economies.

Freedom of navigation and maritime security must be preserved under international law. Small and vulnerable states should never bear the collateral economic costs of conflicts in which they have no part.

Furthermore, we firmly reject unilateral coercive measures that violate international law and inflict disproportionate hardship on innocent populations.

Yet, our global architecture is failing to enforce these principles because its key organs remain outdated. The Security Council’s inability to act decisively in moments of global crisis undermines its very purpose. Its composition reflects a bygone era, not twentyfirst-century geopolitical realities.

Reform is no longer a matter of political convenience—it is a matter of institutional survival and legitimacy.

Seychelles reaffirms Africa’s unified position: our continent must hold no fewer than two permanent seats on the Security Council, with full prerogatives, including the veto for as long as it exists.

Mr. President,

This past June, Seychelles proudly celebrated fifty years of independence. Half a century of self-determination has taught us a fundamental lesson: size does not define sovereignty, and geography does not diminish dignity.

We may be a Small Island Developing State, but we sit as an equal participant in this hall. Every nation—regardless of population or economic power—possesses an inherent right to sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national dignity.

Today, however, sovereignty faces quiet, insidious threats. Transnational organized crime, drug trafficking, and illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing threaten our security, wreck our marine ecosystems, and steal from our people.

Because these threats are interconnected, our response must be equally integrated: stronger international intelligence-sharing, expanded maritime surveillance, and practical law enforcement support. It is unreasonable to expect nations safeguarding vast oceanic domains with modest budgets to meet standards set by heavily resourced states without providing them the tools to do so.

Resilience without resources is not resilience - it is merely survival.

The same logic applies directly to the climate crisis.

For Seychelles, climate change is not a prospective debate; It is a daily reality that strikes at the very foundations of our society. Rising seas threaten our infrastructure, our coastal livelihoods, and our very territory.

The science is undisputed. The targets are clear. What remains missing is political will and execution. Major emitters must display greater ambition, while all nations act according to their responsibilities and capabilities. Economic growth that bankrupts the planet for future generations is not progress.

Seychelles welcomes the Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice on climate change, reinforcing that climate action is rooted in international law, equity, and intergenerational justice. Mitigation, adaptation, technology transfer, and lossand-damage funding are not acts of charity—they are legal obligations.

Our survival is inextricably linked to the health of the ocean. Protecting our marine environment is an economic necessity. As an early ratifying state of the BBNJ Agreement, Seychelles looks forward to its first Conference of the Parties and urges all Member States to finalize their ratifications swiftly.

Yet, our ambitions are hampered by structural economic barriers. Frameworks like the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS and the Sevilla Commitment must be backed by real capital. For small island states, debt sustainability is a matter of national survival.

We require affordable, accessible, long-term financing, meaningful debt relief, and the full implementation of the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index (MVI). Measuring a nation’s development solely by GDP per capita ignores extreme exposure to climate shocks and geographic isolation. If international finance is to serve reality, it must first measure reality correctly.

Looking ahead, we must also address the rapid rise of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies.

While these tools offer immense opportunities for development and ocean management, they also risk widening the global divide and enabling new forms of warfare and cybercrime.

We must ensure technology serves human dignity. We call for global digital governance anchored in human rights, ethical standards, and international law—with the United Nations playing a central role in steering this transformation.

Mr. President,

Excellencies,

Across every crisis we face, one fundamental truth endures: our ultimate duty is to the people we represent—our families, our youth, our coastal communities, and future generations.

Our nations represent a rich tapestry of cultures, languages, and political systems. But diversity need not breed division. Guided by our policy of friend to all and enemy to none, Seychelles believes that our differences can be the dynamic foundation for stronger global cooperation.

Let us restore trust through deliberate action:

By upholding the rule of international law unconditionally; By reforming our global governance institutions to reflect today’s world; By delivering equitable climate and development finance; and By protecting our shared oceans and climate.

Seychelles enters this General Assembly with deep humility, clear conviction, and an unshakable belief in the multilateral system. We may be a small nation, but our voice, our sovereignty, and our aspirations will never be measured by our size on a map.

Let this eighty-first session be remembered not for the divisions we inherited, but for the courage, solidarity, and resolve with which we overcame them.

Let us restore trust. Let us manage transformation. And together, let us build a United Nations that truly delivers for every nation and every human being.

Thank you.

Mr President,

Mr Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished Delegates,

Ekamawir Omo. I bring you warm greetings from my people and my country.

We meet under the theme, “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all.” For my country, that means ensuring no nation — regardless of size or distance — is left behind as the world changes around us.

Mr President,

Let me begin by congratulating you on your election to preside over this eighty -first session. My delegation assures you of our full support, and we thank your predecessor for the stewardship of the eightieth session.

We also pay tribute to Secretary-General António Guterres. This is the last General Debate of his tenure, and my country records its gratitude for a decade in which the smallest States were heard more often than before.

I have travelled far to speak on matters that may seem distinct, but are united by a single, fundamental principle: the right of every people to be treated as an equal, and to speak for itself.

Mr President,

There are moments in the life of a nation when its people are called to remember who they have always been. This is such a moment for us. And so I begin with something deeply personal to my people and my country: our name.

For many years, the world has known our country as Nauru. Nauru is how our name sounded to those who found it hard to say, and the world kept it. But it is not the name our people used among themselves.

I rise on my first point not to announce a change, but to affirm a truth. Long before our country took its place among the family of nations —long before our name appeared on international records—our people knew our homeland by one name: Naoero.

That name carries the memory of our ancestors, our language, and our identity. It has been there all along. Never lost, never absent. Today, we restore Naoero.

We do not make this choice to erase our past. We make it because we honor it. We do so with respect for our history, and with gratitude for the journey “ Nauru” has carried us through to our independence and our place on the international stage.

Mr President,

My Government’s priority is investing in our people and our future generations. Restoring our name gives back to them a piece of their inheritance. Because the identity handed down by our own ancestors has a place in the community of nations. Because their history and language matter.

Because they too have the right to inherit a nation that knows itself, names itself, and speaks for itself.

In light of this year's theme, let me say this: there can be no genuine trust and no true transformation without respect for the identity, history, language, and right of every people to be treated as an equal, and to speak for itself.

I take the opportunity now to convey my sincerest gratitude to the Secretariat, this Assembly, and the many institutions and partners who have taken steps to recognise our restored name. It may seem a small courtesy but it meant a great deal at home.

And so Mr President,

I say this with the greatest pride: Anga dei-Naoero (which means ‘I am from Naoero’). And so is every person I have the honor to speak for today.

We take our seat under that name proud of where we have come from. Confident in who we are.

And determined to carry our name into the future.

What I ask of the world costs nothing. Join us in recognizing and respecting the identity that is already ours.

Say our name. Naoero.

DEEP SEABED Mr President,

Naoero is an ocean State. We are not merely guardians of the ocean, but rightful participants in its future. For Naoero, the ocean represents both opportunity and responsibility. Never one without the other. Both are essential, or the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea is left hollow.

Today, I focus on a part of it that belongs to no one —the deep seabed area beyond national jurisdiction.

Mr President,

The Convention established the International Seabed Authority and charged it with a clear legal obligation to put in place regulations and regulate activities in parallel with sponsoring States. Its role is not to determine whether deep seabed mining is, as a matter of public policy, a correct course of action.

Naoero joined trusting in the commitments set out in the Convention and the 1994 Agreement. For fifteen years, Naoero has invested critical resources in sponsoring the exploration of a portion of the deep seabed. Our sponsored entity, Nauru Ocean Resources Inc, has contributed about one petabyte of data — more than one-third of all Clarion-Clipperton Zone data held in the Authority’s DeepData.

We called on the Authority to seek an Advisory Opinion on the responsibilities of sponsoring States, and we followed it. We established a national regulator with the powers and due diligence obligations that opinion requires.

At every stage, our decisions have rested on the best available scientific evidence, on the Convention, and on that Opinion. At every stage, we have called for the Mining Code to be finished. And when progress stalled, we looked to the 1994 Agreement and invoked the two-year rule. We were told we were rushing. That was five years ago, and the rules remain unwritten.

We are participating in the first contentious proceedings before the Seabed Disputes Chamber, because our obligations as a sponsoring State require legal clarity.

For fifteen years we have done everything a member State can do consistent with our obligations as a sponsoring State. And we continue to wait.

Mr President,

There is a general understanding within the Authority ’s Council that “ nothing is agreed until everything is agreed”. And that the regulations will be adopted by consensus. Achieving that is a great challenge for an institution whose members remain deeply divided on whether deep seabed mining should proceed at all. A question the Convention never asked the Authority to decide.

Naoero welcomes every effort to ensure that seabed mineral development proceeds responsibly.

And I ask this Assembly to reckon with this: a principle declared in 1970, and a bargain struck in 1994 — both in this hall — still wait for the rules that would give them effect.

When a multilateral process cannot deliver, the world does not stand still. Those with the means to act will not wait. And every year of delay makes that more likely, not less.

That is why the theme of this session matters. A multilateral system that cannot deliver for a State like mine does not deliver for all. That holds here in this Assembly, and in any institution we build.

Naoero therefore calls upon the Authority to let the waiting end. Adopt the rules.

Mr President,

My Government’s central purpose is to put Naoero on its own feet.

That work is under way. Our Trust Fund, to which we contribute more than ten per cent of our revenue every single year, so that Naoero has something to stand on when these arrangements end.

Our fisheries. The seabed. Joining the Egmont Group. New revenue through our investment and residence programmes. A virtual asset regulator built with full due diligence obligations before the industry it regulates. Our valuable partnerships. And behind all of it, investment in health, education and sport, so that our people are not only better off but healthier and better prepared.

We are building an economy that does not depend on any single arrangement. And by every measure of fiscal discipline, we have done what was asked of us.

Yet the measure by which we are assessed sees none of it. It sees income, and nothing else. It does not capture the full story of my nation: the true cost of our geographic isolation, the fragility of our limited economic base, or the devastating impact a single disaster can have on our people and our progress.

In January 2027, Naoero will be considered a high -income country in the OECD system. That reflects real progress. But progress should not be punished.

Because fifty-eight per cent of our revenue comes from bilateral arrangements that are not ours to renew. Eighty-seven per cent of the food our people eat is purchased and imported. We have one runway. One port. One road that connects everything we have.

None of that appears in how we are assessed.

That is why we strongly support the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index and the United Nations’ efforts to pilot the tool. Its full implementation is essential to ensuring that countries like ours are fairly assessed and adequately supported. It recognises that vulnerability is complex, and it must be seen, measured, and acted upon.

Mr President,

We acknowledge the significant progress made by some development partners and financial institutions in adopting vulnerability assessments and reviewing their eligibility criteria. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) weighs vulnerability alongside income, and its own policy names my nation as the clearest example of why income alone conceals what small island states face. As a country that is ranked the fifth most vulnerable country in the world on the Index, and the most vulnerable in the Pacific, we welcome these developments as positive steps.

But a gap remains. Not all have taken the necessary steps to truly recognise our realities. I therefore urge all who have yet to do so, including the World Bank, to weigh vulnerability alongside income in decisions on eligibility, as the ADB already does.

If the international community is truly serious about restoring trust and managing transformation, it must demonstrate that commitment where it matters most: with those who are most vulnerable.

PARTNERSHIP Mr President,

I turn to my final point. No country of our size stands alone. Naoero is a friend to all and an enemy to none.

Naoero’s partnerships are not all of one kind. Some are born of kinship. Some of shared interests.

Some have been built through decades of cooperation. And some are grounded in the conviction that when a wrong persists, it must be named and addressed.

Each relationship matters. None is a substitute for another. And none comes at the expense of another.

Mr President,

Small States are increasingly asked to choose. B etween partners, between blocs, between competing visions of the world. Naoero will not be made to choose. We will work with every partner who respects our sovereignty and our right to decide our own future. That is not neutrality.

It is independence.

Partnership does not mean agreement on everything. It means standing together where interests align, and standing on principle where they do not.

A friend I speak for today has been waiting for justice. I am asking this Assembly to honour its word, and I cannot then fall silent when that word is broken for someone else. For thirty-three consecutive years, this Assembly has called for an end to the embargo against Cuba. Naoero reiterates that call and we encourage dialogue grounded in full respect for sovereignty. Because sovereign equality must be more than a principle written in the Charter.

Whatever this Assembly intends to deliver, it will be delivered through partnership and cooperation, or not at all.

So let me extend an invitation to the members of this Assembly.

Invest in our people. Invest in an economy that rests on more than a handful of arrangements.

Invest in institutions that will outlast my Government and the next. Invest in the infrastructure, connectivity and opportunities that distance has too often denied us.

What Naoero offers this Assembly is not dependence, but participation. Not expectation, but contribution. Not a beneficiary, but a partner.

Invest with us, not simply in us.

Mr President,

Everything I have raised today concerns this Organization and what it has promised.

So does this:

The Security Council does not reflect the world as it is. It reflects the world as it was in 1945, when most of the countries in this hall did not yet exist as sovereign States. Naoero therefore calls for reform that expands both the permanent and non-permanent categories.

A body that speaks for all of us should look like all of us.

CONCLUSION Mr President,

As I draw my statement to a close, the matters I have raised may appear separate. They are not.

Our name is about sovereignty. How we are measured is about justice. The deep seabed is about opportunity and responsibility. Our partnerships are about standing as equals. One principle binds them: the right of every people to be treated as an equal, and to speak for itself.

You have convened this Assembly to restore trust, manage transformation, and deliver for all.

Trust is restored when promises are kept. Transformation is managed when decisions lead to action. And we deliver for all only when we deliver for the small.

Everything Naoero has asked for today was agreed in this hall long before I took this floor. I am not asking this Assembly to be braver than it has ever been. I am challenging you to be as good as your word.

Say our name.

Let the waiting end.

Let vulnerability be measured honestly.

Treat us as partners.

May God bless the Republic of Naoero, and may God bless the United Nations.

Mwa tubwa kor. I thank you.

1. Courtesy It is indeed a great honor and privilege to address this Assembly on behalf of H.E. Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan,

President of the United Republic of Tanzania. H.E. the President asked me to convey her fraternal greetings and best wishes for the success of this Session.

Mr. President; Allow me to congratulate you, on your election to preside over the 8 1st Session of the UN General Assembly. Your immense experience and diplomatic skills give us confidence in your ability to guide the proceedings of this Session successfully. Your election is also a fitting tribute to your great country, Bangladesh, with which Tanza nia enjoys excellent relations.

2. Theme of UNGA81 and UN80 Initiatives Mr. President; About eighty years ago, the UN was founded in San Francisco on a simple but enduring principle: that nations can prevent war and advance peace through trust, collective action and respect for the UN Charter. Today, war and insecurity are not the only existential threats to our survival, but a range of challenges including climate change, pandemics, ungoverned Artificial Intelligence and energy insecurity, just to mention a few. These challenges should remind us of a need for a stronger and much more coordinated UN. Therefore, the theme of this session, that is “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All”, is timely for it requires us to revert to the founding principle of maintaining peace and restoring trust.

Managing transformation requires reforming the UN to meet the realities of our time. In that regard, I commend our illustrious Secretary -General, H.E. Antonio Guterres, for championing the UN80 initiative that aims to advance the transformation agenda. In our opinion, the UN80 initiative must go beyond administrative efficiency to include overall Organizational effectiveness, accountability, and representativeness, for the UN to be able to deliver for all. Further, the transformation must be undertaken with utmost caution to avoid going off -track on the development pillar and incapacitating the UN Country offices and programs.

3. Agenda 2030, Vision 2050 and Financing for Development Mr. President, Excellencies and Distinguished Delegates; While we are a few years away from 2030, progress towards attainment of the SDGs is still unimpressive. Given this situation, we need to improve our execution and ensure that every cent invested delivers results. Tanzania remains committed and has made strides in implementing the 2030 Agenda. Tanzania Vision 2050, aim to build an inclusive and competitive economy that ensures quality of life for all. We are investing in our people, productive infrastructure, technology and innovation, while creating greater opportunities for women and young people. Our ambition is to transform economic growth into lasting improvements in people's lives.

These ambitions may not be realized if the international financial architecture is not made to work for development.

Currently, when developing countries are accelerating progress, they are restricted by high borrowing costs, rising debt burdens, and limited access to affordable longterm finance.

Tanzania stresses that improvements must be made to ensure the expansion of concessional financing, mobilization of private investment, improved access to development and climate finance, and giving developing countries a stronger voice in global financial decision making.

It is without a doubt that political commitment is paramount in undertaking focused investment. In that respect, Tanzania has made significant strides in reducing maternal and child mortality by expanding facility delivery from 51 per cent in 2015 to 81 per cent in 2022. Our experience on this demonstrates that when we invest in feasible projects, and remain people -centred, development can move from promises to measurable results.

It is in this spirit that H.E. President Samia Suluhu Hassan, accepted the responsibility of championing Maternal and Child Health for the African Union. Under her leadership,

Tanzania reduced maternal deaths by 80 per cent in just seven years. We now aim to advance the Three Zeros, i.e.,

Zero Preventable Maternal and Child Deaths; Zero home deliveries; and Zero Unvaccinated Children. Our experience shows that this is an agenda that Africa can successfully achieve, but it will require sustained political leadership, adequate financing, and stronger partnerships.

We, therefore, urge the international community to join us in giving this agenda a push.

4. Climate Action Excellencies; Our efforts to address climate-related challenges continue to face unjustifiable obstacles, mainly from those contributing significantly to greenhouse gas emissions.

Global efforts to address climate challenges are being frustrated by withdrawal of financial contributions supporting climate adaptation measures and initiatives by international and regional institutions, as well as individual states. Let us prioritize delivery on the pledges for climate action by increasing long-term concessional financing and deployment of new technology.

On this agenda, Tanzania chose to address the just energy transition component through different measures. Some of these measures include, implementation of the national renewable energy strategy that comprises 2,115MW Julius Nyerere H ydro Power Project, 650MW solar and wind power projects, 130MW geothermal power projects, and the National Clean Cooking Strategy, which aims to ensure that 80% of households adopt clean cooking by 2034. In our efforts to reduce the use of fossil fuels, we have also opted for the electric railway to link the port of Dar es Salaam and neighboring countries of Burundi and DRC.

We, therefore, appeal that climate financing be provided as grants and concessional financing to step up efforts on climate action.

Mr. President; Tanzania joins Small Islands and Coastal States in pushing for a workable solution to address sea-level rise.

We commend the President for convening today the HighLevel Event addressing the existential threats posed by sea-level rise, and we look forward to the adoption of the UN Declaration on Sea -Level Rise, which will provide a comprehensive framework for international cooperation, scientific advancement, adaptation resilience, and legal stability. We welcome the Declaration's legal affirmation on the stability of maritime zones under United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea ( UNCLOS) and the continuity of statehood, even in cases of physical land loss, while encouraging strengthened international cooperation and the protection of human rights. Timely and urgent action is needed to safeguard the future of our coastal communities and island nations.

5. Sanctions and Embargoes Excellencies; Global solidarity must be concurrent with respect of each other's sovereignty. Tanzania stands against the proliferating trend of some states to assume the responsibility of policing and imposing unilateral sanctions on others, thus undermining the principles of sovereignty and peaceful co-existence. As stated previously, Tanzania reaffirms its position to oppose the use of such coercive measures against any Member State and reaffirms its unwavering solidarity with Cuba, Zimbabwe and all other states that are subjected to such unjustifiable constraints.

In line with our resolve to leave no one behind, we call for an immediate and unequivocal lifting of these measures that cause hardships, constrain development and obstruct full enjoyment of human rights.

6. Global Peace and Security Mr. President; Global peace and security are vital for sustainable socio economic development. The United Nations, through its Charter, has remained central to international efforts to maintain peace and security, uphold international law, and promote conditions conducive to development.

However, despite these longstanding commitments, the persistence of armed conflicts around the world reflects the departure from the purposes and principles of the Charter. In addition, there are emerging challenges to the authority of the United Nations Charter and the established principles of international law, often without commensurate accountability. These developments underscore the urgent need to reaffirm multilateralism, strengthen respect for international law, and reinforce the central role of the United Nations in maintaining international peace and security.

In that regard, Tanzania remains firmly committed to supporting the efforts of the U N Security Council to fulfil its primary responsibility, for the maintenance of international peace and security. our commitment is demonstrated by our two terms of service on the Security Council, during which we made substantive contributions to such cause.

Notable achievements include the adoption of Security Council Resolution 1653 (2006) on the Great Lakes Region and Tanzania’s collaboration with Denmark in establishing the Peacebuilding Commission.

Excellencies; Building on this record of service and sustained commitment to multilateralism, I am pleased to inform you that, last month, the African Union formally endorsed Tanzania’s candidacy for a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for the term 2029–2030, during elections to be held by this Assembly in June 2028. I, therefore, seize this opportunity to formally announce our candidature. During our tenure in the Council, we will put forward and prioritize deliberations on matters vital to the maintenance of international peace and security, such as preventive diplomacy and the peaceful Settlement of disputes; women in peacekeeping; youth in peace and security and the Reform of UN Peacekeeping. In the coming days, we will engage with each one of you and present our vision and respectfully seek your valued support to enable Tanzania to serve with a strong African voice, principled leadership, and unwavering commitment to international peace and security.

7. Peace in the Middle East Mr. President; Tanzania is deeply concerned and saddened by the protracted conflict and humanitarian suffering in Gaza and across the Middle East. We continue to call for the protection of civilians, unhindered humanitarian assistance, and renewed diplomacy towards lasting peace.

Furthermore, Tanzania remains firmly committed to the two-State solution, with Israel and Palestine living side by side in peace and harm ony, in accordance with international law and relevant UN resolutions. We reaffirm the right of the Palestinian people to self -determination and believe that lasting peace must guarantee the dignity, security and legitimate aspirations of both peoples. We have been consistent on this for the past 50 years. For us, this is a matter of our foreign principle.

8. Tribute to the outgoing UN Secretary-General Mr. President; On behalf of the people of the United Republic of Tanzania,

I wish to pay tribute to H.E. António Guterres as he concludes his distinguished tenure as the SecretaryGeneral of the UN. During his tenure, he steered the UN through an exceptionally challenging period marked by conflicts, geopolitical tensions, the COVID -19 pandemic, climate emergencies and growing pressure on multilateralism. In all these situations, he remained firm and undeterred.

Tanzania appreciates his support for Africa’s aspirations for peace, sustainable development, climate justice and a fairer international financial architecture, as well as his personal engagement with our country.

Similar accolades are for Ambassador Amina Mohammed,

Deputy Secretary-General, who has played a pivotal role in advancing the SDGs, advocacy for women, children and those whose voices are too often unheard. We shall miss your contribution, but Africa is proud to welcome its daughter back home. To both of you, we wish you every success and fulfillment in the years ahead.

9. Conclusion Mr. President; In conclusion, I wish to underscore that the UN must not merely reflect on the balance of power but serve as a platform for justice, solidarity, and progress. As we take stock of its invaluable contribution to the advancement of humanity, maintenance of international peace and security, socioeconomic progress, and sustainable development over the past 81 years, let us be reminded that there are more mountains to climb and milestones to accomplish. Tanzania believes that it is only by respecting and living by the Charter that we can honor the past and build a safer and better future for all.

Thank you for your attention.
