Mr. President,

Excellencies,

Ladies and gentlemen I stand before you today not as Prime Minister, but as a salesman.

And I am not here to sell you a product. Or a policy.

Or another declaration.

I am here to sell you an idea.

An idea conceived and spearheaded by His Majesty,

King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck.

An idea embraced by the people of Bhutan.

An idea already being built.

That idea is Gelephu Mindfulness City.

GMC.

And my sales pitch is simple:

Come and build it with us.

The world has built new cities before: financial centres, free ports, technology hubs, special economic zones.

But GMC is different.

Gelephu Mindfulness City is a Special Administrative Region - an SAR.

Under its Royal Charter, GMC exercises full autonomy - in governance, legislation and the judiciary.

Think one country, two systems.

Think of the agility of a microstate.

But GMC was not inherited from history. It was not created to manage a transfer of sovereignty.

It is being deliberately created - by Bhutan, within Bhutan, on sovereign Bhutanese territory - for the future.

GMC covers more than 4,000 square kilometres. That is more than five times the size of Singapore.

But its greatest opportunity is not its size.

Its greatest opportunity is an institutional blank slate.

GMC was given something extraordinarily rare: the freedom to design an entire city - and its operating system - from first principles.

So we asked:

If we could begin again, how would we govern?

What laws would we write?

How would we regulate business?

How would we guarantee an independent judiciary?

How would we attract the best talent?

How would we use technology - and especially artificial intelligence?

How would we create wealth while protecting nature?

And ultimately - what would all that prosperity be for?

These were not theoretical questions.

We answered them.

And we are making full use of that blank slate.

If Singapore has legal principles that work, we learn from Singapore.

If Abu Dhabi has financial regulation that works, we learn from Abu Dhabi.

If leading jurists from the United Kingdom can help us build an independent judiciary, we learn from them.

If international experts can strengthen our institutions, we learn from them.

The principle is simple:

Search the world for what works.

Take the best.

Adapt it.

And make it work for GMC.

The result is a core operating system that is now in place - designed to give investors clarity, familiarity and predictability.

But GMC's operating system was designed around a deeper conviction:

That prosperity and values should reinforce one another.

That means rejecting the assumption that we must choose between enterprise and wellbeing. Between technology and humanity. Between development and nature.

At GMC, we believe a balanced approach can deliver substantial profits - while protecting the values that make prosperity worthwhile.

Balance is not the enemy of profit.

It is the foundation of lasting profit.

And at GMC, balance is not a slogan.

It is built into the operating system.

This matters deeply to Bhutan.

Bhutan is peaceful and stable. Our forests are intact.

Our culture is alive. Our people are educated.

But our economy is small. It cannot yet create enough opportunities for our young people.

So too many of them leave home to find opportunity elsewhere.

For a country as small as ours, this is not only an economic challenge.

It is an existential one.

We cannot simply tell them to stay.

We must give them a reason to stay - and a reason to return.

Jobs.

Opportunities.

Enterprise.

A future.

So Bhutan must transform.

But we refuse to believe that transformation requires us to become somebody else.

We want economic growth. We want investment. We want technology. We want successful companies. We want our people to become wealthier.

But we also want to protect what makes Bhutan Bhutan.

That is the driving force behind His Majesty's vision for GMC.

And that is why His Majesty is personally spearheading its development.

GMC is not a project on the margins of Bhutan.

It is at the heart of our national transformation.

Our people have embraced GMC as a People's Project - an investment in our children, our economy and our shared future.

Bhutan is not waiting to see whether the world believes in GMC before committing to it.

We have committed.

Fully.

Now let me tell you why GMC is built to succeed.

Begin with location.

GMC sits directly on the border with India - our closest friend and neighbour.

The vision enjoys the support of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the Government of India and our neighbours across the border in Assam.

Beyond that border lies the world's most populous country - and one of its largest and fastest-growing economies.

GMC is also a gateway to the markets of South Asia and Southeast Asia.

So GMC begins with what many new cities spend decades trying to acquire: access to vast and growing markets, connectivity and, in India, a trusted friend.

Bhutan brings another advantage - one that cannot be constructed or bought.

Trust.

Trust built through peace, political stability, the rule of law and a record of honouring our commitments.

For long-term investors, trust creates something invaluable:

Predictability.

Bhutan has spent generations building that trust.

GMC puts it to work.

Then there is nature.

Imagine GMC early in the morning.

Mist rising from its rivers.

Forests stretching towards the mountains.

Elephants moving through the landscape.

Tigers still roaming its forests.

This is not empty land.

It is a living, carbon-negative landscape.

A biodiversity hotspot.

We will not build over it.

We will build within it - and protect it.

The forests, rivers and wildlife of GMC are not obstacles to development.

They are part of its value.

And then there is energy.

Bhutan is expanding its renewable-energy capacity towards 25 gigawatts by 2040.

That electricity will power GMC - and the industries of the future: advanced manufacturing, scientific research, artificial intelligence and data centres.

Clean, renewable power.

But GMC has another type of power.

A power Bhutan has cultivated for centuries.

Spiritual power.

GMC is being developed as a global centre for Vajrayana Buddhism.

Spiritual masters from across the Buddhist world are already building monasteries, retreat centres, libraries and institutions of learning.

So imagine what will exist side by side:

Entrepreneurs and monks.

Artificial intelligence and human consciousness.

Data centres and meditation centres.

The newest technologies humanity has created alongside some of the world's oldest traditions for understanding the human mind.

Is that a contradiction?

No.

That is the point.

GMC is not asking investors to choose between commercial success and quality of life.

It is designed to offer both.

Because the world's best people choose more than a workplace.

They choose where to build their lives.

Taken together, these advantages create the conditions for businesses to grow - and investors to prosper:

Lower uncertainty.

Abundant clean energy.

Access to growth.

The ability to attract global talent.

And the freedom to create the markets others will later enter.

That is how GMC turns its values into commercial advantage.

You may now reasonably ask:

It sounds wonderful.

But is it real?

Yes.

It is real.

The Royal Charter is in force. Laws have been enacted. Regulators are operating. The framework for an independent judiciary is in place.

GMC has its own government. Its own laws. Its own financial system. And its own gold-backed digital currency.

These are not aspirations.

They are foundations already in place.

The physical city is also taking shape.

Infrastructure is being built progressively - as and when it is needed.

The international airport is under construction. A railway connection to India's vast rail network is being developed. Energy, digital connectivity and urban infrastructure are being added as demand grows.

Artificial-intelligence and data-centre projects are moving forward. And nearly five billion US dollars in projects are under active negotiation.

GMC is not an idea waiting to begin.

The journey has begun.

But there is still an extraordinary opportunity to help define where it goes.

Perhaps the best way to understand GMC is to imagine it as a startup.

A 4,000-square-kilometre startup.

Most startups begin with an idea - then search for the conditions they need to succeed.

GMC begins with many of them already in place:

His Majesty's leadership.

An entire country fully committed.

Land and clean energy.

Full autonomy.

Trusted laws and institutions.

Access to vast and growing markets.

So GMC is a startup designed from the beginning for success.

And there is one guarantee I can give you:

Bhutan will not hedge its bets.

We are all-in.

Every startup needs one more critical ingredient.

Co-founders.

And that, Excellencies, is why this salesman is standing before you.

We want your capital. Your technology. Your talent.

Your ideas. Your enterprise.

And let me be absolutely clear:

We want you to make money.

GMC is not a retreat from capitalism, technology or ambition.

It is designed to harness all three - without sacrificing nature, culture or human wellbeing.

Those who come early can help create the industries and markets that others will later enter.

They can help define GMC's economic journey - and share in the value they create.

That is the first-mover advantage.

At GMC, commercial success and human flourishing are designed to build on one another.

This balance is deeply Bhutanese.

For more than half a century, Bhutan has pursued Gross National Happiness.

It does not reject economic growth.

But it does ask the essential question:

What is growth for?

GMC gives this development philosophy contemporary form - through markets, technology and investment.

But the aspiration itself is older.

For centuries, the Himalayan Buddhist world has carried an ideal of an enlightened society - where material prosperity and spiritual wisdom coexist; where good governance serves human flourishing; and where people live in harmony with one another and with nature.

That ideal is called Shambhala.

Some of our spiritual masters have looked at what is taking shape in GMC and said:

Under an enlightened King, Shambhala is being built.

We make no claim to perfection.

For us, Shambhala points not back to the past, but forward - a promise to carry its wisdom into the future.

To build a city that prospers - and has a soul.

Mr. President,

I told you at the beginning that I came here as a salesman.

Now you know what I am selling.

Gelephu Mindfulness City.

So, to governments and institutions seeking partnership - and to investors, entrepreneurs and companies seeking the next great opportunity:

Do not watch GMC being built.

Come to Bhutan.

Come to GMC.

Help define the journey.

Build it with us.

Become our co-founders.

Because the future does not simply arrive.

The future is built.

And in Bhutan - we are already building it.

Thank you and Tashidelek.

1. Introduction Mr. President, Excellencies,

The international order is experiencing a period of great instability.

The free and open international order based on the rule of law that we have fostered is facing difficult challenges on multiple fronts.

Amid a shifting balance of power and intensifying geopolitical competition, innocent civilian lives are being lost around the world every day.

The “stable post-Cold War era” is now a thing of the past. The distribution of goods is stagnating, people across the world are suffering from high cost of living, progress towards development goals is not on track, and human rights issues are arising in various places around the world.

Against this backdrop, has the United Nations, now eighty years on since its foundation, been failing to fulfill its role in promoting peace and stability around the world? We are even hearing such concerns today.

Mr. President,

Despite these concerns, the United Nations has never been more important than it is today in bringing about peace and stability to the world, and enabling the international community to overcome new challenges and prosper. Japan will continue to fulfill its significant responsibilities towards the United Nations. And I am here today to express that resolve.

This year marks the 70th anniversary of Japan’s accession to the United Nations. In this milestone year, I would first like to address how Japan has been tackling the challenges facing the international community, working hand-in-hand with the United Nations. Then, together with you all, I would like to take this opportunity to revisit the role of the United Nations in the international community.

2. Challenges facing the International Community in light of Escalating International Tensions Mr. President,

First, let us turn our attention to escalating international tensions.

The situation in the Middle East has been growing increasingly tense, and free and safe navigation is increasingly under challenge in the Strait of Hormuz, which is an international public good. Japan, in cooperation with the international community, has been continuing to engage in diplomatic efforts with a view to achieving an early deescalation of the situation across the Middle East.

Furthermore, supply concerns regarding fuel, chemical products, and medical supplies, are causing significant impact on people’s lives and business operations. Due to disruptions in the supply of fertilizers, the risk of a food crisis is mounting, with Africa and Asia being hit particularly hard.

For many years, we have engaged in dynamic trade in the free and open seas spanning the Pacific Ocean to the Indian Ocean, and together, we have built a strong and prosperous region. This holds true also in the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea. We wish to extend this to Africa as well, to turn it into a main artery for growth and prosperity. To that end, exactly ten years ago, former Prime Minister ABE Shinzo advocated a “Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP)” at the Tokyo International Conference on African Development (TICAD) held in Kenya.

However, due to the recent intensification of geopolitical tensions, free trade has been hampered, and stable energy supplies, and supply chains in general, have been disrupted.

Amid this situation, in May this year, I announced the ”Updated Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP)”. There I appealed that it is essential for countries to acquire the capabilities to freely determine their own futures and resilience across economic, social, and security domains.

Japan places particular emphasis on the following three pillars that embody this idea.

First, Japan is engaged in strengthening the resilience of supply chains for energy and critical materials.

For global energy security, it is crucial to ensure free and transparent energy trade, engage in international coordination on strengthening oil stockpiling, and enhance collaboration between producing and consuming countries. Japan has also launched the “Partnership On Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia (POWERR Asia)” to strengthen energy and resource supply resilience in Asia, and has been promoting cooperation in areas such as stockpiling capacity development and credit provision.

Furthermore, Japan is currently formulating a comprehensive cooperation plan aimed at strengthening the economic and energy resilience of the Gulf countries in the Middle East. Through this initiative, we will work to further strengthen the collaboration between the Asia-Pacific region, including Japan, and the Gulf countries to ensure a stable global energy supply.

Moreover, concerns about arbitrary export restrictions are growing throughout the international community. Japan is proposing a vision for strengthening supply chains, which encompasses not only the development of alternative supply sources, but also the enhancement of countries’ ability to respond to supply disruptions, in particular in the field of critical minerals.

One example is the “Resilient and Inclusive Supply-chain Enhancement (RISE) Partnership”. Under this initiative, we are cooperating with countries that produce critical minerals to enable them to play a greater role in mining, refining, and processing. In June, we established “RISE+” under the World Bank Group and pledged a contribution of 20 million US dollars to help develop the infrastructure essential for critical minerals production.

Second, Japan is devoted to enhancing cooperation towards peace and stability.

Since the end of the Second World War, Japan has consistently and seriously pursued efforts towards nuclear disarmament and nonproliferation. At the very heart of our aspiration for “a world without nuclear weapons” lies the earnest plea of the hibakusha: the catastrophic consequences of nuclear weapons must never be repeated.

It is Japan’s mission, as the only country to have ever suffered atomic bombings during war, to lead the efforts of the international community towards a “world without nuclear weapons”. Japan strongly calls for solidarity within the international community to maintain and strengthen the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) regime, to which both nuclear-weapon states and nonnuclear-weapon states are parties. Furthermore, Japan will persistently advance realistic and practical efforts, including enhancing the transparency of nuclear forces, and promoting a deeper understanding of the realities of atomic bombings.

The situations in Ukraine and North Korea have reminded the world of growing risks and threats posed by nuclear weapons. There are also concerns regarding the proliferation of nuclear- and missilerelated technologies through the strengthening of military cooperation between Russia and North Korea. The security of the Indo-Pacific and the Euro-Atlantic is inseparable.

The advancement of North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs, as well as its use of malicious cyber activities, including cryptocurrency thefts as a source of funding, are clear violations of relevant Security Council resolutions and pose a serious threat to international peace and security. The full implementation of Security Council resolutions, under the principle of the complete denuclearization of North Korea, is essential.

Moreover, the issue of abductions by North Korea is an ongoing matter with lives at stake. The abductees are still denied their freedoms, and their families continue to suffer. This is a matter of grave concern not only for Japan, but for the international community. As the abductees and their families are aging, the abductions issue must be resolved immediately.

For the sake of the future of both Japan and North Korea, I am prepared to engage in dialogue and take concrete action to establish a mutually fruitful relationship in accordance with the Japan–DPRK Pyongyang Declaration.

Third, Japan will continue to contribute to the maintenance and development of a free and open international order based on the rule of law.

Any attempts to unilaterally change the status quo by force or coercion are contrary to the principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations and must never be tolerated anywhere in the world.

Russia’s aggression against Ukraine is the most obvious example. A permanent member of the Security Council, with a special responsibility for international peace and security, has initiated an act of aggression against another country, and has vetoed Security Council resolutions concerning its own actions. In this current situation, it must be said that the Security Council is not functioning for international peace.

Since the end of the Second World War, Japan, as a peace-loving nation, has attached great importance to the rule of law in the settlement of any disputes. This is demonstrated by Japan’s consistent support for, and its contributions of judges to, various international judicial organs, such as the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS).

We established a unit for peace mediation within the Government of Japan in March of this year. Japan will play a more proactive role in the peaceful settlement of disputes.

Furthermore, the maritime order based on the rule of law is currently being greatly shaken in the Strait of Hormuz. Ensuring free and safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz for all vessels without additional costs, as has been the case, is extremely important not only for the security of the Middle East, but also for the stability of the global economy as a whole. Similarly, it is essential to ensure stability in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Japan will continue to work closely with relevant countries and the International Maritime Organization (IMO) towards the maintenance of the maritime order in the Middle East.

3. Japan’s Commitment to the United Nations and Multilateralism Mr. President,

Next, I would like to set out Japan’s efforts and commitments towards the United Nations and multilateralism.

Since becoming a Member State of the United Nations in 1956, Japan has acted decisively to address global challenges, such as the eradication of poverty, economic and social development, women’s empowerment, climate change, and global health. We have done so through our Official Development Assistance (ODA), channeled bilaterally or through international organizations, and have deepened our solidarity with the Global South.

To date, Japan has provided ODA totaling over 670 billion US dollars to developing countries and regions, and has dispatched almost 60,000 Japan Overseas Cooperation Volunteers to 99 countries. Additionally, Japan has been promoting initiatives towards achieving universal health coverage (UHC) across the globe.

Since 1993, Japan has co-organized the TICAD together with the United Nations. TICAD has served as a platform for reflecting Africa’s voice in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and for Japan to first put forward the concept of FOIP. Africa is endowed with a dynamic young population and possesses enormous economic potential. Japan will continue to promote its diplomacy towards Africa so that Japan and Africa can become more resilient and prosperous together. For example, we will promote industrial development, job creation, and enhanced connectivity in Africa.

Furthermore, next year, I will host the Pacific Islands Leaders Meeting (PALM) in Yokohama, Japan, which Japan has convened together with the Pacific Islands region since 1997. Japan aims to further deepen our collaboration with the Pacific Island Countries region and promote the stability and prosperity of the region, including addressing common challenges such as maritime security and climate change.

Several large-scale disasters have occurred and continuously caused extreme damage around the world this year, including in Japan.

Natural disasters are becoming more severe and frequent. Japan is striving to become the world’s leading nation in disaster risk reduction. To share Japan’s expertise and technology in disaster risk reduction and contribute to global efforts in this field, I appointed a new Minister of State for International Disaster Risk Reduction Cooperation in my Cabinet reshuffle last week. I myself, in 2015, as Minister for Internal Affairs and Communications, attended the United Nations World Conference on Disaster Reduction, where the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction was adopted.

Promoting this framework remains one of our top priorities to this day. It is in Sendai that Japan will host the Asia-Pacific Ministerial Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction in October next year.

To protect the lives of present and future generations, all States must take serious action to tackle global warming. I believe that climate action and economic growth can go hand-in-hand.

Japan has been advancing Green Transformation (GX) efforts with the goal of achieving net-zero by 2050 by harnessing Japan’s technological capabilities. Such capabilities include establishing the basis for the production and engineering of materials such as green steel, utilizing the world’s most efficient gas-fired power generation, and popularizing the adoption of energy-efficient data centers.

We will enhance these efforts with a view to strengthening the resilience of the energy supply-demand structure and vigorously advance the Policy Package for Wide Energy and Resources Resilience through Green Transformation (POWERR GX).

Furthermore, Japan will contribute to global climate action, including through GX-related efforts, such as the Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC) that simultaneously achieve decarbonization, energy security and economic growth.

Next year, Japan will host the World Horticultural Exposition 2027 in Yokohama, which is an industrial trade fair showcasing green technologies and approaches to sustainable development. We sincerely hope that many of you will come to join this expo.

There are also challenges arising from technological innovation.

Whilst advances in AI bring tremendous opportunities for humanity, they also pose challenges, including those related to national security.

We also urgently need measures to tackle the spread of information not based on facts, as well as the spread of propaganda. Japan took the initiative to launch the “Hiroshima AI Process”, establishing the world’s first international principles and code of conduct to govern generative AI. In parallel, Japan has been working with like-minded partners and Global South partners to co-create a “safe, secure and trustworthy AI” ecosystem, and will enhance cooperation on safety to respond to the risks of highly capable frontier AI. To accelerate these efforts, we intend to host an AI Summit in Japan at the earliest opportunity.

Mr. President,

Since the end of the Second World War, Japan has built the peace and prosperity it has today through the tireless efforts of our predecessors and the goodwill of a large number of countries. In the course of these efforts, Japan itself has consistently acted in the spirit of multilateralism towards addressing challenges facing the international community.

However, these challenges cannot be solved by any single country acting alone. Now, more than ever, the flag of the United Nations must be held high, and under that banner, Member States must mobilize the collective strength of the membership to elaborate new rules and build a framework for cooperation. I am convinced that the United Nations is the only organization capable of taking the helm on a global scale.

To this end as well, reform of the United Nations is essential. The United Nations is a “vessel”, and the responsibility for determining its contents lies with us, namely the Member States. Rather than lamenting the institutional fatigue of the United Nations, Member States should unite with one heart, vigorously advance reform of the United Nations and transform the organization into a more resilient and effective United Nations. Let us move forward, building on the achievements of the current Secretary-General António Guterres.

At the same time, the Charter of the United Nations, which is now 81 years old, should also be reviewed. Regarding the so-called “enemy States” clauses, a United Nations General Assembly resolution was adopted in 2005 to delete references to ‘enemy States’ from the Charter of the United Nations, expressing the resolve of the Heads of State and Government of all Member States. In accordance with this resolution, these clauses must be deleted. I would like to strongly emphasize this position as Japan takes pride and honor in its significant contributions to the efforts of the United Nations for the last 70 years.

Furthermore, as a matter of utmost importance, reform of the Security Council is urgently needed. The current structure of the Security Council, whose mandate is to maintain international peace and security, reflects the international situation as it stood in 1945.

We need to transform it without delay into a structure that truly reflects the current realities of the international community. To this end, it is essential to expand the number of both permanent and nonpermanent members in order to ensure the legitimacy and representativeness of the Security Council. A majority of Member States support the expansion of both categories.

Japan is determined to fulfill its solemn responsibility in these UN reforms.

4. Concluding Remarks Mr. President,

In the 70 years since we became a UN Member State, Japan has consistently contributed to the peace and prosperity of the international community as a peace-loving nation, under its exclusively defense-oriented policy. Furthermore, we have worked hand-in-hand with the United Nations on the two indispensable tasks of establishing rules and institutions and providing support on the ground. This policy will remain unchanged in the future. In light of this history, Japan feels a sense of responsibility to safeguard the ideals of the United Nations as our beacon of hope, and to carry that light forward into the future.

To that end, with its renewed commitment to the United Nations and multilateralism, Japan will continue to steadily take actions.

Now, at a time when the world is in turmoil, the United Nations itself must be reborn as a “more resilient and effective United Nations” and regain the trust of the international community.

Together with this more resilient and effective United Nations, Japan is determined to create peace and prosperity by making the IndoPacific and the international community more resilient and prosperous.

Thank you very much.

Madam President, Your Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, As the new British Prime Minister, I am here today to tell you how Britain will deliver leadership in a changing world for the decade that lies ahead, learning from our experience of the last one. It is now 10 years since Brexit. My country has lived through the disruption it brought, and it has given us a unique perspective that I want to share with you today. Britain is back. restoring our stability, building a more dynamic economy, a nation that wants to trade with the world and work together to solve the shared problems we face. But we have also learned that we need to adapt to meet the challenge of these times. We need to rebalance power in our country and bring it closer to people. We need to work harder to fight the forces of division and instability which threaten us. Not just through hard power but through softer, slower means that sow fear and despair. We need to do more to help people with the everyday cost of living and seize the opportunities that give them hope for the future. And we need to embrace the incredible potential of technology to improve people's lives. That's what I want to talk to you about this evening. How the world can come through the turbulence of today to reach towards something better in the decade ahead. Overcoming the forces of division and instability starts with national security. we will keep investing in our defence, meeting our NATO commitments and strengthening European capabilities. We will be relentless in building up our hard power and deterrence. But we will not play Russia's game of trading escalatory rhetoric. Unlike Russia, we do not seek confrontation. Instead, we will be prepared but not panicked. Clear-eyed but cool-headed and unflinching in defending our people and our allies. True resilience depends on this military strength, but the last 10 years tells us that it is also about something deeper as well. It is about the strength of the social fabric that binds us together. There is no national security without a strong cohesive society underneath it. That's the starting point for everything we hold dear and everything we want to achieve. But the fact is it has been under attack. In recent years, we have seen industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment in the UK and that of many of our allies. Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fears. They've used bots and fake websites, falsified newspaper articles, forged the branding of 28 British organisations including universities and the BBC. They've amplified far-right narratives and we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 general election. We also know that they have tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of horrific events. The idea that anyone would try to use such things to their advantage is just repulsive, but it is what they do. The Kremlin spends around £1.3 billion each year on manipulating information. We're talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people's homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community, creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair. On top of that we have seen cyber attacks on companies and institutions and we know that AI will multiply the threat. We have tiptoed around this for too long. Over the last decade we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative corrosive narrative about life in Britain which bears no resemblance to reality. Well, no more. We are going to face the new decade in a different way, with our eyes wide open. We are going to be much prouder in standing up for our values and the rule of law. And we are going to help our people to strengthen their resilience because faced with this information warfare, security starts in every home. If you're struggling with the cost of living and your life is not improving, or if you're a young person, not in employment, education or training, you are going to be much more vulnerable to this kind of influence. So part of the challenge is to lift our people up and create the opportunities they need. When inequalities grow too wide, our societies are at greater risk. So we will work to make life more affordable for people. That will be at the heart of a new 10-year plan for Britain that we will bring forward later in the year. And we will put in place the architecture to stem this poisonous tide. Today, I am asking our security chiefs in the UK to begin work on a new national centre for information defence. To detect, attribute and disrupt these kinds of hostile state information attacks. To support and defend our democracy. I know this is a shared challenge so we are going to use our experience in the UK and And the fact that we have already been through this shock, starting 10 years ago, to help other countries. We have already supported Moldova to protect its elections from Russian interference. As more elections approach across Europe, more nations are grappling with these issues, some for the first time. So we're ready to share our understanding of how these actors work and how we can respond because this is a vital task for our collective security and resilience. To overcome division and instability, we must also find new ways to bring countries together. We know that we are at our strongest when we unite with others, when we reach across borders to solve shared problems. Being here today, I am reminded of the huge human progress that this organisation has led, like the eradication of smallpox, or the universal declaration of human rights. That is the kind of promise and hope that led Britain to host the very first meeting of this General Assembly in London, and led to the world to create this institution, United Nations, our United Nations. That is the level of ambition that we need now to renew the UN for our times, to tackle challenges like improving global health and preventing future pandemics, to end the wars that are causing so much suffering and instability, including the terrible conflict in Sudan, and to tackle climate change. The climate That crisis is now a national security threat for countries around the world as this summer of extreme heat, wildfires and floods has proved beyond doubt. Britain will continue to lead with others to fight this threat, to protect our children and grandchildren, to protect the natural world and also to seize the benefits for jobs, growth and reindustrialisation that the clean energy transition can bring. So we must raise our sights. And I believe the United Kingdom has a unique position as an honest broker to help drive this forward. We are America's closest ally. We have deep ties with our friends in the European Union and seek to deepen them further. We work with China and emerging powers like India and Brazil. We sit on the UN Security Council in the Commonwealth, in the CPTPP. In a divided world, we have the ability to bring people together and we will. We are going to step into that role and we are going to start with one of the most significant challenges and opportunities of our age, Frontier AI. AI brings together so many of the most pressing issues before us. It is already speeding up cancer diagnosis in the UK, but AI has the potential to go further, not just to help prevent and treat cancer, but to help cure it. AI will also be the key to economic growth, the route to transforming education, and it will be a vital tool to keep us safe. I am announcing today that we are developing a new AI defence partnership with the United States to protect our critical national infrastructure. But we know that AI will also be a source of disruption to the way we live and work, a multiplier of risk. We've all heard the warnings, which we must heed. I know how worried people are, so we have to rise to this moment. Fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance. They must be taken by elected governments who serve working people. And we need to give people the support they need through this change, ensuring that it becomes an engine for re-industrialization and opportunity as well. There is a lesson from the first industrial revolution which started in Northern England two centuries ago. It was a time of incredible technological progress. But for workers, the disruption brought huge suffering and exploitation. Things got a lot worse before they got better. So this time we need to get it right. I believe we're more than equal to the task. The UK has some of the best tech and AI talent anywhere in the world. And when it comes to guarding against the risks, we have our world-leading AI security Institute working hand in glove with the US and the leading labs on AI safety. But we need to go further. Building on the meeting convened by His Majesty King Charles last week, I can announce today that I am going to put AI at the heart of the UK's G20 presidency next year. I look back at how we responded to the financial crisis back in 2008. We moved quickly in the G20 and smaller groups to deliver an urgent practical response. We came together to agree principles which everyone implemented at home in a way that was right for them. And it worked. That is the kind of approach we need now. So we will bring the right people together on the key issues, delivering on the potential of AI for good and dealing with the risks. And we will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure the transparency and access we need to increase our preparedness and to ensure that AI development is safe. This will bring together welcome initiatives from others, like that proposed by Norway this week. That is Majesty said, the task before us is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity. I want to reassure the British people that ultimately we will do whatever is necessary to protect them, including bringing forward new laws if that is what is needed. They need to know that we will protect their interests and we will. But on its own that's not enough, is it? In this dangerous turbulent age it is more important than ever that we give people the power to build their own resilience and do more for themselves and give them the platform to stand up for what they believe in. I am working to rebalance power across all regions of the UK and as part of that I have set up a second Downing Street office in Manchester, we call it number 10 North. that office stands a statue of Abraham Lincoln. It marks the personal connection he made with Manchester and the bond between our two nations, a bond which he described in a letter to the working people of the city as perpetual. This was not due to some military or material support, there was no quid pro quo. It was because Manchester's humble mill workers took a principled stand. During the American Civil War in 1862, despite the hardships it brought them, they refused to touch raw cotton that had been picked by slaves. In 1862, people with little power used it to help those with none on the other side of the world. The best change is change like that, bottom-up change led by people. And whatever distorted view social media offers today the world is still full of good and decent people all over the world who are ready to stand up for what is right. I see that shining through all the time. Nothing brings the British people together across age, race and class more than their hatred of injustice, the misuse of power against the powerless. We will always stand for the underdog against the bully. That's why we are so united behind Ukraine. And let me say, we salute the Ukrainian people. They are showing depths of resilience and courage. That is an inspiration to the whole world. I was in Kiev last month and it gave me a glimpse of life under Russian attack. I went to a bustling market, just a normal scene from any European city. The traders singing the praises of their products, pushing into my hands peaches and plums from Odessa. But their stalls were out on the street because the market hall had been destroyed. In the background there were burned out cars. Behind us a building that had taken a direct hit just a few weeks before. I met people riding the metro home from work, people just getting on with their lives. But at night those same metro stations doubling as shelters for thousands of people. From the elderly to little kids, some who have known nothing but war. People told me about the freezing conditions in the stations last winter, when temperatures dropped below minus 20 degrees outside. Meanwhile, Russia was targeting their energy infrastructure, trying to make them suffer even more. We can't let them do that again this winter, so we're working to help Ukraine protect their skies and civilians. We're leading the charge in raising the cost for Russia of continuing this senseless and illegal war. The Graham Bill, which President Trump signed last week, will make a huge difference to that effort. And we will support Ukraine to repair and protect the heat and power plants that Kiev will depend upon this winter. It is right that we provide that support. But we should call Russia out this time and every time. Everyone in this room knows that strikes on civilian infrastructure are explicitly forbidden by international law. Yet we stand here in the UN announcing funding to mitigate the effects of these war crimes, which we reliably expect to be perpetrated yet again by a permanent member of the Security Council. It must end. Russia could choose a different course tomorrow, except a ceasefire, come to the negotiating table. I urge them to do so. But until then, we will stand with Ukraine, stronger than ever for as long as it takes. This is about upholding the UN Charter and the rule of law. We will stand firm in the face of any threats and challenges to the rule of law, not just from Russia but from others too, including where they threaten the rights of British territories to remain British, such as the Falkland Islands. That's why we're also working with France and other partners to support freedom of navigation in the Gulf. And it's why I have acted on the Middle East. State weeks into becoming Prime Minister, working with my foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, I comprehensively reset our position. And we built an international coalition of countries to come with us. The terrorist attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 was utterly horrific. I have condemned it in the strongest possible terms. We continue to condemn Hamas and And we stand with Israel in the face of the ongoing threats, including from Iran against Israel and Jewish people around the world. But this does not justify the Israeli government's actions in Gaza or the West Bank. Far too many people have died, including so many children. Far too little aid is getting in. And it has gone on for far too long. We will not stand by as the horrific suffering continues to grow and the prospect of a two-state solution, the best hope for peace and stability for both nations, comes under attack. Last month Israel issued tenders for the construction of the E1 mega settlement which would drive a wedge through the West Bank and threaten to put a viable Palestinian state beyond reach. It cannot be allowed to happen. But we have acted by banning trading goods with illegal settlements, recognizing that the Israeli occupation of the Palestinian territory is unlawful and sanctioning those taking part in the construction of illegal settlements. We want to see the suffering and death finally come to an end. We want to see Israeli and Palestinian people living side by side in peace and security. And we will do all we can to keep the hope of that possibility alive. And look, we live in an age of low trust in politics. If we were to continue to talk about the two-state solution, but fail to back those words with deeds, that trust will fall even lower, and our enemies will seek to exploit the alienation that follows from that. We won't let it happen. So Your Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, this is the kind of leadership Britain is here to bring. We need to recommit together to make the decade ahead of us better than the last. My message to our partners around the world is this, you can count on us. Count on us to stand up for those long-standing British values of fairness and justice, our shared values and for the UN Charter. Count on us to fight racism, discrimination and the abuse of power wherever we see it, just as those Manchester Cotton workers did in the 19th century and the country did in the fight against fascism in the 20th century. Count on us to bring people together, not to point towards old problems, but to work towards new solutions for the 21st century. Count on us to meet fear and division with unity and hope. Thank you very much indeed.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen, • We come to this Assembly from countries that differ in size, population, and power.

• Yet here, precisely because of that, every country has its unique experience to share, responsibilities to assume, and a contribution to make.

• Croatia brings the experience of a nation that, within one generation, endured aggression and occupation, defended its freedom, and rebuilt itself.

• It joined UN, NATO and the European Union and developed a flourishing democracy and a growing economy.

• Our path and our transition were neither straight nor easy, but we made it.

• Over the past decade as Prime Minister, I have seen Croatia translate those experiences into progress at home and more responsibility abroad.

• They have reinforced three convictions that speak directly to the theme of this session.

• First, rules are our common compass.

• Second, transformation helps build resilience.

• Third, trust is earned only through delivery.

(First: Rules are our common compass) Ladies and Gentlemen, • Croatia supports rules -based multilateralism as the pinnacle of human cooperation not because we are naive, but because we have seen and experienced the alternative.

• For smaller and medium-sized states, international law is not an abstraction.

• It is the line between order and tyranny, between sovereign equality and the rule of force.

• The rule of force such as witnessed by Croatia during the brutal aggression and occupation of more than one quarter of our territory in the 1990s.

• In the war which claimed nearly 20,000 lives.

• And after which, m ore than three decades later,

Croatia continues to search for 1,725 missing persons – a poignant example that the consequences of war do not end when the weapons fall silent.

• Instead, peace requires courage, credible institutions, and rules that apply equally to everyone.

• Russia's ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine is a direct assault on those rules.

• Croatia will continue to support Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, and a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace based on the UN Charter.

• Peace cannot reward conquest, and recovery cannot be separated from justice.

• The same compass must guide us in the Middle East.

• Protection of civilians, unhindered humanitarian access, respect for international law, and a credible political horizon are essential to breaking the cycle of violence.

• Croatia supports a negotiated two-state solution in which Israelis and Palestinians live in peace and security.

• From Sudan and Myanmar to the Sahel and the Great Lakes region, civilians bear the highest cost when rules are ignored and diplomacy fails.

• And no crisis remains local for long.

• War disrupts food and energy supplies, while insecurity from the Strait of Hormuz to the Black Sea affects shipping, prices, and livelihoods across continents.

• This is why, as a Government, we are dealing with the consequences of energy price pressures by passing decrees to protect Croatian citizens and economy from energy shocks created far away from our shores.

• As distant as they may seem, these shocks are real, as they ripple into domestic inflationary pressures, affecting everything from wages and pensions to food prices and basic services.

• This is why freedom of navigation, maritime security, and the strict implementation of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea matter to everyone.

• For us, freedom of navigation and maritime security are both a national interest and a global responsibility.

• Common rules do not hold us back.

• They provide the stability and predictability necessary for countries to advance their ambitions.

(Second: Transformation helps build resilience) Excellencies, • The world is being transformed by technology, climate change, demographic pressures, illegal migration, and geopolitical rivalry.

• Our responsibility is to govern them so that change expands human freedom and security instead of weakening them.

• The United Nations must begin with its own transformation.

• Croatia supports a UN that is more effective, accountable, and financially sustainable, and stronger across all three pillars: peace and security, sustainable development, and human rights.

• Reform must also produce a more representative and effective Security Council.

• When the Council is blocked, the General Assembly can and must act, but it cannot replace the Council's primary responsibility under the Charter.

• This makes the selection of the next Secretary General all the more relevant.

• I thank Secretary General Guterres for his work over the last decade.

• The United Nations needs leadership capable of bringing member states together, defending the Charter, and turning reform into measurable results.

• No country alone can successfully respond to the global transformations we witness today.

• Artificial intelligence can accelerate development, but its use must remain consistent with legal frameworks, human dignity, and democratic accountability.

• Renewed nuclear rhetoric makes a firm commitment to the Treaty on the Non -Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons more important than ever.

• Climate action should be used to strengthen energy security and social cohesion.

• Our experience shows that the green transition should not be ideological.

• It can endure only when it is technologically realistic, socially fair, compatible with secure and affordable energy, and supportive of overall development.

• For Europe, which imports most of the energy it consumes, the case for producing more renewable energy at home now reaches far beyond climate policy.

• It is a strategic necessity.

• It strengthens Europe’s sovereignty and capacity to act, reduces external dependence, creates economic opportunity, and makes our societies more resilient.

• The same principle applies to illegal migration, which has caused mistrust in Europe and altered the political landscape in many countries.

• This situation is unacceptable and it cannot continue.

• The rule of law must be upheld, and legal procedures must be followed.

• Our primary responsibility is to our citizens.

• And it starts at our borders.

• We are not allowing uncontrolled migration, and we are fighting the criminal networks that facilitate it.

• As an EU external border country, Croatia carries an additional responsibility, and we will fulfill it with full determination.

• Transformation is equally important in our own neighborhood.

• Southeast Europe remains the unfinished part of the European project.

• Croatia will continue to support merit-based EU enlargement.

• EU membership can turn borders of division into lines of cooperation, and reforms on paper into stronger institutions and better living standards.

• But European transformation requires honesty about the past.

• Reconciliation becomes possible when responsibility for the crimes of the past is acknowledged and their glorification rejected.

• That standard allows no national exceptions.

• That means respect for victims and clear rejection of historical revisionism – not the glorification of war criminals.

• Ratko Mladić was a convicted war criminal responsible for the Srebrenica genocide—the first genocide in Europe since the Holocaust.

• While his criminal record reached i ts nefarious culmination in Srebrenica, his trail of war crimes stretches further back—to the shelling of Croatian cities, the murder of civilians, the mining of dams, and the destruction of cultural heritage and industrial facilities.

• The military and official honors accorded to Mladić in Serbia were an affront to his victims and to the judgments of international courts.

• The participation of state representatives and the public acclaim that accompanied the ceremony is totally incompatible with the values of a Union Serbia seeks to join.

• The same commitment to equality and reform should guide Bosnia and Herzegovina.

• As a signatory to the Dayton Peace Accords, and a neighbor and a friend of Bosnia and Herzegovina,

Croatia is one of the strongest advocates of its European future.

• The Dayton Peace Accords ended the war and established the constitutional framework for Bosnia and Herzegovina: one state, two entities, and three constituent peoples —Croats, Bosniaks, and Serbs.

• That balance is the foundation on which peace was built.

• Yet the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina are still being denied legitimate representation, including in the Presidency of the country.

• That is unjust, destabilizing, and contrary to the spirit of Dayton.

• The solution is neither division nor domination.

• It is carefully designed electoral reform that protects every citizen, while ensuring that a basic principle of legitimate political representation of the constituent peoples is restored.

• Croatia will not tire of explaining why this reform is crucial for the entire country to reach its full potential.

• And we will not tire of opposing those political forces whose shortsighted pursuit of political gains jeopardizes equality of constituent peoples and the long-term prosperity.

• Our own history confirms that transformation succeeds when it is rooted in inclusion, responsibility, and reform.

• Over the past decade, Croatia has doubled the size of its economy in nominal terms, while reducing its public debt-to-GDP ratio by 30 percentage points from its pandemic peak.

• Six consecutive sovereign credit -rating upgrades have brought us into the A category.

• We have tripled our defense budget, with approximately one-third of that spending allocated to military modernization.

• In a changed security environment, we are strengthening our security and ensur ing we are better equipped to support international stabilization missions abroad.

• Reforms we are pursuing domestically are increasing our overall resilience and giving us increased capacity to engage in a world which is rapidly changing.

(Third: Trust is earned through delivery) Ladies and Gentlemen, • The international system stutters when the distance between declaration and delivery becomes too wide.

• Trust returns when cooperation produces real, measurable results.

• It returns when a child is in school, a community is protected from violence, a mine is removed from a field, or food reaches a family.

• And it returns when institutions prevent conflict before it even begins.

• Last year alone, the world’s official development assistance was reduced by almost 25% (23.1%).

• This drop is the largest annual contraction on record for international aid.

• Refusing to spiral into negative trends, Croatia is contributing more, not less.

• Between 2016 and 2024, our official development assistance increased fivefold, while our humanitarian assistance grew more than twentyone fold.

• With our UN partners, we are translating our commitment and funds into action.

• We support girls’ education in Kenya, provide humanitarian assistance in Gaza, and assist Syrian refugee children.

• We also advance mine action in Ukraine—drawing on Croatia’s own postwar experience —and protect women and girls from digital violence.

• This practical, inclusive, and human centered approach is also what Croatia brings to ECOSOC.

• If elected to the presidency of ECOSOC for the 2027–2028 cycle, Croatia will work to strengthen coordination and accountability.

• As 2030 approaches, accelerating implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals continues to be a central priority.

• Croatia persistently ranks among the world’s fifteen highest -performing countries in implementing the Sustainable Development Goals.

• Our experience is not a universal prescription but evidence that national reform and international responsibility can and do advance together.

• It is this credibility that is in the foundation of trust in multilateralism that we wish to see rebuilt.

• Credibility which is str ongest when every country, regardless of its size, wealth, or power, has a meaningful voice.

• The answer is therefore not less multilateralism.

• It is multilateralism that delivers.

• It is this approach that Croatia would bring to the Security Council, if elected to serve in 2030–2031.

Excellencies, • Croatia's modern journey began in war, but war did not define its destination.

• Our experience has shaped the way we understand international cooperation and the responsibilities that come with it.

• Rules gave us a compass when force sought to erase our borders.

• Reform gave us a bridge from vulnerability to resilience, and from postwar recovery to membership in the European Union, the euro area, and Schengen.

• Delivery turned those ambitions into institutions, security, and better lives for our citizens—and gave us the capacity to contribute beyond our borders.

• That is the experience Croatia brings to the United Nations.

• Not a claim to perfection, but the perspective of a country that has traveled a difficult road and learned from it.

• The United Nations remains indispensable because no country can navigate today's storms alone.

• Let us therefore re build trust by defending our common compass and managing change so that it strengthens human dignity.

• Let us ensure that our commitments reach the people for whom they were made.

Thank you.

country: Belgium
speaker: Maxime Prévot
title: Deputy Prime Minister
speaker_title: His Excellency

Mr President,

Mr Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Maurice Maeterlinck, born in Ghent and awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1911 (nineteen eleven), wrote a strange, almost unsettling play entitled The Blind.

Twelve people find themselves in a forest on an island.

The guide who led them there is sitting among them.

He is dead, but they do not yet know it.

They are waiting for him to return.

They hear the wind, the sea, the voices around them.

They know they are not alone, yet they can barely tell where the others are.

At one point, one of the characters says: “Years and years we have been together, and we have never seen each other!”

That line comes back to me when I look at our world.

We, too, are together.

We meet constantly.

We exchange statements, messages and positions.

At times, we spend hours around the same tables.

And yet, being in the same room does not mean that we understand one another.

Do we still take the time to hear what others are telling us?

To understand what they fear, what they need, and what the world looks like from where they stand?

That, to me, is where diplomacy begins.

Not when we agree.

But when we no longer do.

Diplomacy is not about erasing disagreements, nor about abandoning our principles to secure consensus at any cost.

It is about continuing to speak, continuing to listen, and finding ways to manage our differences without allowing them to lead to a breakdown in relations or to confrontation.

In the play, one of the characters says something very simple: “Let us try to draw a little closer.”

Maeterlinck wrote those words more than a century ago.

Yet they feel entirely relevant today.

Drawing closer does not mean thinking alike.

It means refusing to let distance turn into indifference, then mistrust, until eventually we stop speaking altogether.

That risk is real today.

It is one of the paradoxes of our time.

We have never been more connected, yet we do not necessarily understand one another any better.

Our economies, societies and technologies have become deeply interdependent, even as the temptation to turn inward returns with force.

In other words, we depend on one another more than ever, at the very moment when we are sometimes tempted to believe that we can do without one another.

The more interdependent we become, the more we need common rules.

Not to erase our differences.

Not to impose a single vision of the world.

But to ensure that we can manage our disagreements without allowing the law of the strongest to become the only law that matters.

In the play The Blind, the characters have lost the person who was meant to show them the way.

We are not in the same position.

No one will come and decide for us which direction to take.

But that does not mean we can move forward without bearings.

Faced with wars, humanitarian crises, climate disruption, pandemics and technological upheaval, the question is ultimately quite simple: do we still have a common compass?

For Belgium, the answer is yes.

That compass is the Charter of the United Nations. It is international law.

But a rule has value only if it continues to apply when respecting it becomes difficult.

It is precisely when the law runs counter to a State’s immediate interest that we discover whether it truly matters.

When a signature loses its value the moment it becomes binding, when a treaty holds only for as long as it suits the party that signed it, it is not merely a legal text that is weakened.

It is trust in a promise made.

And with it, the security of all those who believed they could rely on that promise.

This is why Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine concerns far more than two States.

When a border can be changed by force, every border becomes less secure.

No one in this room needs reminding that international politics is shaped by power and by interests. The Charter does not wish those realities away. It draws a line around what power may be allowed to do.

For Belgium, that line matters in very practical terms. We are an open country, with an economy tied to the world and a security bound up with that of our partners. We depend on States keeping their word, on agreements surviving changes in the balance of power, and on borders not being redrawn at gunpoint.

International law reflects our values, certainly. It also protects our interests.

That is why Belgium stands firmly with Ukraine. Any lasting peace must be grounded in the Charter of the United Nations and in respect for Ukraine’s sovereignty, political independence and territorial integrity.

But we cannot uphold these principles on my continent alone – in Europe – and treat them as optional elsewhere. Sovereignty, territorial integrity and the right of peoples to determine their own future do not change meaning when we cross the borders of our continent.

The same standard must guide us when it comes to international humanitarian law.

Its rules do not apply only when they suit us.

They exist precisely for the moments when respecting them becomes difficult.

In Palestine, Sudan, Myanmar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo,

Haiti, and so many other places scarred by war or armed violence, the circumstances differ.

But no human life is worth less than another.

Civilians remain civilians. They must be protected.

Humanitarian aid must be allowed to reach them.

Everywhere.

This year again, hundreds of millions of people need humanitarian assistance while the resources available to help them are shrinking.

When funding runs out, what do we tell the mother who has walked for hours to reach a clinic with her sick child? That the doors are closed?

What do we tell a family waiting for food? That there will be no delivery tomorrow?

We cannot ask humanitarian workers to give those answers because we have chosen to cut their funding.

This is not the time to treat humanitarian aid as an optional expense.

It is neither a reward nor a bargaining chip.

A hungry child is not responsible for the position taken by his government.

That child has the right to eat, the right to receive care, and the right to be protected.

That is why I urge every one of us not to cut humanitarian funding.

International law does more than contain violence.

It also enables trade, exchange and movement.

That brings me to a freedom that may at first sound rather technical: freedom of navigation.

For my country, it is anything but technical.

As early as the nineteenth century, the port of Antwerp had immense potential.

But ships sailing up the River Scheldt had to pay a toll.

In 1863 (eighteen sixty-three), an international agreement abolished that toll once and for all.

The abolition was to apply to “all flags”.

All of them.

An international route has real value only if it remains open.

Passage cannot depend, each time, on a fresh contest of power.

That is precisely what freedom of navigation represents today.

It is not merely the abstract right of a ship to travel from one point to another.

It allows economies that may share neither the same interests nor the same alliances to remain connected.

It allows a landlocked State to take part in global trade.

It allows grain, medicines, gas and industrial components to cross several maritime areas without their passage having to be renegotiated at every stage.

That seems perfectly normal while everything is working.

It takes only one route closing for us to remember how much it matters.

Think of the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the entrance of the Red Sea, the Suez Canal, the Bosporus, the Strait of Malacca or the Panama Canal.

More than 80 per cent of global merchandise trade by volume is carried by sea.

When a ship is attacked, when a strait becomes dangerous, or when a carrier has to sail around an entire region, the effects are felt thousands of kilometres away.

In our ports, of course.

But also in the price of energy, fertiliser and food.

The price of a tank of fuel.

The price of a loaf of bread. Even having a bread.

And very often, the countries with the least economic room to maneuver bear the greatest burden in proportionate terms.

The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea confers rights, but it also imposes obligations: the safety of navigation, the protection of the marine environment, and respect for the rights of coastal States.

A smaller navy does not mean fewer rights.

Nor does a larger one confer the right to impose its will.

No country should have to surrender the rights the law gives it simply because another can send more ships.

That is why maritime disputes must be settled by law, not by intimidation.

And that is why freedom of navigation depends on common rules: so that every country can exercise its rights while respecting those of others.

But keeping our sea routes open also means keeping them safe, all the way into our ports.

The International Ship and Port Facility Security Code, the ISPS Code, offers a very concrete example of what multilateralism can achieve when it works.

Piracy, terrorism and crime are scourges that we must fight together.

That Code must be strengthened.

Belgium understands its importance.

Freedom and security are not opposing ideas.

Security is a condition of freedom.

I dwell on freedom of navigation because it illustrates something larger.

Sovereignty does not require isolation.

We can defend our interests while accepting that others have rights too.

And when rules are clear and predictable enough, a space of competition can still remain a space of cooperation.

The ocean, moreover, are far more than the highways of our trade.

They feed populations, regulate our climate, and absorb much of the excess heat caused by global warming.

For many small island States, rising sea levels affect the land on which their citizens live, their economy, their culture and, in some cases, their very ability to remain where their families have lived for generations.

The freedom to use the ocean therefore comes with a responsibility: to preserve it.

And on this point, allow me to be optimistic.

The BBNJ Agreement entered into force this year, after almost twenty years of negotiations.

Almost twenty years.

Measured against a political cycle, that is close to an eternity. Measured against the building of international law, it is sometimes the time needed to reach a compromise strong enough to last.

The Agreement proves that, even today, we continue to build international law rather than dismantle it.

Belgium has invested greatly in this process. It helped launch the Blue Leaders, a coalition of countries working to protect at least 30 per cent of the ocean by 2030 (twenty thirty) and secure an ambitious high seas treaty.

The BBNJ Agreement now gives us an essential tool to advance towards that protection goal.

But twenty years of negotiations must not be followed by years of waiting.

It is in that spirit that Belgium is offering to host the treaty’s future secretariat in Brussels.

We are ready to enable it to work from day one. It will be able to draw on our scientific expertise and on a community that brings together international organisations, embassies and civil society.

So that what we have agreed together becomes real protection at sea.

Beneath those same ocean run other vital routes: the cables that connect our continents and carry much of our digital communications and energy.

Here too, our interdependence is plain to see.

A break, an act of sabotage or an attack can have consequences thousands of kilometres away.

Protecting those connections is essential. But our responsibility in the digital world does not end with infrastructure.

Artificial intelligence already confronts us with another question: how can we make full use of the possibilities created by innovation without allowing technology to move faster than our ability to protect people?

I am thinking in particular of children, who are growing up in a world where AI can open extraordinary possibilities, but also create new vulnerabilities.

We must neither hold back innovation out of fear nor assume that it will regulate itself.

At sea as in the digital world, freedom needs rules if it is to remain freedom.

We cannot speak about interdependence without speaking about migration.

People have always moved, and they will continue to do so.

Governments have a duty to manage that movement and to ensure that migration takes place safely, regularly and in accordance with the law.

Order is itself a matter of human rights. When migration is left in the hands of smugglers and traffickers, people are exploited, placed in danger and sometimes lost at sea.

But the way in which governments maintain order matters just as much.

States have both the right and the responsibility to manage their borders.

They must do so in full respect of international law and fundamental rights.

A person’s legal status may change. Their human dignity does not.

Every person counts.

That is why countries of origin, transit and destination must work together. Safe, orderly and regular migration and respect for human rights are not competing ambitions. They must go hand in hand.

We can either manage our interdependence, or be at its mercy.

Health crises have taught us the same lesson.

Outbreaks do not recognise borders.

Cooperation is a necessity.

Those who refuse to cooperate weaken themselves.

But if our commitments are to hold, we also need institutions capable of upholding them.

The law needs guardians.

This year, we mark the 80th anniversary of the International Court of Justice. It settles legal disputes submitted to it by States, peacefully and in accordance with international law.

The International Criminal Court has a different mandate: to fight impunity by prosecuting and trying individuals accused of the gravest international crimes.

Their mandates differ. Their independence must be defended equally.

Both courts rest on the same idea: power cannot be its own judge.

That remains true even when we dislike their rulings or proceedings.

When judges or staff members of an international court face sanctions or pressure for carrying out their mandate, Belgium will always stand with them to protect them.

But the promise of the law does not end in courtrooms or in relations between States.

It concerns people.

Human rights.

The right to think and speak freely.

Freedom of conscience and religion.

And the freedom not to believe.

It concerns the ability of every woman to decide the course of her own life and take her equal place in society.

The ability to love the person we love without fear of prison, violence or persecution.

These freedoms belong to no single continent.

They rest on an elementary conviction: a person’s dignity does not depend on their sex, their origin, their sexual orientation, or what a government thinks of them.

Our societies are different.

They will remain so.

Human dignity does not require us to be alike in order to be equal.

That conviction also guides our diplomacy.

Dialogue is not approval.

Dialogue is not the opposite of resolve.

Diplomacy requires both.

It also requires institutions capable of functioning.

Defending the United Nations does not mean pretending that everything within it works well.

The UN80 process is necessary.

But there is a difference between reforming an organisation and weakening it.

We cannot ask more of it, steadily strip away its resources, and then express surprise when it is not effective enough.

Reform must preserve what gives the Organisation its purpose: peace and security, human rights, and development.

It must also ensure better representation for every region of the world.

More than eighty years ago, Paul -Henri Spaak led the Belgian delegation to the San Francisco Conference that gave birth to the United Nations. A few months later, he became the first President of this General Assembly.

Belgium was emerging from war and occupation.

That is precisely why multilateralism seemed the obvious choice to us.

We are not here to preserve an institution for its own sake.

We are here to preserve what it must make possible.

Peace and security.

Human rights.

And prosperity for all.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Before we were presidents, ministers, ambassadors or diplomats, we were all children.

And despite all that sets them apart, the people we represent often want remarkably simple things.

To come home in the evening.

To watch their children grow up and send them to school without fear.

To work.

To love the person they love.

To make plans for next year.

Not to live with the thought that war, hunger, disease or violence could make everything disappear overnight.

That is the most concrete definition of peace: being able to live your life without constantly fearing that you will lose it.

We can build peace, and we can damage it. We can pass it on, or leave the next generation with the task of starting all over again.

At the beginning of this speech, I spoke of Maurice Maeterlinck’s play The Blind.

Its characters were waiting for someone to show them the way.

We cannot simply wait.

No one will come and decide for us what kind of world we want to live in.

But we are not without bearings.

We have international law.

We have dialogue.

Above all, we have a responsibility to use them both.

A compass cannot prevent a storm.

It helps us hold our course when the storm comes.

Thank you.

Where threats to a peace can be confronted together. Where disputes can be resolved through dialogue, not force. Where international law protects the strong and the weak alike. That was the promise of the United Nations 81 years ago. It reminds our responsibility today. It is not a Christmas wish for this year. We must stand by our principles always. The world has changed. The threats have changed. But our fundamental purpose has not. And the fundamental purpose is to maintain international peace and security. That purpose is worth defending. And this organization is worth reforming so that this organization can deliver. Let us make the United Nations work for peace, for security, and for all of us. Thank you very much.
