Excellences. Excellences, President of the United Nations General Assembly. Excellences, Heads of State and Government. Your Excellency, Secretary-General of the United Nations. Distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. I am particularly proud and honored to address this August Assembly today on behalf of the Republic of Madagascar at this 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly for the rest of my speech. Allow me to now speak to you. and the Malagasy language, my mother tongue, in honor of my country and the Malagasy people. I would like, first of all, on behalf of the Malagasy people, and in my own name, to extend my sincere congratulations to Mr. Khalilor Rahman on his election as President of the First General Assembly as well as to the Vice-Presidents. In this regard, I wish to reaffirm Madagascar's support and its full readiness to work in a genuine spirit of cooperation to ensure the success of all of our work throughout this session. Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, we must acknowledge that the challenges that we have faced for decades, namely food insecurity, disease, armed conflict or natural disasters, are still with us. Thus for Madagascar, as for many other nations, the new emerging challenges must not overshadow the priorities that still require our attention. The theme of this this 81st session calls upon us to assume our shared responsibility for our destiny and for that of future generations with clear vision, placing collective action the common good and the welfare of humanity at the centre of our responses to the profound transformations shaping our world. In light of these intersecting transformations and challenges, the question of trust in our collective action arises with renewed urgency. Indeed, we must admit taking into account all the hopes and expectations that we, the peoples of the United Nations, have placed in our organisation that trust has gradually eroded over time. The most vulnerable populations affected repeatedly or continuously by health crises, food insecurity and hunger, the impacts of climate change, and conflicts exacerbated by current geopolitical tensions sometimes come to feel a certain skepticism regarding our collective capacity within the United Nations system to respond to the scourges of our age, Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen. In this regard, the realities on the ground in my country speak for themselves. In southern Madagascar, mothers walk dozens of kilometers under scorching heat in search of water from the bed of a dried up river. In the east, every year, increasingly violent and destructive tropical cyclones devastate crops, infrastructure and human lives. In other regions, floods engulf rice granaries affecting entire communities, these images illustrate the daily vulnerability of our people, our Malagasy population. Faced with these recurring humanitarian emergencies amplified by climate change, considerable investments are made reflecting the unwavering commitment of our development partners working every year towards the achievement of the sustainable development goals, the SDGs, whether that be fighting hunger, providing education or providing access to basic services for vulnerable populations. And we hope to mobilize $1.5 billion over five years for the implementation of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for the period 2024-2028. Yet beyond commitments and resources mobilised, what matters to us is their tangible impact on the daily lives of our people. Faced with the challenges of a constantly changing world, the Re-Foundation Government that I lead places food sovereignty, health and education at the heart of its action. This priority commitment serves the entire population, particularly women and children, providing our youth with the means to build their future with confidence and contribute to national development, with more than 55 percent of its population under the age of 25. Madagascar enjoys a tremendous demographic dividend. Driven by a firm political determination to build a brighter future for this dynamic youth, we recognise the importance of an education system which is fully aligned with labour market realities, an essential condition for sustainable development, and we hope that cooperation in this area will move beyond a strictly quantitative approach measured only by the volume of infrastructure built or the number of students enrolled, and instead adapt fully to economic realities on the ground. Our aim is to focus on future-oriented sectors, while redefining our indicators of success to prioritise the practical acquisition of skills and medium-term employment outcomes. Mr President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Madagascar's foreign policy is guided above all by the imperatives of economic and social development for the well-being of its people. Madagascar has chosen a policy of engagement in all directions. We are open to all international partnerships capable of meeting the aspirations of our people and supporting the general policy of the State of the Re-Foundation. Madagascar's position of neutrality with regard to global conflicts is consistent with its diplomatic tradition and its desire to preserve constructive relations with all its partners. This idea is not ideological but is based on international partnership that can meet the aspirations of our people in an open spirit without exclusivity, in full respect for national sovereignty. The achievement of our ambitions cannot be separated from the international context in which they are pursued. Excellences, Mr President, Ladies and Gentlemen, Can we speak of development when international peace and security are being tested by multiplying crises around the world and the persistent tensions? Restoring trust requires the United Nations to maintain and to restore peace. We must be concerned that the multilateral system is struggling to contain escalating tensions fueled by geopolitical rivalries. These crises, now affecting different regions of the planet, have consequences for our states. They directly impact our economies and the daily lives of our populations through disruptions in energy supply chains and difficulties in the delivery of essential goods. These are all factors which further aggravate the vulnerabilities that we already face. Confronted with this reality, we must have the courage to recognise and to accept the limitations of the multilateral system in its current form and functioning. It is urgent to initiate concerted and lasting action to guarantee every people the right to pursue their development in dignity and in stability. Mr President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Far from observing the world as a passive spectator, Madagascar positions itself as an actor fully aware of its strategic place and responsibilities. Our country remains a committed and operational partner in the service of peace, development and security. Maritime security in the Mozambique Channel and the western Indian Ocean remains at the heart of the regional initiatives in which Madagascar actively participates. We are determined to strengthen regional and multilateral cooperation founded on respect for national sovereignty, whilst also welcoming partnerships that align with our priorities and serve as genuine drivers of development. We also want to be part of strengthened regional cooperation in order to guarantee the security of our maritime areas. This approach will make it possible to ensure the sustainability of our energy supply chains. Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, What form of United Nations cooperation should we establish to support the contemporary transformation of our world? How can we restore trust? Mr President, ladies and gentlemen, we must look to the future with greater ambition to ensure lasting and measurable impact over the medium and long-term. To do this, we must move on to a new stage, one of increased solidarity that is more integrated and better coordinated. Madagascar advocates for a multilateral system that is not only capable of acting, but that is also capable of supporting member states in their efforts to break the cycles of poverty and insecurity. My country aspires to an international order founded on the primacy of international law and trusts in the virtues of dialogue and diplomatic action. Our commitment to multilateral cooperation remains unwavering. Multilateralism is a privileged forum where states unite in a shared responsibility, enabling them to divine common and appropriate solutions. In the face of challenges such as epidemics and climate disasters, or armed conflicts arising from contemporary geopolitical rivalries, and latent multi-dimensional tensions, history and future generations will judge our organisation according to a single criterion, namely our ability to fulfil our original mission, serving all peoples without exclusion or privilege and in full respect for the sovereignty of nations. It is imperative to restore to the United Nations fully its central role as a guardian of peace, as a strengthened institution capable of restoring order and addressing the challenges of our time. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, our challenge today is therefore to rethink our mechanisms of cooperation through greater synergy between UN agencies and governmental structures in order to optimize the effectiveness of our actions on the ground, but also to provide better visibility of tangible results achieved for the benefit of populations. In this regard, the success of our agenda largely depends on strengthening governance and strengthening institutions, priorities that are fully integrated into Madagascar's process of refoundation. We recognise also the absolute necessity of reforming the United Nations so that it may serve all peoples, and in this spirit we would like to propose the following first. More inclusive global governance. This must begin with a rebalancing of decision-making power, first and foremost, by restoring the General Assembly's full political weight and central place in global governance. It remains, indeed, the only organ where every nation, regardless of power, enjoys an equal and sovereign voice. We must also correct the historical imbalance affecting Africa's representation on the Security Council. Indeed, Africa cannot remain on the margins of decisions. We have 1.4 billion inhabitants, decisions concerning international peace and security. Africa should be granted permanent representation on the Security Council

in accordance with the Ezelwini consensus and the cert declaration, which expresses a common

position grounded in justice, equity and representativeness within the African Union.

We must also strengthen coherence between programs implemented by the UN Resident Coordinator Offices and National Priorities. UN country teams on the ground must listen carefully and respond effectively to priorities defined by host governments, avoiding one-size-fits-all approaches. Secondly, we need a more accessible international financial architecture for effective development support. We must not neglect the reform of the international financial architecture. This means we need to rebalance access to financing. Current aid and lending criteria often relies solely on GDP per capita, excluding many vulnerable countries. The United Nations should therefore take into account the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index so that access to concessional financing reflects climate shocks and external debt burdens. It would also be wise to support durable debt relief. This means advocating a faster, more predictable and more inclusive sovereign debt restructuring mechanism that would allow vulnerable countries to invest in the sustainable development goals rather than servicing unsustainable interest payments. The procedures for accessing UN funds should also be drastically simplified in order to reduce disbursement delays for a vulnerable state facing crisis administrative slowness undermines confidence in the effectiveness of multilateralism. Third, greater effectiveness in responding to climate and humanitarian emergencies. The multilateral system we seek should guarantee the fulfilment of climate finance commitments. should serve both as a catalyst and a guarantor to ensure that developed countries in the north honour their commitments on climate finance. Particularly for the most exposed nations, it's also important to link emergency assistance with long-term structural investments. Mr President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, By embracing this theme, we are undertaking a commitment, namely to not postpone the reforms that are essential for enabling our organisation to act with the integrity required by the challenges of our age, building upon the achievements of the United Nations over 81 Our predecessors were able to build an organization suited to their time. It is now our responsibility to re-found it so that it can address the challenges of today and tomorrow. Let us pass on to future generations, an organization that unites, protects and acts. For its part, Madagascar is preparing at the national level a framework for the effective implementation of this transformation within our means. Indeed, the process of refoundation initiated following the mobilisation of Malagasy youth just one year ago serves as the foundation for responsible governance supported by strong institutions devoted to the public interest and having restored citizens trust in the state. This represents a genuine patriotic awakening driven by the deep conviction that sustainable development requires every citizen to find a full and meaningful place within the nation. To give substance to this vision, we have launched a historic process of inclusive national dialogue bringing together all the vital forces of the nation – young people, men, persons with disabilities, political parties, civil society, the armed forces and the private sector. We have established a clear timetable. Our goal is to hold free, transparent and universally accepted elections before the end of 2027. Mr President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen. This platform, speaking here at this rostrum, also gives me the opportunity to express our gratitude to all our partners for the trust and support that they have provided and for the fraternal support of the Southern African Development Community, SADIC, and the United Nations, going with – standing with us hand in hand since the beginning of the refoundation process. Long live international cooperation and solidarity. Long live the United Nations. I thank you for your kind attention.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished Delegates,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

I congratulate you, Mr President, on your election to preside over the Eighty-First Session of the United Nations General Assembly.

You assume this solemn stewardship at a time of intense geopolitical fragmentation, deepening inequality, and eroded trust in our multilateral system.

Ghana is confident that your proven commitment to inclusive, consultative, and principled dialogue will guide this Assembly well. You have our full support.

I also commend outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres for his dedicated service to our world body over the last 10 years.

Mr. President,

Ghana’s national anthem contains a profound petition. It asks God to make us "bold to defend forever the cause of freedom and of right."

Those words give my compatriots and I the courage to uphold the PanAfrican and anti-colonial heritage bequeathed to us by our forebears.

Another line petitions God to fill our hearts with true humility and make us cherish fearless honesty.

That prayer inspires me today to follow in the footsteps of Kwame Nkrumah, Haile Selassie, Nelson Mandela, and the global icons who have stood at this podium before me and spoken boldly and fearlessly about the state of affairs in our world.

The world may not transform overnight because of the speeches delivered in this August Assembly. But history faithfully records the truth we choose to speak, and the silence we choose to keep, when we are granted the privilege of addressing this global town hall.

Allow me, therefore, to begin by reintroducing myself to the General Assembly.

I stand before you as President of the Republic of Ghana. Yet, we too often ascend these heights draped only in the robes of our titles, forgetting that alongside each of us stands a history, a people, and a legacy.

I was born in Damongo, then a modest town in northern Ghana and now the capital of the Savannah Region.

I was born to Mr Emmanuel Adama Mahama of Bole and Madam Abiba Nnaba Suluwu of Busunu, both of blessed memory.

I belong to them.

I belong to the foremothers and forefathers who birthed them, who named them, nurtured them, and passed down the enduring values by which I live.

I grew up at the crossroads of several Ghanaian cultures.

I speak Gonja, a Guan language.

I speak Akan and Ga.

I am fluent in Hausa, spoken across the West African savannah and Sahel.

I understand some Ewe.

And I speak English.

In a very real sense, I belong to all these peoples because their tongues have become my tongue.

Language creates kinship, regardless of the historical complexities through which the kinship was forged.

Mr. President,

Every person in this Chamber, and every global citizen listening to these words, possesses an origin. We carry inherited memories, values, rich cultures, and distinct identities.

Belonging anchors us; it reminds us that we are part of a human story far larger than ourselves. It is a vital wellspring of dignity and pride.

But belonging also has a dark side.

When weaponised by political expediency, it transforms into nativism, chauvinism, xenophobia and the dangerous prejudices extended to those who are deemed different.

It becomes the pretext for discrimination, displacement, persecution, and war. Yet for this Organisation, the United Nations, the founding principle remains immutable: Every human being belongs to the human family.

No race is superior.

No nation is inferior.

No child’s life is worth less because of the language they speak, the faith they profess, the colour of their skin, or the land of their birth.

This is the unyielding moral foundation upon which the United Nations must stand. I will return to this issue of belonging at the end of my speech.

Mr. President,

Last year, from this podium, I made a solemn pledge on behalf of Ghana, Africa, and the global African diaspora to secure full international recognition of the transatlantic trafficking and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity in human history.

Some cautioned that we were reopening old wounds. But we came not to provoke division or render empty judgment. We came to seek healing. True healing requires truth; truth requires acknowledgement; and acknowledgement must lead to meaningful repair.

For centuries, this tragedy was rendered in the passive voice as though millions of African men, women, and children vanished into the shadows of time.

They did not vanish. They were hunted, captured, trafficked, bought, sold, exploited, and exchanged for profit. They were ripped from the families and communities they belonged to.

Their unpaid labour built the cities, industries, banking institutions, and empires of the modern Western world. Meanwhile, the African continent was left depopulated, with split families, structural disruption, and generational trauma.

On 25 March 2026, the International Day of Remembrance of the Victims of Slavery and the Transatlantic Slave Trade, Ghana had the honour of tabling Resolution A/RES/80/250 in this very August Assembly.

One hundred and twenty-three (123) nations voted to affirm this fundamental truth: the transatlantic slave trade and chattel enslavement were the gravest crimes against humanity.

We thank every nation that voted for justice, and I am deeply grateful to our brothers and sisters in the African Union, CARICOM, CELAC, and our partners across the Global South.

That resolution was not a mere gesture. It was adopted because the structural legacies of those historic crimes continue to fuel systemic racism, economic marginalisation, and a global financial architecture weighted against Africa and people of African descent.

Since the passage of the historic resolution, we welcome the positive overtures from many countries and institutions to join the dialogue on reparatory justice and restitution.

The Netherlands, Germany and France have made positive moves to join the conversation on reparatory justice.

But real repair demands structural transformation. It requires dismantling the persistent engines of exploitation: unfair global trade regimes, predatory resource extraction, discriminatory credit ratings, unsustainable debt burdens, and the continued expo rt of raw materials from Africa while real value addition and job creation occur elsewhere.

Mr. President,

The injustices of the past remain embedded in today's power structures.

Africa is home to 1.5 billion people, over 18 per cent of humanity, and constitutes the largest regional voting bloc in this General Assembly.

Yet, Africa remains without a single permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council.

This is fundamentally unacceptable in the 21st century.

Africa must be granted permanent representation on the UN Security Council, complete with all the rights, responsibilities, and veto powers of such membership.

We cannot credibly champion the sovereign equality of nations while preserving a global governance structure designed for the post-war geopolitical realities.

Security Council reform is not a favour to Africa; it is an imperative for the legitimacy, credibility, and survival of the United Nations.

The same systemic inequality permeates the international financial architecture. Developing nations borrow at interest rates up to eight times higher than industrialised nations.

African and Caribbean nations struck by climate disasters are forced to take on crippling debt to rebuild from floods and droughts they did not cause.

Governments are forced into a tragic choice: to service predatory debt or serve their people.

We demand reform. We need long-term, affordable, and accessible concessionary financing that enables developing economies to invest in human capital, industrialisation, and climate adaptation.

Africa does not seek charity. Africa seeks equal partnership anchored in mutual respect. Our continent possesses the world’s youngest population, vast arable land, unparalleled cultural vitality, and the critical minerals required to drive the global green energy transition.

But Africa will not remain a passive arena for a new scramble for resources. Critical mineral extraction must not replicate colonial-era exploitation.

We will process our minerals at home, build local industries, create dignified jobs for our youth, and retain the value of our natural resources.

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), whose Secretariat Ghana is proud to host in Accra, is our engine for intra-African trade, structural transformation, and industrial growth.

Mr. President,

As we heal historical wounds, we must address the alarming breakdown of global order today.

We are witnessing a dangerous drift toward unilateralism, lawlessness, and the erosion of multilateral norms. The United Nations must learn from the lessons of the League of Nations. The UN Charter must reign supreme over the cynical doctrine that "might makes right."

The veto power must never serve as a license for impunity. Sovereign equality cannot be a privilege reserved only for nations aligned with global superpowers.

Nowhere is this crisis of credibility more painful than in the ongoing persecution of the Palestinian people in Gaza, the West Bank, and the occupied territories.

We must stop using diplomatic euphemisms to veil the human carnage taking place in Gaza.

How many more innocent lives must be lost before the world acts with decisive moral authority? The blood of five-year-old Hind Rajab, and the more than 20,000 children killed in this brutal conflict, cries out to the conscience of the world.

Collective punishment, enforced starvation, and mass displacement are flagrant violations of international law. Ghana remains unwavering in its recognition of the sovereign State of Palestine and its steadfast support for a viable Two-State solution, where Israel and Palestine live side-by-side in peace, security, and guaranteed borders.

At the same time, we condemn all acts of terrorism by Hamas that triggered this conflict. We insist that all parties unconditionally respect international humanitarian law. Our moral standards cannot be selective.

In that same spirit of international legality and human solidarity,

Ghana reiterates its call for the immediate lifting of the decades-long economic, commercial, and financial embargo imposed on Cuba. The world must support Cuba’s new Economic and Social Programme.

Measures that inflict collective economic hardship on ordinary citizens run counter to our shared commitment to human dignity and international law.

We must likewise elevate our global response to the catastrophic conflict in Sudan, which is reported to be the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. We must also exercise solidarity with nations facing the terrorist scourge, especially the Alliance of Sahel States.

The current Middle East crisis is having a deleterious effect on the world economy. We call for a return to the negotiating table. And let me add that no human civilisation deserves to be annihilated, certainly not a member state of the United Nations.

I believe that dialogue can resolve even the most intractable of problems. Across every conflict, whether in Europe, the Middle East, or Africa, the standard must remain uniform: respect sovereign integrity, protect civilians, ensure unhindered humanitarian access, and hold perpetrators of war crimes accountable.

Mr. President,

For those who have declared climate change a hoax perpetrated by geopolitical opponents, the warnings of recent times cannot have been clearer.

Melting glaciers, flash flooding, droughts, record-breaking heatwaves, brush fires, hurricanes and other extreme weather phenomena are unmistakable signals of an overburdened planet.

Climate change is the ultimate test of global equity. Africa contributes less than 4 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet bears some of the heaviest burden of climate devastation.

We face erratic rainfall, our coastal towns suffer relentless erosion, and our Sahelian regions face accelerating desertification. On 29 June this year, Ghana and coastal West Africa faced an unprecedented deluge.

Torrential rain, exceeding 160 millimetres, was dumped on seven coastal regions within 24 hours, resulting in 39 deaths and one still missing.

Climate justice demands that developed nations fulfil their long overdue financial commitments. Mitigation support must be operationalised with predictable, non-debt-creating grants, not loans that further indebt fragile economies.

Similarly, global health security demands true solidarity. Pathogens do not respect national borders or GDP.

We must build an equitable global health architecture that guarantees regional manufacturing of vaccines and therapeutics, strengthens epidemic surveillance, and funds resilient public health infrastructure across the Global South in accordance with the demands of the Accra Reset.

Mr President, Excellencies,

I agree that even as we demand a place at the table and call for a more equitable and just global order, as African leaders, we must also do what is required to put our own houses in order.

As the legal maxim goes: “Whoever comes into equity must come with clean hands.”

African leadership must be transparent and accountable. We must fight corruption and ensure that every dollar of our people’s money counts and is used efficiently in their interest.

Ghana is arguably the most stable democracy in Africa. We believe in the rule of law and have respect for human rights. We are determined to demonstrate that democracy works.

While progress in a democracy may be slow because it must follow constitutional processes, it is more sustainable because it is built through popular participation and consensus-building.

As Ghana addresses these global imperatives, we are leading by example at home through our transformative "Resetting Ghana Agenda."

Less than two years into my administration, through disciplined governance, fiscal prudence, and an uncompromising fight against corruption, Ghana has achieved a dramatic economic turnaround.

Indeed, some circles describe it as the “Ghanaian miracle.”

Our macroeconomic stabilisation measures have restored growth, drastically reduced inflation, stabilised our national currency, and significantly lowered our public debt burden.

This remarkable economic recovery story has been independently validated by multilateral financial institutions and major international credit rating agencies—all of which affirm that Ghana has moved from economic vulnerability to sustained recovery, resilience, and growth.

But macroeconomic indicators mean little if they do not translate into real improvements in our people's daily lives. Economic growth must have a human face.

That is why we are pursuing an aggressive national infrastructure agenda under our Big Push Programme to build roads, expand digital connectivity, and construct schools and health facilities.

This strategic investment is opening up the length and breadth of our country, bridging the rural -urban divide, unlocking agricultural potential, and guaranteeing equitable access to basic services for every Ghanaian, no matter where they live.

Through our flagship 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Programme, and the soon-to-be-launched ‘New Ghana,

New Economy’ policy, we are transforming Ghana into an industrial, high-productivity hub.

We are incentivising round-the-clock commercial operations, driving value addition in agriculture and mining, and creating sustainable, dignified jobs for our vibrant youth and women.

Central to our national reset is a revolutionary expansion of social protection and universal healthcare, delivering on the Sustainable Development Goals, specifically SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being), and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities).

Ghana has officially launched a historic Free Primary Health Care Programme, ensuring that every Ghanaian can access essential primary healthcare services at the community level at zero cost.

Hailed by the World Health Organisation (WHO) and the United Nations as a benchmark paradigm shift for the Global South, this model is currently being studied by other nations seeking to achieve true Universal Health Coverage.

Alongside our National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS), we have introduced a specialised fund officially named the Ghana Medical Trust Fund (and popularly referred to as Mahama Care) that guarantees Ghanaians suffering from Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs) such as renal failure, cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and diabetes receive subsidised, affordable, and life-saving care.

I have always believed that democracy must deliver tangible social benefits. Citizens must experience democracy not only through the ballot box every four years, but through improved access to food, quality education, decent housing, accessible healthcare, and economic opportunity.

Democracy loses its soul when it protects elite privileges while abandoning the vulnerable.

Ghana remains an uncompromising beacon of constitutional democracy, media freedom, the rule of law, and peaceful transitions of power on the African continent.

These domestic achievements set the stage for two historic milestones ahead. In March 2027, Ghana will celebrate its 70th Anniversary of Independence as the first nation in sub-Saharan Africa to break the shackles of colonial rule. And in January 2027, Ghana will proudly assume the Chairmanship of the African Union.

We will use our AU Chairmanship to champion continental integration, accelerate the implementation of the AfCFTA, push for peace and security in conflict zones, and ensure that Africa speaks on the global stage with one resolute, undivided, and confident voice.

Mr. President,

The daunting crises confronting our world are not insurmountable.

What we lack is not resources or intellect; we lack the political courage to see one another as part of a single human family.

We must see each other not as strategic rivals, economic targets, or demographic threats, but as human beings who belong.

The refugee fleeing violence belongs.

The migrant seeking opportunity belongs.

The child in Gaza, Sudan, or Ukraine belongs.

The descendants of enslaved Africans seeking justice belongs.

The indigenous community protecting its ancestral environment belongs.

The small island state threatened by rising oceans belongs.

The poor, the vulnerable, and the marginalised belongs.

They belong to our common human family. And because they belong, we must safeguard their dignity, enforce their rights, and hear their voices.

When Osagyefo Dr Kwame Nkrumah stood on the eve of Ghana’s independence in 1957, he declared that "the independence of Ghana is meaningless unless it is linked up with the total liberation of the African continent."

Today, from this respected global podium, we must expand that historic truth: The freedom of any nation is insecure unless it is linked to the freedom of all humanity. Our national prosperity is fragile unless it is shared.

Our global peace is unviable unless it is anchored in justice. Let this General Assembly recommit itself to a world where belonging is used not to erect walls, but to build bridges; not to exclude, but to unite; not to degrade humanity, but to exalt it.

Let us speak truth with humility.

Let us act with courage.

And let us cherish fearless honesty in the statements we deliver today, and in the choices we make tomorrow.

May God bless our shared world.

May God bless my homeland, Ghana.

And may God bless the United Nations.

I thank you.

In accordance with resolution 81 slash one of September 17th 2026 I Give the floor to the distinguished observer of the observer state of Palestine to introduce an address by the head of state Mr. President Excellencies ladies and gentlemen I have the honor to present a a pre-recorded video statement by His Excellency Mahmoud Abbas, President of the State of Palestine addressing the general debate of the 81st session of the General Assembly pursuant to General Assembly Resolution A-S-R-A-S-A-S-1. Thank you, Mr. President. In the name of Allah, the most gracious, the most merciful. Acccellency Dr. Khalil al-Rahman, President of the General Assembly. Acccellency Mr. Antonio Gutierrez, Secretary General of the United Nations. Acccellencies, Heads and Members of Delegations. For the second consecutive year, the Palestinian delegation was denied the entry visas required required to reach New York and participate in the meetings of the United Nations General Assembly in person. We reject these unlawful, punitive measures, and we reject the accusations and justifications on which they were based. We affirm that we have fulfilled our obligations, carried out a comprehensive national reform program and upheld our commitment to international law, to shunning violence and terrorism, and to the two-state solution, and to peace on the basis of resolutions of international legitimacy. We also affirm that the Palestinian people and its leadership should not be punished for demanding an end for the occupation or for turning to the UN, the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court. Our choice to invoke international law and its institutions is a peaceful and civilized choice and not an act that trans-counter to peace. Denying the Palestinian delegation access to the UN headquarters is a violation of the United States obligations as the host country. Therefore, we call upon the American administration to lift these sanctions and restrictions, return to dialogue and mutual respect, and work with us and with the international community in order to implement the two-state solution on the basis of international legitimacy, and to establish peace rather than punishing the side that has chosen the path of international law and political and diplomatic action in order to guarantee its rights. Mr. President, esteemed member states, I speak to you today as the Palestinian people faces one of the most dangerous times of its history. This is following long decades of historic injustice, uprooting, asylum-seeking, occupation, and the deprivation of its basic right to self-determination, freedom, and independence. In the Gaza Strip, our people are being subjected at the hands of the Israeli occupation forces to killing, destruction, starvation, and attempts at displacement, as well as a genocidal war that has created an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe. It has destroyed neighborhoods, cities, camps, institutions, schools, universities, hospitals, mosques and churches. And it has targeted all the basic necessities of life and the future of entire generations. In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, settler expansion is accelerating. The West Bank is being fragmented and Jerusalem is being isolated and Judaized. Settler terrorism is escalating under the protection of the occupying forces, while the crimes of land theft, home demolition, checkpoints, and raids continue under a system of laws, measures, and practices all built on racial discrimination, ethnic cleansing, and state terrorism. Ladies and gentlemen, we have long warned the international community through the United Nations General Assembly and through the Security Council that these Israeli policies in violation of international law would destroy the two-state solution and that this is what is happening now. Today, we warn of an even greater danger ahead, one that requires international action to address it. The danger is no longer limited to undermining the two-state solution and preventing the realization of the Palestinian state. It has now come to threaten the very life and existence of the Palestinian people on their homeland. What is taking place in Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem are not isolated incidents, but rather a malicious colonial scheme aimed at making the lives of Palestinians more difficult in their homeland and forcing them to leave it. We warn you today, do not allow another Nakba to occur. Do not allow further massacres like those that occurred in 1948. Do not allow terrorist gangs protected by the Israeli occupation forces to burn Palestinian homes while their occupants are sleeping inside them. Do not allow our children to live afraid and threatened. Once again, I ask before this assembly, how much longer will some states continue to remain silent on Israel or supply it with the weapons that it uses against our people? The world has witnessed the tremendous cost in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank. So what is the international community waiting for in order to protect the Palestinian people, ensure their continued presence on their land and the Israeli occupation, and implement the two-state solution on the basis of international legitimacy. This solution guarantees peace for all, instead of the threat emanating from Israeli extremism, which seeks to expand its colonial project towards establishing the so-called Greater Israel and completely erasing Palestinian presence. Mr. President esteemed member states, we welcomed President Donald Trump's 20-point plan. We also welcomed Security Council Resolution 2803 and the roadmap for implementing the second phase. This was to hold the aggression against our people and their humanitarian suffering and secure the withdrawal of the occupation forces from the Gaza Strip and begin rebuilding the Gaza Strip. However, regretfully, we have not seen any of this materialize on the ground. The Israeli killing and aggression continue to claim the lives of men, women and children in Gaza. Nearly a year has passed since the adoption of Resolution 2803 and the establishment of the Board of Peace. and only one year remains of the designated transitional period before the end of 2027. Therefore we call for accelerating the implementation of the second phase rather than wasting any more time. The transitional period must not be allowed to become a permanent or open-ended situation without any clear time-bound political horizon. Rather, it must lead to the reunification of the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, under the authority of the State of Palestine and its legitimate institutions in accordance with the principle of one state, one government, one law, and one legitimate entity authorized to bear arms. Ladies and gentlemen, esteemed member states, the threats and attacks carried out by extremists against Islamic and Christian holy sites, particularly Al-Aqsa Mosque and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem and the Ibrahim Mosque in Hebron, constitute a violation of their historic and legal status and of freedom of worship. They must seize immediately before they devolve into a broader religious conflict in the region and beyond. No one is in need of such an outcome. The ongoing Israeli attacks on United Nations headquarters and institutions in Jerusalem and the West Bank also undermine UNRWA's ability to continue carrying out its duties in providing support and assistance to Palestinian refugees, especially in the fields of education, health care, and vocational training. We call upon all states and international and regional organizations to continue supporting the work of UNRWA, for which there is no substitute so long as the refugee issue remains unresolved. This requires the continued financial support and political backing, as well as an end to these attacks against UNRWA. We particularly warn also against the implementation of the E1 settlement plan. This plan aims to separate the northern West Bank from its south, isolate East Jerusalem from its Palestinian surroundings, and prevent the realization of a geographically continuous Palestinian state. This requires urgent and responsible intervention by the United Nations Security Council. It also requires the implementation of Security Council resolution 2334. This resolution calls for the cessation of all settlement activities in the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem. We highly appreciate the measures taken by the United Kingdom, as well as 12 other countries in order to protect the two-state solution, as well as two ban settlement products. We also commend the call launched by the leaders of France, the United Kingdom, and Canada to convene a summit in New York on this matter. Furthermore, we call upon President Trump to fulfill the commitments he made to the leaders of the Arab and Islamic states last September to prevent the annexation of Palestinian land and to reject displacement. Mr. President, Excellencies, it is impossible to separate Israel's land-seizure practices from the dismantling of Palestinian institutions and the depletion of its financial resources. All of these are tools that lead to one same result, weakening our people's ability to remain steadfast and stay on their land. This leads to undermining our people's national institutions and preventing the realization of its state. The Israeli government is withholding more than $6 billion that belong to the Palestinian people. We are demanding the immediate release of all our with health funds, the guarantee of the regular and full transfer, and the lifting of the financial and economic restrictions and the blockade imposed on our people and our institutions in accordance with the Paris Economic Protocol, which was agreed upon following the Oslo Convention. Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, one year after the International Peace Conference and the adoption of the New York Declaration, I say to you today with full confidence and responsibility, we have fulfilled our pledge. We have fulfilled our pledge. We completed the national reform program to which we had committed before our people and the international community. We strengthened institutional governance, public financial management, transparency, accountability, anti-corruption measures, and the rule of law. We established a unified needs-based national system for social protection and social welfare, abolished the previous laws and regulations on this matter, and obtained an independent international audit confirming the validity of our measures. We also continue to reform the education system and develop criteria and curricula in accordance with international standards and in cooperation with UNESCO in a manner that promotes the values of peace, tolerance, and respect for others while preserving our national identity and the rights of our people. We also proceeded along the path of democratic revival and the empowerment of women and youth. We have held local council elections and elections for the general union of Palestinian students. We are headed towards our legislative elections on the 28th of November of this year. And this will be followed by the completion of the renewal of the institutions of the Palestinian National Council, followed by the Palestinian presidential elections. On behalf of the State of Palestine, I reaffirm the commitments in which we believe. We seek security and peace for all. We reject attacks against civilians by any party whatsoever. We reject terrorism and extremism in all their forms. We combat anti-Semitism, racism, and hatred. And we believe in a culture of peace, dialogue, and coexistence. We seek a democratic Palestinian state that respects the rule of law and human rights. A non-militarized state, a non-militarized state that lives in security and peace alongside the state of Israel. Is this possible? Ladies and gentlemen, our commitment to peace did not begin today. In 1988, our people and its leadership made a historic and difficult decision, and we accepted a historic settlement founded on the two-state solution on the basis of international legitimacy. Today we say to the world, saving the solution begins with preserving the land on which the Palestinian state is to be established and protecting the people who live on it. The Palestinian people will remain on its land. the Palestinian people will not accept displacement, will not accept displacement, and will not disappear. Neither military occupation nor settlement expansion, annexation, nor settler terrorism can be a solution or create lasting security. At the same time, we will not remain in waiting, nor will we accept whatever the governments of the Israeli occupying state decide for us. They have no right to decide for us. No lasting security can be built upon the occupation of another people and the denial of its legitimate rights. We have our own national project. Protecting our people from displacement, preserving our land and its unity, democratically renewing our institutions, and building our state while remaining committed to international law and exercising our right to self-determination, leading to the realization of an independent, sovereign Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital, along with the return of refugees in accordance with UN resolution 194. We do not want a new process for managing the conflict while the face of the land changes every day. We want a process that puts an end to occupation and guarantees freedom and self-determination for Palestinians, a process that guarantees also security and peace for Israelis and the countries of the region. Our vision for peace is clear. A Palestinian people remaining on its own land, determining its future for itself, and the Palestinian state alongside the state of Israel, and the Palestinian-Israeli peace that paves the way to regional integration, cooperation, prosperity and security for everyone. Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, we thank all the countries and peoples that have stood by our people. We thank countries and peoples that have lent political, humanitarian and economic support and helped us preserve our institutions and provide relief to our people. We also thank the countries that have recognized the state of Palestine, which now number 160 states. And we call on those countries that have not yet recognized the state of Palestine to do so. We likewise call for granting the state of Palestine full membership in the United Nations, similar to the rest of the nations and peoples of the world. Finally, I address the sons and daughters of our Palestinian people in their homeland and in the diaspora. You have painted the greatest picture of pride and dignity by holding steadfastly onto your land, your unity, and your legitimate rights. We will not leave our homeland. We will not accept displacement. and we will not allow anyone to decide our future on our behalf. We decide for ourselves. We will extend our hands to a peace based on international legitimacy so that our freedom and independence can be achieved and so that everyone in the region, everyone in the region, may live in security, peace and good neighbourliness. Peace be upon you all and the mercy of Allah and His blessings.

Mr. President,

I extend my congratulations on your election as President of the eighty-first session of the General Assembly. I wish you every success as you undertake this important responsibility at a moment when multilateralism, and indeed the United Nations, faces profound challenges.

I also express my sincere appreciation to your predecessor for her stewardship over the past year.

I take this opportunity to record Guyana’s gratitude to the Secretary-General, His Excellency António Guterres, for his distinguished service to the United Nations and to the cause of humanity. His place in the history of this institution is assured, not merely by the office he has occupied, but by the principles he has steadfastly upheld, the courage and profundity with which he has spoken when silence would have been easier, and his rare ability to hold before the world a clear mirror of the perils that confront our age and the possibilities that still beckon beyond them.

The challenges of our time Mr. President,

One year ago, I stood at this very podium and reminded this Assembly that if the United Nations is to remain humanity’s surest hope for a just and peaceful world, it must have the courage to confront aggression and the wi ll to engage fully with the defining questions of our age. I also argued that we must be bold enough to undertake the institutional reforms necessary to strengthen the Organization, enhance its credibility and enable it to meet the challenges of a changing world.

Indeed, I am pleased that the theme of this year’s assembly, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All” acknowledges the need for this organization to be made fit for purpose to respond to the challenges and to seize the possibilities of our time.

Today, we confront a climate catastrophe; an energy crisis; food insecurity; biodiversity loss; armed conflicts and geopolitical tensions; the horror of genocide; a spiralling cost-of-living crisis; a mounting debt crisis; widening inequalities within and among nations; and, perhaps most troubling of all, a weakening of multilateralism itself.

Yet if history has taught us anything, it is that even when the world seemed to stand at the precipice, humanity has never been entirely without the means to draw it back from the brink. We have ended wars that seemed without end. We have confronted economic calamities that threatened the foundations of societies.

We have overcome dangers that presented existential threats.

Time and again, it has been our inventiveness, our courage and, above all, our willingness to act together that have opened a path where none seemed to exist.

The possibilities of our age This is why I do not wish to linger or lament further upon the difficulties before us. I wish instead to turn our gaze toward the possibilities that lie beyond them. For within every crisis lies a summons to solutions, within every disruption an opportunity for renewal, and within every uncertainty the possibility of shaping a better future.

The possibilities before us are immense.

We have the possibility of silencing the guns through dialogue and diplomacy. The world does not need more sophisticated instruments of destruction; it needs a more sophisticated capacity for peace.

In this regard, I reiterate Guyana’s call for a just and lasting solution to the crisis in the Middle East, one that brings an end to the suffering of innocent civilians and recognises the Palestinian people’s legitimate right to self-determination and to a secure homeland of their own. We reiterate our support for the two-State solution.

We call as well for an end to the Russia-Ukraine war and the war in Sudan, and for peaceful resolution of all conflicts that continue to consume lives, uproot families and extinguish the hopes of millions in other parts of our world.

We reiterate our call for a viable solution for Cuba, one that is peaceful, people centered, development -focused and allows for the full aspirations of the Cuban people to be realized. Guyana reiterates CARICOM’s offer to play a meaningful role in achieving this objective.

In Haiti, resolving the multidimensional challenges remains central to achieving democracy, stability, peace and prosperity for the Haitian people. The sustained support of the international community through the provision of key financial and material resources is critical to realizing t hese objectives.

Ultimately, the future of Haiti must be Haitian-led and Haitianowned.

Mr. President Turning to my own country - Guyana has always advanced the peaceful settlement of the controversy in relation to our border with Venezuela. Despite the historical truth - clearly outlined in the Arbitral Award of 1899 that determined the full, perfect and final settlement of our bord er with Venezuela, we endured long and repeated provocations and aggression.

The matter was referred to the International Court of Justice by the Secretary General, acting pursuant to the Geneva Agreement, and the Court twice pronounced on its jurisdiction to hear the matter. Recourse to the ICJ came after decades of efforts to resolve the controversy bilaterally, including through a mixed commission and the Good Offices of the UN Secretary General.

In full respect for international law, Guyana participated and encouraged Venezuela to participate in the proceedings of the ICJ.

Now that we have both participated in the hearings which were completed in May 2026, we urge Venezuela to abide by the forthcoming ruling in accordance with their obligation under the UN Charter, as Guyana will do.

We look forward to a new era of neighbourly relations in the interest of our peoples, the development of our countries and the stability and prosperity of our region.

Mr. President In pursuit of a stronger and safer region, Guyana is honoured to be a founding member of the Shield of the Americas, launched by President Trump in March 2026.

Since the founding of this initiative, Guyana has worked closely with the United States and thirteen other like -minded nations that believe in building a Western Hemisphere that value s freedom, peace, economic prosperity and have a shared responsibility and commitment to fight ing transnational crime and criminal networks.

It is our collective responsibility to never allow our region to be overtaken by gangs or criminal networks.

We understand that it is only through partnership, shared intelligence, and cooperation that we can effectively tackle the threats they pose to our economies and the livelihoods of our citizens.

This week, I was pleased to join members of the Shield of Americas in adopting a Joint Communique which underscores our collective resolve to strengthen the resilience of our region in Economic, Security and Multilateral Coordination.

Mr. President We stand at the threshold of a new era of technological advancement. Artificial intelligence, biotechnology, digital communications and other extraordinary breakthroughs offer the prospect of transforming health, education, agriculture, productivity and public services on a scale scarcely imaginable a generation ago. But the true measure of technological progress will not be how powerful our machines become, but how much more empowered our people become. Technology must not become the privilege of the few; it must become the servant of all humanity.

Mr. President,

We have before us a new opportunity for sustainable development. Development must not merely make our economies richer; it must make our societies better. We must not allow further slippage in our pursuit of the Sustainable Development Goals. We must renew our commitment to them — not as an inventory of promises, but as a covenant with our peoples and a practical blueprint for ensuring that development reaches every citizen, protects generations yet unborn and creates lasting, inclusive prosperity.

One way to arrest this slippage is, as Guyana is doing, to mainstream the Goals into our national development strategies, public policies and budgets, so that they become embedded in the priorities we set and the resources we commit, rather than remaining aspirations. The SDGs must not only guide our ambitions; they must shape our choices and our national priorities.

In Guyana, we have made significant advances including universal health care, free education, modern infrastructure, accelerated access to affordable housing, opportunities for full employment, acceleration of financing for small and medium sized enterprises, and digitizing service delivery.

Mr. President Two years ago, at this very podium I committed Guyana to provide global leadership on biodiversity. In July 2025, under Guyana’s leadership, the Global Biodiversity Alliance was established as an inclusive platform. In just over one year, the Alliance expanded from 17 to 138 members, bringing together governments, international organization, including the UN, development banks, Indigenous Peoples, local communities, scientists, universities and the private sector.

The second conference of the Alliance, to be held on October 2026, will begin to mobilize the resources and partnerships to deliver its ambitions.

At the same time, w e continue to advance our national Low Carbon Development Strategy focused on turning forest stewardship and climate action into a new model for sustainable development.

Mr. President As we commence this 81 st Session, w e have the opportunity to build a United Nations that is truly fit for purpose.

The crisis confronting multilateralism can become the catalyst for its renewal. The United Nations must not be a monument to the past; it must become an instrument for the future. We need a Security Council that reflects the geopolitical realities of the twenty-first century, not the power structures of 1945; a Council that embraces the emerging multipolarity of our world, including permanent representation from Africa, and Latin America and the Caribbean.

A new multilateralism Mr. President If the United Nations is to remain humanity’s best hope, then this is not the hour to retreat from multilateralism. This is the hour to reclaim and to renew it. For it is in times such as these— when wars rage across borders, when the shadow of existential threats falls across the future of human civilisation, when the old certainties are dissolving before our eyes —that multilateralism must rise.

Multilateralism rests upon the proposition that our destinies are bound together, that the security of one cannot be at the insecurity of another, and that in an interdependent world, cooperation is a necessity; and where t here can be no enduring prosperity where inequality deepen s, and no just international order where rules are applied selectively.

It is to that truth that this eighty -first session of the General Assembly must recommit itself. But recommitment cannot mean merely repeating the language of yesterday. The world has changed, and multilateralism must change with it.

We need a new and invigorated multilateralism —one equal to the turbulence of our age, sufficiently courageous to confront its trials, sufficiently imaginative to navigate its transformations, and sufficiently principled to defend the rule of international law.

To make the United Nations fit for purpose we must make it more transparent, accountable and responsive. We must strengthen the General Assembly and give greater weight to its deliberative and representative authority. We must bring greater coherence to a system too often divided by institutional rivalries, bureaucratic silos and competing mandates. We must ensure that the resources of the UN match the responsibilities we have entrusted to it.

Leadership But institutions do not reform themselves. They require leadership capable of seeing beyond the present and imagining the institution the future demands.

The United Nations needs leadership that can bring its different organs, agencies and programmes into a greater unity of purpose. Leadership that can build bridges where division has become habitual; leadership that can defend the principles of the Charter without fear or favour.

The United Nation s needs its next Secretary-General to work with all member States to restore confidence in the Organization, mobilise its energies, and turn the language of multilateralism from aspiration into action. The reform of the United Nation s, the restoration of trust and the need to manage transformation is, therefore, inseparable from the question of leadership. And the choice of its next Secretary -General will be, in no small measure, a choice about the kind of United Nations we wish to leave to the generations that follow.

Guyana’s nominee for UN Secretary General It is in this spirit that Guyana has put forward the candidature of Her Excellency Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett for the office of Secretary-General of the United Nations. She has served her country, represented the developing world, and worked within the multilateral system with a deep understanding of both its promise and its imperfections.

We believe that her experience, her convictions and her record of service speak directly to the kind of leadership this moment demands.

Her candidature, therefore, acquires special significance amid the profound challenges confronting the United Nations and the international order. We need leadership capable of restoring trust without compromising principle; of listening without surrendering conviction; of building bridges across the widening chasms between North and South, between large states and small, between the developed and developing worlds.

We need a Secretary -General who will defend the Charter not only when it is politically convenient, but precisely when its principles are under pressure.

The responsibility for recommending the next Secretary-General rests, in the first instance, with the Security Council, and we therefore respectfully place before its members the candidature of Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett. Endorsed by the Caribbean Community (CARICOM), we invite all to consider her candidacy on its merits and to judge whether her vision, experience, expertise and record can help restore confidence in the United Nations at this critical moment.

Conclusion Mr. President,

The United Nations was conceived in hope —and that hope remains alive in the pursuit of peace, security and human progress over the perpetuation of division and war. This is why we must not abandon multilateralism because it is imperfect; we must renew it because humanity still needs it.

Let us therefore build a United Nations that does not merely reflect the world as it is, but helps create the world as it ought to be—a world where law restrains power, cooperation overcomes division, and every human being can look to the future with hope.

Guyana believes that the choice remains ours as to whether the divisions of our age will define the future, or whether nations can summon the will to build a more peaceful, secure and prosperous international order. The United Nations must be at the heart of that endeavour—not as an institution looking back at the world it was created to serve, but as one helping humanity shape the world that is yet to come.

I thank you

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished delegates,

Ladies and gentlemen,

It is a great honour to address the eighty -first session of the United Nations General Assembly at a moment of profound uncertainty in our world.

I congratulate His Excellency Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of this session and assure him of Somalia’s full support and cooperation. I also commend Secretary -General António Guterres for his continued service to the United Nations and his steadfast defence of multilateralism. He will be missed very much after he concludes his term as the Secretary General this year. Indeed, his successor will have extremely large boots to fill going forward.

For generations, the United Nations has represented humanity’s shared determination to replace conflict with dialogue, domination with cooperation and despair with hope. Yet today, many of the ideals and values we once collectively defended are being questioned and challenged.

جمهورية الصومال الفيدرالية البعثة الدائمة لدى الأمم المتحدة نيويورك Jamhuuriyada Federalka Soomaaliya Ergada Joogtada ah ee Qaramada Midoobey - New York Federal Republic of Somalia New York 369 Lexington Ave, Suite 14B New York, N.Y. 10017 Tel: (212) 659-5014 Fax: (212) 659-5016 Respect for international law is becoming increasingly selective. Multilateral cooperation is weakening. Conflict, geopolitical rivalry and mistrust are becoming defining features of our time. Uncertainty, unfortunately, has become the new normal.

I remember the sense of optimism that accompanied the transition from the Millennium Development Goals to the Sustainable Development Goals in 2015. There was genuine hope that we were beginning a new chapter -one in which no person, no community or no country would be left behind. Eleven years later, we must have the courage to admit that the world is not where we expected it to be.

Progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030 stands at 36%. This is far too slow. Conflicts between and within States are increasing. Humanitarian needs are rising while the resources available to meet them are rapidly declining. Nationalism, intolerance and political polarisation are weakening the spirit of international cooperation.

At the same time, the climate crisis continues to destroy lives, livelihoods and public infrastructure, particularly across the developing world.

According to the United Nations, over 40% of the global population are vulnerable to the destructive effects of Climate change and governments in developing countries spend over 10% of their GDP to respond to this. These painful fiscal trade -offs come at the expense of investment in education and health which should never be the case.

For millions of vulnerable people, global development can sometimes appear to be moving from one framework to another, from one set of promises to the next, without sufficient transformation in their daily lives. New declarations and targets have value, but they cannot become a substitute for effective implementation.

This is why this year’s theme is both timely and necessary. Trust in the UN will not be restored through declarations alone. It will be restored when our institutions act consistently, uphold international law and produce results that people can see and experience.

Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

The United Nations Charter is founded on sovereign equality, territorial integrity, peaceful coexistence, human rights and the dignity of every person. The most important word in this year’s theme is “ALL.” Not some people. Not a select group of nations. Not only those with the greatest economic or military might.

The promise of the Charter belongs equally to every human being and every Member State. Yet, the United Nations has increasingly become associated with political gridlock in the Security 369 Lexington Ave, Suite 14B New York, N.Y. 10017 Tel: (212) 659-5014 Fax: (212) 659-5016 Council, prolonged negotiations without tangible outcomes and a weakening capacity to mobilise collective action in response to threats to international peace and security.

This should concern all of us, not because the United Nations is not important, but precisely because it is indispensable and appears absent from the global solutions for peace and stability in this dangerous and unpredictable time.

The Security Council must become more representative, transparent and effective. Africa remains unrepresented in the permanent category and not represented enough in the non permanent category. This historical injustice against 54 sovereign states cannot be postponed indefinitely.

Somalia supports the Common African Position and meaningful African representation in both categories of the Council. Given that many of the discussions directly concern African States, they have the right to full representation on equal par with all other Permanent Security Council members.

Reform is not an attack on the United Nations. Reform is necessary to protect its legitimacy, renew confidence in its institutions and ensure that it remains capable of responding to the realities of our time.

Somalia currently proudly serves as a non -permanent member of the United Nations Security Council and as a member of the African Union Peace and Security Council. We carry these responsibilities with great seriousness, humility and determination. In both institutions,

Respect for national sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity is not an abstract principle for Somalia: It is a foundation for peace and stability in our country, our region and the wider international community. Therefore, Somalia firmly rejects unilateral actions that undermine its sovereignty, unity and internationally recognised borders. Disagreements between nations must be resolved through dialogue and in accordance with international law and not through actions that create new tensions or threaten regional stability.

UN Political reform must be accompanied by institutional administrative and operational renewal.

For nearly two decades, we have discussed the need to make United Nations operations more agile, coordinated, cost -effective and capable of delivering measurable results. Some progress has been made, and we recognise the dedication of the many United Nations personnel working under difficult conditions around the world. However, we must also be honest: the results have not yet matched our collective expectations.

In countries like mine, where the United Nations has maintained a substantial presence for more than three decades, operations can become more effective by aligning more closely with our national priorities and using credible national systems.

The majority of UN assistance continues to be delivered through parallel structures, fragmented projects and off -budget arrangements in Somalia. This makes it difficult for governments to plan, coordinate resources, measure results and build the institutions required for long-term stability.

Let us be clear: Somalia is not calling for the United Nations to withdraw. We are simply calling for a more accountable, strategic and result oriented partnership where Somali institutions are in the lead when it comes to implementation. Indeed, Somalia wants a partnership in which international assistance reinforces rather than replaces national leadership. This partnership is one in which national institutions are strengthened rather than bypassed and both governments and international organisations are mutually accountable for results.

The base argument of past UN agencies development thinking that countries like Somalia lack capacity must be condemned permanently to the dustbin of history. It is where it belongs. We now have capable people, institutions and policies that are proudly guiding our national transformation.

We must also ask ourselves why we continue to mobilise vital resources to respond to crises while investing far less in preventing them. The UN office for Disaster Risk Reduction estimates that every $1 invested in proactive measures, resilient infrastructure, or early anticipatory action saves between $3 and $15 in future damages and response costs. Therefore, we cannot remain trapped in a cycle of financing the consequences of conflict while neglecting peacebuilding or responding to humanitarian emergencies while under -investing in resilience and anticipatory action. Prevention is more cost -effective. It is more humane. It is much more sustainable.

We therefore call for predictable and sustainable support for Somalia’s security transition, including adequate financing for the African Union Mission in Somalia. The transition towards full Somali security responsibility must be properly resourced, phased and firmly anchored in capable Somali institutions.

Following debt relief, Somalia’s economy continues to grow on the foundation of strong reforms. Our real GDP growth this year is 3.1% despite all the global shocks we are 369 Lexington Ave, Suite 14B New York, N.Y. 10017 Tel: (212) 659-5014 Fax: (212) 659-5016 experiencing. We are actively working to improve the investment environment to create opportunities for all our people. We also continue to strategically increase investment in education, health and human capital despite the pressures created by geopolitical tensions, recurrent climate shocks and rising global prices.

A serious example of regional tensions negatively impacting Somalia’s development is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz. For Somalia, disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz have serious economic and humanitarian consequences.

As an import-dependent country reliant on the Middle East for much of our food, fuel and trade,

Somalia is already facing rising prices, inflation and increased transport and insurance costs while drought linked to climate change is affecting over 6 million people. The disruption has also contributed to an estimated 40% decline in our customs -based domestic revenue, a critical source of financing for Somalia's economic reforms, growth, and poverty reduction.

Ensuring free and fair navigation through the Strait is therefore essential to protecting vulnerable economies like Somalia and sustaining stability, advancing development, and delivering basic services.

Sustainable development requires strong institutions. In Somalia, we have created institutions capable of translating international commitments into national results. These include the National Climate Fund through which Somalia is mobilising and coordinating urgently needed climate finance, the Independent National Human Rights Commission, established to strengthen the protection and promotion of human rights and the Somali Disaster Management Agency which is on the frontline of responding to humanitarian crises.

Financing is pivotal to development. Therefore, the promise of sustainable development cannot be fulfilled without reform of the international financial architecture. In the same way that the Security Council must reflect today’s political realities, international financial institutions must effectively respond to today’s economic and environmental realities with relevant, affordable and accessible financial products which can be disbursed in a timely manner.
