Mr President, Mr Secretary-General, Excellencies,

It is a special honour to address this Assembly on behalf of Hungary. I speak here to the nations of the world, but also to my fellow citizens watching at home.

For much of my life, I served as a judge, in Hungary and at the European Court of Human Rights. That work taught me a simple lesson: The law must apply even to those in power.

Law does not weaken a state by placing limits on power. It gives citizens a reason to trust the state.

This belief will guide me as President. I will protect the Constitution, the freedom of our institutions and the dignity of every Hungarian citizen.

The state belongs to those who support the government, to those who oppose it and to those who have lost trust in politics altogether. A new political majority must not become the new owner of the state.

This April, the people of Hungary voted for democratic renewal. They expected more than a change of government. They expect public life to change: a state that serves rather than controls, courts that decide without pressure, a press that challenges power and public money that is used for the public good.

There must be accountability for corruption and abuse of power. But there must be no revenge. Justice cannot become a political weapon. A democratic state cannot repair past wrongs by repeating them with new people in charge. The same law must apply to those who governed yesterday, those who govern today and those who may govern tomorrow.

A republic begins where power accepts its limits. That is the republic Hungary must now rebuild.

Trust from our partners will not return because of one election or one speech. Hungary asks to be judged by what we do.

We will be a reliable member of the European Union, a committed NATO ally and an active member of the United Nations. These partnerships do not take away our freedom. They protect it.

Hungary will defend its national interests, but it will do so as a partner. We believe that national interest and international cooperation do not have to stand against each other.

For Hungarians, the reasons are part of our own history.

Seventy years ago, the revolution of 1956 expressed our people's determination to govern themselves. Soviet tanks crushed that hope.

Our appeals reached the United Nations, but the international community could not prevent our defeat.

Many countries represented here opened their doors to Hungarians who fled their country after the revolution. We remember both the cost of losing our independence and the help that allowed our people to start again.

Today, Ukraine is fighting to preserve its independence. Hungary condemns Russia's full-scale war of aggression as a violation of the United Nations Charter and international law.

We affirm Ukraine's right to self-defence, its sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders, and the right of its people to decide their own future.

The freedom Hungarians demanded for themselves in 1956 is a freedom we must uphold for Ukrainians today.

We remember those who have lost their lives in this war, and we want diplomacy to bring the killing to an end. But a lasting peace must respect Ukraine's sovereignty.

If taking territory by force becomes an accepted way of settling disputes, every smaller country will have reason to worry about its own future.

The principles of the Charter therefore matter to all of us.

Human suffering cannot wait for diplomacy to succeed. People in conflict need food, medicine and protection now. Hungary will continue to provide humanitarian aid to people in danger, especially the most vulnerable.

In the Middle East, we call for full respect for international humanitarian law and for aid to reach those who need it safely and without interruption.

Israelis and Palestinians must be able to live in security and dignity. A lasting peace must give their families reason to believe that their children can grow up without the fear that has marked so many lives.

For people forced from their homes by war or persecution, protection may first mean finding safety in another country. Hungary's own history gives us reason to understand that need.

At the same time, every state has the right to protect its borders.

Hungary will do so in accordance with international law. We will fight illegal migration and the criminal networks that profit from it, while respecting human dignity and the protection given to refugees.

But security is not only about borders and wars.

People also need the chance to build a future where they live. They need homes, schools, health care and ways to earn a living. Poverty and the lack of opportunity can drive people from their countries just as conflict can.

Hungary will continue to support development that helps communities build that future, based on their own needs and priorities.

We are ready to share our experience in education, health and digital development.

Water is another area where our interests meet. Drought can destroy crops, threaten food and energy supplies and take away people's income. Climate change is making these pressures greater.

Rivers also cross borders. What one country does can affect the water available to another. This makes cooperation essential.

Hungary has experience in water management, sustainable agriculture and climate adaptation, and we are ready to share it.

For many countries represented in this hall, food, energy, education, health and jobs are immediate concerns. We must give these issues the same serious attention that we ask others to give European security.

International cooperation works best when it responds to people's real needs and when every country has a voice.

Excellencies,

The United Nations faces a crisis of trust.

Too often, it fails to act when powerful states or their friends break the rules. No country should be above the law. We cannot have one rule for our friends and another for others.

But the answer is not to turn away from the United Nations.

We need it, and we need it to work.

It must be able to act, treat all its members fairly and apply the same principles to everyone.

Hungary is ready to do its part. We will stand for human rights, support peacekeeping and work with countries across the world to protect people and help diplomacy succeed.

We must also look beyond the problems of today.

Many of the decisions we make now will shape the lives of people who are not yet born. A school, a strong institution or a safe water system can benefit people for many years.

Future generations must therefore have a place in the decisions we make today.

Hungary supports stronger international action to protect their interests, including the appointment of a United Nations Special Envoy for Future Generations.

The United Nations cannot demand trust. It must earn it.

The same is true of every state and every public institution.

The Hungarian people have asked us to restore their confidence in the future. We will honour that choice by rebuilding trust at home and by becoming a country others can trust when their own future is at stake.

For Hungary, this is a new beginning. But the principle behind it is not new:

Power earns trust only when it accepts the law.

That is the responsibility Hungary accepts, and the work we are ready to undertake with you.

Thank you for your attention.

It is the only realistic way to address the problems of today.

This is why our message is clear: we need multilateralism.

Multilateralism that is strong, effective, representative and capable of delivering for people. Multilateralism that protects human rights, strengthens democracy and advances gender equality.

Multilateralism equipped to address the defining challenges of today: peace, the climate emergency, economic insecurity and Artificial intelligence.

On artificial intelligence and its governance, we need an accountable, transparent and regulated architecture. We need an AI that serves humanity, not controls it. The strength of tomorrow’s multilateral system will depend on this commitment. Thank you, António Guterres.

A stronger multilateral system also requires stronger alliances. The European Union does not seek to impose a model or to establish spheres of influence. The European Union aims to create spaces for progress, peace and shared prosperity together with partners from all regions.

That is why we are continuing to build the world’s largest network of trade agreements, covering 84 countries worldwide. Over the past 12 months, we have concluded negotiations or signed trade agreements with India, Australia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Mercosur and Mexico, benefiting billions of people.

But the value of what we can do with our partners must go beyond trade.

And in no area is action more urgent than in that of sustainable development.

Agenda 2030 is in danger. The funding gap is widening, the climate crisis is worsening and geopolitical divisions are holding back progress. We must continue to work on reforming the global financial architecture.

The European Union remains strongly committed to the Paris Agreement, the Pact for the Future and the Sustainable Development Goals, funded in line with the Sevilla Commitment.

Together, the European Union and its member states account for more than 40 % of official development assistance at international level. And through our Global Gateway initiative, we are investing in all areas, from sustainable infrastructure and connectivity to health, education and poverty eradication.

We cannot afford to lose any more time. That is why the 2027 Sustainable Development Goals Summit must be a turning point: to correct course, to regain momentum and to meet the targets for 2030 and beyond.

The European Union is clear about its choice.

Cooperation over confrontation. about:blank 5/7 Law over power.

Partnership over isolation.

Action over paralysis.

We are ready to work together with all those who share this conviction.

Let us reform.

Let us renew.

Let us reinvest.

And let us act. Together.

Mr. President, Dr. Khalilur Rahman Excellency Mr. António Guterres, Secretary -General of the United Nations,

Your Majesties, Excellencies, Heads of State and Government,

Heads of Delegation,

Distinguished Delegates,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

It is a distinct honour for me to address this Assembly on behalf of His Excellency Mr. Adama Barrow, President of the Republic of The Gambia.

I bring to this Hall the warm greetings of the Government and people of The Gambia, together with our enduring friendship, solidarity and goodwill to all nations represented here.

Mr. President, allow me, at the outset, to congratulate you most warmly on your election as President of the eighty -first session of the General Assembly.

The Gambia assures you of our full support and constructive cooperation as you guide our collective work under the timely theme you have chosen: restoring trust and managing transformation so that the United Nations can deliver for all. That theme speaks directly to the moment in which we meet.

Permit me also to express our profound appreciation to your predecessor, Ms. Annalena Baerbock, for the dedication, dignity and determination with which she presided over the eightieth session of the General Assembly.

I also wish to place on record The Gambia's appreciation for SecretaryGeneral, Mr. António Guterres, and Deputy Secretary -General Amina Mohammed, whose steady and principled leadership through years of compounding global crises has done much to keep the flame of multilateral cooperation alight, even as the winds against it have grown fiercer. We wish them well as they complete their tenure at the end of this year.

Mr. President,

Few institutions embody the principle of sovereign equality as visibly as this Assembly. Within these walls, differences in power, wealth and influence may shape the realities our nations confront, but they do not confer a greater claim to membership or participation.

And, perhaps more than anywhere else, this Assembly reminds us of a simple truth: Our differences are real. But so is our interdependence.

That is why this Organization was created with the understanding that disputes must be resolved through dialogue, human dignity must be protected, and that nations must work together if development, peace, and human rights are to be sustained. In other words, our common future requires common institutions.

Eight decades later, we must ask ourselves whether we have remained faithful to that insight. And perhaps more importantly: Do we still trust one another enough to act on it?

Because today, Mr. President, trust is being tested. Geopolitical divisions are widening. Wars have become more protracted with devastating humanitarian consequences.

Respect for the United Nations Charter and international law is under visible strain, with developing countries facing intensifying debt burdens, climate vulnerabilities, huge gaps between commitments made and implementation, and a feeling of marginalization and inadequate representation in the global system.

Therefore, the task before us is building a stronger, better equipped, representative, responsive, and effective multilateral system and global financial architecture that delivers for all nations and regions.

Mr. President,

The Gambia’s own experience within this Organization gives us grounds for optimism. We have seen, within this very institution, that multilateralism can still deliver.

During the eightieth session of the General Assembly, The Gambia had the honour of chairing the Second Committee at a time of profound disagreement over some of the most consequential economic and development issues before us.

That experience reminded us that multilateralism does not require unanimity on every issue. It requires the willingness to remain at the table, to listen, to negotiate, and to have the courage to compromise.

Our experience demonstrated that even in periods of deep disagreement, progress remains possible when Member States approach negotiations with political will, mutual respect and a shared sense of responsibility.

Mr. President,

The stakes are perhaps greatest in international peace and security, one of the foremost purposes for which this Organization was created.

If diplomacy can bring countries together to find common ground on difficult questions of global development, then surely, we can summon the same political courage to prevent conflicts, resolve wars and build lasting peace.

The Gambia speaks on this not merely from principle, but from experience. In 2017, our country stood at a moment of acute constitutional uncertainty. The democratic choice of the Gambian people faced a grave challenge. At that critical moment, the United N ations' preventive diplomacy, working in partnership with the African Union and ECOWAS, helped uphold the will of the Gambian people and support a peaceful democratic transition.

We have not forgotten that solidarity. It taught us that preventive diplomacy is not an abstract concept. It is a practical instrument for preventing confrontation, creating space for dialogue and protecting institutions. Sometimes, it can change the course of a nation.

That experience also gives us an obligation. If the international community could stand with The Gambia at a moment of fragility, then countries facing similar moments should be able to count on the same solidarity.

Across the world, however, conflicts continue to destroy lives, displace populations and reverse decades of development. Civilians bear the greatest cost, while humanitarian workers operate under increasingly dangerous conditions and the resources availabl e to respond to crises remain far below what is required.

The protection of civilians, respect for international humanitarian law and humanitarian access are not political conveniences. They are legal obligations and expressions of our shared humanity.

We need stronger early-warning systems that enable us to act before crises escalate, timely mediation before positions become entrenched, and peacebuilding that addresses the conditions that allow conflict to take root. The question before us must therefore not only be how to end the ongoing wars, but how to prevent the next war from beginning.

Prevention should not have to wait for a crisis to become sufficiently destructive to attract international attention. It is infinitely less costly, in human, political and financial terms, to prevent conflict than to manage its consequences after violence has begun.

We therefore welcome the Secretary -General’s continued good offices and preventive diplomacy and call for these efforts to be matched with predictable and sustained resources.

Mr. President,

Peace must be built and nurtured through institutions that command public confidence, societies in which trust can be restored and justice pursued, and a future in which women and young people have a meaningful voice and economic opportunity is within reach.

The Gambia has experienced the value of peacebuilding firsthand.

Since our democratic transition, the Peacebuilding Commission and the Secretary-General’s Peacebuilding Fund have been steadfast partners in our nationally led efforts to strengthen instituti ons, advance transitional justice and consolidate peace.

We therefore support a stronger and more responsive Peacebuilding Commission, adequately resourced to support countries emerging from conflict or navigating delicate political transitions.

The implementation of the outcomes of the Peacebuilding Architecture Review must translate into stronger prevention, greater national ownership and closer coordination across the United Nations system.

We also reaffirm our support for United Nations peacekeeping operations and pay tribute to the men and women who serve under the UN flag, including Gambian military and police personnel who have contributed with distinction to international peace and security.

Their safety and security must remain a priority, alongside performance, accountability and strict adherence to international law.

Partnerships between the United Nations and regional organizations, particularly the African Union, must also be deepened with sustained and predictable funding.

Mr. President,

The ongoing conflict in Sudan remains a matter of profound concern to The Gambia. Together with continuing instability across parts of the Sahel, it reminds us that peace cannot be separated from development and governance.

The suffering of civilians in the affected conflict zones globally demands sustained international attention and renewed diplomatic efforts towards de-escalation, dialogue and a durable political settlement.

In the Sahel and other conflict zones, o ur response s must be comprehensive and holistic. Security measures are necessary, but they must be accompanied by increased support for democratic governance, institution-building, education, job creation, development and climate resilience.

Mr. President,

For millions of people around the world, poverty, lack of human rights, democratic governance, etc. continues to pose great insecurity.

The absence of education, healthcare, decent employment, and the loss of homes and livelihoods to climate change leave communities as vulnerable as conflict itself. Our understanding of security must therefore extend beyond the absence of war to include the conditions that allow people to live with dignity, opportunity and hope.

Mr. President,

In The Gambia, this understanding has guided our democratic journey from 2017 to date. We have undertaken the difficult work of rebuilding institutions, strengthening the rule of law, expanding access to justice and confronting the legacy of past human rights violations.

Our transitional justice process continues through implementation of the recommendations of the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission (TRRC). We have strengthened institutional accountability and established the Special Prosecutor's Office to advance investigations and prosecutions arising from the TRRC process.

We are proud of the progress we have made, but we remain conscious that democracy is never a finished project and requires continuous institutional strengthening, adherence to the rule of law, constitutional order, dialogue, and consensus-building.

On 5 December 2026, the Gambian people will again exercise their sovereign democratic right to choose their President. This will be another important milestone in our democratic journey, and we need the support of the international community in this regard.

My Government is committed to ensuring that the elections are peaceful, transparent, credible, and inclusive, and are conducted in accordance with our Constitution, national laws, and democratic standards.

This is the democratic path The Gambia remains committed to pursuing: a path in which institutions are strengthened, citizens are heard, differences are resolved peacefully, and democratic gains are consolidated for future generations.

Mr. President,

On development, The Gambia's Recovery -Focused National Development Plan, YIRIWA 2023 –2027, provides the framework for accelerating our socio-economic transformation.

We are investing in roads, energy, schools, healthcare, agriculture and digital infrastructure, while promoting economic diversification, private-sector investment and value addition.

We are expanding opportunities for women and young people, improving lives and strengthening the human capital upon which our future depends. I seize this opportunity to thank all the bilateral and multilateral partners of The Gambia for your continuous support and partnership.

Mr. President,

The global economic environment remains particularly difficult for developing countries, with declining Official Development Assistance, high borrowing costs, disruptions to international trade, inflationary pressures, food and energy insecurity, narrowing fiscal space, and threats to development gains.

With only a few years remaining to achieve the 2030 Agenda, the time for implementation is now. Following the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, we must translate the Sevilla Commitments into tangible action.

Developing countries need greater access to affordable, long -term finance; meaningful reform of the multilateral development system; sustainable solutions to debt; stronger international tax cooperation; and decisive action against illicit financial flows.

We also need stronger, more resilient supply chains, greater investment in productive capacity, and a global economic system that gives developing countries a fair opportunity to transform their economies.

Trade must remain an engine of development, and developing countries must be enabled to participate more effectively in regional and global value chains.

This would enable developing countries to invest in education, health, agriculture, climate resilience, and other productive sectors to holistically address their interconnected challenges.

Mr. President,

Climate change presents another test of our collective credibility and for The Gambia, it is not a distant threat.

Coastal erosion, changing rainfall patterns, pressure on water resources, food insecurity and environmental degradation are already affecting our communities and livelihoods.

However, w e are responding with determination by investing in renewable energy, coastal resilience, mangrove restoration, disaster risk reduction, early warning systems, water security and nature -based solutions.

National electricity access has reached 90 per cent, with universal access targeted by the end of 2026.

We are expanding solar energy in schools and health facilities, modernizing our electricity network and advancing a 150-megawatt solar park.

We have also adopted our first National Disaster Risk Mitigation Plan and are restoring and sustainably managing more than 100,000 hectares of mangroves.

But we urged that our national ambition be supported by international action to make climate finance accessible, predictable and adequate, including through the sustained implementation of the New Collective Quantified Goal on Climate Finance and effective arrangements to address loss and damage, build climate resilience and a fairer international order in which those who have contributed least to the climate crisis are not left to bear its greatest burdens.

Mr. President,

Artificial intelligence and emerging technologies offer extraordinary opportunities, but opportunity without inclusion can become another source of inequality. The digital divide must not become the next development divide.

Developing countries must not remain passive consumers of technologies designed elsewhere. We need the capacity to participate in research, innovation, entrepreneurship, standard -setting and global technology governance.

Technology must serve humanity, and the governance of artificial intelligence must be inclusive, responsible and grounded in international cooperation.

This is particularly important for the world's Least Developed Countries. As The Gambia prepares to assume greater leadership within the Global Coordination Bureau of the LDC Group, we do so with a clear sense of responsibility.

LDCs continue to face structural constraints, including limited productive capacity, high debt burdens, climate vulnerability, narrow export bases, technological gaps and restricted access to affordable finance.

We will continue to advocate for full implementation of the Doha Programme of Action, with particular attention to productive capacity, structural transformation, industrialization, science and technology, climate resilience and human capital development.

Graduation from LDC status must be a pathway to sustained prosperity and resilience, not a cliff edge leading to the premature withdrawal of essential international support.

South-South and Triangular Cooperation should also remain important complements to North -South cooperation, particularly in knowledge sharing, technology transfer, capacity building and mutually beneficial development partnerships.

Mr. President,

Migration is another area where our collective response must be guided by human dignity and shared responsibility. Migration contributes significantly to economic development, cultural exchange and human progress. Yet irregular migration continues to expos e young people and vulnerable populations to exploitation, trafficking, abuse and tragic loss of life.

We must strengthen cooperation for safe, orderly and regular migration, protect the rights and dignity of migrants and expand lawful pathways for labour mobility as well as investment in young people, women, education, health and social protection to safeguard sustainable development and lasting peace.

With Africa having the world's youngest population, youth employment must remain a development priority. We need greater investment in education, technical and vocational training, entrepreneurship, digital skills and productive employment. Young people must also have a meaningful voice in the decisions that shape their future.

The same is true of women's empowerment, which is essential to peaceful, inclusive and prosperous societies. The Gambia remains committed to expanding women's economic opportunities, strengthening women's leadership and addressing the barriers that limit their meaningful participation in political and public life. We are also strengthening support for women entrepreneurs, survivors of gender -based violence and vulnerable households.

Ensuring food security, building strengthened and resilient health systems, and pandemic preparedness remain equally urgent. The Gambia is investing in agricultural productivity, mechanization, irrigation and climate-smart agriculture, while expanding access to improved seeds, fertilizers, credit and support for farmers. At the global level, we must build food systems capable of withstanding climate, economic and geopolitical shocks.

Mr. President,

The Gambia welcomes the calls for reform of the United Nations.

We recognize the constraints facing the organization with limited resources and increasing demands.

Nevertheless, reforms would strengthen the United Nations' capacity to better serve its Member States and the people of the world and correct the historical injustice that continues to prevail.

We need to embark on reforms that strengthen delivery, protect the universal character of the Organization and enable developing countries to participate meaningfully in decisions that shape their future.

The General Assembly must remain at the centre of global deliberation and policymaking, and the structures of the Organization must also reflect the world as it exists today.

For the Security Council, its reform is not simply about expanding membership. It is about restoring legitimacy and strengthening trust. We need a Council that is more representative, transparent, accountable, effective and responsive to contemporary geopolitical realities.

The Gambia therefore reaffirms its support for the Common African Position reflected in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration and commends the position of African leaders in this regard.

Mr. President,

The General Assembly's decision to move towards a convention on the prevention and punishment of crimes against humanity is an important contribution to addressing a longstanding gap in the international legal framework.

The Gambia is proud of its leading role, alongside Mexico, in advancing this process through more than three years of patient negotiations.

Our conviction is simple: the gravest crimes cannot be met with silence. Victims cannot be forgotten, and impunity cannot become an accepted feature of international relations.

Prevention, accountability and justice are indispensable to reconciliation, healing and sustainable peace.

The rule of law is one of the foundations upon which trust is built.

The continued development of multilateral treaties and the entry into force of the agreement on the conservation and sustainable use of marine biological diversity of areas beyond national jurisdiction also demonstrate what is possible when States negotiate in good faith and persevere.

The Gambia commends Ghana for its historic resolution on the Declaration of Trafficking of Enslaved Africans and Racialized Chattel Enslavement of Africans as the Gravest Crime against Humanity and Togo for the Resolution on Correcting the Map at the General Assembly.

Mr. President,

Our credibility is ultimately tested by how we respond to conflicts and crises that remain unresolved for years. The suffering of the Palestinian people remains a profound test of the credibility of the international system.

The Gambia reiterates its call for the protection of civilians, respect for international humanitarian law, and unhindered humanitarian assistance.

We reaffirm the legitimate and inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, including their right to self -determination, membership of the United Nations, and our support for a just, comprehensive and lasting twoState solution, with Israel and Palestine living side by side in peace, security and dignity.

Furthermore, t he plight of the Rohingya people must also not disappear from the international agenda. The Gambia remains committed to accountability, justice and the protection of their fundamental rights and would continue to need the support of you all in this shared collective endeavour.

On Cuba, we reiterate our longstanding call for an end to the economic, commercial and financial sanctions. Dialogue, engagement and cooperation remain important instruments for improving people's well-being and strengthening peaceful relations among nations.

The Gambia also reaffirms its adherence to the One China Policy and values its partnership with the People's Republic of China, including in development cooperation, infrastructure, South-South and Triangular Cooperation and Partnership.

The leaders of our two countries have raised our bilateral relationship to Strategic Level, and we would continue to grow and deepen this important partnership.

On the question of the Moroccan Sahara, The Gambia supports sustained international efforts towards a peaceful resolution through the United Nations -led political process, and we encourage all concerned parties to engage constructively and in good faith.

The Royal Initiatives of Moroccan Autonomy, the Morocco -Nigeria Gas Pipeline, the Atlantic African Initiative, among others, have provided realistic pathways to a lasting political solution to the dispute over the Moroccan Sahara by giving people the development, human rights, security, and stability they need.

Furthermore, The Gambia welcomes the Kingdom of Morocco’s continued commitment to the ceasefire, full cooperation with MINURSO, and all stakeholders, in line with Resolution 27 97 (2025) and other relevant processes.

We urged all stakeholders, i.e., Polisario, the Kingdom of Morocco,

Algeria, and the Islamic Republic of Mauritania, to continue working to achieve a sustainable political solution to the conflict, and we support the various initiatives of the United Nations in this regard.

Mr. President,

In conclusion, t he United Nations and the m ultilateral system continue to be challenged, but they remain the most reliable guarantor of our collective peace and security and proven mechanisms to confront the challenges facing humanity. Therefore, the task before us is to make the United Nations and the multilateral system more responsive, more representative and better able to deliver for the people that we serve.

What we leave behind should be a legacy of renewed multilateralism, a reformed United Nations, increased international cooperation and solidarity, and an increased trusted global system that sustains peace, advances development, human rights, democracy, and opens the way to a more secure future for all.

The Gambia stands ready to work with every Member State to renew the promise that brought the nations of the world together. My country's journey has taught us that countries and institutions can recover from moments of profound uncertainty and further build trust and confidence.

That is the message we bring to this Assembly.

I thank you, Mr. President.

The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Jose Manuel Restrepo, Vicepresident of the Republic of Colombia.
I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address this assembly.
Mr. Secretary general, Mr. Vice president of the General Assembly, heads of State and government.
Excellencies, ambassadors.

Ladies and gentlemen, I appear today before this assembly representing the president of the Republic of Colombia, Abelardo de la Espriella, who has asked me to be here on his behalf and bring before you a message written by him.
From this moment on, what you will hear are the words of the president of the Republic of Colombia.
I have asked the Vice President of the Republic, José Manuel Restrepo, to read this message on my behalf.
I have done so because I assured the Colombian people that I would not leave the country during the four years of my term, and I am keeping that promise.

47 days ago, a new government took office in Colombia.
Three days later, at 7:34 a.m., the earth shook.
A 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck my country in a matter of seconds.
Homes, hospitals, schools, roads and bridges had been totally destroyed or severely damaged.

The Colombian Geological Service confirmed that this was the strongest magnitude earthquake recorded in Colombia so far this century Hundreds of Colombians lost their lives.
4500 were injured and more than 452,000 people were affected.
36,000 homes were totally destroyed.
They represented the life savings assets of these people.

The government that had barely started its work was forced to confront one of the greatest natural disasters in our recent history.
There was no time to ask whether we were ready.
We had to act, and we did so.
From the very outset.

I gave one unequivocal instruction we had to save human lives.
There was time for everything else.
Appointments to posts could wait, meetings could wait.
But my fellow fellow Colombians trapped underneath the rubble could not.

The government deployed to the affected areas alongside the security forces, emergency services, volunteers and rescue workers.
And from the very beginning, we started receiving the generous assistance from friendly countries and international organizations such as all of you.
And today, from this rostrum, I wish to express the profound and sincere gratitude of the Colombian people to all of you.
The earthquake claimed the lives of many of our fellow Colombians and destroyed thousands of homes and buildings and much infrastructure.

But it also reminded us once again of something that Colombians are very familiar with.
We might fall, we might suffer, and we might weep.
But what we cannot and what we do not know how to do is give up.
But I'm not only going to talk to you about this tragedy.

I want to refer to what Colombia decided to do in its aftermath.
On the 7th of August, I took over a country that had begun to lose something far more difficult to rebuild than a road or a building.
That is trust.
Trust in the law that should protect our citizens.

Trust that working, studying, and doing things well are worthwhile.
Trust in a state that lives up to its duty.
No country, no country can prosper when its people cease to trust in it.
That's why the government that I lead has tasked itself with taking up every possible decision to enable Colombia to believe in itself again, and to ensure that the world can believe in Colombia again.

And I call that overarching purpose the patria milagro, the miracle nation.
The first step is a basic one restoring security.
For far too long, Colombians have had to live alongside situations that no society should accept as normal.
A rural farmer having to ask permission from a terrorist group to work on his land, a shopkeeper having to hand over part of the fruits of his labor to extortionists, a mother increasingly gripped by fear every time their child goes out to play in the park.

That is not, and it cannot become the norm.
Consequently, from the very beginning of my government I gave the security forces one clear instruction to regain territorial control, to fully restore the state's authority and to confront the structures using terrorism.
My government is determined to do away with euphemisms.
Organizations that murder, that kidnap, that use explosives, that recruit children, and that deliberately resort to terror to subjugate a society are terrorist groups.

That is what we call them, and we are facing up to them with the full, legitimate force of the state, within the Constitution and within the law But there is another reality that is very often overlooked.
The illicit drugs produced in Colombia don't end up in Colombia.
Drugs trafficking is a transnational criminal enterprise.
Its routes cross borders.

Its money moves through international financial systems, and its networks operate across numerous countries.
I will do everything necessary to combat that scourge, but a transnational threat requires the international community to play its part as well.
Security, while essential, is not enough.
A territory that provides no opportunities remains vulnerable.

My administration is therefore also focused on ensuring that Colombia grows again.
For years, we have discussed how to better distribute what we have.
That is a legitimate, necessary discussion, but it's absolutely not enough.
We also need to ask ourselves, how are we going to produce more?

In the end?
Governments can't decree economic growth.
What they have to do is lay the foundations for it to occur.
In our miracle nation, we want an idea to be able to come, a business, a business to create jobs, and for jobs to become well-being for our people.

To those of you anywhere else in the world who are wondering where to invest, I would like to invite you to look at Colombia.
It's a country with access to two oceans, productive land, energy resources, enormous biodiversity, an excellent geographical position, and a government that champions private enterprise.

Allow me to begin by clarifying what I mean by that.
I'm not talking about international trade or cooperation among states, nor am I talking about a humanity that shares common problems and responsibilities.
All of those things are absolutely necessary I'm talking about a concept according to which nation sovereignty, distinct identities, traditions, and the values of peoples are obstacles that gradually give way to increasing political and cultural uniformity decided by supranational bodies.

I don't share in that doctrine, which I consider perverse and harmful.
For me, multilateralism isn't about dissolving nations, but rather about facilitating cooperation among them.
Loving one's homeland isn't compatible with respecting others, defending history, culture, values, and traditions doesn't mean disparaging those of another.

That is the international fight against terrorism.

This organization has done significant work here.
Since 1963, the international community has developed 19 universal legal instruments aimed at preventing different terrorist acts.
However, after decades of discussion, there is still no legal definition of terrorism that is universally agreed by member states.
The UN Office of Counterterrorism itself has recently flagged that the lack of a universally agreed definition begets legal uncertainty.

Discrepancies among national laws and causes difficulties in international cooperation.
The Republic of Colombia believes that the time has come to move ahead.
We need a common international definition that is sufficiently clear and precise, compatible with international law and fundamental safeguards, but also useful enough so that states can cooperate effectively in combating acts of terrorism.
A serious definition should avoid two extremes.

On the one hand, a political disagreement being arbitrarily characterized as terrorism, and on the other hand, allowing an organization to hide murders, kidnappings, bombings, or deliberate attacks against civilians behind a political label in order to evade the legal consequences of its actions.
Terrorism must be condemned regardless of the perpetrator, where it is committed or the cause they invoke.
The United Nations has repeatedly reaffirmed that terrorism, in all its forms and manifestations, represents one of the most serious threats to international peace and security.
Now, a better definition is not enough.

States need better tools to combat this phenomenon.
We need faster mechanisms for exchanging information and intelligence.
We need better judicial cooperation, effective tracing, freezing, seizing instruments for assets related to terrorist financing.
And we need closer cooperation to deal with networks that operate simultaneously across different countries.

Colombia stands ready to participate actively in that discussion.
My country wants to see United Nations, where the effectiveness is measured less by the volume of documents it produces, and far more by the results that it delivers.
A UN that is less inclined to multiply processes and more determined to translate international cooperation into concrete action.
That is the sort of multilateralism that Colombia is ready to defend, one that respects the sovereign equality of states as the charter itself provides, but one that is also capable of acting effectively when threats recognize no borders, drugs, trafficking, terrorism, transnational organized crime and illicit economies are precisely those threats.

Specifically, my government's foreign policy is guided by national interests by the defense of our sovereignty, and by the pursuit of results.
That national interest I refer to also has a specific objective that is ensuring the prosperity of our people.

Colombia does not come before the world today to ask others to do for us what it is our responsibility to do for ourselves rebuilding our country, restoring security, growing the economy, protecting our institutions, and giving opportunities back to millions of people are first and foremost responsibilities that fall to Colombians.
But we also know that no nation can turn its back on the world.

The President of the United Nations General Assembly,

Your Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman,

The Secretary-General, Mr. António Guterres,

Fellow Heads of State and Government,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Ni sa bula vinaka, and a very good afternoon to you all.

I bring warm greetings from the people of Fiji, and from the Blue Pacific Continent.

Mr. President,

I congratulate you on assuming the Presidency of the Eighty-First Session of the United Nations General Assembly. Fiji assures you of our full support as you guide this Assembly through a period of profound uncertainty and transformation. Our Prime Ministe r, the Honourable Sitiveni Rabuka, joins me in wishing you and all Member States a peaceful, productive and successful session.

I acknowledge your predecessor, Her Excellency Annalena Baerbock, for her stewardship of the Eightieth Session.

I pay tribute also to Secretary-General António Guterres, who addresses this general debate for the last time in that office.

Through a decade of turbulence he has defended multilateralism and stood with Small Island Developing States. Fiji thanks him.

Mr. President,

The theme of this session — “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All” — speaks directly to the condition of our world.

We face deepening geopolitical rivalry, armed conflict, climate and environmental crises, economic uncertainty, disrupted supply chains, rapid technological change, and an information environment corroded by disinformation.

These crises do not remain where they begin. Conflict raises the cost of fuel and food far beyond its borders.

Carbon emitted far from the Pacific takes our shorelines, our homes and our sacred places.

For Small Island Developing States, distance no longer insulates us from global shocks. Too often, it magnifies their cost.

Trust, therefore, is not restored by declarations alone. It is restored when commitments are kept, when international law is applied consistently, when institutions listen, and when people can see and feel the results of multilateral action in their daily lives.

Mr. President,

Fiji reaffirms an enduring principle: international law is not optional, and peace cannot be secured by power alone.

For small States, the principles of the Charter — sovereign equality, territorial integrity, the peaceful settlement of disputes — are the safeguard against a world in which size or military strength decides whose rights matter.

When the world asks small States to choose between competing power blocs, Fiji chooses principles. We choose the Charter. We choose international law.

We choose dialogue over coercion, human dignity over domination, and cooperation over confrontation.

Fiji calls for the peaceful settlement of conflicts wherever they occur.

We urge all parties to protect civilians, respect international humanitarian law, and return to the negotiating table.

The Charter does not apply differently according to who is involved, or where. Fiji asks the same of every party, in every theatre.

Energy, food security and supply chains are inseparable from peace. The freedoms of navigation guaranteed under international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, must be respected.

Fiji will continue to serve in United Nations peace operations. We ask only that they be properly mandated, properly financed and properly supported — and we support renewed investment in prevention, mediation and the quiet diplomacy that stops wars before they begin.

We carry a simple Pacific conviction: the life of a stranger is worth protecting, dialogue is worth pursuing, and peace, however difficult, is always worth building.

COOPERATION Mr. President,

The Pacific knows the cost of militarization and nuclear testing.

Our ocean carries the memory of decisions made elsewhere but suffered by Pacific peoples. That memory strengthens our determination that the Blue Pacific remain a region of peace.

The Ocean of Peace Declaration expresses a regional vision grounded in sovereignty, international law and the rejection of coercion.

Our message to all partners is clear: the Pacific welcomes friendship, investment and genuine cooperation — but our ocean must not become a theatre in which others settle their rivalries.

For Small Island Developing States, regional cooperation is not an optional layer of diplomacy.

It is a practical necessity. Separated by vast distances, with small populations and narrow economic bases, what is difficult alone becomes possible together. We must take it further still — through connectivity, food and energy security, and Pacific -led f inancing such as something the Pacific has built. The Pacific Resilience Facility is the first climate and disaster financing facility owned, governed and hosted by the States it serves.

Its treaty entered into force in May, it is seated in Tonga, and its first grants are already reaching our communities.

It exists because a village seawall does not need a threeyear accreditation process. It needs money that arrives.

Its initial capitalisation target is five hundred million United States dollars by December, of which one hundred and seventy-three million has been pledged.

I thank those who have come forward, and I ask those able to close that gap to do so.

Cooperation of this kind does not diminish our sovereignty. It strengthens our ability to exercise it.

RENEWAL Mr. President,

The call to restore trust must also apply within our own nations. Fiji's democratic journey has not been easy. We have known political upheaval, constitutional change and periods of deep division. We cannot change that history, but we can learn from it.

This year Fiji undertook a national review of the 2013 Constitution, informed by consultations across the country. On 1 September the Commission presented its report to me as Head of State. That did not end the process; it began the next stage.

The report must now proceed through Parliament and the democratic processes, transparently and in accordance with the rule of law.

What Fiji seeks is not a Constitution for a government, a party or one generation, but a settlement that every Fijian recognizes as their own. Alongside it, our Truth and Reconciliation process continues. Renewal strengthens institutions; reconciliation heals divisions.

Together they can carry Fiji from memory to understanding, and from division to trust.

Mr. President,

If the United Nations is to restore trust, it must also be willing to reform itself.

Fiji supports the UN80 reform agenda to make the Organisation more coherent, efficient and effective. But reform must be judged by a single test: what it improves for people and for Member States.

For Pacific Small Island Developing States, efficiency must not mean distance. The Multi -Country Offices serving our region are essential bridges between global commitments and island realities.

Reform must strengthen, not thin, our capacity to deliver where need is greatest.

This Assembly will also select the next Secretary General. Fiji asks for a process that is transparent and merit-based — and for a Secretary -General who understands the realities of small island States and will act on them. For too long our circumstances h ave been well diagnosed and poorly addressed.

The promise to “deliver for all” must also be measured in development. With 2030 approaching, too many Sustainable Development Goals remain off track.

National income alone cannot capture remoteness, disaster exposure and the repeated burden of rebuilding.

The Multidimensional Vulnerability Index must move from adoption to application.

There is one measure of delivery that reaches Fijian households directly. Remittances are now Fiji’s third largest source of foreign exchange. They pay school fees, rebuild homes after cyclones, and sustain families between harvests. They are not aid. They are the earnings of Fijians abroad, sent home.

Yet Pacific corridors remain among the most expensive in the world through which to send money. In May, in this Hall, we recommitted ourselves to bring transfer costs below three per cent, and to eliminate corridors costing more than five. Pacific corridors are among those. Fiji asks that this be treated as an obligation and not an aspiration.

Labour mobility must also not become a one -way transfer of the people we have trained.

Fiji does not begrudge any Fijian the chance to build a life abroad. We ask only that those who recruit our nurses and teachers invest in the systems that produced them.

And this belongs beside what I have said of reconciliation. Not every Fijian abroad left in search of work. Some left in seasons of upheaval, when they did not feel that the country was theirs. They are Fijians still, and so are their children.

A supreme law that belongs to every citizen must belong to them also. Fiji’s door is open.

This month, Fiji declared a national HIV emergency.

One in sixty of our adults is now estimated to be living with the virus. Fewer than four in ten know it.

I say this plainly, because stigma and silence are how this epidemic grew — and because the late Ratu Epeli Nailatikau, our former Head of State and UNAIDS Goodwill Ambassador for the Pacific, spent his last years telling us so.

This is also a security question. Methamphetamine trafficked into our region by transnational criminal networks is now driving transmission through injecting drug use. Our borders are ocean, our populations are small, and the profits at stake exceed our national budgets. A country of under a million people cannot interdict a global supply chain alone.

So Fiji asks three things: that treatment and diagnostics reach small States at prices we can pay; that the Global Fund and UNAIDS be resourced at a level that does not force triage between regions; and that our partners treat Pacific narcotics interdiction as the shared security interest it is.

These are the same loss. A nurse who emigrates is a nurse Fiji trained and will not have. A Fijian who dies at thirtyfive of a treatable virus is the same subtraction, made permanent, with the cost of care left behind. Small States are not losing workers at the margin. We are losing the capacity to staff our own future.

Mr. President,

Nowhere is the gap between promise and delivery more consequential than in the climate crisis.

For the Pacific, climate change is not a future scenario.

It is saltwater entering farmland, coastal erosion moving closer to homes, stronger storms damaging schools and roads, pressure on fisheries and food security, and communities facing relocation.

This is a question of science. It is also a question of justice.

This Assembly has this week addressed the threats posed by sea-level rise. For Fiji the legal consequences are not abstract. Statehood, once established, continues.

Maritime zones, once lawfully established and deposited with the United Nations, must remain — notwithstanding the physical changes brought by sea -level rise. No State should lose its rights, its identity or its seat in this Hall because others have altere d its coastline. Fiji urges this Assembly to carry that principle from declaration into settled international law.

Fiji welcomes the Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice on the obligations of States in respect of climate change. It confirms that climate responsibility is not only political or moral — it is legal.

The task now is implementation: obligations recognised by the Court must be reflected in national commitments, in the conduct of States, and in the outcomes of our negotiations.

Climate finance must move from promise to access, and from announcement to disbursement. The Loss and Damage Fund must operate at a scale that reflects actual need, and access must be simplified — for small administrations, the cost of applying should never exceed the capacity to apply.

In November, the world gathers in Antalya for COP31.

Before that, Fiji hosts the Pre -COP, and Tuvalu a Leaders’ event, in early October.

To every delegation in this Hall: come to the Pacific. See what a rising sea means to a village that has nowhere to move. Then let us go to Antalya and deliver — on adaptation, on finance, on loss and damage, and on the transition away from fossil fuels.

As a Large Ocean State, Fiji’s identity, economy and future are inseparable from the ocean. Illegal fishing, pollution, biodiversity loss and warming, acidifying seas do not respect national boundaries — and no island nation can meet them alone.

This year, the Agreement on marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction entered into force — a genuine achievement of multilateralism. Fiji calls for universal ratification, for a first Conference of the Parties that delivers a functioning institution, and for capacity building and technology transfer that are real rather than aspirational.

And in the deep sea we ask of others only the discipline we ask of ourselves: that no exploitation proceed until the science is sufficient and the rules are sound. The common heritage of humankind is an obligation owed to those not yet born.

Mr. President,

Fiji comes to this Assembly as a small island State, but not with a small vision.

Our size does not diminish our voice.

Our vulnerability does not diminish our agency.

And our distance from the centres of power does not distance us from its consequences.

Transformation will happen whether we manage it or not. The real question is what kind of transformation we choose.

Will it be governed by law, or by power?

And will this Assembly remain a place where we describe crises — or become an institution that solves them?

Let this Eighty-First Session be remembered not for the depth of our concern, but for the courage of our decisions.

Let us build a United Nations that is trusted because it is fair; relevant because it adapts; and respected because it delivers.

Let us build a Pacific that remains an Ocean of Peace — united in purpose, confident in its identity, and strong enough to shape its own future.

And let us remember that the measure of what we do here will not be found in our speeches. It will be found in whether a coastal community can remain on the land of its ancestors, and whether a young person can trust democracy and find a future at home.

That is the United Nations Fiji believes in.

And that is the trust we must restore — together.

Vinaka vakalevu.

I thank you.

Over the past decade, he has exercised his high office with profound humanity and absolute fidelity to the ideals of the charter of the United Nations in an international context that has been among the most trying in the contemporary history of our organization, Cote d'Ivoire wishes to express its deep gratitude to him for the excellence of our cooperation, which has grown stronger throughout his term.
Mr. Secretary General, President Alassane Ouattara has asked me to convey to you his warmest regards, grounded in high esteem and friendship, as well as his sincere wishes for success in the next chapters of your distinguished career.
Mr. President.

This session is taking place against a deeply troubling international backdrop.
Conflicts and hotspots of tension are multiplying, and geopolitical divisions are deepening.
While the rise of terrorism and violent extremism threatens an ever growing number of regions.

At the same time, climate upheavals are hitting our countries hard, not to mention the humanitarian crises and deep inequalities that are weakening our societies.
Added to this are the very real risks to the survival of humanity posed by the uncontrolled development of artificial intelligence.
The world is thus at a difficult turning point.
It is looking on at the gradual fragmentation of its peace architecture and an alarming reconfiguration of the international landscape before our very eyes.

The trust of peoples, for its part, is nourished by tangible results and by the certainty that the decisions taken on their behalf genuinely serve their security, their dignity, and protect their future.
This year's theme, therefore, aptly captures the expectations of our time.

For Cote d'Ivoire, this means reinvigorating multilateralism and consequently.
Restoring Diplomacy's rightful place and credibility so that it can act effectively.
In light of these challenges, a monumental task awaits the next Secretary General of the United Nations, whose selection process is now well underway.

Cote d'Ivoire hopes that this process will result in the appointment of a figure of the highest caliber, whose moral values independence of mind, diplomatic experience and commitment to dialogue will enable the United Nations to pursue, with ambition and effectiveness its mission in the service of peace, development and solidarity among nations.

Current international events remind us every day of the human, political and economic cost of protracted conflicts.
Cote d'Ivoire remains deeply concerned about the resumption of hostilities in the Near and Middle East, the consequences of which weigh on peace and on food, energy and economic security throughout the world.

And to lend its full support for the many mediation efforts undertaken by the United Nations, the African Union and relevant regional organizations.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies, Heads of State and Government,

Distinguished Delegates,

I extend my warmest congratulations to you, Mr. President, on your election as President of the Eighty -First Session of the United Nations General Assembly and assure you of Nigeria’s full cooperation and support. I commend your predecessor’s stewardship o f this Assembly. I also salute the Secretary General, His Excellency António Guterres, for steering the United Nations through storms that have sharpened our awareness of the cost of inaction.

2. None of us can pretend that conflicts within our borders or in lands far beyond them do not exact a price from us. Such is the reach of our interdependence. Such is the urgency of this session’s sacred duty to restore trust in the international institutions we established to reconcile our differences and advance our common interests.

3. The persistence of conflict across the world recalls the purpose for which the United Nations was founded: to spare succeeding generations the devastation of war. We must therefore return to the founding principles of dialogue, mutual respect and collectiv e responsibility. Nigeria stands by the Charter and its promise of a world in which diplomacy prevails over coercion, cooperation over isolation and international law over the arbitrary exercise of power.

Mr. President,

4. The reform of this institution must begin with the reconstitution of the Security Council, for the world of 2026 cannot remain captive to the distribution of power in 1945. Africa cannot continue to fill the Council’s agenda while remaining absent from its permanent membership. Nigeria demands, in accordance with the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration, at least two permanent seats for Africa, with all the rights and responsibilities of permanent membership, including the veto for as long as it exists, and five non permanent seats in total. The authority to speak for humanity carries an obligation to represent it.

5. Nigeria stands ready to assume greater responsibility on the strength of obligations honoured and sacrifices made over decades in the service of peace. From Liberia and Sierra Leone to Darfur, Mali and The Gambia, we have committed personnel and resources when international solidarity required action. Through ECOWAS, the African Union and our Gulf of Guinea partnerships, we continue to advance mediation, democratic governance, counter -terrorism and maritime security.

Mr. President,

6. Our foreign policy rests on the same conviction that guides our economic reforms. Through sound macroeconomic management, stronger institutions, private -sector development and strategic public investment, we seek to give practical meaning to our sustainabl e development commitments. This purpose binds our national advancement to our continent’s progress and to our responsibility to contribute to a peaceful, equitable and prosperous world.

7. We understand that governments and multilateral institutions earn trust when their decisions improve lives. Yet none of these gains will matter if we turn a deaf ear to the threats gathering around our borders and farther afield. We inhabit the only planet known to sustain human life, and as long as that scientific fact holds, we cannot pretend that we are insulated from conflicts elsewhere. Geography offers no exemption from the consequences of a fractured world.

Mr. President,

8. We reject the false choice between development and climate action. Developing countries must industrialise, eradicate poverty and expand energy access through low -carbon pathways supported by technology transfer, capacity building and climate finance. Africa contributes less than four per cent of greenhouse gas emissions, yet bears disproportionate consequences. Nigeria remains committed to the Paris Agreement and an equitable energy transition that reflects historical responsibility and capacity while protecting people’s right to development.

9. Under our Energy Transition Plan, we are working towards net-zero emissions by 2060 while expanding access to affordable, reliable and sustainable energy. This effort combines renewable energy, clean cooking and gas as a transitional fuel with climate -smart agriculture and nature based solutions. Finance must be governed by equity and shared responsibility rather than charity, with international commitments translated into accessible, predictable and adequately funded mechanisms enabling developing countries to pursue climate action without compromising development objectives.

Excellencies,

10. We refuse to surrender our technological future to paranoia.

An invention can be destructive or beneficial, depending on the purposes it serves and the judgement of those who use it.

A knife can take a life in the hands of an assailant and save one in the hands of a surgeon. We can deploy artificial intelligence t o wage war or use it to transform healthcare, education, agriculture, governance and economic productivity.

Much of the anxiety surrounding AI reflects the distrust we have allowed to grow among us.

11. Nigeria is investing in digital public infrastructure, broadband connectivity, innovation ecosystems, research institutions and technology entrepreneurship. We invite the world to work with our inventive, resourceful and enterprising young people to direct AI towards humanity’s advancement rather than its destruction.

12. Mr. President,

13. One of the greatest obstacles to sustainable development is inadequate financing. Many developing countries devote substantial resources to debt servicing at the expense of education, healthcare and infrastructure. Nigeria therefore calls for reform of the international financial architecture, wider access to concessional financing and debt sustainability frameworks that recognise developmental needs. We also support innovative financing through private capital, blended finance, South-South cooperation and strategic partnerships for sustainable development, climate adaptation and resilient infrastructure.

14. Nigeria further recognises the African Continental Free Trade Area as one of the continent’s most transformative opportunities. It can strengthen regional value chains, expand intra-African trade, promote industrialisation and attract investment. Africa must move beyond its historical role as an exporter of raw materials towards greater value addition, manufacturing, technological innovation and knowledge driven growth. Our abundant natural resources must become engines of shared prosperity rather than sources of perpetual dependency.

Mr. President,

15. No nation, however formidable its defences, can secure itself completely against dangers sustained beyond its borders. Terrorism, organised crime, cyberattacks and illicit finance exploit the gaps between our national responses, drawing strength from the d ivisions that weaken collective action. Nigeria’s prolonged struggle against Boko Haram,

ISWAP and other armed groups has taught us that military victories require enduring foundations in education, economic opportunity, accountable governance and communities whose rights and dignity are protected. Development cannot take root where violence repeatedly uproots livelihoods, and peace cannot endure where injustice and exclusion replenish the ranks of those who threaten it.

16. Our common security therefore demands cooperation equal to the reach of the threats before us. We must exchange intelligence, strengthen institutional capacity, interrupt the financing of violence and prevent weapons from crossing borders that our responses too often fail to cross. The turmoil in the Sahel illustrates how insecurity in one territory can imperil its neighbours, displace populations and frustrate commerce, regional integration and democratic governance.

As a founding member of ECOWAS, Nigeria upholds regional solidarity and African leadership in resolving these challenges, reinforced by principled international partnerships. No country can claim lasting safety while the forces capable of destabilising it retain sanctuary, resources and recruit s elsewhere.

Excellencies,

17. Nigeria remains committed to the peaceful settlement of disputes under the United Nations Charter. The conflicts in Sudan and other war-torn countries demand urgent diplomacy to address their humanitarian, economic and geopolitical consequences. All parties must uphold international humanitarian and human rights law, protect civilians and facilitate humanitarian access. Negotiated settlements must respect sovereignty and territorial integrity. Within and beyond our continent, no claim to security can justify starving children, denying relief to civilians or erasing communities from the land they call home.

18. We should all be afraid of a world in which we can no longer tell the victim from the aggressor. When our investment in propaganda shields perpetrators from justice to the point that telling the truth becomes a crime, the promise of this institution stands betrayed.

19. We place our faith in diplomacy because military victories alone cannot secure lasting peace. Dialogue, reconciliation and inclusive political processes must give people a stake in ending violence and preserving the agreements that follow.

The United Nations must therefore strengthen peacekeeping and give greater attention to peacebuilding, mediation, institution-building and sustainable development. Prevention must command greater resources and political attention.

Mr. President,

20. Africa is ready for the future. Our resilience, our ingenuity, our youthful population, our natural wealth and our expanding markets can make us a major driver of global growth in this century. The African Continental Free Trade Area offers exceptional scope to deepen regional integration, accelerate industrialisation and strengthen our place in global value chains. De veloping countries must be recognised as indispensable partners whose contributions to global solutions and shared prosperity extend far beyond their need for assistance.

21. Such a partnership requires a United Nations that evolves with the aspirations of present and future generations.

Institutions that adapt preserve their relevance; those that resist change imperil it. Nigeria remains optimistic because history shows that countries acting with common purpose and determination can overcome obstacles once considered insurmountable. Our generation has the privilege of shaping the future and the responsibility to answer for it. Those who follow us will judge our courage in reforming outdated institutions, building cooperation across divisions, protecting the planet and directing technology responsibly.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates,

22. Nigeria pledges to choose cooperation over confrontation, dialogue over division, hope over fear and partnership over isolation. These choices must shape institutions that respond to the legitimate aspirations of all nations. Restoring trust requires us to honour our obligations to one another and to manage the changes before us with justice, wisdom and compassion.

23. The world looks to this Assembly for leadership, and our debates must lead to action worthy of that expectation. Nigeria believes that the humanity we share is stronger than the divisions we have made and that cooperation remains wiser than conflict. A ref ormed, inclusive and effective United Nations is indispensable to the peaceful, just and sustainable world that future generations deserve. Whatever our differences, we must remember that humanity is our oldest citizenship, and peace is the inheritance we owe every child.

24. I thank you for your kind attention.

Thank you, Mr. President.
In the name of God, most compassionate, most merciful.
Your Excellency, president of the General Assembly, your Excellency, Secretary General, your Majesties, excellencies Highnesses, ladies and gentlemen, may the peace and blessings of God be upon you.
