We would also like to congratulate His Excellency, Doctor Khalilur Rahman and the Friendly People, People's Republic of Bangladesh on his election as president of the General Assembly.
We affirm our support for His Excellency and we salute his wise choice of theme for this session Restoring Trust and Managing Transformation.
A United Nations that delivers for all.
We would also like to express our gratitude to Her Excellency Miss Annalena Baerbock, for her valued efforts during her presidency of the previous session.

We would be remiss not to applaud the efforts, good offices and initiatives of the Secretary General aimed at strengthening multilateralism and that include initiatives such as UN 80 and the pact for the future, as well as the ongoing efforts to address global challenges, crises, conflicts, wars, climate change and terrorism, as well as the efforts to assist member states in order to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals and to strengthen international cooperation on artificial intelligence.
We hope that these efforts will continue beyond the conclusion of the Secretary General's term in an in a manner to guarantee the continuity of work to reform and develop the organizations bodies to enhance its effectiveness and performance in discharging its responsibilities.
In this context, we emphasize that Security Council reform and the Security Council is the body charged with maintaining international peace and security has become essential to keep pace with the significant increase in the number of member states and the changes in international relations since the establishment of the organization.
There is an urgent need for the Council to become more representative, effective and transparent in carrying out its responsibilities.

Mr. president since last February, the state of Kuwait, the countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council and the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan have been subjected to illegal Iranian aggression involving ballistic, ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones.
All while we are not a party to the conflict in the region.
These attacks are a flagrant violation of the international law, international humanitarian law and the UN charter.
These brutal attacks have systematically and repeatedly targeted civilian objects and critical infrastructure, including Kuwait International Airport, power and water stations, oil facilities as well, revealing a hostile approach aimed at disrupting the foundations of life and critical infrastructure.

These heinous attacks have claimed the lives of several martyrs and innocent civilians.
They have also resulted in numerous injuries and have inflicted material and economic damage.
And furthermore, to inflict harm on the economies of the region and the world, and to disrupt global trade and oil markets, Iran is obstructing maritime navigation and closing the Strait of Hormuz to use it as a bargaining chip in the war in violation of international law and the relevant Security Council resolutions.
In this regard, the State of Kuwait expresses its deep appreciation to the brotherly and friendly nations who have stood by Kuwait and demonstrated solidarity.

We also salute the countries that have sponsored Security Council Resolution 2017 and the other resolutions issued by the Human Rights Council and the International Maritime Organization, which have condemned the Iranian aggression as a threat to international peace and security.
Demanding its cessation and affirming the inherent rights of states to self-defence, as per article 51 of the UN charter.
They have also stressed the importance of guaranteeing freedom of navigation without restrictions or conditions and based on.
Kuwait's belief that the security and stability of the Arabian Gulf region constitutes a fundamental pillar of regional and international security and stability, as demonstrated by the repercussions of the war and Iranian aggressions.

We reiterate the support for all diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalation and a peaceful resolution to the existing dispute, and we applaud the mediation efforts led by Qatar and Pakistan, while emphasizing the need to reach a sustainable regional understanding based on a firm commitment to the principles of good neighbourliness, respect for state sovereignty and non-interference in internal affairs, as well as refraining from the use or threat of use of force.
In addition to ceasing support for proxies and militias and addressing the security concerns of all countries in the region, including.
The Iranian nuclear file, ballistic missiles and drones, while stressing the guarantee of freedom and safety of navigation and the right of passage through the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb.
In accordance with the international law and the 1982 UN convention on the law of the sea.

Mr. president, the State of Kuwait is committed in its foreign policy to the principles of the UN charter, in particular, respect for the principle of good neighbourliness, respect for state sovereignty and non-interference in internal affairs.
Accordingly, the State of Kuwait views the brotherly Republic of Iraq as a neighbour with whom we share close ties as a and our partners in security and stability.
Since the fall of the former regime in 2003, Kuwait has supported and stood by Iraq in facing security, political and economic challenges in order to help Iraq restore its regional and international role and standing.
Kuwait believes that a stable, secure and prosperous Iraq serves the shared interests of Kuwait and the entire region.

In this context, the State of Kuwait commends the measures taken by the Iraqi Prime Minister, Mr. Ali al-Zaidi, to consolidate arms under state control and to strengthen Iraq's bilateral relations with neighbouring countries.
We look forward to enhancing confidence building measures between the two countries and to elevate our bilateral relations to broader horizons, as well as to resolve all outstanding issues.
Most important of these issues are the maritime border demarcation beyond marker 162, as per the rules of International law and the 1982 UN Convention on Law of the sea.
We also emphasize the need to adhere to bilateral security and technical agreements and arrangements signed between the two countries.

Very important among these agreements is the Abdullah Agreement and the 2008 Security Exchange Protocol.
These agreements serve as vital legal and practical instruments for regulating navigation, protecting the environment, combating terrorism, as well as combating the illicit trafficking of arms and narcotics, and enhancing shared security.
The State of Kuwait calls upon Iraq to cooperate with the high level representative of the Secretary-General pursuant to Security Council Resolution 2792, in order to achieve the progress and desired outcomes regarding Kuwaiti prisoners and missing persons, as well as nationals of third countries and the recovery of Kuwaiti property, including the National Archives.
Mr. president, the State of Kuwait reiterates its principled and firm position, condemning the ongoing violations by the Israeli occupation forces against the brotherly Palestinian people.

The Palestinian people continue to suffer under difficult living conditions caused by policies of displacement, arrests and settlement.
We call for the full implementation of the Comprehensive Peace Plan and its subsequent phase adopted by Security Council Resolution 2803.
This includes the complete withdrawal of Israeli occupation forces from Gaza, the assurance of humanitarian aid, access, and the return of the Palestinian Authority to the Gaza Strip.
We affirm that the Gaza Strip is an integral part of the occupied Palestinian territory.

In this regard, we welcome the measures and decisions taken by the United Kingdom, France and several other nations to condemn settlement activities and to impose sanctions against settlers involved in acts of violence and terrorism against Palestinians, as well as banning the import of goods and products originating from the settlements.
The State of Kuwait reiterates that a just, comprehensive and lasting peace in the region remains contingent upon an end to the Israeli occupation of all Arab territories, as well as enabling the Palestinian people to exercise their legitimate and inalienable rights.
It also rests upon the establishment of an independent Palestinian state on the borders of June 4th, 1967, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
Mr. president, the sisterly Republic of Yemen is witnessing a serious military escalation as a result of the attacks by Houthi militias against several governorates and areas along the West Coast aimed at threatening navigation in the Bab el Mandeb Strait.

In this regard, the state of Kuwait reiterates its full support for UN led efforts aimed at a comprehensive, sustainable and Yemeni led settlement.
In accordance with the three agreed references and the relevant Security Council resolutions, in particular resolution 2216.
The State of Kuwait affirms that any political settlement must safeguard Yemen's unity, sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity.
A settlement must end the suffering of the Yemeni people and must open prospects for security, stability and economic development.

We also stress the need to preserve the security and safety of maritime navigation in the Red sea and the Bab el Mandeb Strait.
We also condemn in the strongest terms the attacks by the Houthis against the sisterly kingdom of Saudi Arabia, targeting civilian and economic facilities in several cities.
In this context, we affirm that the security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia is an integral part of the security of the State of Kuwait and the security of the GCC states.
Mr. president, the State of Kuwait reiterates its solidarity with the sisterly Syrian Arab Republic.

We welcome the measures taken by the international community to lift the sanctions against Syria and to remove Syria's name from the list of state sponsors of terrorism.
We also affirm our support for all efforts aimed at rebuilding state institutions and aimed at advancing a Syrian led, comprehensive, inclusive political process led by the Syrians.
With the active participation of all segments of society in Syria and aimed at fulfilling their aspirations for security, stability and a life of dignity.
In this context, we stress the need to respect Syria's sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity We condemn and reject the attacks and incursions by Israeli occupation forces into Syrian territory.

These acts are a serious escalation and a violation of the 1974 Disengagement of Forces agreement.
They undermine security and stability in the region.
With regards to the sisterly Lebanese Republic, the state of Kuwait affirms the importance of Lebanese state institutions and the need to extend their full authority over the entire territory of Lebanon, and to restrict the possession of arms exclusively to the state, thereby reinforcing Lebanon's sovereignty and preserving its security and stability.
Here, we also emphasize the importance of maintaining an international presence along the blue line to ensure the full implementation of UN resolution 1701, and we reiterate our demand for Israel's withdrawal from all occupied Lebanese territories.

And with regards to developments in the Republic of Sudan, the Federal Republic of Somalia and the state of Libya, we affirm the need to adhere to peaceful resolution and to engage in political dialogue to resolve disputes as per the relevant Security Council resolutions and the principles of international law, so as to protect the unity, territorial integrity and sovereignty of these sisterly nations.
Mr. president, since Kuwait's independence, our foreign policy was based on firm principles, namely moderation and balance, and a firm commitment to the charter of the United Nations and International law, and on support for multilateralism and the belief that dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes are the best means to maintain international peace and security.
The State of Kuwait also believes in a complementary relationship between security and development.
There can be no security without development and no development without security.

Accordingly, Kuwait has based its development in humanitarian diplomacy on a pioneering role for the Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development.
Since 1961, the fund has contributed to financing development projects in 107 countries.
This stems from a belief that addressing the root causes of crises is not limited to security measures, but requires supporting development, providing the foundations for a life of dignity, and building more resilient and stable societies.
At the national level, Kuwait is confidently progressing towards its Kuwait Vision 2035 by accelerating the implementation of development projects, diversifying its economy and sources of income, continuing its digital transformation, empowering women and youth, developing its legislation and consolidating governance and transparency.

These efforts should enhance the efficiency of institutions and the competitiveness of the economy, and will establish Kuwait as a leading financial, commercial and control centre in the region.
In conclusion, Mr. President, my country has known the cruelty of occupation and the bitterness of aggression and has suffered from wars that have ravaged and continue to ravage our region for four decades.
From this experience, we have realised that they are the people who pay the price of conflicts.
We have recognised the need for the world to stand together, united in support of justice and in adherence to the UN charter and international law.

Out of our experience, we became firmly convinced that peace is the choice of wisdom and is protected by ability and dialogue does not diminish rights, but preserves them, and that security is not protected by force alone.
But it is anchored in justice, the rule of law, and the principles of international legitimacy.
The message of the state of Kuwait is one that has embraced in both word and deed, and to which it remains committed, that a just peace is the path to stability, and that respect for state sovereignty, the preservation of the rights of people, and recourse to international law for resolving disputes are indispensable pillars for security and stability of all states.
The state of Kuwait shall remain, as the world has known it, to be a voice of wisdom and moderation, a proponent of dialogue, cooperation, and openness to partnerships that serve mutual interests.

A champion of justice and a partner in consolidating international peace and security.
We believe that peace is the path to a future where rights are protected, nations are stable, and generations enjoy security and prosperity, and may the peace and blessings of God be upon you.
On behalf of the Assembly.
I wish to thank the Crown Prince of the State of Kuwait.

Mr. president, excellencies, my friends, we meet at a time when the obstacles confronting human progress are multiplying, obstacles to peace, obstacles to food and clean water, obstacles to finance, medicine and education, obstacles to movement and opportunity.

Obstacles to technology, to the knowledge and infrastructure needed to use it, and increasingly, obstacles between nations, between communities, and between people who no longer agree on the same facts or trust the same institutions.
War continues to destroy lives and communities.
Even though the international community possesses more tools than ever, ever before to prevent conflict and to facilitate dialogue.
The climate crisis is accelerating.

Even though the science is clear enough for us to act, and many of the solutions are already known.
And despite unprecedented global wealth, millions remain without reliable access to food, water, health or shelter.
These challenges, my friends, are creating the crises of which we constantly speak, and at the same time, new challenges are emerging.
Artificial intelligence is opening extraordinary possibilities in health, education, science, and productivity while also creating new risk of exclusion, exploitation, surveillance and the distortion of truth.

It is why I believe the theme this year is so apt.

Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen; The peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan, established on August 8, 2025, with the support and personal engagement of US President Donald Trump, has opened up new opportunities for our region, the South Caucasus.

On this occasion, I would firstly like to address what President Trump referred to from this podium two days ago. I have said it and I reiterate it now: the breakthrough in the establishment of peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan simply would not have been possible without President Trump’s personal engagement and his resolute commitment to establishing peace.

President Trump’s personal presence, by the way, has practical and symbolic expressions on the ground as well.

The fourth paragraph of the Peace Declaration adopted at the Peace Summit held at the White House on August 8, 2025 states (quote): “The Republic of Armenia will work with the United States of America and mutually determined third parties, to set forth a framework for the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP) connectivity project in the territory of the Republic of Armenia. We confirm our determination to pursue efforts in good faith to achieve this goal in the most expeditious manner.”

The implementation of the TRIPP project is thus becoming a reality with tangible steps.

The Framework Agreement on Strategic Cooperation on the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” project signed between Armenia and the United States of America will soon be ratified by the National Assembly of the Republic of Armenia.

We are currently working with the United States government to establish the TRIPP development company and sign a shareholders agreement.

Accordingly, Armenia will initially have a 26 percent stake in the TRIPP development company, and the United States will have a 74 percent stake. The agreement provides that in the event of its extension, in the 50th year, the Republic of Armenia’s share will become 49 percent, without additional investment.

One of the practical expressions of the TRIPP project will be the implementation of paragraph 3 of the Peace Declaration, adopted by me and the President of Azerbaijan on August 8, 2025, and signed by the President of the United States as a witness.

Paragraph 3 of the Declaration states (I quote): “We reaffirmed the importance of the opening of communications between the two countries for intra-state, bilateral, and international transportation for the promotion of peace, stability, and prosperity in the region and in its neighborhood on the basis of respect for the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and jurisdiction of the States.

These efforts are to include unimpeded connectivity between the main part of the Republic of Azerbaijan and its Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic through the territory of the Republic of Armenia with reciprocal benefits for international and intrastate connectivity for the Republic of Armenia.”

The implementation of the TRIPP project will be of historic importance for the Republic of Armenia. For the first time since the early 1990s, Armenia will get railway connection with Azerbaijan, and thus with Russia, Central Asia and China. However, it should be emphasized that after the Peace Summit on August 8, 2025, Azerbaijan opened its railway to Armenia, and now we have a railway connection with Azerbaijan through the territory of Georgia.

The implementation of the TRIPP project will create a direct railway connection between Armenia and Azerbaijan, as well as a railway connection from Azerbaijan to Azerbaijan through the territory of Armenia and from Armenia to Armenia through the territory of Azerbaijan, because Armenia does not have a railway connection between its northern and southern regions, and this is practically possible only through the territory of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic of the Republic of Azerbaijan, while Azerbaijan does not have a railway connection with its Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic and this is practically possible only through the territory of Armenia.

In the near future, we will restore the railway sections of Meghri and Yeraskh in the Republic of Armenia that existed during the Soviet Union and were later destroyed, and the railway connections I mentioned will be opened.

But this will also have a huge international significance, because in parallel with the construction of the aforementioned railways, we are waiting for the opening of the Armenia-Turkey railway.

Together with the TRIPP project, this could become one of the most important events in the field of international logistics in recent decades, because thus a new railway connection will be opened between China, Central Asia, Turkey and the European Union.

All this opens up another crucial opportunity for international logistics, because the restoration of the railway connection between Armenia and the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic of the Republic of Azerbaijan restores the railway connection between the Persian Gulf and the Black Sea. This is an important nuance, because it shows why and how the implementation of the TRIPP project promises great benefits to all countries in our region, and these potential benefits can become a cornerstone of long-term stability and peace.

Especially between Armenia and Azerbaijan. After almost 35 years of conflict, we are now discussing issues of building pipelines, power lines, and roads in addition to the east-west railway within the framework of the TRIPP project, and this will enable not only the Republic of Armenia, but also the entire South Caucasus to become a Crossroads of Peace.

Honorable President of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen; All of this reflects the optimism that has been established in our region and in the Republic of Armenia since the Washington Peace Summit on August 8, 2025.

The citizens of Armenia reaffirmed their optimism in the parliamentary elections held on June 7 of this year, where the overwhelming majority of voters voted in favor of the slogan “Own up the peace,” enabling the “Civil Contract” party to form a parliamentary majority.

The elections took place under special circumstances of external information manipulation, and a number of external and internal forces were developing and implementing a plan to seize the state, using mass disinformation, hybrid and other tools, as well as the distribution of mass voter bribes.

But the democratic and institutional reforms we have implemented in recent years proved their strength, and Armenia's state institutions demonstrated high resilience, preventing state capture and giving the people of Armenia the opportunity to have their say.

The people of Armenia have owned up the peace, and we must consistently engage in the further strengthening and institutionalization of peace.

In the relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan, the clarification of the fate of several thousand missing persons is a matter that needs to be addressed, on which we have reached an agreement to cooperate with Azerbaijan. Armenia is ready to continue and deepen cooperation with Azerbaijan on the issue of demining. And of course, people in the Republic of Armenia are waiting for the return of Armenians who were detained in Azerbaijan as a consequence of the conflict.

Along with these issues still being unresolved, another reason that fuels pessimists is the use of conflict rhetoric from time to time in certain circles of Armenia and Azerbaijan, sometimes at the official level. I think that we, I mean Armenia and Azerbaijan, have achieved more than sufficient results, which should be more valuable for us than the use of conflict rhetoric, whether it is about history or historical-cultural monuments or anything else.

Nurturing the peace, strengthening and making it institutional should be the main theme of cooperation between Armenia and Azerbaijan. For two and a half years now, there have been no casualties or injuries as a result of cross -fire between Armenia and Azerbaijan, and I believe this is the greatest value that has been created as a result of the recent years.

We have never had such a period in the relations between independent Armenia and independent Azerbaijan before, even though Armenians and Azerbaijanis have centuries of experience of peaceful coexistence.

Our task, however, is not to restore that historical experience, but to build interstate relations on the basis of that experience of the peoples, based on respect for each other's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and political independence. This, by the way, is exactly the rhetoric that Armenia and Azerbaijan have already agreed upon and initialed in the text of the agreement on establishing peace and interstate relations between the two countries.

The signing and ratification of the agreement, which was initialed at the Washington Peace Summit, is the next major topic in the joint agenda of Armenia and Azerbaijan, and we will consistently continue to work in this direction.

Ladies and Gentlemen; The balanced and balancing foreign policy adopted by Armenia stems from the logic of multipolarity, which is one of the key principles of the United Nations. In recent years, we have established strategic relations with Georgia, France, China, the Netherla nds,

Kazakhstan, Germany, Luxembourg, the United Kingdom, Bulgaria, Croatia, Lithuania, the United States of America, and the European Union.

Today, by the way, the European Commission approved the decision to adopt autonomous trade measures for Armenia, which is yet another manifestation of the new quality of Armenia-EU relations.

Our relations with Russia are in a transformation phase, and this is a natural process, because throughout the entire preceding period, the largest factor influencing relations between Armenia and Russia was the Armenia-Azerbaijan conflict.

Now that we have established peace with Azerbaijan, Armenia -Russia relations will naturally change, and it is our desire that these relations develop on the basis of the principles of friendship and mutual respect.

We will, of course, continue to develop our relations with our partners located closer to or farther from Armenia, and in this regard, I would like to highlight the countries of Central Asia, with which our relations are also highly dynamic.

But I also cannot but emphasize that the normalization and deepening of relations with our neighbors are nevertheless of key importance for our foreign policy vision. I have already spoken about the dynamics of our relations with Azerbaijan.

We have a high-level dialogue with Turkey, and I want to confirm the words expressed by President Erdogan from this podium the other day, that we are resolutely pushing forward the process of normalizing Armenia-Turkey relations.

Our relations with our two other neighbors, the Islamic Republic of Iran and Georgia, remain of exceptional importance to us, and our good neighborliness continues to develop and deepen.

The Republic of Armenia considers its contribution to the region’s stability and development to be our key task in international peace, stability, and development.

Honorable President of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen; This October, Armenia will host the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, and I invite you all to participate in this very important event for Armenia and for the international biodiversity agenda.

Dear ladies and gentlemen, this is what I wanted to share with you in my speech today.

Thank you for your attention.

Distinguished Delegates, Dear Friends of Georgia, ● It is a privilege to stand before this Assembly on behalf of Georgia - a nation shaped by centuries of history, resilience, and engagement with a changing world.

● We meet at a time of considerable change in the international environment.

● Developments in different parts of the world are challenging existing arrangements and raising questions about the future of the international order.

● In this context, maintaining peace and strengthening international cooperation remain key priorities.

● In light of the growing number of global challenges, сoordinated responses to common obstacles, conflict prevention and the achievement of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development are possible only through strengthened international cooperation and a sh ared commitment to collective action.

● Lasting peace cannot be imposed by force; it must be built through communication and mutual respect.

● Few countries understand the value of peace, stability, and sovereignty as deeply as Georgia does.

● For centuries, we stood at the crossroads of civilizations open to diverse cultures, peoples, and ideas, while steadfastly preserving our own distinct identity and character.

● Georgia’s statehood has been tested more than once, but these challenges have only strengthened our determination to choose our own path.

● The trials of history have also taught us that sovereignty can never be taken for granted, that stability must be protected, and that the strength of the international order ultimately depends on the same principles being upheld for every nation.

● Our commitment to these principles carries particular meaning for Georgia.

● Twenty percent of our country remains under the occupation of the Russian Federation, while hundreds of thousands of our citizens continue to live in displacement, unable to return to their homes.

● While restoring trust is the major theme of this year’s session,

I would like to address our Abkhaz and Ossetian brothers and sisters.

● We have shared a homeland and a history for centuries.

● The divisions of today cannot erase that history, nor should they determine the future of our children.

● We believe that the dividends of peace and economic growth of Georgia should know no artificial boundaries.

● It must reach the people living in our occupied historic regions as well – who remain, and will always remain, part of our shared future.

● The challenges facing our country also remind us that national stability and success cannot be separated from the wider regional context.

● We believe that the South Caucasus should not be defined by the divisions of the past.

● We have consistently sought to act as an honest broker in regional initiatives, fostering cooperation and contributing to peaceful solutions.

● Today, we see a genuine opportunity to turn a new page and build a more peaceful and interconnected region based on shared commitment to a better future.

● This spirit of cooperation must also translate into tangible economic opportunities for the region.

● As an integral part of the South Caucasus and the Middle Corridor, Georgia is well positioned to strengthen connectivity between Central Asia and Europe.

● Our strategic location and direct access to the Black Sea facilitate trade and investment, linking landlocked countries in our wider region to global supply chains.

● Our network of free trade agreements provides access to a market of approximately 2.3 billion consumers.

● To support and further advance connectivity agenda, Georgia plans to invest USD 7 billion by 2032 in major transport infrastructure - modernizing the railway, developing the Anaklia Deep Sea Port, building a new international airport in Tbilisi, and expanding the highway network.

● At the same time, we believe that physical and digital connectivity are two parts of the same strategic agenda.

● Through a Black Sea submarine fiber -optic connection and next-generation data infrastructure, Georgia aims to strengthen secure, resilient, and diversified digital links between Europe and Asia.

● These ambitions are underpinned by Georgia’s strong economic performance.

● Over the past five years, our economy has grown by an average of 9.3 per cent annually, and this momentum has continued in 2026, with growth reaching 7.9 per cent in the first seven months of the year.

● As the International Monetary Fund projects, Georgia will deliver one of the fastest growth rates in the medium term among regional and European countries, averaging 5.4%.

● With one of the fastest-growing economies worldwide, we are actively building an innovation -oriented, business -friendly environment that supports both local and foreign enterprises.

● Despite the global uncertainty, Georgia’s FDI to GDP ratio is one of the highest among peer countries and averaged over 6% of GDP in 2021–2025, highlighting the confidence of investors in the country’s growth potential.

● Georgia’s FDI outlook is supported by a pipeline of large, multi-year investment projects across transport and logistics, energy infrastructure, tourism and real estate.

● Yet the true measure of success is how it improves people’s lives.

● Strong economic performance must translate into tangible social outcomes - higher output per person, rising real wages, declining poverty, better employment opportunities, and greater economic resilience.

● We are already seeing these outcomes reflected in measurable improvements, including a triple decline in Georgia’s poverty rate, which dropped from 21.3 to 7.1 percent since 2020.

● Yet this achievement is only part of the broader transformation we seek to achieve.

● Over the next five years, our focus will therefore be on narrowing disparities between urban and rural communities, expanding opportunities across every region, and ensuring that the benefits of economic growth are shared widely and that no one is left behind.

● These priorities are fully aligned with Georgia’s commitment to the Sustainable Development Goals and are reflected in our new United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for 2026–2030.

● Looking further ahead, our ambition for the coming decade is to transform Georgia from an upper -middle-income country into a high -income economy, underpinned by greater economic diversification, a growing share of knowledge based activities, and broad-based prosperity.

● Excellences, Ladies and Gentlemen, ● The progress we seek at home is inseparable from the cooperation we build beyond our borders.

● Georgia remains open to meaningful engagement with every international partner prepared to engage with us on the basis of mutual respect and sovereign equality.

● We believe that lasting partnerships are built through dialogue and never through pressure or coercion.

● The principles of respect and cooperation are also at the heart of effective multilateralism.

● At a time of growing global uncertainty, the United Nations remains indispensable as a forum for dialogue and collective action.

● In this regard, the UN80 Initiative provides a valuable opportunity to strengthen the effectiveness and capacity of the United Nations, while further enhancing its transparency and accountability.

● Georgia stands ready to work constructively with international partners and contribute actively to this process.

● We firmly support reforms that will strengthen the Organization’s capacity to deliver better and become more results-oriented.

● The choice we make today will shape the world we leave to future generations.

● Let us ensure that we leave them a world that is more peaceful, secure and united than the one we know today.

Mr President, 1.

I congratulate you on your election as President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly. I assure you of our full support and cooperation as you discharge your responsibilities as President. At the same time, I extend my gratitude to the outgoing President, Madam Annalena Baerbock, for her able leadership.

2.

Let me begin by paying my deepest respect to all the martyred freedom fighters of Bangladesh. I respectfully remember the contributions of those who have made the ultimate sacrifice in the struggle to establish democracy, justice and people's rights in our country since independence. I also pay my sincere respect to all those who were martyred and injured in the mass uprising of courageous students and people in July–August 2024 against fascism.

3.

After more than a decade and a half of movement and struggle against fascist rule and exploitation, and through the sacrifice of thousands of lives, Bangladesh is now free from fascism. In a free, fair and impartial national election held on 12 February this year, the people entrusted the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) with the responsibility of governing the country. I congratulate the democracy-loving people of Bangladesh. We believe that the people are the source of all our political power.

4.

Mr President,

Standing on this world stage of the United Nations, I am somewhat nostalgic at this moment. It was from this very world stage that my father, Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman, the proclaimer of Bangladesh's independence, and my mother, former Prime Minister late Begum Khaleda Zia, addressed the world on behalf of the country and its people. Today, I too stand here to speak for the interests of my country and its people, and in the hope of a peaceful world community.

5.

In this age of globalisation, whatever happens in any part of the world has, to varying degrees, a negative impact on every country. Human -made conflicts have created situations of unrest in many countries. Vast numbers of people are being displaced, giving rise to humanitarian crises. Wars and conflicts are placing immense pressure on the global economy. Energy security concerns, disruptions to global energy supply systems and rising inflation are worsening the economic situation.

6.

We believe that every conflict should be resolved through dialogue, diplomatic processes and mutual cooperation.

Equality, fairness, protection of mutual interests, and respect and dignity among disputing states should form the basis of bilateral and multilateral relations. We aspire to a peaceful world, a humane global community where, rather than weapons of destruction, reason and debate, diplomacy, education and humanity become the instruments of change. Bangladesh sees the United Nations as the centrepiece for establishing an accommodative global community based on mutual respect for one another's independence and sovereignty.

7.

Mr President,

The tendency to divert development budgets towards military expenditure in different parts of the world reverses the direction of our journey towards global peace. As a peace -loving nation, Bangladesh remains committed to the goals of complete and general disarmament, preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, and arms control.

I reiterate Bangladesh’s support for any initiative at the United Nations dedicated to establishing world peace and serving humanity.The people of Bangladesh, who believe in democracy, remain deeply concerned about the plight of the freedom seeking Palestinian people. Bangladesh once again reaffirms its unwavering support for their legitimate demands, including their right to self -determination and their right to establish an independent State of Palestine.

8.

Mr President,

In the prevailing global circumstances, the theme of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All”, is highly relevant and timely. Bangladesh remains steadfast in its commitment to multilateralism in maintaining international peace and security.

As Vice-Chair of the Peacebuilding Commission, Bangladesh continues to serve as a strong voice for sustainable peace, conflict prevention and inclusive peace. As a consistent contributor to United Nations peacekeeping missions, Bangladeshi peacekeepers are serving humanity in different parts of the world.

9.

The courageous participation of Bangladeshi women in peacekeeping missions, even under adverse circumstances, reflects our strong commitment to advancing the agenda of “Women, Peace and Security”.

This year, Bangladesh is observing the 40 th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development and the 25 th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action.

Migration is as old as human civilisation. In many countries around the world, migrants make important contributions to the economies of both their countries of origin and their countries of destination. The government of Bangladesh is committed to ensurin g regular, safe and orderly migration. Bangladesh expects stronger global cooperation to ensure the rights, dignity and well-being of migrants.

10.

Mr President,

For more than nine years, Bangladesh has been sheltering more than 1.2 million forcibly displaced Rohingya from Myanmar. This has placed immense pressure on our resources, environment, security and local communities.

As a densely populated country, Bangladesh believes that the source and origin of the Rohingya crisis lie in Myanmar; therefore, its solution also lies there. The only solution to this problem is the early safe return of the displaced Rohingya people to their homeland, Myanmar.

11.

For a lasting solution to this crisis, Bangladesh expects firm and effective support from the United Nations and the international community. At the same time, I call upon the United Nations and the international community to continue life -saving assistance programmes for the displaced Rohingya people until they can be repatriated to their own country, Myanmar.

If the international community fails to ensure justice for the displaced Rohingya people, this could turn into a humanitarian crisis in the near future.

12.

Mr President,

Bangladesh is one of the countries most vulnerable to the adverse impacts of climate change. Although Bangladesh has contributed little to global carbon emissions, it is bearing the adverse consequences of climate change.

In these circumstances, Bangladesh has chosen the path of building resilience and developing the capacity to survive and adapt. Therefore, Bangladesh expects stronger global action at COP31 on climate justice, climate finance and adaptation support.

13.

The government of Bangladesh has strengthened its programmes for environmental protection. As part of these efforts, the government has launched a programme to plant 250 million trees across the country over the next five years.

Emphasis has been placed on the use of clean energy and solar energy. With the aim of freeing the country from the scourge of floods and droughts, the government has also launched a programme to excavate 20,000 kilometres of canals across the country.

14.

The government has also begun work on the Teesta Master Plan and the Padma Barrage project to increase freshwater flows into the world's largest mangrove forest, the Sundarbans, and to conserve water through large reservoirs.

At the same time, while strengthening domestic measures for water conservation and pollution prevention, the Government has reaffirmed its commitment to cooperation on transboundary water management by signing the 1992 Water Convention.

15.

Mr President,

After ending more than a decade and a half of fascist rule and exploitation,

Bangladesh became free from fascism in 2024. Having been freed from the scourges of enforced disappearances, killings, abductions, corruption, plunder and money laundering that ha d become the norm under fascist rule, Bangladesh is now once again embarking on the path of democracy.

To repair a Bangladesh battered by fascist rule and exploitation, the Government is pursuing a 3-R strategy: Recovery, Restoration and Reconstruction.

16.

A vast horizon of opportunities has now opened before Bangladesh. Taking advantage of the demographic dividend, the Government has begun implementing extensive programmes to transform the country's working -age population into a skilled human resource.

The Govenrment has also undertaken some forward -looking i nitiatives to create large-scale employment opportunities and transform Bangladesh into a ‘Manufacturing Hub’.In this endeavour, Bangladesh wants its development partners by its side. To create opportunities for young entrepreneurs, researchers and innovators in the country to pursue start-up initiatives, the Government has allocated US$4 billion in the current fiscal year.

17.

Mr President,

More than half of the country's population is female. Therefore, women are at the forefront of all government plans for socio-economic transformation.

The government is giving priority to women's education, women's employment and the creation of women entrepreneurs. To promote women entrepreneurship, particularly in the small and medium -sized industrial sector, the Government has expanded opportunities for cash financing for women.

Free education opportunities up to the undergraduate level have been opened to women.

18.

The government seeks to ensure not only electoral democracy but also the democratisation of the economy, so that the benefits of economic growth and prosperity reach every family and every citizen.

To achieve this goal, the government has already launched assistance programmes for economically disadvantaged people through various social protection programmes, including the Family Card, Farmers’ Card, Sports Card and e -Health Card.

19.

The government considers the Family Card, issued in the name of the female head of each household, a symbol of women's economic empowerment.

It is also in the government's plans to introduce a Universal Card by integrating the various cards introduced to provide support in different sectors.

20.

Mr President,

The government is implementing the 31 -point programme presented to the people before the national election of 12 February 2026.

At least 73 per cent of the activities under the Government's 31 -point programme have a direct alignment, and 27 per cent an indirect alignment, with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and their guiding principle of “Leave No One Behind.”

21.

The government hopes that through the implementation of these programmes, development disparities between urban and rural areas will be reduced, while accountability and inclusive, sustainable development will be advanced across all areas of the 2030 Agenda.

The government of Bangladesh has accorded special importance to education, health and sports.

The highest budgetary allocation in the country's history have been made in the education sector. Our plan is to increase budgetary allocation to education to 5% of GDP within next five years.

A curriculum has been developed with emphasis on technical and practical education to ensure an employment-oriented education system with strong ethical values.

22.

From the first grade, primary -school students are being provided with schoolbags and clothing, that is, school uniforms, as well as free lunch.

The government hopes that this will increase school enrolment and improve the quality of education.

To establish sports as a profession, sports has been included as a subject in the education curriculum for the first time.

As part of this initiative, more than 2 million students participated in a month -long nationwide football tournament for school students held last June.

23.

Mr President,

Science and technology will shape the future of the world. We are entering a new era of artificial intelligence, biotechnology and science.

Technology is advancing very rapidly, but its opportunities are still not equally accessible to all. Bangladesh's large young population and growing digital capabilities have created new possibilities for us.

To harness these opportunities, access to advanced technology, knowledge and research must be brought within everyone's reach.

24.

We do not want today's digital divide to become tomorrow's artificial intelligence divide.

Bangladesh respects innovation and intellectual property. At the same time, it is essential to ensure technology transfer, skills development and affordable access to modern technologies for developing countries.

25.

No country should be left behind in this scientific advancement. Bangladesh stands ready to work together to build a fair and prosperous future for all.

It is now time for the United Nations to adopt an effective policy framework so that the benefits of the development and rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and social media can be harnessed positively across countries.

26.

Mr President,

Bangladesh is awaiting graduation from the list of Least Developed Countries (LDCs).

For Bangladesh, as well as for all other countries undergoing this process, sustained support in areas such as assured financing, greater market access, technology transfer and capacity -building is essential to make the graduation process sustainable.

27.

In the present world order, all countries are interdependent. Bangladesh believes that, particularly at the regional level, we can help one another achieve prosperity through the facilitation and expansion of trade, effective connectivity and meaningful cooperation.

The COVID-19 pandemic claimed the lives of millions of people around the world.

But it also sent a message to the world: for the global community to survive, mutual assistance, empathy and cooperation are indispensable.

It is essential to ensure sustainable production of vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostic equipment in developing countries so that these are readily accessible to all.

28.

Mr President,

A state can never become strong by keeping its citizens powerless.

Through ensuring the political and economic empowerment of the people, we want to build a prosperous, self-reliant, welfare-oriented democratic state where everyone, irrespective of political affiliation, religion or ethnicity, can live with security and peace, and with equal rights, honour and dignity.

29.

Mr President,

Bangladesh continues to make progress in all areas, including democracy, human rights, good governance, accountability, political stability and the investment environment.

The government is working to establish a safe and stable Bangladesh with a business- and investment-friendly environment.

In today's democratic Bangladesh, we welcome partnership, innovation, and both domestic and foreign investment.

30.

We want to build a Bangladesh where young people can pursue their dreams without fear or hindrance; where women can lead their lives with confidence; where every child grows up with the opportunity to realise their full potential; and, above all, where people are assured of a safe and peaceful life.

That is why we say: “Bangladesh First — Bangladesh for All.”

I conclude my address by reaffirming Bangladesh’s unwavering commitment to the values and principles of the United Nations in order to build a peaceful world.

31.

Mr President,

Thank you.

Bangladesh Zindabad.

Mr President,

Your Excellencies,

Ladies and gentlemen,

Anne Frank was a teenage girl without power or influence.

But she had a pen and a diary.

A diary that would make its way into the world, and inspire millions of people.

I think that one of the reasons people are so inspired by Anne, is that she had an unshakeable belief in the power of people to turn the tide so that good prevails.

She wrote, ‘How wonderful it is that nobody need wait a single moment before starting to improve the world’.

Those words are just as powerful and true today.

This week is the perfect example of that.

I realise that the United Nations does not carry the most positive associations for everyone.

And indeed, there is much that can and must be improved.

But let us not forget what lay behind the founding of the UN, over 80 years ago: the realisation that doing nothing had led to the darkest chapters in human history.

We now live in a different time.

New generations have arisen.

And we face new challenges.

But when we look at the world today, we see similar challenges as which preceded the founding of the UN.

AVT/AZ-260915-002 2 We see that the international legal order is under pressure in more and more places, even though it is the very foundation of our freedom and prosperity.

We see the unending human suffering in Gaza, Sudan and so many other places in the world.

We see violations of international law and of human rights, which are in stark contrast to the UN’s aims.

And we see institutions being undermined.

Institutions that were established to protect people and populations.

We must not be naive about the causes.

These constant threats and attempts to dismantle the legal order are fuelled by people and groups with their own agenda.

One that runs counter to the interests of everyone else.

Yes: everyone.

Even those who don’t feel directly threatened, because they think it doesn’t affect them.

Sooner or later, everyone is affected.

As we saw in the time before the UN.

When major powers choose to pursue only their own interests, it is tempting to respond defensively.

But as Mahatma Gandhi taught us, ‘An eye for eye will only make the whole world blind.’

And so, it is time for us, the global community, to choose to pursue the common interest.

Not by trying to build an entirely new world order.

But simply by working together.

The middle powers must take the lead in fostering such international cooperation.

And everyone must be able to participate, including those countries who are currently too often left on the sidelines.

AVT/AZ-260915-002 3 It is time that countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America had a fullyfledged place.

Not only on the Equal Earth Map, but in the real world too.

To start with, here in the UN, with improved African representation in the Security Council at the very least.

Because if we want to preserve the UN for the future, we must change the balance of power in line with the changing times, and modernise our institutions.

This means that we must focus on core tasks and stable financing, but also that we must work to protect the multilateral order with all our strength.

Because international law either works for everyone, or for no one.

Take the attempts we’ve seen to undermine the International Criminal Court- which is based in my country, in my city.

This undermines the international legal order as a whole.

And that affects us all.

This court was established to protect us against impunity.

This court was built on the foundations of the Nuremberg and Tokyo Trials.

In the words of the Nuremberg chief prosecutor, Robert H. Jackson, ‘one of the greatest tributes that power has ever paid to reason.’

Now, with the ICC under attack, the writing is truly on the wall.

After all, how can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes?

I believe there can be only one response.

To say: hands off the ICC, and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order.

Because the reality is that we still need to fight impunity.

Not least through the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine, which the Netherlands has offered to host in The Hague.

Let me be absolutely clear: we cannot accept impunity.

AVT/AZ-260915-002 4 In this fight, Ukraine has no choice but to defend itself.

But Russia makes a choice every day to wage war.

Russia must be held to account for its flagrant violations of the UN Charter.

For the immeasurable suffering inflicted on so many victims and families in this senseless war.

Since the downing of flight MH17, the Netherlands has come to understand this only too well.

Many others understand it too, with Russia threatening global food security, and millions of people experiencing the consequences.

History teaches us that the only way to resolve conflicts, is through justice.

That was the idea underpinning the establishment, 80 years ago, of the International Court of Justice, the principle judicial organ of the United Nations.

And it’s a conviction that is widely shared, as illustrated by the fact that more and more countries are finding their way to the ICJ.

So let us all continue to stand up for what we have built, and strengthen it further as we go forward.

Ladies and gentlemen,

Cooperation is the cornerstone of our history.

And cooperation is what the world expects of us, now and in the future.

Take the question of how we handle AI.

We face a choice: do we let a small group of companies and countries take all the decisions, while the rest of us simply look on?

Or do we decide, together – within the logical setting of the UN – what our future should look like.

AVT/AZ-260915-002 5 It is also time for us to press forward together and tackle that other great challenge of our age: climate change.

Nowhere on earth is the planet warming faster than in Western Europe.

But in the Caribbean part of our Kingdom – including the countries of Aruba, Curaçao and St. Maarten – the effects of climate change have already been felt for much longer.

And the same is true of many of your countries, as well.

For too long, the consequences of climate change have been trivialised or simply denied.

But after the horrors experienced by Nepal, and a long series of forest fires, the truth should be clear to everyone: the climate crisis will not just disappear if we pretend it doesn’t exist.

We are living on borrowed time.

And the generations that come after us will pay the price.

If we want to prevent that, we must commit now to both mitigation and adaptation.

We all know what needs to be done.

Countless reports are agreed on that.

We have all the technology we need.

And fortunately, we are making progress.

Last year the electric vehicle market grew by 20 per cent.

Wind power capacity grew by 14 per cent, and solar power by more than 30 per cent.

This growth in renewable energy has exceeded even the most optimistic projections from 10 years ago.

The challenge now is to accelerate this transition in all sectors and all parts of the world.

And, at the same time, to reduce carbon emissions and phase out fossil fuels.

AVT/AZ-260915-002 6 That is why the Netherlands and Colombia jointly organised the world’s first conference on ‘Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels’.

This event in Colombia was attended by 57 countries.

Together, these countries account for one-third of global GDP, one-third of energy demand and one-fifth of supply.

And together, we worked to find concrete, practical solutions to take the transition forward.

But climate action requires everyone to contribute.

In November we will gather at the COP in Türkiye.

And I know that many of you don’t have high expectations.

In my view, this can only be explained by the pessimistic idea that we are somehow powerless.

But that is not true.

We have the knowledge and technology to combat climate change.

A better world really is within reach.

Thanks to our joint efforts on the Sustainable Development Goals, 92 per cent of the world’s population now has access to electricity.

Since 2015, we have doubled the amount of renewable energy we generate.

And child mortality has dropped sharply, too.

Climate action can be a catalyst for everyone to work together on solutions that concern us all.

AVT/AZ-260915-002 7 We don’t need to reinvent the wheel.

A lot of good things are happening already.

For decades, the Netherlands has been working with partners around the world to develop climate-smart agriculture and future-proof watermanagement solutions.

We are keen to share our knowledge and know-how, and we want to learn from what other countries are doing.

There are so many great initiatives under way.

But I also know there is much more to be done.

The need to accelerate and scale-up our efforts is only too clear.

And that demands our common commitment.

The Netherlands wants to build practical partnerships with other countries.

So we are once again making funding available for this purpose.

At the same time, we need to adapt to climate shocks that can no longer be avoided.

And these adaptations will require major investment – both public and private.

Because here too: we cannot do it alone.

Today I call on all countries to stick to these ambitions.

Because one way or another, a climate transition is coming.

But we can decide how it will unfold.

It can be chaotic, or it can be carefully planned – with an inclusive approach and economic benefits for all.

Ladies and gentlemen,

As I come to the end of my remarks, I have an even stronger sense of what Anne Frank was telling us.

Because what she wrote is true: we have everything we need to change the world for the better and we don’t have to wait another minute.

We aren’t starting from scratch.

We’ve already come a long way.

And the journey will continue, under the leadership of a new SecretaryGeneral.

AVT/AZ-260915-002 8 Secretary-General Guterres, thank you for all your years of hard work.

You are leaving the UN at a turbulent time.

But we can all take pride in the fact that, as we speak, more than 150 thousand men and women are serving under the blue flag.

Giving vaccinations, providing food aid and serving in peace missions.

Even in these difficult times, when darkness seems to be descending in many places on the high ideals of the UN.

But the light has not gone out.

The torch of peace and justice still flickers and guides us.

Just as it did in my country, more than 80 years ago.

Liberation from the tyranny of unbridled nationalism, racism and fascism came too late for Anne Frank.

In my country, when it did finally come, it was brought by American,

Canadian, British, Polish and other Allied soldiers, many of them not much older than Anne.

Among their many resting places, far from their homes, is an American cemetery in Margraten, in the south of the Netherlands.

A wall stands watch over their graves.

And on it is inscribed a simple epitaph: 'To you from failing hands we throw the torch. Be yours to hold it high.'

Let us pledge, as a new generation, to always hold it high.

Thank you.

Mr. President, excellencies, distinguished delegates,

At the outset, let me congratulate His Excellency Mr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the 81st session of the General Assembly, and I wish him every success in guiding this session.

Allow me to begin my speech by quoting the sentences that I delivered on behalf of Slovenia, on behalf of vast number of current and former heads of states and governments who signed our declaration for this rostrum in 2012. I quote: » This year's theme of the United Nations Assembly is peaceful resolution of disputes... Last year we celebrated the sixtieth anniversary of the entry into force of the Convention on prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide. The Convention was the fruit of the tire less efforts of the Polish jurist of Jewish descent,

Raphael Lemkin...

I would like to remind you that since the end of the Second World War alone; there have been more than 80 countries witnessing mass atrocities. At least 53 million innocent people lost their lives. Behind these numbers are concrete men and women, as well as children. They had a future, but they were not allowed to live that future.

For this reason, I call on the Member States of the United Nations, regional organizations and the Uni ted Nations system to develop a new approach and a strategy for the prevention of genocide and other mass atrocities...

In addition, an intergovernmental forum of like -minded states should be established in order to propose a United Nations resolution that would give a clear mandate for preparation and adoption of an appropriate legal mechanism – legal mechanism that would give the concept of the "responsibility to protect" a new tool, a legal mechanism that will enforce the prevention of crime, a mechanism that will enable a faster and more effective response to acts of genocide and other mass atrocities...

I would like to inform you that this initiative also comes from international civil society.

The Institute for Cultural Diplomacy has gathered thousands of supporters at international non-governmental organizations, among lawyers, students, journalists and others...

As early as 1946, Raphael Lemkin declared: "Our heritage is the result of the contribution of all nations." All nations, as well as the United Nations as a whole, have great responsibility, as well as an enormous opportunity to prevent atrocities in the future. We cannot escape history, but we can learn something from it... I firmly believe that the mistakes we made yesterday we do not want to repeat tomorrow. We took responsibility for this world from our fathers, and we have a great responsibility to make it better for our children. I call on you to improve it by joining all our efforts for a world free from genocide and other mass atrocities." End of quote.

After 14 years, I note that, despite the great initial support, our initiative has not been realized. It has been drowned in new crises, in the incompetence and ignorance of the individuals and institutions responsible, and in the double standards that have further marked the behavior of our United Nations. Today, we are even further away from the goal we tried to achieve 14 years ago.

The theme of this year's session is therefore actually very well chosen. Restoring trust. A United Nations that is here for everyone. Because: Trust begins with a simple question: do we apply our principles consistently, or only when it is politically convenient?

The United Nations was founded on universal principles: sovereignty, equal dignity, the rule of law, the peaceful settlement of disputes, and the protection of human rights.

But principles lose their meaning when they are applied selectively.

Mr. President, distinguished delegates,

Let us be concrete.

For decades, the United Nations has devoted significant institutional attention to the question of Palestine. The General Assembly has adopted resolution after resolution, while the Security Council and Human Rights Council have repeatedly addressed the situation.

Let me be clear: the search for peace and security in the Middle East is of profound importance, and the suffering of Palestinian and Israeli civilians deserves serious and sustained consideration. Every civilian life matters.

But are we applying the same standard of urgency when victims are elsewhere?

Last year alone, over four thousand eight hundred Christians were killed because of their religion. More than three hundred million Christians around the world suffer discrimination and persecution. In Iran, the criminal theocratic regime has brutally murdered tens of thousands of its own citizens this year alone.

After 1948, more than one million Jews fled or were expelled from Arab countries, many amid persecution and violence.

Or consider Nigeria.

For more than a decade, Nigerian communities have faced mass killings, kidnappings, the destruction of villages and places of worship, and the displacement of hundreds of thousands of people. In return, this body produced a single Security Council resolution. Not seventy. Not seventeen. One.

So, we must ask: if every civilian life matters, why does our urgency seem so different from one crisis to another? This does not mean caring less about one crisis but caring more consistently about all of them.

We must also be willing to ask difficult questions about how Palestine is discussed and used politically. A majority position does not, by itself, determine what is right.

The right of a democratic state and its people to defend themselves against terrorism must be recognized and upheld. Civilian suffering is tragic and must be addressed, but it can never justify terrorism or the pursuit of political objectives through violence.

At the same time, criticism of government policy must never become a cover for antisemitism.

If civilian lives are equal, our attention should be guided by the scale, duration and severity of suffering - not primarily by geography, political alliances, media visibility or political influence.

These principles must also guide our approach to Belarus. We condemn the authorities’ systematic repression, arbitrary detention and persecution of political opponents, human rights defenders and independent voices. All political prisoners must be released immediately and unconditionally, and those responsible for human rights violations must be held accountable. Slovenia stands with the Belarusian people and supports a peaceful democratic transformation founded on free and fair elections, the rule of law and full respect for human rights. Belarus belongs in a free and democratic Europe.

Mr. President, distinguished delegates,

Selectivity does more than distort our attention. Over time, it destroys institutions themselves. The United Nations cannot defend the rule of law while silently watching its own mandates, procedures and institutions become instruments of political convenience.

The rule of law must never become merely rule by law. It requires rules to be applied impartially, consistently and transparently.

When the same principles are invoked strictly in one case and conveniently overlooked in another, we do not strengthen international law. We hollow it out.

And when institutions created to protect universal standards are instrumentalized for political purposes, we weaken the very multilateral system they were created to defend.

This inconsistency is particularly difficult to ignore when we consider Iran. Executions, including those involving political prisoners, young intellectuals and others who oppose the regime, demand serious attention. Yet there is often no sufficiently serious condemnation of these executions or of the broader violations of human rights under a system that seeks complete control over social, political and economic life.

The abuse of religion to justify or reinforce such control is another example of how principles can be distorted when institutions and political power are placed above the rights and dignity of individuals. Human rights cannot depend on whether the victims are politically convenient to defend.

The United Nations must therefore defend not only its institutions, but also the integrity of the principles those institutions exist to serve.

Mr. President, distinguished delegates,

Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is a flagrant violation of the United Nations Charter and a direct assault on the sovereignty and territorial integrity of a Member State.

Russia's occupation and attempted illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 challenged a fundamental rule of our international order: territory cannot be acquired by force.

As Mustafa Dzhemilev, the leader of the Crimean Tatars, reminded us at yesterday's Crimea Platform Summit, the international response to Russia's aggression in 2014 was too little, too late. Russia was never effectively stopped. Its impunity began in Crimea. The full-scale invasion of 2022 was the consequence.

The Russian leadership chose this war. Russia is the aggressor. Ukraine is defending its people and its independence.

For Slovenia, sovereignty and territorial integrity are fundamental to our own security.

If a powerful state can seize its neighbour's territory by force, every smaller state becomes less secure.

The United Nations has documented torture and executions of Ukrainian prisoners of war by Russian forces, as well as grave abuses in occupied territory. Those responsible must face justice.

Prisoners of war and civilian detainees must return home. Ukrainian children forcibly transferred or deported must return to their families.

Our goal must remain a just and lasting peace, based on the United Nations Charter and Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Ukraine must participate fully in decisions concerning its future. Any settlement must provide credible security guarantees against renewed aggression.

Slovenia will continue to support Ukraine on its European path. Ukraine's future belongs in the European Union.

A permanent member of the Security Council, entrusted with a special responsibility for international peace, is waging a war of aggression against another Member State.

Russia's permanent seat cannot place it above the Charter. Its veto cannot erase aggression or responsibility for international crimes.

If this Organization wants to restore trust, it should begin by applying its own principles consistently.

I therefore propose two things.

First, this Organization should strengthen transparency around its responses to crises. We should establish an independent mechanism, answerable to this Assembly as a whole, that annually compares the scale, duration and severity of major crises with the scale and nature of the international response. Not to dictate political verdicts, but to make it impossible for us to remain unaware of our own patterns of selectivity.

Second, we should strengthen safeguards against the political instrumentalization of United Nations mandates and institutions. Their credibility depends on transparent procedures, consistent criteria and equal standards of scrutiny for all Member States.

Mr. President, distinguished delegates,

The multilateral system was created to prevent power from replacing principle. We must not allow political convenience to reverse that relationship - so that principle becomes merely a language used by institutions when it serves political interests.

The answer is not to weaken multilateralism. It is to protect it from instrumentalization.

A United Nations that delivers for all cannot mean an organization that responds loudly to some crises and quietly to others.

If we want to speak credibly of the United Nations that delivers for all, then we must be prepared to ask a difficult question: does it really deliver for all?

For those living through war. For those displaced by violence. For states whose concerns receive little international attention. For families struggling to build a future.

We will restore trust when a crisis matters because human beings are suffering, not because the politics surrounding it are convenient.

And we will restore trust when the institutions of multilateralism are strong enough to serve universal principles rather than political convenience.

But restoring trust is not only about correcting what is wrong today. It is about deciding what kind of international system we are willing to pass on to those who come after us.

Mr. President,

A United Nations that cannot uphold its own principles has no standing to ask the world for its trust.

What we owe the people of the world is not sentiment. It is an institution consistent enough, and far-sighted enough, to be worthy of their trust.

Thank you.
