Monsieur le Président,

Heads of State and Government,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

It is a great honor to address the General Assembly for the eighth time as Prime Minister of Greece.

I do so at a moment of particular importance, as Greece reaches the end of our second year on the UN Security Council and is preparing to assume its Presidency next month.

12 months ago, as we marked the 80th anniversary of the United Nations, we spoke of the need to reinvigorate multilateralism.

One year later, that need has only become more urgent as we are living through perilous times. Conflicts are multiplying. Tensions are deepening.

And perhaps most alarmingly, we are witnessing a further erosion of restraint in international affairs.

The rules and understandings that have long provided a degree of stability in relations between states are increasingly being tested.

Secretary-General António Guterres has steered the United Nations through this exceptionally turbulent decade with a steadfast commitment to its Charter and the values it embodies.

The selection of the tenth Secretary -General presents a historic opportunity for the reinvigoration of the Organization when it is most needed.

Ladies and gentlemen,

The first step in restoring confidence in multilateralism is acknowledging where it has actually succeeded.

Few examples are more powerful than the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. With 172 parties, UNCLOS provides the binding legal framework within which disputes can be managed peacefully rather than through force.

From the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea to the Indo -Pacific, strategic maritime routes are increasingly becoming arenas of geopolitical confrontation. Commercial vessels are being targeted and vital trade routes used as instruments of pressure, with grave consequences for supply chains, energy markets and food security worldwide.

Freedom of navigation and uninhibited passage through international straits, as guaranteed by international law, must be championed globally.

It is our collective responsibility to uphold these principles in practice, and to safeguard commercial shipping. As a leading maritime nation, Greece actively contributes to maritime security through the European Union's Operation ASPIDES in the Red Sea.

This topic will remain a high priority when Greece assumes the Presidency of the Security Council next month, with particular attention being placed to the challenges posed by emerging technologies.

Ladies and gentlemen,

Greece’s geography grants it the natural role of serving as a bridge between Europe and its wider neighborhood to the east and south.

We literally sit at the intersection of the shrinking space between the East and West.

My country is a pillar of stability, connectivity, and peace across the Eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East and the Gulf.

Greece has developed strong strategic partnerships with key countries in the region, including Israel, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar.

We are a bridgebuilder not a troublemaker. Yet, putting this vision into practice is rarely simple at a time of tectonic geopolitical changes.

In the Middle East, the Gaza Peace Plan, agreed last year, must be effectively implemented. It is of paramount concern to ensure that Hamas surrenders its arms. It can have no role in Gaza’s future.

At the same time, reconstruction needs to move forward, with Palestinians themselves taking ownership of Gaza’s future.

Greece will continue to advocate for a two-state solution, with Israel and Palestine living side by side in peace and security.

However, developments in the West Bank remain a source of deep concern. Actions that are illegal under international law and undermine the viability of a future Palestinian state cannot be allowed to continue.

We strongly argue that t his is also to the benefit of the long term security of Israel itself. Greece has established a durable strategic partnership with Israel, while maintaining strong ties with the Arab world. It is precisely the strength of this partnership that allows us to engage in an open and candid dialogue.

In Lebanon, there is now a real opportunity to lay the foundations for lasting peace. The US-facilitated negotiations with Israel are an important step forward and should be sustained. Greece strongly supports a sovereign, resilient and united Lebanon, and the Government’s efforts to restore the state’s monopoly over arms.

Ultimately, a stronger Lebanese state will serve both domestic security and regional stability. Therefore, we will continue to deliver concrete assistance to the country, including to the Lebanese Armed Forces. With the UNIFIL’s mandate ending, joint action is crucial to avoid a security vacuum and maintain an effective international and European presence.

Syria is another key part of the region. Lasting stability in the Middle East requires a stable Syria. A Syria that is inclusive, free from foreign interference and regional rivalries, and where every citizen can feel secure.

The new Syrian authorities have taken steps in this direction. Yet further concrete progress must be demonstrated, particularly when it comes to protecting the rights and security of all religious and ethnic communities. This includes the Orthodox Christian minority, which continues to face the violence of Islamist extremists.

This search for stability extends to Libya, a neighbor with whom we share many common interests. We praise all reunification efforts. A stable Libya, free from foreign interference, would benefit not only the Libyan people, but our entire region.

Greece is ready to support Libyan institutions in border protection and migration. We remain committed to reaching an agreement on the delimitation of our maritime zones.

Dear colleagues,

Let me now turn to our relations with our neighbor, Türkiye.

Over the past three years, we have made a sustained effort to improve our relationship, rebuild trust and keep channels of communication open in order to prevent the escalation of tensions that could lead to unwanted crises. It is a delicate relationship, and one that carries the weight of history.

Indeed, given the broader regional challenges, the situation urgently calls for a common understanding o n how we move forward. An understanding grounded in full respect for international law and the principles of good neighborly relations. After all, we cannot change our geography and we are destined to live side by side.

Let me repeat that t he UN Convention on the Law of the Sea provides the only institutional framework to solve our only long standing dispute concerning the delimitation of our continental shelf and exclusive economic zones.

Dialogue is essential for peace and prosperity. But meaningful dialogue cannot coexist with unilateral actions that challenge the international legal order. Nor can meaningful progress be made when faced with threats of war in response to the exercise of lawful rights according to international law. Such actions do not resolve differences. They only deepen them.

And they risk undermining the stability of our wider region. A region which, we should not forget, still bears an open wound: the unresolved Cyprus issue. Fifty-two years have passed since Türkiye’s illegal invasion and the continuing occupation of part of the island. A flagrant violation of international law, whose consequences persist to this day.

For the United Nations, Cyprus remains a litmus test of its credibility: of its ability to uphold its own resolutions and the principles of its Charter.

Greece fully supports the efforts of Secretary -General Guterres to create the conditions for the resumption of substantive negotiations.

We sincerely hope that progress can be achieved during his remaining time in office. And we expect these efforts to continue under his successor with the same objective: the reunification of Cyprus, free of occupation forces, in accordance with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions.

The principles at stake in Cyprus are being tested elsewhere too.

Today, two other major conflicts continue to challenge our ability to defend the values upon which this Organization was founded.

The war in Ukraine is now in its fifth year. Five years since Russia’s full-scale aggression brought war back to European soil.

The Ukrainian people have shown extraordinary courage defending their freedom. Greece continuously stands with them. We strongly condemn attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure.

Diplomacy must now deliver an immediate ceasefire and a lasting peace, anchored in the principles of the United Nations Charter.

Ukraine must have a decisive say in its own future and Europe cannot be absent from negotiations.

Against this backdrop, another devastating war demands our urgent attention. In Sudan, the nearly four-year conflict has resulted in a staggering humanitarian catastrophe. Reports of atrocious war crimes continue to emerge, while the conflict is fueling instability far beyond Sudan’s borders. We should not permit this tragedy to endure.

Foreign interference must also cease with no impunity for war crimes. Ultimately, the way forward lies in a credible, Sudanese-led political process that reflects the aspirations of the citizenry. The European Union ought to leverage its capacity to play a more active role in supporting that proc ess and assisting in bringing this destructive conflict to an end.

After all, it has real skin in the game. Should the devastating war continue, our continent will be the first to suffer from a possible massive new migratory wave.

Ladies and gentlemen,

Greece’s confidence abroad rests on a profound transformation at home. At a time when the effectiveness of governments all over the world is being challenged by populists and extremists and public trust is being eroded in the echo chambers of social media, Greece serves as an example that sound reform-oriented policies can deliver real results for people and improve their lives Of course, significant challenges remain, but the progress Greece has made is impossible to overlook. Seven years ago, my country was still emerging from the most painful economic crisis in its modern history, having lost more than 25% of its GDP. Today, the economy is growing much faster than the European average, while Greece is attracting significant foreign direct investment.

Public finances are solid and our fiscal performance has become a positive example in Europe. Public debt is declining faster than in any other OECD country. Structural reforms and the digitalization of the state, which has helped reduce bureaucracy, have transformed the public administration and restored confidence among investors.

A few days ago, two leading rating agencies upgraded their outlook of the Greek economy. At a time of great turbulence in the global bond markets, this says a lot about the progress that Greece has made. Not many people would have bet a few years ago that today Greece’s borrowing cost would be lower than that of four G7 countries.

This transformation was not easy. It was made possible by the hard work, resilience and determination of the Greek people.

Economic growth is vital because it expands a nation's strategic leverage. It enables a state to bolster its defense, a core commitment this government is proud to adhere to, modernize its infrastructure and invest in innovation, all while safeguarding social cohesion. Economic resilience is, therefore, inherently intertwined with robust institutions and credible deterrent capabilities.

Greece’s ambition is to serve as a nexus through which lasting partnerships are forged. I was reminded of this vision earlier this year when I welcomed President Emmanuel Macron at the Roman Agora in Athens, to discuss Europe’s place amid a shifting geopolitical landscape. The setting was particularly meaningful.

The Agora was a place where commerce, law and public life once converged. There, we reflected on how Europe can transform the crisis into an opportunity for its strategic autonomy and improve its competitiveness.

As we prepare to assume the Presidency of the Council of the European Union in the second half of 2027, we will work for a Europe that is more competitive, more secure, more capable of defending itself and more effective in protecting its external borders.

Another lesson, however, is becoming increasingly clear: connectivity is the tangible face of geopolitics.

The region’s energy landscape is fundamentally transformed.

Electricity grids, energy and digital corridors, ports and shipping routes are levers of power. Geography matters.

Our ambition is to translate our unique position into stronger links between Europe, the Middle East, the Gulf and North Africa.

Therefore, we are investing in a new generation of connectivity projects, such as GREGY, which will bring clean electricity from Egypt to Europe, and the Great Sea Interconnector, which will connect the European electricity grid with Cyprus and Israel.

At the same time, we leverage our unique geographic position to become a provider of energy security to our northern neighbors.

And as the prime min ister of a leading shipping nation, it is worth remembering a stark fact: More than 90% of global trade is conducted by sea. If we systematically threaten the freedom of navigation and do not protect vital sea routes, the global economy risks coming to a grinding halt. And this is something that should be of great interest to every single country represented in th is great Assembly Ladies and gentlemen,

I would like to conclude with a few thoughts on the topic of artificial intelligence. One of my favorite bands when I was growing up was Talking Heads. Little did I know at the time that David Byrne’s iconic song “we are on a road to nowhere” would ring so prescient four decades later.

For the first time in the history of our species, we have created a technology that openly challenges t he supremacy of the human mind as the pinnacle of our evolutionary development. I will not dwell on the transformational potential of this revolutionary technology, w hether in disease eradication, productivity enhancement, or fighting climate change.

However, it is simply impossible to ignore the fact that, at present, the risks of an unchecked and unregulated advance in artificial intelligence could greatly outweigh its potential benefits.

When the people developing the technology tell us openly that, “left unchecked AI could outrun our ability to control these systems” and admit that “we only understand a tiny fraction of what goes on in these models”, alarm bells should ring very loudly for all of us.

In simple words, AI bosses are telling us that they have no idea how recursive self -improvement, the ability of AI to constantly create better versions of itself, actually works.

Add to that the possibility of massive job destruction, the likelihood of unprecedented wealth creation in the hands of very few, and the impact that AI may have on the very nature of human relationships, especially for our kids, and you have all the ingre dients of an unprecedented political and social upheaval.

The idea that the big tech companies will find some voluntary arrangement to self-regulate the development of AI is naive. It flies in the face of everything we know about the history of capitalism.

The prize for the winners is simply too great to believe that benign consideration for the wellbeing of humanity will outweigh the relentless drive of capital to constantly seek better returns.

Given that the leading AI models are being developed here in the United States, this is primarily an issue for the US government to address. Fortunately, t here are prece dents from which to draw lessons.

In the 1940s and 50s, the American government heavily regulated another technology so powerful that its creators believed it could bring about either a golden age in human flourishing or the end of the world. That technology was nuclear.

The same needs to happen now. And it needs to happen fast. AI companies need to be li censed based on specific requirements: adherence to human values, transparency and, most importantly, safety. In order for a new plane to fly, it has to undergo a myriad of rigorous tests approved by the regulator. But the same is not true for a frontier artificial intelligence model.

At the same time, I take the call by leading AI executives for a voluntary pause in the development of their models very seriously.

But only as a temporary measure to buy time for a powerful regulatory authority to be set up.

Liberal capitalism has a history of rei ning in market excesses, whether it was breaking up powerful monopolies or setting rules and standards to allow the market to operate with an eye on the common good. The same needs to happen now.

And as much as the cooperation of China and the rest of the world is necessary to address this huge challenge, the fate of artificial intelligence and the impact it will have on humanity as a whole will not be decided in Brussels, Tokyo, or Brasilia, but primarily here, in the United States.

With great power comes great responsibility. Let us hope our host country will rise to the occasion.

Thank you.

Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

A chairde, friends,

The United Nations is entering its ninth decade at a moment of great uncertainty and challenge for the global community.

Conflicts are having devastating effects on the most vulnerable.

The impacts of the climate crisis are felt in every corner of our world.

Hard won rights are being rolled back.

Narrow self-interest is breaking the bonds of solidarity which have so often lifted us to meaningful progress.

The international legal order is under tremendous strain.

New and emerging technologies that offer unlimited potential could also, without human intervention, create unprecedented dangers.

In such moments of uncertainty, it can be easy to question our foundations.

To retreat.

To turn inward.

To say that international cooperation is too difficult, that multilateralism does not work, that the problems of others are not our problems.

But that would be the wrong conclusion.

Because the answer to a world under strain is not less international cooperation.

It is more.

The answer to the weakening of principles is not to abandon them.

It is to defend them.

And if our multilateral system is not working effectively, the answer is not to walk away from it.

It is to make it stronger, fairer and fit for the world we live in.

That is Ireland’s position.

And that is what all of us as members of the United Nations need to deliver on.

We should also remember what our collective commitment to the United Nations has achieved.

The multilateral system, anchored in the United Nations Charter, has been the foundation of many of humanity’s greatest achievements.

It has driven advances in poverty alleviation, healthcare, education, social protection, and food and nutrition security.

It has championed human rights and dignity and insisted that accountability matters.

It has given voice to the marginalised.

Mr President,

The people of Ireland understand that we live in an interdependent world; that the challenges we face are interconnected, cross borders, and require collective solutions.

Ireland currently holds the Presidency of the Council of the European Union.

Our stewardship of the EU’s agenda is deeply rooted in the principle of strength with unity.

And this principle is at the heart of our vision for the United Nations.

As well as our unwavering commitment to the pillars which guide its work: peace and security, human rights, and development.

These pillars equally bear the weight of our shared ambition for a better, fairer and peaceful world.

Collectively, however, we are not delivering on their ambition. We are not staying the course.

At a time when global needs are increasing and becoming more complex, our responsibility to act does not diminish.

Mr. President,

The denial of the fundamental human rights of millions of people around the world remains one of the defining challenges of our time.

Renewed pressure on women's rights and gender equality is putting hard-won progress at risk.

Women and girls are being told that their ambitions, their education, their voices and their very presence in public life are unacceptable.

The situation in Afghanistan is one of the clearest examples.

The systematic exclusion of women and girls from education, employment and public life is not something that the international community can simply observe from a distance.

It is a profound human rights crisis.

Girls are being denied the education that should shape their futures.

Women are being denied the ability to work, to participate fully in society and to contribute to the economic and social life of their country.

Their freedoms are being progressively erased.

And the world must not become inured to it.

We must not allow the absence of headlines to become an absence of action.

The women of Afghanistan have not disappeared.

And neither should our solidarity.

The same is true elsewhere.

Across the world, women and girls face conflict-related sexual violence, forced displacement, trafficking and discrimination.

Across the world, LGBTQI+ people face growing threats to their rights, safety and dignity.

Ireland remains firmly committed to the universality, indivisibility and equal application of human rights.

These principles are beyond question.

That commitment is why Ireland is seeking election to the Human Rights Council for the 2027–2029 term.

And if elected, we will use that seat to defend the principle that human rights belong to everyone everywhere.

Mr. President,

Today, Russia’s illegal war in Ukraine is more deadly for civilians than at any point since the start of their full-scale invasion.

Russia’s reckless drone and missile attacks, on Ukrainian towns and cities, continue to intensify. These are not the actions of a country interested in peace.

Russia could halt its brutal attacks at any time. Yet it refuses to do so.

Russia’s actions have already had direct global impact, in increased food and energy costs.

This time last year, a bushel of wheat was just over five dollars; this year it is more than seven dollars.

The fact that a permanent member of the Security Council is seeking to change borders by force, in clear violation of the UN Charter, is utterly unacceptable.

Sovereignty and territorial integrity apply equally to all States.

The international community must remain steadfast in our response, in support of the UN Charter and of a comprehensive, just and lasting peace.

Ireland stands in solidarity with Ukraine and will continue to do so.

We will continue to support efforts to hold Russia accountable for its actions.

There can be no impunity for war crimes, not in Ukraine, not anywhere.

That is why Ireland is a steadfast supporter of the International Criminal Court.

Ireland strongly opposes efforts to undermine the Court. All measures against it should be immediately withdrawn.

The international legal order, founded on our agreements to make the world a safer and more secure place is being challenged.

International law represents the collective lessons drawn from conflict, suffering and atrocity.

The rules and institutions that we have built over generations exist to protect the rights, security and sovereignty of all states and all peoples.

When these principles are disregarded, the consequences extend far beyond any single conflict. We all become less secure.

Mr. President,

Twenty years ago, the commission on war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur saw the international community come together to fulfil our collective responsibility to protect.

Despite the extraordinary efforts of the Sudanese people, the cycle of violence has continued.

The conflict has been inflamed and prolonged by harmful outside interference. All States and external actors must cease arming, financing and enabling the war in Sudan.

15 million Sudanese people are displaced from their homes.

Over 19.5 million face crisis levels of hunger.

33 million need urgent humanitarian assistance.

Violations of international law, including targeting on the basis of ethnicity, deliberate destruction of the means of survival, killing, torture, and sexual violence, are again being used as weapons of war.

We need to act decisively to support the people of Sudan to end this conflict. We must support their aspirations for democracy, justice, and development.

Sudan has become a forgotten war, despite its devastating impact.

We must not allow the absence of daily headlines to become a licence for inaction.

The people of Sudan deserve the same attention, urgency and solidarity that we rightly extend to crises elsewhere.

Mr President,

Despite its prevalence, we cannot ever allow ours to become indifferent to conflict and the human suffering it brings.

To do so would deny the shared humanity of its victims.

The peace plan on Gaza agreed last October was welcome, but it has not fundamentally changed the reality on the ground.

Israeli strikes continue. Humanitarian aid remains blocked. Civilians continue to suffer.

We, the collected international community, have failed Palestine.

Ireland, like most gathered here, believes that the only viable solution to the decades of conflict, misery and wasted human lives, is a situation where a State of Palestine and a State of Isreal live side-by-side in peace, security and dignity.

There are modest signs of progress.

More countries have recognised the State of Palestine. An overwhelming majority of UN member states has endorsed the New York Declaration.

More of us have taken steps to push back against the illegal and violent settler occupation of Palestinian land in the West Bank.

But time is running out.

What we are witnessing on the ground is a deliberate attempt by some to make the prospect of a two-state solution impossible.

This is not some mad conspiracy theory – it is the stated intent of the Prime Minister of Israel who said clearly that “we are going to fulfil our promise that there will be no Palestinian state. This place belongs to us” as he permitted the E1 illegal development in East Jerusalem.

And the situation in Gaza remains an affront to all that is decent.

How can we tolerate a situation where civilians are so desperate for shelter that they have to make their homes in war-damaged and unsafe buildings?

Where eight children died because one of them collapsed?

Where the most basic humanitarian aid – food and shelter – is deliberately impeded?

When the full truth of what has happened - what is still happening - in Gaza is finally known, when the evidence is gathered, when the testimonies are heard, when the true horrors are finally and fully revealed, it will shame the world.

Nobody will be able to say that we did not know.

Let it not be said that we did not act.

In the West Bank, the relentless expansion of settlements has reached a scale without precedent, further eroding the prospects for a just and lasting peace.

Violent settlers continue to act with near-total impunity, while Palestinian communities face a sustained campaign of displacement and destruction – amounting to ethnic cleaning.

Entire villages have been razed, homes and vital infrastructure demolished, and thousands of Palestinian families driven from the places they have called home for generations and exposed to intimidation and violence.

The United Nations reports that this year there have been almost 200 attacks against Palestinians every month, a stark reminder of a reality that is deepening conflict, suffering, and despair.

The International Court of Justice has been clear: settlements in occupied Palestinian territory are illegal.

Ireland has acted, alongside others, to prohibit the import of settlement goods.

It is never too late to uphold international law.

Mr President,

The conflict in the Gulf remains deeply concerning and is having a serious impact around the world.

We need to get back to meaningful good faith negotiations by all sides.

Ireland has consistently stated that Iran must cease its attacks on its neighbours and also end its destabilising activities across the region; including strikes on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

Vessels must be allowed to transit the Strait safely and without tolls, in line with international law.

If we are to build greater stability, Iran must never have a nuclear weapon. Iran’s destabilising influence across the region must cease.

We need dialogue to achieve a negotiated settlement.

Mr. President,

Since 1978 Irish soldiers have served with distinction in Lebanon in the UNIFIL peacekeeping operation. Ireland will continue to work with Lebanon, EU and international partners to support Lebanon’s future peace and security.

We have consistently condemned Hezbollah's attacks on Israel, which must cease immediately.

Israel must withdraw its military presence from southern Lebanon and bring an end to its military operations there. Israel's response has been wholly disproportionate.

We honour the courage, professionalism and dedication of all peacekeepers who have served under the UN.

We remember with particular respect those who lost their lives in the cause of peace.

We welcome the Secretary General’s report on the future of peacekeeping, and Ireland will work with others to ensure that this essential tool adapts to the twentyfirst century.

Ireland also welcomes wider reform efforts in the UN system. These are necessary if we are to meet the challenges of our rapidly changing world.

But it is also necessary to point out that no reform process can succeed unless member states are prepared to support the United Nations politically, financially and through their actions.

We need the Security Council to live up to its mandate and respond to the crises around us.

Too long the veto has stymied the Council and eroded its legitimacy.

The Council’s membership must also finally be made representative of the world we live in; starting with the historic under-representation of African countries and ensuring that the voices of small and the most vulnerable states are heard.

Mr President,

I conclude by thanking Secretary-General António Guterres for his principled leadership and steadfast commitment to the United Nations over the past decade.

I especially commend his courage in tackling the climate crisis, the fundamental issue of our time.

From devastating floods in Nepal to wildfires across Europe, communities are increasingly experiencing the consequences of a changing climate.

The Paris Agreement remains a powerful example of what can be achieved when countries work together. Secretary Guterres has been a vital voice in calling Member States to action.

We look forward to working with the next Secretary-General in advancing the Charter's principles and strengthening this institution.

As the leader of a country that fought for its independence and its place among nations, I am deeply conscious of the inheritance we have received.

The United Nations, for all its imperfections, remains one of humanity's greatest achievements: a testament to the belief that peace, dignity and progress are best secured when nations work together.

At a time when that belief is under strain, it is our shared responsibility to renew it, strengthen it, and ensure it endures for generations to come.

Thank you.

ENDS

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished delegates,

Ladies and gentlemen,

I come before you from Nepal - a distant country in the Himalayas - carrying a close warning for humanity.

I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation.

Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions.

About families waiting for loved ones who will never come home.

About communities searching through mud, rocks and water for people whose bodies may never be recovered.

About bridges, roads, schools, homes and livelihoods swept away in minutes.

And about a country whose steady progress to achieve Sustainable Development Goals has been interrupted.

==== Four weeks ago, the world saw the shocking images of the catastrophic flash floods that swept through Nepal’s mountain communities with ferocity many have called a “Himalayan Tsunami.”

The Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster was not just a local tragedy, it was a warning to the world.

And I ask you today: have we really heard that warning?

Nearly three years ago, standing in the shadow of our Mount Everest, the Secretary-General of the United Nations warned humanity about the madness of an impending climate disaster.

That cry from the rooftop of the world was not heard loudly enough.

We in Nepal heard it. Our communities heard it.

Scientists around the world heard it. They repeated it with evidence.

But we, the political leaders of the world, have been negligent to translate those warnings into action at the speed and scale that vulnerable people require.

Last month, we saw the tragic consequences.

=============== A warming climate is destabilizing the fragile Himalayan ecology.

Melting permafrost are fracturing mountain slopes beneath the glaciers and accelerating the risks of ice-rock avalanche, floods, landslides and other cascading hazards.

The resulting devastation unleashed havoc on both sides of the Nepal-China border. The flood continued downstream towards India.

This tells us something fundamental:

Climate change does not recognize borders.

Glaciers and floods do not travel with a visa stamped on passports.

=============== Excellencies,

I am not here to complain but to share some suggestions.

First, I wish to express Nepal's deep gratitude to all those who came to our aid in the aftermath of the deluge.

Our immediate neighbors, India and China, offered prompt and generous assistance.

Other friendly countries, the United Nations system, humanitarian agencies, philanthropies and people around the world stood with Nepal.

To all of them, I say: thank you on behalf of the grateful people of Nepal.

Nepal now faces a massive task of recovery and reconstruction.

After at least 1400 confirmed deaths and over 6,000 people still missing, our rapid assessments peg physical recovery needs at about 10 percent of GDP.

As in rebuilding after past disasters like the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, we count on your solidarity and support.

But we must also understand why this disaster matters beyond Nepal.

Nepal contributes less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions.

We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it.

Our glaciers are retreating. Our mountain slopes are becoming unstable. Our rivers are becoming less predictable.

And every major disaster threatens to erase years of development.

For Nepal, climate catastrophe is not just a humanitarian event, but a development emergency.

It destroys roads, bridges, schools, homes, farms and livelihoods.

It destroys clean energy infrastructure that we need to fuel our future.

And it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause.

=============== But we are not here to blame any country or continent.

We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield.

We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity.

Through the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the international community has already agreed to the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.

Those who have historically contributed more to the problem, and those with greater capacity to respond, must do more.

Climate Justice cannot just remain a beautiful phrase in a United Nations Document.

People of our country be allowed to build their future instead of constantly rebuilding their past.

=============== Excellencies,

The Hindu Kush Himalaya is home to nearly two billion people. These mountains provide water, ecosystems, agriculture and livelihoods to populations far beyond Nepal.

The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system.

That is why, as an urgent first step, we propose that we establish a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, led by Nepal, India and China.

Through this mechanism, let us share satellite data and expertise.

Let us monitor dangerous glacial lakes.

Let us strengthen joint early-warning systems.

And when disaster strikes, let us coordinate assistance across borders.

Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information.

Remarkable for a least developed country, Nepal is already playing a global role exceeding its ecological share.

We have restored forests to cover nearly half our territory.

We are installing hydro power at a pace enough to power all our clean energy needs and displace dirty sources abroad.

We are promoting electric mobility with an adoption rate to match parts of Europe.

We are strengthening climate adaptation at the local level. And we shall do more to withstand increased intensity and frequency of climate disasters.

=============== But, Nepal cannot build resilience alone against a crisis made worse by the failure of global governance.

That is why this Assembly must note six words:

Relief. Rehabilitation. Reconstruction.

And also:

Responsibility. Reparation. Resilience.

The first three are what we need after disaster.

The second three are what we need to ensure that disaster does not become a permanent condition.

When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants.

We need adequate grant-based support from the world. The Loss and Damage Fund, the Global Environment Facility and other relevant financing mechanisms remain grossly inadequate.

Climate finance must not become a bureaucratic maze through which vulnerable countries spend years proving that they need help.

When the house is burning, we do not ask the family to complete fifty forms.

We act.

That is what climate justice must mean.

=============== Excellencies,

This brings me to a larger question:

What kind of international order do we want?

The United Nations was born from humanity's experience of horrific World Wars.

Its promise was that sovereignty would matter.

International law would matter.

The dignity of every human being would matter.

And the weak would not simply have to accept whatever the powerful decide.

Today, that international system is under strain.

Too often, military and economic power determines whose voice is heard.

Nepal believes we need a much fairer global economic order.

=============== In 1994, UNDP’s Human Development Report conceptualized the notion of human insecurity.

It equated security with people rather than territories, and with development rather than arms. It called for the peace dividend to secure freedoms from fear and want.

The new majority government in Nepal, elected through the fairest and most peaceful elections in our history this March, has had to weather many international adversities since.

When a poor farmer in Nepal went to sow her seeds this monsoon, fertilizers didn’t reach her on time. When we wanted to pave a new highway, there was no bitumen. When a family sat down for an evening meal, there was shortage of cooking fuel.

On the one hand, there are melting glaciers and failing harvests to floods arriving without warning. On the other, a global supply chain punishes poor people for causes beyond reason.

Inter-continental missiles arrive on time. Rifles and ammunition cross borders, clear every bottleneck, meet each deadline. But a peasant in Nepal cannot procure his fertilizer or fuel at market price at a time of need.

We have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food.

And this is not Nepal's private misfortune. Ask Bangladesh. Ask Bhutan. Ask India. Ask the Maldives. Ask Pakistan. Ask Sri Lanka. Ask any other country in our region and you will hear the same account: hit by the climate we did not warm, and hit again by the wars we did not start.

This tells us there is a lot more broken than meets the eye in the present order of global cooperation.

Excellencies,

I am told I am the youngest Head of Government to address this Assembly this year.

I did not come here to make that the story.

I came to make sure that whatever else is said from this podium, one thing is said plainly: a country that is willing to pay should be able to buy, and a world that can deliver a weapon anywhere in seventy-two hours has no excuse for leaving a farmer without means for a decent livelihood.

This is why we continue to believe in multilateralism. This is why we need a United Nations in which the presence of small poor countries is felt, and we can work together towards just outcomes.

Climate justice is, therefore, not only about money.

It is about distributive justice - who bears the costs.

It is about procedural justice - who has a voice.

It is about whether the future of mountain communities, small island states, landlocked and least-developed countries, and generations yet unborn count equally.

Starting tomorrow at the “Sagarmatha to the Sea” side-event right here at the United Nations, Nepal is ready to help lead this conversation.

=============== Mr. President & Excellencies,

We are at this General Assembly at a moment of profound global uncertainty — and with a renewed democratic mandate that reflects the aspirations of a new generation.

Our youth have demanded a politics of integrity and accountability.

This generational shift is not only a national story. It is part of a global awakening against conflicts, inequities, and lack of opportunities.

The commitment of my government is clear: to build a state that delivers — decent jobs, social protection, and a fair chance for every Nepali to thrive at home.

The Nepal floods signal a future shaped by rising climate extremes. Our baselines are no longer relevant. And we must move from a d-hoc responses to a culture of preparedness.

Let us finance resilience, and invest in insurance and innovation.

Let us build stronger infrastructure and institutions.

Let us reduce fossil-fuel dependence.

Let us build systems that warn, alert and save lives.

Let us reform the order that leaves the weakest with the least power.

And when the next warning comes from the rooftop of the world:

Let us be ready to hear it, and ready to act.

भगवान पशुपतिनाथले तवश्वको कल्याण गरुन्। (May Lord Pashupatinath bless the world.)

यो तवश्व बुद्धले देखाएको बाटोमा त िंड्न सकोस्। (May this world walk the path illuminated by Lord Buddha.)

धन्यवाद, नमस्िे । (Thank you, Namaste.)

title: Federal Minister for European and International Affairs

24. September 2026 Mr President,

Mr Secretary-General,

Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

There are 193 countries represented in this hall today. 193 States that have signed up to the UN Charter. That have signed up to one essential principle: That relations between States are not governed by sheer power, but by rules.

Today, this commitment is being tested. By conflicts. By shifts in power. By new technologies. And our global institutions are struggling to keep pace.

So, let me ask question that I believe sits underneath everything we are discussing this week:

Who decides?

Who decides whether a border is a line to be respected or a target to be crossed?

Who decides whether a human being or a machine pulls the trigger?

Who decides who gets heard, and who is left waiting outside the room?

For more than eighty years, this organisation has stood for one answer: power must be bound by rules agreed together. That answer secured Austria's sovereignty and our prosperity. It still does.

We are a nation of nine million people. An open, liberal democracy, and we are proud of it. Alone, we cannot keep trade routes open, stabilise energy markets, or prevent wars. Like most countries in this hall, we depend on a world in which borders are respected, agreements are kept, and strength is bound by law.

When that order weakens, the gravest price is paid by those least able to bear it: by countries already in crisis, by populations heavily dependent on food imports and by people caught in conflict. In Austria we are fortunate to live in peace. But the consequences reach us, too: energy prices rise, factories close, and families forced to flee war and seek safety in Europe.

This is why the United Nations matters. It is our life insurance. This is why we are a proud host country of the Organization. Why we - successfully - campaigned for a seat on the UN Security Council.

I would like to thank you wholeheartedly for your support at the elections in June.

Austria will be a reliable partner in the Security Council during the next two years.

Austria – throughout its campaign – has made a promise:

To spare no effort on the Security Council to protect our common rules.

To engage in dialogue with everyone.

And to rebuild trust in our global order that has been eroded by a dangerous zero-sum logic.

But for all of us the road ahead is not easy. Because today, that order is being tested, in conflict after conflict.

For more than four years, Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine has violated the UN Charter, and it still does. During my last visit to Kyiv, I witnessed the pain it causes firsthand.

Austria’s position remains clear: we will not accept a change of borders by force. We need an urgent ceasefire to create a credible path to negotiations between the parties.

In the Middle East, the continuous escalation teaches us a similar lesson. After years of bloodshed and suffering, it is obvious: no one can bomb their way to peace.

We want a prosperous and safe Israel. But the same applies to the Palestinians and to Israel’s neighbours. Israelis and Palestinians deserve to live side by side in peace and security, with a credible path to a two-state solution. Any unilateral actions that undermine this prospect – including the continued settlement expansions in the West Bank – only perpetuate the conflict and must be firmly rejected by all of us.

Palestinians in Gaza desperately need peace and stability, with Hamas disarmed and the IDF withdrawing from the Strip.

Iran and the United States must come back to the negotiating table: to end the suffering, to credibly revive the nuclear talks and to stop holding global supply chains hostage to political ends. Especially when there are bilateral deadlocks and conflicts are impacting the whole world, we must pursue for multilateral solutions.

In Lebanon, we need a sustainable arrangement to support the LAF in disarming Hezbollah. The withdrawal of UNIFIL must not create a vacuum that will leave the region worse off than before.

The same set of international rules must protect civilians in Sudan, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in Yemen, Haiti, Myanmar, Ethiopia and other conflicts that receive far too little international attention.

International law must apply to all states.

It must protect all civilians.

And where violations occur, there must be responsibility and accountability.

This is why Austria will also continue to stand firm in protecting the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court.

Rules do not defend themselves. They need institutions capable of upholding them.

And today, the United Nations too often falls short. Not because it has failed – because we have let it stand still.

There is no alternative to the UN.

There is only the work of making it work.

The United Nations was not created to discuss international problems.

It was created to solve them.

Yet as conflicts and injustice multiply, the UN too often fails to act.

Inside this building, that failure can look like another meeting without a decision.

Outside these walls, it means that wars continue, help does not arrive, and more families bury their dead.

For these families, UN procedures do not matter. What matters to them is whether food arrives, whether a doctor reaches them, whether peacekeepers protect them.

Reform must therefore pass a simple test: does it make the United Nations more able to deliver when people need it?

Austria has been a strong supporter of the reform efforts of the Secretary-General.

And, as an incoming member of the Security Council, we are committed to protect the principles of the Charter. To show to the world, that the Council can act. And to work towards making the decisions we take there more inclusive.

Because it matters who decides.

The United Nations was built to confront the dangers of 1945.

Today, we must face new and rapidly emerging dangers: one of the most urgent threats today is the loss of human control over weapons.

Every Austrian knows the Terminator movies, about a machine, sent to kill humans.

This killer robot was played by a famous Austrian-born, Arnold Schwarzenegger. In the movies, Skynet learns to choose its own targets and starts a war.

In 1984, that was science-fiction.

Today, it is not fiction any more.

Today, weapons with increasing autonomy are already used on the battlefield. The direction is clear: machines are gaining more freedom to find and strike targets.

But a machine cannot understand surrender or mercy. It cannot face a court or answer for a death. It must never have the final say over who lives and who dies.

We therefore need international rules for autonomous weapons, built around one clear principle: no machine may decide to take a human life.

Some will say that agreement is impossible when technology moves so quickly and major powers distrust one another. History says otherwise.

Imagine this hall in December 1953. Austria was still occupied, while the superpowers were testing hydrogen bombs. And yet, from this podium, Eisenhower named two things that did not yet exist: negotiations to restore Austria’s independence and: an international agency that would bring nuclear technology under international oversight. To serve, as Eisenhower said: “the needs rather than the fears of mankind”.

In 1955, Austria was free again. Two years later, the IAEA began its work and Vienna became its home.

The world did not ban atomic energy. It built rules for its peaceful use. But those rules came only after Hiroshima and Nagasaki had shown the terrible cost of waiting.

We cannot afford to wait for a catastrophe to happen.

With artificial intelligence, we can still act first.

For this reason, Austria joins the UN Secretary-General and the President of the ICRC in calling for a legally binding instrument with clear prohibitions and restrictions on autonomous weapons.

Voluntary guidelines are not enough.

We need binding rules that keep human beings in control and ensure accountability.

And we must not drag this out.

Every rule and reform I have spoken about serves one purpose: peace.

During our Security Council term, Austria will make emerging technologies, the protection of civilians, children in armed conflict, and women’s full participation in peace processes priorities. Children must never be treated as collateral damage.

Women must have a real voice at the negotiating table, as leaders and peacebuilders, not as an afterthought.

Peace also requires dialogue. Dialogue is not weakness. It is the refusal to give violence the last word. During the Cold War, states that deeply distrusted one another still met in Vienna. Austria will keep that door open whenever dialogue can prevent bloodshed.

And peace rests on human rights. In Vienna in 1993, the United Nations affirmed that those rights belong to every person, everywhere. That principle is not settled history.

It is a responsibility we must defend today.

I began by asking who decides. Let me end with Austria’s answer.

The strongest voice in the room must not decide alone. Neither should the fastest algorithm. Nor should those with the most tanks or the deepest pockets.

There are 193 countries in this hall. Most of us cannot impose our will on others.

Most of us do not want to live in a world where some can.

Power must answer to rules.

Technology must remain under human control.

Responsibility must always be owned by us, by humans.

And, ultimately: Nations must speak so weapons remain silent.

That is Austria’s answer.

Thank you!

President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly,

Mr Khalilur Rahman,

Secretary-General, Mr Antonio Guterres,

Excellencies, Heads of State and Government,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Mr President Suggestion: This day the 24 th of September is a national day immense significance in South Africa.

We call it Heritage Day. It is a day upon which recommit to not just a United but also a diverse nation. A day where we reassert that diversity is not a cause for division but celebration. Our strength is in our diversity.

In that spirit allow me Mr President to congratulate you in my mother tongue.

(Eka vuyimeri bya Riphabliki ya Afrika Dzonga, ndzi ku amukelesa eku hlawulweni ka wena ku rhangela Nhlengeletano Hikwayo ya vu -81. Ndzi ku tiyisekisa hi nseketelo wa hina hinkwawo loko u ri karhi u hetisisa vutihlamuleri bya wena bya nkoka.)

On behalf of the Republic of South Africa, I congratulate you on your election to preside over the 81st General Assembly. I assure you of our full support as you discharge your important responsibilities.

At the same time, Mr. President, with this being the valedictory UN General Assembly session for Secretary-General Antonio Guteress permit me to salute him for his numerous accomplishments at a time of unprecedented global challenges.

Mr President,

Sixty years ago, in the chambers of this Assembly, the United Nations adopted a resolution condemning apartheid as a crime against humanity.

The demise of apartheid freed the people of South Africa from racial segregation and slaughter, domination and deprivation, humiliation and exploitation.

But it was not only the people of South Africa who were unchained when apartheid collapsed.

The end of apartheid also marked the end of a system that exported violence and instability across southern Africa.

Indeed, the fall of apartheid is a glorious story that attests to what multilateralism can deliver.

Since democratic South Africa took its place in this Assembly, we have pursued a foreign policy anchored in Ubuntu and international law, dialogue and multilateralism, and in the understanding that our fate is tied to the fortunes of our region and continent.

Millions more South Africans have access to education, electricity, water and sanitation, housing and social protection than they did at the dawn of our democracy.

We have built a united nation of a diverse people, steeled in their determination to never let history repeat itself.

In November 2025, South Africa classified gender-based violence and femicide as a national disaster, recognising that dealing with this scourge demands exceptional measures.

We have built a vibrant democracy capable of self-correcting and stepping back from the brink. A democracy strong enough to withstand and resist attempts at external supervision and tutelage.

After the 2024 election, political parties put national stability above narrow interests and formed a government of national unity within two weeks of the announcement of the results.

Since the dawn of our democracy, we have held no fewer than seven free and fair national elections.

As we speak, South Africans are preparing once again to exercise their democratic right, this time in local government elections.

Again, the will of the people will prevail.

Mr President,

The promise of democracy and international cooperation wanes when we cannot demonstrate that they can address inequality and insecurity. Compelled by our unenviable position as the world’s most unequal society, South Africa made inequality a key focus of our G20 Presidency in 2025.

Today, the top 10 percent own roughly 75 percent of global wealth, while the bottom 50 percent own only 2 percent.

This extreme concentration of wealth at the top and poverty at the bottom is neither inevitable nor insurmountable.

Together with Brazil, Norway and Spain, South Africa calls on this Assembly to throw its weight behind the establishment of an International Panel on Inequality.

Mr President,

We know that inequality is at the heart of the rising appeal of politics founded on hate and exclusion. Across the world, citizens who have seen little improvement in their economic fortunes are turning to ideas diametrically opposed to the values of the UN Charter.

As we mark the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, South Africa reaffirms its commitment to confronting racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and all forms of intolerance.

We are determined to confront racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and all forms of intolerance through our Constitution, our laws and our institutions.

Dealing with the root causes and challenges of irregular migration is a shared responsibility of all countries of the world.

Mr President,

We approach our leadership of a regional bloc that is home to a quarter of Africa’s population – the Southern African Development Community (SADC) – with a firm resolve to champion greater regional integration, industrialisation and trade.

We want to increase trade among our countries so that our citizens can share in the prosperity of our region and our economies are better prepared to absorb the shocks of unilateralism.

If multilateralism works at regional level, then citizens have greater reason to believe it can work globally.

Mr President,

Our governments face a difficult choice: whether to meet the needs of their citizens or satisfy the expectations of creditors.

In the last year alone, African countries spent roughly the same amount on servicing debt as is needed to close our infrastructure financing gap.

This grim reality inspired South Africa’s G20 Presidency to focus on debt sustainability.

The Africa Expert Panel report calls for an end to incrementalism.

It supports multilateral efforts to establish a Borrowers’ Club to counter-balance the power of creditors and calls for greater debt transparency and greater scrutiny of credit rating agencies.

To us, Mr President, unsustainable debt betrays the promise of development and destroys the prospects for democracy.

With only 36 percent of the Sustainable Development Goals showing sufficient progress, we are running out of time!

Africa and much of the Global South need multilateral action to free resources absorbed by debt service and redirect them towards development.

We must close the financing gap for the 2030 Agenda and meaningfully advance implementation of the African Union’s Agenda 2063.

Mr President,

Climate disasters and extreme weather patterns threaten our people, our prosperity, and our hard-won development gains.

In the last year, two million people in SADC suffered the combined and debilitating impact of floods, cyclones, wildfires, and disease outbreaks.

Our responses are severely constrained by a climate finance architecture stacked against developing nations.

Global action on disaster resilience and predictable financing for a just energy transition is essential if international cooperation is to deliver for all.

Mr President,

Our continent has the world’s largest reserves of critical minerals.

These critical minerals can help bridge the g ap between wealthy and poor nations and overcome the indignities of poverty and underdevelopment.

We insist, Mr President, that indeed Africa must have a stake in shaping the rules that govern the development and deployment of Artificial Intelligence.

We have a youthful population ready to play a key role in the beneficiation at source of critical minerals and on research and innovation for artificial intelligence.

Mr President,

Restoring trust in multilateralism demands that we demonstrate, as the United Nations, that the peaceful resolution of conflicts is still our mantra.

Unfortunately, much of what we see runs counter to this.

In the last two years, the world spent more on military budgets than on resourcing this important body tasked with maintaining global peace.

We are reminded that meeting the SDGs by 2030, including ending hunger and expanding access to safe water and sanitation, would require no more than 5 percent of the 2.9 trillion US dollars spent on arms.

The result of the choice we are making is an arms race and a world as divided as it is dangerous.

We see the consequences in Sudan, which is today the worst humanitarian crisis in the world.

We see the consequences in the Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, Iran,

Ukraine and elsewhere.

Humanitarian workers are caught in the crosshairs of today’s conflicts. When they are not being obstructed from reaching civilians in need, they are being killed in the line of duty.

To restore respect for international law, we must protect those who deliver humanitarian assistance. That is why South Africa endorsed the Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel, supported by nearly 120 states from all regions of the world.

Mr President Eighty years ago, the first resolution of the General Assembly called for the elimination of nuclear weapons.

Later this year, South Africa will preside over the First Review Conference of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.

As the only country in the world to have voluntarily dismantled its nuclear weapons programme, South Africa stands ready to share this experience as a demonstration that, with political will, credible and verifiable nuclear disarmament is achievable.

In our view, restoring trust in multilateralism will not happen without meaningful reform of global governance, principally the UN Security Council.

African citizens are growing weary of their continent being consigned to the periphery of global governance.

Africa is home to nearly one-fifth of the world’s population and African countries together account for more than a quarter of UN member states.

Yet over the past decade, 70 percent of UN Security Council resolutions have concerned conflicts on the African continent.

If the future belongs to the young, then surely a continent that will be home to one in four of the world’s youth by 2030 deserves a bigger seat at the table.

South Africa therefore reaffirms its support for the Ezulwini Consensus and its call to end Africa’s relegation to the margins of global decision-making.

Permanent seats for Africa in the Security Council, with all the prerogatives of permanent membership, are long overdue.

Mr President,

Nowhere is the need to uphold our shared humanity more urgent than in Palestine.

The rights, dignity and humanity of Palestinians cannot be treated as conditional.

The State of Israel’s continued violations of international and humanitarian law constitute genocide, and we remain steadfast in our view that the international community must act decisively to end this impunity.

In our support for a just and lasting peace and a two -state solution, in accordance with UN resolutions, South Africa is unwavering.

We are steadfast in our longstanding solidarity with the people of Western Sahara.

We reaffirm their inalienable right to self -determination and support a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution consistent with international law and the principles of the United Nations Charter.

Mr President,

We are also deeply concerned by the wielding of economic weapons to coerce countries into abandoning their chosen development trajectories.

The suffering of the Cuban people should command our deepest solidarity.

We reiterate our call for an end to the blockade on the Cuban people.

The designation of Cuba as a State sponsor of terrorism, is similarly unfounded, and it should be removed from that list.

Unilateral coercive measures have negative spillover effects that seriously undermine third countries.

Similarly, we also call for the urgent removal of sanctions against Zimbabwe.

Our current reality demands that we act collectively to protect existing international institutions of justice from sanctions and intimidation. These institutions fulfil important mandates for the benefit of humanity.

As I conclude, Mr President,

South Africa leaves this podium with an important refrain:

The South African nation is the creation and heritage of the international community.

South Africa today stands tall in the family of nations because the United Nations delivered on the promise of its Charter.

As Member States we must continue to support this organisation, our organisation, because as President Nelson Mandela said in his inaugural “The millions across our globe who stand expectant at the gates of hope look to this Organisation to bring them peace, to bring them life, to bring them a life worth living” I thank you.

END

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished Heads of State and Government,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

In the name of the Almighty God, in whom we place our trust in, Kam na bane ni Mauri.

On behalf of the Government and people of Kiribati, I extend our warmest congratulations to you, Mr. President, on your election to preside and lead the Eighty-First (81st) session of the United Nations General Assembly.

Kiribati assures you of our full support and cooperation as you undertake this important responsibility.

The United Nations — Our Family of Nations Mr. President,

We meet today at a difficult moment.

Conflicts continue to claim lives and displace communities. Human rights continue to be violated. Humanitarian crises persist. Development gains are being reversed in many parts of the world. Inequality remains entrenched, while climate change plac es additional pressure on communities already confronting significant development challenges.

We therefore support efforts to strengthen the effectiveness, representativeness and accountability of the United Nations, including its Security Council. Reform should not weaken the organisation, it must enable the UN to fulfil the purposes for which it was created.

We also welcome the UN80 Initiative as an important opportunity to strengthen the effectiveness of the United Nations and acknowledge the work under Workstream 2 on Mandate Implementation Review, and recognise the leadership and contribution of Member States, including New Zealand and Jamaica, in advancing this important process.

Mr. President,

It is therefore fitting that the theme of this eighty-first session is: “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All.”

This theme is both timely and relevant.

Trust cannot be restored by words alone. It must be strengthened through implementation, accountability and results that improve the lives of our people. For Kiribati, the theme reaffirms our shared duty to strengthen the United Nations and ensure it serves everyone.

Ocean Management & Fisheries Mr. President,

Kiribati is an ocean nation. We are a Big Ocean Sustainable State.

Our economy, food security, livelihoods, culture and way of life depend on healthy, sustainable marine resources. Sustainable management is essential to our long -term development and we call for increasing efforts and partnerships to aggregable progress towards SDG 14 “ Conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources for sustainable development.

The 2026 Sustainable Development Goals Report reminds us that our oceans and fisheries continue to face mounting pressures from overfishing, illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, pollution, warming and acidification.

The entry into force of the B iodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction Agreement marks an important step towards stronger and more equitable ocean governance. Kiribati is proud to have signed and ratified this Agreement and calls on Member States to recognise the vital importance of our shared ocean and to work collectively to translate the Agreement’s historic ambition into meaningful global action.

Mr. President,

The sustainability of our oceans and fisheries is closely linked to the changing climate, and the pressures we face on our marine resources are increasingly compounded by its impacts.

Climate change remains one of the most pressing challenges to our development and way of life. Sea -level rise, coastal erosion, saltwater intrusion and extreme weather events continue to place pressure on our communities, infrastructure, water security and livelihoods. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Sixth Assessment Report reinforces the urgency of these challenges and particular ly the risks faced by small island States.

Through our long-term national development vision, the Kiribati Vision for 20 years, and our national priorities under Te Motinnano policies, we continue to invest in resilient infrastructure, water security, coastal protection, disaster preparedness, renewable energy and community -based adaptation. Our objective is clear: to continue building a wealthy, healthy and peaceful Kiribati, where our people can live with dignity, in peace and with opportunities.

Renewable energy is increasingly important to Kiribati’s development and energy access. We therefore see greater investment in renewable energy as an important opportunity to reduce our reliance on imported fossil fuels and strengthen the resilience and sustainability of our energy sector.

But national action must be matched by international action. We call for greater ambition, stronger support for adaptation and climate finance that is adequate, predictable and accessible, particularly for Small Island Developing States.

Kiribati recognises the importance of international law in addressing climate change. The International Court of Justice Advisory Opinion on climate change advances climate justice by affirming that all States have binding duties to protect the climate system and achieve deep, rapid, and sustained greenhouse gas reductions consistent with limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

We welcome growing recognition that climate resilience must be locally owned and driven. The Pacific Resilience Facility is a Pacific -led, Pacificowned mechanism that strengthens the region’s capacity to finance climate and disaster resilience. The Pacific’s co-hosting of COP31 with Türkiye later this year further demonstrates the value of local action. These initiatives also show that strong, genuine partnerships can sustain locally led development.

Mr. President,

Partnership continues to shape international cooperation as we believe that we are stronger when we work together. At a time when multilateralism faces growing challenges, partnership remains one of our most powerful affirmations, of what we can achieve, collectively.

Kiribati reaffirms its support for frameworks that embody this spirit of partnership, including the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS (ABAS) and the Pact for the Future, which provide important foundations for strengthened international cooperation, solidarity and collective action.

As the 2030 Agenda enters its final years, partnership must remain central to accelerating SDG progress.

Kiribati recently presented its Second Voluntary National Review (VNR), reaffirming our commitment to the 2030 Agenda. We value our longstanding diplomatic relations with traditional partners and welcome countries seeking new partnerships based on mutual respect, shared interests, transparency, sovereign equality and respect for our national priorities.

This year, following the submission of our second VNR, my Government convened its first “Development Partners Forum” on Kiritimati Island, which we highly value as the world’s largest coral atoll and the first island to see each new day’s sunrise. The Foru m strengthened partnerships between Kiribati and its Development Partners and showcased two flagship projects critical to accelerating economic growth and sustainable development.

Participants included Australia, the People’s Republic of China, the European Union, New Zealand, Japan, the United States of America, the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, and UN agencies. We thank our partners and look forward to advancing our shared interests under the Forum’s Outcome document, the “Kiritimati Partnership Accord 2026”.

Mr. President,

Ultimately, development depends on people, our most valuable resource, making education a vital investment. Kiribati is committed to expanding access to quality, inclusive, relevant education while strengthening skills development, vocational training, dig ital learning, and opportunities for young people.

Health is equally fundamental. We continue to strengthen our health systems across our widely dispersed and remote islands, improve access to essential services and address both communicable and non-communicable diseases.

A healthy and educated population is the foundation upon which every other national priority rests.

Mr. President,

We cannot speak about development without speaking about women and youth.

Kiribati remains committed to gender equality and empowering women and girls. Our election earlier this year to the Commission on the Status of Women—the first time Kiribati has secured a seat on this UN body —is a significant milestone, reflecting our determination to advance women’s rights nationally and globally. We will expand opportunities, prevent violence, and promote women’s economic empowerment and leadership.

Our youth, meanwhile, represent not simply the future of Kiribati. We must provide them with education, employment, skills, technology, leadership opportunities and spaces where they can contribute. And one of those spaces is sport.

Kiribati will host the 2030 Micronesian Games, which we intend to use to leave a lasting legacy for our young people. We invite our regional and international partners to join us in this endeavour.

Mr. President,

Kiribati is a peaceful nation, yet distance does not make us indifferent to the suffering caused by war and conflict elsewhere. The people of every nation deserve peace. We reaffirm that disputes must be resolved peacefully, in accordance with internationa l law and the principles of the United Nations Charter. For island nations such as Kiribati, respect for international law is fundamental to our security, sovereignty and the stability of the international system.

Kiribati is proud to contribute in our own way to international peace and security, through the service of our police officers under the United Nations flag.

For Kiribati, this is an expression of our belief that even the smallest country can contribute to global peace.

For Pacific peoples, the consequences of nuclear weapons are not merely historical. Our region still bears the human and environmental legacy of nuclear testing. As States Parties to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW), we remain committed to advancing the Treaty’s and the humanitarian objectives and establishing an international trust fund for nuclear-weapons victims. As Co -Chairs with Kazakhstan of the recent International Meeting on Victim Assistance and Environmental Remediation, we thank the Secretary-General for convening this important meeting and for keeping the needs of affected communities at the center of our collective efforts.

Peace and security must also keep pace with emerging threats in the digital domain.

The East Micronesia Cable landed in Tarawa last year, connecting Kiribati with Nauru and the Federated States of Micronesia, transforming our connectivity and digital development. However, it also creates vulnerabilities.

With limited redundancy and technical capacity, island States face threats including cybercrime, critical infrastructure attacks, ransomware and online harms that can undermine security and development.

CONCLUSION Your Excellencies,

Kiribati comes to this Assembly not simply to speak of the challenges we face.

We come to speak of the future we choose.

Mr. President Allow me to close by bestowing upon the United Nations and all its members and all its staff our traditional blessings of Te Mauri, Te Raoi ao Te Tabomoa meaning Abundant Health, Peace and Prosperity.
