Mr President,

Mr Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen.

And a very good morning.

I congratulate you, Mr. President, on your election as President of the eighty-first Session. You can count on the full support of the Maldives as you lead this Assembly.

I also thank the former President of the General Assembly, Her Excellency Annalena Baerbock, for her leadership of the eightieth Session.

This year’s theme, “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all”, captures the task before us.

Trust will not be restored by words alone. It will be restored by what this Organization delivers for every country, large or small.

Thirty-seven years ago, the Maldives asked this Assembly to face a simple truth:

That “Small States can be highly vulnerable to external threats and acts of influence.”

In response, this Assembly adopted Resolution forty -four, fiftyone an initiative led by the Maldives, affirming the importance of protecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of small States.

That was true then and it is true even today. But the threats have evolved.

Insecurity now travels through sea lanes, supply chains, financial markets, digital networks and new technologies.

Today, sovereignty can be weakened without a single border being crossed. It can be undermined when external powers limit a State’s freedom to choose.

This is why the Maldives comes before this Assembly with a clear message: “Every State, large or small must have the freedom and capacity to shape its own future.”

A sovereign future.

And that future begins with peace.

The Indian Ocean must remain peaceful. It must remain as a region where trade can flow and where States can prosper.

Regional competition among major powers must not limit the choices of smaller States.

Conflict does not have to reach our shores to affect us.

In today’s interconnected world, a crisis far away can quickly become a crisis at home.

Interruption to maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz raises fuel prices. It affects food supplies and air travel. The consequences of this are felt across tourism and public finances in the Maldives.

The Maldives condemns the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

The Strait must remain open and safe.

The Maldives further condemns the attacks on Saudi Arabia,

United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Jordan.

The Maldives appreciates the diplomatic efforts of Oman,

Pakistan and Qatar to de-escalate the crisis and bring the parties to dialogue.

The right to a sovereign future must belong to all.

And nowhere is that right more brutally denied than in Palestine.

Israel's genocide and war crimes against Palestinians continue.

And their actions are not confined to Gaza.

Its military attacks across the region have violated the sovereignty of other States.

Security cannot be built by exporting insecurity.

Nor can any country demand respect for its sovereignty while violating the sovereignty of others.

No State should be shielded from accountability by its power or political alliances.

But condemnation alone is not enough.

Every Member State must ask: What have we done to end this violence?

The United Nations must ask itself the same question.

The problem is not a lack of law. The rules are clear. What is absent, is equal application.

International law cannot bind the weak and bend for the powerful. The same rules. The same standard. No exceptions.

Israel’s genocide in Gaza must end.

Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestine and other Arab lands must end.

Illegal settlements must end.

Humanitarian assistance must reach Palestinians safely, rapidly and at scale.

And the decisions of international courts and the resolutions of this Organization must be respected and implemented.

For the Palestinian people, a sovereign future means freedom dignity.

Self-determination.

And the right to live with security in their own State.

The Maldives will always stand with the Palestinian people and their undeniable right for that future.

That is why I reiterate our call for the recognition of an independent and sovereign State of Palestine, based on the pre1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

And if this Organisation is to restore trust and deliver for all,

Palestine must become a full Member of the United Nations.

Conflict is not the only threat to sovereignty. Forces beyond our borders can also limit a State’s freedom to shape its own future.

For SIDS like the Maldives, none is more consequential than climate change.

For SIDS, climate change is altering the very physical foundations of our nations.

Sea level rise is therefore not simply an environmental concern.

It is a matter of national planning and national security.

It is a matter of sovereignty.

Let there be no doubt.

Rising seas may alter our shores.

But they will not erase our statehood.

They will not reduce our rights.

They will not weaken our maritime entitlements.

And they will not diminish our national agency.

Our response must be to adapt innovate and build.

But resilience demands the means to act.

That means finance must reach those who need it.

At the scale.

At the speed.

And on the terms needed to build resilience.

That is why COP31 in Antalya must be a COP of delivery.

Implementation must be the measure of commitment.

We must move faster. We must speed up the 2030 Agenda. And we must turn ABAS into measurable progress for SIDS.

For island nations, that progress cannot be separated from a healthy and sustainably managed ocean. Therefore, the first Conference of the Parties to the BBNJ Agreement must deliver from day one.

Ultimately, global commitments matter only when they enable progress at home.

His Excellency President Dr Mohamed Muizzu has set a clear ambition: for the Maldives to become a developed country by 2040.

We are pursuing that goal by raising productivity, diversifying our economy, building resilient infrastructure, expanding renewable energy and investing in our people.

Our future will be built by Maldivians.

But the international system can widen or narrow our choices.

Technology transfer, resilient supply chains and accessible finance expand choice. Technological dependence, external shocks and unsustainable debt limits it.

This is why reform of the international financial architecture matters.

We must implement the Sevilla Commitment and deliver on its promises on finance, debt, and reform.

Earlier this year, the Maldives joined other developing countries in launching the Borrowers’ Platform.

It must become a lasting mechanism that gives developing countries not just a place in the financial system, but a voice in shaping it.

But for SIDS, greater agency also depends on progress at home.

We must build our institutions, improve stability, and attract responsible investment and meaningful partnerships.

And these partnerships must build national capacity and support national ambitions.

Partnerships must serve national needs strengthen what we have and leave us more capable than before.

Our shared challenges can become shared opportunities.

This is the spirit of President Dr Muizzu’s Maldives First policy.

Partnerships built around respect national interests and mutual contribution.

And the same principl e must guide the technological transformation before us.

Artificial intelligence offers significant opportunities.

For small States, AI can close distance. It can help overcome scale.

And it can put better health care, education, and public services within reach.

But these opportunities must be shared.

Every country must have a voice in shaping the global rules for AI. The digital future should strengthen our ability to serve our people better. Not create new forms of dependence.

And as the world transforms, so must the United Nations.

The UN80 Initiative is an opportunity to reduce duplication, improve accountability, and focus resources on results.

But efficiency must not be measured simply by what we cut. It must be measured by what we deliver.

And the United Nations must not retreat from the countries that need it most, in the name of efficiency.

Reform must preserve a meaningful UN presence on the ground, particularly in SIDS.

The UN Development System must respond to the needs of programme countries and remain guided by relevant international frameworks. The reform process must be MemberState-led. It must be inclusive and transparent.

This is how reform will restore trust. By bringing the United Nations closer to the people and the countries it serves.

Reform must also confront one of this Organization’s oldest weaknesses: Unequal representation.

The Security Council cannot reflect the world of 1945 while deciding for the world of today.

It must be expanded in both permanent and non -permanent categories.

SIDS must have a rotating seat.

Africa must receive the representation long denied to it.

And the veto must be abolished.

After all, representation is not merely symbolic. Who sits at the table shapes what the table sees.

Small States understand how closely climate, finance, trade supply chains and security are connected.

We also know that international law is our strongest safeguard against unequal power. That principle must remain at the heart of the international system.

The Maldives will take its seat on the Economic and Social Council for the 2027 to 2029 term.

We are seeking election to the Human Rights Council for the 2028 to 2030 term.

And we seek the support of Member States for a seat on the UN Security Council for the 2033 to 2034 term.

We do so because small States must be decision -makers, not decision-takers.

Representation matters not only within the bodies of this Organization. But also, in its leadership.

As Secretary-General Guterres approaches the end of a decade of service, The Maldives thanks him for his leadership and commitment to international cooperation. Thank you Secretary General Guterres.

The process to choose his successor must be transparent and based on merit. It must draw from the full breadth of talent available to this Organization.

For more than eight decades, every Secretary-General has been a man. It is time for a woman to lead this Organisation.

A leader who will defend the Charter, without exception. Who can turn reform into delivery. And who will listen to all Member States, including the smallest.

The task ahead is immense. The choice we make must meet it.

So, what should this Assembly do?

The Maldives proposes a simple test for a sovereign future.

When we act on conflict, climate, finance, technology, or institutional reform, let us ask:

Does this decision expand a State’s freedom to choose?

Does it build national capacity and reduce dependence?

Does it protect sovereignty and independent decision-making?

If the answer is no, we must change course.

And we must hold every State to the same standard.

Let this be the measure of international cooperation. Not what we promise, but what we make possible. That is the measure of a United Nations that delivers for all.

In 1989, the Maldives asked this Assembly to protect small States from external threats. Today, we ask it to protect something just as fundamental: Every State’s freedom to choose its own future.

A future chosen by its people.

A future grounded in international law.

A sovereign future for every State.

I thank you.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies,

I ask every nation here - are we still willing to work together?

The principles in the UN Charter, affirmed by each one of us taking our seat in this hall, are now tested not by argument - but by neglect or ill intention.

The credibility and effectiveness of multilateral institutions is imperative for small nations. It is past time to better turn the urgency expressed in political declarations and resolutions into results, not repetition.

We speak from our own experience when we underscore the importance of acting together. An institution that takes decisions collectively must also be accountable, collectively.

Mr. President,

The United Nations is long overdue to reflect and renew the same spirit with which our Marshallese people first came to the UN, by delivering an apology and acknowledgement of the harm caused by impacts from the 67 nuclear weapons tested on our islands during our time as a UN Strategic Trust Territory - between 1946 and 1958. The sacred trust of the UN Trusteeship to ensure our well-being was jeopardized by these tests and the lack of due acknowledgement remains a moral failing.

For generations, our families have testified to displacement, illness, contamination and loss, all of them impacts to our core human rights. As our survivors would say, “this is a song that has been sung far too many times”.

It was in this same building that the UN Trusteeship Council sat in session and voted on Resolutions 1082 and 1493, in 1954 and 1956 respectively, to effectively authorize further nuclear testing over the demands of our local leaders and many citizens.

The United Nations ultimately allowed the testing to continue, but the shock and tragedy of nuclear exposure in the Marshall Islands was a profound driver of the 1963 global ban on atmospheric testing of nuclear weapons.

We acknowledge the ongoing actions, dialogue and complex legacy of the UN’s administering authority, the United States. But the role of the United Nations cannot pass without comment For us – and for fellow member states – this apology is an opportunity to reflect upon the past, to bring healing and closure to the Marshallese people.

We carry no larger agenda – other than to ensure that the United Nations will do better.

Mr. President,

As we face a world in which scientists tell us overshooting the 1.5 degree temperature limit that we agreed in Paris is increasingly likely, we all need to to wake up and act.

Our focus now must be on preventing or minimizing the overshoot, shortening the time we spend above 1.5, and doing everything possible to fight our way back.

As we gather in Tuvalu, Fiji and Turkiye for this year’s climate pre-COP and COP, our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming. A much accelerated transition away from fossil fuels is the only logical response. Continued investment in fossil fuels is not only immoral but irrational. Technologies exist which provide secure, stable, zero-emissions energy. We are employing them in my own country, where, in the next 18 months, renewable energy will cut fossil fuel use in our remote outer atolls by 88%, giving many access to electricity for the first time. We must do everything in our power to accelerate the deployment of renewables, and to reduce fossil fuel production and consumption with equal speed.

This includes shipping, where we have the opportunity at the International Maritime Organisation to adopt binding regulations that will place international shipping on a clear path to net zero by 2050 and generate the revenue required to ensure a just and equitable transition.

Mr President,

The denials and delays that have slowed the transition away from fossil fuels mean that countries like mine are already experiencing grave challenges. We have developed our national adaptation plan, working across ministries and with our people to determine how to make a safe future. Adapting is costly, and takes time, even as we’ve seen schools destroyed by rising seas, salt water poisoning our wells, and disease outbreaks linked to environmental change. This injustice must be addressed. Our communities deserve restitution.

The Marshall Islands, and vulnerable people everywhere, need sufficient, timely and accessible finance for adaptation and loss and damage. Those who have profited to the detriment of the many must pay. We have created home grown institutions that are ready and willing to respond, like the Pacific Resilience Facility

- a regionally managed platform, and the Marshall Islands Adaptation and Resilience Trust Fund, designed to enable donors to support our adaptation efforts.

Mr. President This crisis has the power to divide us, or to prove that we all remain willing to achieve common goals.

This week the Marshall Islands convened the High Ambition Coalition, a diverse group of countries committed to a rigorous response to the climate crisis. We are united in the view that the best available science must lead the decisions we make, the importance of a 1.5 degree celcius temperature limit, an urgent transition away from fossil fuels, and the need for adequate and accessible climate finance, especially for adaptation and loss and damage.

Mr. President,

As a low-lying atoll nation with no higher ground, sea-level rise is an immediate and stark reality. This week’s UN High Level Meeting on Sea-Level Rise has helped achieve new understandings in international law.

It is the seas that are rising around us, and not our islands which are sinking. Our boundaries and baselines of today - the political footprint on the map - will endure in the face of aggressive sea-level rise scenarios. Our collective stability - and security - as Pacific Islands Forum members, and as a UN member state - will be now better addressed.

As an atoll nation - our tide gauge is proof enough that far more action is needed.

And we are acting. Confronted with rising seas on our most vulnerable shorelines, we completed the Ebeye Seawall and Footpath last week, 1.8 kilometers of oceanside protection built with support from the World Bank, the Green Climate Fund, and our own resources. Engineered for rising seas, it now protects 8,400 people and critical energy infrastructure, reduces annual coastal -flooding losses, and anchors resilient future development on Ebeye, including schools, housing, and the proposed new hospital, while providing a safe public space that strengthens community wellbeing. It cost $75 million dollars, took 70,000 tonnes of rocks, took more than a decade to do - and it is just one island of over a thousand. We are taking action, and we urgently need strengthened partnership to better protect our islands, before sea-level rise overtakes us.

Mr. President,

My nation underscores the importance of the Law of the Sea as a key legal pillar of our future. Even before we were a UN member, we fought closely both to participate in UN Law of the Sea negotiations, and to secure these rights in our Constitution. Pacific island leadership, and that of all small island developing states, has defined every multilateral milestone for oceans and fisheries and, we will continue to do so.

As an ocean people, the consequences of getting it wrong are not from distant impacts, but adjacent to our waters - particularly in the North Pacific, both within the International Seabed Authority and unilateral actions. Collectively- the peoples and voices of Micronesia must be heard - we are joined by Guam, Northern Marianas, Federated States of Micronesia, and Palau - in expressing our alarm at seabed mining actions where the decisions are made before impacts are wellunderstood, and where adequate safeguards remain undefined. The Marshall Islands joins 45 nations seeking a moratorium on seabed mining. Responsible and science-driven regulations need to be in place. Going on guesswork for global oceans is beyond dangerous. There are no do-overs.

The Marshall Islands looks forward to the first Conference of Parties to the Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction- to work across silos to advance high seas protection. We urge wide ratification of the Agreement. The Marshall Islands looks forward to supporting its Secretariat in a host nation committed to upholding the Law of the Sea as a matter of both principle and law, in words and in actions.

Mr. President,

Too often the word geopolitics is considered to refer only to the whims of superpowers, and not the reality of our fragile place between them. As a region of vulnerable island nations, we rightly define our own security priorities- and they deeply cut across every sector, placing a safe future for our youngest generations beyond grasp.

As fuel and energy costs are rising beyond our ability to respond, impacts from bigger power plays halfway around the world are amplified tenfold in small, remote economies. The international community is not listening closely to small island developing states, and it is not responding fast enough. Too often, the purported solutions for island nations don’t seem to know the problems.

Mr. President,

The Marshall Islands faces complex challenges in tackling the SDGs, but we are committed with all of our effort to ensure no one is left behind. Our national planning is now firmly linked to SDG goals and targets and our action proves our commitment. We have developed direct assistance to vulnerable groups including mothers and early childhood development- and we are also reaching our entire incountry population with quarterly supplemental income and improved access to digital finance tools. Our aspirations must be better matched by partnership and island-scaled investment and policy innovation.

I must underscore the direct need for data capacity support to measure progress and effectiveness for small island developing states. If we can’t assess the SDGs, we can’t correct course.

Mr. President,

The Marshall Islands affirms the recent Pacific Islands Forum Communique position regarding West Papua, including the 2018 invitation by Indonesia to the UN Human Rights Commissioner.

Further, the Marshall Islands strongly welcomes recent calls for a ministerial summit between ASEAN and the Pacific Islands Forum to take forward our 2023 agreement. Our two regions can stand united as neighbors and close friends.

The Marshall Islands affirms its longstanding support for Japan - and its G4 partners - to achieve permanent membership on the UN Security Council.

Mr, President,

The Marshall Islands expresses its grave concern over increased efforts to spread dangerous disinformation in these halls. Taiwan, and its 23 million people, are an objective reality, and only its democratically-elected government can represent it.

Appropriate ways must be found for Taiwan’s substantive participation in UN meetings - if the UN is to be truly inclusive and effective.

In years to come, every nation in this hall may be told that aggression or coercion upon Taiwan is an internal matter, somehow justified by an ancient UN seating chart resolution - a resolution which doesn’t even reference Taiwan. In years to come, we may all be told that it is futile for a small nation to resist a larger one and that might makes right regardless of the rule book. We all will experience pressure to accept a false narrative, that UN General Assembly resolution 2758 somehow serves as a legal pretext under the UN Charter for coercion or war, impairing freedom of navigation in one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. We will be asked, politely and impolitely, to turn a blind eye and look away.

It is vital that every nation here, including our close partners in our own region, know that appeasement never satisfies an aggressor’s wider agenda, and one taste is never enough. How the UN addresses this very real security dilemma will be a test of its strength and relevance.

Excellencies,

The Marshall Islands stands firm in investing ourselves in this multilateral institution with clear sight of its frustrations and grave errors. Two years ago, I concluded my coral reef where different species of fish congregate to feed and seek shelter.

Today, we are not only being called upon to revitalize this 81 year-old institution created from the ashes of global conflict, but we are being challenged to address the complexities of a rapidly changing world. This United Nations must continue to serve as our primary Wod in Kanol to ensure that no one is left behind.

Thank you and Kommol Tata.

Mr. president, excellencies, distinguished delegates.
Dear friends, the chosen theme for this year's General Assembly is restoring trust, managing transformation.

I don't think that there could be a more appropriate framing for our discussions of this week.
Trust Or more properly.
Properly, the lack thereof is the greatest challenge currently facing our world.
The erosion of trust that has gripped our societies runs deep.

Where once people embraced trust, now people are gripped by suspicion, suspicion of governments, suspicion of institutions, suspicion of businesses, even.
All too often suspicion of each other.
I am talking about suspicion, not skepticism.
Skepticism.

The legitimate questioning of those who hold power over people's lives is the lifeblood of a democratic society.
Suspicion.
However, the assumption that others are automatically looking out for their interests and not those of the common good is poison to any democratic society.
No community can succeed if we blindly believe that our neighbors are out to do us down just as no country can succeed if it blindly believes that its neighbors, even those it may long have considered and seen as friends, are out to get it.

Which means restoring trust, rebuilding alliances, remaking friendships must be the central mission for all of us here at home and abroad.
It must also be the central mission of the remaking of this United Nations To change.
You have to believe.
We know we need to change how the United Nations works, how it takes decisions, and how it delivers on the ground.

But we can only make that change, achieve that transformation if we believe that change is possible.
Nobody ever successfully renovated the House without the faith that however hard the work, however many setbacks faced along the way, the end result would be a real improvement on what went before.
So we need to show faith that however hard the work, however many setbacks faced along the way, the end result of transforming this house, this home of all the nations, will be a real step forward.
And as this United Nations embarks on its ninth decade of service, the need for a step change in how the international community works together solves problems together is arguably needed more acutely now than ever before.

That erosion of trust is leading to the corrosion of the international order, not the improvement of the international order, but the destruction of the international order.
An international order that, for all its flaws and failures, has seen more children escape hunger, more families live in peace, and more children grow into old age than any era before it.
To destroy the international settlement, without any idea of what comes next would be an act of wanton destruction that would rightly never be forgiven or forgotten by the tens of millions whose future it would betray.
So let us be bold and let us say it loud and clear.

Let us be utterly unequivocal.
Now more than ever, is a moment for more cooperation, not less.
More dialogue, not less.
More trust, not less.

That is the only way that we will manage to find paths to progress on the all too many, all true, all too intractable conflicts blighting our world today.
In Malta, the smallest member state of the European Union, we have always been a bridge between Europe and the Middle East.
So allow me to focus on two of those conflicts on our doorstep.
Firstly, Ukraine.

It is all too easy and all too great a mistake for us to fall in the trap that repelling the invasion of Ukraine becomes another never ending conflict, a grinding tragedy on the corner of our continent about which we can do nothing.
Malta will never accept that despair.
Europe must never accept that despair.
The world must never turn its head away in despair.

Malta remains as adamant in our condemnation of that invasion today as we were on day one in February 2022.
And Malta is equally as adamant that a just and lasting peace must guarantee Ukraine's sovereignty within its internationally recognised borders.
That will only come about through a diplomatic process that the Ukrainian people can have full trust in.
They will only have such trust if the process follows a full and unconditional cease fire and the full participation of Ukraine and its people in the subsequent peace talks.

Rightly the Ukrainian people will never have trust in any search for a settlement which involves their government being frogmarched to the table, one arm tied behind its back, whilst the guns still blaze.
The issue of trust is clearly also central to the very worrying situation in Gaza The people of Israel need to have trust that Hamas will be disarmed, and that they will play no future role in the governance or security structures of Gaza.
But the people of Gaza need to have trust that there is a path to a just peace.
It is impossible to build that trust with a humanitarian situation as acute as that being experienced in Gaza right now.

Malta's voice remains unwaveringly with the global calls for safe, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access throughout Gaza in accordance with international law.
We firmly believe that the Gaza peace plan provides the best path towards ending the conflict and advancing credible political progress.
To achieve that progress, all parties and I emphasize all parties must fully respect and implement the objectives and commitments set out in the plan.
And naturally, no progress can be made.

If there is any question of the forced displacement of any of the Palestinian population.
Indeed, it is incumbent on each and every one of us in the international community to rebuild the trust needed to underpin the conditions where genuine progress can be made towards a negotiated and lasting two state solution.
That is the only solution.
Nobody, however, is under any illusion how out of reach?

Unfortunately, that seems at the moment.
But nor is this the moment to shy away or run away from the only goal that will guarantee the people of Israel and Palestine living side by side with the peace, prosperity and stability that they both deserve.
Sadly, any progress towards a long term solution is being endangered by the situation in the West Bank settlement expansion, running directly counter to the resolutions of this General Assembly and designed to undermine the Palestinian territorial integrity, must stop and stop now.
So too, must the violent settler attacks on Palestinian communities increasing at an alarming rate.

Behold, they must be halted.
These are all essential preconditions to a just and lasting peace, as is a credible and reformed Palestinian Authority that can demonstrate to citizens of both Palestine and Israel that it has the transparency, the accountability, the institutional effectiveness, and, above all, the democratic legitimacy to be a truly effective partner for peace.
Malta stands ready to play its part in building the capacity of both a renewed Democratic Palestinian Authority and the robust civil society that must underpin it, not just in Ukraine, Gaza and Israel, but across the world.
Be it the conflict in Sudan, the ongoing violence in Myanmar or the instability across the Sahel.

It is evident that diminished trust means diminished chances of finding solutions.
You could put it as starkly as no trust equals no peace.
Of course, no matter the conflict, each with its own individual and particular circumstances, there is no easy way of building trust.
But equally, there is no easy way of avoiding the need to build trust.

We all know from our lives as much as from the experiences of our own countries, just how hard it is to rebuild trust when it has evaporated.
Yet we also know the consequences if we give up trying, and the rewards that can come.
If, however, slowly and however tentatively, we can start.
If it is hard enough to build trust human to human face to face, it can be, of course, infinitely harder to build trust.

Of machines, of the technology shaping all our lives.
Yet the challenge of how we can manage to trust that technology and the organisations behind it is rapidly becoming the most pressing challenge of our age.
The sheer spread and the sheer power, the sheer speed of artificial intelligence is mind blowing.
It appears to be moving far too fast for anybody let alone governments, to manage to keep pace.

It can seem, whether from the perspective of a leader, consumer or parent, to be overwhelming.
There is no escaping that.
This is the biggest change and the biggest challenge that any of us will experience in our lifetime.
So much so that we barely have the words to describe how monumental a disruption it is proving to be.

The usual phrases step change, paradigm shift just don't seem to capture the scale.
And we should also be under no illusion that the currently existing rules, the traditional models of governance are in any way or manner up to grappling with the revolution that we are living through.
Which is why, if we stand any chance of helping to build citizens trust in these advanced technologies, we need to begin by being honest and transparent that governments, just as individuals, we are still finding our way, that we don't have all the answers.
What we do have, what we must have, is the will and determination to act and the right values to underpin those actions.

And of course, it almost goes without saying that no state, however micro or mighty, has any chance of getting a grip if they try to go it alone.
We only stand a chance as humanity.
On getting a grip on technology that seeks to ape our humanity.
If we collectively work together.

Acknowledging that the rules need to be set globally and they need to be stuck to.
Even as they develop, as the tech develops.
If we are to stand any chance of securing public confidence that AI can enhance and not destroy humanity, we need a set of international rules that reflect international law.
So Malta, my country, wholeheartedly supports the implementation of the global Digital Compact and wider UN efforts to strengthen international digital cooperation.

To fragment is to fail, and that applies equally to fighting the new threats from the new frontline in global conflict and disruption.
Cyber attacks, attacks on critical infrastructure, disinformation, the cutting of the underwater cables that connect us all to each other.
These are not theoretical threats.
They are constant and existential threats.

For a small nation like Malta, a small island in the Mediterranean that relies on our connections to the rest of the world.
They are, yes, existential threats.
Tackling them must be a priority.
The priority for this United Nations.

We need to embrace every emerging technology that can help us fend off those threats and build our digital resilience today.
The guardians of our democracy, of our freedoms are just as likely to be found coding at a keyboard as marching in uniform.
Both must work in lockstep together.
Security will always, of course be physical.

Yes, but now it must also be digital.
The change must then be reflected in the way we work together to achieve our different and common goals.
I know that I am preaching to true believers, Mr. President and Mr. Secretary General, when I say that there must be no letup, no slowing down in the relentless, relentless drive for reform of how disunited nations and its agencies does its business and delivers its services, to take our foot off the gas would be to let down the millions who need this United Nations to do better, be better at tackling the problems that blight their lives.
That is why the goal of this General Assembly, a United Nations that delivers for all, is so important and so urgent.

If we are to have any hope of renewing the trust of the citizens with serving global institutions and the global order.
We have to show that those institutions, this institution, can indeed deliver deliver in ways that change tangibly lives for the better.
We must never lose sight and never lose faith in the values that brought us together in the first place.
As nations united.

Malta is and always, of course, will be a passionate advocate and promoter of and passionately committed to multilateralism.
At the core of all we do must be the code and conscience of the founding charter of this United Nations.
But the implementation of those values, the way we turn those fine words into fine actions, must always be a process of constant evolution.
We can never stand still if we are to keep cooperation alive.

So Malta remains thoroughly committed to the implementation of the pact for the future and all of its associated actions.
Reforms must, yes, remain Member State driven and firmly anchored in the intergovernmental process, and efficiency must not come at the expense of effectiveness on the ground.
Malta solidly backs a strong and effective resident coordinator system as the key anchor of UN action at a country level, and I can't reiterate often enough or restate strongly enough, that the only effective antidote to the cancer of cynicism and suspicion is effective and concerted action to tackle the greatest threat to our people and our planet.
And alongside spreading conflict and the dangers of uncontrolled technology, the greatest threat to us all, and especially island nations like Malta, is man made climate change.

I say, and I express this to all of you.
Just look at the weather extremes we have been experiencing in Europe, particularly during these last weeks, to do nothing, to stand by and just wash our hands of it would be a moral and practical betrayal of the citizens, of the millions of citizens who put their faith in us, that we won't flinch from the biggest problems and the toughest solutions and decisions needed to tackle them So we must not stand by.
We must stand firm.
Stand firm against the torrent of disinformation that fuels the deniers.

Stand firm against the vested interests that seek to block effective action.
Stand firm against the naysayers who say that.
Because all don't choose to act.
Nobody should.

To those cynics, I want to point out an instance that shows how hope can triumph over defeatism.
And I go back to 1967 when representing the then geographically smallest member state of the Europe of the United Nations, a member state that had been a member of the United Nations for less than three years, Arvid Pardo spoke up in this General Assembly in a stirring speech, Malta's permanent representative made a passionate plea to the world's common humanity.
He may have been speaking on behalf of a very small nation, but he had a very ambitious vision.
Pardo Pardo called for the world to treat the resources of the oceans beyond their own borders as the common heritage of mankind.

His demand for a law of the sea was prescient, but to achieve it took persistence.
In fact, it took 27 years before it came into being.
What motivated Malta's action, then, is what motivates Malta's demands now?
Doing nothing meant leaving the world's oceans to the mercy of the world's biggest, strongest and richest nations.

Taking action showed that, and I quote, they belonged to all of humanity.
Those living and those who still had to be born.
That spirit was evident was evident when, in 1988, right at the start of the concern about global warming, Malta proposed the United Nations General Assembly resolution that recognized climate change as a global problem, requiring collective and global solutions suspicion of collective action won't be counteracted by retreat.
It will only be overcome by the strength to turn convictions into action.

The phrase dare to dream has become perhaps the world's most common motivational phrase, imploring us that all we have to do is have the courage to dream, and those dreams will almost automatically become reality.
And yes, we should all indeed dare to dream, to inspire ourselves, to turn hope into achievement, but to turn initial aspirations into sustainable attainment takes something more than just dreams It takes trust.
Trust that by working together, we achieve more than we could ever achieve alone.
It is that belief in the power of trust which underpins the values that brought me into public life.

It is that belief in the power of trust, even now when it can seem a commodity in all too short supply, that convinces me that ultimately it trust will prevail.
That ultimately, we as a world will find the courage to dial down the disbelief and crank up the confidence.
If we don't.
If we don't realise that mutual suspicion can only lead to mutual destruction, if we don't realise that closing our minds to those who don't share our worldview limits our chances of solving the world's biggest problems.

If we don't realise that limiting dialogue only to those who are like minded in reality can only drive us further apart, we face a very bleak future indeed.
I refuse Malta refuses to believe that such a future is any more inevitable than it is desirable There is only one simple antidote to the destructive power of suspicion.
It is one that may not, as of yet, have appeared on many motivational bumper stickers, but it is one that must be our lodestar.
So I say to my fellow leaders, as much as I say to my fellow citizens of this planet, let us dare to trust, dare to realize that even those who we disagree with the most must become a part of the solution, and not a prolonger of pain.

Mr. President of the 81 st Session of the General Assembly,

Excellencies, Heads of State and Government,

Mr. Secretary-General of the United Nations,

Distinguished Delegates,

Mr. President,

At the outset, allow me to extend my warm and heartfelt congratulations to you, on your election as President of the Eighty -First Session of the General Assembly. Your election reflects the confidence of Member States in your steadfast commitment to multilateralism and your vision for a United Nations that is responsive, effective, and capable of delivering for humanity. As you embark on this important journey, my delegation reaffirms its unwavering commitment to working closely with you and all Member States to ensure a productive and successful session.

On behalf of the Government and the people of Lesotho,

I also pay tribute to your predecessor, Her Excellency Ms.

Annalena Baerbock, President of the Eightieth Session of the General Assembly, with whom my delegation had the honour to serve as Vice Preside nt. Her dedicated leadership, zeal, and tenacity of purpose in strengthening multilateral cooperation during a period of profound global uncertainty gave us hope that the future of this Organization can be secured when all nations work together for the common goal of leaving no one behind.

To the Secretary -General, Mr. António Guterres, whose tenure is approaching its end, my delegation commends his exemplary leadership and fidelity to the ideals of the United Nations. During his term, the world confronted unprecedented challenges; from the COVID-19 pandemic to the eruption of new conflicts, the catastrophic effects of climate change and unstable trade regimes.

Throughout these crises, he remained the moral force and steady anchor of the Organization.

We salute him for his distinguished service and will fondly cherish his historic visit to the Mountain Kingdom in December 2024, during which he witnessed firsthand the dividends of the UN’s contributions to Lesotho.

Mr. President,

The theme for this Session, “Restoring Trust,

Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All,” resonates deeply with Lesotho’s aspirations for a more inclusive, transparent, and results-oriented multilateral system; capable of advancing respect for international law, maintaining global peace and security, accelerating sustainable development, protecting human rights, driving climate action and implementing long-overdue institutional reforms.

Lesotho has restored national peace and security following successive episodes of political and security unrest. With the support of the United Nations, the African Union, SADC, and other friendly nations, we have reclaimed our rightful place among the comity of nations as a stable and peaceful country. We therefore attest that preventive diplomacy remains the most effective means of averting conflict and ensuring sustainable peace.

To create an environment conducive to inclusive growth and development, we continue to advance public sector reforms aimed at strengthening democratic governance and the rule of law. We remain committed to accountability, professionalism and respect for hu man rights across all of society. We recognize that sustainable peace requires strong institutions, restored public trust, and an independent judiciary capable of delivering justice impartially and efficiently.

Mr. President,

We must acknowledge that climate change is no longer a future threat but a present reality. Lesotho is increasingly experiencing severe floods and droughts, resulting in unparalleled land degradation and extensive damage to critical infrastructure. Despite contributing minimally to global greenhouse gas emissions, Least Developed Countries like Lesotho bear a disproportionate brunt of climate impact. Global warming and rising sea levels pose existential threats, particularly to small island developing states. We stand in solidarity with these nations and call for greater global action.

To cope with these climate -related challenges, we call upon developed countries to hono ur their commitments by providing new, adequate, predictable and accessible climate finance. Further, we urge developed countries to transfer environmentally sound technology and to strengthen capacity of developing countries to effectively mitigate and ada pt to the adverse effects of climate change. Climate justice demands nothing less.

Just Energy Transition is therefore an imperative if humanity is to be spared from the existential threat of climate change. Under the visionary leadership of His Majesty King Letsie III, Lesotho has launched the ’’His Majesty King Letsie III Just Energy Transition Fund’’, designed not only to decarbonize our economy but to transform it from one historically reliant on migrant labour to one rooted in renewable energy exports. The Fund seeks to attract investment to build new energy generation capacity, unlock energy independence and lay a new foundation for national prosperity that benefits every Mosotho. We therefore call for partnerships to mobilise the requisite resources for clean energy projects, which can create significant employment opportunities for our youth and women.

Our unique topography also presents opportunities for investment in data centres, which underpin the global digital economy. We are proud that Lesotho is the first country to pilot the United Nations Blueprint for National AI Strategies and Data Centres, positioning our nation on a pathway to achieve its AI ambitions for economic development. We are grateful for the UN’s continued support in this digital transformation journey.

Mr. President,

The Kingdom of Lesotho remains committed to the 2030 Agenda. We have accelerated reforms in business development, trade facilitation, public financial management, youth empowerment, and renewable energy. Yet challenges persist: economic diversification remains limited, youth unemployment stands at 38%, and climate -related shocks and inequality continue to constrain inclusive transformation. With only three years remaining until 2030, we appeal to the international community to honour their official development assistance commitments which is an essential step in restoring trust.

We further call for reform of the international financial architecture to make it more equitable, fit for purpose, and responsive to the needs of developing countries, as agreed at the Fourth Summit for Financing for Development (FFD4) held in Seville, Spain. We also urge full implementation of the outcomes of the Third Summit of Landlocked Developing Countries (LLDC3), held in Awasa, Turkmenistan, in August 2025. The unconditional implementation of these outcomes, tog ether with the Pact for the Future, will undoubtedly help restore eroded trust.

Mr. President, Universal health coverage remains central to our development agenda. While investments have been made, we continue to face serious public health challenges, including a high burden of communicable and non-communicable diseases and inequalities in access to healthcare. Lesotho is undertaking reforms to strengthen our healthcare system and invites partnerships to ensure universal access to quality primary healthcare, medicines, vaccines, diagnostics, and robust disease surveillance and pandemic preparedness.

The social and economic costs of cancer are profound.

With support from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Lesotho is developing its first radiotherapy and nuclear medicine facility to provide domestic oncology services. We therefore call for enhanced cooperation in technology sharing, capacity building, and sustainable health financing to build resilient health systems capable of responding to current and emerging challenges.

Mr. President,

Migration is not an abstract concept for the people of Lesotho; it is a daily lived reality. It is woven into our social fabric as human ambition rooted dignity, opportunity and aspiration. Migration benefits both home and host countries, contributing to skills development, cultural exchange and shared economic growth. We must therefore strengthen international cooperation to ensure migration contributes meaningfully to deeper human understanding and sustainable developm ent. Guided by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, we must guarantee the full enjoyment of human rights by migrants, regardless of status. Protecting their dignity and fundamental freedoms is not only a legal obligation, it is a moral imperative.

Mr. President,

We welcome progress under the UN80 Initiative and appreciate efforts to enhance efficiency, effectiveness, and coherence within the UN system. As deliberations continue, reforms must remain guided by intergovernmental agreed mandates and Member State priorities. Any measures undertaken should preserve the UN’s capacity to deliver across all pillars of its work and maintain meaningful impact on the ground.

Mr. President,

As we contemplate the future of multilateralism, we must renew our collective commitment to a United Nations that is more inclusive, effective, and responsive to contemporary global challenges and one in which developing countries, particularly African nations, have a stronger voice in global decision-making. We reiterate our support for comprehensive reform of the Security Council, in line with the Ezulwini Consensus, to make it more representative, equitable, and reflective of current geopolitical realities.

The Kingdom of Lesotho reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the Charter of the United Nations, multilateralism, and the rule of law. International law remains the cornerstone of sovereign equality, peaceful coexistence, and sustainable development.

Mr. President,

The rise in regional conflicts is cause for deep concern.

We call for sustainable diplomatic solutions to secure lasting peace in Ukraine, the Middle East, Sudan and Eastern DRC. We welcome the ceasefire framework and stabilization arrangements in Gaza and call for sustained engagement to achieve a lasting solution based on the 1967 borders, where Israelis and Palestinians coexist in peace and harmony. Regarding the broader conflict in the Gulf, we urge all parties to intensify efforts toward a speedy reso lution, as its economic impact is dire and devastating. For humanity cannot continue to bear the high cost of these wars.

We should draw inspiration from the wisdom of Chief Mohlomi, one of our renowned diplomats, who advised Morena Moshoeshoe, the founding father of the Basotho Nation, that “it is better to thrash corn than sharpen the spear.” As the United Nations, we must continue investing in conflict prevention and building strong democratic institutions grounded in good governance and respect for international law.

Mr. President,

My delegation continues to call for the lifting of longstanding unilateral coercive measures on Cuba and Zimbabwe. These measures are unjust and deprive innocent civilians of their right to development.

In conclusion, Lesotho firmly believes that cooperation, solidarity, and shared responsibility are the only viable path toward a peaceful, prosperous, and sustainable future. Let us recommit ourselves to a multilateral system that delivers tangible results for humanity, protects our planet, promotes peace and international security and ensures that no one is left behind.

I thank you.

Mr. President.

Excellencies.

Distinguished delegates.

1. It is an honour, once again, to address this august Assembly on behalf of the Government and people of Tuvalu.

2. I congratulate His Excellency Khalilur Rahman of Bangladesh on assuming the role of the President for the 81st Session.

3. President Rahman, you can count on the full support of Tuvalu.

4. I also congratulate the outgoing President Her Excellency Annalena Baerbock of Germany for her exceptional and exemplary leadership.

5. Mr President.

Message of condolences

6. Tuvalu extends its deepest sympathies and condolences to all communities worldwide that are affected by ongoing armed conflicts and recent natural disasters, including the devastating floods in Nepal and Myanmar, the earthquake in Colombia, and the tragic loss of lives at sea in Vanuatu.

7. Tuvalu reiterates its hope for peace, stability, and unimpeded humanitarian relief, and reaffirms its solidarity with all those facing violence, insecurity, and loss.

8. Mr President.

Tuvalu’s commitment to multilateralism

9. In less than a week, Tuvalu will celebrate its 48th anniversary of independence, a significant milestone as Tuvalu approaches its golden jubilee of independence.

10. On this month, Tuvalu also celebrates its 26th anniversary of UN membership.

11. Tuvalu reaffirms its strong commitment to the values and principles of the UN Charter and to international law and to a multilateral system that protects the dignity and security of all peoples.

12. This year also marks the historical and first deployment of Tuvalu police officers to serve in the UN mission in South Sudan.

13. A deployment that confirms that even the smallest member of the UN can contribute meaningfully to international peace and security.

14. Mr President.

Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that deliver for all

15. The theme for this session “restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all”, resonates well with the moment of time we find ourselves in right now.

16. There is no denying that the architecture of multilateralism and international law founded on the UN Chater is under enormous stress.

17. And restoring trust in that architecture is critical, particularly for small island developing states like Tuvalu, whose sovereignty and future are anchored in that very architecture.

18. Tuvalu therefore stands in solidarity with fellow Member States in contributing to the restoration of that trust and advancing the necessary reforms and transformations that will enable the United Nations to deliver for all.

19. Mr President.

Managing Transformation: Protecting Our Land,

Preserving Who We Are

20. Tuvalu, like other countries, is being challenged by various enforced transformations that threaten our land, values, knowledge and cultures.

21. Climate change is transforming our physical environment.

22. Technology is transforming how we communicate, govern and preserve knowledge.

23. Artificial intelligence is changing the way economies and society function.

24. The challenge is not to stop transformation.

25. Rather, the challenge is to manage transformation in a manner that protect people, preserve what is valuable, and give every country the capacity to determine its own future.

26. In response to the transformation to Tuvalu’s physical environment caused by rising seas, the Tuvalu coastal adaptation project (TCAP) has already reclaimed on the capital island of Funafuti, 15.3 hectares of elevated and flood free land as part of the reinforcement of the island’s coastal areas.

27. A further 10 hectares is being reclaimed which is significant adjustment for a country with only around 26 square kilometres of land area.

28. While we work to protect our physical territory, we are also contemplating preserving the intangible foundations of our nation, our traditional values, knowledge and cultures.

29. In that regard, we have two digital initiatives.

30. The first is the Tuvalu Digital Nation Initiative that utilizes digital technologies to sustain our sovereignty, institutions and our capacity to deliver services to ensure that our national identity is not lost in the transformation.

31. The second is the Tuvalu Digital Ark Initiative which seeks to preserve Tuvalu’s culture and historical heritage in digital form.

32. Mr. President UN Political Declaration on Sea-Level Rise

33. Less than twenty -four hours ago, Member States endorsed in this very building, the landmark United Nations Political Declaration on Sea-Level Rise.

34. A monumental and gratifying achievement for Tuvalu, because Tuvalu was at the forefront of global efforts demanding for such a declaration.

35. For Tuvalu, sea-level rise is not a future threat, it is a present reality.

36. Tuvalu is therefore overwhelmed with joy and warmly welcome the commitments the Declaration entails namely: (i) It affirms the continuity of statehood and sovereignty despite sea-level rise.

(ii) It safeguards the permanence of maritime zones and rights established under UNCLOS.

(iii) It recognises and protects the rights, dignity, culture, identity, and heritage of affected peoples.

(iv) It commits to strengthened adaptation and resilience.

(v) It calls for accessible, predictable, and needs-based climate finance.

(vi) And it supports science, technology, data, and knowledge systems that enable informed decisionmaking and long-term planning for vulnerable countries.

37. The Declaration affirms that Tuvalu’s nationhood is not negotiable, that our maritime rights are not erasable, and that our people should never be forced to choose between their homeland and their future.

38. Mr. President Sustainable Development Goals

39. For the sustainable development goals (SDGs), Tuvalu is seriously concerned that the world is not on track to achieve them, because the consequences of such shortfall will be acutely felt by small island developing states.

40. Of the SDGs, Tuvalu underscores the urgent need to accelerate progress on SDG 14, Life Below Water which is the least funded and progressed, yet it is the most fundamental to the survival and prosperity of small island developing states.

41. Tuvalu calls on Member States to expedite implementation of the commitments of the Third United Nations Ocean Conference and to build momentum towards the fourth conference in the Republic of Korea in 2028.

42. Mr President Climate Change and the Global Response

43. Climate change is and remains the single greatest existential threat to Tuvalu’s survival, security, and sustainable development.

44. Tuvalu acknowledges the efforts of the international community to address the climate crisis, but the pace and scale of global actions remain insufficient.

45. With a temporary overshoot of the 1.5°C target now inevitable, a fast, fair, just, and orderly transition away from fossil fuels is even more urgent and require serious attention.

46. Although the science may be clear that methane mitigation is the only scalable, near-term solution capable of rapidly slowing global temperature rise and buying time for longterm CO2 decarbonization strategies to take effect.

47. Tuvalu would insist that CO2 mitigation must also remain a top priority and that both methane mitigation and CO2 mitigation should be vigorously pursued simultaneously.

48. Therefore, the Tassiriki Call for a Fossil Fuel Free Pacific and the Funafuti Call for Climate Justice and Climate Action are critical Pacific -led instruments championing Pacific regional survival and global climate actions.

49. Towards that objective, Tuvalu is determined to play its part in driving greater ambition, including hosting the Leaders’ Segment of the Pre -COP31 next month, and co hosting with Ireland in Tuvalu next year the Second Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels.

50. Tuvalu reminds states of their legal obligations to take appropriate action to protect the climate system from greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, as failure to do so constitute an internationally wrongful act as confirmed by the ICJ Advisory Opinion.

51. Tuvalu welcomes the operationalisation of the Loss and Damage Fund and call on countries to honour their pledges and commitments.

52. Adequate, predictable, and timely financing is essential to ensure the Fund can fully deliver on its mandate and provide meaningful support to those most vulnerable to climate related loss and damage including non -economic loss and damage.

53. Finance, therefore, must be provided as grants at the scale required to address the climate impacts already unavoidable and the increasing loss and damage caused by further warming.

54. Tuvalu stands ready to work with all nations to advance climate ambitions, strengthen resilience, and ensure that no country is left behind.

55. Tuvalu’s message is clear: the world must act now decisively, collectively, and with urgency to protect the future for generations to come.

56. Mr President.

Ocean Governance and the Blue Pacific

57. The ocean is central to Tuvalu’s identity and sustainable development.

58. The ocean has sustained Tuvalu for generations and remains at the heart of our existence, our future and our resilience.

59. Tuvalu may have only 26 square kilometres of land, but we are custodians of some 750,000 square kilometres of ocean, which makes Tuvalu a large ocean state.

60. This year, Tuvalu soft -launched its first ever National Ocean Policy, a comprehensive framework to strengthen our stewardship of marine resources, affirms the permanence of our maritime zones, protect biodiversity, and place the ocean at the centre of our resilience and sustainable development.

61. We thank all our partners whose invaluable support helped turn this national vision into reality.

62. For Tuvalu, ocean governance is not simply an environmental policy.

63. It is also an issue of economic security, food security and climate security.

64. Tuvalu has ratified the BBNJ Agreement and looks forward to contributing to the first Conference of the Parties of the Agreement next year.

65. Tuvalu’s objective towards the implementation of the BBNJ is simple in that the ocean areas beyond national jurisdiction belong to our shared future and must be governed responsibly based on science, equity, the precautionary approach and effective international cooperation.

66. Mr. President Financing Resilience at the Speed of the Crisis

67. Tuvalu, like other small island developing states, is highly vulnerable to climate and economic shocks, but the international financing architecture is ill -equipped to respond effectively to those shocks.

68. Earlier this year, Tuvalu declared a national state of emergency due to prolong electrical power disruptions caused by fuel shortages, escalating energy costs and infrastructural deficiencies.

69. Although, Tuvalu did receive with gratitude external assistance, the timing and scale of those responses were slow and insufficient, and this is why access to rapid disbursement and crisis -response financing is essential for the stability and resilience of small island developing sates.

70. Tuvalu, therefore, continues to urge the international community to adopt financial approaches that match the urgency of the crisis with simpler and faster access to climate finance, scaled-up adaptation funding, accessible loss and damage finance, and rapid -disbursement crisis mechanisms.

71. Mr President.

72. In the Pacific, Pacific Leaders have adopted the Pacific Resilience Facility as a regional financing mechanism to help our communities respond effectively to the growing impacts of climate change.

73. Tuvalu calls on the international community and our development partners to support the full capitalisation of the Pacific Resilience Facility, to enable Pacific -led and Pacific-owned solutions to build resilience where it matters most.

74. Mr. President Mobility with dignity

75. Adaptation and building resilience against the impacts of climate change will reduce the severity of climate change but will not eliminate all consequences of climate change.

76. One of those consequences is people deciding to migrate and set up home elsewhere.

77. Although relocation is not part of Tuvalu’s climate change strategy, it is inevitable that some Tuvaluan may decide to migrate and it is incumbent on the Government to ensure that they do so with dignity.

78. Tuvalu has therefore endorsed the Global Principles for Climate Mobility, which are rights-based, people -centred and grounded in international law.

79. We invite all Member States and partners to join us in advancing this framework of cooperation and common ambition.

80. Mr. President Call for support of and condemnations

81. As we call for a multilateral system that delivers for all nations, we must also uphold the principles of dignity, inclusion, and equality for all peoples.

82. Yet too many communities remain outside the structures designed to serve all humanity.

83. Tuvalu therefore calls for arrangements that enable the meaningful participation of the 23.3 million people of Taiwan in the UN and its specialized agencies and mechanisms.

84. Taiwan has consistently demonstrated that it is an able, trustworthy, and a constructive partner in addressing global challenges, and its exclusion undermines both the spirit and effectiveness of multilateral cooperation.

85. Tuvalu is also gravely concerned by the escalating military activities around Taiwan, which threaten stability across the Taiwan Strait, disrupt international transportation and trade, and jeopardize peace and security in the Pacific and beyond.

86. We commend Taiwan for its calm and principled adherence to the values of the UN Charter, and we urge all Member States to uphold those same principles.

87. At the same time, Tuvalu remains troubled by the long standing unilateral economic measures imposed on Cuba.

88. These restrictions continue to inflict hardship on the Cuban people, contravene the human -rights commitments of the UN, and run counter to the cooperative spirit of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

89. The continuation of those economic sanctions deprives Cuba of essential development partnerships and support needed for recovery and future progress, and we call for the lifting of those sanctions.

90. Tuvalu also supports the call for necessary reform of the UN Security Council to ensure that it is more representative, inclusive, transparent, and accountable, and better align with the reality of the twenty -first geo-political landscape.

91. Mr. President Conclusion

92. To conclude, I wish to assure this Assembly that Tuvalu stands in solidarity with the rest of the Member States to play its part in restoring trust and managing transformations to ensure the United Nations delivers for all.

93. Tuvalu has shown that small nations can lead in climate adaptation and resilience, ocean stewardship, digital innovation, mobility with dignity, and the advancement of international law.

94. Tuvalu’s ability to lead is not determined by the extent of our vulnerabilities but national leadership cannot substitute for global responsibility.

95. The United Nations and its charter are the bedrock of international cooperation and multilateralism, and they must be guarded with all seriousness and integrity.

96. Tuvalu will continue to stand firm in its efforts to safeguard its sovereignty, the health of the ocean, and the integrity of its people despite climate change and other global transformations because they are worth fighting for.

97. And Tuvalu invites this Assembly to stand with us in that fight.

98. Tuvalu thanks the outgoing Secretary General for his exceptional and exemplary leadership and wish him well in his retirement and other future endeavours.

99. Thank you and fafetai lasi.

100. Tuvalu mo te Atua, Tuvalu for God.

END

slug: north-macedonia
