Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

A child who will sit at a school desk for the first time this autumn will, in 2040, be a young person just entering adulthood. We do not know exactly what the world in which that young person will live will look like. But we already know that it will be different from our own.

Artificial intelligence will transform professions, industries and the ways in which decisions are made. Energy will be governed by a new configuration and a new logic of operation. Climate change will affect economies, agriculture, cities and the movement of people. Demographic change will reshape labour markets and social protection systems. Security will no longer depend on armies and borders, but also on power grids, data centres, cables, satellites, algorithms and trust in the information we receive every day.

And yet today, as we prepare for that future, millions of people are living through war or under the threat of war. More than one hundred million people have been forcibly displaced. More than 270 million children and young people are not in school.

This is the paradox of our time. Humanity has never possessed such immense scientific and technological capabilities. And yet, it has never been more evident that technological capability does not automatically produce political wisdom.

That is why the real question before this Assembly is not simply how we will manage the crises of 2026. The real question is this: what kind of international order will we leave to the generation that is entering school today?

For a small country like mine, this is not an academic question. It is a question of survival.

Thirty-three years ago since we became part of the United Nations the world looked very different. The Cold War had ended. There was hope that a new era was beginning; an era in which cooperation would gradually replace confrontation.

Our region, however, was living through a very different reality. Yugoslavia was disintegrating in bloodshed. Wars were being fought just beyond our borders. The fear that the violence might spread was real.

And yet, my country chose peace. It chose stability. It was in those circumstances, on our territory, that the United Nations did something it had never done before: it established the first preventive peacekeeping mission in the history of the Organization.

That experience left a profound lesson in our national memory, a lesson to which I will return towards the end of my address.

Peace does not begin when war ends. Peace begins when politics is wise enough to prevent war from beginning.

Perhaps that is why small countries sometimes see international politics differently.

Great powers have room for strategic shifts that small sized states simply do not have. For a great power, a mistaken geopolitical calculation may mean a change of strategy. For a small sized country, the same mistake can mean a lost decade.

That is why we cannot afford to be indifferent to the rules. Nor can we afford to believe that the rules will defend themselves.

The world taking shape before us is a world of sharper competition. Power is being redistributed. Relations among the major powers increasingly shape trade, technology, energy, critical raw materials, transport routes and digital infrastructure.

What we called economic interdependence only yesterday, we increasingly see today also as a matter of national security. Globalization is not disappearing. It is being reshaped. Supply chains are changing. Production is once again becoming a geopolitical question.

States are asking not only where something can be produced most cheaply, but who can be trusted; not only where energy comes from, but whether it will be available when a crisis strikes; not only who develops the next generation of technology, but who will set the rules under which it will operate.

Alliances, too, are changing under the pressure of this same world.

Macedonian citizens know where they belong. We are a NATO Ally. The United States is our strategic partner. Full membership in the European Union is our strategic commitment.

These are not three separate policies. They are one geopolitical orientation, an orientation grounded in democracy, collective security, the rule of law and an open economy.

In a time of uncertainty, our response is not strategic ambiguity. Our response is clarity.

But clarity in our alliances does not mean turning away from the world. Quite the opposite. It is precisely a state that is confident in its democratic and strategic choices that can engage and cooperate with greater confidence with countries that have different histories, different interests and different political perspectives.

The world does not need yet another division into permanent camps. It needs competition with limits and rules that all must respect. Alliances that take responsibility. And international institutions that remain a space for dialogue precisely when dialogue is most difficult.

That is why the United Nations matter.

Not because they can resolve every conflict. Clearly, they cannot. Not because every resolution is given effect. Clearly, that is not always the case.

And that should not discourage us; it should strengthen our determination to protect these United Nations and the rules upon which they are founded, and to stand for multilateralism grounded in values, mutual respect and rules.

Because a world without a place where all states, regardless of their size, can sit under the same roof and invoke the same principles would be even more dangerous than the world we see today.

In 1954, Dag Hammarskjöld reminded us of a thought: The United Nations were not created to take us to heaven, but to save us from hell.

Seven decades later, it is worth understanding the essence of that statement. We should not demand perfection from the United Nations. We should demand relevance.

The capacity to prevent and to mediate. The capacity to protect human dignity. And, ultimately, the capacity to uphold principles even when applying them is politically inconvenient.

Today, trust in the international system is being jeopardized precisely because too many people have a justified sense that the rules do not apply equally. That power sometimes takes precedence over principle. That commitments are conditional.

That agreements last only as long as interests remain unchanged.

For small sized states, this is an especially dangerous world.

Our own history has taught us that international compromises are very difficult, and that peace, stability and integration require political courage and hard sacrifices.

And without wishing to sound patronising, if anyone wants to see an example of a country that has repeatedly given up something that naturally belongs to it as a fundamental right—something that many take for granted—all they need is to look at the recent history of my country.

A history marked by challenges, by security risks of regional proportions, by constant compromises and concessions made in the name of peace and cooperation and the higher goals of integration—often at the expense of our most basic understanding of dignity and justice.

We have taken truly difficult decisions. We have continued forward even when processes lasted longer than one generation of citizens could reasonably have expected.

But precisely for that reason, with the benefit of distance from those decisions and with a clear awareness of reality, I can responsibly say today that trust cannot be a one-way obligation indefinitely.

If small sized states are expected to comply with the rules, then the rules must also provide them with predictability. If candidates for membership in an organization are required to meet certain criteria, then meeting those criteria must lead to progress. If we ask citizens to trust institutions, then institutions must demonstrate that their word has value and that their commitments endure.

The rule that applies today cannot be different tomorrow simply because the balance of power has changed. And a commitment undertaken cannot be a temporary political convenience. It must be a foundation on which people can plan their future.

We ask our citizens to believe in cooperation, in good neighbourly relations, in compromise, and in mutual respect.

We tell them that lasting peace is worth more than a short-term political victory; that respecting agreements is a sign of strength and wisdom, and that it is the right thing to do, not a sign of weakness; that European and Euro-Atlantic integration means accepting rules that apply equally to all.

But that argument becomes much harder to sustain when citizens see that, in international relations, principle sometimes gives way to power; that criteria can change while the process is already under way; or that some are expected to demonstrate consistency that others do not always demand of themselves.

We cannot tell people, “Trust the rules,” when they can see that the rules do not apply equally. We cannot convince them that compromise is a virtue, if every compromise produces a new demand. And we cannot expect trust in international institutions if citizens come to believe that their fate is created more often by the political weight of their state than by the strength of an agreed principle.

This is a question of legitimacy.

Because our authority as elected leaders does not derive from the office itself. It derives from the people who elect us, who hold us to account, and who every day compare what we tell them with what they see.

And today, they see more than ever before.

We live in an age in which information travels around the world in seconds. Never before has humanity had access to so much knowledge. But never before has it been exposed to so much manipulation, half-truths, fabricated images, propaganda and organized disinformation.

That is precisely why politics is entering a new, more difficult and more complex era.

Our task is no longer simply to inform our citizens. We must earn their trust.

It is not enough to tell them what is true. We must build institutions they can trust when the truth is uncomfortable for everyone. It is not enough to speak to them about values. We must show that those values have meaning and carry a cost—even when defending them requires patience, political capital, or choosing the more difficult path.

We are called upon to convince our societies that cooperation is better than isolation, that the rule of law is better than unilateral behavior, that compromise is better than conflict, and that institutions are better than the rule of sheer force.

But for that conviction to carry weight, we ourselves must be consistent.

Values are not sustained by speeches. They are sustained when they are upheld precisely at the moment when it is easiest to abandon them.

And this may be the greatest challenge of our time.

The world is changing at extraordinary speed. The centres of power are shifting.

Technology is changing. Economic relations are changing. Security doctrines are changing. Alliances are changing. History is accelerating once again.

In such periods, there is always a temptation to declare that old principles are no longer practical; that the law must adapt to power; that values are a luxury that can wait until the crisis has passed.

But that is precisely when we need them most.

Because if, in times of change, we abandon the rules that protected us in times of stability, we will not gain greater freedom. We will inherit a world in which every subsequent decision depends on who has more power at that particular moment.

And such a world is especially dangerous for small sized states.

That is why our duty as leaders is not to promise our people a world without injustice, without disappointment, and without conflicting interests. Such a world does not exist.

Our duty is far more demanding.

To preserve faith in the rules even when it is clear that the rules are being broken.

To defend cooperation even when confrontation appears more popular. To sustain trust in institutions not by asking people to look less closely and ask fewer questions, but by making institutions more worthy of their trust.

And not to allow disappointment with the imperfections of the international order to lead us towards something far worse: a world in which there is no order at all.

That, in my view, is one of the greatest political and moral responsibilities of our generation.

It applies to the international system. And it applies to Europe.

We will not abandon the European idea because the European path has been difficult. The European Union remains, for us, our natural political, economic and institutional home.

And we have work to do at home. We must strengthen the rule of law. Build more effective institutions. Build a more competitive economy. And strengthen our citizens ’confidence in their own state.

That is our responsibility, and we will not shift it to Brussels.

At the same time, we expect European integration to remain a merit based-process based on measurable criteria—not a process in which bilateral issues can continually move the goalposts.

We are not asking for an easier path. We are asking for a path governed by rules.

We are not asking for lower standards. We are asking for standards to remain standards.

This is equally important for Europe’s credibility at a time when its geopolitical weight will increasingly depend on its ability to translate its commitments into tangible political outcomes, and on its resolve to uphold the values it espouses and to remain steadfast in advancing them, despite the many challenges it faces.

Excellencies,

The future international order will not be shaped only on battlefields or in diplomatic halls. It will also be shaped in laboratories. In schools. In factories. In energy grids. In data centres. And in the ability of societies to make sense of the changes that technology is bringing.

Artificial intelligence is no longer a subject of the future. It is infrastructure for the present.

Today, the world is once again recognizing the value of resilience. Of reliable energy.

Of infrastructure. Of diversified transport routes. Of nearby and trusted supply chains.

For us, the intensive development of Corridors VIII and X is part of a broader European vision: to better connect the Adriatic, the Black Sea, the Aegean and Central Europe; to provide goods, energy and people with more routes and greater connectivity; and to ensure that the region becomes interconnected in infrastructure rather than remaining on the geopolitical periphery.

Our geography does not have to be our destiny. It can become our advantage if we build the institutions and infrastructure that transform our geographical position into connectivity.

At the same time, we must also approach migration differently.

Migration begins where there is no security, no employment, no education, no access to water, no prospects, or no confidence that tomorrow will be better than today. It is not simply a matter of borders. Responsible policy must bring together security, human dignity, development and the real needs of labour markets.

Climate policy, too, will have to become more grounded in reality.

The green transition is essential. But if we make it socially unsustainable, we will lose the political support that is necessary to implement it. If we make it technologically dependent on a handful of sources, we will create new challenges while addressing old ones. If we expect poorer countries to move at the same pace without providing them with equal access to capital and technology, we will create injustice instead of a transition.

That is why future climate policy must, at the same time, be environmental policy, economic policy and social policy.

Mr. President,

All of this brings us back to the central theme of this session: trust.

Trust is not a sentiment that can be created by adopting a resolution. It is an outcome. It is built when an institution delivers on the purpose for which it was established.

That is why reform of the United Nations is necessary. So that the Organization can become more capable. So that it can deliver greater results. And certainly not to replace the responsibility of national states. But to act where collective action is needed.

Multilateralism does not begin in New York. It begins with the quality of the states that come to New York.

Excellencies,

We are a small sized country. But we refuse to let the smallness of our territory define the scale of our ambition.

Our ambition is to become a serious state. A state that its allies can trust. A state in which young people can plan their future. A state that respects the diversity and multicultural character of its society. A state confident enough to defend its own identity without denying the identity of others. A state that knows its history but is not imprisoned by it. And a state that does not expect others to build it in its place.

That, to me, is modern sovereignty. Not isolation. Capability.

This year, Secretary-General António Guterres reminded us that the Charter begins with the words: “We, the peoples.” And he added: “Not we, the powerful. Not we, the victors.”

In those few words lies the reason why a small sized European country continues to believe in this Organization, even when it is disappointed by it.

Because the alternative to a world governed by rules is not a world in which everyone is free. It is a world in which the strongest are the freest. And everyone else depends on their goodwill.

Such a world may appear effective for a moment. But it is never stable.

Some three decades ago, the United Nations came to our country with a new idea: that the international community does not have to wait for violence to begin before it acts.

Today, we once again need that same political wisdom.

We must not wait for technology to create new inequalities before we establish rules. We must not wait for young people to leave before we build societies in which they see a future worth staying for. We must not wait for institutions to lose all public trust before we reform them. And we must not wait for the world to become fully divided into opposing blocs before we rediscover the value of dialogue.

That child with whom I began will be fourteen years older when the world enters 2040.

None of us today can promise that child a peaceful world. Nor a world without crises. Nor a world without competition.

But we can leave that child something else.

A world in which power is not the only argument. A world in which knowledge is not the privilege of the few. A world in which alliances create security, rather than new lines of fear. A world in which technology serves humanity. And a world in which a small state has the right to the same dignity, the same rules and the same voice as a great power.

That is the promise worth renewing.

Not because we are naive about the world as it is. But because we are realistic enough to understand what happens when the world is left to power alone.

Macedonians and the Macedonian citizens will share their burden of responsibility.

Thank you.

Mr. President,

Secretary-General of the United Nations,

Excellencies,

Distinguished Delegates,

I stand before this Assembly conscious that I speak on behalf of a nation and a people whose future is being shaped in halls like this one.

I bring warm greetings from the people and Government of Solomon Islands, a nation of nearly one thousand islands stretching across as many miles of the Blue Pacific. Our people hold the same hopes as people in every land: to live in peace, and to raise th eir children in dignity.

Mr. President, I congratulate you on your election and assure you of the full support of Solomon Islands. I also commend your predecessor, Her Excellency Ms. Annalena Baerbock, for her determined leadership of the eightieth session.

I pay special tribute to Secretary -General António Guterres as he takes part in his final General Debate in office. Mr. Secretary General, you have been a true champion of multilateralism and of Small Island Developing States. Your unwavering advocacy on climate action and your repeated visits to our region told the world a simple truth: that the Pacific matters, and that our challenges, and how the world responds to them, remain a litmus test for us all.

We meet at a time when multilateralism is under serious strain, and when the notion that might is right appears to be making a return.

Yet we continue to gather, in forums and dialogues around the world and here in the General Assembly, the pinnacle of mul tilateralism.

That, in itself, is cause for hope.

National Priorities Mr. President,

For my people, what is said in this hall is measured not in declarations but in results: classrooms with teachers and books, clinics with medicines, roads that reach markets, and villages that thrive. That is the lens through which Solomon Islands engages with the world.

My government is delivering a programme of national transformation.

We are providing universal free education, so that no child is turned away from school because their family cannot afford the fees. We are strengthening our health system, with a renewed f ocus on tackling the scourge of non-communicable diseases, eradicating malaria and building a new national referral hospital.

We are prioritizing energy and other transformative infrastructure, expanding roads, ports, airports and telecommunications to connect our scattered islands into one national economy. We are reforming our public finance systems so that every dollar delivers for our people. And we are pursuing constitutional amendments to strengthen our democracy. This is the agenda by which our people will judge my government.

International Peace and Security Mr. President,

Over the past year, the international community has faced many challenges. Protracted armed conflicts, an energy crisis and disruptions to global trade have been compounded by destabilization orchestrated by those who pursue their own selfish ambitions.

For small island economies, these are not distant events. Every rise in the price of fuel is felt in the cost of shipping, electricity, food and essential services, placing a heavy burden on communities that have no buffer against external shocks.

These tensions confirm what Solomon Islands has long understood: peace and security are inseparable from development. Neither can be secured without the other.

There are no winners in war, only graves, orphans and the long labour of rebuilding what conflict has torn down.

There is no substitute for dialogue, diplomacy and peaceful negotiation. Solomon Islands calls on all parties to armed conflicts to protect civilians, return to the negotiating table and act in full respect of international law.

And it is why the world needs a stronger, more agile United Nations, one equipped to respond to the realities of today.

Transnational Crime, Illicit Drugs and Ocean of Peace Mr. President,

The Pacific faces a grave and growing threat. Transnational criminal networks are using our ocean as a highway for illicit drugs, undermining our sovereignty and national security, destroying young lives and tearing at the fabric of our communities. Behind every statistic stands a family, a community, and a young life robbed of its promise.

We will not allow criminal networks to profit from the vulnerability of our people. We are amending our Dangerous Drugs Act to introduce stiffer penalties as a deterrent, and we are strengthening law enforcement to prevent and detect these crimes and to ho ld perpetrators accountable.

In August this year, Solomon Islands acceded to the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, a clear demonstration of our resolve to confront this threat.

These are costly and demanding undertakings, and no Pacific country can win this fight alone. We call for stronger international cooperation, greater information sharing, sustained investment in the capacity of our law enforcement agencies, and support for prevention and rehabilitation.

Our vision of a peaceful and secure Pacific extends beyond transnational crime. As enshrined in the Ocean of Peace Declaration, our region must remain free of nuclear weapons and free from destabilizing external influence.

In keeping with that vision, my government has proposed a treaty that would bind Pacific Island countries and like-minded partners to a firm, shared commitment to keep the Pacific an Ocean of Peace.

Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies Mr. President,

Artificial intelligence and emerging technologies present both unprecedented opportunities and serious risks. They can accelerate sustainable development, transform education and health care, strengthen disaster preparedness, and open new economic pathways for developing countries.

But a widening digital divide threatens to leave developing countries further behind. For my government, digital transformation is not about technology for its own sake; it is about connecting our scattered islands and opening the modern economy to every Solomon Islander. The completion of 161 telecommunication towers across the country will lift national broadband coverage from 56 to 86 per cent, expanding access to information, education and digital financial services.

The benefits of AI must be shared by all, not concentrated among a few. Its risks, including its use for non -peaceful purposes, must be governed by all, not left to a few. Solomon Islands therefore recognizes the need for an inclusive and transparent inter national governance framework on AI.

Climate Change Mr. President,

Year after year, Pacific leaders have stood at this podium and urged the world to act on climate change. And yet global action continues to fall short of what the science demands.

With every passing COP, the impacts grow more severe. Our islands are being lost to the sea. Disasters are more frequent and more devastating. Food and water security is under threat, and communities are being forced from their ancestral lands.

Solomon Islands knows this reality first -hand. This year, Tropical Cyclone Maila, a Category 5 storm, tore through our communities, destroying homes, schools, infrastructure and livelihoods. My government has just approved US$9.38 million for shelter recovery.

That is money our essential services urgently need, now diverted to deal with the impacts of this climate extreme.

Like many Pacific Island countries, we are trapped in a relentless cycle of response, recovery and rebuilding.

This is not sustainable, nor is it just. My people did the least to cause this crisis, yet they pay its earliest and heaviest price. That is the moral ledger that lies before this Assembly.

Last year, the International Court of Justice confirmed in its landmark advisory opinion that States have legal obligations to protect the climate system.

Major emitters must make deep emission cuts and transition away from fossil fuels. Climate finance, including support for loss and damage, must be grant -based and channelled through our national budget systems. Project -based financing of climate action is unsustainable and out of step with the scale of a crisis we did least to cause.

Vulnerable countries should not have to choose between climate action and educating their children, caring for the sick or securing food and water. Yet that is the choice we face with every dollar we spend. We therefore call for the full capitalization of the Pacific Resilience Facility and an ambitious and timely third replenishment of the Green Climate Fund.

Our region has long led on climate action, and we will continue to lead. The Pre-COP31 meeting, to be hosted in the Pacific by Australia in partnership with Fiji and Tuvalu, will bring the reality of climate change directly into the heart of the global process. I call on all Parties and partners to come to that meeting, and to COP31, with stronger commitments and concrete action. The communities on the frontline of the climate crisis deserve nothing less.

Sea-Level Rise Solomon Islands welcomes the convening of the Second High -Level Meeting on Sea -Level Rise and the adoption of the first political declaration on sea-level rise.

Every day, our people are defending their coastlines, strengthening their resilience, protecting their food and water security and their cultural heritage, and, where there is no other choice, relocating.

But we cannot do this alone.

I call on this Assembly to match the courage of our Pacific communities with collective international resolve: to scale up adaptation and resilience finance and to support communities facing climate mobility needs.

Solomon Islands reaffirms that maritime boundaries, once established and deposited in accordance with UNCLOS, together with the rights and entitlements that flow from them, shall continue to apply notwithstanding any physical changes caused by climate change-related sea-level rise.

Ocean The ocean is not simply a resource; it is our identity, our heritage and our future. It sustains our livelihoods, our culture and our economy. We do not own the ocean; we belong to it. We hold it in solemn trust for generations not yet born.

Yet our ability to benefit fully from our own ocean is undermined by illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, which costs our region US$300 million every year. Solomon Islands is fighting back, working with the Forum Fisheries Agency and partners inclu ding Australia,

France, New Zealand and the United States to strengthen surveillance and enforcement across our waters.

Mr. President,

SDG 14 remains among the least funded of all the Sustainable Development Goals. With just four years left until 2030, the fourth United Nations Ocean Conference must raise the bar on ocean finance and secure the ocean's place in the development agenda beyond 2030.

Solomon Islands welcomes the entry into force of the BBNJ Agreement and the preparations for the first Conference of the Parties in January. We look to that Conference to establish, without delay, the Secretariat and the institutional arrangements to implement the Agreement.

Plastic pollution is poisoning our ocean and our food. As negotiations resume in Bangkok, Solomon Islands calls for an ambitious, legally binding treaty that addresses the full life cycle of plastics, from production to disposal.

Youth, Women and Persons with Disabilities Mr. President,

Our people are our greatest asset. With more than half of our population under the age of 25, my government is prioritizing legal frameworks that empower young people, advance gender equality, and strengthen the protection of women and children against domestic violence.

We welcome global progress in advancing the rights and full participation of women and persons with disabilities in the economy, and Solomon Islands is committed to accelerating that progress at home.

There can be no sustainable development without equal opportunity for all.

International and Domestic Cooperation Our development partnerships play an indispensable role in expanding infrastructure, maritime connectivity, health and education, and in improving the lives of Solomon Islanders. I thank the Governments and people of Australia, China, Japan, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea and the United States, as well as the European Union, for their contributions to our national development.

South-South cooperation remains an important complement to Official Development Assistance. Partnerships among developing countries have enabled us to share expertise, technology, innovation and practical solutions suited to our circumstances. The support of Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, India and our Pacific family embodies the true spirit of South-South solidarity, and we value it deeply.

We also acknowledge the partnership of multilateral organizations, non-governmental organizations and our private sector in supporting development work in Solomon Islands.

At home, my government is working hand in hand with our churches to build stronger and more inclusive communities.

Cooperation and partnership, at every level and across borders, are critical to nation building, and my government remains fully committed to them.

Financing for Development As a Small Island Developing State, our vulnerability remains a fundamental reality. A single natural disaster can erase years of investment and progress and push a nation backwards.

The Multidimensional Vulnerability Index captures the special circumstances of SIDS in a way that income measures alone cannot.

We call on international financial institutions to integrate the MVI into their financing decisions for SIDS without further delay.

Mr. President,

Last year, the world spent more than US$2.9 trillion on its militaries.

That is more than sixteen times all official development assistance.

In less than 18 days, the world spends more on arms than developed countries provide in a full year of climate finance.

In the same year that military spending reached its highest share of global output since 2009, development aid had its steepest fall on record. Bilateral aid to the least developed countries fell by a quarter.

This imbalance must be corrected. Redirecting even a small share of this spending would fully capitalize the Pacific Resilience Facility and the Loss and Damage Fund, secure the Green Climate Fund's third replenishment, and meet the ODA targets. The resources exist. What is missing is the will. The time to act is now.

LDC Graduation Solomon Islands is due to graduate from Least Developed Country status in 2027.

As part of our preparations, my government is pursuing an ambitious and proactive agenda that uses public-private partnerships to unlock investment in transformative projects, special economic zones and key sectors. A second tuna cannery at Bina Harbour, u pgraded airports, agricultural treatment facilities to support trade, and expanded road networks and maritime ports will shift the trajectory of our economy.

At the same time, my government is strengthening our financial institutions and frameworks to improve revenue collection and accountability, so that we can sustain our development priorities.

These reforms reflect our commitment to a strong and resilient economy that delivers decentralized, people -centred development across the country.

Our ambition is clear: to graduate from LDC status with confidence, to strengthen the foundations of our economy, and to ensure that development delivers lasting opportunities for every Solomon Islander.

UN Reform Mr. President,

As the United Nations marks its eighty -first anniversary, it must continue to evolve to meet today's challenges while remaining faithful to its founding principles. The UN80 reform process must strengthen the Organization's effectiveness and relevance with out diminishing its presence, services or support in the most vulnerable regions, where assistance is needed most. Reform must enhance delivery, not reduce it.

The United Nations is not perfect, but it remains the cornerstone of multilateral diplomacy and the indispensable platform through which nations preserve peace, advance sustainable development, uphold international law and protect human rights.

Solomon Islands looks to the next Secretary -General to lead with vision and to ensure that the Secretariat is accountable to all Member States, serving the interests of small and large States on an equal footing.

Security Council Reform Solomon Islands reiterates its support for comprehensive reform of the Security Council to make it more representative, transparent, accountable and reflective of today's realities. A Council with a dedicated seat for Small Island Developing States would s trengthen the legitimacy and effectiveness of the entire multilateral system.

The veto is a relic of 1945. Too often, it has been used to shield violations of international law and to entrench the double standards that fuel conflict. At a minimum, the veto must never again be used in situations of genocide, crimes against humanity or war crimes.

Ultimately, it should be abolished.

Peacekeeping Mr. President,

It is with great pride that Solomon Islands is once again contributing personnel to United Nations peacekeeping in South Sudan. Despite our small size, our participation reaffirms our enduring commitment to the Charter, to international peace and security, and to the noble work of peacekeepers serving communities affected by conflict.

I thank our partners, including Australia and the United Nations Police, for their support. Solomon Islands looks forward to increasing its peacekeeping contribution in the coming year.

Decolonization Mr. President,

Leaving no one behind demands that we complete the unfinished work of decolonization. Solomon Islands reaffirms its longstanding support for the right to self-determination of the Kanak people of New Caledonia and the Maohi nui people of French Polynesia. The United Nations decolonization process must offer more than hope; it must provide practical pathways to the full emancipation of peoples in Non-Self-Governing Territories, and to their freedom to determine their own political future and development aspirations.

In the same spirit, I turn to West Papua, whose people are our Melanesian brothers and sisters.

Solomon Islands respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Indonesia, and we value our friendship with its Government and people. It is precisely because of that friendship that we speak with candour. Reports of human rights viol ations in West Papua have persisted for far too long. They must be independently verified, not left in dispute.

We therefore renew the call of Pacific Islands Forum Leaders for the Government of Indonesia to facilitate, without further delay, the longawaited visit of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights to West Papua. Such a visit is an act of conf idence between friends, and an affirmation that there is nothing to fear from the light.

Closing Mr. President, in closing, the challenges of our time demand renewed solidarity, stronger multilateralism and genuine commitment to the principles of the UN Charter. But institutions do not have hearts; people do. Charters do not keep the peace; the men and women who honour them do. Beyond every declaration and commitment, each of us carries a profound responsibility: to be agents of peace, champions of goodwill, and keepers of the fragile bonds of friendship among nations. The world has never needed that s pirit more than it does today.

Mr. President, permit me a word from the Christian faith that has shaped my people. Our Constitution was established "under the guiding hand of God," by a people "conscious of our common destiny." We believe that is true not only of Solomon Islands, but of this whole family of nations.

We live in a time when division has become the calling card of the day. Nations are sorted into camps. Neighbours are asked to choose sides. Small States are too often treated as prizes to be won rather than partners to be heard. But the destiny of nations does not finally rest in this general assembly, nor in any capital, however powerful.

King Solomon, among the wisest rulers of antiquity, wrote: "There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless, the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand."

That truth does not make us passive. It makes us humble, and it makes us accountable. So I call on my fellow leaders to do three things.

First, let us ask for wisdom before we ask for advantage. When Solomon was offered anything he wished, he did not ask for riches, or long life, or the defeat of his enemies. He asked for "an understanding heart," so that he might judge his people well. I c an think of no better prayer for every leader in this room.

Second, let us stay at the table. The same king taught that "in the multitude of counsellors there is safety." That is the oldest case I know for what this Organization is meant to be: many nations, large and small, sitting together, because none of us sees far enough alone.

Third, let us measure greatness rightly. "Righteousness exalteth a nation." Not its arsenal, not its alliances, but its justice: how it treats the poor, the displaced, and the small.

Nations rise and nations fall. The purposes of God endure. Let us choose cooperation over division, dialogue over confrontation, peace over hostility, and action over inaction. And let us lead as people who know we will answer for it one day.

Our national motto teaches us that “to lead is to serve”. In that spirit of service, Solomon Islands stands ready to do its part, as a willing partner and a committed Member of this Assembly.

May God bless you all, and may God bless our shared family of nations.

I thank you.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished Delegates,

In 1979, thirty -four (34) years after the creation of this United Nations, my country, Saint Lucia, though small in geography, but large in courage, dignity and conviction, took its seat among the community of nations brimming with hope, optimism and trust in the promise and goals of this body.

Today we meet at a moment of profound international uncertainty. Conflict is spreading, trust is eroding, development gains are being reversed, and the rules intended to protect humanity are too often applied selectively.

For small island developing states, these crises are not abstract. They are lived realities.

Climate change threatens our homes, livelihoods, and very existence. Debt limits our ability to invest in people. Digital technologies are transforming our societi es, but without safeguards, they can reproduce old patterns of domination in a new form. And in our own Caribbean neighbourhood, the people of Haiti continue to endure a humanitarian and security catastrophe that demands more than statements of concern.

The theme before us, “ Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all,” must not remain a slogan. Trust will be restored only when promises are matched by action, when commitments are honoured, and when the United Nations delivers meaningful results for every nation, and when there is due regard for multilateral principles not only for the most powerful, but also for the weakest of us as well.

This Assembly should not be a place where the world expresses sympathy without accepting responsibility.

We need action. We need justice. And we need a renewed international compact based not on power, but on principle; we need multilateralism, not unilateralism. In the words of a former UN Secretary General, “The United Nations was not created in order to bring us to heaven, but in order to save us from hell.”

Climate Change and Climate Finance For Saint Lucia, climate change is not a distant environmental issue. It is a direct threat to national security, economic stability, food and water security, and human survival.

Whilst the world focuses on headline -grabbing events like monster hurricanes, melting glaciers and tidal waves, climate change is affecting Saint Lucia daily in small but significant ways, such as the unusual bouts of drought in the rainy season, unprecede nted floods in the dry season, and the stifling of our beaches and coastlines by sargassum.

Our people contribute little to global emissions, yet these events constantly set back our people’s development and livelihoods and demand that we find the resources to reverse the damage.

Saint Lucia calls for climate finance that matches the scale of the crisis: expanded grants and concessional funding, faster and simpler access, full support for loss and damage, meaningful debt relief, and financing that reaches vulnerable communities directly.

Eligibility for finance must reflect not only income, but climate vulnerability.

Climate finance is not charity. It is about justice, responsibility, and survival.

We must stop confusing loans with solidarity. A loan is not justice when a small vulnerable nation is forced to borrow to repair damage it did not cause.

A United Nations that delivers for all must deliver for those on the front lines of climate change through accessible finance, concrete support and measurable results, not merely through declarations.

International Crises Saint Lucia laments the continued conflicts and human suffering across the globe, including Ukraine, Sudan and the wider Middle East, including Gaza, and calls for renewed efforts towards peace, stability and respect for international law.

In accordance with their right to self -determination and UN resolutions, in particular Resolution 3236 of 1974, the People of Palestine should be allowed their own State and full membership of the UN, alongside the state of Israel.

Haiti: Responsibility to a Sister Nation We also speak today about Haiti.

Member states of this organisation must act in a manner that will restore the trust of the people of Haiti in the United Nations. Some member states have failed to meet their commitments and pledges to the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti, whose one-year mandate ends this month.

The Security Council is urged to renew the Force's mandate, and member states to provide the necessary resources to operate effectively and successfully.

While gang violence is the main factor to be resolved in Haiti, the crisis in this country is multidimensional. The international response must include long -term social and economic assistance that will help restore an acceptable quality of life for the people of Haiti.

That is why the Caribbean Community has been actively engaged in Haiti, a Caribbean Community member state, to assist with a solution to the political and governance dimensions of the crisis. Through its Eminent Persons Group, comprising three former Prime Ministers, it will continue to facilitate dialogue amongst Haiti’s political and civil society stakeholders as they work towards holding the first round of General Elections this year.

Trust in the United Nations will be restored if the daily lives of the people of Haiti are transformed and enhanced.

CUBA It is in a similar quest for trust and transformation that Saint Lucia believes there should be dialogue and the removal of all obstacles that hinder the true development of the people of Cuba.

Cuba has long been celebrated for its continued contribution to health, education and development across our region and beyond. Saint Lucia stands with the Cuban people in their hope for a better future, supported by the friendship and solidarity of the in ternational community.

Republic of China (Taiwan) In the same spirit of transformation and consistent with our commitment to the right of all people to self -determination, Saint Lucia supports Taiwan ’s full membership in the United Nations.

Reform of the Security Council Saint Lucia believes that a truly inclusive United Nations must ensure that its decision-making bodies reflect the world that they serve.

Saint Lucia advocates for a comprehensive reform of the Security Council to enhance its legitimacy and effectiveness in addressing contemporary global challenges, thereby restoring trust and a more inclusive multilateral system.

Mr. President A 21st -century United Nations Security Council could have been more successful in its responsibility for international peace and security had it not been anchored in the world of 1945.

The prolonged reform process must be concluded quickly to include expanded permanent and non-permanent membership for Africa, the Asia -Pacific, and Latin America and the Caribbean regions. This reform is essential to restore trust in the United Nations and ensure it delivers peace and security for all. Saint Lucia pledges its commitment and dedication to work with like-minded nations to achieve the stated reforms.

Secretary General I wish to take this opportunity to thank the outgoing Secretary General, Antonio Guterres, for his sterling service, especially his steadfast solidarity with the Caribbean through the many challenges and disasters our region has faced. We commend him for h is sincere and positive leadership of this organisation. Saint Lucia wishes to express its endorsement of the candidate of the Republic of Guyana, Ms. Caroline Rodrigues-Birkett, for the post of Secretary General.

Her distinguished record of public and international service speaks directly to the kind of leadership this moment demands.

Reparations and Historical Justice Mr. President,

On the 25 th of March, 2026, the General Assembly approved one of its most historic and consequential resolutions that declared the trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as the greatest crime against humanity. This resolution and the subsequent establishment of the High Level Global Advisory Council on Reparatory Justice is a very significant step in the search for reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and the enslavement of Africans in the Americas and the Caribbean.

I want to thank the President of Ghana for spearheading and championing the resolution.

Saint Lucia congratulates the Government of Jamaica on its successful petition to the British monarch for him to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council over the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica.

Mr. President,

Reparations are not about vengeance. They are about truth, acknowledgement, repair and transformation.

Reparations are not about seeking charity or revisiting history for its own sake. History is not behind us when its consequences remain embedded in wealth, power, institutions and opportunity.

Reparations are about addressing the continuing effects of slavery and colonial exploitation, restoring dignity, advancing development and building more equitable relationships with the states and institutions that benefited from these systems.

Digital Colonisation and Digital Sovereignty Digital technology is a new form of power that is rapidly transforming the world, and while it offers enormous opportunities for mankind, it can also create a new hierarchy in which a small number of corporations and powerful states control the systems on which the rest of humanity depends.

We must ensure that artificial intelligence does not widen the gap between the powerful and the vulnerable. Technology must strengthen aspirations, not quietly erode them.

Saint Lucia therefore calls for strong global standards on data protection, privacy and artificial intelligence; equitable access to digital infrastructure, cybersecurity and affordable connectivity; fair technology transfer; transparent algorithms; protec tion from surveillance, disinformation and cyber exploitation; and meaningful participation by small states in shaping global digital rules.

The digital future must not be owned by a few. It must be governed for the benefit of all.

Managing transformation means ensuring that no nation is left powerless in the face of technological change.

A United Nations That Delivers for All Mr. President, my country, Saint Lucia, is small, open, and vulnerable, but our people refuse to impose limits on their aspirations. History has blessed us with unimaginable natural beauty, ambitious, friendly people, and two Nobel Laureates. However, an unfair international financial system threatens the very existence of small island states like Saint Lucia. The rules governing global finance affect our development, and our attempt at economic diversification is hindered by unfair and unequally applied rules.

Oceans of water separate us from the global powers, but our challenges are mainly connected to decisions made in their capitals. Emissions released from these countries affect our climate.

Weapons and drugs trafficked through international networks instiga te violence and gang warfare in our region.

Lack of access to affordable technology slows our development. Mr. President, Saint Lucia refuses to give up. We are educating our people to ensure that their skills are relevant. We are modernising agriculture to ensure our food security. We are dealing with the scarcity of water due to climate change by exploring new sources of groundwater supply and encouraging the harvesting of rainwater. We are reducing youth unemployment through the creation of the successful Youth Economy Agency. We are encouraging t he spirit of entrepreneurship by supporting small and micro enterprises, especially women -owned businesses. We are promoting healthy lifestyles and universal healthcare for the provision of equitable, accessible and affordable healthcare for our citizens.

Mr President, Saint Lucia continues to insist that governance must be about the improvement of the lives of the people. We have maintained fiscal discipline, reduced unemployment as we continue to create new opportunities and an enabling environment for in vestment in tourism and other productive sectors.

Saint Lucia believes that a better world is within our reach if we choose cooperation over coercion and ensure that justice and fairness prevail for all.

The 81st Session of the UN General Assembly must be remembered for turning its laudable theme into actionable commitments and those commitments into meaningful change. As Mahatma Gandhi says, “In a gentle way you can shape the world.”

The people of Saint Lucia remain confident in our collective capacity to shape that better world, even as Saint Lucian Nobel Laureate, Sir Derek Walcott reminds us that “the future happens no matter how much we scream.”

Our task is to meet that future with courage and purpose. Our other Nobel Laureate Sir Arthur Lewis said, “Economic development requires taking risks and embracing change.” And with the speed of Julien Alfred, let us embrace that responsibility together and act with the resolve this moment demands.

I thank you.

Mr. President, Dear representatives of the Peoples of the United Nations,

Gunpowder changed the battlefield. Nuclear fission changed the meaning of human survival.

Artificial intelligence is changing something even more intimate: who can enter the mind of a citizen, imitate a trusted voice, manufacture a reality calibrated to one person’s fears, and do so millions of times at once.

Albania is not a developer of frontier models.

But we are a nation that has already lived the future others are still debating.

And I have come here with a simple message:

The greatest immediate danger is not that artificial intelligence will stop obeying humanity.

The greatest danger is that it will obey the wrong human beings perfectly.

The challenge comes in three layers: what artificial intelligence does instead of us, what it does to us, and who gains the power to reach us.

First, what it does instead of us. The public debate imagines machines that awaken, acquire ambitions and turn against their creators.

But the systems confronting us today do not wake up with hatred in their hearts.

They multiply ours.

They have no ambition of their own.

They serve the ambitions of others.

They carry no flag. But they can be deployed by a state.

They tell no lie for their own benefit. But they can tell a billion lies on our behalf.

The machine has no conscience, but it can borrow the reach of a government, the precision of a weapon and the intimacy of a friend.

At the same time, the economic incentives surrounding artificial intelligence increasingly reward the replacement of human effort, rather than the enlargement of human capacity.

Write the code so that I do not have to understand it.

Draft the report so that I do not have to think through it.

Make the judgment so that I do not have to assume responsibility for it.

When success is measured only by how much work the machine removes from the human being, we may create more efficient institutions but less capable people.

A civilisation that outsources effort may eventually outsource knowledge.

A civilisation that outsources knowledge may eventually outsource judgment.

And a civilisation that outsources judgment will discover that it has also outsourced responsibility.

This is not inevitable. It is a choice. We can build artificial intelligence that teaches rather than merely answers, guides rather than commands, and strengthens the human being instead of making the human being dependent upon it.

The question cannot be only: How quickly did the machine complete the task?

We must also ask: What did the human being learn?

Who understood the decision?

Who can challenge it?

And who answers when it is wrong?

Albania became the first country to bring an artificial intelligence instrument into the architecture of government through Diella, our artificial intelligence minister.

We did not do this to transfer sovereignty from people to a machine.

We did it to make public services more accessible, procedures more transparent and the state more accountable.

No machine possesses democratic legitimacy.

No algorithm inherits constitutional responsibility.

Behind every consequential public decision there must remain a legal mandate, a human institution and a name that can be called to answer.

The second layer is what artificial intelligence can do to us.

Artificial intelligence inside an accountable state can reduce the distance between citizens and public services.

Artificial intelligence outside accountability can eliminate the distance between a lie and the human mind.

Albania experienced this directly.

A fabricated narrative of an Israeli invasion of the Albanian coast, an invasion that had never occurred, was manufactured, personalised and delivered through voices, pages and channels citizens already trusted.

One citizen received a story of national betrayal.

Another received a story of religious provocation.

Another received a conspiracy of foreign occupation.

Different fabrications entered different emotional worlds, all serving the same strategic lie.

The consequences were real. Citizens protested against a phantom enemy.

Antisemitic tropes entered our public discourse.

Fear became anger, anger became mobilisation, and fabrication became political reality.

This was not a laboratory experiment. It was not science fiction.

It was a Tuesday in Tirana. The algorithm did not invent the objective.

A human actor did.

The algorithm did not develop hatred. It discovered how to activate ours.

This is systematic fraud as a service. Election interference no longer requires one television station or one piece of propaganda repeated to an entire population.

It can now operate at the resolution of one voter.

Two neighbours may stand in the same street, vote in the same election and inhabit entirely different realities, each manufactured specifically for them.

When that happens, democracy does not merely lose a debate.

It loses the common ground on which debate is possible.

Sovereignty no longer erodes only at the border.

It erodes in the feed.

In the twentieth century, sovereignty meant control over land, territorial waters and national airspace.

In the twenty first century, it must also mean the capacity of a free society to defend the conditions under which its citizens form their own judgments.

And then comes the third layer: reach. For centuries, the great threat to freedom of speech was censorship.

Today, freedom of speech is also threatened by the weaponisation of freedom of reach.

Speech is the right to express an idea. Reach is the power to place that idea before millions of people.

Speech belongs to human beings. Reach can be purchased, automated, manipulated and secretly assigned by platforms, corporations, criminal networks and foreign states.

The right to speak is universal. But there is no universal right to anonymous, unlimited and artificially amplified reach.

When one lie can be multiplied a billion times, truth does not need to be censored.

It can simply be buried.

The citizen remains formally free to speak, but speaks into a storm that no human voice can match.

Freedom of speech can therefore be defeated without banning a single book, imprisoning a single journalist or deleting a single post.

The answer to bad speech remains more speech.

But the answer to covert, industrial amplification must be exposure.

Who created the message? Who paid for it? Was it spread by people or machines? Why was this citizen targeted?

Was the apparent public reaction authentic, coordinated or foreign-directed?

Defending democracy does not mean controlling what people are allowed to think.

It means revealing the hidden powers seeking to control what people are made to see.

If we protect freedom of speech while leaving the control of reach completely opaque, we defend the door while surrendering the room.

Some respond by demanding that artificial intelligence be slowed or stopped.

Albania respectfully disagrees. A pause by democracies will not produce a pause by dictatorships.

A moratorium observed by responsible states will not restrain hostile powers, criminal networks or industries of manipulation.

We cannot regulate ourselves into helplessness.

On this essential strategic question,

President Donald Trump is right: we cannot stop.

We must accelerate.

But acceleration must have a direction. We need artificial intelligence that is verifiable, transparent and accountable, built by free societies, shared among allies and placed in the service of citizens.

The answer to weaponised automation is not technological surrender.

It is democratic capacity. It is sovereign capability. It is better artificial intelligence in the hands of those who remain accountable under law.

Sovereign artificial intelligence does not mean isolation.

It means that no nation should be helpless before systems it cannot understand, inspect or challenge.

Every country must be able to protect its language, authenticate public communications, detect coordinated manipulation, preserve evidence and inform its citizens without depending entirely on the commercial priorities of a distant corporation.

This is why Albania is building an artificial intelligence based digital Mirror.

The Mirror will identify manipulation in real time, test claims against authoritative information, reveal coordinated patterns and help citizens understand not only what they are seeing, but also how and why it reached them.

It will not tell citizens what they must think.

Truth cannot be decreed by a government.

It must be evidenced, sourced, tested, challenged and defended in the open.

The Mirror is not intended to become an arbiter of opinion.

It is intended to become an infrastructure of transparency.

It does not seek to create a ministry of truth.

It seeks to defend society against an industry of lies.

Albania therefore calls for an international compact for sovereign and democratic artificial intelligence.

First, citizens must know when politically consequential content has been artificially generated or materially manipulated.

Second, the architecture of reach must become transparent.

Citizens and states must be able to know who created, financed, targeted and artificially amplified consequential political content.

Third, every consequential use of artificial intelligence by a public institution must preserve a clear chain of human and legal accountability.

Fourth, democracies must create a shared early warning system so that evidence of artificial intelligence driven manipulation can travel between allies as quickly as the manipulation itself.

And smaller nations and smaller languages must not be abandoned outside this protective architecture.

Digital sovereignty cannot become a privilege reserved for the richest states.

Lies travel without visas. Algorithms cross borders without passports.

Those attacking our societies already cooperate across jurisdictions.

Our democracies must learn to do the same.

This is not ultimately a contest between humanity and machines.

It is a contest between different human purposes, each amplified by machines.

Between those who use artificial intelligence to enlighten and those who use it to obscure.

Between those who use it to empower citizens and those who use it to manipulate them.

Between those who accept responsibility and those who hide behind automation.

We should not fear that machines will become too human.

We should fear that human beings will become invisible behind machines.

Excellencies, Every generation is called upon to defend freedom in the territory where freedom is most threatened.

For one generation, that territory was the battlefield.

For another, it was the ballot box. For ours, it will increasingly be the human mind.

Let us ensure that no citizen is left alone before an algorithmic army.

Let us ensure that no small nation is forced to rent its understanding of reality from beyond its borders.

Let us ensure that no democracy wakes up after an election to discover that its people exercised their freedom of choice inside a world secretly designed for them by someone they could not see.

Artificial intelligence will not decide whether this century belongs to liberty or manipulation.

We will.

The machine will obey. The question is whom it will obey, under what law and in the service of what human purpose.

Albania has made its choice. We choose acceleration, but not surrender.

We choose innovation, but not abdication.

We choose augmentation, not the atrophy of human capability.

We choose sovereignty, but not isolation.

We choose freedom of speech. And precisely because we choose it, we refuse to confuse it with the unchecked freedom of machines, money and foreign powers to reach everyone, everywhere, without disclosure.

We choose truth, not because truth is always easy or comfortable, but because without a shared commitment to reality, there can be no shared public life.

And without a shared world, there can be no United Nations.

Thank you.

Mr. President,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,  I am honoured to address this august Assembly, for the fourth time, on behalf of the 240 million, resilient and peace-loving people of Pakistan.

 I congratulate you, Mr. Khalil ur Rahman, on your election as President of the 81st GENERAL Assembly session, and I assure you, of Pakistan’s full support.

 I thank Her Excellency Ms. Annalena Baerbock, for her able stewardship of the 80th session.

 I also convey Pakistan’s sincere appreciation to UN Secretary-General, Mr. Antonio Guterres, for his dynamic leadership and his strong advocacy, for the UN and the Global South.

Mr. President,  The pursuit of peace is among the noblest of human endeavors.

 The Holy Quran commands: “If the enemy is inclined towards peace, make peace with them.”

(Surah-Al-Anfal, Verse 61)  Pakistan’s founding father, Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah, had famously declared: “We stand by the United Nations Charter, and will gladly make our full contribution to the peace and prosperity of the world.”

 These pearls of wisdom have shaped Pakistan’s national ethos and guided our conduct at home and abroad.

 The unanimous adoption of Resolution 2788, on strengthening mechanisms for peaceful settlement of disputes, under Pakistan’s UN Security Council Presidency, demonstrated our unwavering commitment to global peace.

Mr. President,  Unfortunately, In February this year, conflict engulfed the Gulf and the wider Middle East.

 Precious lives were lost.

 Economies suffered.

 Critical maritime routes — particularly the Strait of Hormuz — came under severe pressure.

 At this critical moment, Pakistan chose to act. swiftly!

 Through concerted efforts, Pakistan successfully brought Washington and Tehran under one roof — in Islamabad.

 From the Islamabad Talks to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, many historic steps were taken to bring an end to this conflict.

 I deeply appreciate Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff, whose relentless efforts, helped create, space for diplomacy under exceptionally difficult circumstances.

 Regrettably, recently we have witnessed a dangerous surge of hostilities.

 Yet, amid the roar of missiles, drones and guns,  the voices for diplomacy must echo even louder.

Mr. President  The Strait of Hormuz and Bab-al-Mandeb are arteries of the global economy.

 They must remain open —  connecting nations, not becoming choke-points of confrontation.

 These waters must carry the promise of prosperity —  not the perils of war.

Excellencies,  We once again condemn, in the strongest possible terms, the recent deplorable attacks by the Houthis against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

 The attempted drone attack on the Holy City of Makkah Al-Mukarramah has outraged,

Muslims across the world.

 Any threat to the safety and sanctity of the Haramain Sharifain is a red line that must never be crossed.

 No Muslim can even dare to think of committing such a heinous act.

 Pakistan stands, in complete solidarity with the brotherly people of Saudi Arabia, as we always have throughout our history.

Ladies and Gentlemen,  Our enduring commitment to peace is also reflected by the historic Makkah Joint Defence Agreement among the brotherly countries Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan.

 This Alliance is not directed against any country.

 It is a collective commitment for defence, stability and peace in the region.

SOUTH ASIA Mr. President,  A year ago, Pakistan faced external aggression from India under a false pretext.

 Pakistan exercised, its inherent right of self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter.

 Our brave and valiant Armed Forces, under the courageous leadership of Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, responded, with precision and professionalism,  They silenced the enemy, repulsed its attacks, and taught it a lesson, it shall, never ever, forget.

 Thanks to President Donald Trump’s resolute and visionary leadership, hundreds of millions of lives in South Asia were saved  His timely intervention came at a decisive juncture when two nuclear-armed neighbours stood, at the brink of an all-out war.

 Who knows, the extent of devastation that could have taken place had President Trump, not stepped in at that critical moment?

Mr. President,  We must therefore ensure that South Asia never reaches that precipice again.

 But this requires, a just and fair solution of the Jammu and Kashmir dispute.

 For eight decades, the Kashmiri people have waited for the United Nations to fulfil, its solemn commitment of a free and impartial plebiscite under its auspices.

 Generations have endured illegal occupation, arbitrary detention, extra-judicial killings, enforced disappearances, sexual violence and collective punishment.

 More recently, there have been attempts to alter, the legal status of Jammu and Kashmir, through demographic re-engineering / and other illegal measures.

 Helpless Kashmiri mothers and fathers yearn for their sons and daughters who never return.

 Their homes lie silent —  under curfew and in grief.

 For many, there is no closure —  only a lifetime spent searching for graves that bear no names.

Mr. President,  From this podium, I assure my Kashmiri brothers and sisters, with fullest authority at my command, that we shall continue to extend our full diplomatic, political, and moral support to them till they are granted their inalienable right to self-determination.

 Kashmir has, and always will be, Pakistan’s jugular vein!

INDUS WATERS Mr. President,  Another foundation of stability in South Asia is now under strain.

 The shared waters of the Indus River system are the lifeblood, not only for the people of Pakistan, but for the entire region.

 India’s unilateral decision, to hold the existing Treaty in abeyance has no legal basis whatsoever.

 In fact, both its claims and actions have been rejected by UN experts and, more recently, by the Court of Arbitration.

 Our legitimate stand that the Treaty remains valid, binding, and fully operative- has been vindicated!

 Water must never be weaponized.

 Rivers should nourish nations —  not divide them.

 Therefore, any attempt to stop, impede, or divert Pakistan’s share of the waters will be treated as an act of war.

 India must, make no mistake about it.

PALESTINE Mr. President,  For generations, Palestinians — particularly women, children and the elderly — have been subjected to occupation, eviction, suffering and death.

 Last year, I had shared with you, the heart-wrenching story of Hind Rajab.

 An innocent Palestinian girl who was brutally shot by Israeli soldiers.

 This year, another tragedy weighs heavy on the heart.

 This time, it is the deafening cries of the sobbing mother of eight-year-old Wafaa Akila, who embraced martyrdom in this senseless aggression.

 What should have been the first day of her school,  Alas, became the last day of her life.

Mr. President  Does not a child born in Gaza deserve the same life, and the same future, as a child anywhere else in the world.

 The tragedies of Hind Rajab, Wafaa Akila, and countless others will echo through history —  As an indictment, of our collective silence and inaction!

Excellencies,  It is deeply worrying, that Israeli violence, has now spread to the West Bank, where the forcible eviction of Palestinians, clearly reflects Israel’s genocidal agenda, which continues, unabated.

 Pakistan believes, that the only, just and lasting solution is the creation of an independent, sovereign, viable and contiguous State of Palestine, based on the pre-1967 borders, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital.

 We also condemn continued Israeli aggression against Lebanon and Syria.

 This, too, must stop immediately.

Mr. President,  Terrorism remains one of the gravest threats to international peace and security.

 As a frontline state in combating the menace of terrorism, we have fought terrorists in our own cities, in our own mountains, and along our frontiers.

 Pakistan has sacrificed, almost 100,000 precious lives and suffered, economic losses, exceeding 150 billion dollars.

 The world is safer today thanks to the valuable sacrifices of our valiant Armed Forces, and brave civilians who took on these terrorists.

 The peace-loving world must never forget this reality.

 Afghan territory continues to be exploited, by the TTP, Fitna-al-Khawarij and the BLA,

Fitna-al-Hindustan.

 These foreign-funded groups, operate from sanctuaries inside Afghanistan with the aim of, destabilizing Pakistan.

 All such attacks including incursions from the territory of Afghanistan must come to a grinding halt.

 The Afghan authorities must fulfil their international commitments and take verifiable, decisive action to ensure, that Afghan soil, is never again used against Pakistan or any other country.

 Fundamental rights of the Afghan people — especially women and girls; must be respected.

Mr. President,  United Nations peacekeeping remains, one of the strongest expressions of collective security.

 For decades, Pakistani men and women have served under the blue flag, protecting civilians and helping countries emerge from conflict.

 We are proud of their valuable, sacrifices.

Ladies and Gentlemen,  The alarming rise in Islamophobia is deeply worrying, as Muslims face hate speech, discrimination, attacks on mosques and desecration of the Holy Quran.

 Just across our border, RSS-driven Hind-dut-va ideology, is fanning religious hatred, leading to lynching, communal violence, attacks on places of worship and restrictions, upon religious freedom.

 The demolition of the 150-year-old mosque in Saharanpur, earlier this month is case in point.

 Religious hatred must have no place in this world.

Mr. President,  Pakistan’s economic revival, remains a defining responsibility of my Government and a mission that is very close to my heart.

 Through difficult, and long-overdue, structural reforms, and stringent fiscal discipline.

 we have restored macroeconomic stability and begun the journey towards sustainable, and inclusive growth.

 We are modernizing agriculture and industry, developing mineral resources, digitalizing our economy and equipping our youth, with modern AI and IT skills.

 We are opening new pathways with China, through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, as well as with the Gulf, Central Asia, and beyond.

 Here, I pay tribute, to the visionary leadership of President Xi Jinping for spearheading the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative, the Global Civilization Initiative and the Global Governance Initiative.

 On these pillars, we can surely build a shared future for mankind.

Mr. President,  Developing countries are in dire need of timely debt relief, affordable long-term financing, and a stronger voice, in global financial institutions.

 Development must receive the same urgency as security.

Ladies and Gentlemen,  Is it not an irony of fate that Pakistan contributes, less than one per cent of global emissions, yet repeatedly bears the horrific consequences of climate change?

 Developed countries must therefore, honour their climate-finance commitments, without delay, fund loss and damage speedily and ensure, support for adaptation and resilience.

Mr. President,  The theme of this session calls upon us to restore trust.

 But trust cannot be restored by words alone.

 It must be earned through action.

 We will restore trust when rivers, become lifelines of cooperation — not fault-lines of conflict.

 We will restore trust when those who fuelled, the climate crisis protect those who suffer most from its devastating consequences.

 And above all —  Trust will be restored when the guns are silenced —  and replaced by handshakes and embraces.

Mr. President,  The UN80 Initiative, should make the United Nations stronger, more coherent and more effective.

 The Security Council, must become more representative, democratic and accountable.

 Reform, must reflect, the interests and aspirations of the overwhelming majority of Member States, not the ambitions of a select few.

 Our motto remains: “Reform for All — Privilege for None!”

Ladies and Gentlemen,  We live at a dangerous moment.

 But our future is not predetermined.

 War is a choice.

 Peace is also a choice.

 And sometimes —  the greater courage, lies, not in starting a war —  but in preventing one.

 Pakistan has made its choice.

 We have chosen dialogue over confrontation.

 We have chosen cooperation over coercion.

 We have chosen peace over war.

 Let this eighty-first General Assembly make it unanimous choice.

 For ourselves.

 For our children.

 And for generations yet unborn.

 Let us restore trust.

 Let us preserve peace.

 And let us prove that even in a divided world —  humanity can still choose to stand together.

I thank you.
