Mr. President,

Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished delegates,

I bring you greetings from Papua New Guinea, a nation of extraordinary diversity, with more than 800 languages and cultures, united under one flag.

Mr. President,

Papua New Guinea comes to this Assembly with profound respect for the Charter of the United Nations and for the principles and purposes upon which this great institution was founded.

The United Nations reminds us that whether we are big or small nations, rich or poor, developed or developing, powerful or less powerful, we are all members of one international community.

The challenges confronting humanity do not recognise the size of our economies, the strength of our militaries or the boundaries on our maps.

No nation can address them alone.

We must therefore continue to work together, respecting the sovereignty of nations, upholding international law and the United Nations Charter, resolving our differences peacefully, and recognising that every nation, regardless of its size or economic strength, has a voice and a place in this Assembly.

For Papua New Guinea, and for the small island nations of the Pacific, multilateralism matters.

The United Nations provides a place where the smallest nations can sit alongside the largest, where our voices can be heard, and where we can work together on the common challenges facing humanity.

Mr. President,

At this time, I also wish to acknowledge Secretary -General António Guterres as he approaches the completion of his tenure.

On behalf of the Government and people of Papua New Guinea, I thank Secretary General Guterres for his strong and consistent advocacy for humanity.

At a time when our world has confronted war, displacement, poverty, inequality, climate change and many other challenges, he has consistently called for peace, human dignity, international cooperation and respect for the principles of the United Nations He has demonstrated the qualities of a global statesman and has used his office to speak for humanity, including those whose voices are too often unheard.

Secretary-General Guterres, Papua New Guinea thanks you for your service to the United Nations and to humanity.

Your advocacy reminds us that beyond our national borders, political differences, cultures and beliefs, we belong to one human family and share one Earth.

Mr. President,

It is in that spirit of our common humanity that I wish to speak about human rights, human freedom and, particularly, freedom of conscience, thought, religion and belief.

At the heart of human rights is a simple truth: every human being has inherent dignity and is entitled to fundamental freedoms.

From my Christian perspective, these freedoms are not gifts bestowed upon humanity by governments, institutions or powerful nations. They are God-given rights inherent in every human life.

And because these rights belong equally to every person, we have a responsibility to respect and protect the rights of others, including those who may not look like us, speak like us, worship like us or believe what we believe.

The strength of a nation, a government, an economy, a technology or a religion should never be used to suppress the fundamental rights of another human being.

The might of military power must not suppress the weak.

The might of economic power must not suppress the poor.

The might of technology must not diminish human dignity or freedom.

And the might of a religious majority must never be used to suppress those who belong to a religious minority.

Human rights have their greatest meaning when they protect those with less power, minorities, vulnerable communities and individuals whose beliefs may differ from those of the majority.

We must therefore learn to live together with mutual respect.

We do not have to agree on everything.

We do not have to share the same religion, culture, political system or worldview.

But we must respect the humanity and fundamental freedoms of one another.

Mr. President,

This principle is especially important when we speak about religion.

Papua New Guinea is a Christian nation, believing that Jesus Christ is our Lord, Saviour and soon-coming King. Christian principles have profoundly influenced our country, our communities and our institutions.

But our Christianity must never become an excuse to deny another human being freedom of conscience.

Section 45 of our Constitution guarantees every person freedom of conscience, thought and religion, and the practice of his or her religion and beliefs.

Our Constitution also protects people against being compelled to participate in religious observance and against attempts to force religion or irreligion upon another person.

Mr. President,

Faith that is forced is no longer faith.

I believe freedom of choice is a God -given right, implanted in the conscience of every human being. Our moral consciousness comes from God.

God does not compel worship. He calls people through love while allowing every person to exercise the freedom of choice He has given them.

True faith therefore cannot be imposed by force, fear, law or persecution.

A person must be free to believe.

A person must be free to worship.

A person must be free to change his or her belief.

And a person must also be free not to profess a religion.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights recognises this principle in Article 18, the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion.

Mr. President,

History teaches us what happens when governments, institutions or majorities use religion to suppress those who believe differently.

Human beings have been persecuted, expelled, imprisoned and killed because of their faith.

Humanity must learn from this history.

A Christian-majority nation must protect people of other religions.

A Muslim-majority nation must protect people of other religions.

A Hindu-majority nation must protect people of other religions.

A Buddhist-majority nation must protect people of other religions.

And every society must respect the rights of those who choose not to profess a religion.

The size of a majority does not diminish the human rights of the minority.

The United States of America, where this Assembly meets, expressed this principle more than two centuries ago through its First Amendment, which prohibits laws “respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof.”

Government should neither impose faith upon its people nor prevent people from practising their faith.

Papua New Guinea supports this principle.

We are proudly Christian.

But the strength of our Christianity should not be demonstrated by suppressing another person’s beliefs.

It should be demonstrated by having the confidence to allow every human being freedom of conscience.

Humanity can be diverse in culture, religion and thought, yet we must be united in respecting and tolerating our differences.

Mr. President,

Papua New Guinea knows something about diversity.

We have more than 800 languages and many different cultures and traditions.

Yet for 51 years as an independent nation, we have remained together as one Papua New Guinea.

We have disagreements and challenges. We do not claim perfection.

But our experience demonstrates something important:

Diversity does not have to mean division.

People can speak different languages and still belong to one nation.

People can come from different cultures and live under one Constitution.

And people can worship differently and still be neighbours, colleagues and fellow citizens.

Mr. President,

Papua New Guinea therefore calls upon all Member States to defend freedom of conscience, thought, religion and belief.

And I respectfully extend this call to every nation that calls Papua New Guinea a friend, every nation with which we have a bilateral partnership, and every nation that seeks friendship and engagement with us.

Look within your own borders.

Ensure that religious minorities are not persecuted, suppressed, intimidated or discriminated against because they practise a religion different from that of the majority.

Whether a country is predominantly Christian, Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist or follows another religious tradition, the faith of the majority must never become an instrument for persecuting the minority.

This message is not directed at one country, one religion or one region.

It is a principle that must apply equally to all of us.

Because human rights cannot be selective.

We cannot demand respect for our own rights while denying those same rights to others.

And we cannot ask the world to respect our beliefs while refusing to respect the freedom of conscience of another human being.

Mr. President,

But there is a wider principle here.

This is ultimately about human dignity.

If we recognise the dignity of every human being, then we must also consider the conditions in which people live — and the Earth we will leave to our children.

The United Nations General Assembly has recognised the human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment.

What value is freedom if a child has no clean water to drink?

What value is development if we destroy the environment that sustains human life?

And what inheritance are we leaving our children if our forests disappear, our oceans become polluted and our climate becomes increasingly unstable?

There is one reality that transcends every political, economic and religious difference between us:

We have only one Earth.

There is no other known habitable planet presently within the practical reach of humanity to which billions of people can simply relocate if we destroy this one.

This Earth is our common home.

Whatever our religion, nationality or political system, we breathe the same atmosphere.

We share the same oceans.

We depend upon the same global climate.

And ultimately, we share the consequences of what humanity does to this planet.

Mr. President,

Think about the children of the world.

A child born today did not create climate change.

That child did not choose the wars of this generation.

That child did not create pollution or environmental destruction.

Yet that child will inherit the consequences of the decisions we make today.

We must therefore be custodians not only of the present, but also of the future.

Future generations cannot stand before this General Assembly today and argue for themselves.

We must consider them when we make decisions about war and peace, development, energy, forests, oceans, minerals and the global economy.

Papua New Guinea understands this responsibility.

We are custodians of great tropical forests, extraordinary biodiversity and a vast ocean space.

For us, the environment is not an abstract international discussion.

It is where we live.

It is where we grow our food.

It is where we fish.

And it is the inheritance we must pass to our children.

Mr. President,

In our interconnected world, decisions made in one country can affect people thousands of kilometres away.

Greenhouse gases do not recognise national borders.

Pollution carried by oceans does not stop at immigration checkpoints.

Wars can disrupt food, fuel, energy, trade and supply chains far from the battlefield.

Economic decisions made in the world’s largest economies can reach an ordinary family in a small developing country.

A mother buying food can feel the consequences.

A farmer buying fuel can feel the consequences.

A small business facing higher transport costs can feel the consequences.

And developing countries trying to build roads, schools and hospitals can feel the consequences.

This is why leadership in powerful nations carries responsibilities beyond national borders.

With greater power comes greater responsibility.

Papua New Guinea respectfully asks the leaders of the world’s major powers to remember the ordinary people whose lives can be affected by decisions made far away from them.

When wars disrupt food, fuel and trade, families far from the battlefield can experience higher prices and economic uncertainty.

When the climate changes, communities that have contributed relatively little to global greenhouse-gas emissions can nevertheless face rising seas, extreme weather, threats to food security and damage to livelihoods.

Mr. President,

My appeal to leaders everywhere is simple:

Put human welfare ahead of war.

Put humanity ahead of narrow geopolitical interests.

Choose dialogue and peaceful settlement wherever possible.

Remember ordinary families when making major economic decisions.

Balance commercial interests with the welfare of people.

Use technology to advance human dignity, not diminish it.

Protect our planet while pursuing development.

And place the interests of our children and future generations at the heart of the decisions we make today.

Leadership is not measured only by the power a nation possesses.

Leadership is also measured by the responsibility with which that power is exercised.

Papua New Guinea does not claim to have all the answers.

We are a developing nation with challenges of our own.

But perhaps our position as a Pacific nation allows us to remind the larger powers of a simple reality:

No nation is so powerful that it can live apart from the Earth.

And no nation is so small that its people should be forgotten when decisions affecting humanity are made.

The military strength of a nation does not make the rights of another nation less important.

The size of an economy does not make the dignity of a poorer person less important.

Technological advancement does not diminish our obligation to protect human freedom.

And the size of a religious majority does not reduce the rights of a minority.

Power in all its forms must be exercised with responsibility.

Mr. President,

We are many tribes.

Many languages.

Many churches.

Many cultures.

But one nation.

And perhaps Papua New Guinea can offer one simple thought to this Assembly:

You do not have to believe what I believe in order for me to defend your human rights.

Let governments govern for people.

Let churches preach.

Let mosques call their faithful to prayer.

Let temples welcome their worshippers.

Let people search their own consciences.

Let economies serve humanity.

Let technology serve humanity.

Let powerful nations exercise their power responsibly.

Let nations resolve their differences peacefully wherever possible.

And let no State compel the human soul.

Mr. President,

We may have different religions, political systems, cultures and national interests.

We may be big nations or small nations.

We may be rich or poor.

We may possess different levels of military, economic and technological power.

But beneath those differences, we share something greater.

We share our humanity.

And we share one Earth.

This is our home.

We must protect it.

We must protect each other.

And we must leave our children a world better than the one we inherited.

Papua New Guinea will remain proudly Christian.

But we will also remain committed to freedom of conscience, thought and religion.

For ultimately, faith cannot be commanded by government.

Faith must come from the heart.

God has given humanity the capacity to choose, and that freedom must be respected.

And God has entrusted this Earth to our generation only for a time.

Let us use our leadership wisely.

Let us pursue peace.

Let us uphold the Charter of the United Nations.

Let us respect the rights and dignity of every human being.

Let us work together — big nations and small.

Let us ensure that power, whether military, economic, technological or religious, is never used to suppress the rights of others.

Let us protect our common home.

And let us remember always the generations who will follow us.

Mr. President,

On this note, I want to thank the United Nations and all those who have stood with Papua New Guinea over the last 51 years of our nationhood.

Amid the challenges we face as a developing nation, we are growing our economy, opening our country through enabling infrastructure, working to provide quality education and health services for all, moving towards cleaner energy, conserving our forests and oceans, strengthening our independent judiciary and free-market economy, and opening our doors to genuine foreign investment.

I want to assure this Assembly that my Government is working to ensure that none of our 11 million people is left behind as we pursue development, opportunity and a better quality of life in our God-given homeland.

May God bless Papua New Guinea.

May God bless all nations and all peoples.

May God protect our children and the generations yet unborn.

And may the United Nations continue to defend peace, human dignity, freedom and the Earth that we all share.

Thank you.

Mr. president.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates:

Congratulations, Your Excellency, Khalilur Rahman, on your election. The Bahamas pledges to you, its full support.

Mr. President:

Every generation inherits a promise it did not make.

The promise of our generation was made eighty-one years ago, with the founding of this United Nations, from the ashes of the worst war in human history.

Its ideals have proven its worth.

No nation is too small to be sovereign.

No people too poor to be equal.

And the strong should be bound by the same law as the weak.

Sad to say, the United Nations has drifted away from its promise.

The Bahamas comes today to insist on it.

Mr. President:

All week we have been told this is an age of uncertainty.

With respect, I do not agree.

Uncertainty is the language of those who have already decided, and do not wish to say so.

Treaties are being torn up. Institutions are being starved. Rules are giving way to deals, and the benefits of the deals go to whoever holds the most leverage.

Once again, we hear the language of Spheres of Influence. Of Backyards and Hemispheres. For 500 years, the Caribbean was somebody's backyard.

We did not win our freedom to once again become somebody's backyard.

The message to small nations is very clear.

Be as sovereign as we allow you to be.

Mr. President:

A sovereignty that must ask permission is not sovereignty. It is a lease.

Our ancestors did not break their chains so that their children could become tenants.

These are not uncertain times.

These times are very certain.

The only uncertain thing is how we respond to the opportunities and challenges of this time.

Mr. President:

People often say that the world lacks political will.

I do not agree.

The world has never lacked political will.

In 2008, when the banks of the richest nations were failing, trillions of dollars were found in a matter of weeks.

When a global pandemic reached the capitals of the powerful, the political will returned.

The will exists. It is simply pointed elsewhere.

Somewhere, a bank is always too big to fail. But a nation should never be too small to be left behind.

What the world lacks is not political will for change. It is political change.

A change in who writes the rules. A change in whose suffering counts. A change in who decides, and who pays.

Political will is a feeling. Political change is a decision about who holds power.

And Mr. President:

That is what I have come to speak about today: Power!

Two and a half thousand years ago, the envoys of Athens stood before the small island of Melos and told its people a simple truth about power.

The strong do what they can. The weak suffer what they must.

Eighty-one years ago, in San Francisco, humanity wrote a different law. The sovereign equality of nations. Not equality of size or wealth. Equality of standing.

The United Nations was the world's answer to Melos.

But in 1945, nearly one in three people on earth still lived under colonial rule, the people of my islands among them.

The Bahamas was not in that room. But we were on the map.

Then came political change. Not granted from above. Demanded from below.

On the eighteenth of September 1973, The Bahamas took its seat in this Assembly.

Then in 1985, Commonwealth leaders met in my own capital and agreed The Nassau Accord against apartheid. We were told pressure would never work. Less than five years later, Nelson Mandela walked free.

None of that happened because the powerful suddenly found their conscience. It happened because the balance of power in the room was changed.

That is the lesson of history. Change is not given, it is organised.

Mr. President:

It is not the small states who are dismantling the rules-based order.

Small countries cannot dismantle a rules-based world. But we will be the first to be crushed beneath its collapse.

Great powers can survive the end of the rules. Small states cannot. For us, a rules based world is our shield.

The rules have not always been applied fairly. But the answer is not a world without rules. It is rules that bind the strong as firmly as the weak.

International order, where rules apply only to the weak, is not order. It is a hierarchy.

When The Bahamas defends multilateralism, we are not defending a bureaucracy. We are defending the only successful arrangement in which a nation of four hundred thousand people can stand at this podium as the sovereign equal of a nation of a billion people.

A world without rules is not a free world. It is Melos.

Mr. President:

I do not appeal to conscience. Small states have done that for decades. Today, I appeal to your interests.

What is in your best interest?

No wall is high enough to keep out rising warming seas. No border strong enough to stop a pandemic.

Narrow self-interest asks what you can take today. Enlightened self-interest asks what kind of world you will have to live in tomorrow.

The international, rules-based order benefits all. They are not arbitrary having been arrived at through lived experience.

Every rule you break today is a rule you will need tomorrow. Every institution you starve is one you will one day call upon. Every small nation you abandon is a crisis you will one day inherit.

Defending the rules is not a favour to the small. It an insurance for the strong.

Mr. President:

Nowhere is that truer than the climate crisis.

Here too, we are told there is uncertainty. There is none.

The sea does not negotiate. It does not read communiqués. And it does not recognise a veto.

In 2024, for the first time, the world was more than one and a half degrees warmer for an entire year. The line which small island states fought to write into the Paris Agreement, has already been crossed.

A new report released only days ago warns that the El Niño phenomenon, now heating the planet, is likely to cost some four hundred and fifty thousand lives by next February.

In 2019, Hurricane Dorian inflicted damage and losses on The Bahamas equal to roughly a quarter of our national output. Families watched the sea take the only land they had.

Most of my country sits barely above sea level. For us, a rising ocean is not a forecast.

It is a boundary inching towards our doorsteps.

That is why The Bahamas proudly endorses yesterday's Declaration on Sea-Level Rise, which affirms that our statehood, our boundaries and our seat in this Assembly will not be washed away by the sea The science is certain. Last year, the International Court of Justice made clear that the law is also certain.

The injustice is certain too. The people who bear least responsibility are asked to adapt first, pay more, and recover from disasters they did not cause.

And the self-interest is certain. People who lose their homes do not disappear. They move, and they arrive at someone's border. Prevention costs less than rebuilding or relocating.

The Bahamas is taking action. But no nation, acting alone, can hold back the tides.

Nor can we build resilience inside a financial system designed at Bretton Woods in 1944, which still declares us too prosperous to help, until the next storm makes us poor.

The Vulnerability Index exists. The Loss and Damage Fund exist. What is missing is the power shift to make them operational and real.

Mr. President:

The next contest for power will not only be fought over land and sea. It will be fought over data.

Our citizens’ data crosses the world without a visa and without a vote. It leaves our shores as raw material, and returns as products we must buy.

We have seen this pattern before. My islands once exported salt, sponge and sisal.

Others set the price. Others kept the profit.

The commodity has changed. The pattern has not.

This is colonisation by data.

It does not arrive with ships and flags. It arrives in a box on a screen and a button that says, I agree.

I am talking about the capacity of a people to govern their own digital lives.

People whose daily lives and histories are being mined, should decide where their data lives, who may use it and on what terms.

Those people should be able to share in the value which their data creates.

It means building artificial intelligence that understands our languages, our laws and our lives, not only the lives of those in the wealthy North and dominate languages and cultures.

And it means taking part in the digital age on our own terms, not as consumers of other people's systems, but as builders of our own.

Data is the newest raw material in the global economy.

The old empires took our lands, plundered them and renamed them. The new ones seek to take our data, and hand us back a picture of ourselves, one we did not paint.

In this modern age, are we expected to be simply the unquestioning suppliers of data, or can we not rightfully expect to participate in processing our own data so as to refine it, govern it and profit from it?

We do not think it outrageous to demand that small states help write the rules of this new age, not simply be shown where to sign.

That is why The Bahamas asks you to support the nomination of Mr. Stephen Bereaux for Deputy Secretary-General of the International Telecommunication Union.

Mr. President:

The Security Council was designed by the victors of a war that ended eighty-one years ago. The world has changed. The Council has not.

Five nations still hold a veto over the peace of one hundred and ninety-three. Most of the nations in this Hall did not exist when that arrangement was made. None of us was asked.

An institution that cannot reform itself cannot hope to reform the world.

Power without legitimacy is not order. It is control. And a peace kept only by the powerful is not peace. It is permission.

That is why The Bahamas seeks a seat on the Council for the 2032–2033 term.

The Bahamas does not seek a seat on the Council to sit quietly inside that arrangement.

We seek it to help change it: a Council that reflects the world as it is, and that gives small island states a dedicated seat at the table where our survival is decided.

Change must also reach the leadership of this Organization.

The Bahamas supports the candidature of Her Excellency Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana for Secretary-General.

A former Foreign Minister who has presided over the Security Council, she understands what rules mean for nations with no other protection.

In eighty-one years, this Organization has had nine Secretaries-General. All of them men. None has come from the Caribbean. The Bahamas believes the time has come for both to change.

Mr. President:

In our own hemisphere, The Bahamas again calls for the lifting of the strengthened blockade against Cuba, an end to the fuel blockade, and Cuba's removal from the unilateral list of alleged state sponsors of terrorism. The Cuban people are suffering.

We call on all states to respect Latin America and the Caribbean as a Zone of Peace.

And we must speak of Haiti.

Haiti was the first nation on Earth born from a successful revolt by enslaved people. For that act of courage, it was made to pay. In 1825, under the guns of a foreign fleet,

Haiti was compelled to compensate its former colonisers for its own freedom. It took Haiti more than a century and a half to pay that compensation.

If you want to see what sovereignty costs when it is only allowed, and never respected, look at Haiti.

When the Security Council meets on the 30th of September, we urge it to renew the mandate under Resolution 2793, and to give the Gang Suppression Force the resources to deliver, in a partnership that respects Haitian sovereignty.

Mr. President:

The injustice of this century has a history. And history presents its bill.

This month, CARICOM advanced its Ten-Point Plan for reparatory justice, building on this Assembly's recognition, in March, of the trafficking and racialised enslavement of Africans, as crimes against humanity.

The wealth of empires was built on the stolen lives of our ancestors, including enslaved children. It is important that the former colonisers have recognised this atrocity, as recognition was a vital step. But recognition without repair is only a sentence on a page.

We call on the nations that profited to engage seriously with reparatory justice: truth, apology, restoration and development.

Mr. President:

The founders of this Organization made their promise in the ruins of war.

We should not need ruins to find our own courage.

The United Nations was not created to manage the decline of its own promise. It was created to build on it.

These are not uncertain times. The only uncertain thing is how we respond.

I challenge you, I dare you, I encourage you, I demand of you:

Let history record that we responded through change.

Thank you.

ENDS

Monsieur le président de l'Assemblée.

President of the General Assembly.
Secretary General, heads of State and Government ministers, permanent representatives, distinguished delegates.
Haitian people.
And taking the floor at this General Assembly, I feel the weight of history.

More than 80 years ago, in the wake of a war that plunged the world into chaos, Haiti, a founding member of the United Nations, joined the nations of the world to make a pledge for peace, for dialogue and respect for human dignity.
Today, while deadly crises and conflicts have proliferated and the climate emergency is intensifying and new divisions are threatening stability in Haiti and throughout the world, this founding endeavor is being put to the test.
It is imperative that, given the crises that Haiti is grappling with and given those that are causing so much upheaval throughout the world, it is imperative for nations to close ranks around what is essential.
That is peace, security and the well-being of all peoples.

This is the whole point of the topic that brings us together this year.
Mr. president, we I congratulate you on your election as president of the General Assembly.
I also wish to hail the Secretary General, Antonio Guterres, for his unwavering commitment to peace.
I still remember fondly his visit to port au Prince on the 16th of June 2026, which bore witness to his solidarity toward the Haitian people in these difficult times that our country is undergoing, Haiti wishes to extend its gratitude to all of its partners and friends that have continued to stand by its side.

The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Eliseu Vieira de Prime Minister of the Republic of Guinea-Bissau.
I request protocol two to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.
Mr. president, distinguished Heads of State and Government.
Mr. Secretary general, ladies and gentlemen.

I have the honour of addressing this August Assembly on behalf of the government and the people of the Republic of Guinea-Bissau.
Allow me to congratulate Mr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as president of the General Assembly of the United Nations.
I am confident that his governmental and diplomatic experience will help guide the work of this Assembly with balance and in a spirit of dialogue.
I also commend Miss Annalena Barbosa Barbosa for the dedication she demonstrated during her term of office, and for her efforts to strengthen multilateralism and international cooperation.

It is a particular pleasure for me to express our appreciation to the Secretary General of the United Nations, Mr. Antonio Guterres, for his tireless commitment to the defense of peace and to the search for solutions to the many challenges facing humanity.
Ladies and gentlemen, yesterday September 24th, the people of Guinea-Bissau celebrated the 53rd anniversary of our national independence.
This date of profound significance for our people invites us to reflect on the value of freedom sovereignty, and the dignity of peoples.
It is in this spirit that I bring to this assembly a message of peace, freedom, and fraternity to all the nations of the world in the firm hope that every people may live in peace, fully exercise its rights, and freely chart its own path towards development and prosperity.

We live in an interdependent world marked by growing uncertainty and by challenges that transcend borders climate change, transnational organized crime, terrorism, structural inequalities, the burden of debt, and insufficient financing for development continue to undermine our efforts towards sustainable development.
Devastating conflicts also persist in several regions of the world, as do security challenges, particularly in the Sahel.
In this context, Guinea-Bissau considers it essential to strengthen the international community's support to the most affected countries in the region.
Ladies and gentlemen, the United Nations remains an essential pillar of multilateralism and a privileged forum for dialogue, cooperation and the search for collective solutions to the challenges facing humanity.

It must be acknowledged, however, that in certain circumstances, the expectations that people have placed in it have not always been met with a response commensurate with their aspirations.
This reality should not lead us to question the foundations of the multilateral system, but rather to strengthen the effectiveness representativeness and capacity for action of international institutions.
It is incumbent upon Member States to renew their commitment to multilateralism that is more effective, more inclusive and more responsive to the aspirations of peoples.
We also consider it urgent to reform the architecture of global governance, so that it reflects the geopolitical realities of the 21st century.

It is essential that Africa have more adequate and effective representation in the international institutions that play a central role in shaping responses to the challenges of peace, security and development The reform of United Nations Security Council Council must reflect the legitimate aspirations of the African continent and ensure fairer, permanent and effective representation.
In keeping with the principle of a more inclusive, equitable and representative international order, Guinea-Bissau welcomes the efforts of the United Nations to achieve achieve a lasting political solution to the question of Western Sahara.
We welcome the adoption of Security Council Resolution 2797 of 2025 and view favourably the Autonomy Initiative presented by the Kingdom of Morocco as a basis for resolving this dispute.
Ladies and gentlemen, on November 26th, 2025, during the electoral process, the constitutional order in Guinea-Bissau was interrupted and transitional bodies were established.

A one year transition period was set with the aim of creating the conditions necessary for the restoration of constitutional order.
Within this framework, the constitutional review process has been completed and the new constitution of the Republic was approved by Popular Referendum on August 30th, 2026.
This process is an important milestone in the transition and in the restoration of constitutional order in the country.
The government is committed to creating the conditions necessary for the presidential and legislative elections scheduled for December 6th of this year, to be held in an inclusive, free, transparent and credible manner.

I take this opportunity to express our gratitude to the Economic Community of West African States, ECOWAS, the African Union, the United Nations and our other institutions international partners for their engagement and support in the efforts to ensure a return to constitutional normalcy in our country.
Ladies and gentlemen, three decades ago, Guinea-Bissau had the honor of serving as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council.
Today, as we reaffirm our commitment to the purposes and principles of the charter of the United Nations and to the promotion of international peace and security, I wish to reiterate that Guinea-Bissau is a candidate for non-permanent membership of the Security Council for the term 2028 2029.
Our vision of the world rests fundamentally on four key words prevention, dialogue, cooperation, peace.

We will work with all Member States to advance essential consensus based priorities for Guinea-Bissau as a developing country, multilateralism and respect for international law are not mere concepts.
They are an existential necessity.
Ladies and gentlemen, Guinea-Bissau follows with concern the humanitarian consequences of the measures imposed against Cuba.
We therefore reiterate our call for the lifting of the economic commercial and financial embargo, as well as other restrictive measures that affect the Cuban people and essential sectors of that country's economy.

Over the past decades, this assembly has built consensus and undertaken numerous commitments towards the achievement of common goals Many of these commitments, however, remain unfulfilled.
Enormous gaps persist in financing for development and climate action, alongside high levels of poverty and social inequality, and a growing and unsustainable debt burden on the economies of developing countries in the face of this reality.
We need more multilateralism, effective international cooperation, and more united and determined collective action.
No country, however powerful, can face today's challenges alone.

It is in this spirit of cooperation, solidarity and peace that Guinea-Bissau will continue to work with all member states to uphold the principles enshrined in the charter of the United Nations and to build a better future, a future of peace, development and well-being for present and future generations.
Guinea-Bissau thanks you and God bless all.
Thank you.

The Assembly will now listen to a statement delivered by His Excellency Dr. Mustafa Kamal Madbouli, Prime Minister of the Arab Republic of Egypt. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly. In the name of God, the merciful, the compassionate, Mr. Khalil-ur-Rahman, President of the first session of the United Nations General Assembly, Mr. Antonio Gutierrez, Secretary General of the United Nations, Your Majesties, Excellencies and Highnesses, Heads of State and Government, Ladies and Gentlemen. At the outset, I am pleased to extend my sincere congratulations to His Excellency Minister Khalil O'Rahman on assuming the presidency of the current session of the General Assembly. We assure him of our full support and confidence in his ability to successfully steer the work of the session. This year, the General Assembly convenes under a theme that accurately reflects the challenge facing the international system, restoring trust and managing transformation. Our word is changing at a pace far exceeding the ability of international governance institutions to respond. crisis does not lie in the absence of charters and principles, but rather in the widening gap between what we proclaim and what we implement, and between those who make decisions and those who are affected by them. Our world does not need a merely symbolic multilateralism that brings together states in open discussions. Rather it needs effective multilateralism in which every state has a voice, and every Many people receive a fair share of decisions, opportunities and resources. It is no exaggeration to say that confidence in the effectiveness of collective action and the multilateral system has declined. There is an urgent need to restore adherence to international law, to avoid policies based on power, polarization and double standards. It is no coincidence that the countries of the global south, which comprised the overwhelming majority of the world's population are among those most harmed by the decline of the rule of international law, the weakening role of international organizations, and the fragility of global governance and international cooperation frameworks. From this perspective, Egypt, as a founding member of the United Nations, believes that restoring trust requires three interconnected pillars – justice in representation and decision-making, justice in the application of the law, and justice in the distribution of development and transformation opportunities. This is not a call to rebuild the international system from scratch. It is a call to fulfill its original promises and purposes, notably sovereign equality among states, respect for law, peaceful settlement of disputes, international cooperation for the benefit of peoples, and enabling them to reap the benefits of accelerating scientific progress. The multilateral international system remains an indispensable choice. However, its survival depends on strengthening justice and ensuring the effectiveness and sustainability of its institutions instead of merely repeating the principles for which it was established without making meaningful action. Mr. President, if justice and the application of rules is the litmus test of the credibility of the international system, then the Palestinian issue remains the clearest example of the existing dysfunction. What the Palestinian people have endured and continue to endure in terms of suffering, repression and violations must not become a normalized reality or a protracted crisis managed from one cycle to the other. Securing the ceasefire and the Gaza Strip, in accordance with President Trump's and the Sharm al-Sheikh Summit peace plan, ensuring full compliance with it, ending daily Israeli violations, completing the withdrawal, guaranteeing the safe and sustainable delivery of humanitarian aid, enabling the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza to carry out its duties, and then moving immediately toward early recovery and reconstruction, these are not merely humanitarian steps. They are also the essential gateway to a serious political process that addresses the root causes of the conflict and resolves them. In this context, Egypt reaffirms its categorical rejection of any attempt to displace the Palestinian people from their land, whether from the Gaza Strip or from the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. The international community as a whole bears a clear responsibility to stop systematic Israeli violations of international law. Peace cannot be built on uprooting a people from their land. Believing that stability can be achieved in the region, while ignoring the suffering of the Palestinian people and merely managing the occupation rather than ending it, is nothing but illusion. The goal remains unequivocally clear. establishment of an independent sovereign and territorially contiguous Palestinian state on the lines of the 4th of June 1967 with East Jerusalem as its capital within the framework of the two-state solution and in accordance with international legitimacy resolutions. This requires preserving the unity of the Palestinian territory and the Palestinian political system, enabling the Palestinian people to manage their own affairs and build their state and ensuring that the international community fulfills its responsibility to protect civilians, reject collective punishment and guarantee respect for international humanitarian law. It also requires recognizing Palestinian rights as inalienable rights, not as bargaining chips to be granted or withheld according to power balances, political posturing or electoral calculations. Egypt has shouldered its responsibility, alongside its partners, secure the ceasefire. It has been the largest provider of humanitarian assistance reaching the Gaza Strip. Egypt will continue to work toward reconstruction and opening a viable political horizon. However, the success of these efforts hinges on an international will capable of transforming legitimacy into decisive international action that moves from managing the tragedy to ending its causes. Mr. President, the experience of our region confirms that managing crises rather than resolving them does not create stability. Rather, it postpones the explosion and increases its costs. Accordingly, Egypt remains committed to a clear vision for regional security based on state sovereignty, territorial integrity, respect for national institutions, rejection of the dismantling of states or the creation of parallel entities, and prioritizing political solutions and inclusive national settlements over the logic of force and the imposition of a FET accompli. In every crisis across the broader Middle East, from the Atlantic Ocean to the Gulf, circumstances and details may differ, but the capable national state that embraces all its citizens and legitimate institutions remain the only true foundation for stability. Security is indivisible. The security of one state cannot be built upon the insecurity of its neighbors or upon threats to shipping, trade and energy routes or violations of state sovereignty through attacks carried out in violation of international law. Likewise, any regional actor that believes that its political or economic interests can be achieved by undermining national state institutions, supporting militias, or promoting separatist agendas and civil conflict, clearly becomes part of the problem. Confronting such actors and their practices becomes the responsibility of the international community as a whole. 4. Regional crises cannot be treated as isolated cases. They must be viewed within an interconnected regional security environment that supports the state's institutions, unity and sovereignty, that encourages political settlements and peacebuilding based on the principle of national and regional ownership of solutions, ending external interferences and preventing crises from turning into arenas for regional and international competition over the resources and capabilities of the peoples of the region. The protection of states and their sovereignty is inseparable from protecting the resources upon which peoples' livelihoods depend. In this context, I wish to state clearly and unequivocally that Egypt's water security is an existential issue that is not open to compromise. Denial is not merely an economic resource. It is the lifeline upon which the existence and development of Egyptian society have depended throughout history. Egypt believes that trans-transt-boundary water resources should be a field for cooperation and integration, not conflict. We also believe that water security and development are not contradictory objectives, but complementary ones when political will exist, when intentions are sincere, and when international law is respected. We do not oppose the right of any people to development, rather we defend a clear and just principle that the development of one party must not be built upon causing harm to others. Trade resources cannot be managed through unilateral measures or FETA-complete policies. They must be managed through cooperation, good-neighborliness, and the conclusion of binding agreements in accordance with international law that preserve the legitimate rights and interests of all parties. In this regard, Egypt reserves its legitimate and internationally recognized ride under the Charter of the United Nations and International Law to protect its water security and preserve the existential resources of its people. Amid the multiple threats facing our region, we call the crisis of Brotherly Sudan, a crisis whose consequences extend beyond military confrontations to affect the security and safety of civilians and threaten to dismantle the state institutions. In confronting these threats and dangers, the Sudan has in Egypt a strong supporter of its people and the right to unity, to institutions capable of safeguarding their resources, and to a justice that upholds their dignity. Mr. President, justice in rules is not complete if the institutions that make decisions do not fairly represent the word they govern. More than eight decades have passed since the founding of the United Nations, yet the structure of the international systems institutions, particularly the Security Council, still reflect historical balances that have become outdated. Institutions that were created for a different word cannot maintain full legitimacy and effectiveness if they do not reflect the word they are meant to serve today, and represent the the concerns and interests of the majority of its population. In this context, Egypt continues to advocate genuine and comprehensive reform of the Security Council, in accordance with the Ezzolwini consensus and the Third Declaration, particularly to mend the historical injustice suffered by Africa. The imbalance in political representation is matched by another imbalance in the global economy. Financing countries are required to accelerate development, create jobs, finance green transitions and adapt to crises, while simultaneously facing growing debt burdens, higher financing costs, and shrinking fiscal space. Therefore, reforming international financial architecture is no longer a luxury, but a necessity. We need financial institutions that are more representative and responsive. We need expanded concessional financing, greater mobilization and lending capacities for multilateral development banks and accelerated debt workout in a fair and effective manner. We need innovative financing tools and a fairer system for assessing countries' needs and investment risks, thus enabling the mobilization of private capital without shifting risks on to the most vulnerable countries. Countries should not be forced to choose between debt servicing and financing education, healthcare, food security, and essential infrastructure. Development is not charity. It is a right and a shared interest. Investing in development is an investment in global stability and in the ability of states to prevent crises before they become cross-border humanitarian and security crises. Mr. President, as we work to correct the imbalances inherited from the last century, we must not allow them to be reproduced in the future. Artificial intelligence opens boundless horizons for growth, knowledge, innovation, and improved services. Yet, it may also create a vast new divide and power, linked to computing capacity, data, models, skills, and financing. Therefore, managing this transformation requires the establishment of governance frameworks for artificial intelligence and emerging technologies on the basis that technology is a global public benefit and not an exclusive privilege enjoyed by a limited number of states or corporations. Egypt supports the role of the United Nations and a global dialogue to develop principles that balance innovation and responsibility, protect privacy, guarantee transparency, accountability, non-discrimination, human oversight, respect for international law, technology and knowledge transfer, financing of digital infrastructure and skills development. This would enable developing countries to become producers and developers of technology rather than merely being markets for its consumption. Artificial intelligence should also reflect the linguistic and cultural diversity of the word. Arab and African languages and communities should receive fair representation in data and models. Egypt has launched the second edition of its national artificial intelligence strategy 2025-2030, grounded in its firm conviction that the safe and responsible use of technology and the development of national capacities are inseparable requirements. The same principle governs the green transition. There can be no trust transition if ambition is dissociated from fair implementation. Climate action must go hand in hand with development, poverty reduction and job creation. Adaptation, water security and food security must receive the priority they deserve, especially in Africa and the country's most vulnerable to the impact of climate change. Drawing on Egypt's experience in hosting the Climate Conference in Sharm-e-Sheikh and the decision it adopted, we can affirm that the gap no longer lies in diagnosing the problem but in implementation, especially in translating commitments into financing flows, projects and technologies that reach the countries and communities most in need. In a world where geopolitical and technological transformations are accelerating, this must not lead us into more dangerous arms races. Therefore, Egypt reaffirms its commitment to a balanced system of disarmament and non-proliferation, free from double standards, and its commitment to the goal of establishing a Middle East free of nuclear weapons and all other weapons of mass destruction. Collective security is not achieved through the accumulation of instruments of destruction, rather it is achieved through equal rules, obligations applicable to all, and a political will that prioritizes the prevention of escalation rather than having a delayed reaction after crises occur. Mr. President, as Egypt presents this vision, it is not merely calling for a reform of the international system. Egypt is putting its experience and capabilities in service of solutions. Drawing upon its Arab, African, and Mediterranean heritage, its historic role in founding the multilateral international order and its principled commitment to its survival and sustainability, Egypt will remain a bridge for cooperation and a partner to all those who seek a more just and effective international system. We will continue investing in partnerships with all parties. We remain open to cooperation and exchange of expertise and working with all nations in both the Global North and the Global South on solutions that do not impose a single model but respect national priorities and are based on shared ownership. Vegetarmacy gains meaning when it produces results. Institutions regain trust when they do justice to those they serve. Trust is not demanded. It is built through justice. Transformation is not imposed. It is managed through participation. Egypt will continue to support every effort that restores trust and effectiveness to our multilateral international system and contributes to managing the transformations of our rapidly changing word in a fair and participatory manner serving the interests of our peoples and future generations. Before concluding, I wish to take this opportunity from this rostrum to extend our sincere thanks and appreciation to Mr. Ghan Antonio Guterres, Secretary General of the United Nations, who has led the organization through one of the most difficult and critical periods in its history with courage, integrity, and a sincere commitment to fulfilling his mandate to protect international law, preserve the standing and role of the United Nations, maintain its credibility and moral authority, and defend the principles upon which the organization was founded. These efforts will remain appreciated and remembered. As I express our profound gratitude for all that he has done, I wish him every success in his future endeavors. Thank you for your attention. On behalf of the General Assembly, I thank his Excellency, Prime Minister of Egypt.

Mr. President Excellencies, Friends I bring greetings from the Government and people of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

Mr. President, we congratulate you on your election to preside over this session of the General Assembly. You can count on our support and cooperation.

Secretary-General, António Guterres, we are extremely grateful to you for your bold leadership and determined advocacy for human rights, justice and peace.

We thank you for standing up for small and vulnerable nations.

Support for Multilateralism The theme "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All" speaks directly to the anxieties of our time and also to the hopes of small states like mine.

As we have heard from many speakers in this chamber, trust in the multilateral system is broken. Hope has retreated while cynicism and doubt have grown.

Nevertheless, we hear the insistent calls for justice, peace, and for a rulesbased international order that applies to all nations.

Mr. President, I come here for the first time representing my country Saint Vincent and the Grenadines with a clear mandate and a commitment that governance must be transparent; that individual actions must consistently reflect integrity; and that public resources must be used to improve the lives of ordinary people.

We are a small, democratic, multi-island Caribbean nation committed to multilateralism and the peaceful resolution of disputes. Those principles serve us well and we believe should bind us all in this chamber.

Vulnerability We in St. Vincent and the Grenadines e xperienced firsthand the vulnerability of living on the frontlines of climate change, having experienced only two years ago the sudden destructive power of a category 5 hurricane.

We also feel the enormous strains imposed on our small, open econom y by distant wars that have disrupted supply chains, and by decisions made in places where our voice is never heard.

Yet, we will not let vulnerability define us or limit our ambitions. We will be resilient and will work individually and collectively to transcend our vulnerability.

So, Mr. President, we come to this august Assembly not as mere petitioners, but as partners seeking to play our part in making our world a better place.

I come at this point in the debate having had the privilege of listening to other leaders who spoke before me. And Mr. President I must tell you, I was moved by the hopeful vision, fiery passion and boundless generosity and caring of many of the speakers.

They lifted my spirit and, I am determined that that is where my spirit shall remain. I owe it to the people who sent me here to be hopeful. I owe it also to people whom I have never met, who come from places I have never been but who, nevertheless, are my brothers and sisters.

And so that brings us to the task at hand.

We all know that t he United Nations has its flaws. But we must not seek to abandon it like a motherless child.

It is what we have made it.

Some, no doubt, are more culpable than others, but in one way or another, we are all involved. We speak of culpability not merely to point a finger of blame, but to understand better where the solutions may lie.

We believe profoundly that more than ever, humanity needs the United Nations. Try to i magine a world without it. Where would we go to have the conversations we are having now and had earlier in the week?

And that is only the beginning!

As a global institution, the United Nations is fundamentally an inclusive space where every nation can play a role in addressing our common problems. A retreat from m ultilateralism undermines the interests of small States and, indeed, of everyone.

But we acknowledge that our support for the United Nations must be matched by our willingness to embrace reform to make it more effective.

Trust cannot be built or restored by declarations alone. It is only when ordinary people see that cooperation makes their lives safer, richer and happier that trust will be restored!

UN REFORM Mr. President, let us restore trust through organizational reform and greater inclusiveness.

The U nited Nations governance model designed in 1945 cannot adequately address the security and economic challenges of today. Therefore, we join with other nations in calling for reform, specifically of the Security Council, to include a permanent member from the continent of Africa with all the attendant rights and privileges. Failure to do so would only confirm that the current composition is not about governance and fairness, but about power.

Further, as we proceed with selecting our next Secretary -General, let us be more open and inclusive.

Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is pleased to join other Caribbean Community members in endorsing the candidacy of Her Excellency Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana and of the region of Latin America and the Caribbean. We know her as a distinguished dipl omat, a principled multilateralist and a compelling advocate for developing countries and small states.

Mr. President, as this is my first visit here, like a tourist I walked the halls of this historic building and admired on the walls the impressive portraits of the nine men who have served as Secretary -General since 1946. And while I appreciated the outstanding caliber and service of those men I, nevertheless, could not resist thinking that after eight decades, surely the time has come for an equally capable woman to be Secretary -General. We believe Ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett is well-suited to be that person.

Climate Finance Reform Mr. President, for Small Island Developing States (SIDS), climate change is not a distant forecast. It is a present danger and recurring financial emergency. We suffer the scourge of sargassum seaweed that damages our tourism, and we worry about the growing problem of Sahara dust that seriously degrades air quality across the Caribbean islands. And we worry constantly about hurricanes!

In July 2024, Hurricane Beryl struck SVG and demonstrated once again how a few hours of extreme weather can destroy homes, livelihoods and infrastructure built over many years, and set back a country.

Small states cannot continue borrowing merely to replace what climate related disasters repeatedly destroy. We cannot continue to walk up the down escalator, pretending it is development.

Mr. President, we renew our call for the full operationalization of the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index, so that access to concessional financing is not constrained by per capita income but reflects the real climate risks small island states face and their limited capacity to respond to such large events.

We also call for the swift implementation of reforms set out in the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS.

Further, we support the continuing work of the Bridgetown Initiative to reform the international financial architecture, including automatic debt -service suspension clauses when disaster strikes, expanded and re -channeled Special Drawing Rights, and multilateral development banks that lend like development partners rather than like commercial creditors.

Mr. President, we must also accept that affordable, patient, concessional capital is not charity to small states; it is justice for states that contribute the least to the climate crisis yet bear the highest costs.

Peace and Security Mr. President, let us restore trust through the pursuit of peace and security.

Trust in the international system begins with the conviction that every one matters, and that the security of small states is as precious as that of great powers.

International conflicts far from our shore s--in Ukraine and the Middle East -- continue to have devastating consequences for our daily lives, disrupting agricultural trade and global food stability and driv ing up fuel prices and shipping premiums.

We therefore join with others here and call for an immediate end to the war in Ukraine with full respect for state sovereignty and territorial integrity under the UN Charter. And Likewise, we call for a permanent ceasefire in the Middle East, the protection of civilians, and the realization of a two -state solution guaranteeing peace and security for Palestine and Israel.

Mr. President, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines does not stand alone. We stand with our brothers and sisters of the Caribbean Community, CARICOM, which is not just a trading bloc but a family whose members in these uncertain times need each other more than ever.

For us in the Ca ribbean, peace and security are paramount concerns in our diplomatic efforts.

Therefore, as we seek to restore trust, we reaffirm that Latin America and the Caribbean must remain a Zone of Peace, where disputes are settled through peaceful means with adherence to international law and the UN Charter. We urge that the territorial dispute between Venezuela and Guyana be resolved in this manner.

Within our hemisphere, other unresolved challenges require immediate, principled engagement.

HAITI Haiti remains our urgent concern.

Nearly four decades ago, the Trinidadian c alypsonian, David Rudder, sang a lament to Haiti. His words are still relevant today. I quote: “When there is anguish in Port-au-Prince, it’s still Africa crying.

We’re outing fires in faraway places when our neighbors are burning.

I refuse to believe that we good people will forever turn our hearts and our eyes...away.

Haiti, I’m sorry.” And the song goes on.

The insecurity of the Haitian people, plagued by gang violence and political uncertainty is a pain felt across our region. We support the efforts of CARICOM and of this organization to help fund and provide security, to build up critical institutions, and create a viable path to general elections. We must confront the reality of arms trafficking, including assault weapons that are terrorizing Haitian communities, and communities across the Caribbean. We don’t make these weapons in the Caribbean. They are manufactured in industrial nations and smuggled across borders into our region and countries. We, therefore, call on all countries to take decisive actions to stem the illicit flow of weapons and ammunition across borders and into the Caribbean.

CUBA Mr. President, Cuba has long been a valued member of our Caribbean family.

For more than three decades, this Assembly has said that the economic embargo imposed on Cuba must end.

Whatever disagreements exist, the collective punishment of an entire population, denying medicine, denying trade, denying fuel, denying ordinary development, cannot be reconciled with the Charter we all signed. My government adds its voice to the call, renewed year after year in this very hall, for that embargo to end.

VENEZUELA When devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela earlier this year, claiming thousands of lives, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines stood up in solidarity, contributing emergency assistance through a coordinated CARICOM relief effort.

Mr. President, when tragedy strikes, we must act as our brothers' and sisters' keepers. This too builds and restores trust among nations and strengthens the UN.

TAIWAN Mr. President, friendship is also a form of trust, and I wish in this august body to recognize our country’s 45 year s of diplomatic ties and friendship with Taiwan that has seen us work together i n development, in disaster response, education and in public health. Taiwan has shown time and again that they are prepared to be a responsible member of the international community. We renew our call for Taiwan's meaningful participation in the United Nations system and its specialized agencies.

Reparatory Justice Mr. President let us also restore trust through support for Reparatory Justice.

The past is not past when its consequences still shape who is rich and who is poor in the world today.

The Caribbean Community has, for over a decade, advanced a Ten-Point Plan for Reparatory Justice, seeking acknowledgment, repair, and genuine partnership to address the historic injustices of the enslavement of African people and the near -annihilation of our indigenous populations. We are encouraged that in March 2026, this assembly strongly adopted a resolution sponsored by Ghana and supported by the African Union and CARICOM, declaring “The Trafficking of Enslaved Africans and Racialized Chattel Enslavement of Africans as the Gravest Crime against Humanity”.

This is a hopeful and historic event, and after the follow-up conference in Accra in June, momentum grows, so necessary actions must follow.

When the continent from which our enslaved ancestors were taken and the islands to which they were brought in chains spoke with one voice, th is Chamber listened—the world listened. We expect that more steps will follow from discussions that will be held as part of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda in November.

CONCLUSION Mr. President, we ask how the United Nations can restore trust while managing transformation.

In summary, trust is restored when the smallest and most vulnerable nations feel they are included and that their concerns met; Trust is restored when a national debt is restructured to be fairer; It is restored when hurricane response arrives in time and when the benefits of new technology such as Artificial Intelligence is shared rather than hoarded or priced out of reach; it is restored when an embargo denounced in this chamber is finally lifted; when peace in a conflict is secured; and when an historical wrong is made right.

Mr. President, we remain hopeful that, with necessary changes in the organization and in the mindset of those of us who shape its work, the UN will live up to its name.

However, we must manage this era of transformation with courage, honesty, and fairness, and including equally the concerns of all the people s of the world, who despite our individual protestations, are inevitably part of our shared humanity.

Thank you. May God bless us all.
