Mr President of the General Assembly,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

I bring you greetings from His Majesty, King Tupou VI and the people of the Kingdom of Tonga.

Nine months into my service as Prime Minister, I stand here mindful that many Pacific leaders have come before me, raising the same warnings and making the same appeals.

Today, I am compelled to make them again.

The question before us is not whether the world has heard our message. It is why it has still not acted?

[Sovereignty and the United Nations] We live in a world more connected than ever. But greater connection has not brought greater unity. We meet amid deepening division, geopolitical competition and rising conflict.

For Tonga, navigating such stormy currents is not new. As descendants of voyagers, “we have been in the survival business much longer than most appreciate.”

Under King George Tupou I, Tonga preserved its independence during an era of colonial expansion. Our Constitution of 1875 secured Tongans’ rights and freedoms more than seven decades before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It reflects our fierce determination to chart our own course.

That is the essence of our sovereignty. Multilateralism allows us to project the power of our ideas, rather than the might of our power. Tonga participates as an equal under the founding principle of the United Nations Charter: the sovereign equality of states.

This is how we must approach our theme, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All.” Enduring trust is restored when commitments produce results.

True transformation is realised when our communities, economies and ecosystems can anticipate change and recover with greater strength. Small Island Developing States must not bear disproportionate costs for challenges they did little to create.

[United Nations Reforms] Mr President,

Too much of the international architecture still reflects the world of 1945 rather than today’s realities. If the United Nations is to remain the principal vehicle through which sovereign nations confront global challenges, it must transform.

We need a United Nations that enables innovation and expands meaningful access to investment and technology, especially for Small Island Developing States too often excluded from both. We need a stronger General Assembly and institutions that respond effectively to the needs of the majority of their members.

We cannot keep negotiating climate, biodiversity and the ocean in separate processes when they form an interconnected ecosystem requiring coherent solutions. Global processes must recognise the ocean–climate nexus and address these challenges together. International commitments must also be capable of implementation nationally.

We need a more inclusive and representative Security Council, equipped for today’s challenges and prepared to recognise the triple planetary crisis as a profound threat to peace and security. We need an international financial architecture that delivers timely, accessible financing to those most in need. Internationally pledged commitments must be acted upon urgently. Sovereign equality must be reflected in how these institutions listen, decide and deliver.

The next Secretary General must understand these realities. It is in this spirit that Tonga has nominated Ambassador Ivonne Baki of Ecuador. Her vision for a renewed and reformed United Nations speaks to the needs of vulnerable states. To restore trust, every Member State, large or small, must have a voice in shaping this Organisation’s future and a stake in its success.

[The Blue Pacific and an Ocean of Peace] Mr President,

The Pacific region spans one third of the Earth’s surface. It is our home. Through the 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent, we have set our own course and identified our priorities. Our Blue Pacific must be defined by those who call it home.

For Tonga, investing in the ocean and nature is foundational to our development ambition.

Protecting and restoring them builds climate resilience, strengthens food security and enables a sustainable blue economy. The financing and partnerships we build around ocean and nature based solutions will help determine our future and sustain our people.

We declared our region an Ocean of Peace in 2025. It sends a clear message: the Pacific must not become a staging ground for military escalation or a battleground for major power rivalry.

Our Ocean of Peace is more than the absence of conflict.

Our most pressing threats are already reaching our shores: transnational crime, illicit drugs, illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, cyber threats, and the unresolved consequences of nuclear testing and radioactive contamination. We will use innovative technologies and work closely with trusted security partners to confront these threats, including through stronger regional cooperation and maritime awareness.

We are committed to protecting the rights of marginalised people and ending violence against women and girls. This year, Tonga ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, reaffirming our commitment to dignity and equal participation for persons with disabilities.

Tonga also acceded to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons and ratified the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. In doing so, we completed the universalisation of the latter treaty in the Pacific.

[Climate Action and Resilience] Mr President,

On climate, the Pacific is already drowning in a crisis that others continue to postpone addressing. The United Nations Environment Programme’s Limiting Overshoot report warns that exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius could occur within the next few years. Crossing that threshold must not become an excuse for abandoning it. We must limit the extent and duration of any overshoot, peak as low as possible and return below 1.5 degrees as quickly as possible. Every fraction of a degree matters.

The Pacific loses an estimated US$500 million each year from cyclones and floods. Early warning systems give communities time to prepare and can reduce these losses. This sum may seem modest in global terms, but it is a heavy burden for Pacific nations. The financing to prevent such losses still falls short.

The Pacific Resilience Facility, our own mechanism for financing community resilience, needs a further US$328 million in pledges to reach its initial capitalisation target of US$500 million. Weather Ready Pacific, our regional mechanism supporting Early Warnings for All, needs a further US$160 million to reach its target. Tonga’s Climate Trust Fund, which provides funding directly to communities and disbursed its first grants this year, also needs significant support. We call on partners to invest in these Pacific-designed and Pacific-owned solutions.

Tonga stands behind the 2026 Pacific Islands Forum Leaders’ Belau Declaration and calls on all major emitters to act urgently. Climate action is a legal obligation. Meeting those obligations will require difficult decisions rooted in science. Climate leadership is not a popularity contest.

Seven of the nine planetary boundaries have been breached by human activity. Climate inaction is not an option. Tonga is accelerating its transition away from fossil fuels, expanding renewable energy and encouraging the shift to electric vehicles. For us, decarbonisation also means greater energy security and protection from global fuel price shocks. Explicit fossil fuel subsidies, estimated by the International Monetary Fund at US$725 billion, must be phased out.

International financial institutions and multilateral development banks must recognise the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index in eligibility and allocation decisions. The index must help unlock affordable and timely support before disasters strike. By any credible index,

Tonga is among the world’s most vulnerable countries.

We call on all nations, especially the world’s largest emitters, to attend the Pre COP31 meetings in Fiji and Tuvalu this October. Come to the Pacific and confront what 1.5 degrees means for our water, our food, our homes and our people.

We welcome the General Assembly’s Declaration on Sea Level Rise, a significant achievement for the preservation of sovereignty and the first common text on sea level rise agreed by all Member States.

Our resilience must account for every hazard confronting our islands. In recent years Tonga has endured cyclones, flooding, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and tsunamis. The developing El Niño intensifies weather patterns and strains water and food security. We need integrated warning, preparedness and response systems that protect communities against the full range of these risks.

[Protecting Our Ocean, Unlocking Prosperity] Mr President,

Tonga has committed to protecting at least 30 per cent of our ocean by 2030. Our ratification of the Agreement on Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction extends that commitment beyond our waters, supporting the protection of marine biodiversity on the high seas. Its implementation must be fair and take account of the circumstances of Small Island Developing States.

Our task is to navigate a course that safeguards the ocean and unlocks its value for our people. This principle underpins Tonga’s Ocean Strategy: responsible management of ocean resources, stronger marine protection and a sustainable blue economy whose benefits reach our communities.

It is in this spirit that we intend to convene a Polynesian Ocean Summit in Tonga in May 2027, moving from shared ambition to practical action. We will bring governments, communities, scientists and partners together to strengthen ocean governance and generate lasting benefits for our people.

Our responsibility does not stop at the boundaries of our Blue Pacific Continent. Consider the humpback whale. Born in Tonga’s warm waters, it migrates to Antarctica to feed on krill before returning to the Pacific to breed. Tonga’s sanctuary protects whales here, but their survival depends on healthy ecosystems at both ends of that journey. What happens in the Southern Ocean near Antarctica is felt in Tonga’s waters. We invite partners to join us with practical commitments that recognise the interconnectedness of these ocean corridors.

[Energy Security and Technological Change] Mr President,

The same principle extends across our development: interconnection must not become dependency. For Tonga, resilience means taking greater control of the forces shaping our future and turning the resources within our geography into greater self sufficiency.

When we import fossil fuels, we also import their volatility. Moving away from them is both a climate imperative and an energy security necessity. We are expanding renewable generation, improving energy storage and strengthening our electricity grid while exploring sources suited to our islands, including geothermal energy.

Tonga is not short of ambition: 70 per cent renewable electricity by 2030 and 100 per cent by

2035. We welcome partnerships that help turn these goals into reliable and affordable power.

The forces shaping our future are increasingly technological. Digital connectivity and rapid technological advancement are transforming how we live. They offer significant opportunities for large ocean sovereign states, but risk creating new inequalities and dependencies.

Those who benefit last from global change often bear its highest costs. We continue to live with that injustice through climate change. We cannot again be asked to adapt only after the systems have been built and the rules written.

For Tonga, submarine cables and satellite links are foundational infrastructure connecting our islands to global opportunities. Connectivity alone is not enough. Digital skills and secure, resilient systems must support it. We will protect children online and retain sovereignty over our national data.

Tonga does not need to be first in artificial intelligence, quantum computing or every technology that follows. But we will not simply endure global transformation. We will exercise sovereignty by helping shape the rules and norms that govern it.

We are looking beyond conventional development models, seeking new forms of finance through the responsible valuation of our natural and ocean assets while exploring the potential of frontier technologies. We will form the right partnerships and direct innovation towards our priorities in climate forecasting, public health, ocean management, clean energy and disaster preparedness.

The Pacific’s data, ocean, biodiversity, critical minerals and traditional knowledge must not power the next technological revolution while returning only a fraction of their value to our people. Small Island Developing States need meaningful access to emerging capabilities and a voice in how these technologies are governed and shared.

[Conclusion] Mr President,

From experience, Tonga knows its challenges, and we will meet them with the determination that has always defined our people. We also know our strengths as a large ocean sovereign state. We are not asking for charity.

We will do our part. We simply ask that others do theirs: uphold the 1.5C degree threshold; help us protect the planet we all share and the ocean that connects us; ensure that everyone benefits from technological advancement; recognise the imbalance between the funds committed to our collective development challenges and those prepared for conflict; and uphold the rules and institutions that allow every nation to participate as an equal sovereign.

That is the promise at the heart of the United Nations. Not that all nations would be equal in power, but that no nation, however powerful, is more sovereign than another.

That is the multilateral system Tonga believes in: an international rules based order founded on the United Nations Charter and the equality of nations. That is the multilateral system we must preserve.

Mr President, I so submit.

Malo ‘aupito.

Let me begin by warmly congratulating His Excellency, Mr. Khalilur Rahman, on his election as President of the 81st Session of the General Assembly. The chosen theme for the general debate, “ Restoring Trust,

Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All,” could not be more timely. It speaks to the reality of the world we face today; a world shaped by uncertainty, disruption and rapid change, but also by hope, innovation and opportunity.

For Samoa, the theme is a promise the world must keep; Can trust be restored? Can transformation protect the vulnerable? The answer lies in the first words of our UN Charter - WE THE PEOPLES. We must always put PEOPLE at the centre of our decisions. For u s, this is underpinned by the core values of our Samoan culture the fa ́asamoa and our faith, such as respect, dignity, love, protection and service.

Excellencies,

Every decision in this Hall shapes the world that every child inherits.

We meet at a pivotal moment in history. Profound and transformative changes are not only necessary, but inevitable. Across many societies, people are increasingly asking whether global institutions are delivering on the promises made to them. We must prepare ourselves to face the challenges ahead with resolve, and use the opportunity to herald in much needed reforms for the benefits of all and leaving no one behind.

For Samoa, multilateralism remains the cornerstone of our international engagement. Only through genuine cooperation and mutual trust can we craft solutions that no single nation could achieve alone.

The UN80 initiative has merits but also its risks, if not fully assessed and understood. Any r eform must strengthen delivery on the ground, by eliminating duplication, improving coherence, and accelerating impact.

Critically, such reforms must not weaken the operations of the UN Multi Country Office s or the Resident Coordinator system. Whilst Samoa reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the United Nations as the premier forum to address global crises, we also caution against premature decisions taken without the full consideration and endorsement by member states.

Excellencies Climate change remains the single greatest threat to Samoa and the global community. Its impacts are more extensively felt by SIDS due to our special circumstances. As the ICJ advisory opinion puts it, climate change is not merely an environmental concern, but “an existential problem of planetary proportions” that requires urgent global action. The United Nations General Assembly welcomed the unanimous ICJ Advisory Opinion, and affirmed its importance as an authoritative contribution to the clarification of existing international law.

Climate finance is the bridge between ambition and action. It must be scaled up, easily accessible, devoid of burdensome conditions, and responsive to the needs of the most climate vulnerable. Resources intended for education, health, water and social protection are now diverted to disaster recovery.

Small nations are being asked to finance both development and survival. No nation should have to borrow its way out of a crisis it did so little to create.

Excellencies,

The world is facing a growing development financing crisis. The gap between commitments and delivery continues to widen. Too often, we simply rebrand and recycle old ideas while failing to deliver tangible progress. Meanwhile multilateralism is under siege, and international financial commitments are being eroded.

The current international financial architecture was designed for a different era. It struggles to adequately recognise vulnerability and fails to fully account for the realities faced by SIDS.

A fairer financial system is not only in the interests of developing countries.

It is in the interests of global stability and shared prosperity.

The implementation of the M ultidimensional Vulnerability Index (MVI) in financing decision -making is essential if we are to genuinely address the financial challenges facing developing countries. We thank the Secretary General and UN DESA for their proactive efforts in moving this issue forward with International Financial Institutions (IFIs). We look forward to the pilot project to demonstrate the MVI can help developing countries in their financing challenges.

On debt, we need to build a sustainable, equitable, and fair debt regime, starting with a robust mechanism for debt restructuring. Debt forgiveness must be linked to measurable progress on resilience -building. Investment in resilience today will reduce the costs of disasters tomorrow. Samoa supports the incorporation of state -contingent clauses in debt instruments, allowing for suspension during crises.

Excellencies,

Energy is both a driver and accelerator for Samoa’s sustainable development ambition. Energy security has become a defining issue for many small island nations.

While we have one of the highest shares of renewable electricity in the Pacific, Samoa remains heavily dependent on imported fuels. Successive energy crises, and the 2026 fuel crisis exposed the economic cost of our energy dependence. We are working towards a whole -of-system transformation that delivers electricity that is reliable and affordable, reduces our dependence on imported fuels, strengthens resilience and supports sustainable development.

The clean energy transition is also an opportunity for Samoa to build a smarter, more resilient and investment-ready energy system.

The digital transformation – including AI and data analytics – offers real opportunities to drive an inclusive, just energy transition, particularly through off-grid solutions and smarter energy planning.

Excellencies The ocean defines who we are as Pacific people. It connects us. Sustains us.

And shapes our identity. Yet our ocean faces increasing pressures from pollution, biodiversity loss, overexploitation and the impacts of climate change.

Pursuing economic growth has c ome at a grave cost to our marine ecosystems. Coupled with the unchecked exploitation of deep seabed mineral resources, our oceans face a crisis of limitless proportions. These planetary changes leave no middle ground. Weak governance frameworks threaten what remains.

Without urgent action, small island states face a future without land and no usable ocean.

It is time to transform how we value and interact with the ocean - from a resource we exploit to one we protect and cherish. We must do more on this front.

Samoa has ratified the BBNJ Agreement, and we remain actively engaged in negotiations towards a global treaty on plastic pollution, particularly to protect our marine environment.

We remain committed to implementing the Apia Commonwealth Ocean Declaration, the 2026 Pacific Islands Forum Leaders’ Ocean Statement, and our own Samoa Ocean Strategy. These are critical to the implementation of SDG14.

Our maritime domain is increasingly exploited by transnational criminal networks involved in illegal trafficking, including illicit drugs moving through our region. Illicit drugs enter homes, harm young people, fuel violence and place increasing pressure on communities and essential services.

Excellencies,

Non-communicable diseases represent one of the most serious development challenges to Samoa ́s public health and economic productivity. In response, we are shifting towards prevention through strengthening health literacy, reforming school nutrition and food environments and early intervention programmes. This includes our Early Childhood development framework, a multisectorial roadmap to ensure every child from pregnancy to age five receives nurturing care, protection and early learning.

Excellencies,

In many of our Pacific countries, our water systems are highly vulnerable to disruption. These realities demand that the global water agenda fully recognize the special circumstances of SIDS.

Samoa’s priorities are four-fold.

First, climate-resilient water systems must be scaled up urgently Second, access to finance must be significantly improved.

Third, capacity and partnerships must be strengthened.

Finally, we need a transnational water governance regime informed by the outcomes of the various water conferences held over the last 8 years.

Excellencies,

Samoa remains a peaceful country, steadfast in our commitment to human rights and justice. We remain concerned by the ongoing wars in Ukraine,

Gaza, and Iran. The terrible loss of civilian lives, displacement of people as well as the destruction of infrastructure and the environment is something we do not condone. The continued supply of weapons to fuel conflicts must end. We also reiterate our longstanding call for meaningful reform of the Security Council to ensure that it remains effective, credible and representative of today’s realities. It is imperative that the UN resolv es disputes peacefully and strengthens international peace and security.

The world needs a stronger commitment to peace. Not more division. Not more conflict. And not more suffering.

Excellencies,

At its heart, Samoa’s development journey is about investing in people. We are strengthening social protection, investing in youth, supporting women and persons with disabilities, and building a resilient economy. These efforts are championed through our District Development Program, delivered across all fifty one districts. Empowering our communities.

Our greatest source of resilience will not be our infrastructure or our institutions alone. It will be our people: healthy, skilled, educated and empowered. This is why the Aiga or family is at the heart of our pathway for development of Samoa.

Excellencies,

I pay tribute to our outgoing Secretary-General, António Guterres, for his steadfast leadership and enduring commitment to the United Nations. His legacy will continue to guide our collective efforts in advancing peace, dignity, and sustainable development for all.

Excellencies,

Before I am a leader, I am first and foremost a mother. History may record our titles, but our children will inherit our choices. This is why, now more than ever, the United Nations matters. We must continue to stan d, as One United Nations Family.

God bless, soifua ma ia manuia.

Mr. President, Secretary-General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, friends, and my fellow Kittitians and Nevisians at home and throughout the diaspora, I bring greetings from the proud twin-island Federation of Saint Kitts and Nevis and our Prime Minister, The Hon. Dr. Terrance Drew.

Mr. President, we extend my congratulations on your election as president of the 81st session of the General Assembly.We also express sincere appreciation o your predecessor for her stewardship over the past year.

I rise before this Assembly at a time when the world is not short of promises, declarations or commitments. What we need is proof that our institutions can respond to the realities people face. For Small Island Developing States like ours, that question is immediate. Saint Kitts and Nevis therefore comes with a clear proposition: trust will be restored not by what we promise, but by what we deliver. The time has come to move from promise to proof.

I come not only to speak about what the world must do, but to account for what we are doing.

National Delivery Under SISA Mr. President, last year our Prime Minister, the Hon. Dr. Terrance Drew, spoke of our Sustainable Island State Agenda (SISA), our national blueprint for transforming Saint Kitts and Nevis into a more resilient, sustainable, inclusive and prosperous society by 2040. Today, we return to demonstrate that it is becoming a record of delivery.

Earlier this year, our second Voluntary National Review to the United Nations High-Level Political Forum showed stronger government coordination, closer alignment with the Sustainable Development Goals, and tangible progress for our people.

Water provides one of the clearest measures of that progress.

One year ago, our two-million-gallon-per-day solar-powered desalination plant was nearing completion. In February, we commissioned it. Through semi airborne drone surveys, we also identified seventeen new potential groundwater sources and, in August, completed drilling at the first rural site. Together with distribution upgrades, these investments are strengthening water security.

In 2022, only about 25 percent of households had 24 -7 water; today, approximately 75 percent do. This is transformation!

On the island of Nevis, we are advancing a 30 -megawatt geothermal power development, with drilling expected by early 2027 and Icelandic Drillers contracted to begin the process. In Saint Kitts, plans for a 50-megawatt solar PV and battery storage project are well advanced. These investments will reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and strengthen economic resilience.

We are also strengthening food security through climate -smart support for farmers and healthcare through our locally developed National Digital Health Information System at the Joseph N. France General Hospital. Sustainability must be practical, people-centred and built to last.

Mr. President, there is more to do. But our experience proves that small states are not powerless. With investment, partnership and political will, small nations can deliver big solutions. Saint Kitts and Nevis is not seeking pity; we are advancing partnership.

A Sustainable Island State is not a distant ambition. We are building it today.

Climate Change Yet even as we advance, the climate crisis is moving the goalposts. This year, our Federation and the wider Caribbean face severe drought; by the end of May, rainfall was 44 percent below the long-term average. We are investing in resilient infrastructure, but no Small Island Developing State can adapt indefinitely to a crisis the world continues to intensify. Adaptation cannot excuse inaction elsewhere.

Distinguished colleagues, the science is unequivocal. The years 2015 to 2025 were the warmest on record, and in 2025 global average temperature remained about 1.43 degrees Celsius above the pre-industrial baseline, while global mean sea level stood approximately eleven centimetres higher than in 1993. For island nations, this is a question of sovereignty and statehood. If our coastlines retreat, our sovereignty must not.

Climate-induced sea-level rise must never erase a State's international legal personality, extinguish its UN membership, deprive its people of nationality, or diminish lawfully established maritime zones and sovereign rights. The International Law Commission has laid foundations for continuity of statehood, sovereignty and maritime entitlements. This Assembly must turn them into firm guarantees.

International law has spoken with increasing clarity. Saint Kitts and Nevis welcomed the International Court of Justice Advisory Opinion on States' climate obligations. Clarification must now become compliance, commitments must become conduct, and promises must become performance. States must reduce emissions, strengthen adaptation, honour climate-finance responsibilities and cooperate with countries bearing consequences vastly disproportionate to their contribution to this crisis.

Those who contributed least must not pay the greatest price.

Our oceans must also move from promises to protection. Saint Kitts and Nevis ratified the BBNJ in 2025. Implementation now matters: large ocean states need access to capacity-building, marine technology, scientific knowledge and financing, while benefits from marine genetic resources must be shared fairly.

For island nations, the ocean is not the space between us and the world; it is our highway, heritage, livelihood and lifeline.

MVI - From Recognition to Application Across climate action, sea-level rise and ocean governance, one reality remains: resilience has a cost. For decades, Small Island Developing States have argued that income is not the same as resilience. Per capita income cannot show exposure to hurricanes, drought, pandemics, shipping disruption, energy shocks, conflict or tourism collapse, nor how quickly one shock can erase years of investment.

This year, Saint Kitts and Nevis stood before the United Nations and completed a pilot Vulnerability and Resilience Country Profile under the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index Framework. And what did we learn? We learnt what our grandparents always knew. A house can look strong from the road and still have rot in the rafters. Vulnerability is not a statistic, it is a roof that was destroyed in hurricane Beryl. It is the school that became a shelter. It is the family rebuilding for the 3rd time in a decade because storms have no patience for GNI per capita.

We are not asking that Gross National Income be discarded; we are asking that it stop being expected to tell a story it was never designed to tell. GNI can count our coconuts and our cruise ships. It cannot count our courage and it cannot count the price we pay to simply remain. It cannot capture the cost of rebuilding the same bridge, clinic or seawall again and again, while nations twice our size and half our vulnerability borrow cheaper than we do.

We therefore call on the World Bank, the IMF, development banks, climate funds and every partner here to incorporate MVI into the architecture of financing. Not as charity, but as arithmetic and justice made real. If vulnerability can be measured, it must be considered.

Artificial Intelligence and the Emerging Digital Divide Mr. President, the next great divide between nations must not be digital. Artificial intelligence offers extraordinary possibilities. Saint Kitts and Nevis intends to participate. But we must ask who will shape this new age and who will live with decisions made elsewhere.

At the end of 2025, some 2.2 billion people remained offline. But the AI divide also concerns computing power, data, research, skills, energy, cybersecurity and capital. With the global AI market projected to reach about US 4.8 trillion dollars by 2033, developing countries cannot simply consume technologies designed and governed elsewhere. We must have a place where AI's future is decided.

Saint Kitts and Nevis welcomes the Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance. Inclusion must lead to capability. Developing countries need affordable computing power, infrastructure, skills and safeguards for privacy, data sovereignty, cybersecurity and rights. At home, we are advancing a Whole-of-Government Technology Strategy, securing digital identity and digital public services. Regionally, the Caribbean AI Task Force supports cooperation on governance, innovation and responsible adoption.

Artificial intelligence is already transforming the world.

Saint Kitts and Nevis chooses to help shape that transformation!

CARICOM, Diplomacy and Global Peace As small states, we know a simple truth: alone, we are small; together, we are formidable. The Caribbean's declaration as a Zone of Peace must retain its force as geopolitical competition moves closer to our shores. Our response must remain anchored in sovereignty, territorial integrity, international law, peaceful settlement of disputes and diplomacy. CARICOM supports the International Court of Justice as the lawful path for resolving the Guyana-Venezuela dispute and the judicial process concerning Belize and Guatemala.

We defend international law because, for small states especially, the alternative is a world where power becomes the rule. Across Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, Yemen,

Chad and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, civilians continue to bear an unconscionable burden. Saint Kitts and Nevis affirms one standard: international law applied consistently, not selectively; and conscience applied evenly, not conveniently.

There can be no hierarchy of human suffering.

Mr. President, the future of multilateralism also depends on its leadership.

Saint Kitts and Nevis proudly joins CARICOM in endorsing Her Excellency Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana for the office of United Nations SecretaryGeneral. Her distinguished record of service, commitment to multilateralism and understanding of the challenges facing developing nations reflect the leadership this moment demands. Her candidature, as an Indigenous woman from a small developing state, also reaffirms that global leadership must be defined not by the size of a nation, but by the vision, integrity and capacity of those called to serve.

Africa - Caribbean Cooperation Mr. President, few bridges carry greater historical meaning or future potential than that between Africa and the Caribbean. The Atlantic, once a passage of forced displacement and separation, is becoming a pathway of return and reconnection. Africa-Caribbean cooperation must move beyond sentiment; our shared history must help build a shared future through capital, trade, technology, knowledge, culture and coordinated diplomacy.

South-South cooperation must be felt in jobs, businesses, knowledge transfer and opportunity. It complements, not replaces, North-South cooperation and the obligations of developed countries.

Greater agency must also include justice. At the Second Africa -CARICOM Summit, our leaders signed the Addis Ababa Declaration, and this year, the African Union's reparations mechanisms and the CARICOM Reparations Commission held their first joint meeting, establishing permanent coordination.

On 25 March 2026, this General Assembly adopted Resolution 80/250, declaring the trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity. Saint Kitts and Nevis welcomed this historic recognition, but recognition cannot be the destination. Reparatory justice must move from recognition to remedy and from words to action.

Haiti, Cuba & Taiwan Distinguished colleagues, when we speak of reparatory justice, sovereignty and solidarity, Haiti cannot be an afterthought. Approximately 1.47 million people are internally displaced, while nearly half the population faces acute food insecurity. In the very near future, the first round of presidential and legislative elections will take place. The Haitian people must choose their leaders freely, credibly and safely. Saint Kitts and Nevis joins CARICOM in calling for the full deployment of the United Nations-authorised Gang Suppression Force and the timely renewal of its mandate, alongside Haitian-led recovery and governance.

Mr. President, we remain deeply concerned about the humanitarian situation in Cuba. St. Kitts and Nevis has contributed humanitarian relief to the Cuban people, and our very own Nationals studying there. We welcome the recent measures undertaken by the Cuban Government to improve the well-being of its people and encourage further meaningful action. We urge constructive dialogue between the Governments of Cuba and the United States. Engagement, mutual respect and cooperation offer the best path towards improving the lives of the Cuban people and advancing peace and stability throughout our region.

Saint Kitts and Nevis remains steadfast in its friendship with the Republic of China (Taiwan) and support for its meaningful international participation. Earlier this year, we joined other Member States in requesting Taiwan's observer participation in the Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly. We continue to support its meaningful participation in the World Health Organization, the International Civil Aviation Organization and other relevant mechanisms, and reiterate that differences across the Taiwan Strait must be resolved peacefully.

To The Young People, The Unseen Majority Mr. President, no generation has a greater stake in our decisions than young people. Half of the world's population is under thirty, yet 67 million young people were unemployed last year and more than a quarter of a billion were neither in employment, education nor training. AI, the green transition and climate change are reshaping their future jobs. We must prepare them.

Last year, our Prime Minister introduced this Assembly to our ASPIRE Programme - Achieving Success through Personal Investment, Resources and Education - for citizens aged 5 to 18. Built on savings, investment and financial education, ASPIRE has opened more than four thousand savings accounts, with our Government committing more than US 2 million dollars to give children a financial foundation for adulthood. We are now piloting our financial education curriculum in schools and training teachers for national rollout. We are not simply giving children money; we are giving them the knowledge to make money work for them. Financial independence must not be reserved for those born into wealth.

Conclusion Mr. President, distinguished colleagues, for eighty-one years this institution has represented a bold conviction: that despite our differences, nations can come together around common rules, responsibilities and human dignity. That conviction is worth defending. But institutions cannot live indefinitely on their founding promises. They must be judged by what those promises produce.

Saint Kitts and Nevis remains ready to do its part and to work with every nation here towards a more peaceful, sustainable, equitable and humane world.

Trust is not something we can demand. It must be earned: by promising less, delivering more, and letting the proof speak where our words once stood alone.

Let this Assembly be remembered not for what was said here, but for what was done after.

The tide is rising. Let our resolve rise faster still.

Thank you.

Your Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman, President of the United Nations General Assembly,

Your Excellency Mr. António Guterres, Secretary -General of the United Nations,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Peace be upon you.

Allow me to congratulate you, Excellency, on your election as President of the eighty-first session of the General Assembly. I wish you every success in conducting the work of this session, and express the Kingdom of Bahrain’s appreciation to your brotherly country, the People’s Republic of Bangladesh, as well as to the Secretary-General for his tireless efforts in the service of international peace and security, and the Sustainable Development Goals.

It is my honour to convey to this distinguished gathering the greetings of His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, King of the Kingdom of Bahrain, and of His Royal Highness Prince Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, Crown Prince and Prime Minister, and their b est wishes for the success of this session.

Mr. President,

You have chosen for this session a theme that speaks directly to the challenges before us: “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that delivers for All.” Trust is not restored through statements or by repeating appeals. It is restored by upholding the law and translating the decisions of this Organization into effective protection for people’s lives, rights and livelihoods.

We meet at a time when the Arabian Gulf is facing a security situation of a severity not witnessed in decades. The States of the Gulf Cooperation Council and the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan have been subjected to waves of unjustified Iranian attacks involv ing ballistic missiles and drones, targeting civilian infrastructure, residential areas, ports, airports and energy facilities, in flagrant violation of international law and the Charter of the United Nations. These are indiscriminate attacks without justification under any law.

My country also condemns the attacks carried out by the Iran -backed terrorist Houthi militia against civilian objects and Islamic holy sites in the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and their threats to freedom of navigation in the Bab Al Mandab and the Red Sea.

Allow me to put the facts before you in numbers. Our countries have been subjected to nearly 7000 attacks, involving 1,700 ballistic missiles, 80 cruise missiles and 5,220 drones.

Two thousand cargo vessels and tankers, with 20,000 seafarers on board, have also been detained, while 72 commercial vessels have been targeted, resulting in the deaths of 2 2 seafarers. These are not merely numbers. Behind every figure is a ship, a port, a market, and families waiting for those that provide for them to return home.

Commercial vessels have been targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, mines have been laid in an international shipping lane, and restrictions on passage have been imposed in contravention of international law. The consequences extend far beyond the Arabian Gulf, affecting energy and food prices, shipping and insurance costs, and supply chains across the world.

As the Kingdom renews its full solidarity with the brotherly countries subjected to these attacks, it commends the professionalism and readiness of the Bahrain Defence Force, and the air defence forces of brotherly countries, in confronting these attacks. It reaffirms the right of these States to take all lawful measures to defend their sovereignty and territorial integrity, in accordance with Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations and the Joint Defence Agreement of the Gulf Cooperation Council States, while continuing to exercise the utmost restraint and seeking to ensure that security and peace prevail for the benefit of the people of the region.

Mr. President,

The position of the Kingdom of Bahrain is grounded in law, not in taking sides. The Strait of Hormuz is an international strait, and the right of transit passage through it is established for the vessels of all States under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.

That right may not be suspended or obstructed, nor may conditions be imposed upon it unilaterally by any State. Accordingly, the Kingdom categorically rejects any permit or fee regime imposed on passage. It rejects the use of international waterways as instruments of pressure, economic coercion or the seizure of vessels. Such actions would set an extremely dangerous precedent, because what is accepted today in one strait may be demanded tomorrow in every international waterway upon which global trade depends.

Alternative routes cannot be treated as a solution to conduct that violates international law.

Mitigation measures are an emergency response. They should not be used as a pretext to claim that the Strait is no longer necessary, or to accept a new status quo. The right of passage does not cease to exist because alternatives are available, nor does a violation cease to be a violation because those affected have found ways to reduce their losses.

This threat is not confined to the Strait of Hormuz. Security Council resolution 2817 also referred to the Bab Al Mandab, recognizing that a threat to one waterway is a threat to navigation through all waterways. The security of navigation in the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the Bab Al Mandab forms part of a single system. We are not defending a regional interest, but a rule that applies to every international waterway, and if it applies to our strait alone, it would cease to be a rule.

The Kingdom of Bahrain has not confined itself to stating its position in principle. On behalf of the Gulf Cooperation Council States and the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, and by virtue of its current presidency of the Gulf Cooperation Council and its non -permanent membership of the Security Council, Bahrain led efforts resulting in the adoption of Security Council resolution 2817, with the historic and unprecedented support of 136 states, which condemned the attacks against our countries, reaffirmed their sovereignty, and rejected any action intended to close the Strait or obstruct navigation through it. The Kingdom also introduced a draft resolution under Chapter VII of the Charter to protect commercial navigation. The resolution adopted by the Council of the International Maritime Organization on 19 March, together with Human Rights Council resolution 61/1, further demonstrated that the international rejection of such conduct extends b eyond the Security Council. We stress the need for the full implementation of these resolutions in a manner that ensures those responsible are held accountable and compensation for the damage caused.

On the seventeenth of this month, the Kingdom convened an Arria-formula meeting of the Security Council dedicated to freedom of navigation. We heard from 53 affected States, the maritime transport sector and relevant international bodies. All delegations expressed one clear conclusion: freedom of passage through international straits is a prerequisite for global economic prosperity.

The Kingdom contributes to the protection of a rules -based maritime order across an area exceeding three million square miles through its hosting in Manama of the headquarters of the Combined Maritime Forces, comprising 47 nations. In this context, the Kingdom welcomes the establishment of the Multinational Maritime Defence Alliance led by the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and is proud to participate as a founding member, in support of efforts to safeguard international trade routes and global energy supplies, in accordance with international law.

As efforts continue in the Security Council, this General Assembly has an equally important role to play as the forum in which all States stand as equals. From this podium, we call upon Member States to support a firm, collective position which upholds freedom of navigation and the right of transit passage in accordance with international law, and which affirms that the security of maritime passages is a collective responsibility that cannot be made subject to bilateral arrangements. This is what restoring trust means in practice.

This is not a call dictated by the present crisis. From this very podium two years ago, His Royal Highness Prince Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, Crown Prince and Prime Minister, said that the systems established to safeguard the international order were under severe strain, and that this Organization must evolve to confront growing threats. He called for comprehensive, consensus -based reform encompassing all decision -making bodies, including the Security Council. What has happened since then has not altered that conviction. It has reinforced it.

Mr. President,

The test of the United Nations ’ credibility is not only confined to our waters. The Palestinian cause remains at the heart of our concerns. The Kingdom reaffirms its steadfast position in support of the establishment of an independent and geographically contiguous State of Palestine, living alongside the State of Israel in peace and security. The Kingdom has also joined the Board of Peace as a founding member, pursuant to Security Council resolution 2803, reaffirming its unwavering support for the rights of the brotherly Palestinian people.

The Kingdom also reaffirms its support for the unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Syrian Arab Republic, as well as for efforts to lift sanctions in a manner that enables the brotherly Syrian people to rebuild their country. In Sudan, we call for an immediate ceasefire, the protection of civilians, unhindered humanitarian access, and a political solution that preserves Sudan’s unity and the institutions of the State. In Yemen, we renew our support for a political solution under United Nations auspices, led by the legitimate Government, and express our appreciation for the efforts of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in this regard.

Our position on other conflicts, including the conflict in Ukraine, is guided by the same principles, regardless of the parties involved: adherence to the Charter, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and the peaceful settlement of disputes.

Mr. President,

The Kingdom of Bahrain, where mosques, churches and temples have stood side by side for generations, believes that tolerance and coexistence are not simply policies to be adopted. They are part of the identity of Bahraini society and a foundation of our na tional unity. It was in this spirit that the Kingdom introduced the initiative adopted by the General Assembly designating 28 January as the International Day of Peaceful Coexistence. His Majesty the King also issued the Kingdom of Bahrain Declaration on religious freedom and freedom of belief; the King Hamad Global Center for Coexistence and Tolerance was established; and the King Hamad Award for Coexistence and Tolerance was launched.

The same approach underpins our development journey. The Kingdom continues to advance its Economic Vision 2030, pursue its commitment to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, and strengthen the status and advancement of Bahraini women. The Kingdom embraces the Women, Peace and Security agenda, and the Youth, Peace and Security agenda, and both are priorities during its membership of the Security Council.

No discussion of development today is complete without addressing the technology that is reshaping it. From this podium two years ago, His Royal Highness the Crown Prince and Prime Minister called for the adoption of an international treaty governing the development of artificial intelligence, to ensure that this technology contributes to peace rather than exacerbating conflict. Since then, the General Assembly has taken positive steps. Dialogue can bring positions closer, but it does not create obligations. The aim is not to halt a technology that no one has the power to halt, but to ensure that its growth is surrounded by safeguards, just as the international community surrounded nuclear energy with safeguards that preserved its benefits without preventing it. This technology recognizes no borders; a safeguard adopted by a single state is no safeguard, just as a rule that applies in a single strait is no rule. We therefore renew our call for a binding international framework to ensure that this technology becomes a driver of innovation rather than division. And this, in our view, is what it means to manage the transformation that you chose as the theme of your session.

Mr. President,

However far apart they seem, all these issues are bound by one fundamental truth: security and prosperity are not parallel objectives. They are a single objective pursued along two paths. There can be no prosperity without security, and no sustainable security without interconnected economies and societies at ease. This is not a Gulf perspective dictated by geography. It is a lesson humanity has learned from its wars, and one Europe learned when it built its peace not through treaties alone, but on interests so intertwined that separating them became costlier than preserving them.

It is in this light that we view freedom of navigation. A waterway is not merely a security issue of concern for coastal States. It is an artery of development through which the food, medicine and energy of nations flow. When a single waterway is disrupted, the cost is felt by a family in a country that does not have a coastline.

An economy that is difficult to disrupt is difficult to coerce, and interdependence, once firmly established, becomes a shield against coercion.

This approach is not a position shaped by the circumstances of the moment. It is what His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, King of the Kingdom of Bahrain, has consistently advocated for, out of a conviction that the security and prosperity of this region are two faces of a single truth, and that a just peace and lasting stability are the path towards a dignified life for all the peoples of the region, whatever their faiths and cultures.

It is on this basis that we reaffirm that what the United Nations needs today is not more resolutions, but a greater capacity to implement them. A resolution adopted but not implemented has no value, and a right that is recognized but not protected has no meaning.

I conclude by saying that the Kingdom of Bahrain continues to be guided by His Majesty’s vision. For peace, as His Majesty sees it, is not declared but built. It can rest only on respect for human beings in their dignity and their beliefs, and on dialogue that is not a concession, but a strength.

The Kingdom will remain faithful to its international commitments and covenants, committed to international law, freedom of navigation, and a just, comprehensive and lasting peace, true to His Majesty’s approach and to the conviction that the security of our region and the prosperity of its peoples are a shared responsibility that can only be safeguarded through our collective efforts.

We pray to Almighty God to grant this session every success, and to bestow upon our peoples and all humanity security, peace, development and prosperity.

Thank you and peace be upon you.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

At the outset, I warmly congratulate His Excellency Mr. Khalilur Rahman on assuming the Presidency of the 81st session of the General Assembly, and wish him every success in this important position.

I also thank His Excellency Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary -General of the United Nations, for his endeavors.

Ladies and gentlemen,

As global challenges become increasingly complex, no country can address them alone. And yet, the growing limitations of multilateral mechanisms continue to undermine our collective ability to respond effectively to current and emerging threats.

Meeting these realities requires joint action, but true transformation is impossible without first restoring trust in the international order and demonstrating that multilateralism can once again deliver tangible results for all.

In an era marked by division, growing intolerance and stark double standards,

Azerbaijan advocates for a reinvigorated and reformed multilateral system, underpinned by strict adherence to consistent and non -selective application of universally accepted norms and principles of international law.

Azerbaijan supports a more effective UN capable of delivering tangible results for Member States, especially in peace and security, development, climate resilience, and humanitarian action.

Through inclusive multilateralism, all States, large or small, particularly developing countries, must have the opportunity to participate equally in global decision -making.

In this context, reform of the UN Security Council is essential to make it more representative, effective, and responsive.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Restoring global trust begins, first and foremost, with respecting international law, sovereign equality, and peaceful coexistence. It is exactly these principles that are guiding our efforts for peace and stability in the South Caucasus.

Even though the decades-long conflict with Armenia brought immense tragedy to our people and left deep scars across our land, Azerbaijan has chosen to look ahead and turn the page of enmity.

We offered Armenia peace fully in line with norms and principles of international law, based on mutual recognition of and respect for each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Our normalization efforts produced historic results at the Washington Peace Summit last August, where the leaders of Azerbaijan and Armenia signed a Joint Declaration witnessed by President Trump of the United States of America. Through this Declaration, both sides confirmed the end of the conflict and their will to jointly chart a peaceful and prosperous future. The sides also initialed the Agreement on Establishment of Peace and Inter-State relations.

Today, we have achieved de facto peace. Moreover, by unilaterally lifting transit restrictions, Azerbaijan facilitates transportation of goods to and from Armenia. We have also established bilateral trade. Azerbaijan provides strategically important oil products to Armenia on a regular basis despite increased volatility in markets and growing international demand for these commodities.

As we proceed with the peace agenda initiated by Azerbaijan, our entire region is now turning into a promising anchor of stability, connectivity, and tangible economic dividends.

To make this process irreversible, it is of crucial importance to eliminate the remaining obstacle, which will allow finalization of the normalization process through the signing of the already initialed bilateral agreement.

Excellencies,

Complementing the regional normalization process, Azerbaijan’s post -conflict rehabilitation agenda aims to ensure that hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis can eventually exercise their right to a safe and dignified return to their homes.

Due to large-scale reconstruction efforts taken by the Government, life is now returning to our liberated territories. Azerbaijan is rebuilding the entire region through “smart cities” and “smart villages” powered by green technology. Areas that were once rubble and ashes are now rising as modern settlements. Today, more than 90,000 people live, study, and work in the liberated territories.

Regrettably, a massive contamination of the territories of Azerbaijan with landmines and other explosive devices remains a serious obstacle. This significantly obstructs the reconstruction and return process. Since the liberation of occupied territories in 2020, more than 400 individuals, including women and children, became victim to landmines. The cumulative toll of landmines over the past 30 years exceeded 3500 persons.

Given the scale of the problem, Azerbaijan considers mine action an essential prerequisite for fulfilling human rights and has formally declared humanitarian demining its 18th National Sustainable Development Goal.

Similarly, the need to clarify the fate and whereabouts of nearly 4000 Azerbaijanis who went missing due to the conflict is essential, not only for accountability and the rights of the victims and their families, but also for post -conflict reconciliation a nd normalization.

Mr. President,

In the face of increasingly complex global challenges, our collective response must be inclusive, equitable and universal.

Azerbaijan’s own experience reflects these principles. Our society is inherently multicultural and multi -confessional, shaped by centuries of peaceful coexistence of diverse ethnic, cultural and religious communities.

This tradition is reflected in Azerbaijan’s international initiatives, including the World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue. Launched in 2008, in the framework of the “Baku Process”, the Forum has evolved into a prominent global platform for advancing intercultural dialogue and cultural diversity, receiving international recognition, including through a series of United Nations General Assembly resolutions.

Building upon these values, under the leadership of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, H.E. Mr. Ilham Aliyev, Azerbaijan has taken important steps to strengthen international solidarity, to build bridges and to mobilize collective responses.

This commitment has also been demonstrated through successful hosting and steering of major global gatherings, including COP29, the 13th session of the World Urban Forum, results -oriented chairmanships of the Non -Aligned Movement, the Organization of Turki c States and the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia, and Azerbaijan’s increasingly active engagement across other international platforms. Azerbaijan’s full-fledged membership in the Consultative Meeting of Heads of State of Central Asia and the C6 format will enhance our contribution to cooperation and connectivity within the region and beyond.

COP29 provided a good example of this approach in practice. As host and Presidency,

Azerbaijan guided negotiations towards ambitious and balanced outcomes while working to ensure that all voices were heard. The conference delivered several historic agreements, including the tripling of the global climate finance goal, full operationalization of Article 6 carbon -market mechanisms, and further advancement of arrangements supporting the Loss and Damage Fund for vulnerable communities affected by climate change.

Our efforts to advance climate action likewise did not end with COP29. Azerbaijan continues to build on its legacy, with particular focus on translating negotiated outcomes into practical implementation. This September, for the first time, Baku hosted the UNFCCC Climate Week, bringing together governments, international organizations, the private sector and other stakeholder s to advance implementation and practical solutions.

Azerbaijan’s commitment to international solidarity and cooperation is equally reflected in our development and humanitarian assistance. In recent years, Azerbaijan has significantly expanded the scope of its international aid, with particular attention to Small Island Developing States and African partner countries. Since 2020, we have provided humanitarian, economic and technical assistance worth approximately USD 400 million to more than 140 countries.

As we mark the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development,

Azerbaijan reaffirms its commitment to partnership -based approaches founded on solidarity, mutual respect and shared development priorities.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

As we inch closer to 2030, it is becoming ever more apparent that the world remains off track in implementing the Sustainable Development Goals.

Azerbaijan is firmly committed to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, having integrated the SDGs into its national development strategies, institutional frameworks, and Voluntary National Review processes, while placing particular emphasis on conn ectivity, green growth, digitalization, and sustainable urban development.

In less than two decades, Azerbaijan’s GDP has increased threefold, while the poverty rate has declined from 49% to around 5%. At the same time, Azerbaijan maintains one of the lowest levels of public external debt globally.

Our commitment also extends to advancing sustainable development through effective and accountable institutions. At Azerbaijan’s initiative, on 30 March 2026, the UN Human Rights Council adopted by consensus, for the third time, the resolution entitled “Promoting Human Rights and the Sustainable Development Goals through Transparent, Accountable and Efficient Public Service Delivery.” Co -sponsored by more than 100 Member States, the resolution underscores the essential role of citizencentered, transparent and efficient public institutions in advancing human rights and accelerating progress towards the SDGs.

Azerbaijan’s innovative ASAN and DOST models of transparent, accessible and citizen-centered public service delivery have gained international recognition and are increasingly being adopted by dozens of partner countries.

Sustainable urbanization is another important pillar of our approach to the 2030 Agenda. Resilient cities are essential to improving quality of life, strengthening communities and promoting inclusive economic and social development. In this context, Azerbaijan’s successful hosting of the 13th session of the World Urban Forum marked an important contribution to the global urban agenda. The key outcomes of the Forum – the Baku Call to Action and the Chair’s Summary – subsequently contributed to the High -level Meeting of the General Assembly on midterm review of the New Urban Agenda, held in New York in July this year.

At the same time, environmental protection remains an important national and regional priority. We are particularly concerned by continuing decline of the Caspian Sea, with serious implications for biodiversity, livelihoods and economic activity across the region. As a challenge shared by all Caspian littoral States, it requires a coordinated, collective and sustained response.

Excellencies,

While remaining firmly committed to our climate goals, we must also recognize that, in the immediate term, development cannot realistically proceed without traditional energy sources.

Energy security, moreover, is closely intertwined with peace, regional connectivity, and sustainable economic development.

As a reliable natural gas supplier to 16 countries, Azerbaijan ranks among the leading pipeline gas suppliers globally and plays a strategic role in strengthening energy security and diversifying supply routes across Europe and beyond.

Azerbaijan’s contribution to global energy security is increasingly complemented by its growing role in the clean energy transition. We are investing in renewable energy, commissioning major solar and wind projects, expanding hydropower capacity and developing new clean energy initiatives together with leading international partners.

Agreements already signed envisage around 6 GW of additional solar and wind capacity by 2030.

By 2030, renewables are expected to generate almost 40% of Azerbaijan’s electricity.

Expansion of renewable power generation will create new opportunities for Azerbaijan to export green electricity to European markets.

This way, our role as a reliable energy partner is evolving alongside the global energy transition.

Energy connectivity is part of Azerbaijan’s broader vision of connecting regions, markets and economies.

Azerbaijan has emerged as a key transport and logistics hub between Europe and Asia, contributing to major trans -regional connectivity initiatives, investing in modern transport infrastructure and expanding cooperation with regional partners.

Since 2022, we have witnessed an increase in cargo volumes along the Middle Corridor by almost 90%. Strategic infrastructure projects along the Middle Corridor spearheaded by Azerbaijan, including the Baku International Sea Trade Port and the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway, are helping to create more resilient, diversified and sustainable supply chains between Asia and Europe.

This growth demonstrates the Middle Corridor’s considerable potential as a key driver of regional connectivity, trade facilitation and sustainable economic development.

Our connectivity agenda extends beyond energy and transport. Digital connectivity offers another important area for regional cooperation. Azerbaijan is advancing new digital links across the region through ambitious initiatives, such as the Digital Silk Way. This project envisages an advanced fiber-optic network across the Caspian Sea, further strengthening Azerbaijan’s role as a regional digital hub and a key link between Europe and Asia.

This broader connectivity agenda is also closely linked to the emerging peace architecture in the South Caucasus.

The “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP), another key outcome of the 2025 Washington Summit, is expected to facilitate unimpeded multimodal connectivity between the main part of Azerbaijan and its Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic and unlock new opportunities for regional trade, economic integration and prosperity as part of the Zangazur corridor.

Mr. President,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

In conclusion, I wish to reiterate that our shared challenges demand renewed global solidarity, more effective and trusted multilateralism grounded in international law, and a reinvigorated system of cooperation.

Trust, however, must be restored through concrete actions. Peace must be built on the ground, commitments must be translated into real outcomes, and sustainable development must deliver meaningful improvements in people’s lives.

Azerbaijan has consistently upheld the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and demonstrated its firm adherence to international law, including respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, non -interference in the internal affairs of States, sove reign equality, dialogue and cooperation, as well as the faithful, consistent and non-selective implementation of agreed commitments.

This is the multilateralism we believe in – principled, inclusive and, above all, capable of delivering tangible results.

I thank you.
