Mr. President,

Distinguished Delegates,

I congratulate His Excellency Mr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the eighty -first session of the General Assembly and assure him that he can count on Kazakhstan’s full support throughout this session.

Excellencies,

Kazakhstan remains firmly committed to the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations and to effective multilateral cooperation.

Guided by a pragmatic and proactive foreign policy, we continue our efforts to strengthen international peace and security and to advance pragmatic solutions to our shared global challenges.

For Kazakhstan, multilateralism is a key instrument for building trust, finding common gro und, and delivering results for our citizens and future generations. It is a key component of our own long-term social economic development.

Kazakhstan has embarked on profound political transformation in response to societal demand and emerging challenges.

Our new Constitution reinforces the foundations of national sustainable development by placing greater emphasis on human dignity, human capital, education, innovation, and environmental responsibility.

We have also continu ed to strengthen the rule of law, public accountability and the protection of human rights. Elections last month to the new Kuryltai brought into parliament a diverse set of voices, including a historic high 34% of women.

Mr. President,

I express my country’s grave concern as the world continues its slide toward uncertainty and division.

The erosion of trust among nations is rapidly reshaping the international order. Our collective inability to prevent conflicts, our collective indiffere nce toward humanitarian crises, and our collective reluctance to seek common solutions to shared challenges are all becoming normalized.

Trust cannot be restored when international law is applied selectively and commitments remain unfulfilled.

Our response must be grounded in the fundamental values we have affirmed together: freedom, equality, justice, and respect for human dignity.

President Tokayev has repeatedly underscored the indispensable role of the United Nations as a single universal platform, uniquely capable of bringing the States together to address the challenges we face.

But to fulfil its potential, UN must be able to act, adapt, and deliver.

We fully support the UN-80 initiative.

The success of the reform should be measured not by what is cut or reorganized, but by whether the United Nations prevents conflict more effectively, responds more rapidly to crises and delivers better results for all member States.

Central to this renewal is reform of the Security Council. Broader representation of Asia, Africa and Latin America in the Council, as well as a greater voice for developing countries and for middle powers is a moral imperative.

Equitable geographical representation must apply throughout the United Nations system as a condition of legitimacy and credibility.

The selection of the next Secretary-General will be one of the defining moments of this session.

Kazakhstan supports a tran sparent, inclusive and merit-based process conducted in full accordance with the Charter.

Mr. President,

The international security environment continues to deteriorate. World military expenditure s reached a record 2.9 trillion dollars in 2025. Our small planet is home to more than twelve thousand nuclear weapons, each one capable of untold damage and sorrow. Every year, we seem to lose more biodiversity yet gain more armaments.

For Kazakhstan, nuclear disarmament in particular is not an abstract doctrine. It is a responsibility born of national experience.

This year marks thirty-five years since the closure of the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site, thirty years since the CTBT opened for signature, and twenty years since the signing of the Semipalatinsk Treaty on a Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone in Central Asia.

Our experience of renouncing the world’s fourth largest nuclear arsenal d id not weaken our State. To the contrary through international trust, it strengthens sovereignty, enhance s security and promotes development.

Today, that trust is again in danger. New START has expired, while the 2026 NPT Review Conference ended without substantive outcome for the third consecutive cycle.

Nuclear weapon states must never confuse the absence of agreement with a vacuum of obligation.

They remain responsible until we secure a world free of nuclear weapons.

Kazakhstan advocates the relaunch of high-level dialogue among nuclear powers and is ready to host one of their next meetings.

We will also continue advancing our earlier proposal to strengthen the BWC through establishing an International Agency for Biological Security.

Distinguished Delegates,

Peace and stability are a prerequisite for sustainable development. We stand firmly for diplomacy and dialogue, and against the escalation of tension and the use of force.

We remain deeply concerned by the Ukrainian crisis, which continues to take lives, erode global trust and undermine international security.

Even the most difficult conflicts must ultimately be resolved through diplomacy and negotiation.

Beyond the tragic loss of life, Kazakhstan strongly condemns the repeated drone attacks against Kazakh crude oil export infrastructure, including against commercial vessels in the Black Sea basin.

Such incidents endanger civilian navigation, disrupt international trade, and threaten the stability of global energy supplies.

We call on all parties to uphold international law and take all necessary measures to protect critical infrastructure and ensure the safety and continuity of civilian commerce.

Political and diplomatic means remain the only viable path towards ending hostilities and achieving a sustainable resolution of the Middle East crisis.

The ongoing escalation carries serious implications for regional and international peace and security, as well as for economic stability, transport connectivity and energy security.

A just and lasting peace in the Middle East requires an independent, sovereign, and viable State of Palestine living side by side with Israel in peace and security.

We support the New York Declaration as a framework for tangible, time -bound and irreversible steps towards the two-State solution.

My country stands ready to support every effort aimed at maintaining unhindered humanitarian assistance, protection of civilians and the recovery of Gaza.

Kazakhstan calls for the full and good -faith implementation of the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict and Security Council resolution 2803.

As a member of the Board of Peace, President Tokayev has committed to contribute to the stabilization of Gaza, by supporting civilian reconstruction, ensuring food security, and providing digital gover nment solutions.

Kazakhstan’s peacekeepers in UNDOF and UNIFIL reflect our readiness to assume practical responsibility and contribute to the internationally mandated stabilization forces in Gaza.

Kazakhstan formally announced its intention to join the Abraham Accords. We see them as an additional platform to reinforce the UN-brokered political process towards a two-State solution.

The long -term stability of Afghanistan remains inseparable from the security and sustainable development of Central Asia. Humanitarian assistance remains indispensable, but it cannot by itself break the cycle of poverty, displacement and dependency.

Kazakhstan supports pragmatic, coordinated and step-by-step international engagement with Afghanistan, with the UN playing the central role.

Finally, we have watched with growing concern in recent years the erosion of the protection of civilians in conflict zones. In response, together with Brazil, China,

France, Jordan, South Africa and the ICRC,

Kazakhstan is advancing the Global Initiative to Galvanize Political Commitment to International Humanitarian Law.

Mr President,

The growing role of middle powers in global affairs is opening new avenues for practical cooperation to achieve SDGs.

Kazakhstan is working with the United Nations to operationalize the United Nations Regional Centre for the Sustainable Development Goals for Central Asia and Afghanistan in Almaty.

Its success should be measured by what it delivers. I thank my colleagues, the Foreign Ministers of Central Asia, for helping s hape a practical and focused agenda for the Centre.

Reaffirming our commitment to (Declaration of AlmaAta and the Declaration of Astana ) advancing primary health care as the cornerstone of universal health coverage, we call upon UN Member States to join the Global Coalition on Primary Health Care.

2026 has been designated by this body as the International Year of Volunteers for Sustainab le Development. This initiative, originally at President Tokayev’s suggestion, has given new impetus to volunteerism as a force for stronger communities, youth engagement, and environmental action.

In Kazakhstan and elsewhere, hundreds of thousands of people have joined volunteer activities.

Excellencies,

Environmental challenges are among the defining issues of our time. Climate change, biodiversity loss, land degradation and the growing frequency of natural disasters are placing increasing pressure on our societies and economies.

The Regional Ecological Summit, held in Astana in April, reaffirmed that climate, water, food and health challenges cannot be addressed in isolation.

Its declaration «Environmental Solidarity of Central Asia», provides a strong foundation for advancing regional cooperation on environmental protection and sustainable development.

On the same day, the Heads of State of the founding countries of the International Fund for Saving the Aral Sea (IFAS) declared an International Day of the Aral Sea and the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, with the aim of raising global awareness of the region’s environmen tal challenges and mobilizing greater international support for their preservation.

We are grateful for the support of UN Member States and partners for President Tokayev’s proposal to proclaim 22 April as the International Day of Greening of the Planet, aimed at amplifying global efforts to restore ecosystems.

Kazakhstan pursues a human-centered approach to contemporary challenges, emphasizing peacebuilding, dialogue, and cooperation as an essential response to the complex global challenges of our time.

This approach is underpinned by a broader mental shift towards environmental stewardship, civic engagement, and care for the public good.

It is reflected in nationwide efforts to improve public spaces, advance large -scale greening, and promote the values of respect for the rule of law, active and responsible patriotism, volunteerism, and compassion as integral elements of everyday life and civic culture.

This brings us to another critical to pic of our days. Healthy ecosystems depend on water. Water security is fundamental to the well-being and resilience of our societies.

Water underpins public health, food and energy security, climate resilience and peace. Yet, despite its fundamental importance, global water governance remains fragmented.

The recent devastating floods in the mountainous regions of Nepal and China remind us of the growing risks associated with water - and climate -related disasters.

In this context, President Tokayev has proposed the establishment of an International Water Organization under the auspices of the United Nations. The purpose is to make international water governance more coherent, accountable and capable of effective implementation.

Kazakhstan calls for an inclusive, Member Stateled process to explore options for strengthening the institutional architecture for water within the United Nations.

We will continue to advance this discussion in the lead-up to the 2026 United Nations Water Conference in Abu Dhabi.

Kazakhstan stands ready to work with all Member States and partners to advance this common agenda.

Distinguished Delegates,

Artificial intelligence and rapid technological change present another area where urgent international cooperation is needed.

At home, we are investing in computing capacity, digital infrastructure and AI skills. We are forging new trusted partnerships on AI governance and emerging technologies. And we have recently adopted a Law on Artificial Intelligence and a new Digital Code.

But without effective governance at all levels, it will also deepen inequality, create new security risks – as we have seen very recently – and widen the digital divide.

We also should not let ethical norms fall behind this rapid evolution. AI must remain human -centered, safe and subject to meaningful human oversight.

These risks are particularly serious in the military domain, where the use of AI in warfare and cyber operations could have far-reaching consequences for international stability.

Kazakhstan supports stronger international rules and cooperation, including through the United Nations Global Mechanism on ICT Security and UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance.

At the regional level, we invite partners to engage with the UN ESCAP Asia -Pacific Digital Solutions Centre in Almaty as a platform for sharing expertise and advancing regional digital cooperation.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

One thing is clear: there is a g lobal trust deficit.

Restoring trust will take time. But greater trust will not just appear like magic, it is the result of increased, not decreased, international cooperation. We must build it.

That system of international cooperation we call multilateralism, in whose famous hall we stand today, depends on us, just as we depend on it. True, the institutions of multilateralism must deliver tangible benefits, but equally true, we the member states must honor our commitments, adhere to global standards, and work together.

Kazakhstan will remain a reliable partner for peace, security and sustainable development. We will continue to choose cooperation over confrontation and work with all Member States to strengthen the United Nations and turn our shared commitments into meaningful action.

I thank you.

Mr. President,

Allow me to congratulate you on your election to the Presidency of the General Assembly and assure you of the support of my delegation.

I also wish to pay tribute to H is Excellency António Guterres for his outstanding dedication and commitment to this Organisation during his two terms as Secretary General. He will be remembered as a leader with a steady hand always guided by principles of fairness, compassion, and dignity for all.

Mr. President,

The United Nations has now completed the first eight decades of its existence.

Eight decades replete with resolutions, declarations and action on decolonization, development, new international order, the new constitution for the oceans, as well as climate and the environment, technology, human rights, international law and peacekeeping.

81st Session of the UN General Assembly Created in the aftermath of the Second World War, the immediate focus was obviously on peace and security. But the UN system has evolved significantly over the decades to expand its scope and sphere of influence, within the confines of its Charter.

However, the UN must now look to the future, building on its record of achievements as well as from lessons learned from what it could not achieve.

UN Reform As we look to the next eighty years, we must ask ourselves a searching question: is the UN fit for the purpose for the 21 st century— not the world of 1945, but the world of today and beyond?

We are entering a new era of international relations defined by unprecedented technological developments.

Often absent from the table where the rules of tomorrow are being adopted, developing countries risk being left further behind.

The same exclusion afflicts the international financial architecture, which remains skewed against the Global South.

Developing nations must have a seat at the table as equal stakeholders.

81st Session of the UN General Assembly We all acknowledge that the three pillars of the UN Charter are: Peace and Security; Development and Human Rights. The twin institutional pillars provided in the Charter were, and still are, the Security Council and ECOSOC as the apex bodies for achieving these purposes. However, over the years, optimal use has been made primarily of only one of these organs.

We need to enhance and accelerate the revitalisation of the General Assembly and that of ECOSOC so that they are not merely forums for debate, but engines of action.

This must be done as we bring about the reform of the Security Council.

The historical injustice regarding the composition of the Council was acknowledged in Action 39 of the Pact for the Future but the process for reform is still stalled. Mauritius fully supports the Common African Position — the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration — calling for no fewer than two permanent and five non -permanent African seats on the Council. Mauritius also supports the call for SIDS to have a seat on a reformed Council.

On the question of the veto, Mauritius aligns itself with the position of a growing number of States that in the event the veto is retained, any new permanent member must have the same rights as the original permanent members.

Mauritius also supports the Franco -Mexican Initiative on the suspension of the veto in cases of mass atrocities.

81st Session of the UN General Assembly We support the positions of the G4 and of L69 on Council reform, and we reiterate our support for India's candidature for a permanent seat, commensurate with its constructive role in global affairs.

Mr. President,

Mauritius welcomes the increasing recourse to the International Court of Justice as a mechanism for the peaceful settlement of disputes and determination of issues of international law. We call upon Member States which have not yet done so to accept the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ.

We welcome the landmark, unanimous Advisory Opinion of the ICJ on the obligations of States in respect of climate change. This was a vindication of the tireless advocacy of Vanuatu and the Core Group of States. Mauritius was proud to stand among them.

We call for the full operationalization of this Advisory Opinion, including through the follow -up action requested by this Assembly, in accordance with the UN General Assembly landmark resolution of 20 May 2026, welcoming the Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice on the obligations of States in respect of climate change.

We also support the legal principle — affirmed by the ICJ - that States are under no obligation to update their maritime baselines or zones to account for climateinduced sea level rise. Mauritius calls for th e principle that statehood and sovereignty are not impacted by sea level rise, to be formally codified.

81st Session of the UN General Assembly Mr President,

Water stands at the frontline of the climate crisis. Water is a major concern globally, and Mauritius welcomes the holding of the UN Water Conference in December this year. We look forward to this crucial global issue being addressed by the international community as a matter of urgency.

We also call for enhanced, accessible, and predictable climate finance accompanied by comprehensive capacity-building and disaster -risk management for the most vulnerable.

I also wish to highlight that Mauritius is currently conducting a constitutional review exercise which will include giving constitutional protection to the Rights of Nature.

Development Financing Mr. President,

The crisis in development financing is deepening. Concessional financing for developing countries is declining precisely when the need is greatest.

The graduation of countries, including Small Island Developing States, should be encouraged and supported and not prejudice access to affordable finance.

Mauritius calls for a review of the criteria for access to concessional financing, that reflect vulnerability rather than income per capita alone.

81st Session of the UN General Assembly We also call for the strengthening of the rules -based multilateral trading system and for fair, transparent, and equitable mechanisms for resolving trade disputes.

Mr. President,

New Technologies The rapid evolution of digital and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, is already shaping economic, social, and institutional developments across the globe. We support the GA resolution establishing the Global Dialogue on AI Governance and welcome the work being done by the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.

For Mauritius, digital innovation is a developmental imperative. We have launched, with UN support, a National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 –2029 and a National Fintech Strategy 2026–2030.

We need an open, transparent and inclusive dialogue on governance of the new technologies which ensures that the benefits of technological progress are shared equitably and that the risks are managed collectively.

Mr. President,

Oceans As a coastal state with an EEZ of 2.2 million square kilometres — that is, more than one thousand times our land mass — Mauritius is profoundly connected to the ocean.

81st Session of the UN General Assembly We reaffirm our unwavering commitment to UNCLOS as the legal framework governing all activities in the oceans including the seabed and subsoil beyond national jurisdiction.

We welcome the decisions of the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf approving the submission lodged by Mauritius in December 2008 and approved in March 2011 as well as the second one filed in May 2009 and approved in July 2026.

We welcome the 100th ratification of the BBNJ Agreement and calls for its prompt and effective implementation. We look forward to its first Conference of the Parties advancing the institutional, financial, and procedural arrangements necessary for the effective implementation of the Agreement.

Collaboration is key to effective maritime security, maritime surveillance and Domain Awareness. We call on the international community to support regional and sub-regional initiatives in this regard. I am pleased to inform that Mauritius, with the support of the European Union and the Commission de l’Océan Indien, will host a Ministerial Conference on Cybercrime and Sea Cables security in the Western Indian Ocean in the first quarter of 2027.

Mr. President,

Mauritius welcomes the major developments taking place across Africa with regard to gre ater integration and pooling of resources particularly in relation to capacity building. I n this regard, Mauritius has initiated action at the UN for 81st Session of the UN General Assembly promoting enhanced regulatory frameworks in developing countries namely through pooling of resources.

Mauritius attaches great importance to the elimination of all forms of racism, racial discrimination, and xenophobia. We welcome the High -Level Meeting on this subject and reaffirm our commitment to the International Decade for People of African Descent.

Mauritius is fully committed to supporting the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women and the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action. Earlier this year, Mauritius adopted new legislation to further enhance the protection of women’s rights.

Mr. President,

SDGs We are deeply concerned by the effects of regional conflicts and instability on development, economic growth, food security and the achievement of SDGs.

The crisis in the Gulf and threats to freedom of navigation have sent shockwaves across the global economy. For a small, open economy such as Mauritius, which depends on maritime trade routes for over 90% of its primary energy imports and more than 70% of its food supply, these effects are felt acutely.

We call for restraint, for dialogue, and for a durable diplomatic resolution.

81st Session of the UN General Assembly Palestine Mauritius reaffirms its longstanding position in support of the inalienable right of the Palestinian people to self -determination and to an independent, sovereign state, with East Jerusalem as its capital, living in peace and security alongside its neighbours. The cycle of violence must end. Too many people have suffered for far too long. We note with deep concern that the establishment of unlawful settlements may be a major obstacle to peace.

Mr. President,

Chagos Archipelago I now come to an issue which for Mauritius is non -negotiable, it concerns our sovereignty over the Chagos Islands. The agreement on the Chagos Archipelago, signed by Mauritius and the United Kingdom in May 2025, stands as living proof that trust in multilateralism and UN judicial organs can achieve the peaceful settlement of disputes and the completion of our nation's decolonisation and restore the rights of Mauritians of Chagossians origin by force of law.

Trust especially amongst neighbours and in the region is reinforced when there is the respect for the rule of law, for the resolutions of the United Nations General Assembly, the ruling of the International Tribunal on the Law of the Sea, and the ICJ’s Advisory Opinion on the Chagos Archipelago, which carries authoritative obligations.

81st Session of the UN General Assembly We trust that States which laid the foundation of the new post war legal order will recommit to full respect and compliance with international law and correct this historical injustice without delay, as William Ewart Gladstone, four -term British Prime Minister and great campaigner for peace and freedom put it, “Justice delayed is justice denied.”

Monsieur le Président,

Tromelin L’île de Tromelin fait partie intégrante du territoire de la République de Maurice.

Nous avons constamment maintenu notre position concernant la souveraineté de la République de Maurice sur cette île.

Nous réitérons notre appel à la France à s’engager de manière constructive en vue du règlement du différend relatif à l’île de Tromelin, dans l’esprit d’amitié qui caractérise les relations entre nos deux pays.

Mr. President,

Social Development Mauritius is committed to uphold ing the pledges made at the Social Summit in Doha last year.

Nowhere is that promise to universal social protection more concrete than in our health services. As Non-Communicable Diseases and a rapidly ageing population place growing pressure on our health system, we are strengthening public healthcare through major investments, improved service delivery, 81st Session of the UN General Assembly expanded specialised care and a greater focus on prevention. Mauritius will continue to offer free and quality public healthcare to each and every citizen. We thus welcome the holding of the 2027 High -Level Meeting on Universal Health Coverage, and Mauritius stands ready to contribute to that global effort.

High-Level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness, and Response Today, t he High-Level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness, and Response met at a decisive moment, and decisive moments demand more than mere intentions. Mauritius supports the conclusion of the terms of BenefitSharing guaranteeing vulnerable countries, real access to affordable, safe, effective and quality medicines, including generics, vaccines, diagnostics and health technologies. It is of crucial importance to widen pandemic financing eligibility, including with the Pandemic Fund, to formally incorporate the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index.

Road Safety Mauritius also welcomes UN initiatives on R oad safety – an issue to which we attach the highest importance, and which acts as a silent epidemic that continues to claim far too many lives, disproportionately in developing countries.

We call for greater international attention and resources for this critical issue.

81st Session of the UN General Assembly Monsieur le Président,

Nous nous trouvons à un tournant décisif dans l’histoire des Nations Unies.

L’organisation fait face à des défis majeurs, tant sur le plan interne que sur le plan externe.

En interne, le processus engagé par le Secrétaire général pour réactualiser la structure administrative et financière de l’organisation pourra permettre à notre organisation d’être mieux équipée pour relever les défis futurs.

Sur le plan externe le rôle et les fonctions de l’organisation ainsi que la composition de ses principaux organes sont remis en question et sont appelés à être redéfinis.

La volonté affichée par la communauté internationale après la guerre, de se doter d’un instrument de collaboration en vue d’instaurer un nouvel ordre mondial est toujours présente. Le fait que le nombre d’acteurs a it plus que triplé durant les huit dernières décennies, reflète un engagement encore plus grand et plus diversifié qu’au moment de la création de l’ONU.

Nous sommes confiants que la communauté internationale, dont environ la moitié est composée de jeunes qui aspirent à protéger la planète, à mieux partager les richesses et à utiliser les nouvelles technologies à bon escient, saura relever les nouveaux défis.

81st Session of the UN General Assembly Nous renouvelons notre attachement au multilatéralisme aussi bien que notre confiance dans sa capacité à répondre aux attentes des peuples.

Je vous remercie, Monsieur le Président.

I now give the floor to His Excellency Carlos Ramiro Martínez Alvarado, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Guatemala.
Senor Presidente.
Mr. president of the General Assembly.
Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the international system that has guided our relations over recent decades is undergoing a profound transformation.

Conflicts, geopolitical tensions, declining resources for development and the fragmentation of spaces for dialogue are testing the principles that have guided coexistence among nations.
At the same time, democracy faces a twofold challenge the resurgence of authoritarian tendencies that seek to undermine the will of the people, and the spread of organised criminal networks that infiltrate institutions, corrupt justice systems, capture economies and territories, and erode public trust.
Transnational organised crime is more than just a threat to public security.
It is a direct threat to democracy the rule of law, and the ability of our peoples to freely determine their future.

Criminal networks do not recognize borders.
They are linked through drug trafficking trafficking in persons, illicit arms trafficking, smuggling, extortion, money laundering, environmental crime and other illicit economies.
They exploit institutional weaknesses, inequality, and a lack of opportunities.
Wherever the state is weakened, these structures seek to replace it, intimidate it, or bend it to serve private interests.

In the face of these realities, the fundamental principles that must guide our collective action have lost none of their relevance.
Preserving peace, combating hunger and poverty.
Ensuring equal rights and opportunities, strengthening justice, protecting our planet, and consolidating democratic institutions remain shared responsibilities.
The Sustainable Development Goals continue to provide an essential roadmap.

It is precisely at moments such as this that international law, multilateralism and democracy show their worth.
Law provides us with common rules.
Multilateralism enables us to turn shared problems into concerted solutions, and democracy ensures that power comes from the people and is exercised for their wellbeing.
I address this assembly on behalf of Guatemala, a country that knows from its own experience the value of these tools.

Our history has taught us that democracy, peace and respect for the law are not permanent achievements.
They are built collectively and each generation must preserve them.
A democracy rests on free elections, legitimate institutions, the separation of powers, freedom of expression, public participation, transparency and accountability But it also requires independent and effective institutions committed to the Constitution, the law and the popular mandate.
Public institutions must not serve criminal networks, private agendas, personal loyalties, or political or economic interests that are at odds with the common good.

They must serve the people, the constitutional order and society's democratic interests.
When an institution strays from that purpose, it does more than simply lose legitimacy.
It weakens the democracy it is meant to protect.
Democracy also earns its legitimacy in everyday life When a family is protected from poverty, when a child learns in a decent school, when a woman lives free from violence, when a community is no longer isolated, and when a young person can envision a future without being forced to leave their country.

That is why in Guatemala, we are restoring the state's capacity to reach those who have been excluded from opportunities for far too long.
The intersectional mano a mano strategy brings together health education, housing, nutrition and community development to address poverty at the local level following crop losses caused by climate related events.
More than 450,000 families have received food assistance, while small scale producers have gained access to seeds, tools, inputs and insurance mechanisms.
Public education is central to this effort.

More than 1 million students have participated in initiatives to strengthen reading comprehension.
We have expanded educational opportunities, promoted scholarships, strengthened instruction in national languages, and accelerated the digital transformation of the school system.
In healthcare, we have expanded and refurbished facilities, strengthened regional services, and made progress in the comprehensive treatment of chronic diseases and cancer.
Alongside the revival of road projects and public works in historically underserved communities, the National Digital Connectivity Plan now provides internet service to 383 public entities.

We have also strengthened early warning systems for earthquakes, tsunamis, floods and volcano hazards, restoring the legitimate presence of the state also means providing security in accordance with the law, strengthening prevention, protecting communities, and pursuing criminal networks rather than only their visible manifestations.
It means improving investigations, institutional coordination, and the tracing of the financial flows that sustain illicit economies.
Guatemala maintains that the charter of the United Nations and international law must remain our common point of reference.
The sovereignty and territorial integrity of states must be respected.

Disputes must be settled by peaceful means.
Human rights must be protected.
International humanitarian law must be observed in all circumstances, and international obligations must be fulfilled.
The law loses its ability to protect us when we accept its selective application.

National and international institutions lose legitimacy when they depart from their mandates in response to pressure, calculations or particular interests.
Their authority rests on independence impartiality, transparency and respect for the law.
There can be no there cannot be one rule for the powerful and another for the weak.
Nor can there be victims whose suffering outrages us and others whose suffering we choose to ignore.

For countries such as Guatemala international law does not constrain our sovereignty.
It is one of its principal safeguards.
Guatemala believes in the peaceful settlement of disputes.
We place our trust in dialogue, negotiation and the mechanisms provided for under international law.

Because even the most complex historical differences can and must be resolved by peaceful means.
We are deeply concerned by the persistence of armed conflicts in different regions of the world, and their devastating consequences for civilians.
In every case, our position rests on the same principles respect for the charter and international law, the protection of civilians, safe humanitarian access and dialogue and diplomacy as indispensable paths towards a just, sustainable and lasting peace.
We must not grow accustomed to war.

We must not accept violence as a permanent condition of our time, or allow entire generations to grow up believing that force is the only way to resolve our differences.
Guatemala stands for peace.
This December, we will mark 30 years since the signing of the agreement on a firm and lasting peace, which brought an end to 36 years of internal armed conflict.
After years of negotiation, we chose to replace armed violence with the pursuit of dialogue.

That is why we understand the value of international support and the role of the United Nations.
Our experience allows us to share one conviction.
Negotiation is not a sign of weakness.
Dialogue does not mean abandoning our principles.

Seeking peace must never mean accepting injustice.
We have also contributed to United Nations peacekeeping operations More than 6300 Guatemalan women and men have served under the United Nations flag in peacekeeping operations in different parts of the world.
A country that knows the cost of war must also take responsibility for helping others preserve peace.
Mr. president, we must strengthen the timely exchange of information, operational and judicial coordination, border security with respect for human rights, the protection of ports and transit routes, financial and asset investigations, and the recovery of assets derived from illicit activities.

We must also work together on prevention.
Lasting security cannot be achieved through law enforcement alone.
It requires education, decent work, resilient communities, accessible institutions and opportunities for young people.
It requires us to reduce the social, territorial and economic spaces that criminal structures exploit to recruit, exert control and supplant the state.

Our regional cooperation must be grounded in trust, shared responsibility and respect for sovereignty.
It must not serve private agendas or become an instrument of interests alien to our peoples.
Climate change, pandemics, transnational organised crime, food insecurity, human mobility and technological transformation all demand cooperation.
Guatemala, a country particularly vulnerable to the effects of climate change, knows that adaptation, risk management and the protection of rural livelihoods require national efforts, but also financing and cooperation commensurate with the needs capable of building capacity and delivering results.

Defending multilateralism does not mean defending the status quo.
The United Nations must become more effective, representative, transparent and responsive to people.
It must make better use of its resources, reduce duplication and respond more swiftly without weakening the purposes for which it was created.
Efficiency must strengthen, not erode, its three pillars peace and security, sustainable development and human rights.

Effectiveness cannot be measured solely in administrative terms, but rather by the ability to prevent a war, protect a population under threat, combat hunger, confront transnational criminal networks, or support a state in strengthening its institutions.
We do not need a United Nations that is smaller in purpose.
We need a United Nations that is stronger in results and firmer in defending democratic principles.
That transformation must also reach the Security Council.

Its composition must better reflect the realities of the 21st century and remedy the long standing underrepresentation of entire regions.
When the veto causes paralysis in the face of serious threats to international peace and security, confidence in the entire system suffers.
We also face an important decision for the future of the organisation the selection of the next secretary general.
Guatemala hopes that the process will be transparent and inclusive, and will identify an independent leader able to build bridges, defend the principles of the charter and lead the reform our organisation needs.

The Latin American and Caribbean region stands ready and prepared to shoulder its responsibility to the international community.
The time has come for a Latin American woman to serve as secretary general of the United Nations.
Excellencies.
Distinguished delegates.

The Republic of Guatemala reaffirms its commitment to the peaceful settlement of disputes and the observance of international law We welcome the fact that the International Court of Justice has set the date for the oral hearings concerning the territorial, insular and maritime dispute with Belize.
For my country, this is more than a procedural milestone.
With the notification of the hearings, the final procedural stage before the court delivers its judgment has begun.
It marks the culmination of a legal dispute that has accompanied the people of Guatemala and successive governments since independence, and whose conclusion we eagerly await.

We recognize that the court's judgment, once delivered, will bring the dispute to an end, and we trust that it will provide legal certainty to both parties and lay the foundations for a new chapter in relations between Guatemala and Belize.
In closing, I wish to say that Guatemala will continue to do its part strengthening democratic institutions capable of meeting the needs of our people, resolutely confronting transnational organised crime, and those who seek to capture institutions defending international law, consistently promoting regional responses based on shared responsibility, and working for a United Nations capable of transforming itself to fulfil the promise contained in the opening words of our charter, we the Peoples.
Restoring trust will depend on our ability to show that even in times of uncertainty and division, we remain capable of building together solutions that none of us could achieve alone.
Thank you very much.

Madam/Mister President, Excellencies I want to tell you about my grandmother, Alice.

Growing up in rural Sweden, as the seventh of eleven siblings, her opportunities were very different from those of her brothers. Her parents expected her to focus first and foremost on family life. Yet she was curious, capable and determined to build a life of her own.

A job at a local bank gave her not only an income, but also independence and confidence. There, at the bank, she met many women with little to no experience with finances and were left vulnerable when circumstances changed.

She wrote in her diary about some of the women she met – many of whom were recently widowed – coming to the bank in tears because they didn’t know anything about their own family finances. Some didn’t know how to fill out a withdrawal slip. One woman came to the bank holding two safe-deposit keys without knowing which bank they belonged to.

My grandmother was as independent as a woman in that time and place could be. But she worried deeply about the consequences for the women who were not.

During her life she witnessed extraordinary progress. But two generations later, far too many women are still entirely economically dependent on men.

Madam/ Mister President 80 years ago, when Sweden joined the United Nations, the foundations of our modern society were being laid.

2(12) In the 1940s and 50s, Swedish women joined the labour market in large numbers. This was not only a matter of principle – it also came from the realisation that our economy needed women in the work force.

Women’s economic empowerment is a matter of freedom. When women work and earn their own money, their self-determination grows.

Gender equality is not only the right thing to do, it’s the smart thing to do. When women work, economies grow.

Madam/Mister President,

Each generation must fight for equality.

In 1919, the same year my grandmother was born, Sweden decided that women should have the same right as men to vote. That very same year, women in Afghanistan were also granted the right to vote.

More than a century later, the contrast between women’s freedoms in our two countries is as striking as it is saddening. It is a painful reminder that progress is never irreversible. Rights once gained can be lost.

Freedoms do not defend themselves. It is up to us to protect them, for women and girls everywhere – and for generations to come.

Madam/Mister President,

When Sweden joined the UN in 1946, the world was emerging from the devastation of war. The lesson from that catastrophe was clear: peace must not be taken for granted.

Defence of sovereignty and territorial integrity have been at the heart of Swedish foreign policy ever since.

Eight decades later, these principles are once again being challenged. Bad faith, conflict and utter contempt for our common rules are weakening the institutions that we built together. These are times of upheaval.

3(12) The number of armed conflicts is growing. And civilians are paying the price. In Ukraine, Sudan,

Yemen, Palestine, Lebanon, Myanmar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and many other conflict zones, millions are suffering.

Madam/Mister President,

Russia’s aggression against Ukraine is a blatant violation of international law. It strikes at the heart of the very principles upon which the United Nations was founded.

Sweden’s support for Ukraine is felt deeply throughout our entire society. It comes from our people, our civil society and the business community. We will support Ukraine for as long as it takes.

Russia has not only violated the UN Charter, it has repeatedly violated international humanitarian law and human rights law. Attacks targeting civilians, forcible transfer and deportation of children, conflict-related sexual violence and torture – the list is far too long.

Ensuring accountability for these violations is crucial. If there is anything that we have learnt from history, it is that there cannot be a just and lasting peace without accountability.

Sweden stands firmly behind the ICC, its independence and integrity, and recognises its vital role not least in Ukraine.

Russia must also be held accountable for its breaches of the Chemical Weapons Convention, both on and off the battlefield.

Russia’s war of aggression against a peaceful neighbour is one of the biggest strategic mistakes and moral failures of the 21st century.

Four and a half years after launching its full-scale invasion, Russia has failed to achieve its objectives. Its economy is under strain, and its casualty numbers are devastating. Ordinary Russians are withdrawing their funds from the bank, and a substantial share of Russia’s young people are dying on the front lines.

The impact of Russia’s war of aggression extends far beyond Ukraine. Russia intensified its systematic attacks on civilian infrastructure and on vessels in the Black Sea this summer. This has 4(12) once again disrupted global food supply chains, exacerbating an already dire situation for vulnerable people across the globe.

To President Putin and Mr Lavrov I say this: the path to peace is clear, the choice should be easy.

Withdraw your troops. End this war.

Madam/Mister President,

Sweden has been an active contributor to the United Nations for 80 years. And we remain committed. But as a staunch partner, we will continue to push for a UN that is more effective, more transparent and better equipped to uphold the principles of its charter. A UN that is resolute.

Sweden’s first peacekeepers, 300 of them, served this organisation during the Suez Crisis in 1956.

Since then, more than 80 000 Swedes have followed in their footsteps.

We have a long tradition of supporting mediation through the UN. It began in 1948 with the UN’s first mediator, Sweden’s Folke Bernadotte.

We have long been a major donor of development assistance. And we remain devoted to tackling global development challenges and contributing to urgent humanitarian efforts.

Sweden remains a generous donor. But development assistance alone will not be enough to meet the challenges before us.

Madam/Mister President,

Reducing emissions to curb climate change is a common and global challenge, and is necessary to safeguard and increase development gains in the coming decades.

Sweden will continue to promote climate action based on urgency and opportunity – urgency based on what science tells us, opportunity based on the economic growth, jobs and strengthened competitiveness that climate transition brings.

Given the state of the world, changes are necessary to ensure the UN’s central role in international affairs and its ability to address today’s challenges.

5(12) An efficient, effective, nimble and well-coordinated UN is urgently needed. Sweden strongly supports the Secretary-General’s UN80 initiative and expects all UN entities to engage fully, with a clear focus on improving delivery at country level.

We also expect Member States to give the UN adequate resources. Assessed contributions must be paid in full and on time. As members, we also need to carefully consider institutional reforms and align mandates with available resources.

UN80 is an opportunity to strengthen the UN’s impact across all three pillars, and to reinforce the international system firmly grounded in the UN Charter and international law.

Madam/Mister President,

Sweden remains firm in its defence of the UN’s normative mandates on human rights, gender equality and sexual and reproductive health and rights.

Everyone has the right to live freely and with dignity. To be who they are and to love whom they choose. Sweden will always stand up for that freedom, and for equal rights of all.

Madam/Mister President,

A balanced expansion of the Security Council would strengthen its credibility and the legitimacy of its decisions.

Sweden would like to see permanent and non-permanent seats added, and a fairer representation of all continents on the Council.

Africa, home to 1.3 billion people and the largest regional bloc in the United Nations, has no permanent seat. This is neither logical nor fair.

Furthermore, the veto should never be used to prevent the UN from acting against serious violations of international law or in humanitarian disasters.

Madam/Mister President,

We must continue to strengthen our United Nations. To make this organisation stronger and better equipped to prevent conflict and meet the challenges of tomorrow.

6(12) We must continue to find common agreements, based on the fundamentals. Every country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Prohibition of the use of force. Respect for international law, human rights and humanitarian principles.

It is our shared responsibility to ensure that the UN remains relevant, effective and resolute. That it becomes greater than the sum of its parts.

To show once again that we can turn the page on conflict and chaos and move toward peace and prosperity.

Madam/ Mister President This year also marks 65 years since Secretary–General Dag Hammarskjöld died. His integrity, conviction and commitment to the vision and values of our organisation are still remembered.

Sweden continues to support the UN investigation aimed at clarifying the circumstances surrounding Secretary–General Hammarskjöld’s death.

I would like to conclude with the words of Mr Hammarskjöld: “It is no news to anybody, but we sense it in different degrees, that our world of today is more than ever before one world.

The weakness of one is the weakness of all, and the strength of one – not the military strength, but the real strength, the economic and social strength, the happiness of people – is indirectly the strength of all.”

Thank you.

NEW YORK President,

Liechtenstein joined the United Nations 36 years ago as its 160th member. We did so driven by the conviction that we, as one of the smallest members of the international community, should be part of the most important conversation on global governance, with the participation of all States, big or small, in developing international norms and standards – and also in upholding respect for them. Sovereignty was a key theme of our domestic discussions resulting in our UN membership. We joined out of enlightened self-interest - the belief that we need the UN to secure respect for our sovereignty, through upholding international law, as the basis for our security and prosperity. To this end, we also decided to make our own contribution, to make best use of the opportunity offered to us as a small State, to be an active part of the biggest peace project in the history of humankind.

President,

Our belief in the United Nations remains steadfast. This is the place where we can make our voice heard, where we can put ideas forward, and where we can gather to try to solve the issues that affect us all. We have greatly benefitted from our membership, and the UN has consistently been a key platform for our foreign policy. Our membership has consistently enjoyed high levels of support in our population.

But today we also find ourselves in a moment where instability and uncertainty dominate the conversation. Our organization no longer seems able to deliver on the key promise of the UN Charter – to save future generations from the scourge of war. It can no longer count on the unconditional support of its most powerful Members for the guiding rules of international law. It is increasingly ignored or sidelined in efforts to address both the traditional and new challenges, such as the regulation of Artificial Intelligence. It is permanently squ eezed financially. Legal obligations to pay are turned into tools to exercise political leverage. As a result, the United Nations has moved down the foreign policy agenda even of States who have a strong history of supporting it. We can no longer take it for granted that our people will continue their strongly positive views of our organization.

President,

This is the difficult moment in which we find ourselves. But rather than engaging in doomsday scenarios, we have to find the opportunities hidden in the challenge. The overwhelming majority of the States present in this room believe in the United Nations. They want to see positive change, for the UN to emerge stronger, more effective, more relevant. But we all have to be prepared to be part of the change that we want to see. Resisting the temptation of collective inertia and of waiting for positive change to happen on its own will require our active political investment.

We are grateful to Secretary -General Guterres for his service to the organization and for his proposals to adapt the organization to the needs of today. On the basis of his ideas, our delegations here have done good work that will show positive results over time. This is important. It shows that we can come together also during times of deep political division. It is also not enough. The steps we have taken are just the beginning of what we need - a political agreement that combines significant structural change with a reliable financial commitment and firm support for the UN Charter from all. This is also the vision we are looking for in the person that will be appointed as the next Secretary -General. We hope that this decision will come very soon, in order to give the new Secretary-General the time she needs to prepare for this most unique of jobs. And we remain convinced that having a woman at the helm of the United Nations is long overdue for an organization that prides itself on its role in gender equality.

President,

At its core, the United Nations is a peace organization. This is the promise of the UN Charter, and this is what our people expect from the UN – and the reason why they hold it in high esteem. Over the past year, we have seen a record number of armed conflicts around the world – and a rapidly diminishing role of the United Nations in ending them. In the Middle East, the UN’s role has been further reduced, in contrast to the central position it has taken up over the years. In Ukraine, there are few prospects for a peace process even though the aggression has now lasted longer than World War I, without even a nominal role for the United Nations. In Sudan, the role of the UN is limited to alleviating the enormous suffering of the civilian population, with no prospect of a political solution and an end to the conflict.

We are well aware of the political dynamic in the Security Council, primarily tasked with matters of peace and security – which severely limits the options for UN action. But the conversation must not end there. There are alternatives for action. This Assembly in particular has wide authority over matters of peace and security – and it is universal in composition. A glance at its history demonstrates its authority in peacekeeping, conflict termination and accountability. It is time that we make better use of this authority. The Veto Initiative, which we were proud to spearhead, provides a platform for such action. What is required is the will to spend our political capital here in this room – on peace rather than force, by dealing with conflict through diplomacy rather than through war.

The United Nations must not accept being reduced to a crisis mitigation organization that distributes States ’ contributions to a skyrocketing humanitarian assistance bill. Instead, we need to see a return to the UN doing political work to prevent, contain and end conflict, through the wide range of peace operations available, and through a strong interplay between a Secretary -General who is proactive and offers creative solutions, backed by the UN membership.

President,

Any successful community must be grounded in the rule of law. And so it is with the international community: our commitment to the law as the foundation for the conduct of international affairs is grounded both in principle and pragmatism. The biggest stre ngth of the United Nations is that it is firmly grounded in rules we have all agreed on – and that we have all agreed apply to all of us. This foundational agreement is increasingly challenged, with alarming trends to dismiss and ignore international law altogether which can only result in a world where might makes right. This would result in catastrophic human cost, a further proliferation of conflict and have devastating effects on development and on human security. We hope that both small and medium -sized States will come together in our common interest for a strong multilateral system, on the basis of respect for international law. This is the moment for us to unify in support of what the United Nations is built on.

President,

Naturally, we are also strong supporters of international courts, the indispensable enforcement mechanisms of international law.

Liechtenstein joined the jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice four decades before we joined the UN. We have made more submissions to the Court over the past decade than in its entire history before. We strongly support its work and its competence in both its advisory and dispute settlement functions. We encourage all to join us in submitting to the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court.

Liechtenstein is also strongly committed to the International Criminal Court, the first permanent international court with jurisdiction over the most serious crimes under international law – genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. We will continue to support the Court and its mandate to ensure acco untability and its central message - that nobody is above the law. In joining the ICC, we have exercised our sovereignty and delegated the jurisdiction we have ourselves to an international Court which we have helped create. We are proud of the way the Court has addressed the challenges to its resilience over the past year, in the face of relentless political attacks and unprecedented sanctions. We hope that more States will join this project, which is one of the landmark achievements in the history of international treaty-making.

The Rome Statute also criminalizes the supreme international crime – the crime of aggression, which complements the prohibition of the illegal use of force, the core piece of the UN Charter. At the international level, by signing the UN Charter we have all agreed to refrain from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another State. This is the most ambitious collective commitment to end war that has ever existed. Amidst accelerating human suffering the world over, it has never been more important for us to implement this commitment.

President,

It has now been many decades since scientists first war ned us of the dangers of Climate Change. Nevertheless, we have continued to run into the climate abyss, leaving the coming chaos for our children and their children. It is almost impossible to believe that we need to reiterate the facts: the climate crisis is real. We are seeing its effects every day, from heatwaves that bake the soil, to heavy rains that turned the parched ground into mud. People are starving in the heat and drowning in the floods. Crops can no longer be sustainably harvested; animals and pollinators are dying out. Liechtenstein commits to working with all States to address these harms and to reverse these trends as much as we still can.

We support the Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice on Climate Change. And this week we were proud to join the adoption of a High-Level Declaration on Sea-Level Rise, including a commitment to the continuity of Statehood for all UN Member States. Only a few years ago,

Member States in this debate wondered aloud if their nameplates would be ‘switched off’. The commitment we made this week is to guarantee that this will not happen. In the face of seas which inundate whole territories, standing up for self-determination is the least we can do for those most affected.

President,

This week has also seen an intense debate on harnessing the potential of Artificial Intelligence. But perhaps what we are discovering in these conversations are our own limits to understanding what that potential might be. Reporting from the most powerful and well -capitalized AI companies tell us that we are on a precipice either of a technology-fueled utopia or an apocalypse. Whether we achieve one or the other, unfortunately, has been treated as a secondary priority to the ‘AI race’ – one that has no clear finish line – and, for that matter, a dubious prize.

Liechtenstein supports the regulation of Artificial Intelligence. Unless we have a clear understanding of the methods, processes, and purposes of the huge variety of AI systems, how can we risk the consequences to human rights, to our environment, to the l ong-term capacities for our critical thinking and ultimately to the future of the human species? We are already seeing the impacts on civilians as armed forces increasingly integrate AI capabilities into their targeting systems in warfare. AI tools have to be made for humanity, lest we become the source material for AI systems to use - or merely the victims in its crosshairs.

President,

Many of us standing here this week have mused about the UN’s imperfections or expressed our concerns about its diminished relevance.

The UN is, indeed, in a fragile place. But very few of us want to live in a world in which the United Nations is rendered obsolete. On the contrary, we realize how much we need the UN. In the often-repeated quote, the UN was not built to take us to heaven. But in an era where it may not even be able to save us from hell, this universal organization retains the unparalleled ability to meet us where we are. It is up to us to do what we can to bring it closer to carrying out its mission under the UN Charter.

Liechtenstein commits to doing our part with you all in service of multilateralism and of the peoples we serve. I thank you.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen.

It is a distinct honor to stand in this historic hall, where so many great leaders have stood before, to deliver my country’s statement to the world. On behalf of Micronesia, I extend my warmest national greeting of Kamorale.

Let me begin by congratulating you, Mr. President, on your election as President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly.

I also extend Micronesia’s appreciation to Secretary-General António Guterres for your dedicated and steadfast service, principled leadership, and personal commitment to the values of the United Nations. As you conclude your tenure, we honor your advocacy for the most vulnerable, and your tireless efforts in strengthening multilateralism.

Mr. President,

The theme of this 81st session "Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all" speaks directly to our realities on our small islands in Micronesia. We need the benefits of digital innovation, artificial intelligence, energy transition, and institutional reforms.

At the same time, we recognize the challenges of climate change, ocean degradation, pollution, and growing inequality.

Micronesia stands in solidarity with all nations that have endured the recent waves of natural disasters around the world. The loss of lives, displacements, and destructions remind us of our common vulnerability. We extend our deepest condolences to the governments and peoples affected, and we honor the courage of those who chose to help in the face of tragedy.

Mr. President,

Today’s security landscape is shaped not only by conflict but by climate-driven fragility.

Extreme weather events, sea-level rise, and resource degradation are eroding stability across vulnerable regions, especially the Pacific. These pressures intensify humanitarian needs, disrupt food and water systems, and strain governance capacities. For Micronesia, climate impacts are a national security concern.

We underscore the importance of safeguarding maritime security across the Blue Pacific. Illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing activities, transnational crimes, and environmental degradation threaten not only our economies but the health of our marine environment as well.

We urge the international community to enhance cooperation, share technology, and support capacity-building to ensure that the ocean remains a zone of peace, governed by international law.

Mr. President,

The challenges that impede our sustainable development are increasing. We must respond by implementing science-based emissions reductions, scale up national climate commitments, and accelerate transition to renewable energy. We demand accessible and predictable adaptation grant financing to support investments in resilient infrastructure. We must operationalize the Loss and Damage Fund. Further, we must keep the 1.5°C goal, and sustain methane reductions.

This is not a substitute for long-term decarbonization, but can slow near-term warming, protect vulnerable communities and oceans, and preserve critical time for those on the front lines of the climate crisis.

Micronesia endorses the proposed Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty. A just and orderly transition away from fossil fuels is now inseparable from the wider geopolitical and economic realities shaping global energy markets. Instability in the Middle East and volatile fuel prices exposed the vulnerability of SIDS to expensive fuel, unstable supply, and widespread economic fragility.

Shift to renewable energy is an economic necessity. Solar, wind, and ocean-based technologies can reduce dependence on external fuel markets, strengthen energy security, and lower emissions in line with science. The world must accelerate the transition to resilient, affordable, and community-centered renewable energy systems.

Mr. President,

Our people are the most valuable national resource. We remain committed to delivering effective public services and advancing Micronesian priorities for our citizens, wherever they reside. I am pleased to announce the adoption of Micronesia’s National Migration Policy, with the technical support of the International Organization for Migration. Micronesia will strengthen the protection, engagement, and well-being of its citizens, including members of diaspora.

Micronesia also aligns itself with the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration, and welcomes its comprehensive framework for promoting humane, orderly, and well-managed international migration.

Mr. President,

Our people’s health has been increasingly affected by more frequent tropical storms, heat waves, and changing tidal patterns. We are seeing a rise in illnesses linked to marine life and vectorborne diseases, in particular dengue and Zika. Already, the burden of non-communicable diseases strains our health system, reduces workforce productivity, and diverts limited resources.

We are strengthening our national health capacity, increasing investments in diagnostics and lifesaving medicine, expanding the use of tele-health to access specialist care and medical education, and partnering with neighboring countries to support regular medical exchange programs that augment our treatment capability in- country. These efforts are essential to safeguard our communities as climate impacts intensify.

Mr. President,

The ocean is the heart of Micronesian identity, livelihoods, and future prosperity. It faces mounting pressures from climate change, sea-level rise, pollution, and unsustainable exploitation. Micronesia ask for a collective effort to fortify ocean governance, sustainable fisheries management, and effective conservation of marine biodiversity. Being the first country to sign the BBNJ Agreement, we are among the first movers, comprising six nations to implement the BBNJ. Micronesia is partnering with GIZ and five co-leading States to develop area-based management tools and marine protected area proposals under the BBNJ framework, translating our commitment to conserve 30 percent of the ocean into concrete, durable protections for areas beyond national jurisdiction.

Mr. President,

On deep-sea mining in the international seabed Area, Micronesia employs a precautionary approach. We stress the need to consolidate comprehensive knowledge, data, and science about the marine environment before any decision is taken on proceeding with exploitation.

Additionally, it is crucial that all stakeholders, including adjacent coastal states, Indigenous Peoples, and local communities in the Pacific, are meaningfully consulted prior to such a decision.

Mr. President,

We must address the growing threat of plastic pollution that degrades the Pacific ecosystems and communities. Marine debris, micro plastics, and associated toxic substances are accumulating on our shores.

Our lagoons, for example, in the State of Chuuk where oil leaks from World War II remnants led to the emergency declaration last year, continue to threaten our livelihood.

These impacts impose disproportionate cleanup and economic burdens on small island governments whose waste-management infrastructure is inadequate. Our national efforts must be matched by strengthened international cooperation, including technical assistance, predictable financing, and collective action across the full plastics life cycle, to prevent pollution at its source and protect the Blue Pacific for present and future generations.

Micronesia calls on the international community to match local action with global responsibility: through sustained funding, meaningful technology transfer, stricter upstream controls on plastic production, and an end to waste exporting. Critically, the international community must complete its work on a new treaty to end plastic pollution, including in the marine environment.

Mr. President,

With less than five years to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, the international community must respond with renewed political resolve, scaled-up financing, and accelerated implementation. The Pacific’s experience underscores this imperative: climate impacts are steadily eroding development gains and placing progress across the Goals further at risk. The recent typhoon and severe flooding in our States, and more frequent king tides affecting our lowlying islands demonstrate that these are no longer isolated events, but recurring pressures that test the resilience of our communities on the front lines of the climate crisis. For us, achieving the SDGs requires accelerated action.

Mr. President,

Our actions on gender equality continues to address barriers to women’s leadership, economic participation, and access to justice, digital safety, and protection from violence—particularly for women and girls in remote and outer island communities. We are mainstreaming gender across state and national planning, strengthening survivor-centered services, expanding women’s economic empowerment and decision-making and engaging in preventing gender-based violence and advancing equality.

Mr. President,

Our youth are taking active roles in community advocacy, climate stewardship, adaptation and mitigation activities, and services across our nation. Building on these achievements, our priorities are clear: strengthening youth voices in decision-making; expanding skills training and pathways to decent work; supporting youth-led climate and community action; addressing substance abuse and mental health; and ensuring that young people have the opportunity to lead, serve, and build the future of our nation.

Mr. President,

We must implement the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index (MVI) into a modern, coherent, and responsive system that moves decisively from concept to practice. Doing so would unlock fair access to concessional financing that reflect structural vulnerabilities faced by small, fragile, and highly exposed economies such SIDS.

Mr. President,

Micronesia reaffirms its strong commitment to the progress of the UN80 reform initiative. In addressing the UN Country Team Reconfiguration, we firmly believe that both the MultiCountry Office and the Resident Coordinator system must remain securely in place. Our distinct geographical landscape features incredibly remote communities. This lived reality is precisely why the UN80 reform initiative matters so deeply to Micronesia. For countries defined by distance, dispersion, and vulnerability, reform cannot be an abstract exercise; it must strengthen the UN’s ability to deliver where the needs are greatest. Our priority is to create a UN architecture that preserves what works, fixes what does not, and ensures that no community, no matter how remote, is left behind.

Mr. President,

Micronesia supports an expanded Council that includes Brazil, Germany, India, and Japan as permanent members, alongside permanent representation for Africa, and a dedicated non‐permanent seat for SIDS, ensuring that those most affected by global decisions are finally present at the table.

Mr. President,

Digital transformation and artificial intelligence offer significant opportunities to improve publicservice delivery, diversify economies, expand market access, and advance climate-resilient development. Although, we are advancing digital connectivity, private-sector development, and trade opportunities, but without adequate investment, capacity-building, and appropriate governance, these technologies may increase inequalities and further heighten exposure to cyber security threats, misinformation, and risks to data privacy. We therefore call upon the international community to strengthen financing for resilient digital infrastructure, with ethical and effective guardrails and governance frameworks.

Mr. President,

The priorities before us mentioned earlier are interconnected tests of whether the United Nations can deliver for all. For Micronesia, success must be measured not by declarations, but by tangible improvements in our people’s lives, security, and dignity. We call for equitable partnership with small island developing States through accessible finance, technology transfer, stronger capacity, and a meaningful voice in global decisions. In the spirit of KAMORALE, let us choose cooperation over division and build a peaceful, just, and sustainable future in which every nation can thrive.

Thank you.
