Mr. President,

Allow me first to congratulate you on your election to the Presidency of the eighty-first session, and to assure you of Belize's full support.

For more than eighty years, this Organisation has done what no single nation could.

It has held back conflict where it could and named it where it could not.

It has given the powerless a language of rights.

It has built, one instrument at a time, the body of international law on which every State in this Hall, large or small, now depends.

It has survived a Cold War, as it has division and doubt, because each generation that came through its doors understood the same simple truth: no nation, however powerful, can secure peace, prosperity or a habitable planet on its own.

That was true in 1945.

It is truer today.

The Charter is hope.

It speaks to our common humanity.

It speaks to the rule of law, to the dignity of every person, to the sovereign equality of States, and to our duty to keep the peace.

These are not the words of one region or one era.

They belong to all of us; they bind all of us.

Few in this Hall would question that mission.

But let us be honest with one another.

Not one of us could fault the people we represent for questioning its delivery.

The world is on course to exceed the 1.5-degree threshold.

Rising seas threaten coastlines, communities and, for some Members, the very territory of the State.

The loss of biodiversity weakens the forests, reefs and mangroves on which our economies depend.

These pressures unfold alongside armed conflict, disrupted supply chains, declining official development assistance and rising debt.

Households face higher food and energy bills.

Governments face higher borrowing costs.

Countries striving to finance the Sustainable Development Goals must absorb shocks they did not create and cannot fairly insure against.

Artificial intelligence adds a further layer.

Well governed, it can widen access to knowledge and improve public services.

Poorly governed, it can deepen inequality, expose critical systems, displace workers and leave developing countries dependent on technologies and rules designed elsewhere.

National legislation alone cannot govern a technology that crosses every border.

These dangers are real.

But danger is not destiny.

We are not without answers.

Indeed, Mr. President, the United Nations has already placed them in our hands.

We have the Paris Agreement,

We have the 2030 Agenda, and the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS.

We have the law of the sea regime, and the Declaration on Sea-Level Rise.

And we have a global dialogue, under this Organization, on the governance of artificial intelligence.

The United Nations is doing its part.

The question before us is whether we will use these tools — whether we have the will to deliver.

Mr. President,

Belize is determined to do so.

We are committed to the Sustainable Development Goals.

And we are making measurable progress.

Multidimensional poverty stands at 19.1 per cent and unemployment at 1.9 per cent.

Public debt has been brought to 66.6 per cent of GDP and, for the first time in a generation, it is on a sustainable path.

These figures are not abstractions.

They are Belizeans at work, families with greater purchasing power, and a Government with room to invest in the future.

Vamos bien.

We are doing well.

But we have further to go.

That is the purpose of the next phase of our national strategy: to create jobs, reduce vulnerability, reduce exposure to imported energy, protect the ecosystems, and equip Belizeans to compete in a changing economy.

Implementation of Plan Belize 2.0 is under way.

Alongside it, my Government has launched the Belize Compact, a landmark grant partnership with the United States that will strengthen our energy security and build the skills of our young people for the workforce of tomorrow.

But the risks are growing.

Hurricanes are more intense.

Weather patterns are less predictable, which makes anticipatory action more complex.

New stressors, such as the unprecedented influx of sargassum along our coast, have no ready-made responses.

Managing them requires innovation, capable institutions and strategies that are properly financed.

Yet even the best national effort will fall short without coordinated international cooperation.

Mr. President,

We are less than four years from 2030.

It is time to consider what follows the Sustainable Development Goals.

The next framework must carry forward what remains undelivered and it must rest on a fairer foundation.

The demand for reparatory justice is no longer a marginal whisper in this Assembly.

It is here, at the centre and it is not going away.

This Assembly has rightly and finally declared slavery as the gravest crime against humanity.

But this recognition is only the beginning of an obligation.

And the obligation is that we must not build the next chapter of development on the foundations of the last.

If we are to be honest about that foundation, then we would acknowledge that the of wealth of the industrial age largely came from the labour of enslaved and colonised peoples, and its rewards flowed almost entirely away from them.

When independence came, the flags changed.

The structures did not.

The terms of trade did not change.

The cost of capital did not change.

Who sits at the table when the rules are written did not change.

The imbalance was not undone; it was inherited.

Now we stand at the threshold of yet another transformation.

Technology is moving faster than any framework we have yet devised to govern it.

Will we do it differently this time, or will we do it again?

Because the question before us is not whether new inequalities may arise.

It is whether the old ones will be written into the code, into who owns the data, who sets the standards, who captures the value, and who, once more, is left to carry the cost.

We do not have to accept that outcome.

A development framework is a choice.

It can be designed to serve the common good, and measured against what our people actually need: dignity, opportunity, and a fair share in what they help to create.

Or it can be left to reproduce what came before and call it progress.

We have the knowledge to choose the first path.

What is needed now is the will.

This, Mr. President, is where trust in multilateralism is won or lost.

Belize has shown that debt can be reduced, that conservation can be financed innovatively and that national reform can succeed.

Yet we still borrow in a system that prices our vulnerability as risk, rather than treating resilience as an investment.

Belize does not seek special treatment.

We seek accurate treatment.

Income per capita does not reveal how much of an economy sits in a hurricane's path, what it costs to serve dispersed communities, or how quickly a climate shock can reverse fiscal gains.

The Multidimensional Vulnerability Index must become a working instrument across the international financial system: in eligibility for concessional finance, in debt sustainability analysis, and in the decisions of the institutions that allocate capital.

Vulnerability should be legible in financial decision-making without small States being required to prosecute their own case again and again.

Mr. President,

The current erosion of international peace and security carries an uncomfortable echo of the League of Nations' final years.

The League did not collapse for want of noble principles but because member states abandoned those principles the moment they became inconvenient or constrained their power.

I therefore cannot speak candidly about multilateralism while looking away from where it is tested most severely.

I begin close to home.

Haiti's crisis is our crisis — Haiti is the Caribbean.

While there are grounds for hope in elections now scheduled for December, there is also grave concern over a spike in violence threatening that process.

Belize echoes the call of the CARICOM Eminent Persons Group.

The Gang Suppression Force must be urgently and fully deployed.

A Haitian-led, Haitian-owned political transition deserves a security environment in which it can actually succeed.

Belize stands with the people of Haiti, and with CARICOM, in asking for nothing less.

Belize stands also with Cuba.

The economic blockade against our sister nation, compounded by restrictions on fuel, has severely damaged the Cuban economy.

This crisis is unnecessary and unjustified.

Belize renews its call for the lifting of the blockade and for Cuba's removal from the list of State sponsors of terrorism.

In Palestine, the legal and moral test is unambiguous.

It is an affront to this Assembly and to humanity to be forced to listen to a man justify apartheid and genocide when he is wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Our complicity lies in decades of failing to ensure Palestinian self determination and in refusing to treat Israel as what it is: a settler colonial state.

The genocide must end.

The apartheid must stop.

End the occupation and decolonise Palestine.

Our Charter summons us to act.

Our actions must extends to every conflict, and to every person displaced, destitute or in despair.

It extends to threats against the sovereignty and territorial integrity of any Member State, as we witness in Ukraine.

If borders can be redrawn by force, then every border is provisional.

We are concerned, too, for the safety and security of the 23 million people of Taiwan, who have no seat and no voice in this Hall.

Taiwan is a friend of Belize.

For more than three decades she has walked with us on our development journey, not as a donor at a distance, but as a partner in the field.

Today that partnership is helping Belize close real gaps: in climate resilience, and in the technical capacity of our agricultural and public infrastructure sectors.

But Taiwan's contribution does not stop at the borders of her small and steadfast allies.

She sits at the heart of global supply chains.

She produces the most advanced semiconductors in the world.

She is a serious presence in artificial intelligence and the other technologies that will shape this century, and she has said plainly that she is ready to share that expertise and those resources with the wider international community.

Belize calls once more for Taiwan's meaningful participation in the United Nations system.

We hold no illusion that a small State can resolve these crises.

But smallness does not relieve us of the duty to speak.

Our voice joins every call for the protection of civilians, for accountability, and for the diplomacy that alone can secure durable peace.

Mr. President,

Forty-five years after independence, Belize continues to pursue the peaceful settlement of its territorial disputes with Guatemala and with Honduras.

Belize has chosen, and will always choose, law over force.

Belize informs this Assembly of a serious breach of international law committed on the night of 23 September 2026, when a Guatemalan military aircraft entered Belize’s sovereign airspace and intentionally disabled its transponder.

This act violates the Chicago Convention on International Civil Aviation, customary norms governing state aircraft, and the inviolability of territorial sovereignty protected under Article 2(4) of the United Nations Charter.

This incursion is not an isolated event.

It forms part of a continuing pattern in which Guatemalan state vessels and personnel operate unlawfully in Belizean territorial waters of the Sarstoon River, which forms part of Belize’s border with Guatemala, in defiance of obligations—binding on both Parties—to refrain from any action capable of aggravating or extending the dispute presently before the International Court of Justice.

The case is scheduled for hearing in February 2027.

Guatemala’s conduct risks prejudicing the Court’s authority and undermines the principle of peaceful settlement of disputes enshrined in Article 33 of the Charter.

Belize therefore calls upon Guatemala to immediately cease all incursions by air, land, or sea; to comply fully with its obligations under the UN Charter, the Chicago Convention, and the OAS Confidence-Building Measures; and to respect the integrity of the ICJ process.

Belize further requests heightened monitoring by the United Nations and the OAS to ensure that no Member State uses military force or intimidation to influence judicial proceedings.

We await the Court's judgments with confidence, and we look forward to borders that are respected by all.

Mr. President,

This is a new dawn for my country, and a moment of renewal for this Organization.

This year the United Nations will select its tenth SecretaryGeneral.

Belize proudly supports the candidacy of Her Excellency Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana, a distinguished daughter of the Caribbean.

A Caribbean woman at the helm of the United Nations would be historic, but history alone is not the argument; her record is.

The next Secretary-General will inherit an institution under strain and a world impatient for results.

Small and vulnerable States must be placed at the centre of the Organization's work, not at the margins of decisions that determine our survival.

The United Nations must become more agile, more representative and better equipped to deliver.

A leaner United Nations is not automatically a better one.

Peace and security cannot be an afterthought to a budget exercise.

Human rights cannot be separated from development, nor development sustained without peace.

Reform must honour all three pillars of the Charter — peace and security, development and human rights — as one indivisible promise.

Mr. President,

Trust will be restored when commitments are kept and law is applied evenly without fear or favour.

Transformation will be fair when small States help to design the future, rather than learning of it afterwards.

Delivery will be real when it reaches beyond conference rooms into the life of a child, the livelihood of a farmer and the resilience of a nation.

Belize will do its part.

We will invest in our people, protect our natural capital, modernise our economy, and choose dialogue over division and law over force.

We ask this Assembly, and its next leadership, to meet the same standard.

Let the smallest voice be heard as clearly as the largest.

Let agreements become action.

Let this United Nations prove that cooperation is not weakness, but the highest expression of our common strength.

Long live Belize. Long live the United Nations.

I thank you, Mr. President.

Mr. President of the General Assembly,

Mr. Secretary-General of the United Nations,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

It is a pleasure to be here, representing Cabo Verde, in this forum where the world comes together to discuss the challenges we share and the future we want to build.

I come from a country made up of ten islands in the Atlantic. A country aware of its vulnerabilities, but one that has learned that the size of a territory must never determine the size of our dreams.

The history of Cabo Verde is also a history of learning. We have learned to confront drought and scarcity, to transform the sea from a barrier into a bridge, but, above all, we have learned that a nation’s greatest wealth lies in its people. We even have a word for this wealth, which is "morabeza", a term that defines the cordiality, determination, and kindness of our people, which the whole world was able to witness a little during this year's Football World Cup.

Amílcar Cabral, one of the great figures of our history, left us a lesson that continues to resonate across generations: “Learn in life, learn from our people, learn from the books and from the experiences of others. Learn always.”

Perhaps this is an ability that the world must rediscover: the ability to learn from history, to learn from one another, and to understand that there can be no lasting development without peace, just as there can be no lasting peace where poverty, exclusion and lack of opportunity persist.

In this spirit, Cabo Verde reaffirms its faith in the United Nations, in dialogue among nations, in cooperation among peoples, and in the primacy of Law over the use of force.

In the face of the wars, inequalities, and crises confronting our world, we reaffirm our unwavering commitment to the Charter of the United Nations, to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of States, to the protection of civilian populations, and to the peaceful resolution of conflicts.

International Law and International Humanitarian Law cannot be applied in a selective manner. They will only be truly strong and fulfill their role when they are respected and upheld by all.

In our region, terrorism, violent extremism and transnational crimes also remind us that peace requires prevention, strong institutions and cooperation.

And requires opportunities.

Africa is the continent with the youngest population in the world. Therefore, investing in our young people, in education, in knowledge, and in the possibility of building a dignified life means also investing in peace.

Excellencies,

Learning also means embracing change.

The world of today is not the world of 1945. The institutions we created to respond to the challenges of that time need to learn with the world that has changed.

Cabo Verde therefore supports a United Nations that is more effective, more transparent, and more representative. The UN80 Initiative presents a n opportunity to modernize th is Organization and strengthen its response capacity.

In this spirit, we also support the reform of the Security Council.

Africa is home to nearly one -quarter of the Member States of this Organization and represents approximately one -fifth of the world’s population, and yet it still lacks the representation it deserves on this Council.

Therefore, we support a more equitable African representation, in accordance with the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration.

A fairer international order also requires fairer and more inclusive institutions.

The election of the next Secretary -General should reflect the same principles: transparency, inclusion, merit and equal opportunities.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

But the United Nations is not just a place where we discuss crises. It is also the space where we build common paths.

The 2030 Agenda, the African Union's Agenda 2063 and the Pact for the Future point us in one direction: sustainable development, centered on the people, capable of transforming global commitments into concrete changes in the lives of populations.

This is also the mission of the new Government of Cabo Verde: to concretely improve the lives of its people.

And we have placed education at the heart of this mission.

Because the school is where a society begins to shape its future. And Education is a powerful development strategy.

We seek to transform knowledge into innovation, decent employment, and opportunities; to strengthen our education and health systems; and to advance progress in digital transformation, gender equality, the energy transition, water security, and the blue economy.

We want to create more opportunities for our young people and build an economy capable of transforming people’s talent into development.

Development is transforming knowledge into opportunity and opportunity into dignity.

Excellencies,

For Cabo Verde and other Small Island States, the climate crisis is not a distant threat; it is a present reality - it’s here: the droughts, desertification, water scarcity, ocean acidification, and rising sea levels.

Just look at what is happening on the island of Sal, where, only two days ago, rising sea waters flooded the avenue in front of the hotels.

It is also a question of justice, because those who have contributed the least to this crisis cannot continue to bear some of its most serious consequences.

Science has shown us the way forward. We must now translate this valuable knowledge into decisions and actions.

Cabo Verde has tried to do its part.

In September 2024, Cabo Verde launched a call for a Global Compact for Climate Mobility, and in June, in Berlin, 57 countries endorsed the Global Consensus on the Principles to Address Climate Mobility.

At the United Nations, Cabo Verde co-facilitated negotiations on the Political Declaration of the Third Conference on the Oceans and the Declaration on Sea Level Rise.

For a country made up of islands, protecting the ocean is not just an environmental policy.

It is protecting the national territory, the economy, the culture, and the future.

In January 2027, Cabo Verde will take over the Presidency of the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS). We will take on this responsibility by working for the unity of Small Island States, the implementation of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda, for fairer financing, for climate adaptation, and for ensuring that the oceans remain at the heart of the global agenda.

And in 2034, we will host the Fifth International Conference on Small Island Developing States, providing an opportunity to share experiences, build common responses, and transform vulnerabilities into opportunities.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

There is also pedagogy in the relationships between Nations.

It begins with the ability to listen.

It entails the humility to recognize that no one country alone has all the answers.

And it makes sense when what we learn together is translated into action.

This, after all, is the essence of multilateralism.

In a time of fragmentation, we need to regain trust. In a time of confrontation, we need to strengthen cooperation. In a time when force so often prevails, we need to reaffirm the Law.

But our history has taught us to engage in dialogue, to build bridges, and to seek consensus.

It also taught us that no country is too small to have a voice and no challenge is too big to tackle when we work together.

The United Nations must continue to be the space for this collective endeavor.

And I will recall what Amílcar Cabral taught us: “Learn always.”

Today, learning also means understanding that educating a child, providing opportunities for young people, protecting the planet, fighting poverty, promoting development, and building peace are not separate missions.

They are, indeed, different ways of caring for the future.

And perhaps this is the greatest lesson that our times require of us: the future is not simply what we receive.

Rather, it is what we are able to teach, learn, and build together.

Thank you for your attention.

Madam Vice President of the General Assembly,

Deputy Secretary General,

Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

This summer, the Republic of Moldova turned thirty -five. For much of that time, the world described us as a country caught between East and West - a place where others decided. I stand here as the new Prime Minister of a country that has decided.

Small countries do not choose their geography or their size. But small, does not mean powerless. Nations, like people, are shaped by the choices they make - whom they trust, whom they elect, whom they call friends, and how they respond when things turn against them.

For a long time, others made many of those choices for us.

Soviet authorities deported our families to Siberia, forced our Romanian language into another alphabet and told us it had another name. After independence, Moscow used gas and trade restrictions as leverage over our country.

Step by step, we began choosing for ourselves. Romanian is again written in the Latin alphabet and spoken freely.

Governments change peacefully at the ballot box. And when our democracy was threatened, Moldovans have defended it through elections and civic action.

We also reduced Russia's economic leverage on us. We diversified our gas purchases. In just five years, renewables grew from almost nothing to around 30%. Our electricity system is increasingly integrated with Romania and the European grid, and our companies sell on some of the most demanding markets in Europe and the world.

But the Kremlin kept trying. Moldova faced illicit financing, disinformation, cyberattacks and vote buying. Russia spent the equivalent of roughly two percent of our GDP trying to influence last year's election.

Moldovans answered that their home is not for sale.

Each of these choices carried a cost. But each taught us the same lesson: we cannot control everything around us, but what we do still matters.

That is the source of our optimism. Our future remains in our own hands.

And nowhere is that choice clearer today than in our European path.

European integration has become our national project. Moldova has been a candidate country since 2022, accession negotiations are underway, and we are moving quickly. Our ambition is clear - to anchor Moldova firmly in the European family.

For us, joining the European Union is not about replacing one sphere of influence with another. It is the opposite. It is our citizens exercising their right to choose. Choose democracy.

Choose prosperity. Choose peace.

That European choice goes hand in hand with a strong transatlantic partnership. For Moldova, these are not competing directions. The United States has been an important partner in strengthening our security, energy independence and resilience. We want the next chapter of that relationship to be increasingly about trade, investment, technology and building things together.

But membership is not only about what Europe can give Moldova. It is also about what Moldova can bring - a democracy that has learned to resist interference, an emerging economy, a country contributing to stability on Europe's eastern frontier, and a small state willing to experiment, reform and move quickly.

Being small imposes constraints. But it can also be an advantage.

Moldova is not a huge domestic market. We cannot outspend the largest economies. So we have to compete differently - with permits in days rather than months, clear regulation, digital public services and rules that change when they no longer make sense.

Technology is moving faster than regulation almost everywhere, and artificial intelligence is widening that gap. Small countries can have a natural edge here.

We want Moldova to become a place where emerging tech can be tested responsibly through regulatory sandboxes - where regulators learn alongside companies, rules adjust with evidence, and good ideas do not wait years to reach the real economy.

When an entrepreneur arrives with a technology for which the law has not caught up, the answer should not simply be: "There is no rule for this." It should be: "Let us find a safe way to test it."

We may never have the deepest pools of capital or the largest GPU clusters. But we can build better rules and be more agile.

Smallness does not have to mean weakness. Sometimes it means turning faster and delivering when larger countries cannot.

And that leads to a broader point about small nations.

Power has never been equal. It never will be. But inequality of power must never become inequality of sovereignty. Countries are not buffers. Nations are not bargaining chips.

Nowhere is that principle being tested more brutally today than next door to us.

Safety is not abstract for me. Kyiv was home for nearly fifteen years, including on 24 February 2022. That morning, as parents, we struggled to explain to our 3 boys - one, ten and twelve at the time - what war actually meant.

Perhaps nothing captures the normalization of this war better than the arithmetic children have learned.

Think of a typical night. A jet-powered Shahed drone is reported heading toward Kyiv. A twelve-year-old checks the map, knows roughly how fast it is travelling, and does the math in his head — before the approaching drone sends him to the bomb shelter.

Children have become frighteningly good at this - the nightly arithmetic of war.

In Moldova, we cannot begin to compare our suffering with Ukraine's. Yet Russian drones have repeatedly violated our airspace and fallen on our territory. The danger is that the unacceptable starts to feel normal.

For us, too, this is about the safety of our families. We must not grow accustomed to it. Repetition does not make a violation acceptable.

And because these are not abstract questions for Moldovans watching at home, allow me to speak to them directly for a moment.

{In Romanian} Dragi moldoveni,

Știu că mulți dintre voi urmăriți cu neliniște știrile despre războiul de alături, despre dronele rusești care s -au întețit, și vă gândiți deja la iarna care vine. Da, ne așteaptă o iarnă grea. Datoria noastră, a Guvernului, este să ne pregătim și să-i ajutăm mai ales pe cei care au cel mai puțin. Pentru asta muncim și despre asta vorbim cu partenerii noștri aici.

Dar vreau să vă rog un lucru important: să ne ținem grămăjoară.

În momentele grele, asta ne -a ajutat de fiecare dată - să nu ne lăsăm singuri unii pe alții, să ne ajutăm vecinii, părinții, oamenii care o duc cel mai greu. Putem avea păreri diferite, putem vota diferit. E firesc într-o țară în care oamenii gândesc liber. Dar grija pentru cei de lângă noi trebuie să ne unească. Suntem o țară mică. Tocmai de aceea e cu atât mai important să știm că nu suntem singuri și că ne putem sprijini unii pe alții.

__ (Translation in to English: My fellow Moldovans,

I know many of you are anxiously following the news about the war next door and the growing threat from Russian drones, and are already thinking about the winter ahead. Yes, a difficult winter awaits us. Our duty as a government is to prepare and to help those who need it most. That is what we are working on, and that is what we are discussing with our partners here.

But I want to ask something important of you: let us stick together. In difficult times, this is what has always helped us through: being there for one another, helping our neighbours, our parents and those struggling the most. We may hold different views. We may vote differently. That is natural in a country where people think freely. But caring for those around us must unite us. We are a small country. That makes it all the more important to know that we are not alone and that we can count on one another.)

___ That solidarity at home must go hand in hand with clarity about the danger around us.

This is not a tragedy without an author. Russia launched a war of aggression against a sovereign neighbour. It occupied territory and continued to attack Ukrainian cities. Ukraine did not choose this war. Russia did.

We often speak about "war fatigue". The phrase is understandable. Governments have other crises. Families have their own worries. Attention moves on.

But being tired of a war you can switch off is different from being tired because an air -raid wakes your children again tonight - and different still from the exhaustion of Ukrainian soldiers spending another cold night in the mud.

Moldova could not choose that this war began next to us. But we could choose our response.

We welcomed people fleeing the war. We kept transport routes open. We reduced the cost of rail transit for Ukrainian cargo with grain.

These decisions were not always cost-free or politically easy at home. We made them because the way this war ends matters far beyond our region.

If aggression is rewarded, it becomes a precedent - for the aggressor and for everyone watching. Peace must protect sovereignty and create the conditions for lasting security.

The same principle applies within our own borders.

Russian military forces remain, illegally and without our consent, in the Transnistrian region of Moldova. We will continue to seek their unconditional withdrawal and the peaceful reintegration of our country, with full respect for Moldova's sovereignty an d territorial integrity.

We want people on both banks of the Nistru to live together in a peaceful, democratic and prosperous Moldova.

And because we believe small states should help shape the international system, not simply depend on it, Moldova is honored to present its candidacy for the Presidency of the 82nd session of the United Nations General Assembly. We want to contribute to a U N that is more effective, more inclusive and focused on results.

Excellencies,

We live in a world with plenty of reasons for pessimism. Moldova chooses something else.

Not naïve optimism. Not the belief that problems disappear if we refuse to see them. The optimism that comes from knowing that our future is still in our own hands.

For too long, Moldovans were told that our country was too small, too exposed, too divided to choose its own future. We have spent enough time believing that. We know our problems.

But we should also know our strength.

We are a free country. Our people are humble, work hard, and put family first. Our diaspora is spread across the world, but stays close to one another and deeply cares about what happens at home. Only when it comes to vineyards does modesty become a little harder for us - we quietly suspect our wines might just be the best in the world.

We have friends across Europe, across the Atlantic and far beyond. And we finally have a realistic path to build a country our children should not need to leave in search of opportunity.

Moldova may never be a great power. But we have everything it takes to be a great country.

I thank you.

Mr. president, I am honored to extend to you and to the distinguished representatives of the Nations Assembly here the warm greetings of His Holiness Pope Leo the 14th, while also congratulating Your Excellency on your election as president of this esteemed Assembly, as the Secretary General, his Excellency Antonio Guterres approaches the end of his term of office.
I wish also to thank him for his service to the United Nations and wish him well.

Mr. President,

1. At the outset, allow me to express my warmest congratulations to His Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly. My delegation assures you of our full support and cooperation throughout your Presidency. I also express our deep appreciation to Her Excellency Annalena Baerbock for her dedicated leadership during the 80th Session.

2. The theme for this session, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All,” arrives at a pivotal juncture. For developing and vulnerable countries, a well-resourced and responsive United Nations is an indispensable anchor. Restoring trust in our international system requires us to uphold predictable support, honour commitments, and reaffirm our fidelity to the UN Charter.

3. For the Lao PDR, restoring and deepening trust begins with a renewed commitment to inclusive multilateralism, with the United Nations at its core. When dialogue is guided by mutual respect, transparency, and genuine cooperation, multilateralism yields tangible benefits for all people.

Mr. President,

4. Our world continues to confront severe, multifaceted crises: geopolitical tensions, macroeconomic instability, supply chain disruptions, and accelerating climate emergencies. These headwinds place immense strain on the most vulnerable economies, where rising energy and food prices jeopardize the livelihoods of millions of people in countries in special situations.

5. The ongoing conflicts in the Middle East demonstrate how rapidly confrontation can destabilize global stability. Sustainable peace cannot be forged through force or unilateral action; it requires diplomacy, respect for sovereign equality and territorial integrity, and strict adherence to international law.

6. The question of Palestine remains an enduring test of multilateral credibility. We remain deeply concerned by the humanitarian catastrophe and immense reconstruction requirements in Gaza, as well as mounting challenges in the West Bank. To prevent the twostate solution from slipping beyond reach, the international community must secure a just, comprehensive, and lasting peace, one that fulfils the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people to selfdetermination through an independent State of Palestine with full membership in the United Nations.

7. In the same vein, the Lao PDR reiterates its principled position against Unilateral Coercive Measures. The prolonged economic, commercial, and financial embargo against the Republic of Cuba continues to inflict hardship on its people. We call for the immediate and unconditional lifting of these sanctions, including logistics and energy blockades, and the removal of Cuba from the list of “State Sponsors of Terrorism.” Such steps are essential first humanitarian measures toward restoring trust and reaffirming the primacy of international law.

Mr. President,

8. The gap between commitments and delivery on climate change equally tests the credibility of multilateralism. Although the Lao PDR has contributed only a small share of global greenhouse gas emissions, our people are increasingly affected by floods, droughts and extreme weather conditions.

9. The Lao PDR remains fully committed to the Paris Agreement and its Nationally Determined Contributions. However, climate ambition must be matched by adequate, predictable, and accessible climate finance, technology transfer, and capacity-building to enable vulnerable developing states to adapt, build long-term resilience, and pursue low-carbon growth pathways.

Mr. President,

10. The Lao PDR welcomes the UN80 Initiative to enhance the coherence, transparency, and effectiveness of the UN System.

Systemic reform must ensure a balanced approach across all three pillars of the Organization: peace and security, sustainable development, and human rights.

11. The implementation of the Pact for the Future and the Global Digital Compact must focus on narrowing the digital divide.

Artificial intelligence and digital technologies must serve human development, strengthen local technical capacities, and respect national development priorities.

Mr. President,

12. As an active member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the Lao PDR reaffirms that a united, integrated ASEAN serves as a cornerstone of regional peace and multilateral stability. We remain steadfast in supporting ASEAN centrality within the evolving regional architecture, where ASEAN -led mechanisms foster trust and practical cooperation.

13. This year carries special significance as we begin implementing the ASEAN Community Vision 2045 alongside its Strategic Plans across all three community pillars. It also marks the 50th Anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia (TAC)—a foundational framework whose core principles of peaceful coexistence and mutual respect remain fully relevant today. ASEAN remains the bedrock of Lao PDR’s regional engagement.

Mr. President,

14. Despite severe external economic shocks and natural disasters, the Lao economy continues its steady recovery through strong national ownership and strategic international partnerships. Guided by our Sovereign and Self-Reliant Economic Policy, the Lao PDR has adopted the 10th National Socio-Economic Development Plan (2026–2030).

15. The 10th NSEDP focuses on six core national outcomes: o First: Executing a sovereign and self-reliant economic policy aiming for steady annual GDP growth of 6% or higher; o Second: Developing high-quality human resources capable of driving technological transition; o Third: Improving living standards, ensuring balanced urbanrural development, and alleviating poverty; o Fourth: Protecting natural resources, building climate resilience, and mitigating disaster risks; o Fifth: Enhancing regional and global economic integration and connectivity; and o Sixth: Strengthening the efficiency and transparency of public administration and governance.

16. Central to this strategy is transforming the Lao PDR from a landlocked country into a land-linked regional gateway. Strategic infrastructure, including the Laos–China Railway, the Laos–Viet Nam Railway project, expanded transit corridors, and access to the sea via Vung Ang International Port are actively driving regional trade and integration. Our long-term vision towards 2055 aims to firmly establish the Lao PDR as an upper-middle-income nation with sustainable, inclusive growth at its core.

Mr. President,

17. This year marks a landmark milestone in our national development. The Lao PDR remains fully committed to its formal graduation from Least Developed Country (LDC) status, in accordance with relevant General Assembly resolutions.

18. As the UN Secretary-General António Guterres rightly stated,

LDC graduation must be “a reward, never a punishment.” To safeguard our hard-won development gains and prevent structural setbacks, we are executing a robust Smooth Transition Strategy (2026–2029). We call on our international partners to provide predictable transition support, extend smooth adjustments regarding International Support Measures (ISMs), and expand concessional financing to build enduring economic resilience.

19. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development remains fully embedded within our national planning. As we prepare to present our Fourth V oluntary National Review (VNR4) at the 2027 HighLevel Political Forum, we remain dedicated to an open, transparent assessment of our progress.

20. For the Lao PDR, the nexus between peace and development is a lived experience. As a country heavily impacted by wartime cluster munitions for over five decades, we have placed unexploded ordnance (UXO) clearance at the heart of our development agenda through the national SDG 18: "Lives Safe from UXO."

Removing UXO is not merely a technical task. It is about restoring fundamental safety, securing agricultural land, and reclaiming development opportunities for our communities.

21. Building on this commitment, the Lao PDR proudly hosted the 3rd Review Conference of the Convention on Cluster Munitions (CCM) early this month in Vientiane under the theme: “Accelerating Progress Towards a World Free from the Threat of Cluster Munitions.” Our Presidency demonstrated that mine action is an indispensable foundation for poverty reduction, human dignity, and sustainable development.

Mr. President,

22. As Secretary-General António Guterres prepares to complete his distinguished tenure at the helm of our Organization, the Government and people of the Lao PDR wish to express our profound appreciation and heartfelt gratitude for his principled leadership, moral clarity, and unwavering dedication to the United Nations. A true and trusted friend of the Lao PDR and fellow peace-loving developing nations across the Global South,

Secretary-General Guterres will be warmly remembered for his tireless advocacy for international financial architecture reform, climate justice, sustainable development financing, and the dignity of countries in special situations. His legacy of solidarity and bold championing of equity will continue to inspire our collective multilateral efforts for years to come.

Mr. President,

23. In conclusion, the Lao PDR firmly believes that the United Nations remains the essential home of global cooperation. No single nation can overcome today's complex global challenges alone. Let us unite our collective strength, renew our trust in multilateralism, and work together to build a peaceful, resilient, and prosperous world where no nation and no person is left behind.

I thank you.

Mr. President of the General Assembly; Mr. Secretary General; The advance of expansionism, usurpation, plunder, conquest as well as military and economic aggression s are alarming. The US government aspiration to impose peace through force is unrealizable.

The fundamental pillars of International Law and the United Nations Organization, such as the sovereign equality among States, are under permanent attack.

The genocidal crime of Zionism against the Palestinian people; the pirate attacks against vessels and the extrajudicial executions in the Caribbean Sea and some areas in the Pacific; the military aggression against the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela and the war against the Islamic Republic of Iran are new expressions of this atrocity.

They are also a reflection of the crisis of identity and relevance imposed on the United Nations Organization, and even on the General Assembly, the most universal, democratic and representative body of the international community.

We are convinced of the need to preserve and strengthen the United Nations, as we make it more democratic and effective; and of placing it closer to the peoples.

As is well known, in Cuba we are facing a multidimensional aggression from the United States government; a permanent, abusive and ruthless hostility that has lasted for almost seven decades already. Since January, 2026, this aggression has strengthened and become crueler and more dangerous, with the imposition of an energy blockade that, by resorting to intimidation and coercion, prevents any country from exporting fuel to Cuba -an equivalent to a naval blockade-, which is classified by International Law as an act of war.

Through the adoption of successive measures, the government of the United States has been applying new prohibitions on all countries with regard to products and services that cannot be exported or transported to Cuba. More than 7 thousand containers remain stranded in different ports; many of them are loaded with foodstuffs, medicines and medical devices and have even been paid for by Cuban private companies.

It is an unusual and unprecedented action. A superpower unilaterally deprives all States of their right to export the commodities that they wish to the country that they wish and continuously and comprehensively violates freedom of trade and navigation.

Added to this is the intimidation of entrepreneurs of different countries so that they abandon, against their will, their investments and businesses in Cuba; the obstacles and tricks to prevent the arrival in Cuba of absolutely legitimate commercial shipments; the pressures to prevent the entry of visitors and tourists; and the efforts aimed at restricting as much as possible Cuba’s legitimate access to financing, technology and markets.

The United States has gone as far as to exert unsuspected pressures on sovereign governments so that they renounce the medical services they requested from us for the benefit of their respective populations and which are offered by Cuban professionals, because the US government is opposed to such cooperation, regardless of the impact and harm this may cause to those populations if they are deprived of free medical care; that is to say, deprived of an elemental human right. On Thursday last, while the General Assembly was in session, the State Department convened a humiliating meeting specifically with the States that are the recipients of this cooperation.

According to the US Secretary of State, the official policy is to shut down every relief valve, block every possible way out and eliminate any form of survival for Cuba.

The impact of such an iron-clad and ruthless siege has a human face.

The economic warfare is aimed against the people. It harms the Cuban people as a whole. It takes a toll on huma n lives. It causes individual and collective pain; it causes anguish. It is not “collateral damage”. It is a policy deliberately designed to wound the deepest sensibilities of Cuban families; disturb their wellbeing and hurt the dignity of the people. It is an act of collective punishment; a crime proscribed by International Humanitarian Law. The obvious short term goal pursued by such policy is to induce a humanitarian crisis in Cuba, which is also a crime.

The government of the United States and the US State Department have been forced to recognize the suffering inflicted on the Cuban people, but they have the impudence and cynicism to insist in putting the blame on the government of Cuba. The executioner blames the victim.

They are following the formula recommended by the State Department since 1960 in the infamous Mallory Memorandum, which established as an official policy, in force up until today, the overthrowing of the Cuban government through the economic suffocation and the extreme suffering of the Cuban people out of material shortages, hunger and desperation.

A few days ago, the President of the United States declared in this room that Cuba was ‘a failed State’. If that were the case, why did they have to impose a fuel blockade? Why did they impose secondary sanctions? Why do they have to threaten, persecute and exert pressures on other States? He also recognized that his government is putting on Cuba the biggest pressure ever applied against any other State. A few months before, he had said that “all that is left is to go in and destroy everything.”

The threat of the use of military force against Cuba persists. This behavior is a violation of International Law and an infringement of the San Francisco Charter.

Should it materialize, it would be a major crime. It would cause the death of Cuban and American youths as well as huge destruction.

Cuba will exercise, with utmost resolve and energy, its legitimate right to defend itself. This aggression is being accompanied by a brutal media and cognitive warfare aimed against the Cuban people, the US citizens and the international public opinion. It is characterized by its gross and brazen attempts to interfere in the internal affairs of Cuba, which is another international crime.

We are often asked what is the US pursuing with such an aggressive behavior, and the question usually surprises us, because the representatives of that government have outrightly declared their purpose to take Cuba, control the country and dominate the economy.

In other words, nullify, through an aggression or economic suffocation, the national so vereignty which several generations of Cuban s have struggled for since the nineteenth century -first to achieve it, and later on, after conquering the full freedom in 1959, to tenaciously defend it against the biggest risks, including that of a holocaust.

The US behavior relies on the fallacy, proclaimed early on this year, that Cuba is an unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security and the foreign policy of the United States -a nonsense shamelessly repeated by that government. In a futile attempt to substantiate such an assertion, the US government inundates its huge communication platforms with false claims using the spokespersons and publications it hires, taking advantage of the increasing control exercised by its government over them. The US President himself repeated it a few days ago in this room.

Any minimally informed observer would understand the unrealistic and evil intention to portray a relatively small and developing nation like Cuba, with a modest economic performance, as a threat to the biggest nuclear, military, technological and econom ic power in the planet.

This Organization and its member States have abundant evidence of the fact that we are a peace -loving country; of the efforts of Cuba in favor of international cooperation, understanding and the peaceful settlement of disputes as well as of the active role that we have played in support of the United Nations. Cuba is not a threat; the blockade is!

We are aware of the immense challenge our country faces in terms of its security, survival, the wellbeing of the people and the destiny of the nation. We are not facing this challenge passively. We are doing it firmly and with dignity. Based on that, we are moving on in a process of changes that would lead to profound transformations of the economic and social model of the country, based on our historical experience.

On July 30 last, during the closing ceremony of the Seventh Session of the National People’s Power Assembly, President Miguel Díaz Canel referred to the origin of the social and economic transformations that the country is introducing. He said, and I quote: “In view of the complex situation I have described, how can we prevail in the construction of socialism? How cou ld we find the material and financial resources needed to preserve the social achievements attained by the Revolution? As it already happened on former occasions, when we were faced with particularly complex situations such as the Special Period -; when, under the guidance, first of Commander in Chief, and later on of Army General Raúl Castro, the economic model was transformed to adapt it to the challenging foreign circumstances demanded by the times, under the leadership of the Party, in a collective and democratic way, in consultation with the people, without compromising the independence, the national sovereignty or the social achievements of the Revolution”, end of quote.

The National People’s Power Assembly has adopted a new program, with new practices, actors and economic concepts. All of that is being done in accordance with the Constitution in force -. which was adopted through a free and universal referendum- and the conception of our socialist State of law and social justice.

As was pointed out by the leader of the Cuban Revolution, Army General Raúl Castro Ruz, the most important thing will be “the appropriate and timely implementation process, with well -defined priorities and the conscious participation of the people.”

This process relies on the strengths that we have built; the potential of our human resources and the determination to respond to the needs of the people with the greatest possible social justice, without ceasing in our efforts to defend, with utmost vigor and resolve, the sovereignty and the right to self-determination.

As a Small Island Developing State, we stand in solidarity with our brothers and sisters who share a similar condition and the warning about the worrying and inexorable advance of climate change.

It is necessary to promote a governance that makes a more intensive use of the new ICTs, particularly the disruptive technologies, such as artificial intelligence.

We reject the implementation of unilateral coercive measures. We express our support to and solidarity with the nations which are victim of them.

We ratify our solidarity with the Government of National Reconciliation and Unity of Nicaragua.

We reiterate our support to the inalienable right of the people of Puerto Rico to self-determination and independence.

The sister nations of Africa and the Caribbean deserve a fair and differentiated treatment, as well as the reparations for the horrors of colonialism and the transatlantic slave trade.

We reaffirm our solidarity with the Saharan people and their right to self-determination.

We ratify our support to the “One China” principle.

We strongly believe that the current trend of international relations of disrespect for International Law and the United Nations, the imposition of the unilateral will of the mightiest over other countries by means of intimidation and coercion, is dangerous and unsustainable.

The law of the jungle cannot be the future of humanity.

To prevent those practices, in addition of promoting peace and justice, the preceding generations founded the United Nations and for decades developed and enriched its activity. Let us recover its role today, when we are perhaps in time to do so, before the Organization goes down in history as an unrealized dream of great promises.

In the year of the centennial birthday of Fidel Castro Ruz, the historical leader of the Cuban Revolution, let us be confident, as he was, that if we struggle with resolve, a better world will be possible.

Homeland or Death, We Shall Overcome!

Mr. President, Excellencies, dear friends,

The United Nations was born from a harsh lesson of history. The generation of 1945 had learned, at terrible cost, that while states can choose their actions, they cannot control all the consequences they set in motion.

That lesson is painfully relevant today.

We are living through a period of profound uncertainty. Power is shifting.

Conflicts are multiplying. And there is a growing tendency to treat the rules and institutions of the international system as constraints belonging to another age.

But the United Nations was built precisely for times of uncertainty: to bring rules and restraint to an unpredictable world, and to prevent conflict from descending into catastrophe.

The task of our generation is both to preserve the institutions built by those that came before us, and to also remember the hard -earned wisdom on which they rest.

Today, that wisdom – and the United Nations that embodies it – is under enormous pressure.

Mr. President,

This year marks eighty years since Iceland joined the United Nations.

For eight decades, Iceland has held that a small state should enjoy the same protection, rights and voice as a powerful one. That idea matters more today, not less.

Despite its shortcomings, the United Nations has mattered. And it has mattered a lot.

UN peacekeeping and peacebuilding operations have helped prevent and contain conflict around the world. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights transformed our understanding of human dignity.

The Convention on the Law of the Sea became the Constitution of the Ocean, on which countries like mine depend, now strengthened further by the BBNJ Agreement.

The International Court of Justice has helped states settle disputes by peaceful means, through law rather than force.

And the International Criminal Court was created to ensure accountability for the most serious crimes.

The United Nations has advanced gender equality, fought racism and discrimination, delivered humanitarian assistance and helped countries build more peaceful and prosperous societies.

But loyalty to the United Nations cannot mean pretending that everything works perfectly. Bureaucracy can be cumbersome, decisions slow and resources fragmented. The Security Council - entrusted with maintaining international peace and security - has too often been paralysed when action was needed most.

Too often, the veto has become a shield against action rather than a tool for preserving peace. So yes, the United Nations needs reform. And Iceland fully supports the UN80 reform process.

We need a United Nations that uses resources effectively and responds quickly when people need it. United Nations that delivers for all.

The deeper chal lenge, however, is p olitical. The strength of the United Nations depends on our willingness to uphold the principles and wisdom on which they were founded.

Mr. President,

The most basic rules of international relations are being tested. Not because we no longer know them. We do.

But because increasingly, governments apply them selectively. Meaning that international law applies - until it becomes inconvenient.

That court decisions must be respected - unless they challenge our own actions or those of our friends.

That sovereignty is sacred - unless someone else's territory stands in the way of our ambitions.

We cannot build courts, celebrate them when they prosecute our enemies, and undermine them when they turn their attention to our friends.

When grave violations go unanswered, they are more likely to be repeated.

And for small states this is existential, not simply a matter of principle.

Russia's brutal war against Ukraine is a clear example. Russia invaded a sovereign neighbour, seeking to change borders by force and deny another nation the freedom to determine its future. Ukrainians have paid an unimaginable price.

Behind every destroyed home is a family. Behind every casualty is someone who was loved.

Iceland's position remains clear. Ukraine has the right to defend itself, to sovereignty and territorial integrity, and to a just and lasting peace on the basis of international law.

Our support for Ukraine defends a principle on which all our countries’ security depends: That no nation gets to decide the future of another.

This principle must apply everywhere. Including in the Middle East.

In Gaza, we continue to witness repeated violations of the ceasefire and continued suffering among civilians, despite the adoption of the twenty point Comprehensive Peace Plan and Security Council Resolution 2803.

The suffering of Palestinian civilians cannot become background noise.

Children are still being killed. Families are still losing their homes. Parents are still trying to keep their children alive. Again. And again. And again.

We cannot accept Gaza being repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt while the underlying cause remains unresolved.

In the West Bank, illegal settlement activity continues to expand. Palestinian civilians face settler violence, too often enabled by impunity, inflammatory rhetoric and permissive policies.

Earlier this month, Iceland joined eleven other states in addressing restrictions on trade in goods from settlements that are illegal under international law.

Our objective remains clear: A viable Palestinian state alongside Israel, with both peoples able to live in security, dignity and peace.

We have heard the words “moral coward s” from this podium. To me, moral cowards are those leaders around the world who refuse to sit down and negotiate a just and lasting peace. Those who deny access to humanitarian aid for people in desperate need. And moral cowards are those leaders who repeatedly go against and disrespect international law.

Mr. President,

We must not allow the horrors in Ukraine and the Middle East to make other crises invisible.

In Sudan, years of civil war have brought atrocities, mass displacement and grave violations of international humanitarian law. As humanitarian leaders have reminded us, Sudan does not suffer from a lack of analysis. It suffers from a lack of action.

Acts that may constitute war crimes and crimes against humanity cannot be met with indifference. We created the International Criminal Court to ensure accountability for the most serious crimes. Accountability matters. So does adherence to international law beyond the battlefield. To be clear: Iceland stands with the ICC.

Obstruction of lawful international transit through the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb threatens not only countries in the region but global energy markets and food security. Disruption falls hardest on the most vulnerable.

The freedoms codified in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea are not optional. For an island nation dependent on open maritime routes, freedom of navigation is fundamental.

Mr. President,

Seventy-five years after the 1951 Refugee Convention, we should have hoped that the need for it would be diminishing. Instead, humanitarian needs and forced displacement have reached staggering levels.

Conflict, poverty, drought, natural disasters and the growing effects of climate change are pushing millions of people from their homes. And just as needs are increasing, funding is falling.

With development cooperation and humanitarian assistance we are investing in stability, resilience and peace. It is not charity offered when times are good. Cutting ODA is shortsighted and risks ma king instability, displacement and conflict worse. The cost will eventually reach us al l. We must not allow today's crises to push the Sustainable Development Goals aside. Iceland will not.

We also must not forget how much progress has bee n driven by economic freedom. Perhaps humanity‘s greatest gift is our c apacity to create. To imagine something that doesn‘t exist and then bring it into being.

Creativity is universal; w hat differ s is whether soc ieties gi ve it roo m to flourish. Open, free markets have given people the oppo rtunity to create, exchange ideas, take risk s and bui ld bet ter lives for themselves and for others.

Mr. President,

Another battle is taking place over what kind of societies we want to be.

Across the world, authoritarianism and political extremism are gaining ground.

We see attacks on democratic institutions, independent media, science and facts in public debate. Too often, these movements target groups whose rights supposedly matter less.

Women. LGBTQI+ people. Minorities. Migrants. People who look different, love differently or live differently. These are not abstract groups. They are our daughters and sons. Our friends. Our neighbours. Our colleagues.

I am deeply concerned by the growing backlash against gender equality and LGBTQI+ rights - including within my own region, Europe.

We hear that equality has gone too far. That diversity has gone too far. That some people demanding the freedom simply to be themselves somehow threaten the freedom of others.

I reject that completely. Human rights are not a zero -sum game. Giving a woman equal rights does not take rights away from a man. Allowing an LGBTQI+ person to live freely does not make anyone else less free. Quite the opposite.

We should be very careful when governments begin telling us that some people's existence threatens society. History has taught us where that can lead.

And l et me be clear: Iceland will not allow others to define our values or dictate the language we use to defend human rights.

Free societies are strongest when people are allowed to be themselves. But freedom that belongs only to people who fit someone else’s definition of normal is not freedom.

A society that strips people of their dignity will eventually undermine its own democracy.

And nowhere is this backlash more extreme than in Afghanistan, where women and girls have been systematically erased from public life. Girls are denied education, women are denied basic freedoms. For me, this can only be described as gender apartheid.

On the Human Rights Council, we have sought to match words with deeds; from Iran and Afghanistan to accountability for violations in Sudan.

Throughout our Council term, Iceland will emphasize gender equality,

LGBTQI+ rights, the rights of children and young people, and the relationship between human rights and the environment.

Human rights are not for some: They are for all.

Mr. President,

The same commitment to facts and responsibility must guide us on climate change.

Leaders who deny or distort science should explain themselves to island communities watching the sea rise around them. To families losing land and livelihoods to drought and erosion - like in the Sahel.

In Iceland, we can see the changes taking place in our own region, the Arctic.

Rising temperatures and receding ice are already changing ecosystems and the lives of communities across the region.

Climate change is not an ideology. Millions already live with its consequences. We need to address it, not ignore it.

Nor can we ignore another transformation already affecting our societies: artificial intelligence. This revolution is changing how we work, communicate and rec eive in formation. It is also making it easier to p roduce convincing falsehoods and manipulate public debate.

Freedom of speech is a fundamental right we must defend. But that does not require passivity when foreign states or other actors spread falsehoods, manipulate democratic processes or use AI to deceive citizens at unprecedented speed and scale.

Governments, businesses and scientists must cooperate internationally to harness the benefits of AI while confronting its risks.

And we need to move faster. Much faster.

Mr. President,

In difficult times, nostalgia tempts us to imagine that the world used to be simpler and safer. It was not.

The decades after the Cold War saw genocide in Rwanda, horrific wars in the former Yugoslavia and the Congo, the rise of international terrorism and devastating civil wars.

Twenty-five years ago this month, terrorist attacks in the United States changed our world profoundly.

Thirty years ago, the Comprehensive Nuclear -Test-Ban Treaty was established, yet the threat of nuclear proliferation remains with us.

What distinguished some of the past's best moments was our response:

Countries came together, built institutions and negotiated treaties. They created the Human Rights Council, OCHA, ICC, UN Women and the UNFCCC.

They placed Women, Peace and Security on the agenda of the Security Council and recognised sexual violence as a weapon and tactic of war. They adopted the Millennium Development Goals and later the Sustainable Development Goals.

To p ut it sim ply: None of t his happened by itself. It h appened b ecause political leaders consciously chose cooperation over retreat. That choice is before us again.

Mr. President,

The United Nations' next Secretary General must continue reforming this organisation, make difficult choices and direct resources where they make the greatest difference.

That will require courage from her.

And so will the choices made by every Member State represented in this Hall.

We must choose whether to uphold the law when it is inconvenient; whether to defend the rights of people who are not our citizens; and whether to protect and respect a system even when that system does not deliver the outcome we want.

That is the real test of our commitment to multilateralism. Not what we say when the rules favour us, but what we do when they do not.

For Iceland, the choice is clear. We choose international law over selective obedience. Accountability over impunity. Cooperation over isolation. Human dignity over division.

The generation that founded the United Nations had seen first -hand what could happen when restraints on power collapsed. The Charter, international law and the institutions that followed were their answer.

In that sense, the United Nations is a gift from a generation that learned that lesson at an extraordinary cost.

And now we need the courage to remember it.
