Mr President,

Imagine if nuclear weapons were developed by private companies.

If stockpiles were located on company grounds. And launch codes locked away in a safe in a CEO’s office.

It ́s a disturbing thought.

When a technology has the power to fundamentally change the world, possibly even determine the fate of humanity – we need to ask:

Who controls it?

Who sets the rules?

Who is accountable?

Today humankind faces another technological revolution that raises exactly these questions.

Engineers have developed a technology that does not need to be launched from a rocket or a submarine to change the course of history.

I am, of course, talking about artificial intelligence.

A technology with seemingly unlimited power.

In the wrong hands, it can upend our economies and threaten our livelihoods.

It has the potential to erode trust within our societies by spreading information that appears real but is, in fact, fake.

A.I. can endanger the infrastructure that keeps our societies running.

And ultimately, it can influence decisions that determine global peace and security.

At the same time, artificial intelligence holds extraordinary promise.

It can accelerate scientific discovery.

Improve healthcare and education all over the world.

Provide opportunities for economic development, overcome inequalities and help us address challenges that no country can solve alone.

Just imagine a world, where with the help of A.I. we can prevent famine and cure cancer.

This is precisely what makes AI so powerful – for better or for worse.

But there is a critical tension.

Only two major countries are home to the companies holding the vast majority of all global A.I. patents.

That puts an enormous amount of influence in the hands of a very few.

Such power carries responsibility – not only towards customers, shareholders or governments. But also to humanity.

And whenever power becomes global, responsibility must become global, too.

The United Nations was created precisely for a moment such as this.

When a challenge is too large for any one nation to address alone.

When risks need to be managed to protect people all over the world, and when opportunities need to be exploited in a way that benefits the largest and the smallest, the richest and the poorest member states.

But today, the United Nations itself is under pressure.

There are great powers that believe they fare better if they ignore the rules enshrined in the UN Charter.

The erosion of international law jeopardises the enormous civilisational progress that the United Nations stands for.

The commitment to peace.

The principle of sovereign equality of all states.

The belief in norms and rules.

The conviction of the dignity inherent in every human being.

The erosion of these principles may serve the interests of a few. Who believe themselves powerful enough to survive in a world without norms – or to write their own rules.

For us, for the overwhelming majority of the 193 states represented in this General Assembly, this is harmful.

We know that the people of this world will pay the price if the respect for international law erodes. And if its institutions are under attack.

For some of us, this erosion of the international order is already catastrophic. If it continues, we all stand to lose.

But this pressure on the international order does not come from political actors alone. It also comes from the forces of technological revolution.

This poses a crucial question: how do we enable our international institutions to keep pace with the technologies that are reshaping our world?

Faced with this question, it will not be enough to invoke what we still have – or once had – in the United Nations.

Nor will it help if we ignore its weaknesses.

What we need is honesty, realism and cooperation.

Honesty in our analysis, realism in our ambition and cooperation as our method.

We must acknowledge that many of the beams of this common house cannot carry the burden we put on them. We must decide: which parts of the house do we preserve, and which do we rebuild?

For this endeavor to succeed we need the new Secretary-General to lead a profound process of reform.

Above all, we must close the gap between what we expect from the United Nations and the capabilities we give to the organisation.

First, we need a functioning UN that plays an active role in resolving conflicts – rather than merely managing them.

In times when the Security Council, as the central decision-making body, is paralyzed, this is more difficult than ever.

We need to keep its reform high on our agenda.

Germany stands up for peace and security.

Today, more people than ever are affected by violent conflict. At the same time, for every member state, resources are limited.

Thus, we have to join forces to bring conflicts to an end.

Today, Germany is the largest supporter of Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. This aggression has been condemned consistently by an overwhelming majority here in the General Assembly.

Russia’s war targets the lives of millions of innocent people, the existence of the Ukrainian state and culture and the European peace order. It puts vital grain deliveries for millions of people at risk, particularly in Africa, Asia and the Middle East. It shows contempt for the Charter and for the common order on which we stand.

That is why we will continue to urge Russia to finally come to the negotiating table. I call on every member state to join us in convincing Russia that the future is built at the negotiating table, not on dead bodies in cities and villages. The day when negotiations finally begin will be a good day for the United Nations.

Germany is also taking on responsibility for peace and security beyond Europe – for example, in Haiti, where we have significantly increased our contribution to the international mission to combat gang crime.

Also, we shall not forget Sudan. At the Sudan conference in Berlin in April, together with our partners we mobilized more than 1,7 billion Dollars to alleviate the biggest humanitarian catastrophe of our time.

Second, we stand for international cooperation that is peaceful, fair and based on equality.

A new nationalism would be a misguided path. Whatever its prophets may preach, the truth is, that it would make our lives narrower, poorer and less secure.

Instead, global trade relations need to be diversified and deepened – in the framework of a fair trading order.

No country should have to accept raw materials being used to force obedience.

Or supply chains becoming instruments of pressure.

None of us is powerless in the face of this. Where we cooperate, we free ourselves from one-sided dependencies and open up new spaces of freedom.

With our partners in the European Union, we have begun this work through new trade accords, cooperation agreements and partnerships. These partnerships are built on mutual respect, on common rules and a shared respect for international law.

They also take into account the fortunate fact that many countries of the Global South are developing with extraordinary success.

The same principle of partnership and cooperation also applies to technology.

Access to computing power, data, expertise and infrastructure will increasingly shape who can innovate – and who merely has to accept the rules set by others.

Cooperation must therefore create capabilities, not new dependencies.

Third, we want to answer the great global questions of our time together.

No one here – not even the largest among us – can do this alone.

Together with all those who are willing to do so, we will continue our work to address human-made climate change and its devastating effects swiftly and effectively.

We are forced to chart new courses, and we must do it with speed.

But nowhere is the need more pressing than in the area of artificial intelligence. It is our collective responsibility to ensure that this technology serves human dignity.

This is particularly urgent because technologies are already changing the foundations of our societies.

A.I. is not waiting for our institutions to catch up.

Our institutions have to catch up with reality.

At the beginning of my remarks, I asked three questions: who controls new technologies? Who sets the rules? And who is accountable?

We cannot answer them by simply trusting that those with the greatest capabilities will always act in the interest of everyone else.

We need to ensure that technological progress is guided by a framework that we all have a say in shaping.

That means building the capacity to understand and assess increasingly capable A.I. systems.

It means making sure that all regions can participate in shaping the rules.

And it means moving from voluntary commitments towards increasing transparency, as well as developing common standards.

That is why Germany calls on UN member states to work towards common safety requirements for the most capable A.I. models.

Providers should be required to test these models before release and report serious safety failures.

These requirements should be supported by effective national and regional oversight.

The A.I. industry will have to play its role in this and continue to bear a responsibility in shaping the trajectory of this technology.

At the same time, we need to ensure accountability, in particular when global peace and security are potentially affected.

In the course of this week, we have intensified our conversation about these questions.

How we address A.I. together, is one of the clearest tests of whether we have the strength and the will to build a United Nations for today’s world.

The next Secretary-General can count on Germany along this path.

Our history, our geography and our constitution bind us to the UN Charter and to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. This is at the very core of our statehood.

The technologies may change.

But one principle will remain: power must be bound by responsibility.

And progress must serve human dignity.

The world has long been in a mode of permanent escalation.

And with it, the UN is navigating stormy waters.

We must decide: are we truly willing to let the boat we all share drift toward capsizing, or will we pool our strength and steer it back on course?

The tools are in our hands.

Together, we can push for renewal and build a peaceful future for generations to come.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

San Marino is the world’s oldest Republic. For more than seventeen centuries, we have survived not through military power, territorial expansion or economic might, but through dialogue, respect for the law, neutrality, and the conviction that the sovereignty of a small State is no less valuable than that of a great power.

Our history has taught us a simple lesson: when power is not enough to protect you, rules matter. When you cannot impose your will, dialogue matters. And when the world is divided, institutions that bring States together matter.

This is why multilateralism is not an abstract concept for San Marino. It is a fundamental principle of our foreign policy, and, in many ways, a lesson drawn from our own history.

Our commitment to cooperation and shared rules is also reflected in our relationship with the European Union.

The forthcoming signing of the Association Agreement with the European Union on 19 October will mark a milestone for our country.

It represents a historic step towards closer cooperation, shared rules and greater integration with the European Union, while fully preserving our sovereignty, identity and institutional specificities.

For San Marino, this is not simply an agreement about economic relations. It is a long-term choice to deepen our engagement with Europe while preserving the distinctive character of our Republic.

It is a choice that reflects a principle at the heart of our history: cooperation does not diminish sovereignty. For a small State, cooperation, rules and dialogue are precisely what allow sovereignty to be exercised and protected.

Today, that principle is under extraordinary pressure.

Eighty-one years ago, the United Nations was created to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.

Yet today, conflicts are multiplying. Inequalities are deepening.

Climate disruption is accelerating. Food and water are increasingly being used as instruments of pressure. And the rules that have governed international relations for decades are being challenged.

We are witnessing the use of force against sovereign States. We are witnessing violations of international humanitarian and human rights law.

At such a moment, the answer cannot be less multilateralism.

It must be more.

And it must be a multilateralism that works: one that protects the weak as well as the strong; one that applies the law equally; and one that gives every State, large or small, a meaningful voice.

Before turning to the challenges before us, allow me to congratulate H.E. Dr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the eighty-first session of the General Assembly.

San Marino supports the priorities of your programme and stands ready to cooperate fully with you and with all Member States in the year ahead.

I also wish to express our appreciation to Secretary -General António Guterres for his leadership at a time of profound international uncertainty, and for his continued efforts to strengthen the United Nations and the multilateral system.

Mr. President,

There can be no world in which might makes right.

Sovereignty, territorial integrity, political independence and self determination matter. These principles are not optional and they cannot depend on the size of a country or the power of a government.

There can be no impunity for violations of international law. The law must apply to all.

For San Marino, this is not an abstract principle. For small States, international law is our protection. It is the ultimate equalizer.

A rules-based international order allows every State, large or small, to have an equal voice and equal legal standing.

This is why San Marino strongly supports the Secretary -General’s UN80 initiative.

The United Nations must become more effective, more efficient and more responsive.

And reform must include the Security Council.

The Council must better reflect today’s world. It must be more representative, transparent and accountable.

San Marino is also a member of the Uniting for Consensus group and supports its efforts to promote a comprehensive and balanced reform of the Security Council, based on greater regional representation, equitable geographical distribution and wider access to elected seats.

Reform must strengthen the voice of all Member States, including small States, and it must be achieved through broad consensus.

We support efforts to restrain the use of the veto, including the French-Mexican initiative and the ACT Code of Conduct in situations involving mass atrocities, alongside the General Assembly veto initiative.

We also reaffirm our full support for the International Court of Justice. Its orders and judgments are legally binding. Respect for the Court is respect for the international legal order.

Mr. President,

The next Secretary-General will carry a vital responsibility.

The United Nations must remain relevant and credible. Above all, it must remain capable of protecting people and upholding the Charter.

San Marino stands ready to contribute.

Mr. President,

I now turn to one of the most painful crises of our time.

The situation in the Middle East demands clarity.

San Marino unequivocally condemns terrorism, including the horrific attacks of 7 October 2023.

But we must be equally clear on another point: the Palestinian people have an inalienable right to self -determination and to their own State.

Statehood is not a reward for terrorism. It is a right.

At the same time, nothing can justify the collective punishment of civilians.

The suffering in Gaza cannot become the new normal.

We call for a permanent ceasefire and for full, safe and unhindered humanitarian access. Humanitarian assistance must reach those who need it. Civilian lives must be protected. UNRWA and other humanitarian organizations must be able to operate.

We call for the permanent disarmament of Hamas and other nonState armed groups, and for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the Gaza Strip.

We support the Palestinian Authority and its reform efforts, including democratic elections.

We urge Israel to release withheld clearance revenues and to facilitate correspondent banking services for the Palestinian Authority.

In the West Bank and East Jerusalem, settlement expansion, settler violence, land appropriation, demolitions and evictions must stop. The situation is rapidly deteriorating amid unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion, including the unacceptable decision to publish tenders for the E1 settlement project.

These developments undermine the possibility of a viable Palestinian State.

The Status Quo of Jerusalem’s holy sites must be respected. All communities, including Christian communities, must be protected.

Last year, San Marino endorsed the New York Declaration for a two-State solution.

Following a unanimous mandate from our Parliament, the Great and General Council, San Marino recognized Palestine as a sovereign and independent State, within secure and internationally recognized borders and in accordance with relevant United Nations resolutions.

We stand by that decision.

There is no alternative to two States living side by side in peace, security and mutual recognition.

The window for that solution is narrowing. We must act now.

Mr. President,

The consequences of the conflict extend far beyond Gaza and the West Bank.

Escalation across the region threatens international peace and security.

We are deeply concerned by hostilities involving Iran and by threats to maritime security in the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz.

Freedom of navigation is essential to global stability. International law, including UNCLOS, must be respected.

In Lebanon, we call for full respect for sovereignty and for the implementation of Security Council resolution 1701. Civilian infrastructure must be protected.

In Syria, we support an inclusive and peaceful political transition that respects sovereignty, protects civilians and strengthens institutions.

Peace cannot be imposed by force. It requires diplomacy and dialogue. And it requires international law.

Mr. President,

Europe is also facing a war that continues to cause immense human suffering.

San Marino condemns Russia’s ongoing aggression against Ukraine.

The bombardment of cities.

The killing of civilians.

Attacks on humanitarian workers.

The unlawful deportation of children.

These are not simply tragedies. They are violations of international law.

No State can be allowed to redraw borders by force.

San Marino therefore reiterates its call for a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire, leading to a comprehensive, just and lasting peace.

Any peace must respect Ukraine’s sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.

Mr. President,

From Ukraine to Gaza, from Sudan to Syria, from the Sahel to Afghanistan, civilians continue to pay the highest price.

Women, Children, Older people. Families forced from their homes.

Hospitals and schools destroyed. Food, water and medicines denied.

International humanitarian law was created precisely for these circumstances.

It does not disappear in times of war. It is not suspended by political convenience. It must be respected.

San Marino strongly condemns the use of explosive weapons in populated areas and calls on all States to implement the Political Declaration on Explosive Weapons in Populated Areas.

Those who deliver humanitarian assistance must also be protected. Aid workers and journalists are not legitimate targets.

San Marino also reaffirms its commitment to the Australia-led Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel, and calls on all parties to armed conflict to respect and protect humanitarian personnel and to ensure that assistance can reach those in need.

Impunity cannot become normal.

San Marino therefore reaffirms its commitment to the Geneva Conventions, the Genocide Convention and the Rome Statute.

And we reiterate our unwavering support for the International Criminal Court.

The Court exists because the gravest crimes cannot go unanswered: genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Accountability is not an obstacle to peace. It is part of lasting peace.

The fight against impunity is also an essential element of the Responsibility to Protect, which must remain a shared responsibility of the international community.

Recent political pressure and coercive measures against the Court, its officials and those who cooperate with it are deeply concerning.

States Parties to the Rome Statute must defend the independence and integrity of the Court.

San Marino also reaffirms its historic commitment to the abolition of the death penalty, which it abolished in 1865. This reflects our enduring conviction that human dignity must be protected even in the face of the gravest crimes.

Justice cannot depend on political power.

Mr. President,

Five years ago, the Taliban seized power in Afghanistan.

Five years is too long for half of a population to be denied its rights.

Afghan women and girls continue to face systematic restrictions on education, employment, movement, public participation and access to justice.

Girls remain excluded from secondary and higher education.

Women are increasingly excluded from public life. This cannot become normal.

San Marino calls for the full restoration of the rights of Afghan women and girls.

Education is a right. Work is a right. Participation in public life is a right. Dignity is a right.

These rights do not disappear because a government chooses to deny them.

The international community must continue to stand with Afghan women and girls.

Humanitarian access must also remain unhindered.

Afghanistan must not be forgotten.

Mr. President,

Children everywhere deserve protection. Children are being killed, maimed, abducted and recruited. They are losing their homes, their schools and their futures.

San Marino remains firmly committed to the Children and Armed Conflict agenda and supports the work of the UN Special Representative for Children and Armed Conflict.

Schools must remain safe places.

We have endorsed the Safe Schools Declaration, the Paris Principles and the Vancouver Principles.

We call on all States to strengthen the protection of children in armed conflict and to ratify the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

Mr. President,

The return of nuclear threats is another source of grave concern.

There can be no acceptable nuclear threat or acceptable use of nuclear weapons.

The modernization and expansion of nuclear arsenals, together with growing military expenditures and the rapid development of artificial intelligence and cyber capabilities, increase the risk of escalation.

The consequences of nuclear use would be catastrophic.

San Marino remains committed to a world free of nuclear weapons.

We support the Treaty on the Non -Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. We also proudly uphold the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which San Marino has signed and ratified.

Diplomacy must prevail over deterrence through fear.

Mr. President,

Peace and security cannot be separated from development. Nor can development be separated from human rights.

Conflict destroys development gains. Poverty fuels instability.

Climate change increases pressure on food, water and communities.

We must also not overlook the devastating humanitarian and socio-economic situation in Cuba, where prolonged hardship is placing an immense burden on the daily lives of the Cuban people.

We must therefore treat peace, security, human rights and sustainable development as parts of the same agenda.

The SDGs remain our common commitment. The Pact for the Future provides an opportunity to strengthen multilateralism and accelerate implementation of the 2030 Agenda.

But commitments are not enough.

We need implementation, financing and accountability.

We also need a fairer and more inclusive international financial architecture, supported by adequate resources and greater financial stability for the UN itself.

The triple planetary crisis - climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution - is already affecting peace and security.

Environmental degradation fuels food insecurity, water scarcity and displacement.

The Paris Agreement must be fully implemented.

The 1.5-degree goal must remain within reach, the transition must be just and no country should be left behind.

Food security must also remain at the heart of our collective efforts.

Conflict and climate shocks are driving hunger and malnutrition.

San Marino believes that reducing food loss and waste is one practical contribution to a more secure and sustainable food system.

Mr. President,

We are also entering a new technological era.

Artificial intelligence and emerging technologies offer enormous opportunities, but they also create new risks.

Technology must serve humanity. It must not be used to undermine human rights, international peace or international humanitarian law.

The rules must keep pace with innovation.

And where new technologies create new risks, our responsibility is not to look away, but to govern them.

This is why multilateralism matters.

Multilateralism is not an outdated idea. It is the only framework capable of managing an interdependent world.

No country can address today’s challenges alone, protect itself from climate change alone, prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons alone or regulate global technology alone.

And no country can build lasting peace alone.

We need cooperation and institutions that work. And we need the political courage to uphold the rules we have created together.

Mr. President,

For more than seventeen centuries, San Marino has shown that a small State can preserve its independence through dialogue, respect for the law and engagement with the international community.

This is why San Marino will continue to defend the United Nations Charter, international law, human rights and multilateralism.

At a time when the world is tempted by division, we must choose cooperation. When force challenges law, we must stand firmly by the law.

And when despair is growing, we must choose peace.

San Marino will do its part.

Together, we must ensure that the United Nations remains what it was created to be: a shield for the vulnerable, a forum for dialogue and a guardian of peace, dignity and international law.

Thank you.

I now give the floor to His Excellency Maxim Ryzhenkov, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Belarus.
Mr. president, ladies and gentlemen, let us begin with the theme of today's debate restoring Trust, managing transformation.
A United Nations that delivers for all.
It is an interesting theme that allows us for a very substantive discussion, which we have been witnessing for a week now.

Indeed, trust among states today is at its lowest point since the Cold War.
The necessary reforms are stalling.
More and more voices are saying that the UN is not working in the interests of all and is incapable of managing change.
This is largely because we, the Member States, have in large part, become mired in endless debates, but have failed to give the organisation a real opportunity to act.

That is precisely why the theme of this session sounds today like a verdict on our collective indecision, and at the same time as a diagnosis, calling for urgent treatment.
We are surrounded by a systemic crisis in international relations.
We see this everywhere.
The air is thick with anxiety from Europe to the Middle East, from Asia to Africa and Latin America.

Wars and conflicts are engulfing the world.
They are claiming lives, tearing families apart, turning thriving cities into ruins and giving rise to ever more waves of mass forced migration.
Global supply chains are being disrupted.
The energy crisis is entwined with the food crisis, and all of this hits the most vulnerable segments of the population the hardest.

And even more alarming sign is the collapse of the system of strategic stability.
For the first time since the 1970s, there are no longer any legally binding limits on strategic arms between the major nuclear powers.
There are no treaties, no verification mechanisms, and no predictability.
Humanity is once again teetering on the brink of existence.

That is a brink that we had hoped we had left for good in the last century.
How did we reach this point?
Well, it is no mere coincidence.
It is the inevitable result of actions by certain states aimed at deliberately undermining the system of international relations so that the world would develop not according to the laws of peaceful coexistence, but rather the principle of might makes right and political selfishness.

If we truly want to restore trust, we must not hide behind diplomatic niceties, but honestly identify the causes of crises.
In 1945, in San Francisco, at the UN founding conference, U.S. president Harry Truman spoke words that today sound like a prophecy.
No matter how great our strength, we must deny ourselves the license to do always as we please.
If all those with great power had acted as Truman said, we would have avoided many wars and conflicts.

Unfortunately, however, the desire to live at the expense of others has remained the dominant narrative in the collective West's development during the Cold War The balance of power was maintained by a system of checks and balances between the two opposing political systems.
But since the 1990s, when that balance collapsed, the policy of unrestrained superiority has begun to grow rapidly, and in recent years this policy has reached its peak.
Western countries have effectively trampled on international law and started to force everyone to act according to so-called rules, destroying countries and suppressing unbowed peoples.
And these rules are like traffic signs in a city that they themselves have designed.

They always have a green light while everyone else faces strict restrictions.
But this isn't about metaphors.
It is about facts that everyone knows Yugoslavia, Iraq, Libya, Syria, Venezuela, Cuba, Iran, Palestine.
And this is by no means an exhaustive list of the countries that have been or remain the focus of greedy Western interests.

Now let's add to that unfair global trade where the rules are written to serve the interests of transnational corporations and also illegal unilateral sanctions that are suffocating entire nations.
And those efforts are intensifying.
But what is the U.N. doing?
The organization has not been able to resolve a single serious conflict.

Its role has instead boiled down to managing concerns, making appeals to those who have already suffered And that is, of course, leading to further escalation.
The leadership of the European Union is particularly worrying.
They have an unbridled desire to preserve their slipping hegemony, and they are attempting to undermine global stability and the maintenance of peace.
And to achieve this, they are prepared to sacrifice even the well-being of their own citizens.

Do the peoples of the United Europe really crave some sort of revenge against Russia, especially at the cost of their own impoverishment?
Of course they don't.
Do they want to be cannon fodder in a war that allegedly European politicians are preparing for by 2030?
Of course not.

And we know this.
But in Brussels, someone is very eager to play toy soldiers and to cement their greatness in history.
This has happened before, more than once, and we know how it ended.
Nevertheless, in the West, they are already beginning to ask questions about their meaning.

They are now being held to account for centuries of colonial plunder, for the destruction of cultures traditions, and identifiers of enslaved peoples, and for the slave trade which claimed millions of lives.
And in line with this, the U.N. General Assembly adopted a resolution in March of this year declaring the trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialized chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity.
Belarus supported this resolution without hesitation.
This is not just a diplomatic gesture.

It is the voice of a country that has itself endured a similar hellish chapter in history.
We know what genocide is.
A third of our population during the war was murdered in cold blood and tortured by civilized Europeans, united by Hitler 85 years ago.
Now their descendants are telling us that they had have nothing to do with this, and nor did their grandfathers, supposedly.

But that village house filled with Belarusian children, the elderly and women, was not burned down by the Führer himself.
And there were thousands of such houses.
We know what the plundering of cultural heritage means.
Our wealth, resources, works of art were all taken to the West.

Mr. President,

On behalf of the Government and people of Jamaica, I congratulate you on your election as President of this eightyfirst session of the General Assembly and assure you of Jamaica’s full support.

I also commend your predecessor, Her Excellency Annalena Baerbock, for her stewardship of the Assembly during its historic eightieth session.

And to Secretary -General António Guterres, I convey Jamaica’s profound appreciation for your committed leadership through a decade of extraordinary global uncertainty.

Mr. President,

Your theme for this session could hardly be more timely.

Because today, trust is in short supply.

Wars and conflicts are devastating communities and displacing millions. Geopolitical tensions are deepening.

Climate change is destroying lives, livelihoods and decades of development in a matter of hours. New technologies, including artificial intelligence, offer extraordinary promise, while presenting risks we have not yet fully understood.

And at the very moment when collective action is most needed, confidence in multilateralism itself is being tested.

Jamaica’s position is clear.

The shortcomings of multilateralism cannot be solved by abandoning multilateralism.

For small states like ours, a rules -based international order is not an abstract diplomatic preference. It is fundamental to our sovereignty, our security and our development.

But neither can we safeguard multilateralism simply by defending it.

We must reform it.

We must make it more representative, more accountable, more efficient — and more responsive to the needs and realities of the people it was created to serve.

That is why Jamaica has chosen not merely to call for reform, but to help lead it.

Our Permanent Representative was privileged to co -chair, with New Zealand, the UN80 Initiative’s Informal Ad Hoc Working Group on Mandate Implementation Review. That work culminated in General Assembly Resolution 80/251 — an important framework for improvi ng how UN mandates are created, implemented and reviewed.

Jamaica now continues that work alongside Norway.

Our objective is straightforward: a United Nations that spends less time sustaining process for its own sake, and more time fulfilling its purpose.

That is the multilateralism Jamaica believes in.

Mr. President,

The selection of the next Secretary-General will be one of the most consequential decisions before Member States this year.

Jamaica proudly joins our CARICOM family in supporting the candidacy of Her Excellency Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of the Cooperative Republic of Guyana.

Her candidacy also speaks to something larger.

Small states have long served this international system as bridge-builders, consensus-makers and problem-solvers.

We learn very early that influence does not depend only on size or power. It can also come from credibility, dialogue, principle and the capacity to bring people together.

These are the strengths which our multilateral system needs now, more than ever.

Mr. President,

For Jamaica, the consequences of global challenges are not theoretical.

On 28 October last year, Hurricane Melissa struck our island.

In a matter of hours, the most catastrophic hurricane in our modern history inflicted damage and losses estimated at 56.7 per cent of our GDP.

Think about that.

More than half the value of an entire year of national economic output, damaged or lost through a single event.

Jamaica had prepared.

Years of fiscal discipline had allowed us to build buffers. We had put in place disaster -risk financing, including catastrophe insurance and an independently sponsored catastrophe bond.

Those measures gave us immediate liquidity.

But no level of prudent national planning can fully insulate a small developing state from a climate event of that magnitude.

And therein lies the fundamental inequity faced by Small Island Developing States.

We can do everything right. In fact, Jamaica’s reforms balanced economic orthodoxy with innovation and expansion of support for the most vulnerable. And yet one hurricane can still erase decades of progress.

We are deeply grateful to our international partners, our CARICOM family, our Jamaican diaspora and the thousands of individuals and organisations wh ich stood with us in our hour of need.

But Jamaica has not simply resolved to recover.

We have resolved to rebuild better and differently.

Our resilience must not be measured by how much suffering we can withstand. It must be measured by how well we prepare, how quickly we recover, how intelligently we adapt — and whether we emerge stronger.

That is why the Government of Prime Minister Andrew Holness established the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority — NaRRA.

Its mandate is to drive reconstruction at speed and at scale; to coordinate major infrastructure projects; crowd in investment; and critically, to embed resilience into the Jamaica we are rebuilding.

We are not simply replacing what Melissa destroyed.

We are building the Jamaica that must withstand the storms of tomorrow.

We have also submitted our updated Nationally Determined Contribution, completed our Long -Term Strategy for a low carbon, climate-resilient future, and advanced our National Adaptation Plan.

But national ambition must be matched by international action.

Climate finance must become more accessible, affordable and predictable.

And the international financial architecture must finally recognise what SIDS have long said: income alone does not and cannot measure vulnerability.

A country does not become less vulnerable to hurricanes and other natural disasters because its per-capita income crosses an arbitrary threshold.

We therefore continue to advocate for the use of measures that go beyond GDP, including multidimensional vulnerability indices, in determining access to concessional and development finance.

Mr. President,

Jamaica brings this message to the international community from a position not only of vulnerability, but one of responsibility.

Over the past decade, we have undertaken difficult reforms and made difficult choices.

Our debt, which once stood at more than 140 per cent of GDP, was brought down to 62 per cent before Melissa, with unemployment then at a historic low of 3.4%.

We built macroeconomic stability, strengthened investor confidence and created the fiscal space that ultimately helped us respond to the greatest natural disaster in our modern history. We are proud and heartened that notwithstanding Melissa, Jamaica’s credit ratings have either been stabilized or upgraded and unemployment still stands at a low of 3.7%.

Those gains did not happen by accident.

They required discipline. Partnership. Sacrifice. Consistency.

And long-term planning.

Our experience has taught us that the strongest response to a crisis begins long before the crisis arrives — in the choices we make, the institutions we build, and the buffers we create.

Jamaica will continue to take responsibility for the things within our control.

But domestic responsibility must be matched by international solidarity and cooperation.

Developing countries cannot reasonably be expected to simultaneously finance climate adaptation, modernise infrastructure, strengthen social protection, manage debt, absorb external shocks and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals without an international financial system responsive to their realities.

We do not ask to be relieved of responsibility. We ask for an international system that gives responsible countries the space to succeed.

Mr. President,

That opportunity increasingly depends on technology.

Jamaica sees digital transformation and responsible artificial intelligence as powerful tools. They can enhance productivity, innovation and sustainable development for our people. Indeed, they can be an equalizing force for the world.

We must therefore not allow AI to deepen old inequalities and create an entirely new global divide.

Developing countries require investment in infrastructure, skills and capacity. And all countries require governance frameworks that safeguard privacy and intellectual property, ensure data integrity and promote the ethical and responsible use of emerging technologies, without stifling innovation.

The Pact for the Future, the Global Digital Compact and the ABAS provide important foundations.

Our task now as a global community, is to translate commitments into action.

Mr. President,

Development also requires peace and security.

For Jamaica and our Caribbean region, transnational organised crime remains a serious threat.

Last year, from this podium, Prime Minister Andrew Holness called for a Global War on Gangs — a coordinated international effort capable of matching the reach, financing and sophistication of transnational criminal networks.

Jamaica reiterates that call today.

Illicit firearms do not manufacture themselves in our communities. They cross borders. Criminal money crosses borders. Criminal networks exploit technology and operate across borders.

Our response must therefore also cross borders.

We call for stronger cooperation in firearms tracing and interdiction, intelligence and information -sharing, financial investigations and law -enforcement capacity -building. We also urge major arms -exporting states to strengthen export controls and post-delivery verification.

At home, Jamaica has invested heavily in our security forces, strengthened legislation, enhanced intelligence gathering, oversight and transformed policing.

The results are remarkable by any standard.

In 2025, Jamaica recorded its lowest number of homicides in more than three decades. And in 2026, the Global Peace Index ranked Jamaica the most peaceful country in the Caribbean.

We recognise that there remains work to be done. But the direction is clear.

Our objective is not merely fewer crimes.

It is a durable ecosystem of peace in which every Jamaican can feel safe, raise a family, do business and fulfil his or her potential and retire in paradise.

Mr. President,

Nowhere in our region is the challenge of criminal gangs more devastating than in our sister nation of Haiti.

Jamaica stands firmly with the Haitian people.

We urge sustained international support for the Gang Suppression Force and for the Haitian National Police and armed forces. This support must include the financial, logistical and operational resources necessary to restore security. We further call for the Security Council to renew the mandate of the GSF at this imperfect but particularly critical juncture. We are at a crossroads. We can lose gains, or we can build on progress made.

The international community must send an unequivocal message: armed gangs cannot be allowed to determine Haiti’s future nor that of the region.

Security must create the space for sustained humanitarian relief, developmental and economic progress. But even more foundationally, s ecurity must create the space for political stability, democratic governance and credible elections, led and owned by the Haitian people.

Mr. President,

Jamaica remains deeply concerned by the terrible human suffering caused by armed conflicts across the world.

Wherever conflict occurs, our principles must remain consistent.

International humanitarian law must be respected.

Civilians must be protected.

International law and the Charter of the United Nations must be upheld.

And diplomacy must remain our first and most persistent instrument for resolving disputes.

Respect for international law — including due regard for the decisions of the International Court of Justice — is indispensable to the peaceful international order on which small states depend.

Similarly, with respect to our neighbour Cuba, Jamaica continues to believe in dialogue and constructive engagement.

We encourage domestic reform and greater integration of Cuba into the international economic system, supported by policies that create pathways for progress and eliminating the dire humanitarian crisis, rather than perpetuating isolation under the blockade. The suffering of the Cuban people is of deep concern.

Mr. President,

Jamaica believes that reparatory justice is, at its heart, about truth, acknowledgement, justice, repair, compensation, development and reconciliation. Jamaica not only supported the resolution put forward by Ghana on March 25th of this year, we also delivered to Buckingham Palace, a petition framing critical questions on the matter of reparations. The petition has now been referred to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.

Mr. President,

Sixty-four years after Jamaica proudly raised our black, green and gold flag as a politically independent nation, we remain clear-eyed about the world around us.

We know its dangers.

But we also believe deeply in its possibilities.

The United Nations must change if it is to remain credible.

Jamaica supports the revitalisation of this General Assembly, meaningful reform of the Security Council, and greater coherence, efficiency and accountability across the United Nations system.

Reform is not an act of disloyalty to this institution.

Reform is how we preserve it.

Ultimately however, Mr. President, multilateralism must mean something beyond these walls.

For a small state like Jamaica, its value is felt when our people are safer; when opportunity is expanded; when vulnerability does not become a barrier to development; when countries that have acted responsibly are not penalised for shocks they did not create; and when the voice of a small nation carries the same dignity as that of a large one.

That is why Jamaica remains committed to this institution — not because it is perfect, but because we are grateful for what is has achieved, and we believe in what it can become.

Small states can help lead that effort.

Our own journey has taught us that vulnerability need not mean helplessness; that discipline creates resilience; that partnership multiplies possibility; and that even in moments of profound crisis, nations can choose to build forward.

So let us restore trust through what we do.

Let us manage transformation with purpose.

Let us bring the same seriousness to preventing crises that we bring to responding to them.

And let us never lose sight of the simple idea on which this institution was founded: that nations working together, can achieve what none of us can achieve alone.

That is the United Nations Jamaica believes in.

And that is the United Nations we will continue working to reform and renew.

I thank you.

I now give the floor to Her Excellency Ilza Maria dos Santos Amado Vaz, Minister of State and for Foreign Affairs, Cooperation and Communities of Sao Tomé and Principe.
Mr. president, Mr. Secretary General, Heads of State and Governments.
Ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honor for me to take the floor before this assembly on behalf of the government and the people of the Democratic Republic of Sao Tomé and Principe.
Allow me, first of all to congratulate His Excellency, Mr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as president of the 81st session of the General Assembly, and to wish him every success in the discharge of his duties.

I would also like to express our appreciation to Her Excellency, Miss Annalena Baerbock, for the work accomplished during the previous session of the General Assembly.
Allow me to pay tribute to the Secretary General, His Excellency Mr. Antonio Guterres, for his commitment to peace, sustainable development, human rights and the strengthening of multilateralism at a time of great challenges.
Excellencies, we live in a context marked by conflicts, geopolitical rivalries, economic uncertainty climate change, forced displacement, inequalities, transnational crime, and rapid technological transformation.
No state can face challenges of this magnitude alone.

For Sao Tomé and Principe, this reality underscores the importance of an international order based on the charter of the United Nations International Law and the sovereign equality of states with principles applied universally and consistently.
As a small island nation, we stand as a consolidated democracy and a state governed by the rule of law, grounded in peace, stability, and harmonious coexistence among our citizens.
It is on the basis of this experience that we reaffirm our confidence in dialogue, diplomacy, cooperation and the peaceful settlement of disputes.
Mr. president, for small island developing states, geographic, economic, financial and social vulnerabilities are compounded by the effects of climate change.

In Sao Tomé and Principe, these impacts are already affecting our coastal areas, infrastructure, marine resources and livelihoods.
Despite our negligible contribution to global emissions.
This reality reflects a profound climate injustice.
Sao Tomé and Principe therefore reaffirms its commitments.

Under the Paris Agreement, its nationally determined contribution and its National Adaptation Plan, while stressing that their implementation requires adequate, predictable and accessible resources.
We also maintain that the vulnerability of small island states should be assessed beyond per capita income, taking into account their specific characteristics and structural constraints.
In this context, we call for the Multidimensional vulnerability index to be translated into concrete eligibility criteria for concessional financing.
We likewise advocate for the full operational operation, rationalization of the fund for responding to loss and damage, and simpler, more effective access to the Green Climate Fund.

The limited institutional capacity of vulnerable countries must not become an obstacle for to accessing the very instruments created to support them.
In the case of Sao Tomé and Principe, this issue is particularly relevant following our graduation to middle income country status, which was an important milestone and a recognition of the progress achieved in human development.
It nonetheless requires appropriate transition measures capable of consolidating these gains and shielding the country from external shocks.
It is as part of this effort of consolidation and that the energy transition finds its place, a transition that is for us an economic, financial, social and environmental necessity.

In an island economy dependent on imported fuel, the cost and reliability of electricity affect every sector.
The implementation of our Energy Transition Programme and the National Energy Compact should contribute to a cleaner, more affordable, secure and stable system.
But it will require investment and international partnerships.
Excellencies, food security and the strengthening of productive capacity are urgent priorities.

We seek to reduce our dependence on imports, increase national production and ensure better market access for farmers so that a greater share of the value generated by quality products such as cocoa and coffee, remains in the country.
If the land is essential to our food security, the sea and our biodiversity represent one of the broadest horizons for our development.
The recognition of our territory by Unesco as a World Biosphere Reserve confirms the exceptional value of our natural heritage and reinforces our responsibility to protect it and make the most of it.
We aim to turn this wealth into opportunities for sustainable development through fisheries, the blue economy, research and nature based tourism that generates jobs and income for local communities.

At the same time, in the face of threats posed by illegal fishing and transnational crime, Sao Tomé and Principe will continue to work with the states of the region and international partners to strengthen maritime security and promote a sustainable blue economy, thus preserving our resources for future generations.
The preservation of these resources and the building of sustainable development ultimately depend on people and on the opportunities afforded to them.
The future of Sao Tomé and Principe hinges on our ability to create opportunities for the next generation.
Our priority is to ensure that young people have the conditions to study, work, start businesses, innovate and fulfil their life aspirations in their own country, in a nation of our size, every talent counts and every young person is an indispensable force for national progress.

Likewise, the Santomean diaspora is an essential part of our human wealth and a strategic partner of the country.
We will continue to strengthen its ties with Sao Tomé and Principe, and to create the conditions for an even greater contribution to investment, entrepreneurship, knowledge transfer and national life.
Mr. president, creating opportunities and ensuring truly inclusive development require strong institutions capable of guaranteeing peace, justice, respect for human rights and the participation of all in the life of the country.
There can be no sustainable development without these conditions, nor without the full participation of women and men in political, economic and social life.

It is in this context that 2026 is a year of particular significance for santomean democracy.
On July 19th, our citizens took part in presidential elections, which were conducted peacefully and transparently, and led to the re-election of His Excellency, Mr. Carlos Vilanova, as president of the Republic.
On September 27th, the people of Sao Tomé and Principe will return to the polls for the legislative, local and regional elections and will exercise their right to vote in large numbers.
These elections are marked by important innovations notably automatic voter registration and the first application of the parity law, which is a significant step towards strengthening the inclusion and participation of women.

With women accounting for 41.4% of confirmed candidacies.
Above the legal threshold of 40%, they will be able to assert a growing presence in decision making spaces.
San Tomé and Principe reaffirms its commitment to constitutional order, political pluralism, fundamental freedoms and respect for the sovereign will of its citizens and will continue to pursue reforms aimed at strengthening justice, security, gender equality, human rights and trust in institutions.
Inclusion and equality must also guide our response to the great transformations of our time.

In the face of the rapid advance of artificial intelligence and the digital transition, Sao Tomé and Principe calls for international cooperation that enables developing countries to access the technology, knowledge, infrastructure and financing they need.
We advocate responsible technology governance centered on human dignity, transparency and fundamental rights, so that innovation translates into better opportunities and services for all.
Excellencies.
The experience of Sao Tomé and Principe as a small democracy also shapes the way we view representation at the international level.

Africa today occupies a demographic, economic and political place that is not yet adequately reflected in the institutions where the most far reaching decisions are taken.
It is in this area that reform of the Security Council becomes imperative.
This is not a concession to Africa.
It is a matter of legitimacy, justice and effectiveness.

An institution responsible for international peace and security cannot remain indefinitely based on a distribution of power inherited from another area.
In the pursuit of greater historical justice and representation.
Sao Tomé and Principe, therefore welcomes the recent decisions that recognize the historical gravity of the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and promoted a more accurate cartographic representation of the size of the continent's correcting distortions that visually diminished Africa.
These acts of recognition must translate into an international order in which Africa participates fully in shaping the future, rather than remaining merely in the position of responding to the decisions taken elsewhere.

Mr. president, peace remains the very raison d'etre of the multilateral system.
Sao Tomé and Principe follows with concern the conflicts in Ukraine, the Sudan, the Sahel, the Great Lakes region, the Horn of Africa and the Middle East and calls for stronger diplomacy and protection of civilians in accordance with the charter of the United Nations and International law.
We likewise call for respect for international humanitarian law, full humanitarian access and the release of hostages.
We reaffirm our support for a two state solution that allows Israel and Palestine to live side by side in peace and security on the basis of international law and the relevant United Nations resolutions.

Excellencies Sao Tomé and Principe will remain faithful to the charter of the United Nations international law, peace, human rights and multilateralism.
Standing as a voice of dialogue and moderation, and as a committed partner for stability in the Gulf of Guinea.

The government has launched reforms and made advances in infrastructure.
The energy transition, digitalization and investment attraction, creating the conditions to mobilise resources needed to meet our population's most pressing needs, particularly in access to health, water, sanitation, justice and security, environmental protection and the infrastructure essential to development.
As aligned with the national strategy based on Sustainable Tourism, 2026 2040, we thank all of our bilateral and multilateral partners who are supporting Sao Tomé and Principe in this process.
However, the challenge before us is to turn these advances into concrete and lasting results, consolidating the foundations for more inclusive, sustainable and resilient development for which ensuring continuity and stability of governance and of governance is paramount.

Mr. president, our vulnerabilities as a small island developing states do not define our horizon.
We therefore reaffirm our determination to turn challenges into opportunities through strategic partnerships based on shared responsibility and mutual benefit.
And we reaffirm our capacity to contribute to peace, uphold the principles of the charter of the United Nations, and participate responsibly in building solutions to the challenges we collectively face We call on all Member States to continue building together a more representative, supportive and just international order founded on respect for the sovereignty of states, international law and equality of opportunity.
It is in this spirit of peace, dialogue and hope that Sao Tomé and Principe will continue to shoulder its responsibility within the international community.

Thank you, Mr. President.

Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished Heads of State and Government,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

We congratulate you, Mr. President, on your election as the President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly and pledge our cooperation and support during your tenure. We also commend the Secretary-General for his strong leadership at a challenging time in our multilateral system. Zambia salutes H is Excellency António Guterres for reminding us that the answer to a more divided and multipolar world is not less multilateralism, but a stronger, fairer and more representative United Nations.

The theme of this session, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation:

A United Nations That Delivers for All,” is both timely and necessary.

Trust is the foundation on which international cooperation is built upon. Yet today, trust in institutions, trust among nations and, most importantly, trust between the institutions that serve the people, is under strain.

Trust means that the founding principles of the United Nations Charter must be respected.

For Zambia, trust begins with keeping promises.

Trust means that international agreements must be honoured.

Trust means that development commitments must be financed.

Trust means that the voices of developing countries matter, in word and in deed.

Trust means that the global system must not protect the interests of the powerful, at the expense of the vulnerable.

And trust means that when the world agrees on a goal, we must have the commitment to implement it.

The world is undergoing profound transformation. Technology is changing economies and societies. Climate change is reshaping livelihoods.

Geopolitical competition is altering global trade and investment patterns.

Conflicts are causing massive displacements and humanitarian suffering.

And yet, Developing countries continue to confront a financing system that does not adequately reflect and respond to their development needs. The question before us is therefore, not whether transformation will happen, but it is rather how we manage transformation, who benefits from it, and whether our multilateral institutions are capable of delivering meaningful results for ordinary people.

For Zambia, our answer is clear: we must restore trust by achieving results, and we must manage transformation by ensuring that no country and no-one is left behind.

Zambia's Democratic Journey and the 2026 Elections Mr. President,

Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights affirms that, “the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government,” expressed through periodic and genuine elections.

It is in this spirit that Zambia recently concluded its general elections, through which our people exercised their constitutional right to choose their leaders.

We thank the people of Zambia for their participation in the democratic process and for renewing their confidence in our leadership. We also express our sincere appreciation to the international Election Observation Missions for their invaluable support and contribution to Zambia’s democratic process.

It is important to emphasize that Zambia is not at war. Zambia is a peaceful, stable and sovereign nation, and the peaceful atmosphere that characterized the country before, during and after the elections is a clear reflection of our people’s enduring commitment to peace, democracy, national unity and constitutional governance.

Despite the political differences that naturally accompany a democratic election, Zambia has demonstrated that such differences can and must be managed peacefully and through the established constitutional and legal institutions. Our democratic process should never be mistaken for conflict or instability.

We therefore reaffirm our unwavering commitment to preserving Zambia’s long-standing tradition of peace. We will continue to ensure that political differences are addressed through the due process of the law and will take all necessary measures, within the confines of our Constitution and laws, to prevent political disputes from degenerating into violence, armed mobilization, insurgency or the emergence of militia groups.

In this regard, we extend a sincere invitation to cooperating partners, international development institutions, investors, the private sector and Zambia’s friends around the world to continue working with us in advancing our Grow Zambia Agenda. Zambia needs partnership s, investment s, innovation, technology, skills and sustained development cooperation in order to unlock its full potential.

We encourage our cooperating partners to view Zambia through the lens of the peace and stability that define our country, and to deepen support for programmes that promote inclusive economic growth, job creation, infrastructure development, human capital development, agriculture, energy, health and other priority areas of national development.

Our message is clear: Zambia is at peace, Zambia is open for partnership, and Zambia is ready to grow.

Zambia: A Stable Partner for Investment and Trade Mr. President,

Peace and stability provide the foundation for economic development.

Zambia is positioning itself as an attractive destination for investment and trade, with opportunities in mining, critical minerals, agriculture, agro processing, manufacturing, energy, infrastructure, tourism and digital services.

Our ambition is to move beyond the export of raw materials and primary commodities towards value addition, industriali zation, job creation and technology transfer as key enablers of our economic transformation agenda.

We welcome investment that creates jobs, develops skills and builds sustainable value chains.

Our message to investors is: Come to Zambia. Invest with us. Produce with us. Trade with us. Grow with us. Zambia is open for investment Climate Change and Environmental Resilience; Water and Sanitation Mr. President,

For Zambia, climate change is not an abstract concept. Our people continue to experience the devastating effects of droughts, floods and changing weather patterns, with significant impacts on agriculture, food security, water availability, energy generation and livelihoods.

The effects of activities transcend our borders and yet our people and the coming generations may pay a heavy price. Zambia recogni zes that countries such as ours cannot finance the climate transition alone, nor should they. This is a collective moral responsibility of the international community, especially the highest contributors to carbon emissions. This is to mitigate the effects of climate change and protect lives and livelihoods.

Those who have contributed least to climate change must not be left to bear its greatest costs.

We therefore call for predictable, accessible and affordable climate finance, technology transfer, and greater investment in adaptation and resilience, consistent with the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.

For Africa, adaptation is not optional. Our farmers require climate -resilient agriculture; our communities and cities need resilient infrastructure; our energy systems must become more diversified; and our water resources, forests and ecosystems must be protected. Zambia is ready to contribute to global climate solutions, but those that have contributed least to climate change must not bear a disproportionate share of its costs.

Water security is integral to climate resilience and sustainable development.

Zambia therefore attaches great importance to international cooperation on water and has actively participated in the preparatory process for the 2026 United Nations Water Confer ence. Together with Finland, Zambia is co chairing the Interactive Dialogue on Water for Cooperation, focusing on transboundary and international water cooperation, scientific cooperation and inclusive governance.

We remain committed to strengthening water security, climate resilience and sustainable management of natural resources, while working with the international community to ensure that climate and water action delivers tangible benefits for our people and future generations.

Health, Human Capital and Inclusive Development Mr. President,

Africa's youthful population is one of our greatest assets and represents an enormous opportunity for global prosperity. According to demographic forecasts, one in every 4 youths on the glob e will be African, by 2050. We have a wealth of young Africans with the potential to become entrepreneurs, scientists, engineers, farmers, innovators, artists and future leaders.

Our responsibility is to equip them with quality education, relevant skills, access to technology, entrepreneurship opportunities and decent employment, so that they can become active drivers of economic transformation and sustainable development.

We are alive to the fact that we should ensure that we keep this youthful and productive population healthy in order to harness positive dividends.

In the health sector, Zambia has increased domestic budgetary allocations from approximately 7 percent to over 10 percent, enabling the recruitment of health workers, expansion and moderni zation of health infrastructure, and improved availability of essential medical supplies. Recogni zing continued vulnerability to epidemics, Zambia calls for the expedited conclusion of negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing Annex under the WHO Pandemic Agreement, alongside strengthened access to technology and preparedness capacities to detect and respond to future health threats.

Zambia is further making efforts toward building capacity for local Vaccine Manufacturing.

Mr. President,

In Zambia, we have taken de cisive steps to expand access to education through the enactment of the Free Education Act, and the strengthening of the school feeding programme, ensuring that more children can access education and remain in school without the burden of fees or hunger standing in their way of learning.

Zambia is equally committed to promoting gender equality and economic empowerment of women and girls. We are expanding opportunities in education, skills development, entrepreneurship, financial inclusion and leadership. For the first time in our history, Parliament now provides for proportional representation of women, you ng people and persons with disabilities, reflecting our conviction that their voices and experiences must be heard in shaping the decisions that affect our nation.

We are also strengthening efforts to end child, early and forced marriage by keeping girls in school and addressing the social and economic factors that place them at risk. Zambia has demonstrated that progress is possible, reducing child marriage prevalence from 29% to 23.9% in four years through comprehensive legal reforms, free education, school re -entry policy, multisectoral support systems like the Keeping Girls in School initiatives and targeted economic investments such as our expanded Constituency Development Fund. We need to continue building on these successes.

We therefore invite Member States to unite behind our global and continental commitments to drive domestic action.

By investing in our people, particularly women, girls and young people, we are investing in Zambia's future. When we empower our people, we strengthen our nation; and when we invest in Africa's young people and women, we invest in the prosperity of our continent and the world. Our commitment is to build an inclusive society in which every citizen, regardless of gender, age or disability, has an opportunity to participate fully in our country's economic and social transformation.

Sustainable Development and the 2030 Agenda Mr. President,

The Sustainable Development Goals remain the most comprehensive expression of our shared ambition to eradicate poverty, reduce inequality and build a sustainable future. Yet we must acknowledge that progress is uneven. The world cannot continue to adopt ambitious commitments while developing countries struggle to finance their implementation.

For Zambia, the SDGs must translate into tangible improvements in the lives of our people: a child receiving quality education; a mother accessing safe healthcare; a farmer having reliable water and markets; a young p erson finding decent employment; a family having access to electricity; a community having accessible roads; access to clean water and sanitation; a small business gaining access to finance. That is what development means.

Sustainable Development Finance and Reform of the Global Financial Architecture Mr. President,

Sustainable development cannot be achieved without addressing the persistent financing gap facing developing countries. High borrowing costs, limited fiscal space and heavy debt -servicing obligations continue to constrain countries’ ability to invest in cl imate action, health, education, infrastructure and other development priorities.

We cannot expect countries to deliver more for their people while resources available are increasingly consumed by the cost of debt. This is not sustainable, nor is it compatible with our collective commitment to leav e no one behind.

Zambia has undertaken significant fiscal reforms and made progress in restructuring our debt, to restore macroeconomic stability and create fiscal space. This demonstrates our willingness to make bold decisions when needed. At the same time, we are strengthening domestic resource mobilization by expanding the tax base, modernizing tax administration and combating illicit financial flows. We cannot continue to lose resources essential to Africa’s transformation while being asked to mobili ze greater financing for development. Africa’s resources must work for Africa’s development.

We support enhanced international cooperation on transparency, beneficial ownership, asset recovery and the prevention of illicit financial flows. We equally support stronger international tax cooperation through the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation, to ensure fairer taxing rights and strengthen domestic resource mobili zation for development.

Zambia therefore calls for greater access to affordable and long -term development finance, increased climate finance—particularly for adaptation and resilience —and innovative financing mechanisms to mobilise private investment for sustainable development.

Africa needs a fairer and more responsive global financial architecture that enables developing countries to finance development as an investment in our shared future.

Multilateralism, Geopolitics, Peace and Security Mr. President,

The United Nations remains indispensable to international peace, security and sustainable development. However, its institutions must evolve to reflect today’s geopolitical, economic and demographic realities. Zambia therefore supports meaningful UN reform, particularly of the Security Council, including permanent African representation in line with the Ezulwini Consensus and Sirte Declaration. We also support reforms to global economic and financial governance, that give developing countries a greater voice in decisions affecting them.

Zambia welcomes the UN80 Initiative as an opportunity to strengthen multilateralism and build a more effective, efficient, equitable and fit -forpurpose United Nations and acknowledge the commendable progress achieved so far.

As efforts are made to attain a more efficient and nimbler United Nations, we must not lose sight of the most important aspect – the effectiveness of the UN in delivering on its mandates. With each crucial question, we must ask ourselves if the reforms will make the world safer and uplift the lives of the most vulnerable in society. We take note of the proposed mergers of some key institutions and emphasize on the importance of protecting their mandates.

We further note the changed landscape for international cooperation that has seen significant declines in official development assistance, which has also affected important UN programmes. We, therefore, call on member states to protect these institutions we trust by ringfencing crucial core funding.

In the face of rising geopolitical tensions and protracted conflicts, we reaffirm our commitment to dialogue, diplomacy and the peaceful resolution of disputes in accordance with the UN Charter and international law. We further support African -led solution s and stronger cooperation between the UN,

African Union and regional organi zations to advance conflict prevention, peacebuilding and collective security.

Conclusion Mr. President,

Zambia remains committed to peace, democracy, multilateralism and sustainable development.

We believe that restoring trust requires delivery; that sustainable development requires genuine international partnership; and that managing transformation requires inclusion.

We call for an equitable global system that provides developing countries with affordable financing and policy space to transform their economies, strengthens climate action through adequate finance, expands opportunities for young people, and reforms inte rnational institutions to reflect today ’s realities.

Let us together strengthen peace through dialogue, respect for human rights, democracy and the rule of law and ensure that the commitments made in this Assembly, translate into tangible improvements in the lives of our people.

Zambia stands ready to work with all nations to restore trust, manage transformation and build a more peaceful, prosperous and equitable world.

I Thank You.

I now invite His Excellency Soggiorno, the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Indonesia, to address the Assembly.
Your Excellency Halil Rahman, president of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, your Excellency Antonio Guterres, Secretary General of the United Nations Excellencies, heads of State and heads of government, ministers, distinguished delegates.
