Your Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman, President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly,

Your Excellency António Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations,

Honourable Heads of Delegation, Distinguished Delegates, Ladies and Gentlemen,

I have the honor to present this statement on behalf of my President, His Excellency Isaias Afwerki,

President of the State of Eritrea.

Allow me to join previous speakers to congratulate Your Excellency for your election to the Presidency of the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly.

On this auspicious occasion each year, the crucial questions that crop to mind, and that we ponder about, are the crucial and novel messages that we should focus on.

Should our annual interventions be confined to sheer and rather routine accounts, or balance sheet, of developments that had transpired during that particular year? Should the forum be seen as essentially and solely a congenial Public Relations platform for eloquent speeches and discourses?

Does the annual forum consist of structured agendas that have continuity and coherence?

What is the context?

What is the overarching mission?

And how do we gauge progress?

... etc. etc.

In previous Summits, I have dwelt on the historical backdrop of the establishment of the UN; the popular aspirations of humanity for peace, growth, and prosperity that underpinned the creation of the UN; the economic injustices that prompted those aspirations in the first place; the innate mission of the UN?

... as well as its structure and operational modality as elaborated in the foundational precepts elabored below.

The first and foremost challenges of humanity are to redress economic injustices; create wealth; and more broadly and accurately, ensure fair distribution of wealth and income.

The prevailing injustices stem from the denial of the rights, as well as enabling environment, for humanity to create and accumulate wealth without any encumbrances on the one hand; and, the usurpation of their right and opportunity for rational distribution of whatever nominal wealth they create under suppressive conditions on the other.

This is precisely the reason why the prevailing international order has become and is dubbed as a "zero-sum order".

In the event, the imperative for installing a new world order predicated on justice and rationality and that jettisons the zero-sum system remains humanity's fundamental individual and collective right.

In this respect, the overarching mission of the endeavor/struggle of mankind can be summed up in: • To fairly own their economic resources and the produce of their work, and march on a sustainable path of generational progress and prosperity by accumulating wealth.

• To secure peace and stability in order to guarantee prosperity and economic growth.

• To ensure prevalence of fairness and justice as vital prerequisites for peace and stability.

• To promote mutual respect, complementarity and cohesion/integration so as to bolster widest regional and global peace and stability as well as mutual growth • To establish appropriate legal executive structure and associated mechanisms for the implementation of these fundamental human aspirations.

The substance of the framework briefly described above evidently requires further expansion and elaboration.

It is not otherwise controversial or novel by any metrics.

In this respect, the main tasks of the annual UNGA Summits ought to focus on rigorous assessment of progress in achieving these goals.

Mr. President,

The events that have unfolded since the 80th Summit of the UNGA are important for gleaning appropriate lessons in comparative terms and within the reality of this international organizations.

They cannot otherwise deflect the attention and focus of the peoples of the world from their chore mission and struggle.

As such: • The impacts and ultimate ramifications that may ensue from President Trump's pronounced MAGA Doctrine; as well as the ongoing war in Iran that must be stopped; The Ukraine war, with all its multi-layered ramifications must also be terminated; • Global climate change and the imperative of finding enduring solutions for its control and reversal; • The urgency of reversing the war and related acts of subversion unleashed in order to foment chaos in our broader neighborhood; i.e. the Nile Basin; the Horn of Africa; the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the Gulf States; the need to terminate debilitating interventions under the rubric of "humanitarian assistance";... are some of the trends and developments that warrant attention.

Against this overall backdrop, it must be recognized that the prime victims of the "zero-sum" global order whose hallmarks are plunder, domination and deceit, are the African peoples who continue to seethe under subsistence economy.

This disconcerting reality impels them to naturally stand at the forefront of the struggle for justice and fairness.

In the event, it behooves on them to formulate appropriate strategies for accomplishing their mission; remove stale and obstructive frameworks and mechanisms; and move forward with greater unity and rigour.

I thank you.

Mr. President; Your Excellencies; Distinguished Delegates,

I have the hono ur and priviledge to deliver this statement on behalf of His Excellency Professor Arthur Pe ter Mutharika, President of the Republic of Malawi, and the people of Malawi.

I congratulate you, Mr. President, and all Vice Presidents, on your election to lead this 81 st Session of the United Nations General Assembly. Malawi pledges its full support to your leadership. We also extend our profound appreciation to the Secretary -General for his unwavering dedication to our shared global values.

Mr. President,

The theme for this session, "Restoring Trust, Managing Tansformation: a United Nations that Delivers for All," strikes at the heart of our current global reality. We live in an era of deep fractures. Trust between nations has eroded. Global systems are failing to manage rapid technological, economic, and environmental shifts equitably. For the United Nations to remain relevant, it must transform into an institution that delivers tangible progress for the most vulnerable, leaving no nation behind. I would, therefore, like to highlight six opportunities for restoring trust, managing transformation and, thereby ensuring a United Nations that delivers for all.

The first opportunity is accelerating sustainable development and economic transformation:

Mr. President, the timeline for the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development is rapidly drawing to a close, yet the promises of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) remain dangerously out of reach for millions. For Malawi, the pursuit of wealth creation, self reliance and economic transformation is not merely a political aspiration; it is an urgent survival strategy. Because of this, we have remained steadfast in implementing the SDGs, in alignment with our long-term development vision, the Malawi 2063. On this note, Mr.

President, I am happy to report that Malawi successfully presented our third Voluntary National Review during the 2026 ECOSOC High -Level Political Forum, thereby reaffirming our commitment to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Malawi 2063, as well as our desire to accelerate sustainable development and economic transformation. The review revealed that even though we face numerous structural challenges, we have made some progress on many of the SDGs.

Mr. President, our goal is to systematically transform our economy by modernizing agriculture, expanding mining and accelerating digitalization. However, national efforts alone cannot dismantle the structural barriers built into the global economic architecture.

Developing nations require deliberate, scaled investment in industrialization, sustainable infrastructure and regional valu e chains to transition from primary commodity exporters to diversified, industrialized economies.

In addition, w e cannot achieve sustainable development while drowning in debt. Malawi, therefore, calls for immediate, comprehensive debt relief and restructuring. The current international financial architecture forces developing nations to choose between servicing predatory debts and investing in health, education and climate resilience. This is a moral failure.

Mr. President,

We also call for a massive sc aling-up of concessional development financing. We need targeted investments in our key productive sectors, namely agriculture, industrialization and infrastructure development as follows:(a) Agricultural modernization through mechanization and commercialization to guarantee food security; (b) Building local industry so that we stop exporting raw materials, and create decent jobs for our youth, who make up nearly 40 percent of the Malawi population; and (c) Developing robust transport, energy and digital infrastructure to connect Malawi to regional and global markets.

We, therefore, call upon our international partners to align their support with national blueprints like the Malawi 2063 in order to generate meaningful job creation and shared prosperity.

The second opportunity is strengthening climate action and resilience:

Mr. President, Malawi contributes negligibly to global greenhouse gas emissions, yet we remain on the frontline of the climate crisis. In recent years, devastati ng cyclones, prolonged droughts and increasingly erratic weather patterns have destroyed infrastructure, devastated crops, displ aced thousands of our citizens and inflicted severe damage on our economy. This year, we face the added threat of El Niño -related extreme weather, which risks further undermi ning livelihoods, food security and economic stability.

As such, we are fighting back by embedding climate resilience into our national development planning and strengthening locally driven adaptation measures. However, our efforts are contin ually outpaced by the scale and speed of climate change. Climate shocks repeatedly destroy infrastructure, decimate agricultural production, exacerbate food insecurity, and erode hard-won development gains.

Mr. President,

The global community must therefore move beyond rhetoric and translate commitments into meaningful action. We call for the full and effective operationalization and capitalization of the Loss and Damage Fund. Major historical and current emitters must honour their climatefinance commitments by providing accessible, predictable, grant -based and highly concessional financing, rather than relying on debt -creating instruments that further burden vulnerable countries already struggling to cope with the consequences of a crisis they did little to cause.

Mr. President,

Malawi, therefore, calls for enhanced, predictable and easily accessible climate finance, with greater emphasis on adaptation and disaster -risk reduction. We need sustain able investment in early -warning systems, climate-resilient infrastructure, sustainable land management, climate-smart agriculture and locally led adaptation.

Climate change is an existential threat to Malawi's development and to the hard-won gains we have made.

Mr. President, the third opportunity is to reform global governance and strengthen multilateralism:

The current global challenges underscore a fundamental truth: our multilateral framework is fractured because its foundational architecture is obsolete. The institutions designed in 1945 no longer reflect the geopolitical and economic realities of 2026.

Malawi reaffirms its unwavering commitment to multilateralism, but it must be a multilateralism that is inclusive, fair, and democratic. We call for an urgent comprehensive reform of the United Nations Security Council to correct the historical injustice done to Africa. Africa deserves permanent representation with full veto privileges, as articulated in the Ezulwini Consensus. Furthermore, the international financial architecture, specifically the IMF and t he World Bank, must be radically overhauled. The current system traps developing nations in cycles of unsustainable debt, forcing governments to choose between servicing foreign loans or funding basic education and healthcare for their citizens.

Mr. President, because Malawi strongly believes in multilateralism, we take responsibility when called upon by the international community to participate in causes that further the aims of this organisation.

Malawi remains firmly committed to the rule of law, acco untability and the peaceful resolution of disputes as indispensable foundations of an effective multilateral system. It is in this spirit that Malawi has presented the candidature of Lady Justice Tujilane Chizumila for election as a Judge of the International Criminal Court for the term 2027–2036. Justice Chizumila is a distinguished jurist with extensive judicial and legal experience at the national, regional and international levels, including her service as a Judge of the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights. Her candidature reflects Malawi’s commitment to strengthening international justice through experienced, independent and highly qualified judicial leadership.

As States Parties prepare to elect six judges to the International Criminal Court in December 2026, Malawi respectfully seeks the valued support of States Parties for the candidature of Lady Justice Tujilane Chizumila. We are confident that her extensive judicial experience, commitment to the rule of law and demonstrated service to justice and human rights would enable her to make a meaningful contribution to the work of the Court. Malawi looks forward to the support of fellow States Parties for her election and to continuing our collective efforts to strengthen the institutions of international justice.

Mr. President, t he fourth opportunity for restoring trust, managing transformation, and thereby ensuring a United Nations that delivers for all, lies in strengthening global health security. Economic transformation and sustainable develop ment are impossible without a healthy population. The vulnerabilities exposed by recent global pandemics continue to linger, reminding us that global health security is only as strong as its weakest link.

Malawi is making strides toward achieving Universal Health Coverage and strengthening our primary healthcare systems. However, systemic global inequities in healthcar e access, medical manufacturing and vaccine distribution remain glaringly unresolved. True global health security demands decentralized pharm aceutical manufacturing capabilities, unrestricted technology transfers and intellectual property waivers during health emergencies. My delegation appeals to all of us here to finali ze a robust, legally binding Pandemic Treaty tha t guarantees equity, solidarity and immediate resource sharing for the Global South.

We also call for collaboration in efforts to build long -term resilience against pandemics, through investments in our domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity. By producing essential medicines within Africa, the entire world gains through stronger health security and stable supply chains, especially through faster outbreak response.

Mr. President, the fifth opportunity is to promote human rights, peace and international security:

Malawi firmly b elieves that development, peace and human rights are inextricably linked. We remain deeply committed to upholding the constitutional rights of all our citizens, strengthen ing our democratic institutions and maintaining an uncompromising stance again st corruption. Further, we strongly defend the right to development as an inalienable human right. True freedom cannot exist in conditions of extreme poverty and systemic economic exclusion.

On the global stage, we view, with great alarm, the proliferation of violent conflicts, unconstitutional changes of government, geo -political fragmentation and acts of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. Mr. President, the Malawi nation is not standing aloof as all these alarming developm ents occur. Malawi continues to play its part in global peace operations, deploying our brave men and women to U nited Nations peacekeeping missions to safeguard stability on our continent. In this regard, let me reiterate the calls for immediate cessation of hostilities in all active conflict zones worldwide. Global resources currently being funneled into destructive warfare should, instead, be redirected toward s eradicating poverty, building schools and financing sustainable development.

We also reaffirm our solidarity with global efforts to combat racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance.

The last, but not least, opportunity is in advancing economic diplomacy and strategic partnerships:

Mr. President, in alignment with the Malawi 2063, our foreign policy prioritizes robust economic diplomacy. Malawi recognizes that navigating the complexities of the 2020s requires a paradigm shift away from traditional, paternalistic foreign aid, toward genuine reciprocal economic diplomacy. For this reason, we are actively strengthening bilateral and multilateral partnerships to attract foreign direct investment, enhance international trade, and mobilize development assistance. Malawi is open for business.

Further to this, Malawi highly values South -South and triangular cooperation. Collaborative initiatives with fellow developing nations allow us to share cost -effective technologies, best practices, and home grown solutions in climate -smart agriculture, renewable energy, and digital governance. We will continue to deepen these alliances to accelerate our national development priorities.

Mr. President, as we take steps to grasp these opportunities, we must also recognize the emergence of Artificial Intelligence, which presents both opportunities and threats to humanity. Malawi welcomes the transformative potential of AI as an expression of human ingenuity and as an increasingly important tool for accelerating sustainable development. For developing countries, including Malawi, AI offers opportunities to strengthen agricultural productivity and food security, improve healthcare and education, enhance climate resilience and disaster preparedness, expand financial inclusion, and improve the efficiency of public services. Malawi believes, however, that technological advancement must remain human -centred: Artificial Intelligence should complement and enhance human capabilities rather than diminish the indispensable role of people in shaping their own development.

At the same time, Malawi recognises that the rapid expansion of Artificial Intelligence presents significant challenges, particularly for developing economies with fragile labour markets and limited technological infrastructure. Automation could disrupt employment and widen existing inequalities, while unequal access to computing capacity, data, digital infrastructure, skills and financing risks creating a new technological divide between and within countries. Malawi therefore calls upon the United Nations to continue promoting an inclusive, ethic al and development -oriented global framework for AI governance—one that safeguards human dignity and employment, builds the technological capacities of developing countries, facilitates equitable access to AI technologies and ensures that the benefits of innovation contribute directly to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. No country should be left behind in the emerging AI-driven global economy.

Mr. President, in conclusion, restoring trust r equires honesty, accountability and action. Ma naging transformation requires courage, vision and solidarity. The choices we make today will reverberate for generations to come. We can choose to retreat into isolationism and protectionism, or we can choose to summon the political cou rage required to build a fairer, more resilient and inclusive world.

Malawi stands ready to play its part. We are transforming our economy, reforming our institutions and investing in our people. But we cannot do it alone in an unfair global environment. We stand ready to wo rk hand -in-hand with all member states to bridge the divides, restore trust in multilateralism and deliver a sustainable dignified future for all humanity Let this 81 st Session of the General Assembly mark the turning point where the United Nations transition s from a forum of speeches to an engine of delivery. Let us build a United Nations that delivers wealth instead of poverty, resilience instead of vulnerability, and peace instead of conflict. A United Nations that truly delivers for all.

Thank you very much for your attention.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Allow me, at the outset, to congratulate you, Dr. Khalilur Rahman, on your election as President of the Eighty -first session of the General Assembly.

On behalf of the Government of Sri Lanka, I wish you every success and assure you of our fullest support in the discharge of your mandate.

We also convey our deep appreciation to your predecessor, Madam Annalena Baerbock, for her able stewardship of the Eightieth session.

Let me also take this opportunity to acknowledge the leadership of Secretary-General António Guterres as he concludes his term.

Mr. President,

Seminal changes are taking place across the world at a pace faster than many institutions are able to adapt or respond. People across the globe are demanding greater clarity, honesty and action from their leaders and institutions.

The theme of this year’s General Debate — “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all” — goes to the heart of this challenge.

The erosion of trust is reflected in unresolved conflicts, humanitarian crises that outpace available resources, increasingly frequent climate disasters, widening inequalities, and technological advances that are moving faster than governance. Together, th ese developments have contributed to a growing perception that global institutions are distant from the people they are meant to serve.

Sri Lanka understands this reality deeply. My country has, on many occasions in the past, experienced the consequences of deficits in trust and breaches of the social contract. Two years ago, marking a watershed moment in our history, the people of Sri Lan ka, representing all communities and walks of life, gave a resounding mandate to the Government of President Anura Kumara Dissanayaka to address these challenges and institute meaningful change. Since then, our Government has been working with determination to rebuild trust from the ground up.

We are building trust through action — not rhetoric; through delivery, discipline and the cour age to confront wrongdoing. Sri Lanka, too, is therefore undergoing a historic transformation and rejuvenation.

Despite conflicts in several parts of the world, including in West Asia, and climate calamities, including the cyclone that struck Sri Lanka, my country has restored macroeconomic stability following the economic crisis of

2022. Today, Sri Lanka has been r eclassified by the World Bank as an upper-middle-income economy, and ratings agencies have recognised this positive trajectory.

However, these developments do not fully reflect the vulnerabilities of countries exposed to debt and external shocks. While we work with our global partners to consolidate this hard-won stability, we remain conscious of the critical need to address the hardships faced by vulnerable communities.

Cyclone Ditwah was one of the worst natural disasters in Sri Lanka’s recent history and devastated several parts of our country. The calamity resulted in the loss of hundreds of lives and affected more than two million people. Livelihoods were disrupted and critical infrastructure was destroyed.

Having experienced this tragedy, we understand deeply the challenge posed by the Himalayan floods to the people of Nepal and China. We extend our deepest sympathies to the victims.

These tragic events demonstrate the enormous human and economic costs of climate change. Sadly, its harshest consequences continue to be borne by countries that have contributed least to global emissions.

The call for action on climate impact is not merely immediate. It is overdue. Climate justice must become an urgent reality. For our part, Sri Lanka is on track towards achieving 70 per cent renewable energy by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2050.

Mr. President,

For three decades, Sri Lanka suffered a protracted conflict that caused enormous loss and suffering to all our communities.

Although the guns fell silent 17 years ago, the deep wounds of that conflict remain, and much remains to be done to heal them. We are determined to prevent a recurrence of such a tragedy and to pursue a path towards national unity and reconciliation. In this regard, our Government is strengthening national institutions to address outstanding issues. Throughout these two years, we have remained firm in our rejection of racism and religious extremism in all its forms and manifestations. We will continue to work tirelessly to build a nation that is more secure, inclusive and united — a nation made stronger by the full richness of its diversity.

Mr. President,

In addition to the consequences of natural calamity, Sri Lanka, like many other countries, is experiencing the severe impact of conflicts in West Asia and elsewhere.

As an island nation situated at the crossroads of the Indian Ocean, and as a country with a large number of migrant workers in West Asia, these developments have direct security, economic and social implications for us.

I am pleased to note that, even during these challenging times, Sri Lanka has continued to uphold its commitments to international law and to ensure sanctity of human life and human dignity.

Mr. President In March this year, amidst a highly volatile geopolitical landscape, Sri Lanka found a ship of a party to a conflict in distress close to our territorial waters with many sailors’ life in peril. We took the difficult path of navigating a wilderness of sensitivities and marshalling our limited national resources to rescue an d look after the wounded and sick. Hard as it was, we went on to rescue hundreds more. We saw human lives in danger, and we acted - founding ourselves on international law and on humanity. While safeguarding our neutrality, we placed humanity above all else. As President Disanayaka has reiterated, “we will never hesitate to protect humanity. If there are actions that must be taken to protect human lives, we will not hesitate to take them under any circumstance”.

This, Mr. President, is the Sri Lanka we wish to bring before the world - a small island nation with a big heart which believes that even in times of conflict and profound division, there remains space for humanity.

And that is also what we wish to see reflected in the world. We need a world where our capacity to uphold humanity grows faster than our capacity to destroy it. That is the transformation we should seek.

It is for these reasons that we are pained by the developments in Gaza and the Occupied Palestinian territories.

Mr. President,

The global security environment has deteriorated significantly in recent years. It is difficult to accept that, in a world with so much wealth and knowledge, vast resources continue to be spent on weapons while children face starvation and are deprived of medicine and education.

Sri Lanka remains deeply concerned by the conflicts in West Asia and by the heavy cost being borne far beyond the region.

International law, including International Humanitarian Law, must be adhered to and respected by all parties. We reaffirm our position that dialogue is the only viable way forward.

Sri Lanka continues to support the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, including their right to self -determination.

We are among the countries that first recognised Palestine as a distinct State in the 1980s. We stand in solidarity with the international community in calling for an independent and sovereign State of Palestine, existing side by side with Israel, in peace, within the pre-1967 borders.

We welcome the resolution of the Security Council on a ceasefire in Gaza and urge all parties to uphold it. Humanitarian assistance must reach civilians without obstruction. The recovery and reconstruction of Gaza must be an urgent priority.

Mr. President,

Sri Lanka is proud of its longstanding contribution to United Nations peacekeeping, in pursuit of global peace and security, having deployed more than 21,000 personnel on numerous missions since 1957.

Our Blue Helmets, through their dedication and service over many years, have earned the trust of local communities and the commendation of UN field missions.

Today, they continue to serve with distinction in some of the most challenging environments under the UN flag — protecting vulnerable civilians, deterring violence and helping war -torn communities transition from conflict to stability.

Sri Lanka has also long championed multilateral disarmament — from our early call for an Indian Ocean Zone of Peace to our leadership at the 1995 NPT Review and Extension Conference.

At a time of rising geopolitical tensions and rhetoric of nuclear escalation, we remain firmly convinced that the only real guarantee against these weapons is their total and verifiable elimination.

Mr. President,

As we approach 2030, we must deliver on the Sustainable Development Goals, which remain our collective blueprint for sustainable development.

Sri Lanka once again calls for reform of the international financial system and for fairer rules governing debt a nd development finance. We welcomed the Seville Commitment last year, including its call for urgent action to close the four -trillion-dollar financing gap for sustainable development in developing countries. It is now time to translate those commitments into concrete action.

We remain steadfast in recognising poverty and inequality as factors requiring our urgent attention.

Our national budget last year made historic allocations to the healthcare and education sectors. We take pride in our longstanding policy of free and universal healthcare and education, and remain committed to strengthening these important pillars of social justice.

While actively implementing all SDGs without discrimination, we fully subscribe to and proactively engage with SDG 16, which underscores the importance of just and inclusive institutions that build and restore public trust and treat all people equally.

Mr. President,

Sri Lanka has long championed and contributed towards a fair and peaceful order at sea under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea — a legal regime which we have helped shape. We also support the work of the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf. We remain committed to preserving the oceans as a shared space for peaceful and sustainable use, and for international cooperation. Our nation’s prosperity is closely linked to the Indian Ocean.

As a founding Member of the Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction, the BBNJ Agreement, we reaffirm our commitment to safeguarding the oceans as a common heritage of humankind for present and future generations.

We look forward to the further operationalisation of the Agreement, complementing the processes of the International Seabed Authority.

Mr. President,

One of the key pillars of the decisive mandate given to us by the people of Sri Lanka was to build a transparent and ethical nation. In delivering on this mandate, we have placed good governance, anti -corruption and institutional transparency at the core of a comprehensive national integrity drive that is being vigorously pursued.

We have seen all too clearly how corruption weakens democracy and destroys trust. We continue to enforce the law against corruption without fear or favour, irrespective of a person’s background or social standing.

Investigations and prosecutions continue t o progress without political interference.

Substantial progress has been made in strengthening the independence of institutions responsible for investigating and prosecuting bribery and corruption.

My President, who addressed this Assembly last year, also highlighted how narcotics and related organised crime have become a menace for many countries, as well as our Government’s comprehensive efforts to address this menace.

One year on, our “United as a Nation” Anti-Narcotics National Programme has made significant progress, including through the arrest of key figures in the narcotics supply chain.

Mr. President,

We reiterate our call on the global community to promote meaningful technology transfers, ensure equitable access for developing nations, bridge the digital divide, and build safe, secure and trustworthy systems that leave no one behind.

Sri Lanka is in the process of building a digital future that includes everyone. We have developed national AI ethical guidelines in line with international frameworks.

We must ensure that emerging technologies and artificial intelligence are developed and used responsibly and consistently with international law, including the well-established principles of international humanitarian law.

Their development and use must contribute to international peace and security while advancing humanity's collective interests.

The interests of humanity must always guide the development and use of these technologies.

Mr. President,

For Sri Lanka, the United Nations is an indispensable partner. The UN has stood with us in challenging times and supported our development.

For many of us in the developing world, the United Nations is also an expression of a fundamental promise: that every nation, large or small, has a voice; that every people has a right to dignity and development; and that, in an interdependent world, no country should be left to confront global challenges alone.

For more than eight decades, amidst its flaws and with much room for improvement, the United Nations has given practical meaning to that promise.

However, genuine faith in multilateralism requires the courage to acknowledge where the system has fallen short, the humility to listen to those who feel unheard, and the determination to make our institutions more effective, more representative and more responsive.

In this regard, Sri Lanka supports the UN80 Initiative as an opportunity to renew and strengthen the United Nations and advance meaningful reform.

Mr. President,

Managing transformation cannot mean managing change for some while asking others merely to adapt to its consequences.

The transformation taking place in our world must be inclusive.

It must narrow, rather than deepen, the divides between North and South; between those who shape new technologies and those who merely receive them; and between those who possess resilience and those who are most exposed to global shocks.

My country comes to this Assembly not with the expectation that the United Nations can solve every problem, but with the conviction that there are problems which no country can solve alone.

Our answer must therefore be a renewed faith in multilateralism and a United Nations that listens more closely, represents more fairly and delivers for all.

I thank you, Mr. President.

Mr. President,

Our region and the world are undergoing a period of rapid transformation, marked by intensifying challenges and divisions.

Amid all this, the United Arab Emirates stands tall — guided by a clear vision and unwavering determination to transform challenges into opportunities, turn ambitions into achievements, and open new horizons for peace, development, and prosperity for our people, the peoples of the region, and the world.

This stems from our principled approach rooted in de escalation, bridge -building, the promotion of diplomacy and dialogue, the peaceful settlement of disputes, and the rejection of the unlawful use or threat of force, as well as coercion. This approach is grounded in full respect for the sovereignty of States, good -neighborly relations, international law, and the Charter of the United Nations.

These values have long underpinned our domestic and foreign policies:

As Iran continues its occupation of the three Emirati islands — Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb, and Abu Musa — which we reject, the United Arab Emirates has consistently called for a peaceful settlement of this conflict, whether through direct negotiations or by recourse to the International Court of Justice.

Amid growing threats to navigation in our region and beyond, my country has continued to emphasize the principles of freedom of navigation and the right of transit passage. We stress the need to secure and protect the safe flow of supply chains, trade, and energy in accordance with international law, including the law of the sea, and the principle of state sovereignty, recognizing these as pillars of food security, development, and prosperity of nations.

The United Arab Emirates has continued to support every sincere effort to achieve peace, particularly in Yemen,

Libya, the Sahel, the Democratic Republic of the Congo,

Myanmar, Haiti, and elsewhere.

We have also supported efforts to reach a sustainable political solution to the Question of the Moroccan Sahara, based on the Moroccan Autonomy Initiative, while affirming the Kingdom of Morocco’s sovereignty over this territory.

Furthermore, we have advocated for a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine, in accordance with international law and the principles of the UN Charter — including respect for sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity. We have remained steadfast in our role as a trusted international mediator, successfully conducting twenty-six mediation s that facilitated the exchange of nearly eight thousand prisoners between Ukraine and the Russian Federation, ensuring their safe return to their homelands and families.

The UAE has also stood ready to support nations undergoing positive transformations — such as Syria and Lebanon — as they move toward s a secure and stable future.

Regarding Sudan, my country has underscored the imperative of ending the humanitarian catastrophe, securing a permanent and unconditional ceasefire that would bring an end to the civil war. This includes launching a comprehensive and credible political process, led by civilians, which would culminate in the formation of a civil government independent of both parties to the conflict and of extremist groups. It is crucial to ensure that neither side of the conflict has a role in the new civilian government.

The future of Sudan must be decided solely by the Sudanese people, and the international community must press the leaders of Port Sudan authorities and those of Rapid Support Forces, as parties to the conflict, to engage seriously with international initiatives.

As for Gaza, the UAE was among the first to support the framework established by the international community to end th e horrific war. We have stressed the need to fully implement the comprehensive plan to end the conflict in Gaza — and the associated roadmap — including Israel’s withdrawal from the Gaza Strip, the disarmament of Hamas, and the advancement of a serious political horizon leading to a just and lasting settlement of the Palestinian Question based on the two -state solution. This entails the establishment of an independent, sovereign Palestinian state living side-by-side with Israel in peace and security.

We also underscore the importance of ensuring the unification of Gaza and the West Bank under a Palestinian authority that, once reformed, will be capable to fulfill its responsibilities and ensure that arms remain solely under its control.

We further underscore the urgent need to halt Israel's dangerous escalation in the West Bank and its settlement activities — which are accompanied by the rise of settler violence, terrorism, and the siege of Palestinian villages, as well as the ongoing violations in East Jerusalem and at holy sites and the attempts to impose new historical and legal realities on the ground. My country condemns all such actions in the strongest terms.

For decades, the UAE's commitment to the Palestinian people has remained unwavering. Today, that commitment continues through our role as the largest provider of humanitarian aid to Gaza, along with our humanitarian and development projects in the West Bank.

This role reflects the core values of our foreign policy, which is driven by the spirit of giving through effective international partnerships while reconfirming the principles of international humanitarian law and the protection of civilians.

Across all these issues, the importance of developing and reforming regional and international multilateral institutions — foremost among them the United Nations, including the Security Council — remains paramount to strengthening their capacity to fulfill the responsibilities they have been entrusted. As the United Nations prepares to transition to new leadership, we look forward to the next Secretary-General using his or her good offices to activate preventive and mediation mechanisms before the first signs of crises emerge, rather than merely reacting once they have erupted. Crises must be addressed at their roots, not simply managed.

Mr. President,

My country has refused to let the crises surrounding us undermine the world -leading achievements we have built over decades. On the contrary, we have pressed ahead with progress across every sector — for this nation was forged not in the absence of challenges, but in defiance of them.

The peoples of our region aspire to stability and prosperity in an environment defined by cooperation, moderation, and tolerance — not by violence, hatred, extremism, or terrorism.

The UAE model has demonstrated its resilience and its capacity to deliver tangible results by investing in the key pillars of national strength, foremost among them strategic independence, industrial capabilities, advanced defense systems, and world-class infrastructure and logistics. This is complemented by the empowerment of human capital, the cultivation of a knowledge -and innovation -based economy, and the harnessing of the opportunities offered by the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreements (CEPAs) concluded with thirty -eight nations —among other frameworks—to diversify markets and supply chains and broaden horizons for trade and investment.

We will continue to cement the UAE's role as a global hub connecting markets and capital, opening ever -broader horizons for growth. This is the promise the UAE makes to its people and to all who call it home — and it is the bedrock of our international partnerships, particularly with the nations of the Global South and Africa, which have matured into an enduring strategic cooperation rooted in mutual respect and shared interests.

The UAE continues to expand its investments in artificial intelligence, emerging technologies, healthcare, and education. We are also strengthening our position as a trusted and responsible leader in the energy sector — balancing the needs of today with bold investment in the solutions of tomorrow and driving the historic commitments of the 'UAE Consensus' toward long -term collective action.

This year, the UAE is preparing to co-host with Senegal the UN Water Conference, recognizing the importance of concerted, coordinated international action in confronting the challenges of water, climate, and food security. We are confident the conference will mark a vital milestone in advancing real, practical solutions for water security. We invite you to participate in the Conference and look forward to welcoming you in Abu Dhabi.

These efforts embody our firm commitment to turning the challenge of water scarcity into an opportunity for innovation and joint international action, including through the Mohamed bin Zayed Water Initiative, which harnesses innovation, partnership, and investment to deliver lasting, sustainable solutions for present and future generations.

Two days ago, Abu Dhabi also hosted the opening of the 15th UN Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, highlighting the need to keep pace with rapid technological advancement and to protect societies from the impacts of crime, violence, and exploitation.

At the same time, we are investing in the values of tolerance, peaceful coexistence, and inclusion through partnerships that bring together diverse nationalities and faiths. We are building a society in which women participate fully, equally, and meaningfully, and in which young people are genuine partners in shaping their future.

In conclusion, Mr. President, my country will remain committed to the path of moderation, the rejection of violence and extremism, and the investment in people and in the vast potential with which our region is so richly endowed. We extend our hands to our partners in the region and across the world to build rather than to destroy, and to unite rather than to divide.

Thank you, Mr. President.

Mr. President,

Mr. President,

Last year we meaningfully celebrated the 80th founding anniversary of the United Nations.

As we marked the watershed in UN history reviewing its past eighty years and looking ahead into the future, mankind ardently desired and aspired to put an immediate end to the current chaos of international relations and regain peace and stability.

Unfortunately, however, what the world witnessed every day for the last one year was a harsh reality rampant with unprecedented mutual distrust and confrontation, infringement on sovereignty, and military conflict s that led to extreme unrest and disorder globally.

The new year started with the most despicable, world startling act of state -sponsored terrorism, followed by worldwide outbreaks of other appalling incidents and events which anyone with common sense and knowledge can hardly imagine. Crises causing insecurity and instability increased further with wars and bloody conflicts.

The effects of disaster -prone abnormal climate ga ve rise to a succession of extreme high temperature, droughts, heavy rains and floods in many countries and regions, seriously threatening the survival of mankind. Humanity desires that the United Nations should fulfill its mission and responsibility as an organization established to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.

Regrettably, however, the Organization still fails to reco ver from functional paralysis owing to the high -handedness and unilateralism of a handful of countries pursuing only chauvinistic interests.

All the crises the international community is faced with point to one clear fact – that infringement on sovereignty, threat to security interests, and denial of right to development of other countries are bound to breed regional instability and crisis and lead to aggression and war.

In order to overcome all the existing crises and challenges and promote peace, security and sustainable development, all member states should seek appropriate solutions to problems while strictly complying with the intrinsic purposes and principles of the UN Charter and giving priority to unity and cooperation among nations.

Mr. President,

The historic 9 th Congress of the Workers’ Party of Korea was held with splendor in February this year in Pyongyang, the capital city of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. During the last five years, the existence and development of humankind were severely constrained by the global pandemic, abnormal weather conditions, geopolitical confrontation and the entailing economic crisis. They were harsh times for our State, too.

The five -year plan for the development of the national economy was successfully accomplished. The economic foundation for production boost was reinforced. Numerous monumental projects were compl eted. Policies for the people that our government invariably pursues are implemented at a higher level. We are seeing the upward trend of comprehensive development conducive to simultaneous and balanced growth in all sectors, fields and regions of the country.

As the first -hand witnesses of the above realities, all our citizens have become all the more confident that the path we have trodden is the most accurate path and that self reliance and self-sustenance of our choice are the surest shortcut to prosperity.

Under the unique leadership of Comrade Kim Jong Un, President of the State Affairs of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, our people have now confidently embarked on new massive projects aimed at building on the successe s in pioneering an era of comprehensive development and leading it to new heights.

The path ahead of us is laden with numerous challenges and difficulties presented by inhumane acts of certain forces that disfavor the DPRK’s very existence, let alone her development. Yet we will surely attain all that we plan to, relying entirely on our own efforts, regardless of changes in the situation.

This is the confidence that every Korean is assured of.

Mr. President,

The sovereignty, security interests and terri torial integrity of sovereign states are ruthlessly trampled upon and the international law and order feebly collapse due to the unilateral high -handedness and tyranny of a hegemonic state. Such a grim reality of international relations teaches us a serious lesson.

A lesson that fair advocacy and earnest desire for compliance with the law and order alone can hardly defend anything.

Like in other parts of the world, a serious landscape of confrontation between justice and injustice and between hegemonic forces and independence forces is being witnessed in Northeast Asia this year.

The U.S.-Japan-ROK military alliance, unmistakably aimed at the DPRK, is being evolved by the United States into a more offensive and aggressiv e military bloc with a nuclear element. This year alone, the U.S. staged a series of bilateral and multilateral military exercises including "Freedom Shield" and "Freedom Edge ", simulating a real war scenario. It didn’t even bother to cover up its dangerous attempt at military confrontation against the DPRK.

The U.S. has approved and is encouraging Seoul’s ambition to possess nuclear powered submarines, while relocating and deploying different military hardware including the latest missiles and drones on the Korean peninsula and in its vicinity. The current military inclination is further aggravating the already vulnerable security landscape in the region.

On the other hand, Japan, an A -class war criminal that inflicted untold sufferings and disasters upon mankind in the last century, is taking advantage of the present international turbulence. It accelerates its attempts at rearmament with an unprecedented commitment including the revision of the Peace Constitution, abandonment of “exclusive defence”, reformation of the military structure and arms build -up. Such actions are casting war clouds over the entire region.

Under the signboard of “counterattack capability”, Japan has buckled down to the development and possession of long -range attack weapons that put neig hbouring countries within a striking range. Its ambition run counter to its obligations as a defeated nation; they are in shameless disregard of the UN Charter and pose a grave challenge to global peace.

The global military and political conte xt is worsening day by day and the unlimited abuse of power has become a commonplace. Under such circumstances, the risky military threat of the U.S., Japan and the ROK go beyond precedent and continue to break the worst records in their scale, intensity, nature and t he dangers, creating security instability on the Korean peninsula on a level different from previous years.

Nevertheless, no physical conflict has occurred on and around the Korean peninsula, a hot spot of the world, and the security index is being maintained at a higher level than any other part of the globe. We owe it to the fact that the DPRK has a war deterrent in place powerful enough to break anyone’s will to start a war of aggression against the DPRK and that we are thoroughly containing and managin g the hostile forces’ intention to use force.

Thus the regional balance of power maintained by the DPRK’s self-defensive capabilities effectively curbs the risk of an armed conflict.

No one can deny such an obvious fact. It further highlights the immutable truth that a just power means the national sovereignty and prestige and a fundamental guarantee of peace and stability.

The Head of State of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea stated that our national sovereignty and security have firmly been en sured by virtue of great strength so far and will invariably be so in the years ahead.

The DPRK’s nuclear deterrent is the absolute might and irresistible force designed, from A to Z, to safeguard the sovereignty, security and peace against aggression and threat from outside.

I would like to reiterate the official position of the DPRK government: the status of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea as a nuclear weapons state, that has been uncompromisingly and permanently fixed both physically and legally with absolutely no turning back, can never be reversed in any circumstances or by any means, no matter how hard and loudly the hostile forces may deny in chorus with all sorts of rhetoric.

The DPRK will continue to strictly control and manage every external threat by dint of her supremacy in overwhelming strength and be all the more faithful and committed to our mission as a responsible nuclear weapons state to firmly defend national sovereignty and fundamental interests and to guarantee peace and sec urity of the region and beyond.

Mr. President,

Large-scale natural calamities claimed tens of thousands of lives in different parts of the world this year. The international community came to realize once again that climate change is a pressing issue that calls for a joint action.

AI and other new cutting -edge technology are transforming every domain of human life, offering great opportunities. But at the same time, they also carry risks of being misused for sinister purposes.

Highly volatile present er a urgently calls for strengthened UN capable of handling challenges and crisis facing humanity in conformity with the common interests of mankind.

It’s about time the UN undertook a reform.

Not the reform centered on specific countries but the one aimed at democratization of the United Nations in the true sense of the word so that the organization would represent the views and interests of the entire membership evenly and equally.

Gone are the days when a n individual member state unilaterally imposed its will on the rest of the world and dominated the international political arena. Instead, multilateralism and multipolarization have emerged as an irresistible aspiration and trend of the times based on justice and equity.

The DPRK will always be with the anti -imperialist, independent countries aspiring after the building of a just and peaceful world and is committed to undertaking the historic mission of leading the movement for globa l independence under the uplifted banner of independence.

Mr. President,

As a UN member state, the DPRK government maintains its invariable stand to actively work towards the establishment of genuine international justice and a new fair international order in compliance with the UN Charter and international law.

In particular, I affirm that the DPRK government led by the present Head of State of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea will direct positive efforts to promote international justice, co -prosperity, and peace and security of the region and beyond while firmly defending her national sovereignty, security interests, and the right to development.

New Zealand Permanent Mission to the United Nations Te Aka Aorere United Nations General Debate of the Eighty-First Session New Zealand Statement delivered by Permanent Representative, H.E. Ms Victoria Hallum Monday 28 September 2026 President,

Over the past week, we have listened to leaders, ministers and representatives from every region of the world.

They have spoken of different priorities and concerns. Yet they have also revealed how much we have in common. We have been reminded that the biggest challenges we face do not respect national borders. And no country, however large or powerful, can address them alone.

It is clear we live in a more contested, fragmented and volatile world.

The number of active conflicts in the world has almost doubled in the past 20 years. The number of conflict -related deaths has reached levels not seen in decades.

Fundamental norms governing state behaviour are being violated with increasing impunity, contravening the UN Charter and other universally applicable rules of international law.

Core human rights that protect the well-being and dignity of our citizens are increasingly being ignored.

Humanitarian needs are growing faster than our collective ability to meet them.

After decades of progress, hard -won development gains have slowed, and it is clear we will fail to meet most of the Sustainable Development Goals by their 2030 target.

Biodiversity loss and pollution are impacting key natural resources in our oceans.

Natural disasters and the growing impacts of our changing climate are becoming more severe and more visible. In our region, these pressures are already affecting lives, livelihoods and long-term development prospects.

All of this is of grave concern to New Zealand, whose sovereignty, security and prosperity depends on a functioning, inclusive multilateral system, grounded in agreed rules and norms with the UN Charter at its centre.

We regard the UN Charter – with its core principles of sovereign equality of states, territorial integrity, the prohibition of the use of force, and respect for human rights - as irreplaceable.

We continue therefore to invest in the United Nations, and agreed international rules, as an exercise of our sovereignty, because we believe it is essential to our interests, and indeed the interests of all. In the face of rising volatility, we need the UN’s stabilising influence, and global solutions, more than ever.

President,

Over recent years, New Zealand has spoken of the importance of leadership. New Zealand thanks Secretary -General Antonio Guterres for his service over the past ten years.

We thank you for your visits to the Blue Pacific, and for your attention to the unique situation of Pacific Islands countries and other Small Island Developing States.

We thank you also for starting the process of essential reform to put this vital organisation on a stronger and more sustainable footing to deal with the challenges of the next 80 years.

Your assignment has not been easy.

As we prepare to appoint the next Secretary-General to lead the UN into the next phase, we should be clear about what this moment requires.

First and foremost, we call on the new Secretary -General to be a courageous guardian of the UN Charter and to assert the UN’s vital role on peace and security.

The United Nations was created to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.

It is ultimately the responsibility of Member States to prevent and resolve conflicts. We cannot outsource that responsibility.

But we need a Secretary-General who is active in conflict prevention, mediation and peace-making.

The Secretary-General should never have to seek permission or forgiveness for acting to prevent or resolve conflict.

As a custodian of the UN Charter, you have the right and the obligation to speak up when its core norms are breached.

We expect you to do so in an objective, impartial, and consistent manner. We will support you when you do.

So we ask you to be active in seeking an end to the horrific conflict in Sudan.

You must be bold in pressing for a sustainable and just end to Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine. One that is consistent with Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and the core principles of the Charter.

You must be determined in your efforts to help alleviate the dire humanitarian situation in Gaza. We ask that you use your influence to progress a fragile ceasefire into a sustainable, durable peace.

And you must be resolute in preserving conditions for a two-state solution. You must take the initiative, despite the challenges and entrenched views, to achieve a just and lasting resolution, where Israel and Palestine can live side -by-side within secure and clearly defined borders.

We urge you to use your good offices to secure a lasting end to hostilities in the Persian Gulf and restore freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, which is a right guaranteed under international law.

Of course, you cannot do this alone. For our part we, as Member States, must provide you with the tools, the resources, and above all the political support to ensure you can play this role effectively.

Parties to conflicts must engage with you constructively and in good faith; while global and regional partners with influence must provide the necessary incentives for the parties to do so.

The UN Security Council needs to fulfil its responsibilities.

Permanent members, in particular, must act in a manner consistent with their special responsibilities under the Charter.

Too frequently has the veto, or the threat of the veto, been abused to block the Council from fulfilling its responsibilities, to the frustration, and sometimes despair, of the global community.

Inevitably, the costs of this failure are borne by those caught in conflict.

This Assembly also has a legitimate and necessary role to play in maintaining peace and security, and we have been pleased to see it step up on occasions when the Security Council has been stymied from acting.

For our part, New Zealand will continue to press for a more effective, credible, transparent and representative Security Council. As a demonstration of our continued commitment to collective security and the UN Charter, New Zealand is seeking a seat on the UN Security Council for 2039-40.

We ask the next Secretary-General to work with us to preserve the integrity of the global disarmament framework, particularly on weapons of mass destruction. The grave dangers of the deterioration of the global nuclear non -proliferation regime should alarm us all.

New Zealand was deeply disappointed at the failure to reach consensus at this year’s Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty Review Conference.

After three consecutive Review Conference failures, we must all do what we can to preserve the health of the NPT and, indeed, strengthen it.

This means tackling persistent violations and cases of non compliance. Iran is not in compliance with its nuclear safeguards obligations. The DPRK’s nuclear weapons and missile programmes continue to threaten its region and beyond.

Halting the NPT’s deterioration also requires concrete action from the Nuclear Weapons States to, at long last, chart a path towards total, verifiable, and irreversible nuclear disarmament.

We also call on you to safeguard the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the “constitution for the oceans”, which provides the framework within which all activities o n the oceans and seas must be carried out. Compliance with these universally applicable rules is essential, not only for maintaining peace and security, but also for protecting prosperity and food security, given the oceans' vital role in supporting trade.

Second, we call on the next Secretary-General to provide strong leadership across the UN’s development and human rights pillars.

The authors of the UN Charter understood that peace and security cannot be sustained without creating the conditions for Member States to provide their citizens with prosperity and the full enjoyment of their human rights.

With significant changes in the global development cooperation landscape, we ask you to ensure the UN is clear about where its comparative advantage lies, alongside the role of governments, regional organisations and International Financial Institutions.

Citizens and donors expect the UN to operate as one, with agencies working together, through a strengthened Resident Coordinator system. We will work with you to ensure the UN is more coordinated and focused on strengthening local capacity and partnerships to address a country’s development needs.

The UN development system must remain relevant, responsive and accessible to all Member States based on need, rather than size, income level or location. We welcome progress in advancing the UN’s Multidimensional Vulnerability Index and want to see further work to ensure its practical application across the multilateral development system.

In the face of contracting development finance flows and increasing debt levels, we need to ensure our ambitions are matched by more sustainable and predictable financing. This will inevitably involve moving beyond an exclusive reliance on traditional sources and approaches.

President,

As Pacific Islands Forum leaders recently reaffirmed in Palau, climate change remains the single greatest threat to the livelihoods, security and wellbeing of Pacific peoples.

While New Zealand will play its part, our efforts will mean little in the absence of determined action by the world’s major emitters.

Rising sea levels threaten the continued viability of many communities and pose a threat to low -lying island states, including some of our Pacific neighbours.

The Political Declaration on Sea Level Rise, endorsed this week, is a demonstration of the UN’s ability to address contemporary challenges affecting its members. We particularly welcome the Declaration’s affirmation of the preservation of maritime zones and the presumption of continued statehood, notwithstanding sea-level rise.

We also expect the new Secretary -General to defend international humanitarian law and international human rights law and its institutions.

The promotion and protection of universal and indivisible human rights is fundamental to the world we live in today and to a collective vision of our future. Societies in which citizens can enjoy their universal human rights have a better chance of avoiding the descent into conflict that tragically impacts so many across the world today.

Over the past decade these norms have often been under threat, sometimes through neglect, sometimes through deliberate and sustained attacks.

The rise in attacks on protected individuals, including civilians and humanitarian and medical personnel, needs particular attention.

It is ten years since New Zealand co-led the adoption of Security Council Resolution 2286 on healthcare in armed conflict. Attacks on medical facilities and personnel in violation of international humanitarian law have grown exponentially worse since then.

Few have been held accountable for these flagrant violations of international humanitarian law.

We ask you to help us reverse these trends, by drawing on the UN’s unique legitimacy to call out egregious and systematic violations of these norms, wherever they may occur and whoever may be perpetrating them, and by providing practical guidance and assistance to help Member States meet their obligations.

Third, we ask the new Secretary -General to maintain momentum and ambition on UN reform.

Confidence in this institution depends on its ability to deliver impact. The next Secretary -General must work with Member States to chart an ambitious vision for the next phase of reform, while ensuring implementation of the decisions already taken.

At a time of multiple and overlapping crises and growing constraints, we need a United Nations that is focused on its core tasks, disciplined and accountable. One where every dollar delivers maximum impact.

One that measures success not by the number of mandates it creates or meetings it holds, but by the difference it makes in people's lives.

Meeting this challenge means exercising your powers to achieve the most impact from the resources available.

It means demanding a culture of continuous improvement, one that focuses on effective implementation and results.

It means setting the highest standards for performance within the Secretariat and holding staff accountable for delivering.

In this regard, we ask you to demonstrate independence in your senior appointments. New Zealand has never accepted the right of any country to assert “ownership” of UN positions by virtue of its power and status.

We encourage all Secretary -General candidates to commit publicly to making senior appointments on the basis of merit.

Reform is a joint responsibility. We as Member States must avoid the trap of regarding reform as something that others will deliver for us and instead live up to our own responsibilities for building the organisation we need.

We cannot expect the UN to continue to lurch on, in a state of constant financial crisis. Member States must meet their financial obligations in full, on time, and without conditions, in accordance with their obligations under the Charter.

We need to focus our attention on the issues that really matter, and that can genuinely deliver benefits for our citizens.

Resolution 80/251 equips Member States to tackle the long standing challenge of mandate accumulation and overload. It commits us all to take a more disciplined approach to setting the Organisation's priorities. It provides the framework we need to create a more focused, coherent and impactful UN.

Yet its success will depend on whether we are prepared to act differently. If we aren’t prepared to make the necessary choices, we will be left with an ever -growing set of responsibilities supported by an ever -shrinking pool of resources. That will do nothing to strengthen confidence in the UN's relevance or effectiveness.

Reform begins with us. It requires Member States to make the decisions that only Member States can make.

That is the only way we can truly achieve an organisation that is fit to meet the challenges that lie before us, and that our citizens need and expect.

Finally, we urge the next Secretary-General to ensure that the UN works for all states.

The sovereign equality of states is one of the most central principles of the UN Charter. It must also be central to your approach.

The fundamental premise of the United Nations is that every state, regardless of its size or circumstances, has a stake in shaping our shared future.

We also call on the President of the General Assembly to remain a steadfast champion of the voices, prerogatives, and interests of the entire UN membership across all pillars of its work.

The next Secretary -General's leadership in these areas will be essential. But we must also find it in ourselves to demonstrate leadership.

Ultimately, the health, relevance, and effectiveness of the United Nations depend s primarily on its members, not its Secretary General. As Member States, we must acknowledge our role in the financial and legitimacy crisis facing the UN. We must ask whether we have the collective will to change our behaviour?

Do we have the discipline to focus our attention and resources on the issues that really matter to our citizens, and deliver impact in their lives? Do we have the honesty to admit what is working and what is not?

Do we have the will to invest in the multilateral system, both politically and financially, to enable it to deliver results where we can truly make a difference?

Coupled with the courage to make bold and consequent decisions on UN reform that can deliver a more effective organisation?

Collective action has changed the course of global challenges before.

These achievements were not inevitable. They were the result of political leadership, persistence, and a willingness to work together despite differences to build understanding, and compromise.

The most fundamental step we can all take to revive this organisation is to unequivocally recommit ourselves – both in words and in deeds - to the principles that the Charter requires us to follow in our relations with other states - respect for sovereignty, international law, the pursuit of dialogue and cooperation, and the peaceful settlement of disputes.

At a time when conflict is rising, trust is eroding, and geopolitical competition is intensifying, we should not conclude that multilateralism has failed.

We should conclude that it is needed more than ever.

Thank you.
