Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, Ladies and Gentlemen,

First of all, I have the honour to convey, on behalf of the President of Turkmenistan, His Excellency Mr. Serdar Berdimuhamedov, greetings and wishes of peace and prosperity to the peoples of your countries.

Allow me to congratulate you, Mr Khalilur Rahman, on your election as President of the eighty -first session of the United Nations General Assembly and to wish you every success in discharging your important responsibilities.

I would also like to express our appreciation to Ms Annalena Baerbock for her leadership of the General Assembly during its previous session.

Distinguished Participants,

The current international environment requires all States to demonstrate a high degree of responsibility, political foresight and readiness for concerted action. Rising conflict potential, the erosion of trust, economic instability, climate risks and the rapid development of new technologies are becoming increasingly intertwined, directly a ffecting the security and well- being of peoples.

In these circumstances, it is particularly important to uphold the common purposes enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations; ensure respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of States, their sovereign equality and noninterference in their internal affairs; and strengthen the rule of international law.

Turkmenistan firmly believes that the United Nations must continue to serve as the universal and legitimate foundation of international cooperation and as the principal mechanism for reconciling interests and developing solutions in the areas of peace, security and sustainable development.

It is from this perspective that our country approaches the work of the eighty-first session of the General Assembly.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Ensuring international peace and security remains a key priority for Turkmenistan. The permanent neutrality of our country, recognized three times by the General Assembly, provides a practical foundation for advancing political and diplomatic methods, preventive diplomacy, mediation and the peaceful settlement of disputes.

We consider it essential to consistently foster a culture of trust and dialogue and to restore the legal and humanistic foundations of international relations.

In this regard, Turkmenistan intends to convene, under the auspices of the United Nations, intergovernmental consultations on the elaboration of a Global Peace Strategy founded on the principles of peace, security and preventive diplomacy.

As a furt her step in this direction, we propose proclaiming a United Nations Decade of Dialogue and Preventive Diplomacy. We believe that such a Decade would lend a systematic character to the efforts of States to prevent conflicts, build trust and establish sustainable channels of political communication.

Turkmenistan will also propose the establishment, within the United Nations, of a Group of Friends of Multilateralism and the Sovereign Equality of States. Its activities could contribute to safeguarding the fundamental principles of the Charter of the United Nations, strengthening dialogue among equals and preventing the emergence of dividing lines in international cooperation.

We attach particular importance to supporting the United Nations Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for Central Asia, headquartered in Ashgabat. The year 2027 will mark the twentieth anniversary of its establishment. We regard this milestone as a unique opportunity to take stock of the Centre's work and identify new avenues for its practical contribution to peace, stability and cooperation in Central Asia.

To this end, during the current session Turkmenistan will submit a further draft General Assembly resolution on the role of the Regional Centre. We trust that the document will reaffirm our shared interest in further strengthening its mandate and operational capacity.

In consistently promoting education and scientific cooperation as important pillars of peacebuilding, Turkmenistan will continue its engagement with the United Nations on the initiative to establish a University of Peace and Neutrality. As a practical first step, we will begin consultations on the establishment of an Academic Centre for Peace, Neutrality and Preventive Diplomacy at the Institute of International Relations of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Turkmenistan.

Distinguished Participants,

Digital transformation is becoming an increasingly important factor in sustainability and development. Artificial intelligence offers broad opportunities, while also requiring responsible international governance to prevent its use to the detriment of peace, security and trust.

In this regard, Turkmenistan proposes the development, under the auspices of the United Nations, of an International Code for the Peaceful Use of Artificial Intelligence in International Relations and Diplomacy. To support this work, we propose convening in Ashgabat an international expert dialogue on digital trust and the responsible use of artificial intelligence.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Peace and development are inextricably linked. For Turkmenistan, a key priority in this area is the development of sustainable, safe and inclusive transport systems.

The proclamation, at the initiative of Turkmenistan, of the United Nations Decade of Sustainable Tra nsport for 2026- 2035 has launched an important mechanism for systematic work, coordinated by the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, to put into practice the Decade's Implementation Plan. Within the framework of this long-term undertaking, our country will continue its work towards the creation of a Global Atlas of Sustainable Transport Connectivity - a comprehensive analytical and informational tool for assessing progress, identifying infrastructure gaps and coordinating international efforts.

During the eighty -first session, Turkmenistan will actively support the implementation of the Awaza Programme of Action for Landlocked Developing Countries for the Decade 2024 -2034 and the Awaza Political Declaration. In this context, we particularly welcome the election of Turkmenistan as Chair of the Group of Landlocked Developing Countries for 2027- 2028. We regard the confidence placed in us as both a great responsibility and an opportunity to work together with the States of the Group to give fresh impetus to the practical implementation of the Awaza Programme of Action in such priority areas as transport and energy connectivity. We proceed from the need to translate the agreements reached into concrete infrastructure, trade and investment projects.

We propose considering the establishment in Turkmenistan, under the auspices of the United Nations, of an International Centre for Sustainable Trade Logistics and Customs Cooperation. Such a Centre could serve as a practical platform for harmonizing procedures, exchanging best practices, digitalizing transit and expanding developing countries' access to global markets.

Our country also proposes the establishment, under the auspices of the United Nations, of a transregional transport corridor linking South and Central Asia with Europe through the Caspian Sea.

We are confident that its development would help diversify routes, strengthen connectivity, expand trade and promote closer economic ties among the regions.

Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates,

Environmental security, climate change and the sustainable use of energy resources are integral components of common security.

In this area, Turkmenistan will continue to promote multilateral dialogue by proposing the establishment of the Ashgabat Climate Dialogue - an open multilateral platform for regular political and expert engagement, the advancement of practical climate initiatives and the strengthening of international partnerships.

We believe particular attention must be paid to strengthening the climate resilience of regions severely affected by drought and water scarcity. This requires coordinated solutions combining modern technologies, financing, data exchange and regional cooperation.

In pursuance of the General Assembly resolution entitled "Key role of reliable and stable energy connectivity in ensuring sustainable development",

Turkmenistan will continue consultations in preparation for the High -level Forum on Sustainable Energy for All. We view the Forum as an effective platform for developing practical approaches to ensuring a reliable, affordable and sustainable energy supply.

In the socioeconomic sphere, Turkmenistan will continue its active and responsible work as a member of the United Nations Economic and Social Council for the period 2026- 2028, as well as its constructive engagement in the work of the Council's subsidiary bodies.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Turkmenistan attaches great importance to the humanitarian dimension of international cooperation. Lasting peace is impossible without the f ull participation of women and young people, the preservation of human dignity, mutual respect and equal opportunities.

Our country will continue to advance the Women and Peace and Security agenda, including by developing the Central Asian Women's Dialogue and expanding its cooperation with the United Nations Peacebuilding Commission and UN-Women.

At the same time, we will support the activities of the Central Asian Youth Dialogue and promote the broader and more meaningful participation of young people in international and regional peace initiatives in accordance with the Youth and Peace and Security agenda.

Distinguished Participants,

Turkmenistan regards the strengthening of international law as an essential condition for a just and sustainable international order. We welcome the consensus adoption of the General Assembly resolution initiated by our country proclaiming 2028 the International Year of Law.

As part of the preparatory process, we propose convening in Turkmenistan in 2027 an International Forum devoted to the interrelationship between international law, disarmament, neutrality, preventive diplomacy and sustainable development. We believe that the Forum will help strengthen respect for the Charter of the United Nations, enhance the role of legal mechanisms and engage the younger generation in the study and development of international law.

Mr. President,

All initiatives of Turkmenistan are united by a common purpose: to strengthen peace and trust, advance cooperation among equals and create the conditions for a dignified future for present and succeeding generations.

We stand ready to work with all Member States, the United Nations Secretariat and international partners towards the practical implementation of the proposals outlined above.

We are co nfident that, with political will, mutual respect and commitment to dialogue, the international community can overcome existing differences and achieve tangible progress towards the purposes of the United Nations.

Turkmenistan will continue to firmly uphold the principles of permanent neutrality, good-neighbourliness, peacefulness and constructive engagement, contributing to the strengthening of the central role of the United Nations in international affairs.

Thank you for your attention.

Mr President,

Mr Secretary-General,

Distinguished Heads of State and Government,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

We meet once again at a moment when history asks difficult questions of this institution.

Can multilateralism still protect the weak as well as the strong?

Can international law restrain power, rather than merely record its consequences?

Can development remain a promise for all, rather than a privilege for some?

For Antigua and Barbuda, these are not philosophical questions. For Small Island Developing States, they are questions of survival.

As we begin the eighty-first session of this General Assembly, we stand between two eras: one ending, and another waiting to be shaped.

At the end of this year, His Excellency António Guterres will complete his tenure as Secretary-General.

Antigua and Barbuda places on record its profound appreciation for his service to this Organization and to the international community. For my country, that appreciation is deeply personal.

In 2017, Hurricane Irma devastated Barbuda. The entire population had to be evacuated.

Homes were destroyed. Livelihoods disappeared. An island community was brought to its knees.

Secretary-General Guterres came to Antigua and Barbuda. He saw the devastation. He listened to our people. And he understood what Small Island Developing States have been telling the world for decades: climate change is not waiting for the future. It is already destroying lives, economies and communities.

He continued to stand with SIDS. He returned to Antigua and Barbuda for the Fourth International Conference on Small Island Developing States. He championed vulnerable countries and supported the international effort that brought the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index into being.

Whether confronting climate change, challenging inequality or calling for reform of the international financial system, he was a fearless and principled advocate. He never relented in demanding a fairer world, and he consistently placed the concerns of small island states before the international community.

For that solidarity, we thanked him.

But gratitude for the past must now be matched by courage in shaping the future.

The next Secretary-General will inherit a United Nations confronting wars and conflicts that devastate lives and undermine international stability. Deep geopolitical divisions, financial constraints, the climate emergency and declining trust will test the Organization’s capacity to respond.

Excellencies, the choice before us is about more than selecting an individual. It is about the future direction of this Organization.

That is why Antigua and Barbuda has nominated María Fernanda Espinosa to serve as the next Secretary-General.

We believe she is the right leader for this moment.

After more than eighty years, no woman has ever served as Secretary-General.

The time has come.

Our case for María Fernanda Espinosa rests on more than gender. It rests on competence, experience, independence and leadership. At a time of fragmentation, the United Nations needs a credible bridge-builder capable of restoring confidence in multilateralism.

Antigua and Barbuda believes that María Fernanda Espinosa can provide that leadership.

Mr President,

Multilateralism is under profound strain. Economic uncertainty continues to grow.

Technology is racing ahead of governance.

Artificial intelligence offers extraordinary possibilities, but it also raises profound concerns about who will control its development and share its benefits. Small states must not be left as spectators in this new era.

Nor can we accept an international system in which rules are binding upon the weak but negotiable for the powerful.

International law must apply equally. Sovereignty cannot depend upon power, nor justice upon the identity of one’s friends.

Antigua and Barbuda commands neither a great army nor a large market. International law, cooperation and multilateralism are fundamental to our security and stability.

For us, the United Nations is not optional. It is essential to our survival.

We support a more efficient, coherent and accountable United Nations. But efficiency cannot become another word for retreat.

The UN80 reform process must be judged by whether this Organization serves people better. For SIDS, that means protecting the development pillar, advancing implementation of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS, and bringing effective support closer to those who need it.

Mr President,

Trade disputes, tariffs and economic fragmentation raise the costs of food, transport and development. Too often, small states pay the price for disputes we did not create.

We call upon the major economies to choose dialogue and cooperation.

Fairness must also govern international finance.

A hurricane does not check GDP before destroying a school. A rising sea does not consult income classifications before entering a home or village.

That is why the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index matters. It provides a fairer measure of the structural vulnerabilities that GDP alone cannot capture.

Excellencies,

Nowhere is the urgency greater than in the climate crisis.

For Small Island Developing States, climate change is not a warning about tomorrow. We are experiencing it today. Warmer oceans fuel more destructive hurricanes. Coastlines are retreating. Salt water contaminates freshwater supplies, forcing countries such as mine to rely on increasingly costly means of securing safe water.

The General Assembly’s High-level Meeting on Sea Level Rise placed before the international community fundamental questions of statehood, sovereignty, maritime rights, displacement, culture and identity.

Climate change must never be allowed to erase a nation’s sovereignty, its statehood or the rights of its people.

Antigua and Barbuda and other vulnerable states sought clarity on the obligations of States in relation to climate change. The International Court of Justice has now spoken. Climate obligations are not acts of generosity. They are responsibilities under international law.

For small states, international law is more than a moral aspiration. It is a strategic shield.

For SIDS, climate justice is survival.

Our survival is inseparable from the ocean.

The entry into force of the BBNJ Agreement is therefore an important achievement for multilateralism. But implementation will be the real test.

SIDS must share fairly the benefits arising from marine genetic resources. Capacitybuilding must be meaningful, and marine technology must be accessible.

Mr President,

Climate justice cannot be separated from historical justice.

The Caribbean did not arrive at this moment on equal terms. Centuries of enslavement and colonial extraction transferred wealth from our societies and denied generations the means to build prosperity.

Political independence did not erase that harm.

Today, countries that contributed least to climate change must borrow at high cost to rebuild from disasters driven overwhelmingly by emissions accumulated elsewhere.

That is where climate debt meets historical debt.

Antigua and Barbuda stands firmly with CARICOM and Africa in demanding reparatory justice for people of African descent.

Reparatory justice requires acknowledging responsibility, repairing continuing harm and correcting structures that still reproduce inequality.

Expressions of regret are not enough. Justice requires honest dialogue followed by concrete measures for repair, restitution and development.

Reparatory justice is not a favor. It is a claim grounded in responsibility, equality and human dignity.

Mr President,

Development finds its true meaning in the lives and dignity of people.

Non-communicable diseases cut short too many lives and diminish the quality of life of too many of our citizens. Preventing these diseases, detecting them early and ensuring effective treatment are national development priorities.

Mental health challenges are increasing. Preventable vision impairment denies thousands of our people opportunities to learn, work and live independently.

Antigua and Barbuda will continue to champion mental health, strengthen our universal health programmes to address non-communicable diseases, and place eye health firmly within our development priorities.

This November, Antigua and Barbuda will host a Global Eye Health Summit to move the international community from advocacy to action against the growing burden of preventable sight loss.

We invite Member States and partners to join us and support an Eye Health Compact that expands access, strengthens prevention and treatment, mobilizes finance, and integrates eye health into development.

Excellencies,

Two years ago, the international community gathered in Antigua and Barbuda and adopted the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS—ABAS—our ten-year framework for sustainable development and resilience.

Now comes the harder part: implementation.

SIDS need finance, technology, capacity and institutions that recognise vulnerability.

The SIDS Centre of Excellence will help turn ABAS commitments into practical solutions through better data, innovation, investment and support for debt sustainability.

ABAS must move from commitment to implementation—and SIDS must move from vulnerability towards resilience.

International financial architecture must also change.

The Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development in Sevilla placed debt and development finance closer to the center of the international agenda. That progress must now become action.

Small states cannot develop sustainably when they must repeatedly borrow to rebuild.

We cannot fulfil the promise of ABAS while carrying unsustainable debt. Nor can we build resilience when the cost of capital itself penalizes vulnerability.

For too long, the international financial architecture has asked vulnerable countries how much debt they can carry.

It must also ask how much development they can achieve.

How can countries realize their potential when debt service, repeated shocks and high borrowing costs consume the resources needed for schools, hospitals and resilient infrastructure?

Finance must create fiscal space for development.

Vulnerable states need greater access to long-term, affordable and predictable financing, together with debt solutions that respond to their real circumstances.

We call for the launch of the intergovernmental process on debt agreed in Sevilla.

Mr President,

There can be no sustainable development without peace.

But peace begins long before guns fall silent.

It begins when young people see a future; when societies provide food, education, employment and opportunity; and when injustice is addressed before it becomes instability and conflict.

In a fractured world, the United Nations must renew both its operational relevance and its moral clarity.

It must help forge a new compact between developed and developing countries, connect finance to resilience, and support local leadership with global solidarity.

Development is an instrument of peace.

The United Nations must invest as seriously in preventing wars as it does in responding after they begin. Diplomacy, mediation and development must be central to that work.

Throughout every crisis, one principle must remain constant: international law must apply equally to all.

The credibility of the international system depends upon that consistency.

Mr President,

United Nations reform must extend to the Security Council—its composition, its decisions and its capacity to act.

Antigua and Barbuda welcomes the initiative led by France and Mexico calling on permanent members to refrain voluntarily from using the veto in situations involving mass atrocities. We will join the growing number of Member States supporting this call.

The veto must not paralyse the Council or prevent it from fulfilling its responsibility to maintain international peace and security.

Reform must also address representation. Africa’s continued exclusion from permanent membership is an injustice that must be corrected. Africa must have permanent representation of the Council.

Small Island Developing States must also have an assured voice at this table. Antigua and Barbuda calls for a dedicated SIDS seat on a reformed Security Council.

Mr President,

The Council’s credibility depends equally on its response to those who urgently need its support.

The crisis in Haiti is a human tragedy and a challenge to Caribbean stability and democratic progress.

We call on the Security Council to renew the mandate of the Gang Suppression Force and international partners to provide the personnel, equipment and sustained financing needed to make that mandate effective.

Excellencies,

The hardship facing the Cuban people also demands our attention.

Antigua and Barbuda calls on the United States and Cuba to return to the table of diplomacy and work as good neighbors towards resolving their longstanding differences.

The Cuban people must not bear collective punishment for political disagreements. Their well-being must remain central to efforts to find a peaceful and lasting solution.

Across our region, our purpose is clear: to protect human dignity, strengthen stability and ensure that dialogue and cooperation prevail.

Excellencies:

The world is changing—its climate, its technology and its balance of economic power.

This United Nations must change with it.

But its founding principles must endure: the equality of nations, the dignity of peoples, the sovereignty of States and respect for international law.

Mr. President:

Let United Nations reform strengthen multilateralism.

Let international law protect every nation.

Let finance serve development rather than deepen debt.

Let us implement ABAS, protect our ocean and invest in human dignity.

And as this Organization prepares for new leadership, let us choose leadership equal to this moment.

Excellencies,

History will not judge us by the number of resolutions we adopt.

It will judge us by whether we acted when the seas rose, inequality deepened, international law was violated and multilateralism faltered.

Let us enter this new era with courage in our leadership, fairness in our decisions and hope in our common future.

And it is our hope that this United Nations can still fulfil the promise of its Charter.

I thank you.

Mr. President,

Distinguished Heads of State and Government,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Let me thank the Government and People of Grenada for this privilege bestowed on me. And thank Grenada’s visionary Prime Minister, Honourable Dickon Mitchell for the trust.

Grenada congratulates you Mr. President as President of the Eighty First Session of the General Assembly, and thank the former President, Annalena Baerbock.

Mr. President,

One year ago, standing at this very podium, the Prime Minister of Grenada addressed this General Assembly not only as our Head of Government, but as a proud son of the Caribbean. He reminded us that our Region continues to literally and figuratively weather storms, yet continues to rise with resilience, dignity and hope.

Today, as I stand before you representing th e people of Grenada, I speak of transformation - Because resilience alone is no longer enough. Our task cannot simply be to survive one crisis after another. We must transform the conditions that make people vulnerable in the first place. We must renew our global systems, strengthen our multilateral partnerships and summon the collective will necessary to build a world worthy of the next generation. And that transformation must begin with people.

Haiti: From Solidarity to Action Mr. President,

Grenada joins CARICOM in calling for the timely renewal of the mandate of the Gang Suppression Force, its full and rapid deployment in close partnership with the Haitian National Police, and the provision of the personnel, financing, equipment and logistic al support necessary for it to fulfil its mandate effectively with appropriate human-rights safeguards. These security efforts are essential to creating the conditions for credible, free, fair and inclusive Haitian -led elections, the strengthening of national institutions and the restoration of constitutional governance.

Haiti is not a failed state. Haiti represents a promise yet to be fulfilled.

It is a promise to the Haitian people that the international community must honour, not with pity - but with purpose; not temporarily - but sustainably. And even as we respond to the security crisis, humanitarian assistance must remain at the centre of our efforts.

Cuba: Partnership Must Prevail Over Isolation Mr. President,

Grenada remains deeply concerned about the continuing hardship endured by the Cuban people. Our humanitarian conscience cannot be indifferent to the circumstances of ordinary households, particularly children, the elderly and other vulnerable persons, whose difficulties deepen with each passing day that the present impasse remains unresolved. We call for constructive engagement that places the well-being of the Cuban people at its centre and opens a path towards meaningful relief, improved living conditions and renewed opportunities.

Mr. President,

As we speak of transforming our multilateral system, we must also ensure that its leadership reflects the diversity, experience and aspirations of the people it serves.

Grenada therefore proudly joins our CARICOM family in giving our unequivocal support to the candidacy of Ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana for the position of Secretary -General of the United Nations. CARICOM Heads of Government have endorsed her as the region’s candidate, recognising the experience and leadership she brings to this important moment for global multilateralism. Her distinguished service as Guyana’s Foreign Minister and Permanent Representative to the United Nations, has demonstrated a deep commitment to diplomacy, dialogue and international cooperation.

The Caribbean has long demonstrated that size does not determine the strength of our ideas, the quality of our leadership, or the value of our contribution to the international community. We believe, Ambassador Rodrigues -Birkett is eminently qualified to serve the entire United Nations membership. Her election would represent a historic milestone for our Caribbean Region and a powerful affirmation that every region, including Small Island Developing States, can contribute to leadership at the highest levels of our multilateral system.

Restoring Trust Through Transformation Mr. President,

We meet at a time of significant global transformation.

The challenges before us are complex, but they also present an opportunity to renew our commitment to cooperation and create practical solutions that improve the lives of our people.

The theme of this session, “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all,” challenges us to move beyond declarations toward delivery.

For Grenada, restoring trust means demonstrating through our actions that international cooperation produces results.

It means listening to one another.

It means respecting the voices of small states as much as those of large ones.

It means building genuine partnerships.

And it means ensuring that every country has the opportunity to pursue its legitimate development aspirations.

Grenada approaches this General Assembly in a spirit of partnership, optimism and constructive engagement.

We remain firmly committed to the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations, international law, peaceful dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes.

In an increasingly interconnected world, cooperation is not merely desirable.

It is indispensable.

Vision 75: Grenada's Transformation Mr. President,

The transformation we advocate internationally must also take place at home.

Grenada is advancing an ambitious long-term roadmap towards our 75th anniversary of independence.

Anchored in our National Sustainable Development Plan 2020 –2035, Vision 75 charts a transformational course for our Nation, rooted in sustainability, resilience, equity and opportunity.

At the heart of Vision 75 are five strategic pillars:

Education and Skills Training. Healthcare. Agriculture and Food Security.

The Environment and Energy. And Housing.

These are not simply sectors of government policy. They are investments in people.

We are investing in health and wellness, education and skills, food security, renewable energy, digital innovation and environmental sustainability.

We are creating greater opportunities for our young people and preparing them not simply for the jobs that exist today, but for the industries that will define tomorrow.

For Grenada, transformation must always be people-centred.

It means building resilience while creating opportunity.

Expanding our economy while protecting our environment; and,

Embracing technology while safeguarding humanity.

SIDS, Climate and Resilience Mr. President,

As a Small Island Developing State, Grenada understands resilience. But experience has also taught us that resilience cannot begin after disaster strikes.

We must invest before the storm.

Prepare before the emergency.

Build before the damage is done.

And finance resilience before countries are forced to borrow simply to rebuild what they have lost.

This requires greater international cooperation in climate adaptation, disaster preparedness, resilient infrastructure and accessible financing. Small Island Developing States should not be viewed simply as victims of climate change. We are also laboratories of resilience.

From Climate Vulnerability to Opportunity Climate action remains one of the areas in which collective effort can make a profound difference.

Grenada remains committed to strengthening resilience and advancing sustainable and low -carbon development. But ambition without implementation is merely aspiration.

For vulnerable countries, climate commitments must be accompanied by reliable access to the resources required to deliver them. Climate financing must become more accessible, predictable and responsive.

Our objective should not simply be to help vulnerable countries recover from the next disaster.

Our objective must be to transform vulnerability into resilience and resilience into sustainable opportunity.

Financing Development Differently Mr. President,

This transformation must also take place in the international financial system.

Grenada welcomes growing recognition that development and vulnerability cannot be assessed by income alone.

The Multidimensional Vulnerability Index offers an important opportunity to better recognise the structural circumstances of Small Island Developing States.

Our vulnerabilities are shaped by exposure to climate change, natural disasters, external economic shocks and other circumstances that cannot adequately be captured through income per capita.

Grenada therefore encourages Member States, development partners and international financial institutions to advance vulnerability -informed approaches to development financing.

Greater access to concessional financing, climate finance, disaster-risk financing and innovative financial instruments can help countries move from vulnerability to resilience, and from recovery to sustainable growth.

Young People, Technology and AI Mr. President,

At the centre of all of this must be our young people. Their creativity, energy and ideas are among our greatest national and global assets. Our responsibility is to give them the education, skills, technology and opportunities necessary to shape the world they will inherit.

Digital transformation and emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, offer enormous possibilities for education, healthcare, agriculture, public administration and economic development.

But access must be equitable.

The technologies shaping humanity's future must not create another divide between those countries that can afford to innovate and those that cannot.

And access alone will not be enough.

As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in our economies and societies, we must develop credible AI governance frameworks that encourage innovation while protecting people, privacy, security, democratic values and public trust.

Technology must remain a tool for human development, not a replacement for human responsibility.

We must prepare young people not only to use new technologies, but to question them, govern them, and deploy them ethically.

Global Call to Action Mr. President,

Grenada approaches the future with confidence. We recognise the challenges before us, but we also see enormous possibilities.

Our Vision 75 embodies our determination to build a stronger, healthier, more resilient and more prosperous Grenada. Our commitment to the Sustainable Development Goals reflects our belief in shared global progress.

And our engagement in this United Nations reflects our conviction that partnership remains one of humanity's greatest sources of strength. But partnership must deliver.

So let this Assembly send a clear message:

Let us restore hope in Haiti.

Let us protect children and civilians wherever conflict threatens their future.

Let us choose dialogue over division.

Let us allow cooperation with Cuba and with all nations to be guided by the interests and well-being of people.

Let us ensure that Small Island Developing States have fair access to the financing necessary to build resilience before disaster strikes.

Let us equip our young people to lead the technological transformation rather than become casualties of it.

Let us protect our oceans and our planet.

And let us transform our multilateral institutions so that they deliver not simply promises, but progress.

The measure of this United Nations cannot only be the resolutions we adopt.

It must be the lives we improve.

The children we protect.

The conflicts we help prevent.

The opportunities we create.

And the hope we restore.

Mr. President,

Grenada stands ready to work with all Member States and international partners in advancing a future that is peaceful, resilient, inclusive and sustainable.

One year ago, Grenada came before this Assembly with a message about resilience and education.

Today, we build upon that message.

Resilience gives us the strength to endure. Transformation gives us the power to change. Partnership gives us the ability to do both.

Together, through renewed trust and genuine partnership, we can build a United Nations that delivers.

A United Nations that protects. A United Nations that listens. A United Nations that acts.

And ultimately, a world in which no country, no community and no person is left behind.

May God bless the United Nations.

I thank you, Mr. President.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished Delegates,

I bring you warm greetings and best wishes from His Excellency Salva Kiir Mayardit, President of the Republic of South Sudan, the Government and the people of South Sudan, together with a message of peace, unity, development and an unwavering commitment to international cooperation.

I wish to congratulate you, Mr. President, on your election to preside over the EightyFirst Session of this esteemed Assembly. I also express South Sudan’s appreciation to the Secretary-General, His Excellency António Guterres, for his continued service to the United Nations and commitment to the principles of its Charter.

Mr. President,

The theme of this Session, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All, ” speaks directly to the experience and aspirations of South Sudan. As the world ’s youngest nation and the 193rd Member of the United Nations, South Sudan understands both the promise and the responsibility of multilateralism.

South Sudan also understands that trust is fundamental to peace: trust among citizens; trust between citizens and their institutions; trust among nations; and trust between Member States and the international institutions created to serve them.

South Sudan remains committed to the United Nations and to the purposes and principles of its Charter. We recognize and appreciate the contribution the United Nations has made to South Sudan, from humanitarian assistance and the protection of civilians to peacebuilding, development and institutional support.

However, restoring trust also requires honest reflection. Our experience has shown that international institutions can sometimes be slow to adjust to changing circumstances on the ground. Approaches designed to respond to conflict must be capable of evolvi ng as nations move toward peace, recovery, institution -building and national ownership.

For South Sudan, therefore, restoring trust must mean strengthening partnership between the United Nations and Member States, respecting national ownership, recognizing progress while acknowledging remaining challenges, and ensuring that international engagement ultimately strengthens the capacity of nations to assume responsibility for their own future.

Mr. President,

To understand where South Sudan seeks to go, one must understand where South Sudan has come from. The history of South Sudan did not begin with independence on 9 July 2011. It was shaped by more than half a century of struggle, sacrifice, displacement and an unwavering desire for freedom and self-determination. Dr. John Garang de Mabior summarized the aspirations of that struggle when he spoke of “freedom, liberty, equality, justice, human rights and democracy.” Those aspirations did not end with independence. They remain part of the ongoing work of nation-building.

The Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 2005 provided the political framework that transformed decades of armed struggle into a peaceful exercise of self determination. South Sudan therefore continues to recognize the indispensable contribution of IGAD and our African brothers and sisters, as well as the support of the Troika, the United States, the United Kingdom and Norway and the wider international community.

South Sudan also remembers the extraordinary contribution of churches and faith leaders. During some of the darkest years of conflict, the churches remained with the people. They educated children, assisted displaced communities, mediated disputes and kept alive the belief that reconciliation was possible.

That tradition continued with the historic Ecumenical Pilgrimage of Peace to South Sudan by His Holiness Pope Francis, the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Moderator of the Church of Scotland. Their message reinforced something South Sudan has learned through painful experience: Peace requires political agreements, but lasting peace also requires reconciliation, forgiveness and courage.

Mr. President,

His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit belongs to the generation that carried the struggle for liberation. Following the passing of Dr. John Garang, President Kiir assumed responsibility for safeguarding the Comprehensive Peace Agreement and leading the people of South Sudan toward the referendum on self -determination. In January 2011, the people of South Sudan spoke overwhelmingly through the ballot.

And on 9 July 2011, President Salva Kiir Mayardit stood before the people as the flag of the Republic of South Sudan was raised for the first time.

Fifteen years later, South Sudan has travelled a difficult road. There have been achievements. There have also been setbacks. South Sudan experienced internal conflict shortly after independence. Implementation of the Revitalized Peace Agreement has taken longer than originally anticipated. Economic and humanitarian challenges remain significant. The Government does not deny these realities, but neither should these challenges be allowed to erase the progress made or define permanently the identity of South Sudan.

Throughout the transition, President Kiir has repeatedly made one commitment clear: he will not take South Sudan back to war. This commitment has guided his approach to the peace process and remains fundamental to his vision for the next chapter of South Sudan.

The mission before President Kiir today is therefore different from the mission of the liberation years. The liberation struggle sought to give the people of South Sudan the right to determine their destiny. The responsibility today is to consolidate peace, strengthen institutions and create the conditions through which the people of South Sudan can once again determine their political future through democratic means.

Mr. President,

When the people of South Sudan voted for independence, they were voting for more than the creation of a new State. They were voting for a dream: • They dreamed of peace after generations of war; • They dreamed of schools for their children; • Healthcare for their families; • Roads connecting their communities; • Food security and economic opportunity; • Justice and equality; • Strong national institutions; and • A government whose authority ultimately derives from the will of its people.

The difficulties of the last fifteen years have not extinguished those dreams. They remain alive among the people of South Sudan. And it is precisely for this reason that His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit remains committed to paving the way towards general elections scheduled for December 2026. These elections are intended to mark the conclusion of the transitional period and provide the people of South Sudan the opportunity to democratically choose their leaders.

We recognize that important work still in progress. Electoral institutions require adequate resources. Political dialogue must continue. Security arrangements must advance. Civic and voter education must reach communities. Women and young people must parti cipate meaningfully. Refugees and internally displaced persons must not be left out. And an environment must be created in which political competition can occur peacefully. The Government remains committed to working towards these objectives.

For too long, South Sudan has often been seen internationally through the lens of conflict, humanitarian need and political crisis. President Kiir’s vision is to create the conditions in which the world can once again see the people of South Sudan for who they truly are: a resilient people who struggled for freedom, voted peacefully for independence, and continue to aspire for peace, dignity, democracy and prosperity.

The people of South Sudan must increasingly speak for themselves. And they must speak through the ballot. Our journey therefore continues: • from liberation struggle to the Comprehensive Peace Agreement - to the Referendum - to independence; • from conflict to peace; and now • from transition towards democratic governance.

Mr. President,

The message of President Kiir remains clear: South Sudan must not return to war.

Political disagreement must be addressed through dialogue. Political competition must never again become armed confrontation. The ballot must replace the bullet.

South Sudan recognizes that conducting peaceful elections requires security and strong institutions. The Government bears the primary responsibility for protecting its citizens, maintaining public order and safeguarding the electoral process.

South Sudan therefore continues to call for constructive engagement with the Security Council concerning restrictive measures, including the arms embargo.

South Sudan’ s objective is not militarization. The objective is to develop professional, unified, disciplined and accountable security sectors operating under civilian authority and the rule of law.

South Sudan believes that accountability and national capacity should reinforce one another. We therefore call for the lifting of all restrictive measures. Sanctions must remain instruments for achieving clearly defined objectives; they should not become permanent substitutes for political engagement and institution-building.

Mr. President,

South Sudan remains grateful for the contribution of the United Nations Mission in South Sudan. We recognize the men and women who have served under the United Nations flag, particularly those who have lost their lives in the service of peace. As South Sudan advances its transition, however, international engagement must also evolve.

President Kiir’s vision is not for South Sudan to remain indefinitely dependent upon international peacekeeping. The objective must be a South Sudan capable of sustaining its own peace. South Sudan therefore calls for greater emphasis on peacebuilding, institutional development and continuous capacity building. We are keen on establishing partnership: • Invest in South Sudan’s police and judiciary; • Invest in public administration; • Invest in education and healthcare; • Invest in infrastructure; • Invest in women and young people; and • Invest in the institutions that will sustain peace long after peacekeepers have departed.

The ultimate measure of successful peacekeeping should be the establishment of conditions under which peacekeeping is no longer required. South Sudan therefore seeks a responsible transition from managing crises towards building lasting national capacity.

Mr. President,

Peace cannot be sustained without development. At independence, South Sudan inherited extremely limited infrastructure and institutional capacity. Nation building, state -building and service delivery have therefore had to proceed simultaneously. His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit has placed particular emphasis on agriculture, infrastructure, education, healthcare and economic diversification.

South Sudan possesses millions of hectares of arable land, significant water resources, livestock, fisheries, natural resources and one of the youngest populations in the world. South Sudan therefore seeks to transition progressively from humanitarian dependency to self -reliance and to towards sustainable development and investment.

For a farmer, a road to market is development. For a child, a functioning school is development. For a mother, access to healthcare is development. For a young person, employment is development. And for South Sudan, development is one of the strongest foundations for lasting peace.

We therefore invite international partners and responsible investors to look beyond South Sudan’s current challenges and recognize its potential. Do not ask only what South Sudan needs. Ask what South Sudan can offer.

Mr. President,

South Sudan continues to face severe consequences from climate shocks despite contributing minimally to global emissions. Recurrent floods, drought, displacement and food insecurity are affecting millions of South Sudanese. South Sudan therefore reiterates its call for predictable and accessible climate financing, investment in adaptation, resilient infrastructure, renewable energy, agriculture and technology transfer. Climate justice must be reflected not only in commitments, but in implementation.

Mr. President,

Women and young people remain central to President Kiir’s vision for South Sudan.

The Revitalized Peace Agreement provided for 35 per cent representation of women in public institutions. South Sudan continuous on working to translate that commitment into meaningful participation at all levels.

South Sudan also has an overwhelmingly young population. These young people should not inherit the conflicts of previous generations. They should inherit the opportunities of peace: Education, vocational training, technology, entrepreneurship, agriculture and sports, that is the future they deserve.

Mr. President,

Decades of conflict scattered South Sudanese across the world. But the South Sudanese diaspora should not be viewed only through the history of displacement.

It is also an extraordinary national resource. Our national basketball team, the Bright Stars, demonstrated this before the world.

South Sudanese whose journeys had taken them across different countries and continents came together under one flag. Under the leadership of Luol Deng and the South Sudan Basketball Federation, South Sudan qualified for the FIBA Basketball World Cup and su bsequently for the Olympic Games. They showed the world another image of South Sudan: not conflict; not displacement; but talent, discipline, unity and excellence. This experience offers a model for national development.

South Sudanese doctors abroad can contribute to healthcare. Engineers can contribute to infrastructure. Academics can strengthen education. Entrepreneurs can invest and create employment. Technology professionals can connect South Sudan to the digital economy. And successful South Sudanese around the world can mentor another generation.

To the international community, we need to create strong partnership that would enable our South Sudanese Diaspora to transfer their skills and professional experience; in order to contribute to the ongoing development in the Republic of South Sudan.

To the South Sudanese Diaspora, our message is simple: South Sudan needs you.

Bring your knowledge. Bring your experience. Bring your investment. Bring your networks. Where physical return is not possible, allow your skills and experience to contribute to South Sudan.

The same spirit that brought South Sudanese athletes from around the world together under one flag can help bring South Sudanese expertise together for one national purpose. South Sudan’s greatest resource is ultimately its people, both at home and abroad.

Mr. President,

South Sudan stands in solidarity with the people of Sudan. South Sudan and Sudan share history, families, economic interests and one of the longest borders in the region. South Sudan therefore reiterates and continues to support all efforts leading to the consolidation of peace in Sudan.

South Sudan knows from experience that military confrontation ultimately requires a political solution. Even the longest conflict must eventually reach a negotiated settlement. South Sudan therefore supports regional and international efforts aimed at achieving peace in Sudan. Outstanding matters arising from the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, including border issues and the final status of Abyei, also require continued peaceful engagement between South Sudan and Sudan.

Mr. President,

Restoring trust also requires reform of the institutions of global governance. The composition of the Security Council does not adequately reflect realities of today; Africa with fifty-four Member States remains without permanent representation on the Council.

South Sudan therefore reaffirms its support for the Common African Position reflected in the Ezulwini Consensus and Sirte Declaration. Africa must be appropriately represented in both the permanent and non -permanent categories.

Similarly, developing countries must have a stronger voice in international financial institutions and in decisions concerning development financing, debt, climate and technology. Reform does not weaken multilateralism. Reform strengthens its legitimacy.

Mr. President,

Fifteen years after independence, South Sudan remains a young nation undertaking the difficult work of building a State while consolidating peace and delivering development. The journey has not been easy. But South Sudanese have never been a people defined by easy journeys. The generation of liberation fought for freedom.

The generation of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement secured the pathway to selfdetermination. The people of South Sudan chose independence through the ballot.

And His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit carried the responsibility of leading South Sudan through the Referendum and into statehood.

Today, President Kiir’s vision is directed toward another historic responsibility: to preserve peace, strengthen national institutions and pave the way toward elections through which the people of South Sudan can determine the next chapter of their nation. This is ultimately about completing the promise of independence. A South Sudan at peace with itself. A South Sudan governed through strong institutions. A South Sudan where political competition does not lead to war.

A South Sudan where women participate fully. Where young people have opportunities. Where refugees can return home. Where the diaspora contributes to national development. And where children grow up knowing South Sudan not through memories of war, but through the possibilities of peace.

Dr. John Garang once challenged the people of South Sudan to “unite and dream together.” That dream did not end with independence. It continues. And today, the responsibility of President Salva Kiir Mayardit, his Government, the political leadership and indeed every South Sudanese is to transform that dream into a functioning, peaceful and prosperous Republic.

To our international partners who stood with South Sudan during the struggle for peace, during the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, during the Referendum and at independence, we say: Stand with South Sudan again. But let this next chapter be a partnership that strengthens national ownership. A partnership that builds institutions. A partnership that recognizes progress while helping address remaining challenges. And a partnership that enables South Sudan progressively to stand on its own.

Mr. President,

For South Sudan, restoring trust means delivering on the promise of peace.

Managing transformation means moving from conflict to institutions, from dependency to national capacity, and from transition toward democratic governance.

And a United Nations that delivers for all must ultimately help nations develop the capacity to deliver for their own people.

South Sudan remains committed to the United Nations. South Sudan remains committed to Africa. South Sudan remains committed to peace. And under the leadership of His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit, South Sudan remains committed to the long journe y of transforming the sacrifices of liberation into the peace, dignity, development and democratic future for which the people of South Sudan have waited for generations. That is the promise of independence. That is the responsibility of this generation. And that is the future South Sudan seeks to build.

May the Lord Almighty bless the people of South Sudan.

And may the Lord Almighty bless all nations represented in this Assembly.

I thank you.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates,

A compass does not change with the weather. It helps you find the way; in fair weather as well as in storm.

Eighty-one years ago, the world gave itself a compass.

We named it the United Nations Charter. It has helped us stay the course, even when the seas have been anything but calm.

It has pointed us toward a world of equal rights, selfdetermination of peoples and territorial integrity of all states, large and small.

Toward a rules-based international order.

The progress has been real. More than a billion people lifted out of poverty. Standards of living transformed.

Colonial empires brought to an end. Independent nations emerged. Peoples gained the right to shape their own future.

That progress was made possible because we kept consulting the compass. Because, we stayed the course.

Today, it seems we are losing our way.

Wars and conflicts are at the highest level since World War II. Extreme poverty is on the rise. Extreme weather and climate-related disasters are hitting record highs.

Mistrust, polarisation and divisions are growing, both among states and within societies.

Even the most basic principles of international law, including international humanitarian law, are violated with impunity.

To get back on track, we must turn our attention to the compass.

*** Excellencies,

Respect for the Charter, for human rights, for international law, is not a courtesy we extend when convenient. These are binding obligations we all agreed to. Respecting them is the precondition for international peace and security.

We see this clearly in Ukraine. Russia's illegal war of choice could end tomorrow, if Russia withdrew to its own territory and stopped trying to redraw borders by force.

The vast majority of UN member states and the UN Secretary General support calls for an immediate and comprehensive ceasefire in Ukraine.

It is the only basis for good-faith talks aimed at a just and lasting peace in line with international law, including the UN Charter. Ukraine has been offering this for a year now.

Denmark's support for Ukraine will remain steadfast.

This is not only a matter of helping Ukraine defend itself.

It is a matter of defending the universal principles upon which this Organisation was built.

*** Excellencies,

In Sudan, the war continues to inflict immense human suffering.

Millions are displaced. Famine has been confirmed. And the international community has been warned of mass atrocities over and over again, but has failed to act. The responsibility for this horrific war lies in the hands of the warring parties. Yet, it is fuelled by outside actors and permitted by international inaction.

We must act now to prevent further mass atrocities against the Sudanese people. We must put our political will and weight behind a stronger demand for peace and accountability.

The warring parties must come to the negotiation table.

Engage in dialogue. And agree on a much-needed truce.

Denmark fully supports the Quintet’s efforts to advance a civilian-led political process and welcomes the improved coordination among mediators.

*** Excellencies,

In Syria, the fall of the brutal Assad-regime offers a historic opportunity to build a brighter future for all Syrians. Denmark is committed to supporting the people of Syria in a Syrian-led and owned transition. It is a glimpse of hope in a troubled region.

And a stark contrast to the destabilizing actions of Iran, whose consequences are felt far beyond the region.

Denmark’s position remains clear: Iran must never be allowed to develop or acquire a nuclear weapon. We strongly support continued diplomatic efforts to restore effective international verification of Iran’s nuclear programme. And we deeply regret the unwillingness of a few Council members to acknowledge that sanctions measures have been reinstated in full accordance with Security Council resolution 2231.

At the same time, we urge Iran to comply fully with resolution 2817. Cease attacks against countries in the region and refrain from any actions or threats that undermine freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

*** Excellencies,

Last year, this Assembly endorsed the New York Declaration – a roadmap toward the two-state solution. A path to lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians.

Since then, the Comprehensive Plan to end the Gaza Conflict has been endorsed by the Security Council. Now it must be implemented in full. We call on all parties to stay committed to the plan.

Yet in Gaza, civilians continue to pay the price. Far more must be done to secure humanitarian access and longterm peace.

And in the occupied West Bank, settler violence and settlement expansion threaten the daily lives of Palestinians – and undermine the prospects for a future Palestinian state. This has to stop.

*** Excellencies,

As an elected member of the Security Council, Denmark strives to ensure that the Council fulfils its mandate.

At times, we succeed. This June, the Security Council unanimously adopted resolution 2823 [Twenty-eight twenty-three] on accountability for crimes against UN peacekeepers – led by Denmark and Pakistan, and backed by a record 153 member states. A clear signal of commitment to the safety and security of the brave men and women who serve under the UN flag.

And a clear demonstration that the Council can still come together and speak with one voice.

Too often, however, the Security Council is blocked by geopolitical divisions. Unable to act. Meanwhile, the costs of inaction are felt by civilians across the world as the disrespect for international humanitarian law is allowed to fester.

*** Excellencies,

Our collective inability to halt the killings, suffering, and injustices in Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan and beyond, must not prompt us to surrender to a world ruled by brute force.

On the contrary, it must inspire us to work harder to sustain and strengthen the structures, instruments and mechanisms, we have built over the past 81 years.

To Denmark, this includes maintaining our firm support for the ICJ and ICC as core international justice institutions. This year, Denmark nominated its first-ever candidate for judge at the ICC, reaffirming our unwavering support for the Court at a critical time.

It also means continuing to meet the UN target of providing 0.7 per cent of GNI for official development assistance.

For more than 45 years, Denmark has consistently delivered on this goal. We do so, not as an act of altruism, but because it is in our shared interest: It creates jobs, opportunities and hope where people live, allowing them to build a future at home, increasing stability and mutual prosperity. We call on fellow member states to join us.

At the current juncture, however, sustaining an order with the UN at its core, means working for reform.

Reform is how we keep this Organisation fit for the world we live in.

Denmark continues to call for fundamental Security Council reform: we wish to expand the Council with more members in both categories, including permanent seats for underrepresented regions. And we wish to commence text-based negotiations. Only then can we begin to redress historical injustices.

Denmark also strongly supports the UN80 reform process. We applaud the results so far and call for ambitions to be raised. We must strive to build a more efficient and inclusive UN.

A UN that delivers better – on its core mandates, and on the ground, where it matters most.

To enable this, we call on all UN Member States to meet their financial obligations to the UN. In full and on time.

*** Excellencies,

Let’s be real. We need the UN, not for the sake of the UN, but in order to address challenges that face us all.

Because no single country can manage climate change, global health threats, or the governance of emerging technologies on its own.

The climate crisis makes the point starkly. We see it in droughts and wildfires. In record-breaking heat. And in the growing pressure on food, water and energy accessibility and security.

The challenge before us is no longer a lack of solutions.

We have the solutions. We know what is required. Now we need to deliver.

Therefore, COP31 must be a COP of implementation.

Turning ambition into action and real-world results.

Delivering on the objectives of the Paris Agreement and its 1.5-degree Celsius temperature goal.

With only four years left to 2030, we must also be honest about where we stand with the Sustainable Development Goals. Both in terms of achievements and challenges.

Let’s make the upcoming SDG Summit a turning point.

2030 must not be a missed deadline.

*** Excellencies,

This year, we will be selecting a new Secretary-General.

Denmark thanks the outgoing Secretary-General Guterres for a decade of dedicated service to this Organisation – often under exceptionally difficult circumstances.

The next Secretary-General will take over an organisation under strain and under scrutiny.

To bring the UN safely into the future, we must select a person who can work to restore global trust in the UN and among its member states.

*** Excellencies,

In closing, I am happy to inform you that last week - in this very building - Denmark, Greenland and the United States signed an agreement on security, which strengthens the defence of Greenland, the NATO area and the American continent. The agreement is good for Greenland, for Denmark, for the USA, and for NATO and Europe.

Progress can still be made, when we consult the compass.

I thank you.
